Medinan, and it has two hundred and eighty-six verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif-Lam-Mim. Know that the names by which the letters are spelled out (yatahajja, i.e. pronounced individually) are the names of the simple letters from which words are composed. Your saying "ḍād" is a name given to "ḍih" (the spelled-out form) of "ḍaraba" (he struck), when you spell it out; and likewise "rā" and "bā" are names for your saying "rih" and "bih". In this naming a subtle point has been observed: since the named items (al-musammayat) are, like their names, letters that stand alone, and the number of letters in the names rises to three, a way opened for them to indicate the named item in the naming, so they did not neglect it, and they made the named letter the first element of each name, as you see, except for the alif, where they borrowed the hamzah in place of its named item, because it can only be unvoweled (sakin).

Among what resembles these in placing a word to indicate a meaning are: the tahlil (saying lā ilāha illā Allāh), the ḥawqala (saying lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh), the ḥay'ala (saying ḥayya 'ala), and the basmala (saying bismillāh). Their rule, so long as governing particles do not affect them, is that their final parts are unvoweled and pause-ended, like the names of the numbers. It is said "alif, lām, mīm," just as it is said "wāḥid, ithnān, thalāthah." But when governing particles come after them, inflection (i'rāb) takes hold of them. You say: "hādhihi alif," "katabtu alifan," "naẓartu ilā alif." Thus every name that you intend merely to express its essence, before any of the effects of governing particles have touched it, it is right that you pronounce it pause-ended. Do you not see that when you want to throw to the calculator different kinds for it to compute their sum, how do you do it, and how do you throw them free of the mark of inflection? You say: "dār, ghulām, jāriyah, thawb, bisāṭ." If you inflected them, you would commit an error.

If you say: Why did you assign these expressions the status of nouns? Why not claim they are letters, as the earlier scholars' expressions have it? I say: It has been made clear by the luminous proof that they are nouns, not letters; so you know that their saying is to be read as a loose usage. We have found them loose in naming many nouns, whose nounhood is not disputed, such as the adverbs and others, with the name "letters," using the letter to mean the word. For your saying "alif" indicates the middle letter of "qāla" and "qāma" in the same way that "faras" (horse) indicates the specific animal; there is no difference in the naming between the two indications. Do you not see that a letter is that which indicates a meaning in something else, whereas this, as you see, indicates a meaning in itself? Also, these are subject to inflection by imāla (fronting of the vowel), as in your saying "bā," "tā"; and by tafkhīm (velarization), as in your saying "yā," "hā"; and by definiteness, indefiniteness, plurality, diminutive form, description, predication, annexation, and all that belongs to the inflected nouns.

Then I came upon a text on this from al-Khalīl's side. Sībawayh said: Al-Khalīl said one day, asking his companions: "How do you say when you want to pronounce the kāf that is in *laka* and the bā' that is in *ḍaraba*?" It was said: "We say *bā'*, *kāf*." He said: "You have only brought the noun, and have not pronounced the letter; I say: *kih*, *bih*." [Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "Al-Khalīl asked his companions how they pronounce the kāf ... etc." Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: He also asked them how they pronounce the qāf in *man yaqbal*? They said: *qāf*, as their first saying. He answered them as he had answered the first time, and said: "As for me, I say: *iqh*." So he (may God be pleased with him) first added the hā' of pause to it, because the letter pronounced is moving; and second the hamzat al-waṣl, because it is quiescent.]

Abū ʿAlī mentioned in *al-Ḥujja* concerning *Yā-Sīn*, the imāla of *yā*: that they said "yā Zayd" in the vocative and fronted it, although it is a letter. He said: If they have fronted what cannot be fronted of the letters because of the *yā*, then fronting the noun that is *Yā-Sīn* is all the more fitting.

Do you not see that these letters are nouns for what is pronounced by them? If you say: What kind of noun are they, inflected or indeclinable? I say: Rather they are inflected nouns, and their quiescence is the quiescence of Zayd and ʿAmr and other nouns, where inflection does not touch them for lack of a governing factor and its cause. The proof that their quiescence is a pause and not a built (indeclinable) state is: that if they were indeclinable, they would be treated like *kayfa*, *ayna*, and *hā'ulā'*; and one would not say *ṣ*, *q*, *n* gathered together with two quiescent letters. If you say: Why, when they are spelled out, is the one ending in alif pronounced short (maqṣūr), but when inflection touches it, it is lengthened, so you say "hādhihi bā', yā', hā'", which suggests that their pattern is like your saying "lā" short, and when you make it a noun you lengthen it and say "katabtu lā'?" I say: This supposition is dispelled by the proof and cause I have summarized: that the state of spelling out is fit for the lighter and more concise form, and their use in it is more frequent; and when inflection touches them, they are lengthened.

If you say: It has become clear that they are nouns for the letters of the alphabet, and that they belong to the inflected category, and that the quiescence of their final parts when spelled out is because of pause; so what is the reason for their coming in this form as openings of the surahs? I say: There are several aspects. The first, which the majority agree upon: they are the names of the surahs. The author of the book (Sībawayh) titled the chapter in which he dealt with them, in the definition of what is not inflected, "chapter on the names of the surahs." They are of two kinds. One is that which does not admit inflection, such as *Kāf-Hā-Yā-ʿAyn-Ṣād* and *Alif-Lām-Rā*. The second is that which admits inflection, and it is either a single noun like *Ṣād*, *Qāf*, *Nūn*, or a group of names whose total is in the pattern of a singular noun, like *Ḥā-Mīm*, *Ṭā-Sīn*, *Yā-Sīn*, for they match *Qābīl* and *Hābīl*; and similarly *Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm* admits its nūn to be opened, and the mīm becomes pronounced with a ḍamma attached to *Ṭā-Sīn*, so that they become one name like *Dārābjird*. The first kind is merely quoted and nothing else; but the second kind allows both: inflection and quotation. The slayer of Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa al-Sajjād, who was Shurayḥ ibn Awfā al-ʿAbsī, said [the verse, with the commentary of al-Zamakhsharī and its sources, reads as follows:]

*Verse:* "Hām-Mīm reminds me, while the spear is splintering, / why did he not recite Ḥā-Mīm before advancing?"

[The chain of this verse and its context: Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa was at the Battle of the Camel with his father; ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) forbade killing him... Shurayḥ struck him, and he fell on his hands and face. Commentary of the verse words: "*shājir*" means the spear is mixed in his garments and ribs; "*fa-hallā*" carries a note of reproach.]

Inflected *Ḥā-Mīm* and denied it the diptote (ṣarf), and likewise every one of its sisters that is inflected, because two causes for denying ṣarf have gathered in it: definiteness as a proper name and feminine gender. Quotation means that you bring the saying after transferring it while keeping its original form, as in your saying: "Leave me with *tamratān*"; "I began with *al-ḥamdu lillāh*"; "I recited *sūratun anzalnāhā*." He said:

*"We found in the book of the Banū Tamīm / that the most deserving of horses for the lent racing..."*
[The commentary explains the words "rakḍ," "muʿār," "yuḍmar," "al-aṣā'il," "nahd," "aqab," "muqallaṣ," "al-ifwirār," "al-sarāt," "al-waḥīf," "al-ribw," and the grammar of "fa-aḥaqqu" as subject with "al-muʿār" as predicate.]

And Dhū al-Rummah said:

*"I heard people seeking rain, / so I said to Ṣaydaḥ: 'Seek Bilāl'..."*
[The commentary explains that this is an address to Bilāl Abū Burayda, the governor and judge of Baṣra, and the grammar of "al-nās" as nominative, and the variant reading.]

And another said:

*"They called out to depart tomorrow, / and in their departure is my soul..."*
[The commentary explains the variant readings *al-raḥīl* (nominative), *ghadan*, and the metaphor.]

It is recited with the nominative and genitive. The people of the Ḥijāz, when asking one who says "raʾaytu Zaydan," say: "*man Zaydan?*"

Sībawayh said: I heard from the Arabs: "*Lā min ayna yā fatā*."

If you say: What is the reasoning of those who read *Ṣād*, *Qāf*, *Nūn* with fatḥa? [Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: what is the reasoning of one who reads Ṣād, Qāf, Nūn with fatḥa..." Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: His speech on the first aspect requires that they be inflected; on the second aspect it may be that he meant the fatḥa arose from quiescence of quotation, for they are quoted as quiescent, bare of the mark of inflection, so the vowel is not then inflection, since there is no governing factor with the quotation, nor building, since in his view they are inflected on this supposition. It may also be that he meant they are indeclinable, so the vowel is a building vowel like in *ayna* and *kayfa*. The first is the apparent meaning of his purpose, since he had earlier decided they are inflected. Sībawayh stated in his book what was quoted verbatim: "As for *Ṣād*, it does not need to be made a foreign noun, because its pattern exists in their speech; but it may be a name of the surah, so it is not declined. It may also be that *Yā-Sīn* and *Ṣād* are two non-fully-declinable nouns, so they require fatḥa, as non-fully-declinable nouns are required to take vowels, like *kayfa*, *ayna*, *ḥaythu*, and *ams*." End of Sībawayh's words. In it is a rebuttal of al-Zamakhsharī, may God have mercy on him, in his insistence that they be inflected and that their fatḥa is either naṣb or the result of the meeting of two quiescent letters from the quotation, as appears from his speech above; and he will later also say something indicating that building them is not permitted at all. I say: Given the assumption that the first is the apparent meaning of his purpose, what he reported on Sībawayh's authority does not bear on him, since he chose one of the two options.]

I say: The better view is that it is said: that is naṣb, not fatḥa; and it is not accompanied by tanwīn because of the prohibition of ṣarf as I mentioned. Its being in the accusative is by a hidden verb, such as *udhkur* ("mention"). Sībawayh has allowed the like in *Ḥā-Mīm*, *Ṭā-Sīn*, *Yā-Sīn* if it were recited that way. Abū Saʿīd al-Sīrāfī related that some read *Yā-Sīn*. It is permitted to say it was moved because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, as one who read *wa-lā al-ḍāllīn* did.

If you say: Why not assume they are things sworn by? [Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "Why not claim they are things sworn by..." Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: He has the option to keep them in the accusative by the oath, with the wāw as conjunction, according to al-Khalīl's and Sībawayh's school in such examples; and in conjoining one follows the path of: "nor one who precedes anything when it comes", for the thing sworn by, though accusative, since it is a known position and contains the predicate, is conjoined in the genitive out of regard for that known position. Here it is more fitting to be correct than the verse of Zuhayr that is mentioned, because the accusative of the thing sworn by arose from deleting the genitive particle, which is the basis of the oath, whereas the accusative of the predicate of *laysa* is not basic in itself and does not arise from deletion; its extent is that the genitive particle may accompany its predicate as an intruder, so observing the basis is more worthy than observing the accident. Thus two possibilities have been established for the fatḥa of *Ṣād*: one is that it is an inflection, either following the aspect Zamakhsharī presented, or the accusative on the aspect I quoted from Sībawayh; the second is that it is neither inflection nor building, but it came up as the pause of quotation.] I say: the better view is that they are in the accusative: "*naʿam Allāh la-afʿalanna*" and "*āy Allāh la-afʿalanna*," by deletion of the genitive particle and governance of the oath verb? Dhū al-Rummah said:

*"Oh, many a man whose heart to God is an adviser, / and whose heart toward me is among the swift gazelles..."*
[The commentary explains: "man" is an indefinite relative, "qalbī" is subject, "Allāh" is an oath in the accusative by deletion of the particle and the implied verb; "nāṣiḥ" is the predicate; "al-sawānīḥ" are those that pass on the right side as "al-bawāriḥ" pass on the left; the poet wants to say that his beloved is like a gazelle.]

Another poet said:

*"When bread is seasoned with meat,*
*then that is the trust of Allah, the tharid."*

The *ma* here is superfluous (*za'ida*). The verb *adama*, *yadamu*, follows the pattern of *darraba*, *yadribu*, and means to make something suitable and put it right. Likewise *ādama*, with a lengthened hamza, means the same. So *ta'dimahu* means to make it good and prepare it for eating. *Amanatu Allah* is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with the predicate omitted, meaning "my oath." Or it is in the accusative, governed by an assumed verb of swearing after the particle has been dropped, meaning "I swear by the trust of Allah." Or it is in the genitive, governed by an assumed oath-particle *waw*. However, the Basran grammarians restricted this last construction to the word *Allah*.

The poet means that when bread is seasoned with meat and mixed with it, that dish is the *tharid*, and nothing else is, and this is the due of the trust of Allah.

If it is objected that the Qur'an and the pen, after these disjointed letters, are sworn by, so that if you say the letters are oaths too you would combine two oaths on one sworn thing, and they disliked that, I answer: Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said concerning the verse ﴿By the night when it covers, and by the day when it shines, and by Him who created the male and the female﴾: the last two *waws* are not on the same level as the first. Rather, they are the *waws* that join nouns to nouns, as in your saying "I passed by Zayd and 'Amr." The first is on the level of the *ba'* and the *ta'*.

Sibawayh said: I said to al-Khalil, "Why are the last two not on the level of the first?" He said: "He swears by these things in order to affirm something. If his oath with the first had been completed on a particular matter, it would be permissible to use another statement, as in your saying 'By Allah, I will do it,' 'By Allah, I will go out today.' It is not strong to say 'By your life and the life of Zayd, I will do it.' The last *waw* is an oath-*waw*, and it is not permissible except in a strained way." He said: "You say 'By my life, then your life, I will do it,' where *thumma* here functions like the *waw*."

Furthermore, in the matter we are dealing with, there is no way to make the *waw* a conjunction, because the second word differs from the first in its grammatical case (*i'rab*). If you say: then consider it genitive by an assumed *ba'* of swearing, not by its deletion, for it has come from them as "Allah, I will do it" in the genitive. Its parallel is their saying *lāhu abūka*, except that it is given the open vowel in the genitive position because it is not declined. And make the *waw* a conjunction, so that your path to what you have pointed to is secured. I answer: This is not far from the truth, and it is supported by what they narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Allah swore by these letters."

[Narration cited: this is a mawquf report transmitted by al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, from the route of Mu'awiya ibn Salih, from 'Ali ibn Talha, from him, with the wording: "The disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs are all oaths, which Allah swore by." Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it by this route in the tafsir of *Ta-Ha*, saying: "*Ta-Ha* and its like are an oath which Allah swore by, and they are among the names of Allah, exalted is He."]

If it is asked: What is the reasoning behind some reciters reading *Sad* and *Qaf* with a kasra? I answer: Its reasoning is what you mentioned about the movement to avoid the meeting of two consonants.

[Note by Ibn al-Munayyir, may Allah have mercy on him: al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, what is the reasoning behind some reciters reading *Sad* and *Qaf* with a kasra?" Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This shows you that his position contradicts what I quoted from the text of Sibawayh, that these letters are not fully declinable (*ghayr mutamakkina*). What shows you that the fatha he earlier said was due to the meeting of two consonants is a fatha of indeclinability (*fathat bina'*), is that he only meant the accidental quiescence in quotation, not the quiescence of indeclinability. This too contradicts Sibawayh's text, as I pointed out.]

The explanation for the one who sets the movement is this: since pausing (*waqf*) has continued on these names, they came to resemble the indeclinable words that end with two consonants. So they are treated sometimes like *al-an* and sometimes like *ha'ula'*.

If it is asked: Does it allow me, in the quoted form, to intend the meaning of an oath as it allowed me in the declined form? I answer: It is no concern of yours in that. You may assume the oath particle is implied in such a verse as ﴿Ha-Mim. By the Clear Book﴾, as if it were said: "I swear by this surah and by the Clear Book: We have made it..." As for his peace and blessings be upon him saying "Ha-Mim, they will not see," [this is a hadith transmitted by the authors of the three Sunan, from the narration of al-Muhallab, from one who heard the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, say: "If the enemy attacks your house, let your watchword be Ha-Mim, they will not see." Al-Hakim said: the unnamed narrator is al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also narrated by an-Nasa'i, and in the matter there is a report from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, in *al-Awsat* of at-Tabarani; in *ad-Dala'il* of Abu Nu'aym from him concerning the battle of Hunayn; from Shayba ibn 'Uthman in at-Tabarani as well; and from Abu Dujana al-Ansari at the end of *ad-Dala'il* of al-Bayhaqi, in a long hadith.] it is appropriate to judge that it may be given both the genitive and the accusative, by deleting the particle and assuming it.

If it is asked: What is the meaning of naming the surahs with these particular expressions? I answer: The meaning in that seems to be to signal that the Furqan (the Criterion, i.e., the Qur'an) is nothing but words in Arabic whose composition is known, made from the names of these letters, as the Mighty One said: ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾.

If it is asked: Why are they written in the Mushaf in the form of the letters themselves, not in the form of their names? I answer: Because words are composed of the letters themselves, and the custom has continued that when one spells something out, or when the scribe is told "write such and such," he pronounces the names while the letters themselves appear in writing. So the writing of these openings was done in this familiar pattern. Also, because of the fame of this matter, the tongues of the common folk and the elite are upon it, and because one who utters them without spelling them out gains nothing from them, and because some of them are single letters that do not come to mind as anything but what they are in their context, you are safe from confusion over them. Many features have come about in the Mushaf's script that lie outside the rules on which the science of orthography and spelling is built. Yet that brings no defect or shortcoming, since the wording stays correct and the memorization is preserved, and following the script of the Mushaf is a Sunna that must not be contradicted.

['Abd Allah ibn Darastawayh said in his book, known as *al-Mutarjam* or *Kitab al-Kitab al-Mutammim*: In orthography and spelling there are two scripts that are not measured by rules: the script of the Mushaf, because it is a Sunna, and the script of prosody, because in it one records what the wording records and drops what it drops.]

The second aspect: that these names come in this manner, recited in sequence in the form of enumeration, like an alert and the striking of a staff for one who was challenged by the Qur'an and its strange composition, and like a stirring of attention to the fact that what is recited to them is a composition made of the very same materials from which they make their own speech, so that their reflection leads them to become certain that their power did not collapse short of it, and their miraculous ability did not appear as able to produce its like after prolonged exchanges. They were the commanders of speech and the leaders of debate, eager to compete in the composition of impromptu speeches, and passionately devoted to excelling in poetry and rajaz. Yet the Qur'an did not reach the limit of eloquence and beautiful arrangement that surpassed the rhetoric of every speaker, split the dust of every competitor, and exceeded the limit that issues from the powers of the eloquent. It did not fall beyond the aspirations of the sight of the discerning except because it is not the speech of humans, but the speech of the Creator of powers and destiny. This view is firm and worthy of acceptance by its strength and its creative force. Whoever supports the first view may say: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, poured into their methods and usages, and the Arabs did not go beyond naming with a compound of two names, and no one among them was named with a compound of three, four, or five names. The claim that these are names of the surahs in their literal sense leads to something outside the language of the Arabs and results in the name and the named becoming one thing.

If you object to him that this is an opinion that has been said across time and that there is no way to refute it, he answers you that it has a meaning other than what he proceeds to, and that it is like the saying of people: "So-and-so recites *qifa nabki*" and "*'afat al-diyar*," and a man asks his companion, "What did you recite?" and he says "*al-hamdu lillah*," "*bara'atun min Allah wa rasulihi*," "*yusikum Allah fi awladikum*," and "*Allahu nuru al-samawati wa al-ard*." These sentences are not the names of those poems, these surahs, and these verses. Rather, they mean the transmission of the poem whose opening is that, and the recitation of the surah or verse whose opening is that. When speech followed the style of one who intends naming, and what is derived from it is what is derived from naming, they said that by way of metaphor rather than literal meaning. For one who answers the two objections on the first view, he may say: Naming with three names or more is, by my life, objectionable and a departure from the speech of the Arabs. But if it is made one name, in the manner of *hadrmawt* [the place name], then there is no objection. As for a non-compound listed loosely, like the listing of numerals, there is no objection to it, because it belongs to the class of naming with what should be reported as a report, just as they named people *bi-ta'abbata sharran*, *bi-baraqa nahruhu* ["Lightning his chest"], *bi-shab qarnaha* ["Gray her horns"], and as if one named someone *bi-Zayd munṭaliq* ["Zayd departs"] or a line of verse. It is enough that Sibawayh equated naming by a phrase or a line of poetry with naming by a group of letters of the alphabet, which is a decisive proof of the soundness of this. As for naming the entire surah by its opening, it does not make the name and the named one thing, because it is naming a composite by itself, and the composite is different from the simple. Do you not see that they made the name of a letter composite, from it and two letters joined to it, as in their saying *Sad*? So there was no making of the name and the named one thing, given that the name is composite and the named is simple.

The third aspect: that the surahs are introduced with these letters so that the first thing that strikes the ears stands independently with a feature of grammar, as a prelude of the signs of inimitability. This is because pronouncing the letters themselves was something in which the Arabs were equal in footing, the unlettered among them and the People of the Book alike. This is unlike pronouncing the names of the letters, which was specific to one who wrote, read, mixed with the People of the Book, and learned from them. For an unlettered man to speak them was considered strange and unlikely, just as writing and reading were, as the Mighty One said: ﴿You did not recite any scripture before it, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾. So the judgment on pronouncing these, along with the widely known fact that he had not acquired anything from their people, is the judgment on the stories mentioned in the Qur'an, of which Quraysh and those who followed their religion had no comprehensive knowledge. Thus it is acquired by him through revelation, and it is evidence of the truth of his prophethood, as if he spoke a foreign tongue without having heard it from anyone.

Know that when you reflect on what Allah, mighty in authority, has presented in the openings of these names, you will find them to be half the names of the letters of the alphabet.

[Note by Ibn al-Munayyir: Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Know that when you reflect on what Allah, mighty in authority, has presented in the openings of these names, you will find them to be half the names of the letters of the alphabet..." Ahmad said: What remains from the categories is the strong letters (*al-huruf al-shadida*). He mentioned half of them: the hamza, expressed by the alif, the kaf, the qaf, and the ta'. And the emphatic letters (*al-mutbaqa*), of which he mentioned half: the sad and the ta'.]

And the open letters, of which half has been mentioned: alif, ḥāʾ, rāʾ, sīn, ʿayn, qāf, kāf, lām, mīm, nūn, hāʾ, and yāʾ. The sibilants (ḥurūf al-ṣafīr) are three: sīn, ṣād, and zāy. Since they are three, they have no exact half, so he mentioned two of them: sīn and ṣād. That is the familiar practice in whatever is intended to be halved when halving is not possible, so the fraction is completed. Do you not see the divorce of a slave and the waiting period of a slave-woman, and similar cases? The soft letters (ḥurūf al-līn) are three: alif, yāʾ, and wāw. He mentioned two of them, alif and yāʾ, like the sibilants. The repeated letter (al-mukarrar) is rāʾ. The airy letter (al-hawāʾī) is alif. The deflected letter (al-munḥarif) is lām, and he has mentioned it. None of the categories of letters remains outside this pattern except what lies between the plosive (al-shadīd) and the fricative (al-rakhw). He did not limit himself to half of it, because what was mentioned of it exceeded half and merged into the other categories, so it was not possible to limit it, like the plosive and the fricative, and so it received no attention. As for the letters of fluency (ḥurūf al-dhalaqa) and the closed letters (al-muṣmata), the correct view is that they are not two separate categories. Whoever counts them as two distinct categories has a long dispute about the basis of their distinction, to the point that al-Zamakhsharī, in his al-Mufaṣṣal, went too far in distinguishing them, saying: "The letters of fluency are those on which the speaker relies on the tip (dhalq) of the tongue, that is, its edge." This is a very rejectable distinction, because among them are mīm, bāʾ, and fāʾ, and the edge of the tongue has no role in them. Furthermore, the matching of these with the closed letters does not hold under this distinction, since he defines the closed letters as those that come from the structure of a quadriliteral word or longer, until one of the letters of fluency is merged with them. How then can the emergence from the edge of the tongue be contrasted with closure? The truth is that they are two categories whose distinction is weak, so their running in the continuous pattern is not considered, unlike the other categories whose distinctness is clear. Al-Zamakhsharī counted the letters of echo (ḥurūf al-qalqala) in this pattern, and he mentioned that the half of them mentioned are qāf and ṭāʾ. This is a mistake, for they are five letters, and of them only the two mentioned appear in the openings. In general, the observer should not put forward an explanation of what has not come about in this pattern of categories in a way that can be relied upon.

Fourteen letters, equally, are: alif, lām, mīm, ṣād, rāʾ, kāf, hāʾ, yāʾ, ʿayn, ṭāʾ, sīn, ḥāʾ, qāf, and nūn, in twenty-nine sūrahs, corresponding to the number of the letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al-muʿjam). Then, when you examine these fourteen, you find that they include halves of the classes of letters. The explanation is that among them, half of the voiceless letters (al-mahmusa) are: ṣād, kāf, hāʾ, sīn, and ḥāʾ. Half of the voiced letters (al-majhūra) are: alif, lām, mīm, rāʾ, ʿayn, ṭāʾ, qāf, yāʾ, and nūn. Half of the plosive letters are: alif, kāf, ṭāʾ, and qāf. Half of the fricative letters (al-rakhwa) are: lām, mīm, rāʾ, ṣād, hāʾ, ʿayn, sīn, ḥāʾ, yāʾ, and nūn. Half of the emphatic letters (al-muṭbaqa) are: ṣād and ṭāʾ. Half of the open letters (al-munfatiha) are: alif, lām, mīm, rāʾ, kāf, hāʾ, ʿayn, sīn, ḥāʾ, qāf, yāʾ, and nūn. Half of the elevated letters (al-mustaʿliya) are: qāf, ṣād, and ṭāʾ. Half of the lowered letters (al-munkhafiḍa) are: alif, lām, mīm, rāʾ, kāf, hāʾ, yāʾ, ʿayn, sīn, ḥāʾ, and nūn. Half of the letters of echo are: qāf and ṭāʾ. Then, when you survey the words and their compositions, you find that the letters which God has left unmentioned from these counted categories are abundant among the mentioned ones. So glory be to Him in whose every thing His wisdom is subtle. You know that the majority of a thing and most of it takes the place of its whole. This is consistent with the subtleties of the revelation and its abbreviations. It is as if God, exalted be His name, enumerated for the Arabs the letters of which their speech is composed, as an indication of what I have mentioned: rebuking them and binding them with proof.

And among what indicates that He singled out for mention the most frequently occurring letters in the compositions of words is that alif and lām, since their occurrence is so frequent, came repeated in most of these openings. They are: the openings of the sūrahs al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān, al-Rūm, al-ʿAnkabūt, Luqmān, al-Sajda, al-Aʿrāf, al-Raʿd, Yūnus, Ibrāhīm, Hūd, Yūsuf, and al-Ḥijr.

If you ask: why were they not all enumerated at the beginning of the Qur'an, and why did they come dispersed across the sūrahs? I answer: because repeating the reminder that what is challenged is composed of these alone, and renewing it in more than one place, reaches the goal and establishes it in the ears and hearts more than mentioning it once. Likewise, every repetition that comes in the Qur'an aims at fixing the repeated matter in souls and confirming it. If you ask: why did they not come in one pattern, and why do the numbers of their letters differ, so that ṣ, q, and n occur as one letter; ṭ-h, ṭ-s, y-s, and ḥ-m as two letters; a-l-m, a-l-r, and ṭ-s-m as three letters; a-l-m-ṣ and a-l-m-r as four letters; and k-h-y-ʿ-ṣ and ḥ-m-ʿ-s-q as five letters? I answer: this is a renewed exercise of their varied styles of speech, their manipulation of it in diverse ways and varied schools. Just as the patterns of their words are one letter, two letters, up to five letters and do not exceed that, these openings were made to follow that same course.

If you ask: what is the reason for the particular opening that each sūrah is singled out with? I answer: when the purpose is alerting, and all the openings are equal in fulfilling this purpose without any preference, seeking the reason for the specific assignment falls away, just as when a man names one of his sons Zayd and another ʿAmr, one does not say to him: why did you single out this son with Zayd and that one with ʿAmr? Because the purpose is distinction, and this is achieved by whatever is used. For this reason one does not say: why was this species called "man" and that one "horse"?

Why was the act of striking called ḍarb, standing called qiyām, and its opposite called quʿūd? If you ask: why did they count some of these openings as verses and not others? I answer: this is a matter of revelation (tawqīf), in which analogy has no room, like knowing the sūrahs themselves.

As for a-l-m, it is a verse wherever it occurs among the sūrahs that open with it, and there are six of these. Likewise, a-l-m-ṣ is a verse. Al-r is not counted as a verse; r is not a verse in its five sūrahs. Ṭ-s-m is a verse in its two sūrahs. Ṭ-h and y-s are two verses. Ṭ-s is not a verse. Ḥ-m is a verse in all its sūrahs. Ḥ-m-ʿ-s-q is two verses. Kh-y-ʿ-ṣ is one verse. Ṣ, q, and n, all three, are not counted as verses. This is the view of the Kufans and others, who do not count any of them as a verse. If you ask: how then is what is in the status of one word counted as a verse? I answer: just as al-Raḥmān alone and muhdhāmmatān alone are counted as two verses, by way of revelation. If you ask: what is their ruling regarding pausing (waqf)? I answer: one pauses on all of them with a complete pause (waqf al-tamām) when they are taken to have an independent meaning, not requiring what follows them. That is when they are not made names of the sūrahs and are not uttered as one utters sounds, or when each one alone is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject, as in the saying of the Exalted, who says: "a-l-m, Allāh" — meaning: this is a-l-m — then He begins, saying: "Allāh, there is no god but Him." If you ask: do these openings have a place in i'rāb (grammatical analysis)? [Mahmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: what is the place of these openings in i'rāb?..." Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: The accusative with the oath is permissible only where no coordinated genitive follows it. As for what is followed by a coordinated genitive, like ṣ, q, and n, the accusative with the oath is absolutely not permitted there, and one takes it to imply an omitted verb, or to be that the fatḥa is in a place of genitive. As for their position at the beginning of what came before, the accusative with the oath is permitted in all of them, so renew the attention to it. On the accusative with an implied verb, Sībawayh analyzed them in his book.] I answer: yes, they have a place according to those who make them names of the sūrahs, because according to them they are like the rest of proper names. If you ask: what is their place? I answer: it may take the three cases. As for the nominative, it is by way of being the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ). As for the accusative and the genitive, it is by the soundness of swearing by them, and their being in the position of Allāh, and Allāh in both dialects. Whoever does not make them names of the sūrahs cannot conceive of their having any place in his view, just as there is no place for the independent sentences and the enumerated single words.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

If you say: Why is the demonstrative "that" (dhalika) used for something that is not distant? [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "If you say, why is the demonstrative 'that' (dhalika) used for what is not distant...?" Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: Because the distance here is by way of the elevation of rank, and the rank of the one pointed to is distant from the rank of every other book. They also use thumma (then) to signal the remoteness of ranks, and the conjoined may precede the conjoined-to in existence, and similar cases will come.]] I say: The pointing was made to alif-lam-mim after it had been spoken and concluded, and what has been concluded is in the position of the distant. This is the case in every speech. A man narrates a story and then says: "That is beyond doubt." A reckoner reckons and then says: "That comes to such and such."

God Most High said: ﴿Neither old nor virgin, but of middle age between that﴾ [Q 2:68 / 5 / 66 type usage], and He said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Q 12:37]. Also, since it has passed from the sender to the one sent to, it has entered the category of distance, as you say to your companion when you have given him something: "Keep that safe." It was also said that its meaning is: that Book which they were promised. If you say: Why is the demonstrative noun used when the referent is feminine, being the sura? [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "If you say, why is the demonstrative noun used...?" Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: Had he illustrated it with the saying of the speaker, "Hisan was your mount," it would have been more upright and safer than the distinction made by the ambiguity in the word "man" which is suitable for both the masculine and feminine referent. A similar case is God's saying: ﴿They think every shout is against them; they are the enemy﴾ [Q 63:4], for one who joins the sentence makes ﴿they are the enemy﴾ a clause in the position of the second object of "think," and he departs from saying "it is the enemy," considering the second object, which in meaning is a predicate about the shout; so he used the masculine and plural because the subject is, in meaning, the predicate. Shaykh Abu Amr has given the explanation of al-Zamakhshari's statement, and the clause is called by the feminine and masculine forms after his saying: "Speech is what is composed of two words," in accordance with this explanation.]] I say: I cannot avoid making the Book either its predicate or its attribute. If I make it its predicate, then it is in its meaning and designation the same as it, so it is permissible to apply its rule to it in the masculine, as it was applied to it in the feminine in their saying: "Whoever your mother was." If I make it its attribute, then it is pointed to the Book explicitly, because the demonstrative noun is used to point to the genus that is in apposition to it. You say: "Hind, that person, or that individual, did such and such." And al-Dhubyani said:

"I was informed that Nu'mā, reproaching me over the separation, [said]: 'Watering and pasturing for that reproachful one (al-'Atib al-Zari)'"

[[Awiju fa-hayyū li-Nu'ma dimnat al-dār... ma dhā yuhayyūna min nu'an wa-aḥjār / la-qad arānī wa-Nu'mā lāhīyayna bihā... wa-l-dahr wa-l-'ayysh lam yuhimma bi-imrār / nubbi'tu Nu'mā 'alā al-hijrān 'ātibatan... suqyā wa-ra'yā li-dhāka al-'ātib al-zārī.]] By al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani. Al-'awj: turning the camel's head with the rein. Nu'mā: the name of his beloved. Al-dimna: what has become matted of dung, ash and refuse, and the intended meaning is traces in general. Al-nu'y: the barrier around the tent so that water does not enter it. What is meant by al-ahjār: the three stones on which pots are set, or the remaining walls. Hamma bi-l-shay': he intended it; its root is idgham, and its unfolding here is a dialect form, i.e. neither of them was intending. Al-imrār: a thing becoming bitter, and al-ihlā': its becoming sweet; and making a taste bitter, or making it sweet. It is also narrated as zāriya instead of 'ātiba. Al-zārī: the faultfinder; one says: zarā 'alayhi yazrī if he found fault with him. His saying "mādhā tuhayyūn" is an expression of regret for the error in the command to greet and a retraction from it, since it is of no benefit. "Min" is an explanation of "mādhā," and in it is a sense of belittling. Nu'mā is coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative, and the waw is for the circumstantial state, meaning: while the time and life had not changed, each of them, into misery. He likened them to what can be the object of will by way of metaphor, so he attributed intention to them by imagination, or he metaphorically borrowed "intention" for approach and nearness explicitly; and he likened them to something eaten and attributed bitterness to them, or borrowed it for their turbidity and disturbance, with the common element of the soul's aversion to each. "'Alā al-hijrān" means: with her separation, or because of my separation from her. Suqyā and ra'yā are accusatives in the sense of the verbal noun, meaning: may God water her and pasture her. And "dhālika" refers to the person or individual, which is the intended meaning, and she is described with the masculine form to magnify her and exalt her status.]] If you say: Inform me about the construction of "that is the Book" together with "alif-lam-mim." I say: If you make "alif-lam-mim" the name of the sura, there are several constructions: that "alif-lam-mim" is the first subject, "dhālika" is a second subject, and "al-Kitāb" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the first subject. Its meaning: that Book is the complete Book, as if whatever other books there are are deficient in comparison with it, and that it is the one deserving to be called a Book, just as you say: "He is the man," meaning the perfect one in manliness, combining what is praiseworthy among men in qualities. As someone said:

"They are the people, all the people, O Umm Khalid"

[[And verily those whose blood was spilled at Falaj... they are the people, all the people, O Umm Khalid.]] By al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla; it was also said to be by Hurayth ibn Mikhfad. Al-ladhī: its origin is alladhīna, with the nūn dropped for lightness; and it is narrated as "wa-inna al-ulā" which has the sense of alladhīna, and they are those mentioned at the beginning of the verses, which is: "Have you not seen that after 'Amr and Malik, 'Urwa and Ibn al-Hawl, I am not immortal?" Ḥānat: its time of destruction arrived, and it is a metaphor for destruction. It is said: ḥāna ḥīnahu: he perished, and aḥānahu Allāh: God destroyed him, which is literal. Falaj, with a fatḥa, is the name of a place on the road to Basra, and dimā'uhum: their souls. "They are the people, all the people": that is, they are the ones specialized with all the praiseworthy qualities of men, to the exclusion of others.]]

And the Book may be an attribute; its meaning: it is that promised Book. And "alif-lam-mim" may be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e. "these are alif-lam-mim," and "dhālika" would be a second predicate or an apposition, with the Book then being an attribute. Or: "these are alif-lam-mim" as one clause, and "that is the Book" as another clause. And if you make "alif-lam-mim" like a sound, then "dhālika" is the subject whose predicate is "al-Kitāb," i.e. that revealed Book is the complete Book. Or the Book is an attribute and the predicate is what follows it, or an omitted subject is supposed, i.e. it, meaning what is composed of these letters, is that Book. Abdullah read: "Alif-lam-mim, the sending down of the Book, there is no doubt in it." The construction of this is evident.

"Rayb" (doubt) is a verbal noun of rābanī, when you come to have doubt. The true meaning of doubt is the restlessness and agitation of the soul. From this is what al-Hasan ibn 'Ali narrated: he said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi at the end of Medicine, al-Hakim in Judgments and in Sales, al-Tabarani and al-Bazzar. al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Shu'ab with the wording: "for indeed evil is doubt and good is tranquility."]], for indeed doubt is a doubt, and truthfulness is tranquility," meaning: for the matter being doubted is something that disturbs the soul and it does not settle, while its being correct and true is something the soul is at rest with and calm. From this also: "the doubts of time," which is what disturbs souls and startles hearts of its calamities. And from it: that he passed by a bent gazelle [[His saying "that he passed by a bent gazelle" perhaps means: that he (ﷺ) passed... In al-Sihah it says that he, peace be upon him, passed by a gazelle, bent in the shade of a tree, meaning one that curved and twisted in its sleep. (Ibn Ma'ruf?)]] and said: "Let no one disturb it with anything [[Narrated by Malik in al-Muwatta', al-Nasa'i in al-Hajj, and Ibn Hibban from the narration of Umar ibn Salama al-Damri from al-Bahzi: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out intending Mecca while in ihram, until when he was at al-Atha'iya between al-Ruwaythah and al-'Arj, behold, a gazelle was in the shade and in it an arrow. He commanded a man to stand by it, that no one among the people should disturb it until they passed it. And in Ishaq's Musnad: he said to some of the people: "Stay until the people pass, and let no one disturb it with anything." The name of al-Bahzi, in Musnad Abi Ya'la, is said to be Mukhawwil, and its wording: I followed my snares at al-Abwa', and a gazelle fell into them, and I released it while the snare was on its leg, and I went out to chase it, and a man got ahead of me and embraced it, then we brought the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he divided it between us in halves.]]." If you say: How is doubt negated in a comprehensive way when many doubt it? I say: It does not negate that no one doubts it; rather what is negated is that it is the object of doubt and the occasion for it, because of the clarity of its indication and the brightness of its proof, such that it is not fitting for a doubter to fall into it. Do you not see God's saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We sent down upon Our servant, then bring a sura like it﴾ [Q 2:23]. How far is the existence of doubt from them? Rather He showed them the way to remove doubt, which is that they should measure themselves and test their strength in eloquence, whether it is complete for opposition or shrinks before it, so that when they are unable they will be certain that there is no room in it for suspicion nor entrance for doubt. If you say: Why not place the adverbial phrase before "doubt," as it was placed before "intoxication" in His saying: ﴿Neither in it is intoxication﴾ [Q 37:47]? I say: Because the purpose in putting the particle of negation before "doubt" is to negate doubt from it, and to affirm that it is truth and sincerity, not falsehood and lying, as the polytheists used to claim. If the adverbial phrase were placed first, it would aim at what is far from the meaning, namely that another book has doubt in it, not in this one, just as in His saying ﴿neither in it is intoxication﴾ the aim is to prefer the wine of Paradise over the wines of this world, in that it does not confound the intellects as they do, as if it were said: there is not in it what there is in others of this defect and deficiency. Abu al-Sha'tha' read: "lā rayb fīhi" with a raised rafʿ. The difference between it and the well-known reading is that the well-known reading entails comprehensiveness, while this one permits it. Pausing on "fīhi" is the well-known practice. From Nafi' and 'Asim that they paused on "lā rayb," and the one pausing must intend a predicate.
Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They said: no harm﴾ [Q 26:50], and the Arabs' saying: "lā ba's" (no harm), and it is abundant in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.
The estimated reading is: "there is no doubt in it."

﴿In it is guidance﴾: guidance (hudā) is a verbal noun of the form fu'l, like al-sura and al-bukā, and it is the indication that leads to the desired goal, as is proven by the occurrence of error in opposition to it. God Most High said: ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [Q 2:16]. And He said: ﴿Surely we, or they, are upon guidance, or in manifest error﴾ [Q 34:24]. It is said: "mahdī," in a place of praise, like "muhtadī," and because "ihtadā" is the intransitive form of "hadā," and the intransitive form does not go against the meaning of its origin. Do you not see the likes of: "ghammahu fa-ghtamma" (he grieved him, so he grieved), "kasarahu fa-nkasara" (he broke it, so it broke), and similar. If you say: Why is it said: "guidance for the God-fearing," when the God-fearing are already guided? [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "If you say, why is it said 'guidance for the God-fearing,' when the God-fearing are guided...?" Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: Guidance is used in the Qur'an in two senses: one is direction and clarifying the path of truth, from which is His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Q 41:17]. On this basis guidance is for the one who is astray, in that he was led to the truth, whether or not guidance was attained by him. The other is that God Most High creates guidance in the heart of the servant, and from it: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [Q 6:90]. When it is established that it occurs in both senses, it is possible in this verse that both senses are intended together. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that the Qur'an cannot be guidance for those whose remaining in error is known, that is correct only if guidance is taken to mean the creation of guidance in their hearts. But if its first meaning is intended, there is no impossibility that God Most High directed all creatures and clarified to people what was sent down to them; some of them were guided, and others upon whom error was decreed. This is the doctrine of the People of the Sunna.]] I say: It is like your saying to the honored noble: "May God honor you and exalt you," meaning to seek increase on top of what is established in him and its continuation, like His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [Q 1:6]. Another aspect: He named them, when they were on the verge of clothing themselves in the garment of piety, "God-fearing," like the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever kills a slain man, for him is his spoil" [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Qatada, with its story. al-Tibi erred in reading it as in Abu Dawud from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both; what is in it is that he said on the day of Badr: "Whoever kills a slain man, for him is such and such," and did not say "for him is his spoil."]]. And from Ibn 'Abbas: "If one of you intends to perform the Hajj, let him hasten, for illness afflicts the sick, the lost is lost, and need is restrained" [[Mawquf (a statement of Ibn 'Abbas). al-Tibi attributed it to Abu Dawud alone as marfu' and said: it does not contain the additions, meaning his saying: "for illness afflicts" to the end. Ended. The whole hadith is in Ibn Majah, and Ahmad and Ishaq in their Musnads as marfu', and in it is Abu Isra'il al-Makki, who is truthful but poor in memory.]]. So he named the one on the verge of death, sickness and going astray: "a slain man," "a sick one," and "one astray." And from it His saying: ﴿They will not beget but a wicked disbeliever﴾ [Q 71:27], i.e. one heading toward wickedness and disbelief. If you say: Why not say "guidance for the astray"? I say: Because the astray are of two groups: a group known to remain in error, namely those upon whose hearts a seal is set, and a group known to be heading to guidance. So guidance cannot be for the remaining group in error, and it remains that it is guidance for these. Had the expression explicitly stated that, it would have been said: "guidance for those heading to guidance after error," so the speech was abbreviated by treating it in the way we mentioned, and it was said: "guidance for the God-fearing." Also, this was made a stepping stone to introducing the sura, which is the first of the two bright ones, the hump of the Qur'an and its first of the oft-repeated, by mentioning the friends of God and His chosen servants.

The "muttaqi" in language is an active participle, from the saying: "waqāhu fa-ttaqā" (he protected him, so he guarded himself). The "wiqāya" is extreme protection. From it: a "wāqin" horse, and this animal is protected from its hoof-soreness when it is struck by a stone (dal') from the hardness of the ground and the thinness of the hoof, so it protects its hoof from anything that would hurt it [[His saying: "from its hoof-soreness, when it is struck by a stone": in al-Sihah: al-wajy: pain in the hoof. al-dal': inclination and crookedness; al-dalᶜ: a limp in the gait of a camel.]]. In the Shari'a, it is the one who protects himself from engaging in what would merit punishment, by act or omission. There is disagreement regarding minor sins [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "And there is disagreement regarding minor sins..." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: As for the Qadariyya's desire regarding God Most High, their belief is that minor sins are erased from them if they avoid major sins, and that God must pardon them for the one who avoids major sins, just as according to them He must not pardon the one who commits major sins; and this is manifest error, and opposition to the clear verses of God and the sound sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ). The truth is that forgiveness of minor sins, even when major sins are avoided, is committed to His will, just as forgiveness of major sins is committed to it too. Those who do not hold this, namely the Qadariyya, are compelled to stop at His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [Q 99:7-8], for it clearly speaks of accountability for minor sins. And they are bewildered at His saying: ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾ [Q 39:53], for it explicitly speaks of forgiveness of major sins. As for the People of the Sunna, they reconciled these two verses with His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that He be associated with, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [Q 4:48], for the restriction by will in this verse governs the two unrestricted verses.]] It was said: the correct view is that it does not include them, because they fall as expiated for one who avoids major sins. It was said: the name "believer" is applied to a man on the basis of outward condition, while "God-fearing" is applied only on the basis of experience, just as "just" may not be applied except to one who has been tested.

The position of ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ is in the nominative, because it is a predicate of an omitted subject, or a predicate along with ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ for that, or a subject if the preposed adverbial phrase is made the predicate of it. It is permissible to put it in the accusative as a circumstantial state, with the governing element being the sense of the demonstrative or the adverbial phrase. What is more deeply rooted in eloquence is to disregard these positions altogether, and to say that His saying "alif-lam-mim" is a sentence by itself, or a group of letters of the alphabet standing alone. "That is the Book" is a second clause. "There is no doubt in it" is a third. "Guidance for the God-fearing" is a fourth.

The finest point of eloquence (balagha) and the reason for the beauty of its composition (nazm) are found in its arrangement. The verses come in this harmonious order without any conjunctive particle (harf nasq), because they are linked like brothers, each one embracing the next. The second is joined to the first and embraces it, and so on to the third and the fourth.

The explanation is this. First, it draws attention to the fact that this is the speech with which the challenge was issued. Then it is pointed to as the Book described with the utmost perfection. This confirms the aspect of the challenge and strengthens its supports. Then it denies that any shred of doubt may cling to it. This is a testimony and an attestation of its perfection, for there is no perfection more complete than that which belongs to truth and certainty, and no deficiency more deficient than that which belongs to falsehood and dubious suspicion. It was said to one of the scholars: "In what do you find your delight?" He said: "In a proof that struts with clarity, and in a doubt that shrinks in disgrace." Then it informs that it is "guidance for the God-conscious," thereby establishing that it is a certainty around which doubt does not hover, and a truth that falsehood does not approach from before it or behind it.

Moreover, after these four were arranged in this elegant order and composed in this marvelous fashion, each one of them is not free of a subtle point of weighty significance. In the first there is ellipsis (al-hadhf) and an allusion to the purpose in the most refined and graceful manner. In the second there is the majesty found in the definite form. In the third there is what lies in placing the doubt before the adverbial phrase. In the fourth there is ellipsis, and the verbal noun "hudan" (guidance) is placed in the position of the active participle "hadin" (one who guides), and it is brought in indefinite form. And there is brevity in mentioning "the God-conscious."

May God increase us in insight into the secrets of His speech, in clarifying the subtleties of His revelation, and in granting us success in acting upon what it contains.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 3:

﴿Those who believe﴾ may be a relative clause describing "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin), in the genitive as an attribute, or in the accusative as an expression of praise, or in the nominative with an implied subject, meaning "I mean those who believe," or "they are those who believe." Or it may be separated from "the God-fearing" and put in the nominative as a new subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being ﴿those are upon guidance﴾. If it is a relative clause, then stopping at "the God-fearing" is acceptable but incomplete (hasan ghayr tamm). If it is separate, then stopping there is a complete pause (waqf tamm).

If you ask: what is this attribute? Is it coming to explain and clarify the God-fearing? Or is it listed alongside "the God-fearing" to convey a meaning other than theirs? Or did it come as praise and commendation, like the attributes of God which follow Him to glorify Him? I say: it may come as explanation and clarification, because it contains what the state of the God-fearing is founded upon, namely doing good deeds and abstaining from evil. As for the doing, it is folded into the mention of faith, which is the foundation and rank of good deeds, and the mention of prayer (salah) and almsgiving (zakat), because these two are the mothers of bodily and financial acts of worship, and they are the measure by which others are judged. Have you not seen how the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called prayer the pillar of religion, and made the dividing line between Islam and unbelief the abandoning of prayer, and called zakat the bridge of Islam? [[As for the first hadith, al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Shu'ab through the chain of 'Ikrimah from 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), in a hadith which at its end says: "and prayer is the pillar of religion." He said: 'Ikrimah did not hear from 'Umar. He said: I think it is from Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both). It has a supporting report from the hadith of 'Ali (may God be pleased with him) with the wording "prayer is the pillar of Islam," recorded by al-Asbahani in al-Targhib. Ibn al-Salah overlooked this in Mushkil al-Wasit and said: this is a hadith that is not known. I say: al-Tibi attributed it to the takhrij of al-Tirmidhi in the hadith of Mu'adh, where it says "and its pillar is prayer," and its distance is not hidden.

As for the second hadith, Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Jabir (may God be pleased with him) with the wording: "Between a man and unbelief is the abandoning of prayer."

As for the third hadith, Ishaq recorded it in his Musnad from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' (may God be pleased with him), the same. In its chain is al-Dahhak ibn Humuq, and he is weak.]] And God Most High said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat﴾. Since these two are of this standing, it is their nature to draw along and bring after them the rest of the acts of worship. Hence the speech was abbreviated, by dispensing with enumerating the acts of obedience, through mentioning what serves as their heading, which, when present, the rest do not fail to accompany, along with what this contains of revealing the excellence of these two acts of worship. The same applies to abandoning (sins). Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾?

It may also be that it is not an explanation of the God-fearing, but a separate attribute indicating the performance of acts of obedience, and "the God-fearing" is meant as those who avoid acts of disobedience.

It may also be that it is praise for those described with piety, and the singling out of belief in the unseen, establishing prayer and giving zakat by mention, to show their superiority over the rest of what falls under the reality of this name of good deeds and faith.

"Iman" (faith) is a form (if'al) from "amn" (security). It is said: amantuhu (I made him secure) and a'manta-hu (I gave him security) for someone else. Then it is said: amanahu (he believed him) when he confirmed him as truthful. Its basic meaning is: "security from denial and opposition." As for its being transitive with the preposition ba' (bi-), this is because it is taken to include the meaning of aqarra (to acknowledge) and i'taraf (to confess). As for what Abu Zayd related from the Arabs: "ma amintu an ajida sahabatan" (I did not feel secure that I would find a companion), meaning "ma waththaqtu" (I did not trust), its basic meaning is: "I became one having security in it," meaning one having tranquility and calm. Both interpretations are good for ﴿they believe in the unseen﴾, meaning they acknowledge it or are confident that it is true.

It is permissible that "bil-ghayb" (in the unseen) is not connected to "believe," but is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "they believe while absent from the one believed in." Its basic meaning is: "in a state of being with the unseen," like His saying: ﴿those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾ and ﴿that He may know that I did not betray him in the unseen﴾. This is supported by what is related: "that the companions of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) mentioned the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) [[It is a mawquf (a report ending with a companion). Al-Hakim recorded it through the chain of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd: "they mentioned in the presence of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud..." etc., and its chain is sound.]] and their faith, and Ibn Mas'ud said: The matter of Muhammad was clear to whoever saw him. By Him besides whom there is no god, no believer has believed better than the faith of one who believes in the unseen," and then he recited this verse. If you ask: then what is meant by "the unseen" if you take it as connected to the verb, and what if you take it as a circumstantial clause? I say: if you take it as connected, it means "the absent," either as a verbal noun (taslimatan bil-masdar) from your saying "ghaba al-shay' ghaybан" (the thing went absent), just as the witnessed is called "shahada" (witness). God Most High said: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The Arabs call a low-lying land "ghayb." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "The camels drank until they filled the hollows of their ribs (ghuyub kulaha)." He means by "ghayb": the hollow which is in the place of the kidney, when the animal's belly is distended, it swells. Or it is fa'il (an intensive form) which was lightened, as in what is said "qil" (said), whose original is: "qayl." The meaning of it is the hidden, which does not penetrate at first except through the knowledge of the Subtle, the All-Aware, and we only know from it what He has made us know, or what He has set up as evidence for us about it. For this reason it is not permitted to say without qualification: "So-and-so knows the unseen." This is like the Creator and His attributes, prophethood and what relates to it, resurrection, gathering, reckoning, promise and threat, and other things. If you take it as a circumstantial clause, it means absence and concealment. If you ask: what is true faith? [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "If you say, what is the meaning of true faith... etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: by the sinner he means neither a believer nor an unbeliever, and this is among the names which the Qadariyya (determinist-rationalist school) invented, and God sent down no authority for them. The creed of Ahl al-Sunna (people of the Sunna) is that one who affirms the oneness of God, whose creed has no defect, is a believer even if he commits major sins. This is the correct view linguistically and legally. Linguistically, faith is affirmation, and it is affirmation. Legally, the clearest evidence for it is this verse, for when it coordinates righteous deeds with faith, it shows that faith is conceivable without them. If righteous deeds were part of faith, the coordination would be a repetition. Look at al-Zamakhshari's trick in bringing his doctrine close to the language, by his saying: "The believer is one who holds the truth as belief, expresses it with his tongue, and confirms it with his deeds." So he made affirmation part of the share of deeds, so that it would be established for him that whoever does not act has forfeited the affirmation which is faith linguistically. We have clarified that affirmation is only in the heart and its existence does not depend on the deeds of the limbs, which confirms the creed of Ahl al-Sunna that whoever believes in God and His Messenger and then dies before any deed of the limbs becomes obligatory upon him, is a believer by consensus even though he did not act. The most truthful evidence of this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed one of you does the deeds of the people of the Fire until there remains between him and it only the distance of a she-camel's milking, then he does the deeds of the people of Paradise and is written among the people of Paradise." He (ﷺ) only illustrated with the distance of a she-camel's milking because it is the extreme of brevity, and in such a time only the right intention is conceivable, yet he counted him among the people of Paradise. The believer enters Paradise by the agreement of both groups, and the evidence for this makes the condition a part of it. I say: defining the sinner as neither a believer nor an unbeliever, as is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school), is not sound, and what he did not state explicitly we are not obliged to state and define, for in our view "the astray" is one who neglects action, and he is a sinner.]] I say: it is to believe the truth, express it with the tongue, and confirm it by deed. Whoever neglects affirmation of the heart, even if he bears witness and acts, is a hypocrite. Whoever neglects testimony is an unbeliever. Whoever neglects action is a sinner.

The meaning of "establishing prayer" is straightening its pillars and guarding it from deviation in its obligations, sunan (recommended practices) and etiquette. It comes from "aqama al-'ud" (he straightened the stick) when he made it straight, or from constancy in it and guarding it, as He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿those who are constant in their prayer﴾ and ﴿those who guard their prayers﴾, and from "qamat al-suq" (the market stood) when goods sold well, and "aqamaha" (he made it stand). Someone said: "Ghazala made the market of striking stand (for the people of the two Iraqs) for a full year." [[It is by Ayman ibn Khuzaym. Ghazala was the wife of Shabib al-Kharijī, whom al-Hajjaj killed, and she fought him for a full year. "The market of striking" is a metaphor for the battlefield, or a likeness of spear-thrusting and sword-striking to goods bought and sold in the market, by way of metaphor (makniyya), and the "market" is an imaginative element (takhyil). The two Iraqs are Basra and Kufa. "Qamit" is a confirmatory adjective meaning complete. It is said: "qamata al-ta'ir untha-hu" (the bird mounted its female), meaning mated with her. The qimat is a rope with which captives and reed huts are bound, so the root indicates encompassing and gathering.]]

Because when it is guarded, it becomes like a valuable thing toward which desires are directed and for which those who attain it compete. When it is neglected and wasted, it becomes like a worthless thing that no one desires. Or it means exerting oneself and being alert for performing it, and that there should be in its performer no slackness or negligence, from the expressions "qama bil-amr" (he took up the matter) and "qamat al-harb 'ala saqihā" (the war stood on its leg). Its opposite: "qa'ada 'an al-amr" (he sat back from the matter) and "taqa'ada 'anhu" (he withdrew from it), when he shrank back and hesitated. Or it means performing it, and the performance is expressed by "establishing," because standing is part of its pillars, just as it is expressed by "qunut" (qunut is standing), and by bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud). They also say "sabbaha" (he glorified) when he prayed, because glorification exists in it. ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify (God)﴾.

The word "salah" (prayer) is a form (fi'la) from "salla," like "zakah" from "zakka." Its writing with a waw (ṣalawāt) follows the emphatic pronunciation. The basic meaning of "salla" is: he moved the two "salawayn" (the two bones of the hips/the two sides of the spine), because the one who prays does this in his bowing and prostration. Its parallel is the Jew's "kafara" (bowing) when he lowered his head and bent at the glorification of his companion, because he bends on the two "kadhatayn" [[His saying "on the two kadhatayn": in al-Sihah it says: "al-kadhatan" are what grows of flesh at the top of the thighs, (ʿ)]], which are the two "kafiratan" (the two thigh-tops). And the one who makes supplication was called "musalli" (one who prays), by way of comparison, in his humility, to the one who bows and prostrates.

The attribution of provision to Himself [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "He attributed provision to Himself to inform that they spend only from pure lawful sustenance... etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: this is a Qadari innovation, for they hold that God Most High provides only what is lawful, and that the servant provides himself with what is unlawful, to the point that they divide provisions into two parts: this is for God in their claim, and this is for His partners. When they affirm a creator other than God, they do not hesitate to affirm a provider other than Him. As for the people of the Sunna, there is no creator or provider in their creed except God, Glorified is He, in confirmation of His saying: ﴿Is there any creator other than God who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? There is no god but He, so how are you deluded?﴾ O Qadariyya.]] is to inform that they spend the lawful pure (sustenance) which deserves to be attributed to God and called provision from Him. [[His saying "that they spend the lawful" is based on the view that provision is specific to the lawful, which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. According to Ahl al-Sunna, provision is more general. (ʿ)]] He placed "min" (of) as partitive, to protect them and restrain them from extravagance and wastefulness, which are forbidden. He put the object of the verb first to show that it is more important, as if he said: they single out some of the lawful wealth to give it in charity. It is permissible that it means obligatory zakat, since it is linked with its sister and twin, which is prayer, and that it means it and other expenditures in the ways of good, since it came unrestricted and can include every spender.

"Anfaqa al-shay'" and "anfadahu" are two synonyms. Ya'qub said: "nafaqa al-shay'" and "nafada" are one and the same. Every word whose first letter is nun and whose middle letter is fa' indicates the meaning of going out, departing, and similar things, if you reflect upon it.

If you say: Are those who believe (wa-alladhīna yu'minūna) other than the former (al-awwalīn), or are they the former themselves? The conjunctive particle (al-ʿāṭif) is placed in the middle, just as it is placed between attributes in your saying, "He is brave and generous," and in the verse of the poet:

"To the noble king (al-malik al-qarm) and the son of the resolute one (ibn al-hammām), and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

[[The prepositional phrase "to" (ilā) in the poem is linked to what precedes it. Al-qarm, with a fatḥa on the qāf, originally means a noble stallion that is exempted from work because of its honour and because it is kept for mating with camels. The poet uses it metaphorically for a lord, a chief, or a horseman prepared for hardships. The Qāmūs appears to mean by it, literally, a lord. The waw is placed between the epithets to emphasise their connection to the described noun. Al-hammām is one of great resolve, of penetrating determination.

He uses "lion" (layth) metaphorically for the brave man, by way of explicit metaphor. Al-katība is an organised, ordered army. Al-muzdaḥam is the battlefield, because it is the place of crowding; its original form was "muztaḥam" from the iftiʿāl pattern, its tāʾ changed to dāl.]]

And his saying:

"Alas for Zayyāba for al-Ḥārith, the one who shouts (al-ṣābiḥ), then the one who seizes spoils (al-ghānim), then the one who returns (al-āyib)?"

[[Alas for Zayyāba for al-Ḥārith, the one who shouts, then the one who seizes spoils, then the one who returns.

By God, if I met him alone,
he would return with two swords alongside the victor.

This is said by the son of Zayyāba in reply to al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, when the latter said to him:

"O son of Zayyāba, if you meet me,
do not meet me in the wide open pasture (al-naʿam al-ʿāzib)."

"And if you meet me, he will pull me on a bare-haired, swift-stepping mount, broad of chest like a rider."

Al-ʿāzib, with a zāy, means one far from his people. He alludes that Zayyāba is a herdsman of camels, not a brave man. Al-ajrad is one whose hair is shorn. Al-barka in a camel or a horse is the protruding bone in their chest, and its size is praised in both. He compared it to a rider in the length and extension of its neck. It is also possible that the meaning is that its rider is likewise broad-chested, not humbled or shrunken. He says: alas for my father's grief over him, because of al-Ḥārith, who has achieved his aim from me. There is in it a kind of mockery, if his threat was then followed by turning back on his heels. It is said that it is on its literal sense: then he swore that if he found him he would kill him, but he presented the speech in the form of implication for the sake of fairness in speech. The return of the two swords with the victor is a metaphor for killing the defeated and stripping him of his weapon.]]

I say: It is possible that by "these" is meant the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his like from among those who believed. Their faith then encompasses every revelation sent down from God, and they became certain of the Hereafter with a certainty by which there disappeared what they had held, namely that no one enters Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a few counted days. Their agreement on affirming the other creation and the return of souls into bodies, then their division into two groups: some of them said that their condition in enjoying food, drink and marriage would proceed on the same course as in this world; and others rejected this, claiming that such things are needed in this abode for the growth of bodies and for procreation, while the people of Paradise are free of this, so they take pleasure only in fragrant breezes, sweet scents, delightful music, joy and happiness. Their disagreement concerns permanence and cessation, so the conjoined word is other than the one it is conjoined to. It is also possible that the meaning is a description of the former. The conjunctive particle is placed in the middle to mean that they combine those attributes and these.

If you say: If by "these" is meant others than those, do they enter into the category of the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn) or not?

I say: If you join them to (alladhīna yu'minūna bil-ghayb), they enter, and the attribute of God-consciousness includes both groups, the believers from the People of the Book and others. If you join them to (lil-muttaqīn), they do not enter. It is as if it were said: guidance for the God-fearing, and guidance for those who believe in what has been sent down to you.

If you say: His saying "what has been sent down to you" (bimā unzila ilayka), if it means the entire Qur'an and the whole Sharīʿa from beginning to end, then it was not sent down at the time of their belief, so how is it said "was sent down" in the past tense? And if it means the portion that had already been sent down at the time of their belief, then it is faith in part of what was sent down, while faith that encompasses the whole, both what came before and what is awaited, is obligatory.

I say: What is meant is the whole of what was sent down, and it is expressed in the past tense even though part of it is still awaited, giving precedence to the existent over what has not yet existed, just as the speaker takes precedence over the addressee, and the addressee over the absent party. One says: "You and I did it," and "You and Zayd will do it." Also, when part of it has descended and part is awaited, it is treated as if all of it had descended and its descent had ended. This is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book sent down after Moses﴾, and they had not heard the whole Book, nor was all of it yet sent down; but its course is the course we have mentioned. A parallel to it is your saying: "Everything that so-and-so has delivered in speech is eloquent, and he has said nothing except that it is rare." You do not mean by this the past alone to the exclusion of the future, because its parts are tied to one another and its future is bound to its past.

Yazīd ibn Quṭayb read "bimā unzila ilayka wa-mā unzila min qablika" with the verb in the passive form, in the pattern of what has not named its agent. In placing "bil-ākhira" first and in the construction of "yūqinūn" upon "hum," there is a pointed reference to the People of the Book and to what they held: affirming the matter of the Hereafter contrary to its reality, and that their saying does not proceed from certainty, and that certainty is what those hold who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you. Al-yaqīn (certainty) is the perfection of knowledge with the absence of doubt and suspicion from it. "Bil-ākhira" is the feminine of al-ākhir, the opposite of al-awwal, and it is a description of the abode, as shown by His saying: ﴿That is the Last Abode﴾, and it is one of the dominant attributes, as is al-dunyā. It is reported from Nāfiʿ that he lightened it by dropping the hamza and placing its vowel on the lām, as in His saying ﴿dābbat al-arḍ﴾.
