Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī read "yūqinūn" with a hamza, placing the ḍamma of the waw as though it were on it, then changing it as the waw of "wujūh" and "wuqqitat" is changed. Similar to it is the verse:

"How I love the two fire-kindlers to me, Mūsā and Jaʿda, when the blaze lit them up."

[[This is by Jarīr in praise of Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and his son Mūsā, and Jaʿda, his daughter; it was said that she was also his son, but that is not so. The lām is for oath. Ḥabba is originally ḥababa, like ẓarufa; the vowel of the bāʾ was moved to the ḥāʾ and then the two were assimilated. Its meaning is the expression of praise, like naʿama, and it also conveys wonder, like "mā aḥabbahu." Its ḥāʾ may be given a fatḥa when its subject is dhā. "Al-mūqidān" with a hamza is the subject. Mūsā also with a hamza. Jaʿda, the one singled out for praise, follows the pattern "naʿama rajulan Zayd." "Ḥabba" is transformed from the triliteral ḥabba, like ḍarraba, although the more common form is the quadriliteral "aḥabba," because praise is formed only from the triliteral. If you ask: Is it transformed from ḥabba with the active subject, or from ḥabba in the passive? I say: If it is from the active, then the two fire-kindlers are the ones loved; if it is from the passive, then the transformation is presumed. The apparent view is that it is derived from the root without considering the construction. It is permissible that the original is ḥubbiba, like ḍuriba in the passive, so "al-mūqidān" is the deputy subject, and Mūsā and Jaʿda are an apposition or clarification. The meaning is then a statement rather than an expression. It is also reported as "aḥabba al-mūqidīn," with the comparative form of the elative added to the plural form, so Mūsā and Jaʿda are the predicate. The waw of "al-mūqidīn" and "Mūsā" was permitted to become a hamza because the letter before it is ḍammed, so it is as though it were ḍammed, and when it is ḍammed it is replaced by a hamza. One says "aḍā'a al-makān" and "aḍā'ahu al-sirāj." What occurs here is the second form, transitive, in the sense that the blaze lit them up. "Al-wuqūd" with a ḍamma is the blazing of the fire, namely the kindling of the fire of hospitality and its flaming. With a fatḥa it is what is kindled. The original form of fa'ūl is an intensive form of the active, like ḍarūb, and it often means what the act is done to, like wuqūd and suḥūr, so it may be of the passive object type, and it may be of the instrument type, irregularly. The meaning is: how I love them to me at the time when the fire that they kindle for the guests' hospitality showed them to me.]]

The sentence ﴿Those are upon guidance﴾ is in the nominative position if ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and otherwise it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). The construction works on both readings. If you intend ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ as a subject, you have taken it as a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question). When it was said ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾, and the God-conscious were singled out as those to whom the Book is guidance, a questioner could ask: "What is the matter with the God-conscious that they alone are so distinguished?" So the words ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ up to its end come as an answer to this implied question. The attribute of the God-conscious is brought in, comprising their distinctive qualities for which they deserve that God show them kindness and do for them what He does not do for those who lack their attribute. That is, those whose beliefs and deeds are these are worthy that God guide them and grant them success. A parallel to this is your saying: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) loved the Ansar who fought beside him and relieved his distress; those are people worthy of love." If you make it a follower (tabi') of ﴿the God-conscious﴾, then the resumption falls on ﴿those﴾, as if it were said: "What of those who possess these attributes, that they have been singled out for guidance?" The answer is that those described are not unlikely to attain guidance over other people in this world and success in the next. Know that this type of resumption comes sometimes by repeating the name of the one about whom the discourse is resumed, as when you say: "You have done good to Zayd; Zayd deserves kindness." And sometimes by repeating his attribute, as when you say: "You have done good to Zayd, your old friend, who deserves that from you." The resumption by repeating the attribute is better and more eloquent, because it contains an explanation and summary of the reason.

If you ask: may the first relative pronoun be made to refer to the God-conscious, and the second be nominative as a subject with ﴿those﴾ as its predicate? I answer: yes, on the basis that their singling out for guidance and success is an allusion (ta'rid) against the People of the Book who did not believe in the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while thinking they are upon guidance and hoping they will attain success with God.

The demonstrative ﴿those﴾ (ulā'ika) indicates that what follows it is attributed to those mentioned before it, as they are worthy of acquiring it because of the excellent qualities enumerated for them. As Hatim said:

*"God has a vagabond [a poor man of spirit] — then he enumerated for him distinguished qualities,*
*Then he followed the enumeration with his saying:"*

فَذلِكَ إنْ يَهْلِكْ فَحسْبى ثَنَاؤُهُ ... وَإنْ عاشَ لَمْ يَقْعُدْ ضَعِيفاً مُذَمَّمَا

*"So that one: if he perishes, his praise suffices me,
and if he lives, he will not sit weak and blamed."*

[[ويغشى إذا ما كان يوم كريهة ... صدور العوالي وهو مختضب دما

أو الحرب أبدت ناجذيها وشمرت ... وولى هدان القوم أقدم معلما

فذلك إن يهلك فحسبي ثناؤه ... وإن عاش لم يقعد ضعيفا مذمما

*"And he advances, when there is a day of dread, upon the spears' breasts, while he is dyed with blood.*
*Or when war has bared its molars and rolled up its sleeves, and the blockhead of the people has fled, I advance, marked."*

*"So that one: if he perishes, his praise suffices me,
and if he lives, he will not sit weak and blamed."*

By Hatim al-Ta'i, lamenting a man, saying that he was lofty in aspiration, and when there was a day of battle he would go to the breasts of the lances and descend among them, while he was dyed with their blood. His saying "or war" is coordinated with his saying "when there was a day of dread." Attributing the baring of the molars and the rolling up of the sleeve to war as a figure is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli), because it is the cause of the horsemen doing that. It may also be that he likened war in its strength and intensity to a brave man who does that, by way of metaphor (kinaya), and the baring of the molar and the rolling up are imaginative depiction (takhyil). The nājidh (molar) is the last of the teeth, the tooth of wisdom. The hadān, on the pattern of kitāb, is the foolish and heavy one; its plural is hudūn, from the hudna, which is calm. "Aqdam" is the answer of the conditional, marking himself for the people as so-and-so in the manner of horsemen, or marking his horse with its markings. So that one, described by those attributes and singled out for those qualities, is the one deserving to be said of: if he perishes and dies, his praise will suffice me as a source of pride, that is, his mention among people with goodness. His saying "if he lives" is a condition that does not imply occurrence, but mentioning it indicates that he is praiseworthy in his deeds in any case. His saying "he will not sit" is apparently little praise but to the discerning it is much: that is, rather, he will sit in his well-known state and praiseworthy qualities.]]

The meaning of elevation in His saying ﴿upon guidance﴾ is a figure for their being firmly established in guidance, their settling upon it, and their holding fast to it. Their state is likened to the state of one who mounts a thing and rides it. Similar to it: "He is upon the truth" and "upon falsehood."

They have indeed stated this in their saying: "He made error a mount, and he rode ignorance (imtaṭā al-jahl), and he settled upon the back of desire (iqta'ada gharib al-hawā)."

[[His saying "imtaṭā al-jahl" means he took ignorance as a mount and took desire as a riding-camel. The qu'ūd of camels is the young camel at the moment it is ridden. The gharib is what lies between the hump and the neck, as in the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

The meaning of ﴿from their Lord﴾ is that they were granted it from Him, and were given it from before Him, and it is the gentle kindness and divine success by which they were aided in performing good deeds and in ascending to what is better and then better still. ﴿Guidance﴾ is indefinite (nakkara) to convey a kind of ambiguity that does not reach its reality nor is its measure determined, as if it were said: "upon what kind of guidance!" just as you say: "If you had seen so-and-so, you would have seen a man." Al-Hudhali said:

فَلَا وَأَبِى الطّيْرِ المُرِبَّةِ بالضُّحَى ... عَلى خالِدٍ لَقدْ وَقَعْتِ على لَحَم

*"So by the father of the birds gathered at midday,
upon Khalid, you have indeed alighted upon flesh."*

[[فلا وأبى الطير المربة بالضحى ... على خالد لقد وقعت على لحم

فلا وأبى لا يأكل الطير مثله ... عشية أمسى لا يبين من السلم

*"So by the father of the birds gathered at midday, upon Khalid, you have indeed alighted upon flesh.*
*So by my father, no bird eats the like of him, on an evening when he became one who is not distinguished from the salam tree."*

By Abu Kabir al-Hudhali, lamenting Khalid ibn Zuhayr. The "la" before the oath is superfluous. He magnified the birds alighting upon him, so he swore by them, and referred to them by "father of the birds" just as one refers to a great man as "father of so-and-so." The original of "abī" here is "abīn," on the pattern of the sound masculine plural, its nūn dropped for the idafa (construct). It may be singular, meaning the vulture, because it is called "father of the birds." It may also be that by "father of the birds" he means Khalid, because they alighted on him, or that he means its origin. It is reported: "By the life of the father of the birds gathered in the morning..." etc. It is also reported with "al-ṭayr" in the nominative. Perhaps it is in the nominative as subject, or as predicate of an omitted subject, or on the supposition of vocative, and "ilā" is attached to a pronoun of the speaker, like the one after it.

It is said: "arraba bi-l-makān" and "alaba bihi": he stayed in the place and kept to it. So "al-murbbah" is the one who stays and is devoted at the time of midday upon Khalid the slain. He turned to address the birds, saying to them: "You have indeed alighted." It is reported "'alaqat" (you clung), upon "lahm," with the vowel on the lām as a dialect form. Its indefiniteness is for magnification, i.e., upon a great flesh. He made it feminine because "birds" is a collective in meaning. If the tā' is read with fatḥa, it is clear. He addressed it as if it were rational, then swore by his father that no bird eats the like of Khalid in size, on an evening when he became one who does not appear to us from the salam, which is the acacia-type tree, as a metonymy for his being slain in it with the birds around him on that tree. In the two lines there are two shifts of grammatical person (iltifat).]]

The nūn in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ is assimilated, with ghunna (nasal resonance) and without ghunna. Al-Kisā'ī, Ḥamza, Yazīd, Warsh in one transmission, and al-Hāshimī from Ibn Kathīr did not give it ghunna. The rest gave it ghunna, except Abū 'Amr, from whom two transmissions are related.

In the repetition of ﴿those﴾ there is an indication that just as the distinction of guidance is established for them, so the distinction of success is also established for them; each of the two distinctions was made to distinguish them in a position where, if either stood alone, it would suffice to distinguish them on its own.

If you say: why does it come with the conjunction? And what is the difference between it and His saying: ﴿Those are like cattle, nay, they are further astray; those are the heedless﴾? I answer: the two predicates differ here, so the conjunction is present; unlike the two predicates there, which are the same, because the attribution of heedlessness to them and their likening to animals are one thing, so the second sentence confirms what is in the first, and therefore it is outside coordination.

﴿Their Lord﴾ is a separator (fasl, a pronoun of separation). Its function: to show that what comes after it is a predicate and not an adjective; and emphasis; and the necessity that the benefit of the predicate belongs to the subject and not to anything else. Or it is a subject, with ﴿the successful﴾ as its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of ﴿those﴾.

The meaning of the definite article in ﴿the successful﴾ is to indicate that the God-conscious are the people about whom you were informed that they will succeed in the Hereafter, just as when you are informed that a man among the people of your town has repented, you ask who he is, and it is said: "Zayd the penitent," that is, he is the one whose repentance you were informed of. Or it is that they are those who, if the attribute of the successful is realized and their reality is verified, and they are conceived in their true form, then they are they, and do not exceed that reality. As you say to your companion: "Have you known the lion and what it is created with of excessive boldness? Indeed Zayd is he." So observe how God, mighty and majestic, repeated the alert to the singling out of the God-conscious for attaining what no one else attains, by various paths: the mention of the demonstrative, its repetition, the definiteness of ﴿the successful﴾, and the placement of the separator between it and ﴿those﴾, so that He may show you their ranks, and make you desire what they sought, and invigorate you to advance what they advanced, and deter you from empty greed, false hope, and wishing upon God what His wisdom does not require and what His word has not preceded. O God, adorn us with the garment of God-consciousness, and gather us in the company of those whose mention opens the chapter of al-Baqara.

The successful (al-mufliḥ) is the one who attains his aim, as if the doors of victory were opened to him and were not locked against him. Al-muflaj, with jīm, is the same. From it comes the saying of the divorced woman: "istafliḥī bi-amrik" (decide your affair), with ḥā' and with jīm. The root denotes the meaning of splitting and opening, and likewise its sister roots with fā' and 'ayn, such as: falaqa, faladha, and falā.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 6:

When he had first mentioned His friends and the purest of His servants, with the qualities that made them fit to attain nearness to Him, and had shown that the Book is guidance and special kindness for them, he followed this with the mention of their opposites: the obstinate and rebellious disbelievers, for whom guidance is of no benefit and kindness brings them no profit, and for whom it makes no difference whether the Book exists or not, and whether the Messenger warns them or remains silent. If you say: why is the story of the disbelievers cut off from the story of the believers, and not joined by a conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in the Blaze﴾, and the many other verses like it? I say: the relation of these two stories is not the relation you mention, because the first, in what we are dealing with, is brought to mention the Book and that it is guidance for the God-fearing, while the second is brought because the disbelievers have such-and-such qualities. Between the two sentences there is a difference in purpose and style, and they are on a level where there is no room for a conjunction. If you say: this holds if you suppose that ﴿those who believe﴾ is a continuation of the God-fearing; but if you begin afresh and build the speech on the qualities of the believers, then follow it with another statement about the qualities of their opposites, it would be like those verses recited. I say: I have already explained that the sentence begun after the God-fearing is by way of resumption (isti'naf), and that it is built upon an assumed question; so this is an inclusion of it within the ruling of the God-fearing, and it follows them in meaning, even though it is a new beginning in wording; in reality it is like what runs on from them.

As for the definite article in ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, it may be for a specific reference (al-'ahd), and they may be meant as particular individuals, such as Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their like; or it may be for the category (al-jins), encompassing everyone who has firmly resolved upon his disbelief, such that he does not turn back after it, and others. That it includes those who persist is shown by the discourse about them, that warning and not warning are equal regarding them. ﴿Sawa'un﴾ is a noun in the sense of equality, and it is described by it just as verbal nouns are described. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Come to a word that is equal between us and you﴾, and ﴿in four days, equal for those who ask﴾, meaning "even" (mustawiyah). Its being raised is because it is the predicate of inna. And ﴿a-anzartahum am lam tunzirhum﴾ is in the position of the subject that it raises, as if it were said: "Indeed those who disbelieved, your warning them and not warning them is equal for them", just as you say: "Indeed Zayd, his brother and his cousin are disputing."

Or ﴿a-anzartahum am lam tunzirhum﴾ is in the position of the beginning (mubtada'), and ﴿sawa'un﴾ is a predicate placed before it, meaning: "Your warning them and not warning them is equal for them," and the clause is the predicate of inna. If you say: a verb is always a predicate, not a subject, so how is it valid to make it the subject of a statement in this sentence? I say: this is of the type of speech in which the wording is set aside in favour of the meaning, and we have found the Arabs inclining markedly, in some of their speech, towards meanings, as in their saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk," meaning: "Let there not be from you the eating of fish and the drinking of milk," although the apparent wording would be what is not valid, namely conjoining a noun to a verb. The interrogative particle hamza and ''am'' are stripped of meaning for equality. Sibawayh said: this has been applied to the interrogative particle as it has been applied to the vocative particle, as in your saying: "O Allah, forgive us, O group (ayyatuha al-'isabah)", meaning that this has taken the form of the interrogative while there is no question, just as that has taken the form of the vocative while there is no call. The meaning of equality is their equality in the knowledge of the one questioned about them, for it is known that one of the two matters exists, either warning or not warning, but not specifically; so both are known through an indefinite knowledge.

It has been read: ﴿a-anzartahum﴾ with both hamzas clearly pronounced; the lightening is more eloquent and more common; and with the second lightened between the two (bayn bayn); and with an alif inserted between them, both clear; and with it inserted and the second between the two; and with the interrogative particle omitted; and with it omitted and its vowel thrown onto the preceding consonant, as ﴿qad aflaha﴾ was read.

If you say: what do you say about one who changes the second into an alif? I say: he is a solecist, outside the speech of the Arabs in two respects: one is his venturing to join two quiescent letters contrary to its rule, whose rule is that the first is a soft letter and the second an assimilated letter, as in His saying ﴿al-dallin﴾, and "khuwaysatu" (in the hadith). The second is his error in the path of lightening: the path of lightening a moving hamza whose preceding letter is open is to bring it out between the two; as for changing it into an alif, it is the lightening of a quiescent hamza whose preceding letter is open, like the hamza of ra's. And al-Indhar: the warning of the punishment of Allah by deterring from acts of disobedience. If you say: what is the position of ﴿la yu'minun﴾? I say: either it is a clause emphasizing the clause before it, or it is the predicate of inna, and the clause before it is a parenthetical interjection.

The seal and the covering are brothers, because when you secure something by stamping a seal upon it, you conceal it and cover it so that it cannot be reached or seen.

Ghishawah (covering) is on the pattern fi'alah, from ghashahu, meaning he covered it. This pattern denotes something that wraps around a thing, like a headband (*'isabah*) or a turban (*'imamah*).

If you ask: what is the meaning of sealing upon the hearts and the hearing, and covering the sight? I say: there is no sealing and no covering [[His words "there is no sealing and no covering" mean: no covering either.]] in the literal sense. It is figurative, and it may include both of its types, which are *isti'arah* (metaphor) and *tamthil* (figurative comparison). As for metaphor, it is that you treat their hearts as though the truth does not penetrate them or reach their inner selves, because of their turning away from it and their arrogance in refusing to accept and believe it. Their hearing is treated as though it rejects the truth, recoils from listening to it, and disdains to hear it, as if it were secured with a seal. Their sight is treated as though it does not behold God's signs displayed before it or His proofs set up, as the eyes of the attentive and perceptive behold them, as if it were covered over and screened, and as if a barrier stood between it and perception.

As for figurative comparison, it is that you picture them, since they did not benefit from the faculties in the religious purposes for which they were charged and for which they were created, as though those faculties had been given things over which a screen was placed, preventing their benefit, by sealing and covering. Some of the Mazini grammarians made the stammering and incapacity of the tongue a seal upon it, saying:

*God has set a seal upon the tongue of Udhafir,*
*a seal, so he has no power over speech.*
*When he wants to speak, you think his tongue*
*is a piece of flesh that a hawk pecks, moving it.* [[By a man of Fazarah. He used the seal, which prevents the addition to or subtraction from a book, as a metaphor for preventing speech. Udhafir, with a dammah, is the name of a man, and it is also applied to the strong and mighty, and to the lion. The verse's meaning is a report about the condition of Udhafir, which is what the sequence of the verses shows, and it is far-fetched that it is a supplication against him. The doer of "yuharrik" (moves it) is Udhafir. He likened his tongue to the flesh that the hawk pecks, with the common element of constant movement without straightness and without articulated speech. This shows that the verse is a report, not a supplication.]]

If you ask: why did he attribute the sealing to God, exalted is He? [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why did He attribute the sealing to God, exalted is He... etc.?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is the first blind camel that stumbled into a pit of desires and descended into it, for he came down from the platform of the explicit text to the lowland of its interpretation, seeking discord and preserving what was decreed for him of trial. So his words contain errors which I set out and refute:

The first: opposition to the rational proof of God's oneness. Its implication is that nothing occurs except by the power of God, without partner. Refusing to accept the truth is among the occurrences, so it must be included within the scope of what falls under the all-encompassing power that relates to all existents and possibilities.

The second: opposition to the transmitted proof that parallels the rational proof, such as His words: ﴿God is the Creator of all things﴾ and ﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾ This verse too attributes the sealing to God explicitly. Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, does not deny this, but claims that he resorted to interpreting it because of a proof that appeared to him. But if the rational proof is established as agreeing with what the text indicates, it is obligatory for him to keep the verse on its apparent meaning. Indeed, even if it came apparently contrary to that, it would be obligatory to interpret it by the proof, in harmony between reason and transmission.

The third: fleeing from attributing to God what he considers ugly, out of glorifying Him, on his supposition that associating partners with Him consists in believing that Satan creates the sealing, and that the disbeliever imposes it upon himself by his power, contrary to his Lord's will. He has thus found the waters of the sunnah unwholesome and entered the hot springs of innovation, which are the sources of punishment.

The fourth: the error of believing that what is ugly in the witnessed world is ugly in the unseen. Since refusing to accept the truth is ugly in the witnessed world, he supposes it must be ugly in the unseen. This is a principle whose falsehood has already been settled in its own discipline.

The fifth: his belief that if this were assumed to exist by God's power, it would be injustice. God is exalted above injustice by His words: ﴿I am not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ Clear injustice includes ignorance of the reality of injustice, which is acting upon the property of another without his permission. How then can the reality of injustice be conceived of as attributed to God? Every assumption is bounded by the limits of His dominion, exalted is He: ﴿The dominion is God's, the One, the Subduer.﴾

The sixth: he fled from the belief that injustice is attributed to God, and so he fell into it up to his neck. For he has affirmed that refusing to accept the truth, if it were from God's act, would be injustice. It should be said to him: the proof has been established that it is from God's act, so it necessarily follows for you that it is injustice, exalted is God far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. The fancy around which these people revolve is that if the acts of the servant were created by God, He would not have forbidden them to His servants, nor punished them, nor would God's proof have been established against them. These doubts have been circulated in the folds of his earlier speech. It is said to them: why have you said that if they were created by God, He would not have forbidden them to His servants? If they hold this implication, as they do, to the principle of the good and the ugly, and say: punishing a person for an act of another is ugly in the witnessed world, especially when the punishment comes from the agent, then it necessarily follows that this should be extended to the unseen. It is said to them: it is also ugly in the witnessed world that a man enable his slave to commit abominations and vices in his sight and hearing, and then punish him for them, while having the power to restrain him and prevent him from them from the outset. You, the Qadariyyah, claim that the power by which the servant creates vices for himself is created by God, knowing that the servant creates these by it for himself. This is like giving a sharp sword to a wicked man, knowing that he will cut the road with it and take captive the women, and that is definitively ugly in the witnessed world. They will say: Indeed, it is ugly in the witnessed world, but there is a wisdom which God has kept to Himself, which distinguishes the witnessed from the unseen, so that it is good in the unseen for God to enable His servant to commit vices while having the power that nothing from him occurs, but it is not good in the witnessed. At this point their feet slip and their banners are overturned, when the decisive certainties and the flashes of proofs appear to them. It is said to them: what prevents those acts from being created by God, and the servant being punished for them for a benefit and wisdom which God has kept to Himself, as you have just concluded, equally? Why does not one of you take the more just path, consider the outcome of this matter, so that the last becomes the first, and entrust the matter from the beginning to his Creator, receiving God's proof against him with acceptance and submission? Let him travel guided by the light of reason and following the evidence of the Law on the straight path. If the soul contends with him and anxious thoughts assail him, and he desires some support from speculation to find comfort in the wastelands of thought, then let him consider what is mentioned here, which is known to every sensible person, the distinction between voluntary and compelled movement, and he will find no doubt in this distinction. When he perceives this, let him be watchful, for he has been kindly guided away from the narrows of determinism, fearing that the devil of misguidance will lead him toward the deserts of Mu'tazilism. Let him restrain himself from that by the rein of the proof of oneness, that there is no agent and no creator except God, exalted is He. When he halts, he halts only upon the straight path and the best way, passing over it swifter than the lightning that tears and the wind that drives. Let the examiner ponder this section and take it as his guide in the principle of acts, and he will arrive at the truth, God willing, exalted is He.]] Attributing it to Him indicates the prevention of accepting the truth and of reaching it by its paths, and that is ugly, and God, exalted is He, is above committing what is ugly, [[His words "God is exalted above committing what is ugly": this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. As for the People of the Sunnah, it is permissible for God, exalted is He, to create evil and to will it, just as He creates and wills good, though He commands only good. For them, the sealing upon the hearts is the creation of misguidance in them, as is explained in the discipline of the doctrine of divine unity. (ʿ)]] a great exaltation, because He knows its ugliness and knows that He has no need of it.

He has explicitly affirmed the exaltation of His essence by His words: ﴿I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾, ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers﴾, ﴿God does not command indecency﴾, and similar verses that the revelation has articulated. I say: the intention is to describe the hearts as being like something sealed upon. As for attributing the sealing to God, exalted is He, it is to draw attention to the fact that this quality, in its complete firmness and steadfastness, is like an innate thing, not an accident. Do you not see how they say: so-and-so is disposed to such-and-such and created upon it, meaning that he is deeply persistent in it? How can what you imagined be conceived of, when the verse censures the disbelievers for the vileness of their attribute and the ugliness of their state, and attaches to it a severe punishment?

It is also permissible to take the expression as it is, that is, the sealing of God upon their hearts, as a figure of speech, like their saying: the valley carried him away, meaning he perished, and the phoenix flew away with him, meaning he stayed away for a long time. The valley has no role in his perishing, nor the phoenix in his long absence. It is only a figure: his state in perishing is pictured as the state of one carried off by a valley, and his state in long absence as the state of one carried off by the phoenix. Likewise, the state of their hearts in what they were upon of aversion from the truth is pictured as the state of hearts upon which God has set a seal, such as the hearts of the dull [[His words "such as the hearts of the dull": in the Sihah it says: the ghatmah is incomprehensibility, and the aghtam is the foreigner who does not speak clearly. The plural is ghutm. (ʿ)]] who, in their emptiness of understanding, are like the hearts of beasts, or the state of the hearts of beasts themselves, or the state of hearts for which God is imagined to have set a seal, so that they perceive nothing and understand nothing. He, exalted is He, has no act in their aversion from the truth and their rejection of accepting it, and He is exalted above that. It is also permissible that the attribution in itself, from something other than God, be borrowed for God, so that the sealing is attributed to the name of God by way of metaphor, while it is literal for something else. The explanation of this is that an act has various accompanying relations: the agent, the object, the verbal noun, the time, the place, and the one who causes it. Its attribution to the agent is literal, but it may be attributed to these other things by way of metaphor, called *isti'arah*, because they resemble the agent in being connected to the act. Just as a man resembles a lion in boldness, so his name is borrowed for him. It is said of the object: a pleasant life (*'ishah radiyah*), and gushing water (*ma' dafiq*). And in the reverse: a flooding torrent (*sayl mif'am*). Of the verbal noun: a poetic feeling (*sha'r sha'ir*), and a dragging hem (*dhayl dha'il*). Of time: its day is fasting, and its night is standing in prayer. Of place: a traveling road (*tariq sa'ir*), and a flowing river (*nahr jari*). The people of Makkah say: the Maqam prayed (*salla al-maqam*). Of the cause: the prince built the city, and a she-camel that is tested for fatness (*naqah dabuth*) and milked. And someone said:

*Then do not ask me, but ask about my nature,*
*when the remnants of the pot push away whoever borrows it.*
*So they sat around it, watching over it,*
*and she was the young woman of the tribe who lends it.* [[By 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas al-Bahili. It is also said to be by al-Kumayt. He says: do not ask me about my nature, but ask others about it, at the time when the remnant of the pot, meaning the seeker of sustenance that is in it, prevents whoever wants to borrow it to cook in it. The attribution of "repelling" to the remnant is a figurative attribution of reason, because the one who prevents, in reality, is the owner of the pot, because of the seeker of sustenance; he did not attribute it to himself, to disclaim the attribution of repulsion to himself, unless what is meant is the kind of pot and not his pot alone. The meaning is: when the time becomes barren, as will come. The plural pronoun in "they sat" is because the one who remains (*'afi*) is plural in meaning, meaning: it is as though the seekers of food were sitting around it, waiting for what is in it to ripen. "The young woman of the tribe" means the young woman of his tribe, and she is among those who lend the pot. It is also permissible that the pronoun in "they sat" refers to those who borrow it. It is also possible that "the remnant of the pot" is the rest of the broth that was in it, and the attribution is also figurative, meaning that whoever borrows it finds it occupied, and this is evidence of his much hospitality to guests. It is also permissible that what is meant is that the situation is barrenness, to the point that the owner of the pot repulses the borrower out of greed for what is in it, even a little of the broth. Then the pronoun in "they sat" refers to those who borrow it. It is also permissible that "remnant of the pot" is the object of a verb whose accusative is not shown because of the meter, and "whoever borrows it" is the subject, because it was a custom of the Arabs in times of drought to repel the borrower, giving the lender some of the remaining broth in the pot. So it is a metonymy for drought, but the fit with what follows is not complete. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when the borrower of the pot prevents its remnant, that is, the seeker of sustenance from it, due to his stinginess and the absence of guests at his place, he owns no pot for himself. So when he borrows a pot to cook in it once, the seeker of sustenance prevents him from it. On this basis it is possible that it is a plural whose noun-ending was dropped for the annexation, so its accusative is marked by the *ya*. These are four aspects.]]

So the devil is the one who seals in reality, or the disbeliever. But since God, exalted is He, is the one who empowered and enabled him, the sealing was attributed to Him, just as an act is attributed to its causer. A fourth aspect: since they were, with certainty and decision, among those who will not believe, and signs and warnings do not avail them, and the beneficial divine favors, even if given to them, do not profit them, then after the firm knowledge that there is no way for them to believe willingly and by choice, there remains no way to their belief except compulsion and constraint. And when there is no way left but that God compel them and constrain them, yet He does not compel them and does not constrain them, lest the purpose of obligation be frustrated, the abstention from compulsion and constraint is expressed by the sealing, to indicate that they are those whose affair has reached the point of determination upon disbelief and insistence upon it, to a degree that they will not desist from it except through compulsion and constraint. This is the utmost extent in describing their obstinacy in error and the spread of their misguidance and rebellion. A fifth aspect: that it is a report of what the disbelievers used to say in mockery of them, from their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a deafness, and between us and you there is a veil﴾. Its counterpart in reporting and mockery is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them the clear evidence﴾. If you ask: the wording allows that the hearing be included both in the ruling of the sealing and in the ruling of covering. [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "The wording allows that the hearing be included in the ruling of the sealing and in the ruling of covering..." etc. Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: my grandfather, may God have mercy on him, used to mention this and add that since the hearing and the heart are enclosed, the use of sealing for them is more fitting, while since the sight is exposed and its perception relates to its surface, covering is more suitable for it.]] Upon which of the two shall one rely? I say: upon its inclusion in the ruling of the sealing, because of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart, and He placed upon his sight a covering﴾, and because they stopped at their hearing and not at their hearts.

If you ask: what is the benefit of repeating the preposition in His words: ﴿and upon their hearing﴾? I say: if it were not repeated, it would have joined the hearts and the hearing under one governing term. But when a separate governing term was introduced for the hearing, it indicates more clearly the intensity of the sealing in both places. And the hearing is singular, just as the belly is singular in the saying: "eat from some of your bellies and you will be healthy." They do this when there is no ambiguity. When ambiguity is feared, as in your saying "their horse" or "their garment" while you mean the plural, they reject it. And you may say: the hearing is originally a verbal noun, and verbal nouns are not pluralized. The original sense is indicated by the plural of "ear" in His words: ﴿And in our ears is a deafness﴾. And you may posit an omitted annexed noun, meaning: and upon the faculties of their hearing. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "and upon their hearings" (*asma'ihim*). If you ask: why did not the letter of elevation in "absarihim" (their sights) prevent Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i from *imalah* (inclining the vowel)? I say: because the kasrah on the *ra'* overcomes the elevated letter, due to its repetition, as if it contained two kasrahs, and that is the greatest help toward inclination, and that which would not be inclined becomes inclinable. Basar (sight) is the light of the eye, and it is that by which the seer sees and perceives the visible things, just as *basirah* (insight) is the light of the heart, and it is that by which one perceives and reflects. As if they were two subtle substances which God created in them as instruments of seeing and insight.

"Ghishawah" has been read with a kasrah and a nasb; with a dammah and a raf'; with a fathah and a nasb; "ghishwah" with a kasrah and a raf'; "ghishwah" with a fathah and raf' and nasb; and "'ishawah" with an unpointed 'ayn and raf', from al-'Asha.

Al-ʿadhāb: in form and meaning it is like al-nakāl (the punishment that deters), for you say aʿdhaba ʿan al-shayʾ, meaning he refrained from it, just as you say nakala ʿanhu. From the same root comes al-ʿadhb (sweet water), because it quenches thirst and repels it, unlike brackish water, which increases it.

This is confirmed by their naming sweet water naqākh, because it breaks (yanqukhu) thirst, that is, it shatters it, and furāt, because it makes it easy to swallow (yarfituhu ʿalā al-qalb). Then the word was extended so that every severe pain is called ʿadhāb, even if it is not nakāl, that is, a punishment by which the wrongdoer is deterred from returning to the offense.

The difference between ʿaẓīm (great) and kabīr (big) is that ʿaẓīm is the opposite of ḥaqīr (contemptible), while kabīr is the opposite of ṣaghīr (small). Thus ʿaẓīm is above kabīr, just as ḥaqīr is below ṣaghīr. Both are used of physical bodies and of abstract matters alike. You say rajul ʿaẓīm and rajul kabīr, meaning his body or his standing. The indefiniteness (al-tankīr) in ʿalā abṣārihim ghishāwatun means that upon their eyes is a kind of covering other than what people are accustomed to, namely the covering of blindness to the signs of Allah. And for them, among the great pains, there is a great kind whose true nature no one knows except Allah.

O Allah, protect us from Your punishment and do not afflict us with Your wrath, O You of vast forgiveness.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 8–10 (part 1 of 2):

He (glorified is He) began by mentioning those who sincerely devoted their religion to Allah, whose hearts agreed with their tongues, whose inner state matched their outward state, and whose speech matched their deeds. Then He followed with those who openly and inwardly, in heart and tongue, purely embraced disbelief (kufr). Then He moved to the third group: those who believed with their mouths while their hearts did not believe, who concealed the opposite of what they displayed, and they are those of whom He said: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾. He named them the hypocrites (munafiqun), and they were the most wicked of the disbelievers and the most hateful to Him and the most abhorrent in His sight, because they mixed disbelief with deception (tamwih) and fraud (tadlis), and with polytheism, mockery and trickery. For this reason He revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾. He described the condition of those who disbelieved in two verses, and the condition of those who were hypocritical in thirteen verses, in which He censured their wickedness and their cunning, exposed their folly and their foolishness, deemed them ignorant, mocked them, ridiculed their deeds, recorded their transgression and their blindness, called them ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾, and coined for them abominable similitudes. The story of the hypocrites, from beginning to end, is linked to the story of those who disbelieved, as one sentence is linked to another.

The original form of (nas) is (unas); its hamza was dropped for lightness, as it is said: "luqah" for "al-luqah" (the cream). [[His saying "as it is said: luqah for al-luqah": al-luqah and al-aluqah mean cream (zubdah). Reported by al-Sihah (ʿ)]]. Dropping it together with the definite article as a constant feature is such that one hardly says "al-unas". Its original form is supported by insan, unas, unasi and ins.

They were named (nas) for their visibility, and because they are perceived (yu'nasun), meaning they are seen, just as the jinn (jinn) were named for their concealment (ijtinan). For this reason they were also called bashar (human beings).

The pattern of nas is fa'al, because the morphological pattern follows the root letters. Do you not say, in the pattern of "qih" (protect), "if'al", while you have only the ʿayn with you? It is among the collective nouns, like rakhal (ewes). As for nuways, it is a diminutive that deviates from its magnified form, like unaysiyan and ruwayjil. The definite article in it is for the genus (li-l-jins). It may be for specific reference (li-l-ʿahd), pointing to those who disbelieved mentioned earlier, as if it were said: "And among these are those who say." They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and whoever was in their condition from among those firmly set upon hypocrisy. Its position is like the position of "al-qawm" in your saying: "I alighted among the Banu So-and-so and they did not host me, and the people are miserable."

The relative word man in man yaqulu is descriptive (mawsufah), as if it were said: "And among the people are people who say such-and-such," like His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men﴾, if you make the article generic. If you make it specific, it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾. If you say: how can they be some of those, when the hypocrites are not those whose hearts are sealed?

I say: disbelief gathers both groups together and makes them one genus. The hypocrites being a species of one of the two species of this genus, differing from the other species by an addition they added to the common disbelief, namely deception and mockery, does not take them out of being part of the genus, for genera are differentiated only by differences that occur between some of them and others, and those differences produce species-distinctions but do not prevent entry under the genus.

If you say: why were belief in Allah and belief in the Last Day singled out for mention? I say: singling them out reveals their excessive wickedness and their persistence in corruption, because these people were Jews, and the belief of the Jews in Allah is not belief, by their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾. Likewise their belief in the Last Day, because they hold it contrary to its true description. So their saying: ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾ was a doubled wickedness and a manifest disbelief, because if this statement had come from them not in the manner of hypocrisy, while their belief was what it was, it would be disbelief, not faith.

When they said it in the manner of hypocrisy, as deception of the Muslims and mockery of them, and showing them that they were like them in genuine faith, it was wickedness upon wickedness and disbelief upon disbelief. Moreover, by this utterance they gave the impression that they had taken faith from both its sides, surrounded it from both its flanks, and encompassed both its beginning and its end. And in the repetition of the preposition bi (in) is that they claimed each of the two faiths to be in a state of soundness and firmness.

If you say: how does His saying ﴿And they are not believers﴾ correspond to their saying ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾, when the first concerns the state of the act and not the agent, and the second concerns the state of the agent and not the act? I say: the intention is to deny what they claimed and to negate it, so He followed a route that leads to the desired aim. In it there is emphasis and exaggeration not found elsewhere, namely the removal of their selves and persons from being a group among the groups of believers, because of what is known of their condition, which contradicts the condition of those who enter faith. When they are testified against as being in themselves in this state, the negation of what they claimed to affirm for themselves, categorically and decisively, is included within that testimony. Similar is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it﴾, which is more eloquent than your saying: "they do not come out of it." If you say: why did faith come unrestricted in the second and restricted in the first? I say: it may be intended to be restricted, and the restriction is left to the indication of what was mentioned; or the unrestricted sense may mean that they have no share of faith at all, neither faith in Allah and the Last Day, nor faith in anything else.

If you say: what is meant by the Last Day? I say: it may be meant as the time that has no limit, which is everlasting eternity that does not end, since it is later than the times that have passed. Or it may be meant as the limited period from resurrection until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, because it is the last of the limited periods, after which there is no limit to time.

Al-khada (deception): that one leads his counterpart to believe other than what one intends for him of harm, from the saying of the Arabs: "a dhabb is khadi' and khadi'," when the hunter passes his hand over the entrance of its burrow or intends to approach it, then it leaves by another entrance. If you say: how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid? [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this section of al-Zamakhshari's words gathers together the lean and the fat. We point out what is in it of froth, so that the reader may take what is in it of the Sunnah, safe from entanglement in the filth of innovation, seeking help from Allah, and He is the best helper. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in is his saying that Allah, exalted be He, is knowing by His essence, meaning He does not know. This is one of the things by which the Mu'tazilah were marked in the introduction, that they deny the attributes of divine perfection, desiring by that their claim of tawhid and tanzih. The creed of the People of the Sunnah is that Allah, exalted be He, knows with an eternal, pre-eternal knowledge, related to every knowable thing, whether necessary, possible or impossible, and nothing escapes His knowledge, not the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven, nor smaller than that nor greater, except that it is in a clear Book. It suffices you that this verse confirms their belief in the affirmation of the attribute of knowledge for Him, exalted be He, and in the generality of its relation to universals and particulars, along with what lies beyond that of the theological proofs for it. We are not concerned to mention them in this book. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in: his belief that among existing things there is something not created by Allah, exalted be He, because it is ugly in his view, as is understood from deception in this verse. What drove him to these two errors is only his belief that the impossibility of His being deceived is not established except by His knowing by His essence, so that His knowledge encompasses every existent, and thus He cannot be deceived, since the relation of the essence to existents is one relation; and that the impossibility of His being a deceiver is not established except by the impossibility of some existents issuing from Him, because it is ugly in their view. This transcendence has rested on what it does not rest on and what is not conditioned by it.

We, the community of the People of the Sunnah, believe that Allah, exalted be He, knows by a knowledge, and yet we believe it impossible that He be deceived, because His knowledge, in our view, has a general relation as we have described. We believe that no existent comes into being except from His power alone, and yet we refuse to attribute deception to Allah, exalted be He, because its apparent meaning suggests that it arises from incapacity to confront and from revealing what is hidden. This is the meaning that is conceived from it in absolute terms; but where He, exalted be He, uses it in contrast to what He mentioned of the hypocrites' deception, like the contrast of plotting with their plotting, we know that what is meant is that He did toward them an act which He named deception by way of correspondence and parallelism; otherwise He is capable of tearing away their veil and sending punishment upon them before their eyes. This is the creed of the People of the Sunnah concerning this verse and its like, not like al-Zamakhshari and his partisans, who claim that they affirm divine unity while denying, and that they declare Allah transcendent while associating partners with Him. And Allah is the Granter of success to the truth. Likewise the deception attributed to them is by way of metaphor, for their engaging in the acts of a deceiver according to their own supposition; and the clearest witness that it is a metaphor is the negation of it immediately after its affirmation in His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive﴾. In this continuation, then, the possibility of literal meaning is negated so that the direction of metaphor becomes determined. Among the things which the rhetoricians count as evidence of metaphor is the truth of its negation. So reflect upon this section, for it has superiority over all other sections.]] because the knowing one whom nothing hidden escapes cannot be deceived, and the wise one who does not do ugly things cannot be deceived, and the believers, though it may be possible that they be deceived, it is not possible that they be deceived [in this manner].

Do we not see his saying: "They sought rain from Quraysh, every one who is deceived; indeed, the generous, when you deceive him, is deceived." The Arabs, when drought struck them, would turn to Quraysh to seek rain for them, because they were the custodians of the House of Allah and the guardians of its sanctuary, as the people of 'Ad did when they suffered drought. Likewise 'Umar sought rain through al-'Abbas, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). And Abu Sufyan asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for rain, and he granted it, despite the enmity that was between them. He says: the people sought from every deceived one of Quraysh rain, that is, they asked him to pray for rain for them. Al-Sayyid said: "wa-stamtiru" means "istaqu" and "talabu", thus indicating that it is in the imperative form. In al-Sihah: that is, ask him to give as rain, for example, and this supports the words of al-Sayyid. It is also permissible to liken every deceived one of Quraysh to a cloud by way of metaphor (makniyyah), so rain is sought from him. Al-munkhada' is the one overcome by his generosity, and his saying "indeed the generous" explains it. The verse is related thus:

"There is no good in love whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for, so seek rain from Quraysh, every deceived one."

It is also related as "from firq" instead of "from Quraysh". His saying "whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for" is a circumstantial clause for love. Firq is a particular place in the Hijaz.

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

"That girl whom I hung upon accidentally: indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

This is by Dhu al-Rummah concerning his beloved Mayy. Safarat the woman: she uncovered her face. It is also related: "isfaran" instead of "ibhajan". The meaning is that her delight to the eye increases when she unveils, and the eye is bewildered in her when she veils. "Kharajat al-'ayn" (the eye was bewildered), like "ta'abat", means it was perplexed. It is also related "minha" instead of "fiha", that is, on account of her. Tantaqibu: she lets her veil fall over her face. "'Aradan": without intention or awareness. Khalaba (from the pattern of qatala) means deceived; that is, she is the young woman whose love confronted me without my awareness. Then he consoles himself that the intelligent Muslim is often deceived.

Thus the attribute of being deceived has come, but not deception. I say: there are several aspects to this. One: it may be said that the form of their action toward Allah, in that they display faith while being disbelievers, is the form of the action of deceivers; and the form of Allah's action toward them, in that He commanded that the rulings of Muslims be applied to them while He regards them among the most evil disbelievers and the people of the lowest depth of the Fire, is the form of the action of a deceiver; likewise the form of the action of the believers toward them, in that they obeyed Allah's command concerning them and applied their rulings to them. The second: that this is an expression of their belief and their supposition that Allah is one who can be deceived, for whoever claims faith in Allah while being a hypocrite is not one who knows Allah or His attributes, nor that His essence is related to every knowable thing, nor that He is free from doing ugly things; so it is not remote from such a person to permit that Allah in his supposition may be deceived and afflicted with harm from a hidden direction, and to permit that He may deceive His servants and mislead them. The third: that Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned while the Messenger (ﷺ) is intended, because he is His successor on His earth and the one who speaks for Him with His commands and prohibitions among His servants, as one says: "the king said such-and-such and decreed such-and-such," while the speaker and decreer is in fact his vizier or some of his close attendants whose words are his words and whose decrees are his decree. Its confirmation is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they pledge allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The fourth: that it may be from the saying: "Zayd pleased me and his generosity," so the meaning is: they deceive those who believe in Allah. The benefit of this manner is the strength of particularization; and since the believers have a standing with Allah, He took them along this course. Similar is: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and likewise: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. Its parallel in their speech is: "I knew Zayd to be excellent," where the purpose is to mention the comprehensiveness of knowledge of Zayd's excellence, not Zayd himself, since he was already known to him from of old; as if it were said: "I knew the excellence of Zayd," but mentioning Zayd is a preface and paving for mentioning his excellence. If you say: is there a valid aspect to restricting "khadaʿa" (deceived) to one object? I say: its aspect is that it is said that it is taken in the sense of "fa'ala", but it is brought in the pattern of "fa'ala", because the pattern in its origin is for contest and rivalry, and when an action is contested by its doer it comes out more eloquent and more firm than when he practices it alone without a contender or rival, due to the increased strength of motive toward it. It is supported by the reading of one who recited: ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾, which is Abu Haywah. And "yukhadi'una" is an explanation of "yaqulu". It is also permissible that it be a new sentence, as if it were said: "Why do they claim faith falsely, and what is their aim in that?" and it is answered: "They deceive." If you say: from what were they deceiving?

I say: they were deceiving them for purposes they had and aims among which were: their being left alone and their exemption from war, and from what they were plotting against others among the disbelievers. Among them: their being favored by the treatment with which they favored the believers, honoring them, doing good to them, giving them shares of the spoils, and similar benefits. And among them: their being informed, through their mixing with them, of the secrets which they were eager to spread to their opponents. If you say: then why did He not make them known to them, so that they would not reach these aims by deceiving them? I say: He did not make it known to them because of the interests which He encompassed in knowledge, which, if made known, would turn into corruptions; and the reprieve of Iblis and his offspring and their leaving alone, and what they are upon of misleading the hypocrites and instructing them in hypocrisy, is even graver than that. But the cause in it is what Allah, exalted be He, knew of the interest. If you say: what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves﴾? I say:

It may be meant: and they do not deal in that dealing which resembles the dealing of deceivers except with themselves, because its harm befalls them and its deceit returns upon them, just as you say: "So-and-so harms so-and-so, and he harms only himself," meaning: the circle of harm returns to him and does not pass beyond him. It may also be meant the literal reality of deception, that is: while they are in that, they deceive themselves, since they promise themselves falsehoods and lie to it in what they tell it, and their selves likewise promise them and speak to them of wishes. And it may be meant: "and they do not deceive," expressed in the form of "yufa'iluna" for emphasis. It is also read: "wa-ma yakhda'ina" and "yakhda'una" from "khada'a", and "yakhda'una" with the yā' vowelled (fatha) in the sense of "yakhda'una", and "yakhdi'una" and "yukhadi'una" in the form of the passive voice. The nafs (self): the essence and reality of a thing. It is said: "indi kadha nafsan" (I have such-and-such in my self). Then it was said of the heart:

Nafs (soul, self) because the self is by it. Do you not see their saying: "The man is by his two smaller parts" (the tongue and the heart)? Likewise nafs means spirit (rūḥ), and blood has a nafs because its subsistence is by blood. Water has a nafs because of its great need of it. Allah the Exalted said: "And We made from water every living thing." The literal sense of "nafs" for a man is an eye that has been struck, as in their saying: "So-and-so consults his two nafs's" when he hesitates over a matter and two opinions and two impulses appear to him, and he does not know which of them to incline toward. It is as if they meant the impulse of the nafs and the whisper of the nafs, and they called them "two nafs's", either because they issue from the nafs, or because the two impulses, being like advisers to him and commanders over him, were likened to two persons, and so they were called "two nafs's". The intended meaning of "al-anfus" here is their persons (dhawāt). The meaning of "by deceiving their persons" is that the deception clings to them and does not pass beyond them to others or leap over them to anyone else. It is also permissible that what is meant is their hearts, their impulses and their opinions.

And "shu'ūr" is knowledge of a thing by way of sensation (ʿilm ḥiss), from "ash-shiʿār" (the undergarment). The "mashāʿir" of a human being are his senses. The meaning is that the harm of that befalls them is like something perceptible, and they, because of the prolongation of their heedlessness, are like one who has no sense.

The use of "maraḍ" (sickness) for the heart may be literal or metaphorical. The literal sense is that pain is intended, as you say: "There is a sickness in his belly." The metaphorical sense is that it is borrowed for some of the heart's attributes, such as bad belief, rancour, envy, inclination to sins, resolve upon them, the feeling of desire, cowardice, weakness, and other things that are corruption and affliction resembling sickness, just as health and soundness are borrowed for their opposites. What is meant here is what is in their hearts of bad belief and disbelief, or of rancour, envy and hatred, because their breasts used to seethe against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers with rage and fury, and they hated them with the hatred that Allah the Exalted described in His saying: "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater." And they burn with envy against them: "If a good thing touches you, it grieves them." And enough of what occurred from Ibn Ubayy, and the saying of Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Pardon him, O Messenger of Allah, and overlook, for by Allah, Allah has given you what He has given you, and the people of this town had agreed to crown him with a diadem; but when Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked with that." [Agreed upon, from the narration of ʿUrwa from Usāma ibn Zayd, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode on a donkey with a saddle-blanket, and Usāma ibn Zayd rode behind him, going to visit Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda, and he mentioned it at length.]

Or what is meant is what has penetrated their hearts of weakness, cowardice and feebleness, because their hearts had been strong, either from the strength of their hope in what they used to speak of: that the wind of Islam blows for a time and then subsides, and its banner flutters for days and then settles; so they weakened when despair overcame them upon Allah's sending down victory to His Messenger and the manifestation of the religion of truth over all religion. Or because of their boldness and daring in wars, they weakened into cowardice and feebleness (khawar) when Allah cast terror into their hearts and they witnessed the might of the Muslims and Allah's support for them with the angels. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been helped with terror over a distance of a month's journey."

The meaning of Allah's increasing them in sickness is that whenever revelation was sent down upon His Messenger and they heard it, they disbelieved in it, and so they increased in disbelief along with their disbelief. It is as if Allah is the One who increased them in what they increased, by attributing the action to its cause, as He attributed it to the surah in His saying: "So it increased them in filth along with their filth," because it was the cause. Or, whenever His Messenger increased in victory, expansion in the lands, and reduction of the borders of the earth, they increased in envy, rancour and hatred, and their hearts increased in weakness, in scarcity of hope in what they had based their expectations upon, and in cowardice and feebleness. It is also possible that the increase of sickness means the seal (ṭabʿ) upon their hearts.

Abū ʿAmr, in the narration of al-Aṣmaʿī, recited "marḍ" and "maraḍan" with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

It is said: "alama" (to pain) — "fa-huwa alīm" (he is painful), like "wajaʿa" (to ache) — "fa-huwa wajīʿ" (he is aching). Its description of punishment with it is like His saying: "Their greeting therein is a painful blow" (wajīʿ). [The verses: "Does the remembrance of Rayḥāna, the hearing caller, keep me awake while my companions sleep? / And the driving of a battalion that advanced upon another, whose size seemed like a bald head / And horses that advanced against horses, their greeting among them a painful blow." Said by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, companion of Rayḥāna, sister of Duraid ibn al-Ṣimma, who sought her in marriage from him but he postponed it. It is said that Rayḥāna is the name of a specific place. "Al-samīʿ" may be "the one made to hear" in the sense of maf ūl, or "the heard," or "the one who makes to hear" in the sense of fāʿil, or "the hearer." The original form fa ʿīl is for the meaning of fāʿil, like ʿalīm, and likewise what comes in the meaning of maf ʿūl, like jarīḥ and qatīl. There occurs from the quadriliteral, in the meaning of mufʿil as an active participle, like wajīʿ, and in the meaning of mufʿil as a passive participle, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. And samīʿ in the sense of mufāʿil is common, like jalīs and sharīk.

"Samīʿ" is the subject, and its predicate is "yu'arriqunī", i.e., does the impulse of longing from Rayḥāna keep me awake, while my companions are asleep? The interrogation is for wonder. "Wasawq kattība" is conjoined with "al-dāʿī" or with the pronoun in "yu'arriqunī". "Al-kattība" is the gathered, arranged, organized group. "Dalafa dalafan" from the door of taʿiba means to walk slowly; it is also said: to advance and hasten. "Kāna zahāʾahā" means its quantity. "Al-ṣalīʿ" is one without hair, and perhaps he likened it to that head in bareness, exposure, prominence and completeness, as one says: "an army that is bald (aqraʿ)", "a thousand bald," meaning complete, figuratively. "Khayl": that is, and companions of horses have advanced against it with its like. "Al-taḥiyya" is supplication for life, so he informed about it with a painful blow, by way of mockery.

The pronoun in "baynahum" refers to the horses in the sense of the army. He moved from mentioning Rayḥāna to mentioning war because he had raided Duraid in pursuit of her.]] This is in the manner of their saying: "Jadd jaddahu" (his fortune was in his fortune). The pain in reality belongs to the one who causes pain, just as the fortune belongs to the fortunate one.

What is meant by their lying is their saying "We believe in Allah and the Last Day." In it is an allusion to the ugliness and vileness of lying, and an imagining that the painful punishment befalls them because of their lying. Similar to it is His saying: "Because of their sins they were drowned," though the people were disbelievers. The sins were specified only to magnify them and to deter from committing them.

Lying is reporting a thing contrary to what it is, and it is wholly ugly. As for what is related from Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), that he lied three lies, the meaning is allusion (taʿrīḍ). But since its form resembles the form of a lie, it was named as such. And from Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it is related as a marfūʿ hadith: "Beware of lying, for it is far from faith." [It is related as marfūʿ and mawqūf upon Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him).]

It is recited "yukadhdhibūn" (they make others lie / they are called liars), from "kadhdhaba," which is the opposite of "ṣadaqa," or from "kadhdhaba," which is intensive of "kadhaba," as intensive form is used for "ṣadaqa" and it is said "ṣaddaqa." Similar to them are: "bāna al-shayʾ" and "bayyana," and "qalaṣa al-thawb" and "qallaṣa." Or in the sense of abundance, like their saying: "mawwatat al-bahāʾim" (the beasts died in numbers) and "barakat al-ibil" (the camels knelt), or from their saying: "kadhaba al-waḥshī" when the wild animal ran a course and then stopped to look at what was behind it, because the hypocrite is hesitant and wavering in his affair; for this reason he is called "mudhabdhab" (wavering). The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like the wavering sheep between two flocks, going to this one once and to that one once." [Related by Muslim from the narration of Mūsā ibn ʿUqba from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both). His saying "taʿīr" with an unpointed letter means "tataraddad" (wavers).]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 8–10 (part 1 of 2):

He (glorified is He) began by mentioning those who sincerely devoted their religion to Allah, whose hearts agreed with their tongues, whose inner state matched their outward state, and whose speech matched their deeds. Then He followed with those who openly and inwardly, in heart and tongue, purely embraced disbelief (kufr). Then He moved to the third group: those who believed with their mouths while their hearts did not believe, who concealed the opposite of what they displayed, and they are those of whom He said: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾. He named them the hypocrites (munafiqun), and they were the most wicked of the disbelievers and the most hateful to Him and the most abhorrent in His sight, because they mixed disbelief with deception (tamwih) and fraud (tadlis), and with polytheism, mockery and trickery. For this reason He revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾. He described the condition of those who disbelieved in two verses, and the condition of those who were hypocritical in thirteen verses, in which He censured their wickedness and their cunning, exposed their folly and their foolishness, deemed them ignorant, mocked them, ridiculed their deeds, recorded their transgression and their blindness, called them ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾, and coined for them abominable similitudes. The story of the hypocrites, from beginning to end, is linked to the story of those who disbelieved, as one sentence is linked to another.

The original form of (nas) is (unas); its hamza was dropped for lightness, as it is said: "luqah" for "al-luqah" (the cream). [[His saying "as it is said: luqah for al-luqah": al-luqah and al-aluqah mean cream (zubdah). Reported by al-Sihah (ʿ)]]. Dropping it together with the definite article as a constant feature is such that one hardly says "al-unas". Its original form is supported by insan, unas, unasi and ins.

They were named (nas) for their visibility, and because they are perceived (yu'nasun), meaning they are seen, just as the jinn (jinn) were named for their concealment (ijtinan). For this reason they were also called bashar (human beings).

The pattern of nas is fa'al, because the morphological pattern follows the root letters. Do you not say, in the pattern of "qih" (protect), "if'al", while you have only the ʿayn with you? It is among the collective nouns, like rakhal (ewes). As for nuways, it is a diminutive that deviates from its magnified form, like unaysiyan and ruwayjil. The definite article in it is for the genus (li-l-jins). It may be for specific reference (li-l-ʿahd), pointing to those who disbelieved mentioned earlier, as if it were said: "And among these are those who say." They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and whoever was in their condition from among those firmly set upon hypocrisy. Its position is like the position of "al-qawm" in your saying: "I alighted among the Banu So-and-so and they did not host me, and the people are miserable."

The relative word man in man yaqulu is descriptive (mawsufah), as if it were said: "And among the people are people who say such-and-such," like His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men﴾, if you make the article generic. If you make it specific, it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾. If you say: how can they be some of those, when the hypocrites are not those whose hearts are sealed?

I say: disbelief gathers both groups together and makes them one genus. The hypocrites being a species of one of the two species of this genus, differing from the other species by an addition they added to the common disbelief, namely deception and mockery, does not take them out of being part of the genus, for genera are differentiated only by differences that occur between some of them and others, and those differences produce species-distinctions but do not prevent entry under the genus.

If you say: why were belief in Allah and belief in the Last Day singled out for mention? I say: singling them out reveals their excessive wickedness and their persistence in corruption, because these people were Jews, and the belief of the Jews in Allah is not belief, by their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾. Likewise their belief in the Last Day, because they hold it contrary to its true description. So their saying: ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾ was a doubled wickedness and a manifest disbelief, because if this statement had come from them not in the manner of hypocrisy, while their belief was what it was, it would be disbelief, not faith.

When they said it in the manner of hypocrisy, as deception of the Muslims and mockery of them, and showing them that they were like them in genuine faith, it was wickedness upon wickedness and disbelief upon disbelief. Moreover, by this utterance they gave the impression that they had taken faith from both its sides, surrounded it from both its flanks, and encompassed both its beginning and its end. And in the repetition of the preposition bi (in) is that they claimed each of the two faiths to be in a state of soundness and firmness.

If you say: how does His saying ﴿And they are not believers﴾ correspond to their saying ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾, when the first concerns the state of the act and not the agent, and the second concerns the state of the agent and not the act? I say: the intention is to deny what they claimed and to negate it, so He followed a route that leads to the desired aim. In it there is emphasis and exaggeration not found elsewhere, namely the removal of their selves and persons from being a group among the groups of believers, because of what is known of their condition, which contradicts the condition of those who enter faith. When they are testified against as being in themselves in this state, the negation of what they claimed to affirm for themselves, categorically and decisively, is included within that testimony. Similar is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it﴾, which is more eloquent than your saying: "they do not come out of it." If you say: why did faith come unrestricted in the second and restricted in the first? I say: it may be intended to be restricted, and the restriction is left to the indication of what was mentioned; or the unrestricted sense may mean that they have no share of faith at all, neither faith in Allah and the Last Day, nor faith in anything else.

If you say: what is meant by the Last Day? I say: it may be meant as the time that has no limit, which is everlasting eternity that does not end, since it is later than the times that have passed. Or it may be meant as the limited period from resurrection until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, because it is the last of the limited periods, after which there is no limit to time.

Al-khada (deception): that one leads his counterpart to believe other than what one intends for him of harm, from the saying of the Arabs: "a dhabb is khadi' and khadi'," when the hunter passes his hand over the entrance of its burrow or intends to approach it, then it leaves by another entrance. If you say: how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid? [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this section of al-Zamakhshari's words gathers together the lean and the fat. We point out what is in it of froth, so that the reader may take what is in it of the Sunnah, safe from entanglement in the filth of innovation, seeking help from Allah, and He is the best helper. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in is his saying that Allah, exalted be He, is knowing by His essence, meaning He does not know. This is one of the things by which the Mu'tazilah were marked in the introduction, that they deny the attributes of divine perfection, desiring by that their claim of tawhid and tanzih.
