The creed of the People of the Sunnah is that Allah, exalted be He, knows with an eternal, pre-eternal knowledge, related to every knowable thing, whether necessary, possible or impossible, and nothing escapes His knowledge, not the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven, nor smaller than that nor greater, except that it is in a clear Book. It suffices you that this verse confirms their belief in the affirmation of the attribute of knowledge for Him, exalted be He, and in the generality of its relation to universals and particulars, along with what lies beyond that of the theological proofs for it. We are not concerned to mention them in this book. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in: his belief that among existing things there is something not created by Allah, exalted be He, because it is ugly in his view, as is understood from deception in this verse. What drove him to these two errors is only his belief that the impossibility of His being deceived is not established except by His knowing by His essence, so that His knowledge encompasses every existent, and thus He cannot be deceived, since the relation of the essence to existents is one relation; and that the impossibility of His being a deceiver is not established except by the impossibility of some existents issuing from Him, because it is ugly in their view. This transcendence has rested on what it does not rest on and what is not conditioned by it.

We, the community of the People of the Sunnah, believe that Allah, exalted be He, knows by a knowledge, and yet we believe it impossible that He be deceived, because His knowledge, in our view, has a general relation as we have described. We believe that no existent comes into being except from His power alone, and yet we refuse to attribute deception to Allah, exalted be He, because its apparent meaning suggests that it arises from incapacity to confront and from revealing what is hidden. This is the meaning that is conceived from it in absolute terms; but where He, exalted be He, uses it in contrast to what He mentioned of the hypocrites' deception, like the contrast of plotting with their plotting, we know that what is meant is that He did toward them an act which He named deception by way of correspondence and parallelism; otherwise He is capable of tearing away their veil and sending punishment upon them before their eyes. This is the creed of the People of the Sunnah concerning this verse and its like, not like al-Zamakhshari and his partisans, who claim that they affirm divine unity while denying, and that they declare Allah transcendent while associating partners with Him. And Allah is the Granter of success to the truth. Likewise the deception attributed to them is by way of metaphor, for their engaging in the acts of a deceiver according to their own supposition; and the clearest witness that it is a metaphor is the negation of it immediately after its affirmation in His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive﴾. In this continuation, then, the possibility of literal meaning is negated so that the direction of metaphor becomes determined. Among the things which the rhetoricians count as evidence of metaphor is the truth of its negation. So reflect upon this section, for it has superiority over all other sections.]] because the knowing one whom nothing hidden escapes cannot be deceived, and the wise one who does not do ugly things cannot be deceived, and the believers, though it may be possible that they be deceived, it is not possible that they be deceived [in this manner].

Do we not see his saying: "They sought rain from Quraysh, every one who is deceived; indeed, the generous, when you deceive him, is deceived." The Arabs, when drought struck them, would turn to Quraysh to seek rain for them, because they were the custodians of the House of Allah and the guardians of its sanctuary, as the people of 'Ad did when they suffered drought. Likewise 'Umar sought rain through al-'Abbas, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). And Abu Sufyan asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for rain, and he granted it, despite the enmity that was between them. He says: the people sought from every deceived one of Quraysh rain, that is, they asked him to pray for rain for them. Al-Sayyid said: "wa-stamtiru" means "istaqu" and "talabu", thus indicating that it is in the imperative form. In al-Sihah: that is, ask him to give as rain, for example, and this supports the words of al-Sayyid. It is also permissible to liken every deceived one of Quraysh to a cloud by way of metaphor (makniyyah), so rain is sought from him. Al-munkhada' is the one overcome by his generosity, and his saying "indeed the generous" explains it. The verse is related thus:

"There is no good in love whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for, so seek rain from Quraysh, every deceived one."

It is also related as "from firq" instead of "from Quraysh". His saying "whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for" is a circumstantial clause for love. Firq is a particular place in the Hijaz.

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

"That girl whom I hung upon accidentally: indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

This is by Dhu al-Rummah concerning his beloved Mayy. Safarat the woman: she uncovered her face. It is also related: "isfaran" instead of "ibhajan". The meaning is that her delight to the eye increases when she unveils, and the eye is bewildered in her when she veils. "Kharajat al-'ayn" (the eye was bewildered), like "ta'abat", means it was perplexed. It is also related "minha" instead of "fiha", that is, on account of her. Tantaqibu: she lets her veil fall over her face. "'Aradan": without intention or awareness. Khalaba (from the pattern of qatala) means deceived; that is, she is the young woman whose love confronted me without my awareness. Then he consoles himself that the intelligent Muslim is often deceived.

Thus the attribute of being deceived has come, but not deception. I say: there are several aspects to this. One: it may be said that the form of their action toward Allah, in that they display faith while being disbelievers, is the form of the action of deceivers; and the form of Allah's action toward them, in that He commanded that the rulings of Muslims be applied to them while He regards them among the most evil disbelievers and the people of the lowest depth of the Fire, is the form of the action of a deceiver; likewise the form of the action of the believers toward them, in that they obeyed Allah's command concerning them and applied their rulings to them. The second: that this is an expression of their belief and their supposition that Allah is one who can be deceived, for whoever claims faith in Allah while being a hypocrite is not one who knows Allah or His attributes, nor that His essence is related to every knowable thing, nor that He is free from doing ugly things; so it is not remote from such a person to permit that Allah in his supposition may be deceived and afflicted with harm from a hidden direction, and to permit that He may deceive His servants and mislead them. The third: that Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned while the Messenger (ﷺ) is intended, because he is His successor on His earth and the one who speaks for Him with His commands and prohibitions among His servants, as one says: "the king said such-and-such and decreed such-and-such," while the speaker and decreer is in fact his vizier or some of his close attendants whose words are his words and whose decrees are his decree. Its confirmation is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they pledge allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The fourth: that it may be from the saying: "Zayd pleased me and his generosity," so the meaning is: they deceive those who believe in Allah. The benefit of this manner is the strength of particularization; and since the believers have a standing with Allah, He took them along this course. Similar is: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and likewise: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. Its parallel in their speech is: "I knew Zayd to be excellent," where the purpose is to mention the comprehensiveness of knowledge of Zayd's excellence, not Zayd himself, since he was already known to him from of old; as if it were said: "I knew the excellence of Zayd," but mentioning Zayd is a preface and paving for mentioning his excellence. If you say: is there a valid aspect to restricting "khadaʿa" (deceived) to one object? I say: its aspect is that it is said that it is taken in the sense of "fa'ala", but it is brought in the pattern of "fa'ala", because the pattern in its origin is for contest and rivalry, and when an action is contested by its doer it comes out more eloquent and more firm than when he practices it alone without a contender or rival, due to the increased strength of motive toward it. It is supported by the reading of one who recited: ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾, which is Abu Haywah. And "yukhadi'una" is an explanation of "yaqulu". It is also permissible that it be a new sentence, as if it were said: "Why do they claim faith falsely, and what is their aim in that?" and it is answered: "They deceive." If you say: from what were they deceiving?

I say: they were deceiving them for purposes they had and aims among which were: their being left alone and their exemption from war, and from what they were plotting against others among the disbelievers. Among them: their being favored by the treatment with which they favored the believers, honoring them, doing good to them, giving them shares of the spoils, and similar benefits. And among them: their being informed, through their mixing with them, of the secrets which they were eager to spread to their opponents. If you say: then why did He not make them known to them, so that they would not reach these aims by deceiving them? I say: He did not make it known to them because of the interests which He encompassed in knowledge, which, if made known, would turn into corruptions; and the reprieve of Iblis and his offspring and their leaving alone, and what they are upon of misleading the hypocrites and instructing them in hypocrisy, is even graver than that. But the cause in it is what Allah, exalted be He, knew of the interest. If you say: what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves﴾? I say:

It may be meant: and they do not deal in that dealing which resembles the dealing of deceivers except with themselves, because its harm befalls them and its deceit returns upon them, just as you say: "So-and-so harms so-and-so, and he harms only himself," meaning: the circle of harm returns to him and does not pass beyond him. It may also be meant the literal reality of deception, that is: while they are in that, they deceive themselves, since they promise themselves falsehoods and lie to it in what they tell it, and their selves likewise promise them and speak to them of wishes. And it may be meant: "and they do not deceive," expressed in the form of "yufa'iluna" for emphasis. It is also read: "wa-ma yakhda'ina" and "yakhda'una" from "khada'a", and "yakhda'una" with the yā' vowelled (fatha) in the sense of "yakhda'una", and "yakhdi'una" and "yukhadi'una" in the form of the passive voice. The nafs (self): the essence and reality of a thing. It is said: "indi kadha nafsan" (I have such-and-such in my self). Then it was said of the heart:

Nafs (soul, self) because the self is by it. Do you not see their saying: "The man is by his two smaller parts" (the tongue and the heart)? Likewise nafs means spirit (rūḥ), and blood has a nafs because its subsistence is by blood. Water has a nafs because of its great need of it. Allah the Exalted said: "And We made from water every living thing." The literal sense of "nafs" for a man is an eye that has been struck, as in their saying: "So-and-so consults his two nafs's" when he hesitates over a matter and two opinions and two impulses appear to him, and he does not know which of them to incline toward. It is as if they meant the impulse of the nafs and the whisper of the nafs, and they called them "two nafs's", either because they issue from the nafs, or because the two impulses, being like advisers to him and commanders over him, were likened to two persons, and so they were called "two nafs's". The intended meaning of "al-anfus" here is their persons (dhawāt). The meaning of "by deceiving their persons" is that the deception clings to them and does not pass beyond them to others or leap over them to anyone else. It is also permissible that what is meant is their hearts, their impulses and their opinions.

And "shu'ūr" is knowledge of a thing by way of sensation (ʿilm ḥiss), from "ash-shiʿār" (the undergarment). The "mashāʿir" of a human being are his senses. The meaning is that the harm of that befalls them is like something perceptible, and they, because of the prolongation of their heedlessness, are like one who has no sense.

The use of "maraḍ" (sickness) for the heart may be literal or metaphorical. The literal sense is that pain is intended, as you say: "There is a sickness in his belly." The metaphorical sense is that it is borrowed for some of the heart's attributes, such as bad belief, rancour, envy, inclination to sins, resolve upon them, the feeling of desire, cowardice, weakness, and other things that are corruption and affliction resembling sickness, just as health and soundness are borrowed for their opposites. What is meant here is what is in their hearts of bad belief and disbelief, or of rancour, envy and hatred, because their breasts used to seethe against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers with rage and fury, and they hated them with the hatred that Allah the Exalted described in His saying: "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater." And they burn with envy against them: "If a good thing touches you, it grieves them." And enough of what occurred from Ibn Ubayy, and the saying of Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Pardon him, O Messenger of Allah, and overlook, for by Allah, Allah has given you what He has given you, and the people of this town had agreed to crown him with a diadem; but when Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked with that." [Agreed upon, from the narration of ʿUrwa from Usāma ibn Zayd, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode on a donkey with a saddle-blanket, and Usāma ibn Zayd rode behind him, going to visit Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda, and he mentioned it at length.]

Or what is meant is what has penetrated their hearts of weakness, cowardice and feebleness, because their hearts had been strong, either from the strength of their hope in what they used to speak of: that the wind of Islam blows for a time and then subsides, and its banner flutters for days and then settles; so they weakened when despair overcame them upon Allah's sending down victory to His Messenger and the manifestation of the religion of truth over all religion. Or because of their boldness and daring in wars, they weakened into cowardice and feebleness (khawar) when Allah cast terror into their hearts and they witnessed the might of the Muslims and Allah's support for them with the angels. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been helped with terror over a distance of a month's journey."

The meaning of Allah's increasing them in sickness is that whenever revelation was sent down upon His Messenger and they heard it, they disbelieved in it, and so they increased in disbelief along with their disbelief. It is as if Allah is the One who increased them in what they increased, by attributing the action to its cause, as He attributed it to the surah in His saying: "So it increased them in filth along with their filth," because it was the cause. Or, whenever His Messenger increased in victory, expansion in the lands, and reduction of the borders of the earth, they increased in envy, rancour and hatred, and their hearts increased in weakness, in scarcity of hope in what they had based their expectations upon, and in cowardice and feebleness. It is also possible that the increase of sickness means the seal (ṭabʿ) upon their hearts.

Abū ʿAmr, in the narration of al-Aṣmaʿī, recited "marḍ" and "maraḍan" with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

It is said: "alama" (to pain) — "fa-huwa alīm" (he is painful), like "wajaʿa" (to ache) — "fa-huwa wajīʿ" (he is aching). Its description of punishment with it is like His saying: "Their greeting therein is a painful blow" (wajīʿ). [The verses: "Does the remembrance of Rayḥāna, the hearing caller, keep me awake while my companions sleep? / And the driving of a battalion that advanced upon another, whose size seemed like a bald head / And horses that advanced against horses, their greeting among them a painful blow." Said by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, companion of Rayḥāna, sister of Duraid ibn al-Ṣimma, who sought her in marriage from him but he postponed it. It is said that Rayḥāna is the name of a specific place. "Al-samīʿ" may be "the one made to hear" in the sense of maf ūl, or "the heard," or "the one who makes to hear" in the sense of fāʿil, or "the hearer." The original form fa ʿīl is for the meaning of fāʿil, like ʿalīm, and likewise what comes in the meaning of maf ʿūl, like jarīḥ and qatīl. There occurs from the quadriliteral, in the meaning of mufʿil as an active participle, like wajīʿ, and in the meaning of mufʿil as a passive participle, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. And samīʿ in the sense of mufāʿil is common, like jalīs and sharīk.

"Samīʿ" is the subject, and its predicate is "yu'arriqunī", i.e., does the impulse of longing from Rayḥāna keep me awake, while my companions are asleep? The interrogation is for wonder. "Wasawq kattība" is conjoined with "al-dāʿī" or with the pronoun in "yu'arriqunī". "Al-kattība" is the gathered, arranged, organized group. "Dalafa dalafan" from the door of taʿiba means to walk slowly; it is also said: to advance and hasten. "Kāna zahāʾahā" means its quantity. "Al-ṣalīʿ" is one without hair, and perhaps he likened it to that head in bareness, exposure, prominence and completeness, as one says: "an army that is bald (aqraʿ)", "a thousand bald," meaning complete, figuratively. "Khayl": that is, and companions of horses have advanced against it with its like. "Al-taḥiyya" is supplication for life, so he informed about it with a painful blow, by way of mockery.

The pronoun in "baynahum" refers to the horses in the sense of the army. He moved from mentioning Rayḥāna to mentioning war because he had raided Duraid in pursuit of her.]] This is in the manner of their saying: "Jadd jaddahu" (his fortune was in his fortune). The pain in reality belongs to the one who causes pain, just as the fortune belongs to the fortunate one.

What is meant by their lying is their saying "We believe in Allah and the Last Day." In it is an allusion to the ugliness and vileness of lying, and an imagining that the painful punishment befalls them because of their lying. Similar to it is His saying: "Because of their sins they were drowned," though the people were disbelievers. The sins were specified only to magnify them and to deter from committing them.

Lying is reporting a thing contrary to what it is, and it is wholly ugly. As for what is related from Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), that he lied three lies, the meaning is allusion (taʿrīḍ). But since its form resembles the form of a lie, it was named as such. And from Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it is related as a marfūʿ hadith: "Beware of lying, for it is far from faith." [It is related as marfūʿ and mawqūf upon Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him).]

It is recited "yukadhdhibūn" (they make others lie / they are called liars), from "kadhdhaba," which is the opposite of "ṣadaqa," or from "kadhdhaba," which is intensive of "kadhaba," as intensive form is used for "ṣadaqa" and it is said "ṣaddaqa." Similar to them are: "bāna al-shayʾ" and "bayyana," and "qalaṣa al-thawb" and "qallaṣa." Or in the sense of abundance, like their saying: "mawwatat al-bahāʾim" (the beasts died in numbers) and "barakat al-ibil" (the camels knelt), or from their saying: "kadhaba al-waḥshī" when the wild animal ran a course and then stopped to look at what was behind it, because the hypocrite is hesitant and wavering in his affair; for this reason he is called "mudhabdhab" (wavering). The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like the wavering sheep between two flocks, going to this one once and to that one once." [Related by Muslim from the narration of Mūsā ibn ʿUqba from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both). His saying "taʿīr" with an unpointed letter means "tataraddad" (wavers).]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 8–10 (part 1 of 2):

He (glorified is He) began by mentioning those who sincerely devoted their religion to Allah, whose hearts agreed with their tongues, whose inner state matched their outward state, and whose speech matched their deeds. Then He followed with those who openly and inwardly, in heart and tongue, purely embraced disbelief (kufr). Then He moved to the third group: those who believed with their mouths while their hearts did not believe, who concealed the opposite of what they displayed, and they are those of whom He said: ﴿Wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾. He named them the hypocrites (munafiqun), and they were the most wicked of the disbelievers and the most hateful to Him and the most abhorrent in His sight, because they mixed disbelief with deception (tamwih) and fraud (tadlis), and with polytheism, mockery and trickery. For this reason He revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾. He described the condition of those who disbelieved in two verses, and the condition of those who were hypocritical in thirteen verses, in which He censured their wickedness and their cunning, exposed their folly and their foolishness, deemed them ignorant, mocked them, ridiculed their deeds, recorded their transgression and their blindness, called them ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾, and coined for them abominable similitudes. The story of the hypocrites, from beginning to end, is linked to the story of those who disbelieved, as one sentence is linked to another.

The original form of (nas) is (unas); its hamza was dropped for lightness, as it is said: "luqah" for "al-luqah" (the cream). [[His saying "as it is said: luqah for al-luqah": al-luqah and al-aluqah mean cream (zubdah). Reported by al-Sihah (ʿ)]]. Dropping it together with the definite article as a constant feature is such that one hardly says "al-unas". Its original form is supported by insan, unas, unasi and ins.

They were named (nas) for their visibility, and because they are perceived (yu'nasun), meaning they are seen, just as the jinn (jinn) were named for their concealment (ijtinan). For this reason they were also called bashar (human beings).

The pattern of nas is fa'al, because the morphological pattern follows the root letters. Do you not say, in the pattern of "qih" (protect), "if'al", while you have only the ʿayn with you? It is among the collective nouns, like rakhal (ewes). As for nuways, it is a diminutive that deviates from its magnified form, like unaysiyan and ruwayjil. The definite article in it is for the genus (li-l-jins). It may be for specific reference (li-l-ʿahd), pointing to those who disbelieved mentioned earlier, as if it were said: "And among these are those who say." They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and whoever was in their condition from among those firmly set upon hypocrisy. Its position is like the position of "al-qawm" in your saying: "I alighted among the Banu So-and-so and they did not host me, and the people are miserable."

The relative word man in man yaqulu is descriptive (mawsufah), as if it were said: "And among the people are people who say such-and-such," like His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men﴾, if you make the article generic. If you make it specific, it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾. If you say: how can they be some of those, when the hypocrites are not those whose hearts are sealed?

I say: disbelief gathers both groups together and makes them one genus. The hypocrites being a species of one of the two species of this genus, differing from the other species by an addition they added to the common disbelief, namely deception and mockery, does not take them out of being part of the genus, for genera are differentiated only by differences that occur between some of them and others, and those differences produce species-distinctions but do not prevent entry under the genus.

If you say: why were belief in Allah and belief in the Last Day singled out for mention? I say: singling them out reveals their excessive wickedness and their persistence in corruption, because these people were Jews, and the belief of the Jews in Allah is not belief, by their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾. Likewise their belief in the Last Day, because they hold it contrary to its true description. So their saying: ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾ was a doubled wickedness and a manifest disbelief, because if this statement had come from them not in the manner of hypocrisy, while their belief was what it was, it would be disbelief, not faith.

When they said it in the manner of hypocrisy, as deception of the Muslims and mockery of them, and showing them that they were like them in genuine faith, it was wickedness upon wickedness and disbelief upon disbelief. Moreover, by this utterance they gave the impression that they had taken faith from both its sides, surrounded it from both its flanks, and encompassed both its beginning and its end. And in the repetition of the preposition bi (in) is that they claimed each of the two faiths to be in a state of soundness and firmness.

If you say: how does His saying ﴿And they are not believers﴾ correspond to their saying ﴿We believe in Allah and in the Last Day﴾, when the first concerns the state of the act and not the agent, and the second concerns the state of the agent and not the act? I say: the intention is to deny what they claimed and to negate it, so He followed a route that leads to the desired aim. In it there is emphasis and exaggeration not found elsewhere, namely the removal of their selves and persons from being a group among the groups of believers, because of what is known of their condition, which contradicts the condition of those who enter faith. When they are testified against as being in themselves in this state, the negation of what they claimed to affirm for themselves, categorically and decisively, is included within that testimony. Similar is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it﴾, which is more eloquent than your saying: "they do not come out of it." If you say: why did faith come unrestricted in the second and restricted in the first? I say: it may be intended to be restricted, and the restriction is left to the indication of what was mentioned; or the unrestricted sense may mean that they have no share of faith at all, neither faith in Allah and the Last Day, nor faith in anything else.

If you say: what is meant by the Last Day? I say: it may be meant as the time that has no limit, which is everlasting eternity that does not end, since it is later than the times that have passed. Or it may be meant as the limited period from resurrection until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, because it is the last of the limited periods, after which there is no limit to time.

Al-khada (deception): that one leads his counterpart to believe other than what one intends for him of harm, from the saying of the Arabs: "a dhabb is khadi' and khadi'," when the hunter passes his hand over the entrance of its burrow or intends to approach it, then it leaves by another entrance. If you say: how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid? [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, how is that, when deceiving Allah and the believers is not valid... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this section of al-Zamakhshari's words gathers together the lean and the fat. We point out what is in it of froth, so that the reader may take what is in it of the Sunnah, safe from entanglement in the filth of innovation, seeking help from Allah, and He is the best helper. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in is his saying that Allah, exalted be He, is knowing by His essence, meaning He does not know. This is one of the things by which the Mu'tazilah were marked in the introduction, that they deny the attributes of divine perfection, desiring by that their claim of tawhid and tanzih. The creed of the People of the Sunnah is that Allah, exalted be He, knows with an eternal, pre-eternal knowledge, related to every knowable thing, whether necessary, possible or impossible, and nothing escapes His knowledge, not the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven, nor smaller than that nor greater, except that it is in a clear Book. It suffices you that this verse confirms their belief in the affirmation of the attribute of knowledge for Him, exalted be He, and in the generality of its relation to universals and particulars, along with what lies beyond that of the theological proofs for it. We are not concerned to mention them in this book. Among what he contradicted the Sunnah in: his belief that among existing things there is something not created by Allah, exalted be He, because it is ugly in his view, as is understood from deception in this verse. What drove him to these two errors is only his belief that the impossibility of His being deceived is not established except by His knowing by His essence, so that His knowledge encompasses every existent, and thus He cannot be deceived, since the relation of the essence to existents is one relation; and that the impossibility of His being a deceiver is not established except by the impossibility of some existents issuing from Him, because it is ugly in their view. This transcendence has rested on what it does not rest on and what is not conditioned by it.

We, the community of the People of the Sunnah, believe that Allah, exalted be He, knows by a knowledge, and yet we believe it impossible that He be deceived, because His knowledge, in our view, has a general relation as we have described. We believe that no existent comes into being except from His power alone, and yet we refuse to attribute deception to Allah, exalted be He, because its apparent meaning suggests that it arises from incapacity to confront and from revealing what is hidden. This is the meaning that is conceived from it in absolute terms; but where He, exalted be He, uses it in contrast to what He mentioned of the hypocrites' deception, like the contrast of plotting with their plotting, we know that what is meant is that He did toward them an act which He named deception by way of correspondence and parallelism; otherwise He is capable of tearing away their veil and sending punishment upon them before their eyes. This is the creed of the People of the Sunnah concerning this verse and its like, not like al-Zamakhshari and his partisans, who claim that they affirm divine unity while denying, and that they declare Allah transcendent while associating partners with Him. And Allah is the Granter of success to the truth. Likewise the deception attributed to them is by way of metaphor, for their engaging in the acts of a deceiver according to their own supposition; and the clearest witness that it is a metaphor is the negation of it immediately after its affirmation in His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive﴾. In this continuation, then, the possibility of literal meaning is negated so that the direction of metaphor becomes determined. Among the things which the rhetoricians count as evidence of metaphor is the truth of its negation. So reflect upon this section, for it has superiority over all other sections.]] because the knowing one whom nothing hidden escapes cannot be deceived, and the wise one who does not do ugly things cannot be deceived, and the believers, though it may be possible that they be deceived, it is not possible that they be deceived [in this manner].

Do we not see his saying: "They sought rain from Quraysh, every one who is deceived; indeed, the generous, when you deceive him, is deceived." The Arabs, when drought struck them, would turn to Quraysh to seek rain for them, because they were the custodians of the House of Allah and the guardians of its sanctuary, as the people of 'Ad did when they suffered drought. Likewise 'Umar sought rain through al-'Abbas, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). And Abu Sufyan asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for rain, and he granted it, despite the enmity that was between them. He says: the people sought from every deceived one of Quraysh rain, that is, they asked him to pray for rain for them. Al-Sayyid said: "wa-stamtiru" means "istaqu" and "talabu", thus indicating that it is in the imperative form. In al-Sihah: that is, ask him to give as rain, for example, and this supports the words of al-Sayyid. It is also permissible to liken every deceived one of Quraysh to a cloud by way of metaphor (makniyyah), so rain is sought from him. Al-munkhada' is the one overcome by his generosity, and his saying "indeed the generous" explains it. The verse is related thus:

"There is no good in love whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for, so seek rain from Quraysh, every deceived one."

It is also related as "from firq" instead of "from Quraysh". His saying "whose supererogatory acts are not hoped for" is a circumstantial clause for love. Firq is a particular place in the Hijaz.

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

"That girl whom I hung upon accidentally: indeed the forbearing one and the one of Islam are deceived."

This is by Dhu al-Rummah concerning his beloved Mayy. Safarat the woman: she uncovered her face. It is also related: "isfaran" instead of "ibhajan". The meaning is that her delight to the eye increases when she unveils, and the eye is bewildered in her when she veils. "Kharajat al-'ayn" (the eye was bewildered), like "ta'abat", means it was perplexed. It is also related "minha" instead of "fiha", that is, on account of her. Tantaqibu: she lets her veil fall over her face. "'Aradan": without intention or awareness. Khalaba (from the pattern of qatala) means deceived; that is, she is the young woman whose love confronted me without my awareness. Then he consoles himself that the intelligent Muslim is often deceived.

Thus the attribute of being deceived has come, but not deception. I say: there are several aspects to this. One: it may be said that the form of their action toward Allah, in that they display faith while being disbelievers, is the form of the action of deceivers; and the form of Allah's action toward them, in that He commanded that the rulings of Muslims be applied to them while He regards them among the most evil disbelievers and the people of the lowest depth of the Fire, is the form of the action of a deceiver; likewise the form of the action of the believers toward them, in that they obeyed Allah's command concerning them and applied their rulings to them. The second: that this is an expression of their belief and their supposition that Allah is one who can be deceived, for whoever claims faith in Allah while being a hypocrite is not one who knows Allah or His attributes, nor that His essence is related to every knowable thing, nor that He is free from doing ugly things; so it is not remote from such a person to permit that Allah in his supposition may be deceived and afflicted with harm from a hidden direction, and to permit that He may deceive His servants and mislead them. The third: that Allah, exalted be He, is mentioned while the Messenger (ﷺ) is intended, because he is His successor on His earth and the one who speaks for Him with His commands and prohibitions among His servants, as one says: "the king said such-and-such and decreed such-and-such," while the speaker and decreer is in fact his vizier or some of his close attendants whose words are his words and whose decrees are his decree. Its confirmation is His saying: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you, they pledge allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The fourth: that it may be from the saying: "Zayd pleased me and his generosity," so the meaning is: they deceive those who believe in Allah. The benefit of this manner is the strength of particularization; and since the believers have a standing with Allah, He took them along this course. Similar is: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and likewise: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. Its parallel in their speech is: "I knew Zayd to be excellent," where the purpose is to mention the comprehensiveness of knowledge of Zayd's excellence, not Zayd himself, since he was already known to him from of old; as if it were said: "I knew the excellence of Zayd," but mentioning Zayd is a preface and paving for mentioning his excellence. If you say: is there a valid aspect to restricting "khadaʿa" (deceived) to one object? I say: its aspect is that it is said that it is taken in the sense of "fa'ala", but it is brought in the pattern of "fa'ala", because the pattern in its origin is for contest and rivalry, and when an action is contested by its doer it comes out more eloquent and more firm than when he practices it alone without a contender or rival, due to the increased strength of motive toward it. It is supported by the reading of one who recited: ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾, which is Abu Haywah. And "yukhadi'una" is an explanation of "yaqulu". It is also permissible that it be a new sentence, as if it were said: "Why do they claim faith falsely, and what is their aim in that?" and it is answered: "They deceive." If you say: from what were they deceiving?

I say: they were deceiving them for purposes they had and aims among which were: their being left alone and their exemption from war, and from what they were plotting against others among the disbelievers. Among them: their being favored by the treatment with which they favored the believers, honoring them, doing good to them, giving them shares of the spoils, and similar benefits. And among them: their being informed, through their mixing with them, of the secrets which they were eager to spread to their opponents. If you say: then why did He not make them known to them, so that they would not reach these aims by deceiving them? I say: He did not make it known to them because of the interests which He encompassed in knowledge, which, if made known, would turn into corruptions; and the reprieve of Iblis and his offspring and their leaving alone, and what they are upon of misleading the hypocrites and instructing them in hypocrisy, is even graver than that. But the cause in it is what Allah, exalted be He, knew of the interest. If you say: what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they deceive only themselves﴾? I say:

It may be meant: and they do not deal in that dealing which resembles the dealing of deceivers except with themselves, because its harm befalls them and its deceit returns upon them, just as you say: "So-and-so harms so-and-so, and he harms only himself," meaning: the circle of harm returns to him and does not pass beyond him. It may also be meant the literal reality of deception, that is: while they are in that, they deceive themselves, since they promise themselves falsehoods and lie to it in what they tell it, and their selves likewise promise them and speak to them of wishes. And it may be meant: "and they do not deceive," expressed in the form of "yufa'iluna" for emphasis. It is also read: "wa-ma yakhda'ina" and "yakhda'una" from "khada'a", and "yakhda'una" with the yā' vowelled (fatha) in the sense of "yakhda'una", and "yakhdi'una" and "yukhadi'una" in the form of the passive voice. The nafs (self): the essence and reality of a thing. It is said: "indi kadha nafsan" (I have such-and-such in my self). Then it was said of the heart:

Nafs (soul, self) because the self is by it. Do you not see their saying: "The man is by his two smaller parts" (the tongue and the heart)? Likewise nafs means spirit (rūḥ), and blood has a nafs because its subsistence is by blood. Water has a nafs because of its great need of it. Allah the Exalted said: "And We made from water every living thing." The literal sense of "nafs" for a man is an eye that has been struck, as in their saying: "So-and-so consults his two nafs's" when he hesitates over a matter and two opinions and two impulses appear to him, and he does not know which of them to incline toward. It is as if they meant the impulse of the nafs and the whisper of the nafs, and they called them "two nafs's", either because they issue from the nafs, or because the two impulses, being like advisers to him and commanders over him, were likened to two persons, and so they were called "two nafs's". The intended meaning of "al-anfus" here is their persons (dhawāt). The meaning of "by deceiving their persons" is that the deception clings to them and does not pass beyond them to others or leap over them to anyone else. It is also permissible that what is meant is their hearts, their impulses and their opinions.

And "shu'ūr" is knowledge of a thing by way of sensation (ʿilm ḥiss), from "ash-shiʿār" (the undergarment). The "mashāʿir" of a human being are his senses. The meaning is that the harm of that befalls them is like something perceptible, and they, because of the prolongation of their heedlessness, are like one who has no sense.

The use of "maraḍ" (sickness) for the heart may be literal or metaphorical. The literal sense is that pain is intended, as you say: "There is a sickness in his belly." The metaphorical sense is that it is borrowed for some of the heart's attributes, such as bad belief, rancour, envy, inclination to sins, resolve upon them, the feeling of desire, cowardice, weakness, and other things that are corruption and affliction resembling sickness, just as health and soundness are borrowed for their opposites. What is meant here is what is in their hearts of bad belief and disbelief, or of rancour, envy and hatred, because their breasts used to seethe against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers with rage and fury, and they hated them with the hatred that Allah the Exalted described in His saying: "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater." And they burn with envy against them: "If a good thing touches you, it grieves them." And enough of what occurred from Ibn Ubayy, and the saying of Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Pardon him, O Messenger of Allah, and overlook, for by Allah, Allah has given you what He has given you, and the people of this town had agreed to crown him with a diadem; but when Allah turned that away by the truth He gave you, he choked with that." [Agreed upon, from the narration of ʿUrwa from Usāma ibn Zayd, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rode on a donkey with a saddle-blanket, and Usāma ibn Zayd rode behind him, going to visit Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda, and he mentioned it at length.]

Or what is meant is what has penetrated their hearts of weakness, cowardice and feebleness, because their hearts had been strong, either from the strength of their hope in what they used to speak of: that the wind of Islam blows for a time and then subsides, and its banner flutters for days and then settles; so they weakened when despair overcame them upon Allah's sending down victory to His Messenger and the manifestation of the religion of truth over all religion. Or because of their boldness and daring in wars, they weakened into cowardice and feebleness (khawar) when Allah cast terror into their hearts and they witnessed the might of the Muslims and Allah's support for them with the angels. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been helped with terror over a distance of a month's journey."

The meaning of Allah's increasing them in sickness is that whenever revelation was sent down upon His Messenger and they heard it, they disbelieved in it, and so they increased in disbelief along with their disbelief. It is as if Allah is the One who increased them in what they increased, by attributing the action to its cause, as He attributed it to the surah in His saying: "So it increased them in filth along with their filth," because it was the cause. Or, whenever His Messenger increased in victory, expansion in the lands, and reduction of the borders of the earth, they increased in envy, rancour and hatred, and their hearts increased in weakness, in scarcity of hope in what they had based their expectations upon, and in cowardice and feebleness. It is also possible that the increase of sickness means the seal (ṭabʿ) upon their hearts.

Abū ʿAmr, in the narration of al-Aṣmaʿī, recited "marḍ" and "maraḍan" with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

It is said: "alama" (to pain) — "fa-huwa alīm" (he is painful), like "wajaʿa" (to ache) — "fa-huwa wajīʿ" (he is aching). Its description of punishment with it is like His saying: "Their greeting therein is a painful blow" (wajīʿ). [The verses: "Does the remembrance of Rayḥāna, the hearing caller, keep me awake while my companions sleep? / And the driving of a battalion that advanced upon another, whose size seemed like a bald head / And horses that advanced against horses, their greeting among them a painful blow." Said by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib, companion of Rayḥāna, sister of Duraid ibn al-Ṣimma, who sought her in marriage from him but he postponed it. It is said that Rayḥāna is the name of a specific place. "Al-samīʿ" may be "the one made to hear" in the sense of maf ūl, or "the heard," or "the one who makes to hear" in the sense of fāʿil, or "the hearer." The original form fa ʿīl is for the meaning of fāʿil, like ʿalīm, and likewise what comes in the meaning of maf ʿūl, like jarīḥ and qatīl. There occurs from the quadriliteral, in the meaning of mufʿil as an active participle, like wajīʿ, and in the meaning of mufʿil as a passive participle, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. And samīʿ in the sense of mufāʿil is common, like jalīs and sharīk.

"Samīʿ" is the subject, and its predicate is "yu'arriqunī", i.e., does the impulse of longing from Rayḥāna keep me awake, while my companions are asleep? The interrogation is for wonder. "Wasawq kattība" is conjoined with "al-dāʿī" or with the pronoun in "yu'arriqunī". "Al-kattība" is the gathered, arranged, organized group. "Dalafa dalafan" from the door of taʿiba means to walk slowly; it is also said: to advance and hasten. "Kāna zahāʾahā" means its quantity. "Al-ṣalīʿ" is one without hair, and perhaps he likened it to that head in bareness, exposure, prominence and completeness, as one says: "an army that is bald (aqraʿ)", "a thousand bald," meaning complete, figuratively. "Khayl": that is, and companions of horses have advanced against it with its like. "Al-taḥiyya" is supplication for life, so he informed about it with a painful blow, by way of mockery.

The pronoun in "baynahum" refers to the horses in the sense of the army. He moved from mentioning Rayḥāna to mentioning war because he had raided Duraid in pursuit of her.]] This is in the manner of their saying: "Jadd jaddahu" (his fortune was in his fortune). The pain in reality belongs to the one who causes pain, just as the fortune belongs to the fortunate one.

What is meant by their lying is their saying "We believe in Allah and the Last Day." In it is an allusion to the ugliness and vileness of lying, and an imagining that the painful punishment befalls them because of their lying. Similar to it is His saying: "Because of their sins they were drowned," though the people were disbelievers. The sins were specified only to magnify them and to deter from committing them.

Lying is reporting a thing contrary to what it is, and it is wholly ugly. As for what is related from Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), that he lied three lies, the meaning is allusion (taʿrīḍ). But since its form resembles the form of a lie, it was named as such. And from Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it is related as a marfūʿ hadith: "Beware of lying, for it is far from faith." [It is related as marfūʿ and mawqūf upon Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him).]

It is recited "yukadhdhibūn" (they make others lie / they are called liars), from "kadhdhaba," which is the opposite of "ṣadaqa," or from "kadhdhaba," which is intensive of "kadhaba," as intensive form is used for "ṣadaqa" and it is said "ṣaddaqa." Similar to them are: "bāna al-shayʾ" and "bayyana," and "qalaṣa al-thawb" and "qallaṣa." Or in the sense of abundance, like their saying: "mawwatat al-bahāʾim" (the beasts died in numbers) and "barakat al-ibil" (the camels knelt), or from their saying: "kadhaba al-waḥshī" when the wild animal ran a course and then stopped to look at what was behind it, because the hypocrite is hesitant and wavering in his affair; for this reason he is called "mudhabdhab" (wavering). The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like the wavering sheep between two flocks, going to this one once and to that one once." [Related by Muslim from the narration of Mūsā ibn ʿUqba from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both). His saying "taʿīr" with an unpointed letter means "tataraddad" (wavers).]

And when it is said to them, [﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾] is coordinated with [﴿يَكْذِبُونَ﴾ (they lie)]. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with [﴿يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾ (says, "We believe")], because if you said, "And among the people are those who, when it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption,'" it would be sound. But the first is more apt.

Corruption (fasad) is the departure of a thing from its state of soundness and its being beneficial. Its opposite is reform (salah), which is attaining the upright, beneficial state. Corruption in the land is the stirring up of wars and strife, because in that is the corruption of what is in the land and the loss of uprightness in the conditions of people, their crops, and their religious and worldly benefits.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾, and ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ From this comes the name given to a war that took place between the tribe of Tayy: "the War of Corruption" (harb al-fasad). The corruption of the hypocrites in the land was that they inclined toward the disbelievers and sided with them against the Muslims by disclosing their secrets to them and inciting them against the Muslims. That leads to the stirring up of strife among them. Since this conduct of theirs led to corruption, it was said to them, "Do not cause corruption," just as you say to a man, "Do not kill yourself with your own hand" or "Do not throw yourself into the fire," when he undertakes what has such an outcome.

"Innama" (indeed/only) is used either to restrict the judgment to a thing, as in your saying, "Only Zayd speaks," or to restrict a thing to a judgment, as in your saying, "Zayd is only a writer." The meaning of ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ (we are only reformers) is that the attribute of reformers is purely theirs, unmixed with any flaw from any aspect of corruption.

﴿ألا﴾ (Alā) is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negative particle, to give the meaning of alerting to the certainty of what follows. The interrogative, when it enters upon a negation, conveys affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and earth able to create the like thereof?﴾ Because it holds this position of emphasis, the clause after it almost never occurs except beginning with something like what introduces an oath. Its sister, "amā," is among the introductions and forerunners of an oath: "Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu" (By He who knows the unseen, besides whom there is none...) [[

"Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu... wa-yuhyī al-ʿiẓāma al-bīḍa wa-hiya rameem
Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā ṭawā al-ḥashā maḥādhiratan min an yuqāla laʾeem
Wa-innī la-astaḥyī yamīnī wa-baynahā wa-bayna famī dājī al-ẓalāmi bahīmu"

[These are] by Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

The origin of "amā" is composed of the interrogative hamza and "mā" remaining, and it became a particle introducing an oath and emphasizing speech. He swore by the One who knows the unseen and the inner thoughts, who is Allah the Exalted, because the answer to the oath is of this kind. Mentioning "the white" (al-bīḍ) is to dispel the assumption that they are the bones of the marrow-filled kind, or it is a metaphor for the length of their period being bare of flesh, so that their whiteness intensifies from the dryness of their marrow, "and they are crumbling" (rameem), decayed. The use of the masculine and feminine alike in fa'īl in the sense of fā'il, as here, is rare; the common usage is in the sense of maf'ūl. "Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā": that is, I used to gather guests and honor them. It may also be narrated as "ajnāz al-qirā" with a jīm and zāy and a ḍamma on the qāf, describing himself as chaste. And it is narrated "akhtāru al-jawā," meaning the burning of the heart from hunger or the like, while I was chaste. According to the first reading, the meaning is: while I was hungry, "qaṭīy al-ḥashā," that is, the stomach and the intestines, as a metaphor for that. The use of "ṭayy" in this sense became so common that from it was said: "ṭawā yaṭwī," like "riḍā yarḍā," meaning he went hungry; so he is "ṭayyān," like "jaw'ān" in form and meaning. "Maḥādhiratan": that is, out of fear of people's saying that he is base and not generous. He was ashamed to extend his hand to food to his mouth, although the night was very dark and a barrier between them, which prevented him from seeing it. "Al-bahīm" is that in which things are made indistinct by its darkness.]]

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak" [[

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak wa-lladhī
amāta wa-aḥyā wa-lladhī amruhu al-amru
Laqad tarakatnī aḥsudu al-waḥsha an arā
ulayfayni minhā lā yurwiʿuhumā al-dhaʿru"

By Abū Ṣakhr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salmā al-Hudhalī. "Amā" is an introductory particle, a prelude to an oath. The "wa" after it is for the oath: that is, "by the right of He who causes to weep and causes to laugh" in truth, or "He who gladdens and afflicts" as a metaphor, and this is more fitting to the context. "Wa-lladhī amruhu": that is, His decree is the executing decree, or "He whose command, when He wills something, is the Command," that is, His word "Be!" It is narrated "amr" without the lām: that is, a great and true matter. "Laqad tarakatnī": the answer to the oath: that is, He made me envy the wild beasts for seeing two companions among them whom fear does not frighten. "Lā yurwiʿuhumā" means it does not frighten them, because fear inflicts "rawʿ" (with a ḍamma), which is the heart. "Dhaʿara dhaʿran," like "taʿiba," meant he feared with fear; and "dhaʿartuhu dhaʿran," like "ḍaraba ḍarban," means I frightened him. That is, the frightening does not frighten them. It is also permissible for "al-dhaʿr" to mean a frightening matter. It is narrated: "lā yurwiʿuhumā al-nafr," that is, neither of them flees from the other and thus frightens him by that.]]

Allah's rejection of their claim to be included among the reformers is the most eloquent and most evident rejection, indicating great wrath. The emphasis in it comes from the resumptive construction (istiʾnāf), from what is in each of the two words "alā," and from the two emphasizers "inna" and "min," the definite predicate, and the placement of the separating pronoun (faṣl).

As for His saying ﴿وَلَكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (but they do not perceive): it refutes their advice in two respects. The first is the censure of what they were upon, because it is far from correctness and leads to corruption and strife. The second is showing them the straight path, away from following the people of understanding, and their entering into their number. So their response was to call them fools (sufahāʾ) because of their extreme foolishness, and to call them ignorant because of the persistence of their ignorance. In this there is consolation for the scholar for what he suffers from the ignorant.

If you ask: how is it correct to attribute "qīla" (it was said) to "lā tufsidū" and "āminū," when attributing an action to an action is not correct? I say: what is not correct is attributing an action to the meaning of an action. This, however, attributes it to its wording, as if it were said: "When this statement and this speech is said to them." It is like your saying: "alif" is a kind of three letters. And from this: "They claim is the mount of falsehood" [[

Ibn Saʿd related it in al-Ṭabaqāt from the narration of al-Aʿmash from Sharīḥ, who said: "They claim" is the kunya of falsehood. The author mentioned it as a marfūʿ ḥadīth in Sūrat al-Taghābun, but I have not found it with this wording. What is in al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhārī, from the ḥadīth of Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfūʿ ḥadīth: "Evil is the mount of a man: 'they claim.'" Likewise Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Abū Yaʿlā related it, and it is from the narration of Abū Qilāba from him. In al-Bukhārī's narration, between Abū Qilāba and Abū Masʿūd is Abū al-Muhallab.]].

The "mā" in "kamā" (as) may be a kāfa (preventing its governing effect), like it in "rubbamā" (perhaps), and it may be a maṣdariyya (verbal), like it in "bi-mā raḥubat" (with what it was spacious).

The "al" in "al-nās" (the people) is for the specific known referent: that is, "as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him believed." Or they are known people, like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, because they were of their own kind and of their species, meaning: as your companions and brothers believed. Or it is for the genus, meaning: as those perfect in humanity believed. Or the believers are made as if they were "the people" in reality, and whoever else is like the animals in lacking the discernment between truth and falsehood.

The interrogative in ﴿أَنُؤْمِنُ﴾ (Shall we believe?) carries the meaning of denial. The "al" in ﴿السُّفَهاءُ﴾ (the fools) has its inclination toward "the people," as when you say to your companion, "Indeed Zayd has informed on you," and he replies, "Has the fool really done so?" It is also permissible that it be for the genus, and it includes under it those mentioned, according to their own claim and belief, because among them they were the most deeply rooted in foolishness.

If you ask: why did they call them fools and deem their minds deficient, when they were the wise and the superior ones? I say: because in their ignorance and their neglect of reflection and of being fair to themselves, they believed that what they were upon was the truth and that whatever else was falsehood. Whoever mounts the back of falsehood is a fool. Also, they were in a middle-level leadership among their people and in prosperity, while most of the believers were poor, and among them were clients such as Ṣuhayb, Bilāl, and Khabbāb. So they called them fools to belittle their status. Or they meant ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, and their leaving their religion, and what their Islam had cast down and weakened their support. They said this as a show of forbearance, to guard against the gloating over them, while knowing that they were far from foolishness. Foolishness is the weakness of reason and lightness of forbearance.

If you ask: why was this verse concluded with ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they do not know), while the preceding one was concluded with ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (they do not perceive)? I say: because the matter of religion, and the realization that the believers are upon the truth while they are upon falsehood, requires reflection and inference until the reflecting person acquires knowledge.

As for hypocrisy, and what it contains of transgression that leads to strife and corruption in the land, it is a worldly matter based on custom, known among people, especially among the Arabs in their Jāhiliyya and what existed among them of raids, mutual enmity, warfare, and factionalism. So it is like the perceived and witnessed. And because foolishness, which is ignorance, was mentioned, mentioning knowledge with it is a better antithesis (ṭibāq) to it.

The context of this verse differs from the context in which the beginning of the story of the hypocrites was presented, so it is not a repetition. For that was to explain their doctrine and to express their hypocrisy, while this is to explain what they used to do with the believers: denying them, mocking them, meeting the faces of the sincere ones and making them think they were with them. Then when they separated from them to the devils of their religion, they confirmed to them what was in their hearts. It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions went out one day and encountered a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAbd Allāh said: "Look how I will repel these fools from you." He took the hand of Abū Bakr and said: "Welcome, O al-Ṣiddīq, lord of the Banū Taym, shaykh of Islam, second of the Messenger of Allah in the cave, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿUmar and said: "Welcome, lord of the Banū ʿAdī, al-Fārūq, strong in the religion of Allah, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of Allah and his son-in-law, lord of the Banū Hāshim, apart from the Messenger of Allah." Then they separated, and he said to his companions: "How did you see me act?" They praised him well, and so it was revealed.

It is said "laqītuhu" and "lāqaytuhu" when you meet him closely; and he is "jārī mulāqī" and "murāwiqī." Abū Ḥanīfa recited: ﴿وَإِذا لاقوا﴾.

"Khalawtu bi-fulān" and "ilayhi" means when you are alone with him. It is also permissible that it comes from "khalā" meaning "passed away," and "khalāka dhamm" means: he passed you and went by you. From it: "al-qurūn al-khāliya" (the past generations). And from "khalawtu bihi" when you mock him, from your saying: "Khalā fulān bi-ʿarḍ fulān," meaning he played with his honor. The meaning is: "When they carried the mockery of the believers to their devils and told them of it," just as you say: "I convey to you such-and-such and I blame him to you." Their devils are those who resembled the devils in their rebelliousness. Sībawayh made the nūn of "shayṭān" (devil) original in one place of his book and extra in another. The evidence for its originality is their saying "tashayṭana" (to act like a devil), and its derivation is from "shaṭana," meaning to be far, because of its distance from righteousness and goodness; and from "shāṭa," meaning to perish, if its nūn is taken as extra. And among its names is falsehood.

﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ (We are with you): we are your companions and your agreers in your religion. If you ask: why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence, while to their devils it was in the nominal sentence confirmed by "inna"? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He built this exposition on the premise that the nominal sentence is more firm than the verbal, especially when emphasized with "inna" and followed by "innamā," while he has also related the faith of the sincere believers in the verbal sentence in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger﴾. In general, al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, did excellently in his exposition, achieving what he wished and summarizing what he intended.]] I say: what they addressed the believers with is not worthy of the strongest and most emphatic of the two statements, because they were claiming the recent appearance and emergence of faith from them, not claiming that they were unique in faith, with no dust of doubt on it. This is either because their own selves do not assist them in it, since they have no motive or driver from their beliefs, and so is every statement that does not proceed from enthusiasm, true desire, and conviction. Or because it would not be accepted from them had they said it with the form of emphasis and exaggeration. How could they say it and hope for its acceptance while they were among the Emigrants and Helpers, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel?

Do you not see Allah's relating the speech of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed believed﴾? As for addressing their brothers, they, in what they reported about themselves, were firm in Judaism and persistent in the belief of disbelief, far from turning away from it, with true desire, abundant energy, and joy in speaking it. What they said of that was accepted from them and received from them, so it was a place for confirmation and a sign of emphasis.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ (we are only mockers) relate to ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾? I say: it is an emphasis of it, because their saying ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ means steadfastness in Judaism. And their saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ is a rejection of Islam and a repelling of it from them, because one who mocks a thing and belittles it denies it and repels its being regarded. Repelling the opposite of a thing is either a confirmation of its firmness or a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), as if they were objected to when they said to them ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾, so they said: "Then what about you, if it is established that you are with us, agreeing with the people of Islam?" So they said ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾.

Mockery (istihzāʾ) is ridicule and belittling. The root of the matter is lightness, from "al-hazʾ," which is quick killing; and "hazaʾa yahzaʾu" means he died on the spot. From some Arabs: "I walked and became tired, and I thought I would die on my spot." And "his she-camel hazaʾa by him," meaning she hastened and was light.

If you ask: mockery cannot be attributed to Allah the Exalted, because He is exalted above the ugly, and ridicule belongs to the category of defect and ignorance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾? So what is the meaning of His mocking them? I say: its meaning is the inflicting of humiliation and lowliness upon them, because the mocker's aim, which he is shooting at, is seeking lightness and disparagement from the one he mocks, and bringing humiliation and lowliness upon him. The derivation, as we mentioned, is evidence for this. Mockery (tahakkum) has become frequent in the speech of Allah the Exalted toward the disbelievers, and its purpose is belittling their status, despising their affair, and indicating that their doctrines deserve to be ridiculed by mockers and laughed at by laughers. It is also permissible that it is meant in the sense mentioned in ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ (they deceive), that the rulings of Muslims apply to them outwardly, while He conceals what is intended for them. It is said: the recompense for mockery was named by its name, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, and ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner﴾.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾ (Allah mocks them) begin as a new sentence and is not coordinated with what precedes it? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'Allah mocks them' begin and is not made coordinated...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If someone says, "Is this meaning not derived from the coordination?" It is said to him: had it been coordinated, it would indicate that the aim is wholly the gathering of the content of both sentences, and it would turn away from this meaning which the resumptive construction alone conveys.]]. I say: it is a resumptive sentence of extreme eloquence and grandeur. In it is that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who mocks them with the most eloquent mockery, whose mockery against Him is not mockery and does not count in comparison to it, because of the punishment that descends upon them and the humiliation and abasement that settles on them. In it also is that Allah is the One who undertakes mocking them as vengeance for the believers, and does not oblige the believers to oppose them with a similar mockery. If you ask: why was it not said, "Allah is a mocker of them," so that it would correspond to His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'Allah is a mocker of them'...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: For this difference between the verb and the noun, the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered﴾.

Since the frequent and renewed occurrence of mockery and the gathering of the birds with it is a constant matter, the mockery was expressed with a verbal form and the gathering with a nominal form. Further elaboration on this will come, God willing.

I say: because "yastahzi'" (He mocks) indicates that mockery occurs and is renewed time after time. Likewise were God's punishments upon them and the afflictions that descended upon them. "Do they not see that they are tested every year, once or twice?" [9:126] And they were not free, for most of their time, from the tearing of veils and the exposure of secrets, and revelation concerning them, and a sense of dread lest something be revealed about them: "The hypocrites fear that a surah may be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts." [9:64] "Say: Mock on; surely God will bring forth what you fear." [9:64]

"And He extends them in their transgression" (yamudduhum fi tughyanihim): from the verb madda (to supply) an army, meaning to increase it and add to it what strengthens and multiplies it. Likewise madda the inkwell (addadha): he added to it what improves it. And I madadtu the lamp and the land: when I improved them with oil and manure. And the Devil "mad-dahu fi al-ghayy" and amadahu: when he continues to supply him with whisperings until his error follows on and increases.

If you ask: why do you claim it is from the root madd (supply) and not from madd in the sense of lengthening (life), granting respite or delaying? I reply: sufficient proof that it is from madd (supply) and not from madd (lengthening) is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-yamudduhum" (with the ḍamma on the yāʾ and the doubled dāl), and the reading of Nafi': "wa-ikhwanuhum yamudduunahum" (and their brothers supply them). The meaning of granting respite is, in that case, expressed with the lām, as in amla lahu (he granted him respite).

If you ask: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression, when this is the act of the devils? Do you not see His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error" [7:202]? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: What prevents him from upholding it according to its apparent sense and leaving it in its place is only that it is pure monotheism and true reality, while the Qadariyya are far from monotheism by stages.]

I say: either it is understood that when God withheld from them the graces He bestows upon the believers, and forsook them because of their disbelief and persistence in it, their hearts remained with an increase of rust and darkness, just as the believers' hearts increased in expansion and light; that increase is called "supply." It is attributed to God, the Exalted, because it is caused by His action toward them on account of their disbelief. Or it is understood as a denial of compulsion and coercion. Or the Devil's action is attributed to God because it is by His enabling, His empowering, and His leaving free between him and the misguiding of His servants.

If you ask: what led them to interpret the supply in transgression as respite, when the lexical meaning, as you mentioned, does not accommodate it? I reply: fear of taking the step of attributing to God what they attributed to the devils drove them to it. But the correct meaning is that which the wording matches and which confirms its soundness; otherwise it would be like the wild sheep among ostriches.

It is incumbent upon the interpreter of the Book of God, which is overwhelming and whose speech is inimitable, to take care in his interpretations that the composition remains in its beauty, that eloquence retains its perfection, and that what the challenge was made with remains free from any defect. If he does not observe the conventions of the language, then his observance of composition and eloquence is in stages. What we have said is supported by al-Hasan's saying in his tafsir: "In their misguidance they persist, and these are of those sealed." Transgression (tughyan) is excessiveness in disbelief and exceeding the limit in insolence.

Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with him, read "fi tughyanihim" with a kasra, and both are dialects, like laqiyan and laqiyan, and ghaniyan and ghaniyan. If you ask: what is the point in attributing it to them? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: what is the point of attributing transgression to them...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Every act that proceeds from the servant by choice has two considerations. If you look at its existence, its origination, and the particular aspects of its specification, attribute that to God's power and will alone, with no partner. If you look at its distinction from compulsion that is necessary, attribute it in this respect to the servant, which is the attribution expressed in the Sharia as acquisition (kasb), as in His saying: "for what your hands have earned" [42:30]. This is also realized if you present to your mind the necessary trembling movement and the voluntary one, for you will necessarily distinguish between them by that attribution. Once the plurality of considerations is established, their supply in transgression is created by God, so He attributed it to Himself, and inasmuch as it occurs from them by way of choice, which is expressed as acquisition, He attributed it to them. Build your branches upon the principles of the Sunnah, and the fruits of your branches will be good in Paradise, not as the Qadariyya build, for they dig but only against themselves. May God grant us realization and strengthen us with success.]

I say: in it is that transgression and persistence in misguidance are among what their souls have committed and their hands have wrought, and that God is free of it, refuting the belief of the disbelievers who say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]" [6:148], and negating the notion of whoever might imagine, when the supply is attributed to His essence, that if transgression were not attributed to them, it would be a flaw. He thus removes doubt and uproots it, and repels it from the breast of whoever deviates regarding His attributes. [Mahmud's statement "and negating the notion of whoever might imagine..." intends a refutation of the People of the Sunnah, who say that God, exalted, is in reality the doer of good and evil, and it champions the Mu'tazila who say that He does not do evil nor will it.] The evidence for this is that when He attributed the supply to the devils, He left "ghayy" unrestricted and did not qualify it with an attribution in His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error."

"Al-'Amah" (blindness of heart) is like "al-'Amá" (blindness), except that "al-'Amá" is general for sight and opinion, while "al-'Amah" is specific to opinion: it is bewilderment and hesitation, not knowing where to turn. From it is His saying: "among the ignorant and bewildered" [in the poetic sense: those who have no judgment or insight into the paths]. And "salaka ardan 'amhā'" means he traversed a land with no landmarks. [The sense of "salaka ardan 'amhā'" is that from the same root is the saying of the Arabs...]

The meaning of "buying error in exchange for guidance" is choosing it over it and substituting it for it, by way of metaphor, because buying involves giving a substitute and taking another. [Mahmud said: "Buying requires giving a price..." Ahmad said: From this category is Malik's prohibition, may God be pleased with him, of buying one of two slaughtered geese chosen by the buyer, since he is considered to have chosen each of them, and then a seller of each for the other, so usury enters; this is what later companions of his express by whether one who has the right to own is considered owner or not, and they sometimes say: whoever is given a choice between two things is considered to have transferred to one of them, according to one opinion.]

From it is the poem:
I took with the abundant hair a bald head, and with the bright long teeth a crumbling one,
And with the tall-lived a short one, as the Muslim bought when he became Christian.

[Notes on the poem: "al-Jumma" is abundant hair; the bāʾ is for exchange; "azar" means little hair. The thanāyā are the front teeth, meaning the whole mouth. "Al-Dardar" means the separated teeth. "Al-Haydar" means short. "Ishtara" means "exchanged." The meaning is that he took an old ugly woman in exchange for a young beautiful one. It is related that Jabalah ibn al-Ayham came to Mecca and circumambulated the Kaaba; a man stepped on his waist-wrap, and he struck him. He complained to Umar, may God be pleased with him, who ruled retaliation against Jabalah; he asked for a delay until the next day, fled by night to the Byzantines, and became Christian after Islam. Then he regretted what he had done, and so he became a proverb.]

It is related from Wahb that God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, in reproaching the Children of Israel: "You learn religion for other than religion, you teach for other than practice, and you sell the hereafter for the works of the world." [Attributed as a reproach.]

If you ask: how did they buy error in exchange for guidance when they were not upon guidance? I reply: they were made as if it were in their hands because it was available to them and presented itself to them; so when they left it for error, they had abandoned it and exchanged it for error. Also, the upright religion is the natural disposition (fitra) of God upon which He created people; so whoever goes astray has substituted what contradicts the fitra.
