Or the believers are made as if they were "the people" in reality, and whoever else is like the animals in lacking the discernment between truth and falsehood.

The interrogative in ﴿أَنُؤْمِنُ﴾ (Shall we believe?) carries the meaning of denial. The "al" in ﴿السُّفَهاءُ﴾ (the fools) has its inclination toward "the people," as when you say to your companion, "Indeed Zayd has informed on you," and he replies, "Has the fool really done so?" It is also permissible that it be for the genus, and it includes under it those mentioned, according to their own claim and belief, because among them they were the most deeply rooted in foolishness.

If you ask: why did they call them fools and deem their minds deficient, when they were the wise and the superior ones? I say: because in their ignorance and their neglect of reflection and of being fair to themselves, they believed that what they were upon was the truth and that whatever else was falsehood. Whoever mounts the back of falsehood is a fool. Also, they were in a middle-level leadership among their people and in prosperity, while most of the believers were poor, and among them were clients such as Ṣuhayb, Bilāl, and Khabbāb. So they called them fools to belittle their status. Or they meant ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, and their leaving their religion, and what their Islam had cast down and weakened their support. They said this as a show of forbearance, to guard against the gloating over them, while knowing that they were far from foolishness. Foolishness is the weakness of reason and lightness of forbearance.

If you ask: why was this verse concluded with ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they do not know), while the preceding one was concluded with ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (they do not perceive)? I say: because the matter of religion, and the realization that the believers are upon the truth while they are upon falsehood, requires reflection and inference until the reflecting person acquires knowledge.

As for hypocrisy, and what it contains of transgression that leads to strife and corruption in the land, it is a worldly matter based on custom, known among people, especially among the Arabs in their Jāhiliyya and what existed among them of raids, mutual enmity, warfare, and factionalism. So it is like the perceived and witnessed. And because foolishness, which is ignorance, was mentioned, mentioning knowledge with it is a better antithesis (ṭibāq) to it.

The context of this verse differs from the context in which the beginning of the story of the hypocrites was presented, so it is not a repetition. For that was to explain their doctrine and to express their hypocrisy, while this is to explain what they used to do with the believers: denying them, mocking them, meeting the faces of the sincere ones and making them think they were with them. Then when they separated from them to the devils of their religion, they confirmed to them what was in their hearts. It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions went out one day and encountered a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAbd Allāh said: "Look how I will repel these fools from you." He took the hand of Abū Bakr and said: "Welcome, O al-Ṣiddīq, lord of the Banū Taym, shaykh of Islam, second of the Messenger of Allah in the cave, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿUmar and said: "Welcome, lord of the Banū ʿAdī, al-Fārūq, strong in the religion of Allah, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of Allah and his son-in-law, lord of the Banū Hāshim, apart from the Messenger of Allah." Then they separated, and he said to his companions: "How did you see me act?" They praised him well, and so it was revealed.

It is said "laqītuhu" and "lāqaytuhu" when you meet him closely; and he is "jārī mulāqī" and "murāwiqī." Abū Ḥanīfa recited: ﴿وَإِذا لاقوا﴾.

"Khalawtu bi-fulān" and "ilayhi" means when you are alone with him. It is also permissible that it comes from "khalā" meaning "passed away," and "khalāka dhamm" means: he passed you and went by you. From it: "al-qurūn al-khāliya" (the past generations). And from "khalawtu bihi" when you mock him, from your saying: "Khalā fulān bi-ʿarḍ fulān," meaning he played with his honor. The meaning is: "When they carried the mockery of the believers to their devils and told them of it," just as you say: "I convey to you such-and-such and I blame him to you." Their devils are those who resembled the devils in their rebelliousness. Sībawayh made the nūn of "shayṭān" (devil) original in one place of his book and extra in another. The evidence for its originality is their saying "tashayṭana" (to act like a devil), and its derivation is from "shaṭana," meaning to be far, because of its distance from righteousness and goodness; and from "shāṭa," meaning to perish, if its nūn is taken as extra. And among its names is falsehood.

﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ (We are with you): we are your companions and your agreers in your religion. If you ask: why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence, while to their devils it was in the nominal sentence confirmed by "inna"? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He built this exposition on the premise that the nominal sentence is more firm than the verbal, especially when emphasized with "inna" and followed by "innamā," while he has also related the faith of the sincere believers in the verbal sentence in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger﴾. In general, al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, did excellently in his exposition, achieving what he wished and summarizing what he intended.]] I say: what they addressed the believers with is not worthy of the strongest and most emphatic of the two statements, because they were claiming the recent appearance and emergence of faith from them, not claiming that they were unique in faith, with no dust of doubt on it. This is either because their own selves do not assist them in it, since they have no motive or driver from their beliefs, and so is every statement that does not proceed from enthusiasm, true desire, and conviction. Or because it would not be accepted from them had they said it with the form of emphasis and exaggeration. How could they say it and hope for its acceptance while they were among the Emigrants and Helpers, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel?

Do you not see Allah's relating the speech of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed believed﴾? As for addressing their brothers, they, in what they reported about themselves, were firm in Judaism and persistent in the belief of disbelief, far from turning away from it, with true desire, abundant energy, and joy in speaking it. What they said of that was accepted from them and received from them, so it was a place for confirmation and a sign of emphasis.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ (we are only mockers) relate to ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾? I say: it is an emphasis of it, because their saying ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ means steadfastness in Judaism. And their saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ is a rejection of Islam and a repelling of it from them, because one who mocks a thing and belittles it denies it and repels its being regarded. Repelling the opposite of a thing is either a confirmation of its firmness or a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), as if they were objected to when they said to them ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾, so they said: "Then what about you, if it is established that you are with us, agreeing with the people of Islam?" So they said ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾.

Mockery (istihzāʾ) is ridicule and belittling. The root of the matter is lightness, from "al-hazʾ," which is quick killing; and "hazaʾa yahzaʾu" means he died on the spot. From some Arabs: "I walked and became tired, and I thought I would die on my spot." And "his she-camel hazaʾa by him," meaning she hastened and was light.

If you ask: mockery cannot be attributed to Allah the Exalted, because He is exalted above the ugly, and ridicule belongs to the category of defect and ignorance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾? So what is the meaning of His mocking them? I say: its meaning is the inflicting of humiliation and lowliness upon them, because the mocker's aim, which he is shooting at, is seeking lightness and disparagement from the one he mocks, and bringing humiliation and lowliness upon him. The derivation, as we mentioned, is evidence for this. Mockery (tahakkum) has become frequent in the speech of Allah the Exalted toward the disbelievers, and its purpose is belittling their status, despising their affair, and indicating that their doctrines deserve to be ridiculed by mockers and laughed at by laughers. It is also permissible that it is meant in the sense mentioned in ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ (they deceive), that the rulings of Muslims apply to them outwardly, while He conceals what is intended for them. It is said: the recompense for mockery was named by its name, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, and ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner﴾.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾ (Allah mocks them) begin as a new sentence and is not coordinated with what precedes it? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'Allah mocks them' begin and is not made coordinated...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If someone says, "Is this meaning not derived from the coordination?" It is said to him: had it been coordinated, it would indicate that the aim is wholly the gathering of the content of both sentences, and it would turn away from this meaning which the resumptive construction alone conveys.]]. I say: it is a resumptive sentence of extreme eloquence and grandeur. In it is that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who mocks them with the most eloquent mockery, whose mockery against Him is not mockery and does not count in comparison to it, because of the punishment that descends upon them and the humiliation and abasement that settles on them. In it also is that Allah is the One who undertakes mocking them as vengeance for the believers, and does not oblige the believers to oppose them with a similar mockery. If you ask: why was it not said, "Allah is a mocker of them," so that it would correspond to His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'Allah is a mocker of them'...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: For this difference between the verb and the noun, the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered﴾.

Since the frequent and renewed occurrence of mockery and the gathering of the birds with it is a constant matter, the mockery was expressed with a verbal form and the gathering with a nominal form. Further elaboration on this will come, God willing.

I say: because "yastahzi'" (He mocks) indicates that mockery occurs and is renewed time after time. Likewise were God's punishments upon them and the afflictions that descended upon them. "Do they not see that they are tested every year, once or twice?" [9:126] And they were not free, for most of their time, from the tearing of veils and the exposure of secrets, and revelation concerning them, and a sense of dread lest something be revealed about them: "The hypocrites fear that a surah may be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts." [9:64] "Say: Mock on; surely God will bring forth what you fear." [9:64]

"And He extends them in their transgression" (yamudduhum fi tughyanihim): from the verb madda (to supply) an army, meaning to increase it and add to it what strengthens and multiplies it. Likewise madda the inkwell (addadha): he added to it what improves it. And I madadtu the lamp and the land: when I improved them with oil and manure. And the Devil "mad-dahu fi al-ghayy" and amadahu: when he continues to supply him with whisperings until his error follows on and increases.

If you ask: why do you claim it is from the root madd (supply) and not from madd in the sense of lengthening (life), granting respite or delaying? I reply: sufficient proof that it is from madd (supply) and not from madd (lengthening) is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-yamudduhum" (with the ḍamma on the yāʾ and the doubled dāl), and the reading of Nafi': "wa-ikhwanuhum yamudduunahum" (and their brothers supply them). The meaning of granting respite is, in that case, expressed with the lām, as in amla lahu (he granted him respite).

If you ask: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression, when this is the act of the devils? Do you not see His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error" [7:202]? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: What prevents him from upholding it according to its apparent sense and leaving it in its place is only that it is pure monotheism and true reality, while the Qadariyya are far from monotheism by stages.]

I say: either it is understood that when God withheld from them the graces He bestows upon the believers, and forsook them because of their disbelief and persistence in it, their hearts remained with an increase of rust and darkness, just as the believers' hearts increased in expansion and light; that increase is called "supply." It is attributed to God, the Exalted, because it is caused by His action toward them on account of their disbelief. Or it is understood as a denial of compulsion and coercion. Or the Devil's action is attributed to God because it is by His enabling, His empowering, and His leaving free between him and the misguiding of His servants.

If you ask: what led them to interpret the supply in transgression as respite, when the lexical meaning, as you mentioned, does not accommodate it? I reply: fear of taking the step of attributing to God what they attributed to the devils drove them to it. But the correct meaning is that which the wording matches and which confirms its soundness; otherwise it would be like the wild sheep among ostriches.

It is incumbent upon the interpreter of the Book of God, which is overwhelming and whose speech is inimitable, to take care in his interpretations that the composition remains in its beauty, that eloquence retains its perfection, and that what the challenge was made with remains free from any defect. If he does not observe the conventions of the language, then his observance of composition and eloquence is in stages. What we have said is supported by al-Hasan's saying in his tafsir: "In their misguidance they persist, and these are of those sealed." Transgression (tughyan) is excessiveness in disbelief and exceeding the limit in insolence.

Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with him, read "fi tughyanihim" with a kasra, and both are dialects, like laqiyan and laqiyan, and ghaniyan and ghaniyan. If you ask: what is the point in attributing it to them? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: what is the point of attributing transgression to them...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Every act that proceeds from the servant by choice has two considerations. If you look at its existence, its origination, and the particular aspects of its specification, attribute that to God's power and will alone, with no partner. If you look at its distinction from compulsion that is necessary, attribute it in this respect to the servant, which is the attribution expressed in the Sharia as acquisition (kasb), as in His saying: "for what your hands have earned" [42:30]. This is also realized if you present to your mind the necessary trembling movement and the voluntary one, for you will necessarily distinguish between them by that attribution. Once the plurality of considerations is established, their supply in transgression is created by God, so He attributed it to Himself, and inasmuch as it occurs from them by way of choice, which is expressed as acquisition, He attributed it to them. Build your branches upon the principles of the Sunnah, and the fruits of your branches will be good in Paradise, not as the Qadariyya build, for they dig but only against themselves. May God grant us realization and strengthen us with success.]

I say: in it is that transgression and persistence in misguidance are among what their souls have committed and their hands have wrought, and that God is free of it, refuting the belief of the disbelievers who say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]" [6:148], and negating the notion of whoever might imagine, when the supply is attributed to His essence, that if transgression were not attributed to them, it would be a flaw. He thus removes doubt and uproots it, and repels it from the breast of whoever deviates regarding His attributes. [Mahmud's statement "and negating the notion of whoever might imagine..." intends a refutation of the People of the Sunnah, who say that God, exalted, is in reality the doer of good and evil, and it champions the Mu'tazila who say that He does not do evil nor will it.] The evidence for this is that when He attributed the supply to the devils, He left "ghayy" unrestricted and did not qualify it with an attribution in His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error."

"Al-'Amah" (blindness of heart) is like "al-'Amá" (blindness), except that "al-'Amá" is general for sight and opinion, while "al-'Amah" is specific to opinion: it is bewilderment and hesitation, not knowing where to turn. From it is His saying: "among the ignorant and bewildered" [in the poetic sense: those who have no judgment or insight into the paths]. And "salaka ardan 'amhā'" means he traversed a land with no landmarks. [The sense of "salaka ardan 'amhā'" is that from the same root is the saying of the Arabs...]

The meaning of "buying error in exchange for guidance" is choosing it over it and substituting it for it, by way of metaphor, because buying involves giving a substitute and taking another. [Mahmud said: "Buying requires giving a price..." Ahmad said: From this category is Malik's prohibition, may God be pleased with him, of buying one of two slaughtered geese chosen by the buyer, since he is considered to have chosen each of them, and then a seller of each for the other, so usury enters; this is what later companions of his express by whether one who has the right to own is considered owner or not, and they sometimes say: whoever is given a choice between two things is considered to have transferred to one of them, according to one opinion.]

From it is the poem:
I took with the abundant hair a bald head, and with the bright long teeth a crumbling one,
And with the tall-lived a short one, as the Muslim bought when he became Christian.

[Notes on the poem: "al-Jumma" is abundant hair; the bāʾ is for exchange; "azar" means little hair. The thanāyā are the front teeth, meaning the whole mouth. "Al-Dardar" means the separated teeth. "Al-Haydar" means short. "Ishtara" means "exchanged." The meaning is that he took an old ugly woman in exchange for a young beautiful one. It is related that Jabalah ibn al-Ayham came to Mecca and circumambulated the Kaaba; a man stepped on his waist-wrap, and he struck him. He complained to Umar, may God be pleased with him, who ruled retaliation against Jabalah; he asked for a delay until the next day, fled by night to the Byzantines, and became Christian after Islam. Then he regretted what he had done, and so he became a proverb.]

It is related from Wahb that God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, in reproaching the Children of Israel: "You learn religion for other than religion, you teach for other than practice, and you sell the hereafter for the works of the world." [Attributed as a reproach.]

If you ask: how did they buy error in exchange for guidance when they were not upon guidance? I reply: they were made as if it were in their hands because it was available to them and presented itself to them; so when they left it for error, they had abandoned it and exchanged it for error. Also, the upright religion is the natural disposition (fitra) of God upon which He created people; so whoever goes astray has substituted what contradicts the fitra. "Ḍalāla" means deviation from the right course and loss of guidance. It is said: "ḍalla manzaluh" (his dwelling was lost), "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" (the jerboa's young lost its burrow). [The proverb "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" means its den.] It is then borrowed for going astray from the right path in religion. "Al-Ribḥ" (profit) is the surplus over capital, and for this reason the surplus is called "al-shaff"... [The text continues in the same sense.] "Tijāra" (trade) is the profession of the merchant, who sells and buys for profit. A "nāqa tājira" is a she-camel that, from her beauty and fatness, seems to sell herself. Ibn Abi Ablah read "tijārātuhum."

If you ask: how is loss attributed to trade when it belongs to its practitioners? I reply: it is attribution by metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), namely attributing the verb to something that is clothed with what is in truth its own, just as trade was clothed with the buyers. If you ask: is it valid to say "your slave profited and your slave-girl lost" by metaphorical attribution? I reply: yes, when the context indicates it. Likewise the condition for the validity of "I saw a lion" when you mean a brave man is that a context indicates it; otherwise it is invalid.

If you ask: grant that buying error in exchange for guidance was metaphorical in the sense of substitution; what is the point of mentioning profit and trade? As though there were an actual transaction. [Mahmud said: "Grant that buying error in exchange for guidance..." Ahmad said: this kind is close to the "completion" (tatmīm) which the rhetoricians illustrate with al-Khansa's words: "Indeed Sakhr is followed by the guided, as if he were a banner with fire at its top."] I say: this is of the beautiful craft that carries metaphor to its highest peak, namely that a word is driven in the manner of metaphor and then followed by terms similar to it and its sisters; when they follow one another you will not see a speech more beautiful in finish, richer in lustre and brilliance. This is the "tarshīḥ" (nurturing) metaphor. Like the Arabs' saying about the dull: "as if the ears of his heart were a stripped palm-frond," where they liken him to a donkey, then nurture it by claiming for his heart two ears and claiming for them drooping, to represent his dullness in a manner that joins it to the dullness of a donkey in visible observation. Similar is: "When I saw the eagle overcome the son of Dayah [the crow], and nest in his two nests, my chest stirred for him." [Likening white hair to an eagle by the common whiteness, and youth to a crow by blackness; the nesting is nurturing.] Likewise the saying of one of their outlaws about his mother: "Though Umm al-Radin is proud, she is not knowing of the ways of the noble; when the Devil crept into her nape, we pursued him with the twisted rope." [The metaphor of the jerboa's hole, "qaṣʿa" and "tanaffaqa," is used for the Devil's entry and expulsion.] That is: when the Devil enters her nape, we extract him from his exit with the twisted rope. He means: when she is angry and bad-tempered, we strive to remove her anger.

He first borrowed "qaṣʿa," then added "tanaffaqa," then "the twisted rope." So likewise, when God mentioned buying, He followed it with what resembles it and fits it, and what completes it by joining it, representing their loss and depicting its reality. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "so their trade did not profit, nor were they guided"? I reply: what traders seek in their dealings is two things: the safety of capital and profit. These have lost both aims together, for their capital was guidance, so nothing remained for them with error. When nothing remained in their hands but error, they were not described as attaining profit, even if they gained some worldly aims, because the one who is astray is a lost loser, and one whose capital is not preserved is not said to have profited. And they were not guided to the ways of trade, as merchants who manage affairs and know what profits and what loses are.

And when it is said to them, [﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾] is coordinated with [﴿يَكْذِبُونَ﴾ (they lie)]. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with [﴿يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾ (says, "We believe")], because if you said, "And among the people are those who, when it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption,'" it would be sound. But the first is more apt.

Corruption (fasad) is the departure of a thing from its state of soundness and its being beneficial. Its opposite is reform (salah), which is attaining the upright, beneficial state. Corruption in the land is the stirring up of wars and strife, because in that is the corruption of what is in the land and the loss of uprightness in the conditions of people, their crops, and their religious and worldly benefits.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾, and ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ From this comes the name given to a war that took place between the tribe of Tayy: "the War of Corruption" (harb al-fasad). The corruption of the hypocrites in the land was that they inclined toward the disbelievers and sided with them against the Muslims by disclosing their secrets to them and inciting them against the Muslims. That leads to the stirring up of strife among them. Since this conduct of theirs led to corruption, it was said to them, "Do not cause corruption," just as you say to a man, "Do not kill yourself with your own hand" or "Do not throw yourself into the fire," when he undertakes what has such an outcome.

"Innama" (indeed/only) is used either to restrict the judgment to a thing, as in your saying, "Only Zayd speaks," or to restrict a thing to a judgment, as in your saying, "Zayd is only a writer." The meaning of ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ (we are only reformers) is that the attribute of reformers is purely theirs, unmixed with any flaw from any aspect of corruption.

﴿ألا﴾ (Alā) is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negative particle, to give the meaning of alerting to the certainty of what follows. The interrogative, when it enters upon a negation, conveys affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and earth able to create the like thereof?﴾ Because it holds this position of emphasis, the clause after it almost never occurs except beginning with something like what introduces an oath. Its sister, "amā," is among the introductions and forerunners of an oath: "Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu" (By He who knows the unseen, besides whom there is none...) [[

"Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu... wa-yuhyī al-ʿiẓāma al-bīḍa wa-hiya rameem
Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā ṭawā al-ḥashā maḥādhiratan min an yuqāla laʾeem
Wa-innī la-astaḥyī yamīnī wa-baynahā wa-bayna famī dājī al-ẓalāmi bahīmu"

[These are] by Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

The origin of "amā" is composed of the interrogative hamza and "mā" remaining, and it became a particle introducing an oath and emphasizing speech. He swore by the One who knows the unseen and the inner thoughts, who is Allah the Exalted, because the answer to the oath is of this kind. Mentioning "the white" (al-bīḍ) is to dispel the assumption that they are the bones of the marrow-filled kind, or it is a metaphor for the length of their period being bare of flesh, so that their whiteness intensifies from the dryness of their marrow, "and they are crumbling" (rameem), decayed. The use of the masculine and feminine alike in fa'īl in the sense of fā'il, as here, is rare; the common usage is in the sense of maf'ūl. "Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā": that is, I used to gather guests and honor them. It may also be narrated as "ajnāz al-qirā" with a jīm and zāy and a ḍamma on the qāf, describing himself as chaste. And it is narrated "akhtāru al-jawā," meaning the burning of the heart from hunger or the like, while I was chaste. According to the first reading, the meaning is: while I was hungry, "qaṭīy al-ḥashā," that is, the stomach and the intestines, as a metaphor for that. The use of "ṭayy" in this sense became so common that from it was said: "ṭawā yaṭwī," like "riḍā yarḍā," meaning he went hungry; so he is "ṭayyān," like "jaw'ān" in form and meaning. "Maḥādhiratan": that is, out of fear of people's saying that he is base and not generous. He was ashamed to extend his hand to food to his mouth, although the night was very dark and a barrier between them, which prevented him from seeing it. "Al-bahīm" is that in which things are made indistinct by its darkness.]]

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak" [[

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak wa-lladhī
amāta wa-aḥyā wa-lladhī amruhu al-amru
Laqad tarakatnī aḥsudu al-waḥsha an arā
ulayfayni minhā lā yurwiʿuhumā al-dhaʿru"

By Abū Ṣakhr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salmā al-Hudhalī. "Amā" is an introductory particle, a prelude to an oath. The "wa" after it is for the oath: that is, "by the right of He who causes to weep and causes to laugh" in truth, or "He who gladdens and afflicts" as a metaphor, and this is more fitting to the context. "Wa-lladhī amruhu": that is, His decree is the executing decree, or "He whose command, when He wills something, is the Command," that is, His word "Be!" It is narrated "amr" without the lām: that is, a great and true matter. "Laqad tarakatnī": the answer to the oath: that is, He made me envy the wild beasts for seeing two companions among them whom fear does not frighten. "Lā yurwiʿuhumā" means it does not frighten them, because fear inflicts "rawʿ" (with a ḍamma), which is the heart. "Dhaʿara dhaʿran," like "taʿiba," meant he feared with fear; and "dhaʿartuhu dhaʿran," like "ḍaraba ḍarban," means I frightened him. That is, the frightening does not frighten them. It is also permissible for "al-dhaʿr" to mean a frightening matter. It is narrated: "lā yurwiʿuhumā al-nafr," that is, neither of them flees from the other and thus frightens him by that.]]

Allah's rejection of their claim to be included among the reformers is the most eloquent and most evident rejection, indicating great wrath. The emphasis in it comes from the resumptive construction (istiʾnāf), from what is in each of the two words "alā," and from the two emphasizers "inna" and "min," the definite predicate, and the placement of the separating pronoun (faṣl).

As for His saying ﴿وَلَكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (but they do not perceive): it refutes their advice in two respects. The first is the censure of what they were upon, because it is far from correctness and leads to corruption and strife. The second is showing them the straight path, away from following the people of understanding, and their entering into their number. So their response was to call them fools (sufahāʾ) because of their extreme foolishness, and to call them ignorant because of the persistence of their ignorance. In this there is consolation for the scholar for what he suffers from the ignorant.

If you ask: how is it correct to attribute "qīla" (it was said) to "lā tufsidū" and "āminū," when attributing an action to an action is not correct? I say: what is not correct is attributing an action to the meaning of an action. This, however, attributes it to its wording, as if it were said: "When this statement and this speech is said to them." It is like your saying: "alif" is a kind of three letters. And from this: "They claim is the mount of falsehood" [[

Ibn Saʿd related it in al-Ṭabaqāt from the narration of al-Aʿmash from Sharīḥ, who said: "They claim" is the kunya of falsehood. The author mentioned it as a marfūʿ ḥadīth in Sūrat al-Taghābun, but I have not found it with this wording. What is in al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhārī, from the ḥadīth of Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfūʿ ḥadīth: "Evil is the mount of a man: 'they claim.'" Likewise Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Abū Yaʿlā related it, and it is from the narration of Abū Qilāba from him. In al-Bukhārī's narration, between Abū Qilāba and Abū Masʿūd is Abū al-Muhallab.]].

The "mā" in "kamā" (as) may be a kāfa (preventing its governing effect), like it in "rubbamā" (perhaps), and it may be a maṣdariyya (verbal), like it in "bi-mā raḥubat" (with what it was spacious).

The "al" in "al-nās" (the people) is for the specific known referent: that is, "as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him believed." Or they are known people, like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, because they were of their own kind and of their species, meaning: as your companions and brothers believed. Or it is for the genus, meaning: as those perfect in humanity believed. Or the believers are made as if they were "the people" in reality, and whoever else is like the animals in lacking the discernment between truth and falsehood.

The interrogative in ﴿أَنُؤْمِنُ﴾ (Shall we believe?) carries the meaning of denial. The "al" in ﴿السُّفَهاءُ﴾ (the fools) has its inclination toward "the people," as when you say to your companion, "Indeed Zayd has informed on you," and he replies, "Has the fool really done so?" It is also permissible that it be for the genus, and it includes under it those mentioned, according to their own claim and belief, because among them they were the most deeply rooted in foolishness.

If you ask: why did they call them fools and deem their minds deficient, when they were the wise and the superior ones? I say: because in their ignorance and their neglect of reflection and of being fair to themselves, they believed that what they were upon was the truth and that whatever else was falsehood. Whoever mounts the back of falsehood is a fool. Also, they were in a middle-level leadership among their people and in prosperity, while most of the believers were poor, and among them were clients such as Ṣuhayb, Bilāl, and Khabbāb. So they called them fools to belittle their status. Or they meant ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, and their leaving their religion, and what their Islam had cast down and weakened their support. They said this as a show of forbearance, to guard against the gloating over them, while knowing that they were far from foolishness. Foolishness is the weakness of reason and lightness of forbearance.

If you ask: why was this verse concluded with ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they do not know), while the preceding one was concluded with ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (they do not perceive)? I say: because the matter of religion, and the realization that the believers are upon the truth while they are upon falsehood, requires reflection and inference until the reflecting person acquires knowledge.

As for hypocrisy, and what it contains of transgression that leads to strife and corruption in the land, it is a worldly matter based on custom, known among people, especially among the Arabs in their Jāhiliyya and what existed among them of raids, mutual enmity, warfare, and factionalism. So it is like the perceived and witnessed. And because foolishness, which is ignorance, was mentioned, mentioning knowledge with it is a better antithesis (ṭibāq) to it.

The context of this verse differs from the context in which the beginning of the story of the hypocrites was presented, so it is not a repetition. For that was to explain their doctrine and to express their hypocrisy, while this is to explain what they used to do with the believers: denying them, mocking them, meeting the faces of the sincere ones and making them think they were with them. Then when they separated from them to the devils of their religion, they confirmed to them what was in their hearts. It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions went out one day and encountered a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAbd Allāh said: "Look how I will repel these fools from you." He took the hand of Abū Bakr and said: "Welcome, O al-Ṣiddīq, lord of the Banū Taym, shaykh of Islam, second of the Messenger of Allah in the cave, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿUmar and said: "Welcome, lord of the Banū ʿAdī, al-Fārūq, strong in the religion of Allah, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of Allah and his son-in-law, lord of the Banū Hāshim, apart from the Messenger of Allah." Then they separated, and he said to his companions: "How did you see me act?" They praised him well, and so it was revealed.

It is said "laqītuhu" and "lāqaytuhu" when you meet him closely; and he is "jārī mulāqī" and "murāwiqī." Abū Ḥanīfa recited: ﴿وَإِذا لاقوا﴾.

"Khalawtu bi-fulān" and "ilayhi" means when you are alone with him. It is also permissible that it comes from "khalā" meaning "passed away," and "khalāka dhamm" means: he passed you and went by you. From it: "al-qurūn al-khāliya" (the past generations). And from "khalawtu bihi" when you mock him, from your saying: "Khalā fulān bi-ʿarḍ fulān," meaning he played with his honor. The meaning is: "When they carried the mockery of the believers to their devils and told them of it," just as you say: "I convey to you such-and-such and I blame him to you." Their devils are those who resembled the devils in their rebelliousness. Sībawayh made the nūn of "shayṭān" (devil) original in one place of his book and extra in another. The evidence for its originality is their saying "tashayṭana" (to act like a devil), and its derivation is from "shaṭana," meaning to be far, because of its distance from righteousness and goodness; and from "shāṭa," meaning to perish, if its nūn is taken as extra. And among its names is falsehood.

﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ (We are with you): we are your companions and your agreers in your religion. If you ask: why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence, while to their devils it was in the nominal sentence confirmed by "inna"? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He built this exposition on the premise that the nominal sentence is more firm than the verbal, especially when emphasized with "inna" and followed by "innamā," while he has also related the faith of the sincere believers in the verbal sentence in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger﴾. In general, al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, did excellently in his exposition, achieving what he wished and summarizing what he intended.]] I say: what they addressed the believers with is not worthy of the strongest and most emphatic of the two statements, because they were claiming the recent appearance and emergence of faith from them, not claiming that they were unique in faith, with no dust of doubt on it. This is either because their own selves do not assist them in it, since they have no motive or driver from their beliefs, and so is every statement that does not proceed from enthusiasm, true desire, and conviction. Or because it would not be accepted from them had they said it with the form of emphasis and exaggeration. How could they say it and hope for its acceptance while they were among the Emigrants and Helpers, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel?

Do you not see Allah's relating the speech of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed believed﴾? As for addressing their brothers, they, in what they reported about themselves, were firm in Judaism and persistent in the belief of disbelief, far from turning away from it, with true desire, abundant energy, and joy in speaking it. What they said of that was accepted from them and received from them, so it was a place for confirmation and a sign of emphasis.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ (we are only mockers) relate to ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾? I say: it is an emphasis of it, because their saying ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ means steadfastness in Judaism. And their saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ is a rejection of Islam and a repelling of it from them, because one who mocks a thing and belittles it denies it and repels its being regarded. Repelling the opposite of a thing is either a confirmation of its firmness or a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), as if they were objected to when they said to them ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾, so they said: "Then what about you, if it is established that you are with us, agreeing with the people of Islam?" So they said ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾.

Mockery (istihzāʾ) is ridicule and belittling. The root of the matter is lightness, from "al-hazʾ," which is quick killing; and "hazaʾa yahzaʾu" means he died on the spot. From some Arabs: "I walked and became tired, and I thought I would die on my spot." And "his she-camel hazaʾa by him," meaning she hastened and was light.

If you ask: mockery cannot be attributed to Allah the Exalted, because He is exalted above the ugly, and ridicule belongs to the category of defect and ignorance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾? So what is the meaning of His mocking them? I say: its meaning is the inflicting of humiliation and lowliness upon them, because the mocker's aim, which he is shooting at, is seeking lightness and disparagement from the one he mocks, and bringing humiliation and lowliness upon him. The derivation, as we mentioned, is evidence for this. Mockery (tahakkum) has become frequent in the speech of Allah the Exalted toward the disbelievers, and its purpose is belittling their status, despising their affair, and indicating that their doctrines deserve to be ridiculed by mockers and laughed at by laughers. It is also permissible that it is meant in the sense mentioned in ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ (they deceive), that the rulings of Muslims apply to them outwardly, while He conceals what is intended for them. It is said: the recompense for mockery was named by its name, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, and ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner﴾.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾ (Allah mocks them) begin as a new sentence and is not coordinated with what precedes it? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'Allah mocks them' begin and is not made coordinated...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If someone says, "Is this meaning not derived from the coordination?" It is said to him: had it been coordinated, it would indicate that the aim is wholly the gathering of the content of both sentences, and it would turn away from this meaning which the resumptive construction alone conveys.]]. I say: it is a resumptive sentence of extreme eloquence and grandeur. In it is that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who mocks them with the most eloquent mockery, whose mockery against Him is not mockery and does not count in comparison to it, because of the punishment that descends upon them and the humiliation and abasement that settles on them. In it also is that Allah is the One who undertakes mocking them as vengeance for the believers, and does not oblige the believers to oppose them with a similar mockery. If you ask: why was it not said, "Allah is a mocker of them," so that it would correspond to His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'Allah is a mocker of them'...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: For this difference between the verb and the noun, the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered﴾.

Since the frequent and renewed occurrence of mockery and the gathering of the birds with it is a constant matter, the mockery was expressed with a verbal form and the gathering with a nominal form. Further elaboration on this will come, God willing.

I say: because "yastahzi'" (He mocks) indicates that mockery occurs and is renewed time after time. Likewise were God's punishments upon them and the afflictions that descended upon them. "Do they not see that they are tested every year, once or twice?" [9:126] And they were not free, for most of their time, from the tearing of veils and the exposure of secrets, and revelation concerning them, and a sense of dread lest something be revealed about them: "The hypocrites fear that a surah may be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts." [9:64] "Say: Mock on; surely God will bring forth what you fear." [9:64]

"And He extends them in their transgression" (yamudduhum fi tughyanihim): from the verb madda (to supply) an army, meaning to increase it and add to it what strengthens and multiplies it. Likewise madda the inkwell (addadha): he added to it what improves it. And I madadtu the lamp and the land: when I improved them with oil and manure. And the Devil "mad-dahu fi al-ghayy" and amadahu: when he continues to supply him with whisperings until his error follows on and increases.

If you ask: why do you claim it is from the root madd (supply) and not from madd in the sense of lengthening (life), granting respite or delaying? I reply: sufficient proof that it is from madd (supply) and not from madd (lengthening) is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-yamudduhum" (with the ḍamma on the yāʾ and the doubled dāl), and the reading of Nafi': "wa-ikhwanuhum yamudduunahum" (and their brothers supply them). The meaning of granting respite is, in that case, expressed with the lām, as in amla lahu (he granted him respite).

If you ask: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression, when this is the act of the devils? Do you not see His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error" [7:202]? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: What prevents him from upholding it according to its apparent sense and leaving it in its place is only that it is pure monotheism and true reality, while the Qadariyya are far from monotheism by stages.]

I say: either it is understood that when God withheld from them the graces He bestows upon the believers, and forsook them because of their disbelief and persistence in it, their hearts remained with an increase of rust and darkness, just as the believers' hearts increased in expansion and light; that increase is called "supply." It is attributed to God, the Exalted, because it is caused by His action toward them on account of their disbelief. Or it is understood as a denial of compulsion and coercion. Or the Devil's action is attributed to God because it is by His enabling, His empowering, and His leaving free between him and the misguiding of His servants.

If you ask: what led them to interpret the supply in transgression as respite, when the lexical meaning, as you mentioned, does not accommodate it? I reply: fear of taking the step of attributing to God what they attributed to the devils drove them to it. But the correct meaning is that which the wording matches and which confirms its soundness; otherwise it would be like the wild sheep among ostriches.

It is incumbent upon the interpreter of the Book of God, which is overwhelming and whose speech is inimitable, to take care in his interpretations that the composition remains in its beauty, that eloquence retains its perfection, and that what the challenge was made with remains free from any defect. If he does not observe the conventions of the language, then his observance of composition and eloquence is in stages. What we have said is supported by al-Hasan's saying in his tafsir: "In their misguidance they persist, and these are of those sealed." Transgression (tughyan) is excessiveness in disbelief and exceeding the limit in insolence.

Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with him, read "fi tughyanihim" with a kasra, and both are dialects, like laqiyan and laqiyan, and ghaniyan and ghaniyan. If you ask: what is the point in attributing it to them? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: what is the point of attributing transgression to them...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Every act that proceeds from the servant by choice has two considerations. If you look at its existence, its origination, and the particular aspects of its specification, attribute that to God's power and will alone, with no partner. If you look at its distinction from compulsion that is necessary, attribute it in this respect to the servant, which is the attribution expressed in the Sharia as acquisition (kasb), as in His saying: "for what your hands have earned" [42:30]. This is also realized if you present to your mind the necessary trembling movement and the voluntary one, for you will necessarily distinguish between them by that attribution. Once the plurality of considerations is established, their supply in transgression is created by God, so He attributed it to Himself, and inasmuch as it occurs from them by way of choice, which is expressed as acquisition, He attributed it to them. Build your branches upon the principles of the Sunnah, and the fruits of your branches will be good in Paradise, not as the Qadariyya build, for they dig but only against themselves. May God grant us realization and strengthen us with success.]

I say: in it is that transgression and persistence in misguidance are among what their souls have committed and their hands have wrought, and that God is free of it, refuting the belief of the disbelievers who say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]" [6:148], and negating the notion of whoever might imagine, when the supply is attributed to His essence, that if transgression were not attributed to them, it would be a flaw. He thus removes doubt and uproots it, and repels it from the breast of whoever deviates regarding His attributes. [Mahmud's statement "and negating the notion of whoever might imagine..." intends a refutation of the People of the Sunnah, who say that God, exalted, is in reality the doer of good and evil, and it champions the Mu'tazila who say that He does not do evil nor will it.] The evidence for this is that when He attributed the supply to the devils, He left "ghayy" unrestricted and did not qualify it with an attribution in His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error."

"Al-'Amah" (blindness of heart) is like "al-'Amá" (blindness), except that "al-'Amá" is general for sight and opinion, while "al-'Amah" is specific to opinion: it is bewilderment and hesitation, not knowing where to turn. From it is His saying: "among the ignorant and bewildered" [in the poetic sense: those who have no judgment or insight into the paths]. And "salaka ardan 'amhā'" means he traversed a land with no landmarks. [The sense of "salaka ardan 'amhā'" is that from the same root is the saying of the Arabs...]

The meaning of "buying error in exchange for guidance" is choosing it over it and substituting it for it, by way of metaphor, because buying involves giving a substitute and taking another. [Mahmud said: "Buying requires giving a price..." Ahmad said: From this category is Malik's prohibition, may God be pleased with him, of buying one of two slaughtered geese chosen by the buyer, since he is considered to have chosen each of them, and then a seller of each for the other, so usury enters; this is what later companions of his express by whether one who has the right to own is considered owner or not, and they sometimes say: whoever is given a choice between two things is considered to have transferred to one of them, according to one opinion.]

From it is the poem:
I took with the abundant hair a bald head, and with the bright long teeth a crumbling one,
And with the tall-lived a short one, as the Muslim bought when he became Christian.

[Notes on the poem: "al-Jumma" is abundant hair; the bāʾ is for exchange; "azar" means little hair. The thanāyā are the front teeth, meaning the whole mouth. "Al-Dardar" means the separated teeth. "Al-Haydar" means short. "Ishtara" means "exchanged." The meaning is that he took an old ugly woman in exchange for a young beautiful one. It is related that Jabalah ibn al-Ayham came to Mecca and circumambulated the Kaaba; a man stepped on his waist-wrap, and he struck him. He complained to Umar, may God be pleased with him, who ruled retaliation against Jabalah; he asked for a delay until the next day, fled by night to the Byzantines, and became Christian after Islam. Then he regretted what he had done, and so he became a proverb.]

It is related from Wahb that God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, in reproaching the Children of Israel: "You learn religion for other than religion, you teach for other than practice, and you sell the hereafter for the works of the world." [Attributed as a reproach.]

If you ask: how did they buy error in exchange for guidance when they were not upon guidance? I reply: they were made as if it were in their hands because it was available to them and presented itself to them; so when they left it for error, they had abandoned it and exchanged it for error. Also, the upright religion is the natural disposition (fitra) of God upon which He created people; so whoever goes astray has substituted what contradicts the fitra. "Ḍalāla" means deviation from the right course and loss of guidance. It is said: "ḍalla manzaluh" (his dwelling was lost), "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" (the jerboa's young lost its burrow). [The proverb "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" means its den.] It is then borrowed for going astray from the right path in religion. "Al-Ribḥ" (profit) is the surplus over capital, and for this reason the surplus is called "al-shaff"... [The text continues in the same sense.] "Tijāra" (trade) is the profession of the merchant, who sells and buys for profit. A "nāqa tājira" is a she-camel that, from her beauty and fatness, seems to sell herself. Ibn Abi Ablah read "tijārātuhum."

If you ask: how is loss attributed to trade when it belongs to its practitioners? I reply: it is attribution by metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), namely attributing the verb to something that is clothed with what is in truth its own, just as trade was clothed with the buyers. If you ask: is it valid to say "your slave profited and your slave-girl lost" by metaphorical attribution? I reply: yes, when the context indicates it. Likewise the condition for the validity of "I saw a lion" when you mean a brave man is that a context indicates it; otherwise it is invalid.

If you ask: grant that buying error in exchange for guidance was metaphorical in the sense of substitution; what is the point of mentioning profit and trade? As though there were an actual transaction. [Mahmud said: "Grant that buying error in exchange for guidance..." Ahmad said: this kind is close to the "completion" (tatmīm) which the rhetoricians illustrate with al-Khansa's words: "Indeed Sakhr is followed by the guided, as if he were a banner with fire at its top."] I say: this is of the beautiful craft that carries metaphor to its highest peak, namely that a word is driven in the manner of metaphor and then followed by terms similar to it and its sisters; when they follow one another you will not see a speech more beautiful in finish, richer in lustre and brilliance. This is the "tarshīḥ" (nurturing) metaphor. Like the Arabs' saying about the dull: "as if the ears of his heart were a stripped palm-frond," where they liken him to a donkey, then nurture it by claiming for his heart two ears and claiming for them drooping, to represent his dullness in a manner that joins it to the dullness of a donkey in visible observation. Similar is: "When I saw the eagle overcome the son of Dayah [the crow], and nest in his two nests, my chest stirred for him." [Likening white hair to an eagle by the common whiteness, and youth to a crow by blackness; the nesting is nurturing.] Likewise the saying of one of their outlaws about his mother: "Though Umm al-Radin is proud, she is not knowing of the ways of the noble; when the Devil crept into her nape, we pursued him with the twisted rope." [The metaphor of the jerboa's hole, "qaṣʿa" and "tanaffaqa," is used for the Devil's entry and expulsion.] That is: when the Devil enters her nape, we extract him from his exit with the twisted rope. He means: when she is angry and bad-tempered, we strive to remove her anger.

He first borrowed "qaṣʿa," then added "tanaffaqa," then "the twisted rope." So likewise, when God mentioned buying, He followed it with what resembles it and fits it, and what completes it by joining it, representing their loss and depicting its reality. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "so their trade did not profit, nor were they guided"? I reply: what traders seek in their dealings is two things: the safety of capital and profit. These have lost both aims together, for their capital was guidance, so nothing remained for them with error. When nothing remained in their hands but error, they were not described as attaining profit, even if they gained some worldly aims, because the one who is astray is a lost loser, and one whose capital is not preserved is not said to have profited. And they were not guided to the ways of trade, as merchants who manage affairs and know what profits and what loses are.

And when it is said to them, [﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾] is coordinated with [﴿يَكْذِبُونَ﴾ (they lie)]. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with [﴿يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾ (says, "We believe")], because if you said, "And among the people are those who, when it is said to them, 'Do not cause corruption,'" it would be sound. But the first is more apt.

Corruption (fasad) is the departure of a thing from its state of soundness and its being beneficial. Its opposite is reform (salah), which is attaining the upright, beneficial state. Corruption in the land is the stirring up of wars and strife, because in that is the corruption of what is in the land and the loss of uprightness in the conditions of people, their crops, and their religious and worldly benefits.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾, and ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ From this comes the name given to a war that took place between the tribe of Tayy: "the War of Corruption" (harb al-fasad). The corruption of the hypocrites in the land was that they inclined toward the disbelievers and sided with them against the Muslims by disclosing their secrets to them and inciting them against the Muslims. That leads to the stirring up of strife among them. Since this conduct of theirs led to corruption, it was said to them, "Do not cause corruption," just as you say to a man, "Do not kill yourself with your own hand" or "Do not throw yourself into the fire," when he undertakes what has such an outcome.

"Innama" (indeed/only) is used either to restrict the judgment to a thing, as in your saying, "Only Zayd speaks," or to restrict a thing to a judgment, as in your saying, "Zayd is only a writer." The meaning of ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ (we are only reformers) is that the attribute of reformers is purely theirs, unmixed with any flaw from any aspect of corruption.

﴿ألا﴾ (Alā) is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negative particle, to give the meaning of alerting to the certainty of what follows. The interrogative, when it enters upon a negation, conveys affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and earth able to create the like thereof?﴾ Because it holds this position of emphasis, the clause after it almost never occurs except beginning with something like what introduces an oath. Its sister, "amā," is among the introductions and forerunners of an oath: "Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu" (By He who knows the unseen, besides whom there is none...) [[

"Amā wa-lladhī lā ya'lamu al-ghayba ghayruhu... wa-yuhyī al-ʿiẓāma al-bīḍa wa-hiya rameem
Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā ṭawā al-ḥashā maḥādhiratan min an yuqāla laʾeem
Wa-innī la-astaḥyī yamīnī wa-baynahā wa-bayna famī dājī al-ẓalāmi bahīmu"

[These are] by Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī.

The origin of "amā" is composed of the interrogative hamza and "mā" remaining, and it became a particle introducing an oath and emphasizing speech. He swore by the One who knows the unseen and the inner thoughts, who is Allah the Exalted, because the answer to the oath is of this kind. Mentioning "the white" (al-bīḍ) is to dispel the assumption that they are the bones of the marrow-filled kind, or it is a metaphor for the length of their period being bare of flesh, so that their whiteness intensifies from the dryness of their marrow, "and they are crumbling" (rameem), decayed. The use of the masculine and feminine alike in fa'īl in the sense of fā'il, as here, is rare; the common usage is in the sense of maf'ūl. "Laqad kuntu akhtāru al-qirā": that is, I used to gather guests and honor them. It may also be narrated as "ajnāz al-qirā" with a jīm and zāy and a ḍamma on the qāf, describing himself as chaste. And it is narrated "akhtāru al-jawā," meaning the burning of the heart from hunger or the like, while I was chaste. According to the first reading, the meaning is: while I was hungry, "qaṭīy al-ḥashā," that is, the stomach and the intestines, as a metaphor for that. The use of "ṭayy" in this sense became so common that from it was said: "ṭawā yaṭwī," like "riḍā yarḍā," meaning he went hungry; so he is "ṭayyān," like "jaw'ān" in form and meaning. "Maḥādhiratan": that is, out of fear of people's saying that he is base and not generous. He was ashamed to extend his hand to food to his mouth, although the night was very dark and a barrier between them, which prevented him from seeing it. "Al-bahīm" is that in which things are made indistinct by its darkness.]]

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak" [[

"Amā wa-lladhī abkā wa-aḍḥak wa-lladhī
amāta wa-aḥyā wa-lladhī amruhu al-amru
Laqad tarakatnī aḥsudu al-waḥsha an arā
ulayfayni minhā lā yurwiʿuhumā al-dhaʿru"

By Abū Ṣakhr ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salmā al-Hudhalī. "Amā" is an introductory particle, a prelude to an oath. The "wa" after it is for the oath: that is, "by the right of He who causes to weep and causes to laugh" in truth, or "He who gladdens and afflicts" as a metaphor, and this is more fitting to the context. "Wa-lladhī amruhu": that is, His decree is the executing decree, or "He whose command, when He wills something, is the Command," that is, His word "Be!" It is narrated "amr" without the lām: that is, a great and true matter. "Laqad tarakatnī": the answer to the oath: that is, He made me envy the wild beasts for seeing two companions among them whom fear does not frighten. "Lā yurwiʿuhumā" means it does not frighten them, because fear inflicts "rawʿ" (with a ḍamma), which is the heart. "Dhaʿara dhaʿran," like "taʿiba," meant he feared with fear; and "dhaʿartuhu dhaʿran," like "ḍaraba ḍarban," means I frightened him. That is, the frightening does not frighten them. It is also permissible for "al-dhaʿr" to mean a frightening matter. It is narrated: "lā yurwiʿuhumā al-nafr," that is, neither of them flees from the other and thus frightens him by that.]]

Allah's rejection of their claim to be included among the reformers is the most eloquent and most evident rejection, indicating great wrath. The emphasis in it comes from the resumptive construction (istiʾnāf), from what is in each of the two words "alā," and from the two emphasizers "inna" and "min," the definite predicate, and the placement of the separating pronoun (faṣl).

As for His saying ﴿وَلَكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (but they do not perceive): it refutes their advice in two respects. The first is the censure of what they were upon, because it is far from correctness and leads to corruption and strife. The second is showing them the straight path, away from following the people of understanding, and their entering into their number. So their response was to call them fools (sufahāʾ) because of their extreme foolishness, and to call them ignorant because of the persistence of their ignorance. In this there is consolation for the scholar for what he suffers from the ignorant.

If you ask: how is it correct to attribute "qīla" (it was said) to "lā tufsidū" and "āminū," when attributing an action to an action is not correct? I say: what is not correct is attributing an action to the meaning of an action. This, however, attributes it to its wording, as if it were said: "When this statement and this speech is said to them." It is like your saying: "alif" is a kind of three letters. And from this: "They claim is the mount of falsehood" [[

Ibn Saʿd related it in al-Ṭabaqāt from the narration of al-Aʿmash from Sharīḥ, who said: "They claim" is the kunya of falsehood. The author mentioned it as a marfūʿ ḥadīth in Sūrat al-Taghābun, but I have not found it with this wording. What is in al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhārī, from the ḥadīth of Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfūʿ ḥadīth: "Evil is the mount of a man: 'they claim.'" Likewise Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Abū Yaʿlā related it, and it is from the narration of Abū Qilāba from him. In al-Bukhārī's narration, between Abū Qilāba and Abū Masʿūd is Abū al-Muhallab.]].

The "mā" in "kamā" (as) may be a kāfa (preventing its governing effect), like it in "rubbamā" (perhaps), and it may be a maṣdariyya (verbal), like it in "bi-mā raḥubat" (with what it was spacious).

The "al" in "al-nās" (the people) is for the specific known referent: that is, "as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him believed." Or they are known people, like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, because they were of their own kind and of their species, meaning: as your companions and brothers believed. Or it is for the genus, meaning: as those perfect in humanity believed. Or the believers are made as if they were "the people" in reality, and whoever else is like the animals in lacking the discernment between truth and falsehood.

The interrogative in ﴿أَنُؤْمِنُ﴾ (Shall we believe?) carries the meaning of denial. The "al" in ﴿السُّفَهاءُ﴾ (the fools) has its inclination toward "the people," as when you say to your companion, "Indeed Zayd has informed on you," and he replies, "Has the fool really done so?" It is also permissible that it be for the genus, and it includes under it those mentioned, according to their own claim and belief, because among them they were the most deeply rooted in foolishness.

If you ask: why did they call them fools and deem their minds deficient, when they were the wise and the superior ones? I say: because in their ignorance and their neglect of reflection and of being fair to themselves, they believed that what they were upon was the truth and that whatever else was falsehood. Whoever mounts the back of falsehood is a fool. Also, they were in a middle-level leadership among their people and in prosperity, while most of the believers were poor, and among them were clients such as Ṣuhayb, Bilāl, and Khabbāb. So they called them fools to belittle their status. Or they meant ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, and their leaving their religion, and what their Islam had cast down and weakened their support. They said this as a show of forbearance, to guard against the gloating over them, while knowing that they were far from foolishness. Foolishness is the weakness of reason and lightness of forbearance.

If you ask: why was this verse concluded with ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (they do not know), while the preceding one was concluded with ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (they do not perceive)? I say: because the matter of religion, and the realization that the believers are upon the truth while they are upon falsehood, requires reflection and inference until the reflecting person acquires knowledge.

As for hypocrisy, and what it contains of transgression that leads to strife and corruption in the land, it is a worldly matter based on custom, known among people, especially among the Arabs in their Jāhiliyya and what existed among them of raids, mutual enmity, warfare, and factionalism. So it is like the perceived and witnessed. And because foolishness, which is ignorance, was mentioned, mentioning knowledge with it is a better antithesis (ṭibāq) to it.

The context of this verse differs from the context in which the beginning of the story of the hypocrites was presented, so it is not a repetition. For that was to explain their doctrine and to express their hypocrisy, while this is to explain what they used to do with the believers: denying them, mocking them, meeting the faces of the sincere ones and making them think they were with them. Then when they separated from them to the devils of their religion, they confirmed to them what was in their hearts. It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his companions went out one day and encountered a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAbd Allāh said: "Look how I will repel these fools from you." He took the hand of Abū Bakr and said: "Welcome, O al-Ṣiddīq, lord of the Banū Taym, shaykh of Islam, second of the Messenger of Allah in the cave, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿUmar and said: "Welcome, lord of the Banū ʿAdī, al-Fārūq, strong in the religion of Allah, the one who gave his soul and wealth for the Messenger of Allah." Then he took the hand of ʿAlī and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of Allah and his son-in-law, lord of the Banū Hāshim, apart from the Messenger of Allah." Then they separated, and he said to his companions: "How did you see me act?" They praised him well, and so it was revealed.

It is said "laqītuhu" and "lāqaytuhu" when you meet him closely; and he is "jārī mulāqī" and "murāwiqī." Abū Ḥanīfa recited: ﴿وَإِذا لاقوا﴾.

"Khalawtu bi-fulān" and "ilayhi" means when you are alone with him. It is also permissible that it comes from "khalā" meaning "passed away," and "khalāka dhamm" means: he passed you and went by you. From it: "al-qurūn al-khāliya" (the past generations). And from "khalawtu bihi" when you mock him, from your saying: "Khalā fulān bi-ʿarḍ fulān," meaning he played with his honor. The meaning is: "When they carried the mockery of the believers to their devils and told them of it," just as you say: "I convey to you such-and-such and I blame him to you." Their devils are those who resembled the devils in their rebelliousness. Sībawayh made the nūn of "shayṭān" (devil) original in one place of his book and extra in another. The evidence for its originality is their saying "tashayṭana" (to act like a devil), and its derivation is from "shaṭana," meaning to be far, because of its distance from righteousness and goodness; and from "shāṭa," meaning to perish, if its nūn is taken as extra. And among its names is falsehood.

﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ (We are with you): we are your companions and your agreers in your religion. If you ask: why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence, while to their devils it was in the nominal sentence confirmed by "inna"? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why was their address to the believers in the verbal sentence...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He built this exposition on the premise that the nominal sentence is more firm than the verbal, especially when emphasized with "inna" and followed by "innamā," while he has also related the faith of the sincere believers in the verbal sentence in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger﴾. In general, al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, did excellently in his exposition, achieving what he wished and summarizing what he intended.]] I say: what they addressed the believers with is not worthy of the strongest and most emphatic of the two statements, because they were claiming the recent appearance and emergence of faith from them, not claiming that they were unique in faith, with no dust of doubt on it. This is either because their own selves do not assist them in it, since they have no motive or driver from their beliefs, and so is every statement that does not proceed from enthusiasm, true desire, and conviction. Or because it would not be accepted from them had they said it with the form of emphasis and exaggeration. How could they say it and hope for its acceptance while they were among the Emigrants and Helpers, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel?

Do you not see Allah's relating the speech of the believers: ﴿Our Lord, we have indeed believed﴾? As for addressing their brothers, they, in what they reported about themselves, were firm in Judaism and persistent in the belief of disbelief, far from turning away from it, with true desire, abundant energy, and joy in speaking it. What they said of that was accepted from them and received from them, so it was a place for confirmation and a sign of emphasis.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ (we are only mockers) relate to ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾? I say: it is an emphasis of it, because their saying ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ means steadfastness in Judaism. And their saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾ is a rejection of Islam and a repelling of it from them, because one who mocks a thing and belittles it denies it and repels its being regarded. Repelling the opposite of a thing is either a confirmation of its firmness or a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), as if they were objected to when they said to them ﴿إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾, so they said: "Then what about you, if it is established that you are with us, agreeing with the people of Islam?" So they said ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾.

Mockery (istihzāʾ) is ridicule and belittling. The root of the matter is lightness, from "al-hazʾ," which is quick killing; and "hazaʾa yahzaʾu" means he died on the spot. From some Arabs: "I walked and became tired, and I thought I would die on my spot." And "his she-camel hazaʾa by him," meaning she hastened and was light.

If you ask: mockery cannot be attributed to Allah the Exalted, because He is exalted above the ugly, and ridicule belongs to the category of defect and ignorance. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾? So what is the meaning of His mocking them? I say: its meaning is the inflicting of humiliation and lowliness upon them, because the mocker's aim, which he is shooting at, is seeking lightness and disparagement from the one he mocks, and bringing humiliation and lowliness upon him. The derivation, as we mentioned, is evidence for this. Mockery (tahakkum) has become frequent in the speech of Allah the Exalted toward the disbelievers, and its purpose is belittling their status, despising their affair, and indicating that their doctrines deserve to be ridiculed by mockers and laughed at by laughers. It is also permissible that it is meant in the sense mentioned in ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ (they deceive), that the rulings of Muslims apply to them outwardly, while He conceals what is intended for them. It is said: the recompense for mockery was named by its name, like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, and ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner﴾.

If you ask: how does His saying ﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾ (Allah mocks them) begin as a new sentence and is not coordinated with what precedes it? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: how does His saying 'Allah mocks them' begin and is not made coordinated...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If someone says, "Is this meaning not derived from the coordination?" It is said to him: had it been coordinated, it would indicate that the aim is wholly the gathering of the content of both sentences, and it would turn away from this meaning which the resumptive construction alone conveys.]]. I say: it is a resumptive sentence of extreme eloquence and grandeur. In it is that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the One who mocks them with the most eloquent mockery, whose mockery against Him is not mockery and does not count in comparison to it, because of the punishment that descends upon them and the humiliation and abasement that settles on them. In it also is that Allah is the One who undertakes mocking them as vengeance for the believers, and does not oblige the believers to oppose them with a similar mockery. If you ask: why was it not said, "Allah is a mocker of them," so that it would correspond to His saying ﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾? [[

Maḥmūd, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'Allah is a mocker of them'...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: For this difference between the verb and the noun, the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered﴾.

Since the frequent and renewed occurrence of mockery and the gathering of the birds with it is a constant matter, the mockery was expressed with a verbal form and the gathering with a nominal form. Further elaboration on this will come, God willing.

I say: because "yastahzi'" (He mocks) indicates that mockery occurs and is renewed time after time. Likewise were God's punishments upon them and the afflictions that descended upon them. "Do they not see that they are tested every year, once or twice?" [9:126] And they were not free, for most of their time, from the tearing of veils and the exposure of secrets, and revelation concerning them, and a sense of dread lest something be revealed about them: "The hypocrites fear that a surah may be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts." [9:64] "Say: Mock on; surely God will bring forth what you fear." [9:64]

"And He extends them in their transgression" (yamudduhum fi tughyanihim): from the verb madda (to supply) an army, meaning to increase it and add to it what strengthens and multiplies it. Likewise madda the inkwell (addadha): he added to it what improves it. And I madadtu the lamp and the land: when I improved them with oil and manure. And the Devil "mad-dahu fi al-ghayy" and amadahu: when he continues to supply him with whisperings until his error follows on and increases.
