If you ask: why do you claim it is from the root madd (supply) and not from madd in the sense of lengthening (life), granting respite or delaying? I reply: sufficient proof that it is from madd (supply) and not from madd (lengthening) is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin: "wa-yamudduhum" (with the ḍamma on the yāʾ and the doubled dāl), and the reading of Nafi': "wa-ikhwanuhum yamudduunahum" (and their brothers supply them). The meaning of granting respite is, in that case, expressed with the lām, as in amla lahu (he granted him respite).

If you ask: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression, when this is the act of the devils? Do you not see His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error" [7:202]? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: how is it permissible that God should grant them supply in transgression...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: What prevents him from upholding it according to its apparent sense and leaving it in its place is only that it is pure monotheism and true reality, while the Qadariyya are far from monotheism by stages.]

I say: either it is understood that when God withheld from them the graces He bestows upon the believers, and forsook them because of their disbelief and persistence in it, their hearts remained with an increase of rust and darkness, just as the believers' hearts increased in expansion and light; that increase is called "supply." It is attributed to God, the Exalted, because it is caused by His action toward them on account of their disbelief. Or it is understood as a denial of compulsion and coercion. Or the Devil's action is attributed to God because it is by His enabling, His empowering, and His leaving free between him and the misguiding of His servants.

If you ask: what led them to interpret the supply in transgression as respite, when the lexical meaning, as you mentioned, does not accommodate it? I reply: fear of taking the step of attributing to God what they attributed to the devils drove them to it. But the correct meaning is that which the wording matches and which confirms its soundness; otherwise it would be like the wild sheep among ostriches.

It is incumbent upon the interpreter of the Book of God, which is overwhelming and whose speech is inimitable, to take care in his interpretations that the composition remains in its beauty, that eloquence retains its perfection, and that what the challenge was made with remains free from any defect. If he does not observe the conventions of the language, then his observance of composition and eloquence is in stages. What we have said is supported by al-Hasan's saying in his tafsir: "In their misguidance they persist, and these are of those sealed." Transgression (tughyan) is excessiveness in disbelief and exceeding the limit in insolence.

Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with him, read "fi tughyanihim" with a kasra, and both are dialects, like laqiyan and laqiyan, and ghaniyan and ghaniyan. If you ask: what is the point in attributing it to them? [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: what is the point of attributing transgression to them...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Every act that proceeds from the servant by choice has two considerations. If you look at its existence, its origination, and the particular aspects of its specification, attribute that to God's power and will alone, with no partner. If you look at its distinction from compulsion that is necessary, attribute it in this respect to the servant, which is the attribution expressed in the Sharia as acquisition (kasb), as in His saying: "for what your hands have earned" [42:30]. This is also realized if you present to your mind the necessary trembling movement and the voluntary one, for you will necessarily distinguish between them by that attribution. Once the plurality of considerations is established, their supply in transgression is created by God, so He attributed it to Himself, and inasmuch as it occurs from them by way of choice, which is expressed as acquisition, He attributed it to them. Build your branches upon the principles of the Sunnah, and the fruits of your branches will be good in Paradise, not as the Qadariyya build, for they dig but only against themselves. May God grant us realization and strengthen us with success.]

I say: in it is that transgression and persistence in misguidance are among what their souls have committed and their hands have wrought, and that God is free of it, refuting the belief of the disbelievers who say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated [others with Him]" [6:148], and negating the notion of whoever might imagine, when the supply is attributed to His essence, that if transgression were not attributed to them, it would be a flaw. He thus removes doubt and uproots it, and repels it from the breast of whoever deviates regarding His attributes. [Mahmud's statement "and negating the notion of whoever might imagine..." intends a refutation of the People of the Sunnah, who say that God, exalted, is in reality the doer of good and evil, and it champions the Mu'tazila who say that He does not do evil nor will it.] The evidence for this is that when He attributed the supply to the devils, He left "ghayy" unrestricted and did not qualify it with an attribution in His saying: "and their brothers supply them in error."

"Al-'Amah" (blindness of heart) is like "al-'Amá" (blindness), except that "al-'Amá" is general for sight and opinion, while "al-'Amah" is specific to opinion: it is bewilderment and hesitation, not knowing where to turn. From it is His saying: "among the ignorant and bewildered" [in the poetic sense: those who have no judgment or insight into the paths]. And "salaka ardan 'amhā'" means he traversed a land with no landmarks. [The sense of "salaka ardan 'amhā'" is that from the same root is the saying of the Arabs...]

The meaning of "buying error in exchange for guidance" is choosing it over it and substituting it for it, by way of metaphor, because buying involves giving a substitute and taking another. [Mahmud said: "Buying requires giving a price..." Ahmad said: From this category is Malik's prohibition, may God be pleased with him, of buying one of two slaughtered geese chosen by the buyer, since he is considered to have chosen each of them, and then a seller of each for the other, so usury enters; this is what later companions of his express by whether one who has the right to own is considered owner or not, and they sometimes say: whoever is given a choice between two things is considered to have transferred to one of them, according to one opinion.]

From it is the poem:
I took with the abundant hair a bald head, and with the bright long teeth a crumbling one,
And with the tall-lived a short one, as the Muslim bought when he became Christian.

[Notes on the poem: "al-Jumma" is abundant hair; the bāʾ is for exchange; "azar" means little hair. The thanāyā are the front teeth, meaning the whole mouth. "Al-Dardar" means the separated teeth. "Al-Haydar" means short. "Ishtara" means "exchanged." The meaning is that he took an old ugly woman in exchange for a young beautiful one. It is related that Jabalah ibn al-Ayham came to Mecca and circumambulated the Kaaba; a man stepped on his waist-wrap, and he struck him. He complained to Umar, may God be pleased with him, who ruled retaliation against Jabalah; he asked for a delay until the next day, fled by night to the Byzantines, and became Christian after Islam. Then he regretted what he had done, and so he became a proverb.]

It is related from Wahb that God, the Mighty and Majestic, said, in reproaching the Children of Israel: "You learn religion for other than religion, you teach for other than practice, and you sell the hereafter for the works of the world." [Attributed as a reproach.]

If you ask: how did they buy error in exchange for guidance when they were not upon guidance? I reply: they were made as if it were in their hands because it was available to them and presented itself to them; so when they left it for error, they had abandoned it and exchanged it for error. Also, the upright religion is the natural disposition (fitra) of God upon which He created people; so whoever goes astray has substituted what contradicts the fitra. "Ḍalāla" means deviation from the right course and loss of guidance. It is said: "ḍalla manzaluh" (his dwelling was lost), "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" (the jerboa's young lost its burrow). [The proverb "ḍalla dirṣ nafaqihi" means its den.] It is then borrowed for going astray from the right path in religion. "Al-Ribḥ" (profit) is the surplus over capital, and for this reason the surplus is called "al-shaff"... [The text continues in the same sense.] "Tijāra" (trade) is the profession of the merchant, who sells and buys for profit. A "nāqa tājira" is a she-camel that, from her beauty and fatness, seems to sell herself. Ibn Abi Ablah read "tijārātuhum."

If you ask: how is loss attributed to trade when it belongs to its practitioners? I reply: it is attribution by metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), namely attributing the verb to something that is clothed with what is in truth its own, just as trade was clothed with the buyers. If you ask: is it valid to say "your slave profited and your slave-girl lost" by metaphorical attribution? I reply: yes, when the context indicates it. Likewise the condition for the validity of "I saw a lion" when you mean a brave man is that a context indicates it; otherwise it is invalid.

If you ask: grant that buying error in exchange for guidance was metaphorical in the sense of substitution; what is the point of mentioning profit and trade? As though there were an actual transaction. [Mahmud said: "Grant that buying error in exchange for guidance..." Ahmad said: this kind is close to the "completion" (tatmīm) which the rhetoricians illustrate with al-Khansa's words: "Indeed Sakhr is followed by the guided, as if he were a banner with fire at its top."] I say: this is of the beautiful craft that carries metaphor to its highest peak, namely that a word is driven in the manner of metaphor and then followed by terms similar to it and its sisters; when they follow one another you will not see a speech more beautiful in finish, richer in lustre and brilliance. This is the "tarshīḥ" (nurturing) metaphor. Like the Arabs' saying about the dull: "as if the ears of his heart were a stripped palm-frond," where they liken him to a donkey, then nurture it by claiming for his heart two ears and claiming for them drooping, to represent his dullness in a manner that joins it to the dullness of a donkey in visible observation. Similar is: "When I saw the eagle overcome the son of Dayah [the crow], and nest in his two nests, my chest stirred for him." [Likening white hair to an eagle by the common whiteness, and youth to a crow by blackness; the nesting is nurturing.] Likewise the saying of one of their outlaws about his mother: "Though Umm al-Radin is proud, she is not knowing of the ways of the noble; when the Devil crept into her nape, we pursued him with the twisted rope." [The metaphor of the jerboa's hole, "qaṣʿa" and "tanaffaqa," is used for the Devil's entry and expulsion.] That is: when the Devil enters her nape, we extract him from his exit with the twisted rope. He means: when she is angry and bad-tempered, we strive to remove her anger.

He first borrowed "qaṣʿa," then added "tanaffaqa," then "the twisted rope." So likewise, when God mentioned buying, He followed it with what resembles it and fits it, and what completes it by joining it, representing their loss and depicting its reality. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "so their trade did not profit, nor were they guided"? I reply: what traders seek in their dealings is two things: the safety of capital and profit. These have lost both aims together, for their capital was guidance, so nothing remained for them with error. When nothing remained in their hands but error, they were not described as attaining profit, even if they gained some worldly aims, because the one who is astray is a lost loser, and one whose capital is not preserved is not said to have profited. And they were not guided to the ways of trade, as merchants who manage affairs and know what profits and what loses are.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

When He had stated the reality of their condition, He followed it with a parable, as an addition to the disclosure and a completion of the clarification. The use of parables by the Arabs, and the citing by scholars of similes and analogues, is a matter well known for bringing forth the hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, so that it shows you the imagined in the form of the certain, the presumed in the guise of the assured, and the absent as though it were witnessed. It also serves to rebuke the most contentious adversary and to subdue the wild, stubborn one. For this reason God has multiplied parables in His Manifest Book and in all His other scriptures, and they became widespread in the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in the speech of the prophets and the wise. God the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [29:43]. Among the surahs of the Gospel is the Surah of Parables. The word mathal (parable) in its original usage means "likeness" (mithl), that is, "analogue" (nazir). It is said: mathal, mathal and mathil, like shabah, shabah and shabih. Then the term was applied to the widely circulating saying whose point of application matches its source: mathal (proverb).

They did not coin a parable, nor did they regard it as worthy of being transmitted and accepted, except for a saying that has some strangeness in certain respects. For this reason it was preserved and protected from alteration. If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ and ﴿The likeness of the hypocrites and the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾, such that one of the two likenesses is compared with its companion? I say: the term mathal is used metaphorically, like "lion" for a brave man, for a state, an attribute, or a story, when it has a significant and strange character. It is as if it were said: "Their strange condition is like the condition of one who kindled a fire." Similarly His words ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ [13:35], meaning: "And among what We have related to you of wonders is the story of the wondrous Garden," and then He proceeded to explain its wonders. And ﴿To God belongs the highest likeness﴾ [16:60], meaning: the attribute that has a dignity of greatness and majesty.

﴿Their likeness in the Torah﴾ [48:29]: that is, their attribute and their condition that is marvelled at. Because of the sense of strangeness inherent in mathal, they said: "So-and-so is a mathal in good and evil," and so they derived from it an adjective for one whose condition is wondrous.

If you ask: how is the group likened to the singular? I say: alladhi (the one who) is placed in the position of alladhina (those who), as in His words ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged﴾ [9:69]. What permitted placing alladhi for alladhina, while it was not permissible to place qa'im for qa'imin or similar attributes, are two factors:

The first: that alladhi, being a link to describe any definite noun by a clause, and its frequent occurrence in their speech, and because it is extended by its relative clause, is deserving of lightening; for this reason they wore it down by elision, dropping its yā', then its kasra, and then they restricted it to the lām alone in the forms of the active and passive participles. The second: that its plural is not like the plural of other words formed with wāw and nūn. That is merely a sign of increased indication. Do you not see that all the other relative pronouns have plural forms while the singular in them is singular? Or the intention is the genus of those who kindle, or the plural is intended, or the group that kindled a fire. Moreover, the hypocrites and their persons were not likened to the person of the one who kindled, so that a likening of the group to the singular would follow; rather, their story was likened to the story of the one who kindled. Similar to this is His words ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾ [62:5], and His words ﴿They look at you with the look of one fainting from death﴾ [33:19].

Wuquad al-nar (the kindling of the fire) is its blazing and the rising of its flame. Among its cognates: "wa-qal fi al-jabal" when it ascends and rises. Nar (fire) is a fine, luminous, hot, burning substance. Nur (light) is its brightness and the brightness of anything shining, and it is the opposite of darkness. Its derivation is from nara yanur, meaning to flee, because in it there is movement and agitation, and nur is derived from it. Idā'a (illumination) is the excess of lighting. The confirmation of this is His words ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [10:5]. In the verse, the verb ḍā'at is transitive. It may also be intransitive, with its subject being what surrounds it. The feminine form is used in accordance with the sense, because what surrounds the kindler is places and things. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah (ḍā'at). There is another possibility, namely that a pronoun referring to the fire is concealed in the verb, and the shining of the fire's light around it is treated as the shining of the fire itself, with mā being either superfluous or a relative pronoun in the sense of "places." Ḥawlahu is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and its formation signifies circling and encompassing; and the year is called ḥawl because it revolves.

If you ask: where is the response of lammā?
I say: there are two possibilities. One is that its response is dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim (God took away their light). The second is that it is omitted, as it is omitted in His words ﴿So when they had taken him away﴾ [12:15]. Its omission is permissible because the sentence is lengthy while there is no ambiguity, the indicator being present. Omission is preferable to mention because of its concision, while expressing the state in which the kindler found himself with what is more eloquent than the word in conveying the meaning, as if it were said: "So when its surroundings were lit, it went out, and they remained stumbling in darkness, bewildered and grieving over the loss of the light, disappointed after the toil of kindling the fire."

If you ask: then if the response is considered omitted, to what does dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim attach? I say: it is a resumptive sentence, as if, when their state was likened to the state of the kindler whose fire was extinguished, a questioner intervened and said: "What is the matter with them that their state has been likened to the state of this kindler?" So it was said to him: "God took away their light." Or it may be a substitute for the whole simile by way of explanation. If you ask: in this possibility the pronoun has returned to the hypocrites, so what is its referent in the second possibility? [Note: "its referent in the second possibility" is probably the earlier one. (ʿ)] I say: its referent is alladhi istawqada (the one who kindled), because it has the sense of a plural. As for the plurality or singularity of this pronoun in ḥawlahu, it is by agreement with the wording at one time and with the sense at another.

If you ask: what is the meaning of ascribing the verb to God the Exalted in His words dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim? I say: when fire is extinguished by a heavenly cause, wind or rain, then God has extinguished it and taken away the light of the kindler. And there is another possibility, namely that the kindler in this case is one who kindles a fire that God does not approve of. Then this fire is either a metaphorical fire, like the fire of sedition and enmity to Islam, and such a fire is short in the duration of its blaze and brief in its survival. Do you not see His words ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ [5:64]? Or it is a real fire, kindled by the deceivers so that they might reach some sin through the illumination it gives, and grope their way along the paths of folly; then God extinguished it and frustrated their hopes.

If you ask: how is it valid for a metaphorical fire to be described as illuminating what surrounds the kindler? I say: it is in the manner of the metaphor that is nurtured (al-majaz al-murashshah), so consider it well.

If you ask: why was it not said "God took away their radiance," in accordance with His words ﴿When it lit up﴾? I say: mentioning the light (nur) is more eloquent, because radiance (ḍaw') implies increase. If it had been said "God took away their radiance," it would have suggested the removal of the increase while what is called light remains; whereas the purpose is the removal of light from them altogether and its complete obliteration.

Do you not see how He mentioned after it ﴿and left them in darknesses﴾ [2:17], and darkness is an expression for the absence and obliteration of light, and how He put it in the plural, and how He made it indefinite, and how He followed it with what indicates that it is a dark, indistinct darkness in which no two shapes can be discerned, namely His words ﴿they do not see﴾. If you ask: then why was it described with illumination? I say: this is according to the manner of their saying: "Falsehood has a momentary assault and then vanishes; the wind of misguidance has a gust and then subsides; and the fire of the 'arfaj (a bush) is a likeness of the momentary elation of every arrogant one."

The difference between adhhaba-hu and dhahaba bi-hi is that the meaning of adhhabahu is: he removed it and caused it to go away. One says dhahaba bi-hi when he takes it along and goes off with it. Dhahaba al-sultan bi-mali-hi means he seized his property. ﴿So when they had taken him away﴾ [12:15]; ﴿Then each god would have taken away what he created﴾ [23:91]. From this is "dhahabat bi-hi al-khuyala' (pride carried him away)." The meaning is: God took hold of their light and held it back, ﴿and whatever He withholds, none can release﴾ [35:2], so this is more eloquent than causing it to go away. Al-Yamani recited adhhaba Allahu nurahum (God caused their light to go away). And tarak means to cast off and leave; when it is attached to one object, as in the saying "taraka-hu tarka zabyi zillahu" (he left him like a gazelle leaves its shadow), it means that. When it is attached to two objects, it is considered to bear the meaning of ṣayyara (to make), and so it follows the course of verbs of the heart, like the saying of 'Antara:

[Verse quoted in the commentary:]
So I struck his garments with the hard, unyielding spear, for the noble is not forbidden from the spears.
So I left him as a portion for the beasts of prey, tearing at him, nibbling at his fine fingers and wrist.

These are the verses of 'Antara ibn Shaddad al-'Absi from his mu'allaqa. He means: I tore his garments with the dry, hard spear, that is, his heart and inner organs, so it is a metonymy for them. Or: I pierced his garments, meaning I strung them upon his body by inserting the spear into them. Another version reads "ihābahu," that is, his skin. "For the noble is not..." to the end: a parenthetical clause indicating that it is the custom of the noble to be generous with everything, even with their lives, to the spears. There is in it a kind of mockery.

Fa-taraktu-hu: that is, I made him. Jizr al-siba' (with a vowel on the zay) means their portion and food of flesh. Nahsha and nasha'a: to take with the mouth and tear it. Qadama and yaqdimu, of the patterns 'alima and daraba: to bite with the front teeth. So His saying "yaqdimna" is an apposition. He used "fine" for a fine thing by exaggeration: that is, they devour his fine fingers and his fine wrist. Another version has in place of this half-line: "between the top of his head and the wrist." Ma is superfluous, and "bayna" is an adverb for the tearing. It is permissible that ma is a relative pronoun, a substitute for the object pronoun. Qullat al-ra's is its highest point, like the summit and peak of a mountain.

From the same usage is His words ﴿and left them in darknesses﴾; its original form is: "they are in darknesses," then taraka was introduced and it governed the two parts.

Ẓulmah (darkness) is the absence of light. It is said: it is an accident that opposes light. Its derivation is from the saying "mā ẓalamaka an taf'ala kadhā" (what prevented you and occupied you from doing such and such), because it blocks sight and prevents vision. Al-Hasan recited ẓulumāt with a sukūn on the lām, and al-Yamani recited fī ẓulmah in the singular. The omitted object of "lā yubṣirūn" (they do not see) is of the kind that is left out and cast aside, which the mind does not turn to bring to attention, not of the kind that is supposed and intended; as if the verb were not transitive at all, like "ya'mahūn" (they wander blindly) in His words ﴿and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [7:186]. If you ask: in what respect was their state likened to the state of the kindler? I say: in that after the illumination they stumbled into darkness and became entangled in bewilderment. If you ask: where is the illumination in the state of the hypocrite? Is he ever anything but one bewildered and stumbling in the darkness of disbelief? I say: what is meant is the slight benefit they gained from the light of the word uttered upon their tongues; and beyond their illumination by the light of this word lies the darkness of hypocrisy, which casts them into the darkness of God's wrath and the darkness of everlasting punishment. It is also permissible that the comparison is to God's taking away the light of the kindler as God's exposure of their secrets and what they were disgraced by among the believers, and the mark of hypocrisy with which they were branded. The more apt view is that it refers to the seal (ṭab') upon them, in accordance with His words ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [2:18].

There is another explanation of the verse: when they were described as having bought error in exchange for guidance, this simile was appended to it, so that their guidance which they sold is likened to the shining fire surrounding the kindler, and the error they purchased and over which their hearts were sealed is likened to God's taking away their light and leaving them in darkness. The indefiniteness of "fire" is for magnification. Their senses were sound, but when they stopped their ears against hearkening to the truth, and refused to speak it with their tongues, and to look and perceive with their eyes, they were treated as though their faculties had been dulled and the structures by which they were built for perception and comprehension had been broken down, as in the saying:

"Deaf when they hear good spoken of me, but when ill is mentioned of me in their presence, they are all ears."

These are the verses of Qu'nab ibn Umm Sahib, son of Ḍamrah, whose father was Ḍamrah, and Umm Sahib is the kunyah of his mother. He says: "If they hear slander or falsehood which they spread about me, they spread it like birds flying among people out of their joy at what they hear of my faults; but whatever good they hear, they bury it." "Deaf when they hear good spoken of me..." Another version reads "ya'dhanū" (they would take notice) instead of "adhinū," like "yasma'ū" in metre and meaning. "Jahla 'alayya" (ignorance against me) and cowardice before their enemy; the two qualities are wretched, ignorance and cowardice.

The metaphor of flying is clearly stated. Ibn Malik, following al-Farra', said: it is permissible to answer the present tense with the past, though the majority forbid it in the chosen usage. "Whatever they heard of good speech from Ṣāliḥ they hid, so burying is also an explicit metaphor." "They are deaf": that is, like the deaf, which is an eloquent simile and metaphor according to the differing views. "If he is mentioned in their presence with evil, they listen and are silent." Another version reads "sabbah" with a damma: that by which one is reviled. It may also be read "sab'ah" with a sukūn on the ya' then a hamza. Another version reads "wa-mā yasma'ū." Another reads "ṣammū" in the past form instead of "ṣumm." Another reads "bi-sū'in kullu-hum adhun": that is, "all of them are ears," which is on the assumption of the fa', because it is the response of the conditional. It may also be taken as inverted order: that is, "all of them are ears if ill is mentioned," and this is more fitting with what precedes. Making them the very substance of ears is exaggeration. It is also permissible that adhun is a descriptive term applying to the singular and the plural, and that is because of their ignorance and their arrogance towards me, and their cowardice and weakness before their enemy. It is said that it is on the assumption that they collectively gathered ignorance. "Al-khalatān" means the two qualities, and "al-jubn" with two dammas is a dialectal variant of it. There is in it an instance of ītāb through the device of expansion (tawshi'), since he used the dual and explained it with two nouns, the second of which is conjoined to the first, and this is good.

ASamm 'amma sā'ahu samī' (I am deaf to what displeases him, and hearing)

Ṣamma ṣammam, like ta'iba ta'aban. So aṣamm, with fatḥ on the ṣād, is a present-tense verb. Had you made it a noun in the predicative sense with a suppressed pronoun, it would have suited asma' which is conjoined to it. The meaning is that my state is like the state of the deaf, which is a metaphor for that. Asma': that is, I act in accordance with hearing, which is also a metaphor. It is permissible that it is a metonymy. He says: I do not listen to what I dislike, and I listen to the words of God's creatures when I desire them, that is, when they are beloved to me, or when I wish to hear.

Fa-aṣmamtu 'Amran wa-a'maytu-hu ('an al-jūd wa-l-fakhr yawma al-fakhār) (So I made 'Amr deaf and blinded him, from generosity and boasting, on the day of boasting)

He says: when I displayed my glories and my nobility, I made 'Amr deaf, that is, I made him like the deaf, and I blinded him, that is, I made him like the blind. So deafness and blindness are explicit metaphors. The meaning is that I silenced him and made him unable to speak of glory and generosity at the time of my boasting against him. It is also said: "I made him deaf and blind" means: I found him deaf and found him blind, that is, as if he were so, as has passed.

If you ask: what is the method of these metaphors according to the scholars of rhetoric? I say: it is like the saying "hum layth" (they are lions) for the brave, and "bahr" (seas) for the generous. Except that this is in attributes, and that in nouns; and metaphor has come in nouns, attributes and verbs alike. You say: "I saw lions," "I met people deaf to good," "the Islamic dawn," and "the truth shone forth."

If you ask: is what is in the verse called a metaphor? I say: it is a matter of dispute. The scholars of verification hold that it is called an eloquent simile, not a metaphor, because the thing compared (al-musta'ār lahu) is mentioned, and they are the hypocrites. Metaphor is applied only where the thing compared is omitted, and the speech is left devoid of it, fit to be understood as referring to the source and the target alike, were it not for the indication of the situation or the sense of the discourse, like the verse of Zuhayr:

"Before a lion, armed and fearsome, with a mane, whose claws have not been trimmed."

These are the verses of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma from his mu'allaqa praising Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḍamḍam, that he charged upon his enemy with fine strategy, and so he did not frighten many houses. Or the meaning is: he charged against him alone, and he did not frighten houses, that is, people of houses who would assist him. "Ḥayth" (where) is a substitute for "ladā" (before), and it may be that ladā is for an indefinite place, with ḥayth added to a clause. "Umm Qash'am" is a name for death; he likened it to the traveller on the road, by way of the implicit metaphor. "Al-raḥl" (the saddle) is an imaginative figure, and the second "ladā" is a substitute for the first. He abstracted from the praised person another figure, for his perfection in courage, and he metaphorically applied the lion to him by explicit metaphor. "Shākī al-silāḥ": that is, fully armed; this is an abstraction, since it suits the thing compared. Al-Farra' said: it is an inversion of shāyik, that is, one possessing a spike and sharpness. "Muqadhdhaf": that is, large, as if he were thrown with flesh and cast. "Lahu libad": that is, hair matted upon his shoulders. "Aẓfāruhu lam tuqallam" (whose claws have not been trimmed): all of this is a development (tarshīḥ), since it suits the thing used for comparison. In his saying "whose claws have not been trimmed" there is a kind of amplification called īghāl, with which the line is concluded for the sake of exaggeration in the simile, like the saying of al-Khansa' about her brother Ṣakhr: "as if he were a banner of fire on his head."

Therefore you find the most skilful of the eloquent among them seem to forget the simile and turn away from imagining it, overlooking it entirely.

Abu Tammam said:

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 2 of 2):

*"And he ascends until the ignorant man thinks / that he has a need in the sky."* [This is by Abu Tammam, praising Khalid ibn Yazid al-Shaybani and mentioning his father. The pronoun in "ascends" refers to Yazid. He used *al-su'ud* (ascending) as a metaphor (*isti'ara*), borrowing it from the literal height to the figurative height, in the explicit form (*tasrih*). Then he built upon it what is built upon height in place, as an elaboration (*tarshih*) and completion (*tatmim*) of the exaggeration (*mubalagha*) in the comparison (*tashbih*), because that thinking can only be based on seeing him actually ascending. Thinking, like knowing, takes its object directly at times and through a preposition at others. He singled out the ignorant man to show that this thinking is an error. It may resemble an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the metaphor, but the elaboration concealed it. Al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) stated that mentioning the ignorant man is a safeguard against the suspicion that the praised person or the context requires something, given the claim that he is at the utmost level of perfection. The transmission *la-zanna* (with the verb in the past) is well known, and it is on the assumption of an oath with *qad*: that is, "By God, the ignorant man has indeed thought that."]

And someone else said:

*"Do not suppose that within his garment there is a man, / for in it is rain and a lion, with trailing and cubs."* [This is by al-Zamakhshari. He likened the praised person to rain in abundance of goodness and generosity, and to a lion in abundance of courage, and used both as metaphors in the explicit form. On this he built the prohibition against people thinking that there is a man in his garment, to indicate the forgetting of the comparison and the claim of identity (*idda'a al-ittihad*). *Musbil* means one who pours down abundantly, and this refers to the rain. *Mushbil* means one whose cubs have multiplied, that is, whose young are lions, and this refers to the lion. So there is a *laff wa nashr* (arrangement of references). There is also a contrast-like figure (*shibh al-tadad*), in that he combined what is feared with what is hoped for. There is also the *jinas al-lahiq* (near-paronomy) between *ghayth* and *layth*, and between *musbil* and *mushbil*.]

It is not for a speaker to say: he omitted mentioning them from the sentence by deleting the subject, so he climbs thereby to calling it a metaphor, because it is in the status of what is pronounced. Its parallel is the saying of one addressing al-Hajjaj:

*"A lion against me, yet in battles an ostrich, / a fearful bird fleeing at the whistle of the whistler."*

*"Why did you not charge at Ghazala in the fighting? / Rather, your heart was in the wings of a bird."*

[These are by Imran ibn Hittan, the slayer of al-Hajjaj. It is related that Shabib the Kharijite, his mother Jahayza, and his wife Ghazala were of extreme courage. They entered Kufa with thirty thousand horsemen, while al-Hajjaj was there with thirty thousand fighters. They fought him for a full year until he fled from them, and Imran reproached him for this. That is, "You are like a lion." It is not valid as a metaphor according to the majority, given the intention to mention the thing compared. Al-Taftazani permitted it on the basis that what is mentioned is an individual of its individuals, not its very essence. *"Ala"* is connected to *asad* (lion), because of the meaning of courage and strength in it, and *"fi al-hurub"* (in battles) is connected to *na'ama* (ostrich), because of the meaning of cowardice and weakness in it. This is clear according to the view of al-ʿAllama, because *asad* is a metaphor for any brave man, and *na'ama* for any coward. As for the view of the majority, the two words are fixed (*jamidan*), since they remain on their literal meaning, unless it is said that, being in the context of comparison, they were given the attribute upon which the resemblance is built. They may also be connected to a meaning of comparison, or to an omitted circumstantial element (*hal*) from the omitted subject, according to the opinion of Sibawayh. *Al-fatkh* (with vowel a) is softness and separation in the fingers and wings, and *al-fathkha'* is its adjective. *Tanfur* is an attribute of *na'ama*: that is, it is alarmed and frightened from fear of the slightest sound it hears. He described it with utmost weakness to show that the likened one is also like this, then he rebuked him with his saying: "Why did you not charge at that woman in battle?" You did not do that; rather, your heart was pounding and trembling, as if it were in the wings of a bird. This is an eloquent comparison (*tashbih baligh*). It is also narrated as: "Why did you not come out against Ghazala?"]

The meaning of *"fa-hum la yarji'un"* (﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾) is that they will not return to guidance after they have sold it, or away from error after they have bought it, as a seal upon them by the imprinting of nature. Or it means that they are like the bewildered who remain fixed in their place, not moving, not knowing whether to advance or to retreat. And how can they return to where they began?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

When He had stated the reality of their condition, He followed it with a parable, as an addition to the disclosure and a completion of the clarification. The use of parables by the Arabs, and the citing by scholars of similes and analogues, is a matter well known for bringing forth the hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, so that it shows you the imagined in the form of the certain, the presumed in the guise of the assured, and the absent as though it were witnessed. It also serves to rebuke the most contentious adversary and to subdue the wild, stubborn one. For this reason God has multiplied parables in His Manifest Book and in all His other scriptures, and they became widespread in the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in the speech of the prophets and the wise. God the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [29:43]. Among the surahs of the Gospel is the Surah of Parables. The word mathal (parable) in its original usage means "likeness" (mithl), that is, "analogue" (nazir). It is said: mathal, mathal and mathil, like shabah, shabah and shabih. Then the term was applied to the widely circulating saying whose point of application matches its source: mathal (proverb).

They did not coin a parable, nor did they regard it as worthy of being transmitted and accepted, except for a saying that has some strangeness in certain respects. For this reason it was preserved and protected from alteration. If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ and ﴿The likeness of the hypocrites and the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾, such that one of the two likenesses is compared with its companion? I say: the term mathal is used metaphorically, like "lion" for a brave man, for a state, an attribute, or a story, when it has a significant and strange character. It is as if it were said: "Their strange condition is like the condition of one who kindled a fire." Similarly His words ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ [13:35], meaning: "And among what We have related to you of wonders is the story of the wondrous Garden," and then He proceeded to explain its wonders. And ﴿To God belongs the highest likeness﴾ [16:60], meaning: the attribute that has a dignity of greatness and majesty.

﴿Their likeness in the Torah﴾ [48:29]: that is, their attribute and their condition that is marvelled at. Because of the sense of strangeness inherent in mathal, they said: "So-and-so is a mathal in good and evil," and so they derived from it an adjective for one whose condition is wondrous.

If you ask: how is the group likened to the singular? I say: alladhi (the one who) is placed in the position of alladhina (those who), as in His words ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged﴾ [9:69]. What permitted placing alladhi for alladhina, while it was not permissible to place qa'im for qa'imin or similar attributes, are two factors:

The first: that alladhi, being a link to describe any definite noun by a clause, and its frequent occurrence in their speech, and because it is extended by its relative clause, is deserving of lightening; for this reason they wore it down by elision, dropping its yā', then its kasra, and then they restricted it to the lām alone in the forms of the active and passive participles. The second: that its plural is not like the plural of other words formed with wāw and nūn. That is merely a sign of increased indication. Do you not see that all the other relative pronouns have plural forms while the singular in them is singular? Or the intention is the genus of those who kindle, or the plural is intended, or the group that kindled a fire. Moreover, the hypocrites and their persons were not likened to the person of the one who kindled, so that a likening of the group to the singular would follow; rather, their story was likened to the story of the one who kindled. Similar to this is His words ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾ [62:5], and His words ﴿They look at you with the look of one fainting from death﴾ [33:19].

Wuquad al-nar (the kindling of the fire) is its blazing and the rising of its flame. Among its cognates: "wa-qal fi al-jabal" when it ascends and rises. Nar (fire) is a fine, luminous, hot, burning substance. Nur (light) is its brightness and the brightness of anything shining, and it is the opposite of darkness. Its derivation is from nara yanur, meaning to flee, because in it there is movement and agitation, and nur is derived from it. Idā'a (illumination) is the excess of lighting. The confirmation of this is His words ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [10:5]. In the verse, the verb ḍā'at is transitive. It may also be intransitive, with its subject being what surrounds it. The feminine form is used in accordance with the sense, because what surrounds the kindler is places and things. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah (ḍā'at). There is another possibility, namely that a pronoun referring to the fire is concealed in the verb, and the shining of the fire's light around it is treated as the shining of the fire itself, with mā being either superfluous or a relative pronoun in the sense of "places." Ḥawlahu is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and its formation signifies circling and encompassing; and the year is called ḥawl because it revolves.

If you ask: where is the response of lammā?
I say: there are two possibilities. One is that its response is dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim (God took away their light). The second is that it is omitted, as it is omitted in His words ﴿So when they had taken him away﴾ [12:15]. Its omission is permissible because the sentence is lengthy while there is no ambiguity, the indicator being present. Omission is preferable to mention because of its concision, while expressing the state in which the kindler found himself with what is more eloquent than the word in conveying the meaning, as if it were said: "So when its surroundings were lit, it went out, and they remained stumbling in darkness, bewildered and grieving over the loss of the light, disappointed after the toil of kindling the fire."

If you ask: then if the response is considered omitted, to what does dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim attach? I say: it is a resumptive sentence, as if, when their state was likened to the state of the kindler whose fire was extinguished, a questioner intervened and said: "What is the matter with them that their state has been likened to the state of this kindler?" So it was said to him: "God took away their light." Or it may be a substitute for the whole simile by way of explanation. If you ask: in this possibility the pronoun has returned to the hypocrites, so what is its referent in the second possibility? [Note: "its referent in the second possibility" is probably the earlier one. (ʿ)] I say: its referent is alladhi istawqada (the one who kindled), because it has the sense of a plural. As for the plurality or singularity of this pronoun in ḥawlahu, it is by agreement with the wording at one time and with the sense at another.

If you ask: what is the meaning of ascribing the verb to God the Exalted in His words dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim? I say: when fire is extinguished by a heavenly cause, wind or rain, then God has extinguished it and taken away the light of the kindler. And there is another possibility, namely that the kindler in this case is one who kindles a fire that God does not approve of. Then this fire is either a metaphorical fire, like the fire of sedition and enmity to Islam, and such a fire is short in the duration of its blaze and brief in its survival. Do you not see His words ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ [5:64]? Or it is a real fire, kindled by the deceivers so that they might reach some sin through the illumination it gives, and grope their way along the paths of folly; then God extinguished it and frustrated their hopes.

If you ask: how is it valid for a metaphorical fire to be described as illuminating what surrounds the kindler? I say: it is in the manner of the metaphor that is nurtured (al-majaz al-murashshah), so consider it well.

If you ask: why was it not said "God took away their radiance," in accordance with His words ﴿When it lit up﴾? I say: mentioning the light (nur) is more eloquent, because radiance (ḍaw') implies increase. If it had been said "God took away their radiance," it would have suggested the removal of the increase while what is called light remains; whereas the purpose is the removal of light from them altogether and its complete obliteration.

Do you not see how He mentioned after it ﴿and left them in darknesses﴾ [2:17], and darkness is an expression for the absence and obliteration of light, and how He put it in the plural, and how He made it indefinite, and how He followed it with what indicates that it is a dark, indistinct darkness in which no two shapes can be discerned, namely His words ﴿they do not see﴾. If you ask: then why was it described with illumination? I say: this is according to the manner of their saying: "Falsehood has a momentary assault and then vanishes; the wind of misguidance has a gust and then subsides; and the fire of the 'arfaj (a bush) is a likeness of the momentary elation of every arrogant one."

The difference between adhhaba-hu and dhahaba bi-hi is that the meaning of adhhabahu is: he removed it and caused it to go away. One says dhahaba bi-hi when he takes it along and goes off with it. Dhahaba al-sultan bi-mali-hi means he seized his property. ﴿So when they had taken him away﴾ [12:15]; ﴿Then each god would have taken away what he created﴾ [23:91]. From this is "dhahabat bi-hi al-khuyala' (pride carried him away)." The meaning is: God took hold of their light and held it back, ﴿and whatever He withholds, none can release﴾ [35:2], so this is more eloquent than causing it to go away. Al-Yamani recited adhhaba Allahu nurahum (God caused their light to go away). And tarak means to cast off and leave; when it is attached to one object, as in the saying "taraka-hu tarka zabyi zillahu" (he left him like a gazelle leaves its shadow), it means that. When it is attached to two objects, it is considered to bear the meaning of ṣayyara (to make), and so it follows the course of verbs of the heart, like the saying of 'Antara:

[Verse quoted in the commentary:]
So I struck his garments with the hard, unyielding spear, for the noble is not forbidden from the spears.
So I left him as a portion for the beasts of prey, tearing at him, nibbling at his fine fingers and wrist.

These are the verses of 'Antara ibn Shaddad al-'Absi from his mu'allaqa. He means: I tore his garments with the dry, hard spear, that is, his heart and inner organs, so it is a metonymy for them. Or: I pierced his garments, meaning I strung them upon his body by inserting the spear into them. Another version reads "ihābahu," that is, his skin. "For the noble is not..." to the end: a parenthetical clause indicating that it is the custom of the noble to be generous with everything, even with their lives, to the spears. There is in it a kind of mockery.

Fa-taraktu-hu: that is, I made him. Jizr al-siba' (with a vowel on the zay) means their portion and food of flesh. Nahsha and nasha'a: to take with the mouth and tear it. Qadama and yaqdimu, of the patterns 'alima and daraba: to bite with the front teeth. So His saying "yaqdimna" is an apposition. He used "fine" for a fine thing by exaggeration: that is, they devour his fine fingers and his fine wrist. Another version has in place of this half-line: "between the top of his head and the wrist." Ma is superfluous, and "bayna" is an adverb for the tearing. It is permissible that ma is a relative pronoun, a substitute for the object pronoun. Qullat al-ra's is its highest point, like the summit and peak of a mountain.

From the same usage is His words ﴿and left them in darknesses﴾; its original form is: "they are in darknesses," then taraka was introduced and it governed the two parts.

Ẓulmah (darkness) is the absence of light. It is said: it is an accident that opposes light. Its derivation is from the saying "mā ẓalamaka an taf'ala kadhā" (what prevented you and occupied you from doing such and such), because it blocks sight and prevents vision. Al-Hasan recited ẓulumāt with a sukūn on the lām, and al-Yamani recited fī ẓulmah in the singular. The omitted object of "lā yubṣirūn" (they do not see) is of the kind that is left out and cast aside, which the mind does not turn to bring to attention, not of the kind that is supposed and intended; as if the verb were not transitive at all, like "ya'mahūn" (they wander blindly) in His words ﴿and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [7:186]. If you ask: in what respect was their state likened to the state of the kindler? I say: in that after the illumination they stumbled into darkness and became entangled in bewilderment. If you ask: where is the illumination in the state of the hypocrite? Is he ever anything but one bewildered and stumbling in the darkness of disbelief? I say: what is meant is the slight benefit they gained from the light of the word uttered upon their tongues; and beyond their illumination by the light of this word lies the darkness of hypocrisy, which casts them into the darkness of God's wrath and the darkness of everlasting punishment. It is also permissible that the comparison is to God's taking away the light of the kindler as God's exposure of their secrets and what they were disgraced by among the believers, and the mark of hypocrisy with which they were branded. The more apt view is that it refers to the seal (ṭab') upon them, in accordance with His words ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [2:18].

There is another explanation of the verse: when they were described as having bought error in exchange for guidance, this simile was appended to it, so that their guidance which they sold is likened to the shining fire surrounding the kindler, and the error they purchased and over which their hearts were sealed is likened to God's taking away their light and leaving them in darkness. The indefiniteness of "fire" is for magnification. Their senses were sound, but when they stopped their ears against hearkening to the truth, and refused to speak it with their tongues, and to look and perceive with their eyes, they were treated as though their faculties had been dulled and the structures by which they were built for perception and comprehension had been broken down, as in the saying:

"Deaf when they hear good spoken of me, but when ill is mentioned of me in their presence, they are all ears."

These are the verses of Qu'nab ibn Umm Sahib, son of Ḍamrah, whose father was Ḍamrah, and Umm Sahib is the kunyah of his mother. He says: "If they hear slander or falsehood which they spread about me, they spread it like birds flying among people out of their joy at what they hear of my faults; but whatever good they hear, they bury it." "Deaf when they hear good spoken of me..." Another version reads "ya'dhanū" (they would take notice) instead of "adhinū," like "yasma'ū" in metre and meaning. "Jahla 'alayya" (ignorance against me) and cowardice before their enemy; the two qualities are wretched, ignorance and cowardice.

The metaphor of flying is clearly stated. Ibn Malik, following al-Farra', said: it is permissible to answer the present tense with the past, though the majority forbid it in the chosen usage. "Whatever they heard of good speech from Ṣāliḥ they hid, so burying is also an explicit metaphor." "They are deaf": that is, like the deaf, which is an eloquent simile and metaphor according to the differing views. "If he is mentioned in their presence with evil, they listen and are silent." Another version reads "sabbah" with a damma: that by which one is reviled. It may also be read "sab'ah" with a sukūn on the ya' then a hamza. Another version reads "wa-mā yasma'ū." Another reads "ṣammū" in the past form instead of "ṣumm." Another reads "bi-sū'in kullu-hum adhun": that is, "all of them are ears," which is on the assumption of the fa', because it is the response of the conditional. It may also be taken as inverted order: that is, "all of them are ears if ill is mentioned," and this is more fitting with what precedes. Making them the very substance of ears is exaggeration. It is also permissible that adhun is a descriptive term applying to the singular and the plural, and that is because of their ignorance and their arrogance towards me, and their cowardice and weakness before their enemy. It is said that it is on the assumption that they collectively gathered ignorance. "Al-khalatān" means the two qualities, and "al-jubn" with two dammas is a dialectal variant of it. There is in it an instance of ītāb through the device of expansion (tawshi'), since he used the dual and explained it with two nouns, the second of which is conjoined to the first, and this is good.

ASamm 'amma sā'ahu samī' (I am deaf to what displeases him, and hearing)

Ṣamma ṣammam, like ta'iba ta'aban. So aṣamm, with fatḥ on the ṣād, is a present-tense verb. Had you made it a noun in the predicative sense with a suppressed pronoun, it would have suited asma' which is conjoined to it. The meaning is that my state is like the state of the deaf, which is a metaphor for that. Asma': that is, I act in accordance with hearing, which is also a metaphor. It is permissible that it is a metonymy. He says: I do not listen to what I dislike, and I listen to the words of God's creatures when I desire them, that is, when they are beloved to me, or when I wish to hear.

Fa-aṣmamtu 'Amran wa-a'maytu-hu ('an al-jūd wa-l-fakhr yawma al-fakhār) (So I made 'Amr deaf and blinded him, from generosity and boasting, on the day of boasting)

He says: when I displayed my glories and my nobility, I made 'Amr deaf, that is, I made him like the deaf, and I blinded him, that is, I made him like the blind. So deafness and blindness are explicit metaphors. The meaning is that I silenced him and made him unable to speak of glory and generosity at the time of my boasting against him. It is also said: "I made him deaf and blind" means: I found him deaf and found him blind, that is, as if he were so, as has passed.

If you ask: what is the method of these metaphors according to the scholars of rhetoric? I say: it is like the saying "hum layth" (they are lions) for the brave, and "bahr" (seas) for the generous. Except that this is in attributes, and that in nouns; and metaphor has come in nouns, attributes and verbs alike. You say: "I saw lions," "I met people deaf to good," "the Islamic dawn," and "the truth shone forth."

If you ask: is what is in the verse called a metaphor? I say: it is a matter of dispute. The scholars of verification hold that it is called an eloquent simile, not a metaphor, because the thing compared (al-musta'ār lahu) is mentioned, and they are the hypocrites. Metaphor is applied only where the thing compared is omitted, and the speech is left devoid of it, fit to be understood as referring to the source and the target alike, were it not for the indication of the situation or the sense of the discourse, like the verse of Zuhayr:

"Before a lion, armed and fearsome, with a mane, whose claws have not been trimmed."

These are the verses of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma from his mu'allaqa praising Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḍamḍam, that he charged upon his enemy with fine strategy, and so he did not frighten many houses. Or the meaning is: he charged against him alone, and he did not frighten houses, that is, people of houses who would assist him. "Ḥayth" (where) is a substitute for "ladā" (before), and it may be that ladā is for an indefinite place, with ḥayth added to a clause. "Umm Qash'am" is a name for death; he likened it to the traveller on the road, by way of the implicit metaphor. "Al-raḥl" (the saddle) is an imaginative figure, and the second "ladā" is a substitute for the first. He abstracted from the praised person another figure, for his perfection in courage, and he metaphorically applied the lion to him by explicit metaphor. "Shākī al-silāḥ": that is, fully armed; this is an abstraction, since it suits the thing compared. Al-Farra' said: it is an inversion of shāyik, that is, one possessing a spike and sharpness. "Muqadhdhaf": that is, large, as if he were thrown with flesh and cast. "Lahu libad": that is, hair matted upon his shoulders. "Aẓfāruhu lam tuqallam" (whose claws have not been trimmed): all of this is a development (tarshīḥ), since it suits the thing used for comparison. In his saying "whose claws have not been trimmed" there is a kind of amplification called īghāl, with which the line is concluded for the sake of exaggeration in the simile, like the saying of al-Khansa' about her brother Ṣakhr: "as if he were a banner of fire on his head."

Therefore you find the most skilful of the eloquent among them seem to forget the simile and turn away from imagining it, overlooking it entirely.

Abu Tammam said:

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 17–18 (part 2 of 2):

*"And he ascends until the ignorant man thinks / that he has a need in the sky."* [This is by Abu Tammam, praising Khalid ibn Yazid al-Shaybani and mentioning his father. The pronoun in "ascends" refers to Yazid. He used *al-su'ud* (ascending) as a metaphor (*isti'ara*), borrowing it from the literal height to the figurative height, in the explicit form (*tasrih*). Then he built upon it what is built upon height in place, as an elaboration (*tarshih*) and completion (*tatmim*) of the exaggeration (*mubalagha*) in the comparison (*tashbih*), because that thinking can only be based on seeing him actually ascending. Thinking, like knowing, takes its object directly at times and through a preposition at others. He singled out the ignorant man to show that this thinking is an error. It may resemble an abstraction (*tajrid*) of the metaphor, but the elaboration concealed it. Al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) stated that mentioning the ignorant man is a safeguard against the suspicion that the praised person or the context requires something, given the claim that he is at the utmost level of perfection. The transmission *la-zanna* (with the verb in the past) is well known, and it is on the assumption of an oath with *qad*: that is, "By God, the ignorant man has indeed thought that."]

And someone else said:

*"Do not suppose that within his garment there is a man, / for in it is rain and a lion, with trailing and cubs."* [This is by al-Zamakhshari. He likened the praised person to rain in abundance of goodness and generosity, and to a lion in abundance of courage, and used both as metaphors in the explicit form. On this he built the prohibition against people thinking that there is a man in his garment, to indicate the forgetting of the comparison and the claim of identity (*idda'a al-ittihad*). *Musbil* means one who pours down abundantly, and this refers to the rain. *Mushbil* means one whose cubs have multiplied, that is, whose young are lions, and this refers to the lion. So there is a *laff wa nashr* (arrangement of references). There is also a contrast-like figure (*shibh al-tadad*), in that he combined what is feared with what is hoped for. There is also the *jinas al-lahiq* (near-paronomy) between *ghayth* and *layth*, and between *musbil* and *mushbil*.]

It is not for a speaker to say: he omitted mentioning them from the sentence by deleting the subject, so he climbs thereby to calling it a metaphor, because it is in the status of what is pronounced. Its parallel is the saying of one addressing al-Hajjaj:

*"A lion against me, yet in battles an ostrich, / a fearful bird fleeing at the whistle of the whistler."*

*"Why did you not charge at Ghazala in the fighting? / Rather, your heart was in the wings of a bird."*

[These are by Imran ibn Hittan, the slayer of al-Hajjaj. It is related that Shabib the Kharijite, his mother Jahayza, and his wife Ghazala were of extreme courage. They entered Kufa with thirty thousand horsemen, while al-Hajjaj was there with thirty thousand fighters. They fought him for a full year until he fled from them, and Imran reproached him for this. That is, "You are like a lion." It is not valid as a metaphor according to the majority, given the intention to mention the thing compared. Al-Taftazani permitted it on the basis that what is mentioned is an individual of its individuals, not its very essence. *"Ala"* is connected to *asad* (lion), because of the meaning of courage and strength in it, and *"fi al-hurub"* (in battles) is connected to *na'ama* (ostrich), because of the meaning of cowardice and weakness in it. This is clear according to the view of al-ʿAllama, because *asad* is a metaphor for any brave man, and *na'ama* for any coward. As for the view of the majority, the two words are fixed (*jamidan*), since they remain on their literal meaning, unless it is said that, being in the context of comparison, they were given the attribute upon which the resemblance is built. They may also be connected to a meaning of comparison, or to an omitted circumstantial element (*hal*) from the omitted subject, according to the opinion of Sibawayh. *Al-fatkh* (with vowel a) is softness and separation in the fingers and wings, and *al-fathkha'* is its adjective. *Tanfur* is an attribute of *na'ama*: that is, it is alarmed and frightened from fear of the slightest sound it hears. He described it with utmost weakness to show that the likened one is also like this, then he rebuked him with his saying: "Why did you not charge at that woman in battle?" You did not do that; rather, your heart was pounding and trembling, as if it were in the wings of a bird. This is an eloquent comparison (*tashbih baligh*). It is also narrated as: "Why did you not come out against Ghazala?"]

The meaning of *"fa-hum la yarji'un"* (﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾) is that they will not return to guidance after they have sold it, or away from error after they have bought it, as a seal upon them by the imprinting of nature. Or it means that they are like the bewildered who remain fixed in their place, not moving, not knowing whether to advance or to retreat. And how can they return to where they began?

Then Allah, glorified is He, reinforced the matter concerning them with another parable, so that it would be a further unveiling of their condition and a clarification following a clarification. Just as the eloquent speaker, in places where brevity and concision are called for, must be concise and brief, so too his duty in places where detail and fullness are called for is to elaborate and to be thorough. Al-Jahiz recited:

They deliver long sermons, and at other times
they convey (their meaning) by the glances of the eye, fearing the watchers.

[Al-Jahiz recited it. Another version reads "yarmun" (they throw). He used the metaphor of "throwing" for bringing out speech from the mouth in abundance, in the manner of explicit statement.
It is said: wahá lahu, wa ilayhi wahyan, and awḥá lahu wa ilayhi īḥāʼan, meaning: he conveyed speech to him, or signaled to him with it, or inspired him with it. So al-waḥy is a verbal noun of wahá, or a nominal form of the verbal noun of awḥá. Al-laḥẓ is signaling with the corner of the eye to the right or to the left. Al-lāḥiẓ is originally a descriptive term, but it is also the name of the corner of the eye. That is why it was pluralized as lawāḥiẓ, and waḥy was attributed to it because it is the instrument. It is also possible that it is the plural of lāḥiẓa, like a female neck. The meaning: they speak long sermons at times when they feel safe, and they convey the message by glances at other times, out of fear of the watchers. So for every situation they have a suitable speech.]

Among the parables that Allah reinforced in the Revelation is His saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike, nor the darknesses and the light, nor the shade and the scorching heat. And the living and the dead are not alike.﴾ Have you not seen how Dhu al-Rummah acted in his poem?

Is that (the wild ass) or a mottled one whose forelegs are marked with white patches ...
Is that or one dyed with the red of the sī, whose pasture ...

[Dhu al-Rummah, describing his she-camel, first likened her to a wild ass, then said: "Is that the wild ass which my she-camel resembles, or a mottled one (tamash)?" Tamash, with a fatḥa-less pattern, means varied in color; kaḥadhir means varied in color. Al-washy is a color differing from the rest of the thing. Al-akraʻ is the plural of kurāʻ, the shank. Al-masfa‘ is the black one, from al-sufʻa, which is blackness. Al-nāshiṭ is one that leaves one land for another. Al-shabab, like kaḥadhir, is an old male wild cow. Then he said: "Is that the bull she resembles, or the dyed one?", meaning the male ostrich whose shanks have turned red or yellow from eating spring herbage. Al-sī is level ground and also the name of a specific place. Al-marta‘ is a verbal noun or a place noun governed by the adverb within a wider area. Munqalab means returning from pasture to its thirty chicks. It is at its fastest, so she too is swift in her course.
Akra‘uhu is the agent of the adverb, or the agent of tamash. Mar‘atuhu is its agent for the adverb, or a subject whose predicate is the adverb.]

If you say: In the first parable the hypocrite was likened to one who kindles a fire, his display of faith to illumination, and the cessation of his benefit to the extinguishing of the fire. Then what is he likened to in the second parable, with the rain-cloud, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning and the thunderbolts? I reply: One may say that the religion of Islam is likened to the rain-cloud, because hearts come alive through it as the earth comes alive through rain. What is connected to it, the disbelievers, is likened to the darknesses. What it contains of promise and threat is likened to thunder and lightning. What afflicts the disbelievers of fear, calamities and trials from the people of Islam is likened to thunderbolts. The meaning is: "Or like those of a rain-cloud," that is, like a people whom the sky overtook in this condition, and they suffered what they suffered.

If you say: This is the comparison of things with things; where then is mention of the things compared, and why was it not stated explicitly, as in His saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike, nor those who believe and do righteous deeds and the wrongdoer﴾, and in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry,
beside their nest are the jujube and the decayed date?

[Imru' al-Qays describes the eagle which eats the young of birds except their hearts, which is why they are abundant near it, and describes himself as courageous, since he reached the sight of that. He says: as if the hearts of the birds, some moist and some dry, were, while at the eagle's nest, that is its nest, al-‘unnāb, which is a red moist fruit, referring to the moist part. Al-ḥashf is the dry, poor, decayed date that has perished, referring to the dry part. There is thus lafʿ and nashr in ordered arrangement, and antithesis between moist and dry.
It is permissible that raṭaban and yābisan are in the accusative as a substitute for qulūb al-ṭayr, meaning as if the moist and dry of them were the jujube and the decayed date. A partial substitute does not require a pronoun returning to the substituted noun, though the better practice is that it does.]

I say: Just as that is stated explicitly, so it has also come with its mention concealed, in the manner of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet and palatable in its drink, and this one is salty and bitter﴾, and ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a man in whom are partners at odds, and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾. The sound position, which the scholars of rhetoric hold and do not transgress, is this: both comparisons belong to the composite similes, not the separate ones, in which each individual element is not forced to have its own counterpart. This is the decisive opinion and the strong position. Its explanation: the Arabs take things singly, each isolated from the others, none taking hold of another's belt, and compare them with their counterparts, as Imru' al-Qays did and as occurs in the Qur'an. They also compare a state resulting from the combination of several things that have been joined and adhered until they become one thing, with another like it, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah﴾ up to the verse. The purpose is to compare the condition of the Jews in their ignorance of what the Torah contained and its striking signs, with the condition of a donkey in its ignorance of the books of wisdom it carries, the two states being equal to him whether he carries books of wisdom or other burdens; he perceives from it only the toil and fatigue on his back. And like His saying: ﴿And strike for them the parable of the life of this world: like water which We sent down from the sky﴾. The intent is the brevity of the lasting of the world's splendor, like the brevity of the lasting of the green vegetation. But to intend that individual things be compared with individual things, without some of them being bound to others and becoming one thing, is not so.

Likewise, when He described the hypocrites' falling into their error and the bewilderment and confusion into which they plunged, their bewilderment and the severity of their situation were compared with one who suffers when his fire is extinguished after being kindled in the darkness of night, and likewise one whom the sky overtakes on a dark night with thunder, lightning, and fear of thunderbolts.

If you say: What you were estimating in the separate comparison, namely the omission of the modified noun in "Or like those of a rain-cloud", would you estimate the same in the composite comparison? I reply: Were it not for the need of a returning pronoun in His saying: ﴿They put their fingers into their ears﴾, to which it would refer, I would not need to estimate it, because I consider the configuration abstracted from the whole discourse. It makes no difference to me whether the particle of comparison is followed by a single noun to which the comparison can apply or not. Do you not see His saying: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only﴾ the verse, how the particle "ka" (like) was followed by water, while the purpose is not to compare this world with water, nor with some other single thing that would need contrived estimation? Clear in this is the verse of Labid:

And the people are only like the dwellings and their inhabitants,
in them on the day they settled, and on the morrow, desolate ruins.

[He did not intend to compare people with the dwellings themselves, but intended to compare their condition with the world with the condition of dwellings with their inhabitants. His saying "and its inhabitants in it" is a circumstantial clause. "The day they settled it" is in the accusative governed by the preposition-phrase before it, which is deleted. "Ghadwan balāqiʿ" means: and on the morrow they are desolate ruins. The plural of baluqʿ is "bala'ī", meaning empty waste. "Al-ghad" is commonly used like "al-yad", so its original waw appears here. He used "ghad" meaning near time, as one says "af'aluhu bukrah" (I will do it early). The meaning is after a few days. The common element is the swift passing and disappearance after brightness and freshness. You may also take it as a comparison of a single thing with a single thing, the common feature being that people have life-spirits in them, so they are radiant and splendid, then those spirits are removed and they become empty and vacant, like a house inhabited by people which becomes a ruin. This is on the nominative reading of "ahluha". If it is read in the genitive, coordinated with "al-diyar", the first interpretation is required, and "bihā" is then attached to a deleted circumstantial element describing "ahluhā". The bāʼ means "fī" in both readings.]

He did not compare people with dwellings; rather he compared their existence in the world and the swiftness of their passing and annihilation with the settling of the people of dwellings in them and the imminence of their departure from them, leaving them empty and vacant. If you say: Which of the two comparisons is more eloquent? I reply: The second, because it indicates more clearly the extreme bewilderment, the severity of the matter and its horror. That is why it was placed last, since they proceed in such matters from the easier to the more severe. If you say: Why was one of the two comparisons joined to the other by the particle of doubt? I reply: "Aw" originally is used to equate two or more things in doubt, then its use was extended and it was employed for equivalence not in doubt. An example is your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning they are equal in the appropriateness of sitting with them. From this is His saying: ﴿Do not obey from them a sinner or an ingrate﴾, meaning the sinner and the ingrate are equal in the obligation of disobeying them. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud﴾ means that the manner of the story of the hypocrites is comparable to the manners of these two stories, and the two stories are equal in that each one independently serves as a mode of comparison. So whichever of them you compare it to, you are correct, and if you compare it to both together, that is likewise.

Ṣayyib: the rain that pours down, that is, descends and falls. The cloud itself is also called ṣayyib. Al-Shammakh said:

And a dark, near, true-thundering, rain-pouring one.

[Two lines before this: "Traces of a new sign of Su'ad avoided, the abandoned encampment of the forefathers' garden has been effaced by it, a valley..." The verse is attributed to al-Shammakh, and also to al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, and to al-Haytham ibn Kharijah. "Janabahu" means he kept far from it or reached its side. "‘Afā al-manzil" means it was effaced and perished; the wind effaced and erased it. "Al-jadd" with a damma is a well in a place of abundant pasture. "Al-judud" are hard lands, opposite of soft sands. "Al-ajdād" is a plural of the first or the second. "Al-judud" are winding streaks in sand. It is possible that "ajdād" is also its plural, but in the reading "rawḍah" in the accusative with a pronoun attached, and "al-ajdād" in the nominative. "Al-naqb", like "al-shiʿb", is a depressed path in a mountain; "naqaba al-makān" means it became full of passes, and similarly "shaʿaba" means it became full of valleys.
This indicates that it is with ʿayn replacing qāf, meaning it became desolate, from "al-nuqba" which is desolation. "Al-āy" is the singular "āyah", meaning signs and traces.
He likened the alternation of winds in fixed ways to weaving, by explicit metaphor. "Al-asḥam" is black, a description of clouds. "Al-dānī" is near. Another reading is "dāj", and "al-dājī" is dark. "Ṣayyib" is one with many rains. The interrogative is exclamatory. He says: "Do I marvel at our being far from the new traces of Su'ad's house, or do I marvel at passing by the side of the new traces of Su'ad whose marks have perished so that they became wide tracks?" What erased its trace was the alternation of winds and successive rains. So "‘afā" is a rhetorical resumption. He likened the cloud to a truthful man whose promise is true, by metaphor in the form of personification (al-makniyya); "truthfulness and promise" is imaginative. The variant "al-ra‘d" with rāʾ likens its thunder to a true report.
"Ṣayyib" is fayʿil from ṣāba yaṣūbu, when it descends inclining to a direction, like sayyid from sāda yasūdu.]

The indefiniteness of "ṣayyib" is because a type of rain is intended, severe and terrifying, just as "nār" was made indefinite in the first comparison.

It is read "ka-ṣāʾib", but "al-ṣayyib" is more intensive. "Al-samāʾ" here is the canopy. From al-Hasan: it is a suspended wave.

If you say: His saying "min al-samāʾ", what is the benefit of mentioning it, since rain-cloud comes only from the sky? I reply: The benefit is that by bringing "al-samāʾ" in the definite form it negates that it pours from one sky, that is, from one horizon among the other horizons, because each horizon of it is a sky, just as each layer of the layers is a sky, in His saying: ﴿And He revealed in each sky its command﴾. The evidence is the verse:

Alas for remembering her whenever I remember her,
and from far away, a land and sky between us.
