[ "Awh" with shadda and fatha or kasra on the waw is an indeclinable form meaning an expression of pain, a verb-form. "Mā" after "idhā" is extra, indicating generality of times. He says: I grieve whenever I remember the beloved, and from the distance between us, a piece of earth and a piece of sky facing it. He applied "earth" and "sky" to parts of each, and mentioned them to convey that. But the established position among them is that tanwīn indicates partiality among individuals, not parts. So what was said does not hold unless one claims that "sky" applies to part of that canopy and "earth" to part of this eyeball, so that the part becomes an individual and not a component. Mentioning the sky indicates the extremity of distance on earth, because it appears there before it appears in the sky. It is also possible that the intent is to compare the distance between them to the distance between sky and earth. On this, the tanwīn is for magnification and grandeur.]

The meaning is that it is a cloud enveloping, seizing the horizons of the sky, as it came as a rain-cloud. In it there are exaggerations in construction, form, and indefiniteness. He emphasizes this by making it enveloping. In it also is that clouds descend from the sky and take their water from it, not as some claim that they take it from the sea. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in them﴾.

If you say: With what is "ẓulumāt" raised? I reply: By the adverbial phrase, by agreement, because it depends on a modified noun. "Al-raʻd" is the sound heard from the cloud, as though the bodies of the cloud tremble and quake when the wind drives them, and then they make a sound from the trembling. "Al-barq" is the light that gleams from the cloud, from "barraqa al-shayʾ" meaning it shone. If you say: He has made the rain-cloud a place for the darknesses, so it must be that either the cloud or the rain is intended; whichever is intended, what are its darknesses? I reply: As for the darknesses of the cloud, when it is black and enveloping, then the darkness of its density, plus its enveloping, is added to the darkness of the night. As for the darknesses of the rain, there is the darkness of its thickening and its compactness with successive drops, and the darkness of its cloud shading, together with the darkness of night. If you say: How can the rain be a place for lightning and thunder, when their place is the cloud? I reply: When they are at its top and its outpouring, and are attached to it in a general sense, then they are in it. Do you not say: "So-and-so is in the city," though he is only in a space occupied by his body?

If you say: Why did he not combine "thunder and lightning" as the more eloquent, as in al-Buhturi's:

O cloud wrapped in its striped garments,
strutting between its lightnings and its thunders!

[Al-Buhturi addresses the cloud, likening it, because of its density and piling, to a man wrapped in his garments. Attributing wrapping in garments and strutting is imaginative, and upon that is built attributing will, and the plural of lightning and thunder, though both are verbal nouns, indicates multiplicity and repetition. "Al-‘Aqīq" and "al-Zarūd" are two specific places. "Al-manʿaraj" on the pattern of the passive participle is the place where the traveler bends right and left. "Al-Lawā" is a twisted sand dune. "Al-aghyad" is soft and beautiful, its feminine is ghaydāʾ, and "al-ghīd", like "al-bīḍ", is its plural. "Al-jūd" means rains.
He asks the cloud crossing the horizon to rain in the abode of the beloved, in the bending place, then he describes the abode as a barren waste without vegetation, where the loneliness of wild beasts replaced the comfort of beloveds.]

And as it was said, "darknesses," what is the reason? I reply: There are two aspects. One is that "eyes" is intended, but since both were originally verbal nouns (one says "the sky thundered, a thundering, and lightened, a lightening"), the rule of their origin was observed, so their plural was dropped even though plurality is meant. The second is that the events are intended, as if it were said: "and thundering and lightening." These things came indefinite because what is meant is kinds of them, as if it were said: "in it are dense darknesses, a crashing thunder, and a flashing lightning." It is permissible that the pronoun in "yajʿalūna" returns to the people of the rain-cloud though the rain-cloud is deleted and stands in its place, as in His saying: ﴿or they were resting at noon﴾, because the deleted element, though its wording is omitted, remains in meaning. Do you not see how Hassan relied on the survival of its meaning in his verse:

By the god of the company that kept me company
one day in Jalliq in the former age,
they are given to drink from the watering place of al-Barīṣ, over them
the Barada, clapping with the sealed wine.

...for Hassan ibn Thabit, describing the days of the Ghassanid kings of Syria. *Al-'iṣāba* (the group): a company united upon one opinion. *Jalaq*, with the doubled *lam*, is a non-Arabic name for a town. "*Fi al-zamān*" is dependent on an omitted predicate, as an attribute of *yawm al-wāqi'* (the day of the event), and as an adverbial complement of *al-mundamah* (the drinking companionship), which is conversation over wine. *Al-Burays* is the name of a valley. It is also transmitted with two *fatḥah*s (*al-Baraḥ*?) as the name of a river in Damascus, a mountain in the Hijaz, and the name of the sea. *Yuṣaffiqu* means "it is mixed." It has also been said that it means "it is clarified," that is, transferred from one vessel to another. Perhaps he transmitted it as *yuṣaffā*, from *al-taṣfiyah* (clarification). *Al-raḥīq* is the pure. *Al-salsal* is the easy to swallow. "*Wa-man warada*" is the first object, and "*'alayhim*" has been said to be dependent on an omitted predicate, serving as a circumstantial complement of the implied pronoun in *warada*. Apparently it is dependent on *warada* itself, meaning "came and alighted." "*Barada*" is the second object. "*Yuṣaffiqu*" is a circumstantial clause. The meaning is that whoever comes to them at al-Burays, they give him water of Barada, while it is being mixed as explained above. It is also permissible that its meaning be that its waves clash, so the *bā'* expresses accompaniment. It is possible that there is inversion here, and the original is "*yuṣaffiqu al-raḥīqu al-salsalu bihi*" (the pure, easy wine is mixed with it). Perhaps this is a metaphor for their generosity, due to their abundant giving. It has been said that *al-raḥīq al-salsal* is pure, easy wine. The meaning is then by way of comparison, that is, with water that is like wine. The apparent meaning is that it remains literal, and this would be before its prohibition, which is more fitting in a context of praise. If you say: "*Barada*" is feminine, so why did he say "*yuṣaffiqu*" in the masculine? I say: there is an omitted masculine modified noun, and the modifier stands in its place in grammatical case and gender. The original is "water of Barada."

[[Ḥaythu dhakara yuṣaffiqu]] because the meaning is "water of Barada." The phrase "*yajʿalūna*" has no place in the grammar, being a resumptive new sentence. For when He mentioned thunder and lightning, which indicate severity and terror, it is as if a questioner asked: "What is their state with such thunder?" So it was said: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾. Then he said: "What is their state with such lightning?" So it was said: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾. If you say: "The fingertip is what is put into the ear, so why not say 'their fingertips'?" I say: this is one of the broad usages of the language which no limiter can fully restrict, as in His saying ﴿wash your faces and your hands﴾ and ﴿cut off their hands﴾, meaning part of them, that which reaches to the elbow and that which reaches to the wrist. Also, mention of the fingers contains an emphasis absent from mention of the fingertips. If you say: "The finger with which the ear is blocked is a specific finger, so why was the general term mentioned rather than the specific?" I say: because the index finger is *fa'ālah* from *al-sabb* (cursing), so avoiding it is more fitting to the courtesy of the Qur'an. Do you not see that they found it abhorrent and so referred to it by *al-musabbiḥah* (the glorifying one), *al-sibāḥah* (the swimmer), *al-muhallilah* (the one that says "there is no god but God"), and *al-du'ā'ah* (the supplicating one)? If you say: "Why not mention some of these euphemisms?" I say: they are newly coined expressions that people had not commonly used in that era, and they were coined only later. His saying ﴿because of the thunderclaps﴾ is connected to *yajʿalūna*, meaning: because of the thunderclaps they put their fingers in their ears, like your saying "he gave him drink from *al-ʿayma*" (thirst for milk). It has been said *al-ʿayma* is intense craving for milk, and *Al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon) reports it. *Al-ṣā'iqah* is a crack of thunder that falls with a piece of fire. They say it is ignited from the cloud when its bodies collide, and it is a subtle, sharp fire that passes over nothing without consuming it, except that, despite its sharpness, it is quick to extinguish. It is related that it fell upon a palm tree and burned about half of it, and then went out. It is said: "The thunderbolt struck him" when it destroys him, so he *ṣa'iqa*, that is, died, either from the intensity of the sound or from the burning. From this is His saying ﴿and Moses fell down in a swoon﴾. Al-Ḥasan recited *min al-ṣawāqiʿ* (from the thunderbolts) and that is not a transposition of *al-ṣawāʿiq*, because both forms are equal in their usage, and when they are equal, each is a form in its own right. Do you not say: *ṣaqaʿahu ʿalā raʾsihi* (he struck him on his head), *ṣaqaʿa al-dīk* (the rooster crowed), and *khaṭīb miṣqaʿ* (an orator who makes his speech loud)? Its counterpart is *jabadha* alongside *jadhaba* (he pulled), which is not a transposition, because both are equal in usage. Its form is either an attribute of the thunderclap or of the thunder, and the *tā'* is for emphasis, as in *rāwiyah* (a great transmitter), or it is a verbal noun, like *al-kādhibah* and *al-ʿāfiyah*. Ibn Abi Layla recited *ḥadhara al-mawt* (fearing death), and it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, like the poet's saying:

*And I overlook the faults of the noble for the sake of storing them up,*
*and I turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity.*

[[And a crooked fault I have turned from, so it did not harm me,
and a crooked one whose bend I straightened, so it became straight.

And I overlook the faults of the noble for the sake of storing them up,
and I turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity.

These are by Hatim al-Ta'i. It is also said they belong to al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays. He says: "Many a fault, that is a blemish," I turned away from it so it did not harm me. "And many a one with a crookedness," that is, a bend, like a bent staff, I straightened and corrected by force, so it became straight. He divided the turning away into two parts, each with its specific cause, and said: "And I overlook the faults of the noble," that is, his blemish, because of storing it up for him. So *ādikhāruhu* is an object of purpose in the accusative governed by *aghfiru*, even though it is definite by annexation. "And I turn away from the abuse of the base out of generosity on my part, so that I do not become like him." It is also permissible that the meaning is: I turn away from punishing the base for his abuse of me, out of generosity on my part. Then *tukarruman* is an accusative object governed by *a'riḍu*. The claim that *tukarruman* is the cause for both *a'riḍu* and *aghfiru* is the claim of one who has not tasted the flavour of speech.]]

Death is the corruption of the animal's constitution. It has been said: an accident that prevents perception and is opposed to life. "*Iḥāṭat Allāh bi-al-kāfirīn*" (God's encompassing of the disbelievers) is metaphorical. The meaning is that they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses him in reality. This clause is parenthetical and has no grammatical place. *Al-khaṭf* is taking quickly. Mujahid recited *yakhṭifu* with a *kasrah* on the *ṭā'*, but the *fatḥah* is more eloquent and more elevated. From Ibn Mas'ud: *yakhtaṭif*. From al-Ḥasan: *yakhṭifu* with the *yā'* and *khā'* vowelled with *fatḥah*, and its origin is *yakhtaṭif*. Also from him: *yakhiṭu* with both vowelled with *kasrah*, making the *khā'* follow the *yā'*. From Zayd ibn ʿAlī: *yakhṭifu*, from *khaṭafa*. From Ubayy: *yatakhaṭṭafu*, from His saying ﴿they are snatched away from around them﴾.

*Kullamā aḍā'a lahum* (whenever it shines for them) is a third new sentence, as if it answered one who asks: "How do they act in the two states of the lightning's flashing and its dimness?" This is an illustration of how severe the matter is for the hypocrites, as it is severe for the people of the rain-cloud, and of their utmost bewilderment and ignorance about what they should do or leave undone. When they encounter a flash of lightning, while fearing it will snatch away their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few short steps. When it fades and its brightness weakens, they remain standing, restrained from movement. If God willed, He would intensify the crash of the thunder and deafen them, or the light of the lightning, and blind them. *Aḍā'a* may be transitive, meaning: whenever it lit up for them a path and a way, they took it, and its object is omitted. Or it may be intransitive, meaning: whenever it flashed for them, they walked in the place of its light and the spot where its brightness fell. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi ʿAblah: *kullamā ḍā'a lahum*. *Al-mashy* is the general class of a particular movement. When it intensifies it is *saʿy* (striving), and when it intensifies further it is *ʿadw* (running). If you say: "Why is *kullamā* used with illumination, and *idhā* with darkness?" I say: because they are eager for the existence of what their concern is bound to, namely the possibility and availability of walking. So whenever they encounter an opportunity, they seize it. This is not the case with stopping and being detained. *Aẓlama* may be intransitive, which is the apparent meaning, or transitive, transposed from *ẓalama al-layl* (the night was dark). This is confirmed by the reading of Yazid ibn Qutayb: *uẓlima*, in the passive. There occurs in the poetry of Ḥabīb ibn Aws:

*They two darkened my state, then they revealed*
*their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man.*

*Ḥaddidh*... [[Have you tried to guide me, when my intellect is my guide?
Or has the age of trouble disciplined me, when my era is my disciplinarian?

They two darkened my state, then they revealed
their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man.

Stuck in the throats of misfortunes, a bone that rises in the east and sets in the west.

These are by Abu Tammam. It is said they belong to Ḥabīb ibn Aws. *Ḥāwala al-shay'* means he desired it and circled around to obtain it. *Istāma al-shay'* means he aimed at it and traced its marks and recognised it by them. It is transmitted as: "Or has he longed for?" His saying "from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man" contains abstraction, meaning from the face of a man who is beardless, a metaphor for good character. "Grey-haired" is a metaphor for the sound judgment necessary for full manhood. The first is a metaphor for persisting on the paths of jest, and the second a metaphor for persisting on the paths of seriousness, which is why both are gathered together in one time. It is possible that he became grey despite being beardless, due to the abundance of the calamities of the age. *Al-shajī* is what lodges in the throat and neither rises nor descends. *Al-mushriq al-mughrib* means departing east and west, and the intended meaning is generality. *Al-tarhah* is a Persian loanword meaning a small path that is not a main road, and its plural is *tarahāt* and *tarārī*. Then it was used metaphorically for falsehood and became its name. The meaning: if you want a guide, it is my intellect, or a disciplinarian, it is my age. The interrogative is thus used with the sense of a condition, figuratively. It is possible that it is reproachful, and the *fā'* is causal for an omitted clause, meaning: it is not right to desire my guidance or my discipline, for my age and my intellect have undertaken that. He explains this by saying "they two darkened," and using *aẓlama* transitively is a poor usage. *Ḥālī* is the object. Darkening is a metaphor for the troubling of life and the clouding of the mind. *Ajlayā* means they removed and uncovered their darkness. *Al-ẓalāmayn* is a metaphor for turbidity and disturbance. His saying *shajī* is an apposition for "beardless," meaning "like one who is stuck." He likened the calamities to animals that have throats, by way of metonymy, and "throats" is an imaginative depiction of that. The meaning is that the calamities no longer affect him, and his resolve has carried him through all paths of jest just as it carried him through paths of seriousness. Between *mushriq* and *mughrib* is an antithetical contrast.]] Although he is a later poet whose verses are not cited as evidence in the language, he is among the scholars of Arabic, so consider what he says as equivalent to what he transmits. Do you not see the saying of the scholars: "The proof for it is the verse of *al-Ḥamāsah*," and they are satisfied with that because of their trust in its transmission and mastery. The meaning of *qāmū* is they stood and stayed firm in their place. From this: *qāmati al-sūq* (the market became stagnant) when it went slack, and *qāma al-mā'* (the water became still) when it froze. The object of *shā'a* is omitted, because the answer indicates it. The meaning: if God willed to take away their hearing and sight, He would take them away. This omission of the object with *shā'a* and *arāda* is very frequent. They rarely express the object except in something surprising, as in the poet's saying:

*If I wished to weep blood, I would have wept it,*
*but the courtyard of patience is wider.*

*Mulaktu dumū'a al-ʿayni ḥīna radadtuhā*
*ilā nāẓirī wa-al-ʿaynu ka-al-qalbi tadmaʿu*

*Wa-law shi'tu an abkiya daman labakaytuhu*
*ʿalayhi walākin sāḥatu al-ṣabri awsaʿu*

These are by Ibn Yaʿqūb, Isḥāq ibn Ḥassān al-Khudhaymī, lamenting Abu al-Haythām ʿĀmir ibn ʿAmmār, commander of the Arabs of Syria. He says: my eyes' tears overpowered me, and I was able to hold them back when I turned them back to their place. It is transmitted as "then I turned them back," and the eye, while weeping tears like the heart in redness and burning, or weeping tears in a subordinate way to the heart. It is transmitted as "the eye is in the heart," an exaggeration of his thought and his hidden grief within it. Mentioning the object of the will, though in their usage it has become forgotten, is good here because it is something surprising. *Abkā* is given the meaning of *adma'a* (to shed tears), so it governs "blood," although it only governs the one wept over. He likened patience to a generous person, or to a house with a courtyard, by metonymy. The meaning is that he abandons anxiety and turns to patience, so he is characterised by it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence﴾ [21:17], ﴿If God had wished to take a son﴾ [39:4].

Meaning: if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing with the crash of thunder and their sight with the flashing of lightning. Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited *la-adhhaba bi-asmāʿihim* with an added *bā'*, like His saying ﴿and do not cast your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [2:195]. *Al-shay'* is that which is valid to be known and spoken of. Sibawayh, in the chapter headed "The Course of the Final Endings of Words in Arabic," says: "Femininity is only derived from masculinity. Do you not see that *shay'* applies to everything spoken of before one knows whether it is male or female?" *Shay'* is masculine, and it is the most general of the general, just as God is the most specific of the specific. It applies to substance, accident, and the eternal. You say: "a thing unlike other things," meaning known, unlike other known things, and it applies to the non-existent and the impossible. If you say: "How is it said ﴿God is competent over all things﴾ when among things there is that to which the competent has no relation, such as the impossible, and the act of another competent being?" I say: the commentator (al-Zamakhsharī) said: "Among things there is that to which the competent has no relation, such as the impossible..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: What he has raised here is an error both according to the root and the branch. As for the root, the Sunnis hold that *shay'* only applies to the existent. As for the branch, even if we branch from the view of the Qadariyyah, for whom *shay'* applies to the existent and to the non-existent that can exist, and so does not apply to the impossible, then on that branching it is not a correct refutation on either doctrine. As for what is decided between two competent beings, it is a predicament which only the Qadariyyah are driven into, those who believe that what the servant's power is related to cannot be related to the Lord's power, since the servant's power is creative, so the act is independent of another creator's power—exalted is God above what they associate. As for the Sunnis, the competent creator is one, namely God, the One, the Unique, so His power relates to the act, and He creates it, and the servant's power relates to it by concomitance, not by effecting. For this reason, on this interpretation, what is decided between two competent beings is not created. The commentator (al-Zamakhsharī) has in the folds of this discourse denied and rejected the eternal power, and made God competent through His essence rather than through power. He concealed this under his saying "in what there is no relation to the essence of the competent," and did not say "to the power of the competent." So beware of its hidden meanings. How many errors he has smuggled into this doctrine. And God is the Granter of success. If it is said: "O Ash'arites, if the thing according to you is the existent, what is the meaning of power over it after its existence and its continuance, when God says, and He is the truest of speakers: ﴿Indeed, God is competent over all things﴾?" We say: power relates to its object and brings it into existence, and then it is a thing. Since what power relates to necessarily becomes a thing, it is correct to apply the name "thing" to it. This is of the kind of: "Whoever kills a slain man, to him is his spoil." When they name a thing by the name of what it generally becomes, then what it necessarily becomes is more fitting.

Then if you say: "*Qadīr* (competent) is derived from what?" I say: from *taqdīr* (measuring out), because he brings about his act in accordance with the measure of his strength and capacity, and what distinguishes him from the incapable.

Then Allah, glorified is He, reinforced the matter concerning them with another parable, so that it would be a further unveiling of their condition and a clarification following a clarification. Just as the eloquent speaker, in places where brevity and concision are called for, must be concise and brief, so too his duty in places where detail and fullness are called for is to elaborate and to be thorough. Al-Jahiz recited:

They deliver long sermons, and at other times
they convey (their meaning) by the glances of the eye, fearing the watchers.

[Al-Jahiz recited it. Another version reads "yarmun" (they throw). He used the metaphor of "throwing" for bringing out speech from the mouth in abundance, in the manner of explicit statement.
It is said: wahá lahu, wa ilayhi wahyan, and awḥá lahu wa ilayhi īḥāʼan, meaning: he conveyed speech to him, or signaled to him with it, or inspired him with it. So al-waḥy is a verbal noun of wahá, or a nominal form of the verbal noun of awḥá. Al-laḥẓ is signaling with the corner of the eye to the right or to the left. Al-lāḥiẓ is originally a descriptive term, but it is also the name of the corner of the eye. That is why it was pluralized as lawāḥiẓ, and waḥy was attributed to it because it is the instrument. It is also possible that it is the plural of lāḥiẓa, like a female neck. The meaning: they speak long sermons at times when they feel safe, and they convey the message by glances at other times, out of fear of the watchers. So for every situation they have a suitable speech.]

Among the parables that Allah reinforced in the Revelation is His saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike, nor the darknesses and the light, nor the shade and the scorching heat. And the living and the dead are not alike.﴾ Have you not seen how Dhu al-Rummah acted in his poem?

Is that (the wild ass) or a mottled one whose forelegs are marked with white patches ...
Is that or one dyed with the red of the sī, whose pasture ...

[Dhu al-Rummah, describing his she-camel, first likened her to a wild ass, then said: "Is that the wild ass which my she-camel resembles, or a mottled one (tamash)?" Tamash, with a fatḥa-less pattern, means varied in color; kaḥadhir means varied in color. Al-washy is a color differing from the rest of the thing. Al-akraʻ is the plural of kurāʻ, the shank. Al-masfa‘ is the black one, from al-sufʻa, which is blackness. Al-nāshiṭ is one that leaves one land for another. Al-shabab, like kaḥadhir, is an old male wild cow. Then he said: "Is that the bull she resembles, or the dyed one?", meaning the male ostrich whose shanks have turned red or yellow from eating spring herbage. Al-sī is level ground and also the name of a specific place. Al-marta‘ is a verbal noun or a place noun governed by the adverb within a wider area. Munqalab means returning from pasture to its thirty chicks. It is at its fastest, so she too is swift in her course.
Akra‘uhu is the agent of the adverb, or the agent of tamash. Mar‘atuhu is its agent for the adverb, or a subject whose predicate is the adverb.]

If you say: In the first parable the hypocrite was likened to one who kindles a fire, his display of faith to illumination, and the cessation of his benefit to the extinguishing of the fire. Then what is he likened to in the second parable, with the rain-cloud, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning and the thunderbolts? I reply: One may say that the religion of Islam is likened to the rain-cloud, because hearts come alive through it as the earth comes alive through rain. What is connected to it, the disbelievers, is likened to the darknesses. What it contains of promise and threat is likened to thunder and lightning. What afflicts the disbelievers of fear, calamities and trials from the people of Islam is likened to thunderbolts. The meaning is: "Or like those of a rain-cloud," that is, like a people whom the sky overtook in this condition, and they suffered what they suffered.

If you say: This is the comparison of things with things; where then is mention of the things compared, and why was it not stated explicitly, as in His saying: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike, nor those who believe and do righteous deeds and the wrongdoer﴾, and in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry,
beside their nest are the jujube and the decayed date?

[Imru' al-Qays describes the eagle which eats the young of birds except their hearts, which is why they are abundant near it, and describes himself as courageous, since he reached the sight of that. He says: as if the hearts of the birds, some moist and some dry, were, while at the eagle's nest, that is its nest, al-‘unnāb, which is a red moist fruit, referring to the moist part. Al-ḥashf is the dry, poor, decayed date that has perished, referring to the dry part. There is thus lafʿ and nashr in ordered arrangement, and antithesis between moist and dry.
It is permissible that raṭaban and yābisan are in the accusative as a substitute for qulūb al-ṭayr, meaning as if the moist and dry of them were the jujube and the decayed date. A partial substitute does not require a pronoun returning to the substituted noun, though the better practice is that it does.]

I say: Just as that is stated explicitly, so it has also come with its mention concealed, in the manner of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet and palatable in its drink, and this one is salty and bitter﴾, and ﴿Allah strikes a parable: a man in whom are partners at odds, and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾. The sound position, which the scholars of rhetoric hold and do not transgress, is this: both comparisons belong to the composite similes, not the separate ones, in which each individual element is not forced to have its own counterpart. This is the decisive opinion and the strong position. Its explanation: the Arabs take things singly, each isolated from the others, none taking hold of another's belt, and compare them with their counterparts, as Imru' al-Qays did and as occurs in the Qur'an. They also compare a state resulting from the combination of several things that have been joined and adhered until they become one thing, with another like it, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah﴾ up to the verse. The purpose is to compare the condition of the Jews in their ignorance of what the Torah contained and its striking signs, with the condition of a donkey in its ignorance of the books of wisdom it carries, the two states being equal to him whether he carries books of wisdom or other burdens; he perceives from it only the toil and fatigue on his back. And like His saying: ﴿And strike for them the parable of the life of this world: like water which We sent down from the sky﴾. The intent is the brevity of the lasting of the world's splendor, like the brevity of the lasting of the green vegetation. But to intend that individual things be compared with individual things, without some of them being bound to others and becoming one thing, is not so.

Likewise, when He described the hypocrites' falling into their error and the bewilderment and confusion into which they plunged, their bewilderment and the severity of their situation were compared with one who suffers when his fire is extinguished after being kindled in the darkness of night, and likewise one whom the sky overtakes on a dark night with thunder, lightning, and fear of thunderbolts.

If you say: What you were estimating in the separate comparison, namely the omission of the modified noun in "Or like those of a rain-cloud", would you estimate the same in the composite comparison? I reply: Were it not for the need of a returning pronoun in His saying: ﴿They put their fingers into their ears﴾, to which it would refer, I would not need to estimate it, because I consider the configuration abstracted from the whole discourse. It makes no difference to me whether the particle of comparison is followed by a single noun to which the comparison can apply or not. Do you not see His saying: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only﴾ the verse, how the particle "ka" (like) was followed by water, while the purpose is not to compare this world with water, nor with some other single thing that would need contrived estimation? Clear in this is the verse of Labid:

And the people are only like the dwellings and their inhabitants,
in them on the day they settled, and on the morrow, desolate ruins.

[He did not intend to compare people with the dwellings themselves, but intended to compare their condition with the world with the condition of dwellings with their inhabitants. His saying "and its inhabitants in it" is a circumstantial clause. "The day they settled it" is in the accusative governed by the preposition-phrase before it, which is deleted. "Ghadwan balāqiʿ" means: and on the morrow they are desolate ruins. The plural of baluqʿ is "bala'ī", meaning empty waste. "Al-ghad" is commonly used like "al-yad", so its original waw appears here. He used "ghad" meaning near time, as one says "af'aluhu bukrah" (I will do it early). The meaning is after a few days. The common element is the swift passing and disappearance after brightness and freshness. You may also take it as a comparison of a single thing with a single thing, the common feature being that people have life-spirits in them, so they are radiant and splendid, then those spirits are removed and they become empty and vacant, like a house inhabited by people which becomes a ruin. This is on the nominative reading of "ahluha". If it is read in the genitive, coordinated with "al-diyar", the first interpretation is required, and "bihā" is then attached to a deleted circumstantial element describing "ahluhā". The bāʼ means "fī" in both readings.]

He did not compare people with dwellings; rather he compared their existence in the world and the swiftness of their passing and annihilation with the settling of the people of dwellings in them and the imminence of their departure from them, leaving them empty and vacant. If you say: Which of the two comparisons is more eloquent? I reply: The second, because it indicates more clearly the extreme bewilderment, the severity of the matter and its horror. That is why it was placed last, since they proceed in such matters from the easier to the more severe. If you say: Why was one of the two comparisons joined to the other by the particle of doubt? I reply: "Aw" originally is used to equate two or more things in doubt, then its use was extended and it was employed for equivalence not in doubt. An example is your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning they are equal in the appropriateness of sitting with them. From this is His saying: ﴿Do not obey from them a sinner or an ingrate﴾, meaning the sinner and the ingrate are equal in the obligation of disobeying them. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud﴾ means that the manner of the story of the hypocrites is comparable to the manners of these two stories, and the two stories are equal in that each one independently serves as a mode of comparison. So whichever of them you compare it to, you are correct, and if you compare it to both together, that is likewise.

Ṣayyib: the rain that pours down, that is, descends and falls. The cloud itself is also called ṣayyib. Al-Shammakh said:

And a dark, near, true-thundering, rain-pouring one.

[Two lines before this: "Traces of a new sign of Su'ad avoided, the abandoned encampment of the forefathers' garden has been effaced by it, a valley..." The verse is attributed to al-Shammakh, and also to al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, and to al-Haytham ibn Kharijah. "Janabahu" means he kept far from it or reached its side. "‘Afā al-manzil" means it was effaced and perished; the wind effaced and erased it. "Al-jadd" with a damma is a well in a place of abundant pasture. "Al-judud" are hard lands, opposite of soft sands. "Al-ajdād" is a plural of the first or the second. "Al-judud" are winding streaks in sand. It is possible that "ajdād" is also its plural, but in the reading "rawḍah" in the accusative with a pronoun attached, and "al-ajdād" in the nominative. "Al-naqb", like "al-shiʿb", is a depressed path in a mountain; "naqaba al-makān" means it became full of passes, and similarly "shaʿaba" means it became full of valleys.
This indicates that it is with ʿayn replacing qāf, meaning it became desolate, from "al-nuqba" which is desolation. "Al-āy" is the singular "āyah", meaning signs and traces.
He likened the alternation of winds in fixed ways to weaving, by explicit metaphor. "Al-asḥam" is black, a description of clouds. "Al-dānī" is near. Another reading is "dāj", and "al-dājī" is dark. "Ṣayyib" is one with many rains. The interrogative is exclamatory. He says: "Do I marvel at our being far from the new traces of Su'ad's house, or do I marvel at passing by the side of the new traces of Su'ad whose marks have perished so that they became wide tracks?" What erased its trace was the alternation of winds and successive rains. So "‘afā" is a rhetorical resumption. He likened the cloud to a truthful man whose promise is true, by metaphor in the form of personification (al-makniyya); "truthfulness and promise" is imaginative. The variant "al-ra‘d" with rāʾ likens its thunder to a true report.
"Ṣayyib" is fayʿil from ṣāba yaṣūbu, when it descends inclining to a direction, like sayyid from sāda yasūdu.]

The indefiniteness of "ṣayyib" is because a type of rain is intended, severe and terrifying, just as "nār" was made indefinite in the first comparison.

It is read "ka-ṣāʾib", but "al-ṣayyib" is more intensive. "Al-samāʾ" here is the canopy. From al-Hasan: it is a suspended wave.

If you say: His saying "min al-samāʾ", what is the benefit of mentioning it, since rain-cloud comes only from the sky? I reply: The benefit is that by bringing "al-samāʾ" in the definite form it negates that it pours from one sky, that is, from one horizon among the other horizons, because each horizon of it is a sky, just as each layer of the layers is a sky, in His saying: ﴿And He revealed in each sky its command﴾. The evidence is the verse:

Alas for remembering her whenever I remember her,
and from far away, a land and sky between us.

[ "Awh" with shadda and fatha or kasra on the waw is an indeclinable form meaning an expression of pain, a verb-form. "Mā" after "idhā" is extra, indicating generality of times. He says: I grieve whenever I remember the beloved, and from the distance between us, a piece of earth and a piece of sky facing it. He applied "earth" and "sky" to parts of each, and mentioned them to convey that. But the established position among them is that tanwīn indicates partiality among individuals, not parts. So what was said does not hold unless one claims that "sky" applies to part of that canopy and "earth" to part of this eyeball, so that the part becomes an individual and not a component. Mentioning the sky indicates the extremity of distance on earth, because it appears there before it appears in the sky. It is also possible that the intent is to compare the distance between them to the distance between sky and earth. On this, the tanwīn is for magnification and grandeur.]

The meaning is that it is a cloud enveloping, seizing the horizons of the sky, as it came as a rain-cloud. In it there are exaggerations in construction, form, and indefiniteness. He emphasizes this by making it enveloping. In it also is that clouds descend from the sky and take their water from it, not as some claim that they take it from the sea. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in them﴾.

If you say: With what is "ẓulumāt" raised? I reply: By the adverbial phrase, by agreement, because it depends on a modified noun. "Al-raʻd" is the sound heard from the cloud, as though the bodies of the cloud tremble and quake when the wind drives them, and then they make a sound from the trembling. "Al-barq" is the light that gleams from the cloud, from "barraqa al-shayʾ" meaning it shone. If you say: He has made the rain-cloud a place for the darknesses, so it must be that either the cloud or the rain is intended; whichever is intended, what are its darknesses? I reply: As for the darknesses of the cloud, when it is black and enveloping, then the darkness of its density, plus its enveloping, is added to the darkness of the night. As for the darknesses of the rain, there is the darkness of its thickening and its compactness with successive drops, and the darkness of its cloud shading, together with the darkness of night. If you say: How can the rain be a place for lightning and thunder, when their place is the cloud? I reply: When they are at its top and its outpouring, and are attached to it in a general sense, then they are in it. Do you not say: "So-and-so is in the city," though he is only in a space occupied by his body?

If you say: Why did he not combine "thunder and lightning" as the more eloquent, as in al-Buhturi's:

O cloud wrapped in its striped garments,
strutting between its lightnings and its thunders!

[Al-Buhturi addresses the cloud, likening it, because of its density and piling, to a man wrapped in his garments. Attributing wrapping in garments and strutting is imaginative, and upon that is built attributing will, and the plural of lightning and thunder, though both are verbal nouns, indicates multiplicity and repetition. "Al-‘Aqīq" and "al-Zarūd" are two specific places. "Al-manʿaraj" on the pattern of the passive participle is the place where the traveler bends right and left. "Al-Lawā" is a twisted sand dune. "Al-aghyad" is soft and beautiful, its feminine is ghaydāʾ, and "al-ghīd", like "al-bīḍ", is its plural. "Al-jūd" means rains.
He asks the cloud crossing the horizon to rain in the abode of the beloved, in the bending place, then he describes the abode as a barren waste without vegetation, where the loneliness of wild beasts replaced the comfort of beloveds.]

And as it was said, "darknesses," what is the reason? I reply: There are two aspects. One is that "eyes" is intended, but since both were originally verbal nouns (one says "the sky thundered, a thundering, and lightened, a lightening"), the rule of their origin was observed, so their plural was dropped even though plurality is meant. The second is that the events are intended, as if it were said: "and thundering and lightening." These things came indefinite because what is meant is kinds of them, as if it were said: "in it are dense darknesses, a crashing thunder, and a flashing lightning." It is permissible that the pronoun in "yajʿalūna" returns to the people of the rain-cloud though the rain-cloud is deleted and stands in its place, as in His saying: ﴿or they were resting at noon﴾, because the deleted element, though its wording is omitted, remains in meaning. Do you not see how Hassan relied on the survival of its meaning in his verse:

By the god of the company that kept me company
one day in Jalliq in the former age,
they are given to drink from the watering place of al-Barīṣ, over them
the Barada, clapping with the sealed wine.

...for Hassan ibn Thabit, describing the days of the Ghassanid kings of Syria. *Al-'iṣāba* (the group): a company united upon one opinion. *Jalaq*, with the doubled *lam*, is a non-Arabic name for a town. "*Fi al-zamān*" is dependent on an omitted predicate, as an attribute of *yawm al-wāqi'* (the day of the event), and as an adverbial complement of *al-mundamah* (the drinking companionship), which is conversation over wine. *Al-Burays* is the name of a valley. It is also transmitted with two *fatḥah*s (*al-Baraḥ*?) as the name of a river in Damascus, a mountain in the Hijaz, and the name of the sea. *Yuṣaffiqu* means "it is mixed." It has also been said that it means "it is clarified," that is, transferred from one vessel to another. Perhaps he transmitted it as *yuṣaffā*, from *al-taṣfiyah* (clarification). *Al-raḥīq* is the pure. *Al-salsal* is the easy to swallow. "*Wa-man warada*" is the first object, and "*'alayhim*" has been said to be dependent on an omitted predicate, serving as a circumstantial complement of the implied pronoun in *warada*. Apparently it is dependent on *warada* itself, meaning "came and alighted." "*Barada*" is the second object. "*Yuṣaffiqu*" is a circumstantial clause. The meaning is that whoever comes to them at al-Burays, they give him water of Barada, while it is being mixed as explained above. It is also permissible that its meaning be that its waves clash, so the *bā'* expresses accompaniment. It is possible that there is inversion here, and the original is "*yuṣaffiqu al-raḥīqu al-salsalu bihi*" (the pure, easy wine is mixed with it). Perhaps this is a metaphor for their generosity, due to their abundant giving. It has been said that *al-raḥīq al-salsal* is pure, easy wine. The meaning is then by way of comparison, that is, with water that is like wine. The apparent meaning is that it remains literal, and this would be before its prohibition, which is more fitting in a context of praise. If you say: "*Barada*" is feminine, so why did he say "*yuṣaffiqu*" in the masculine? I say: there is an omitted masculine modified noun, and the modifier stands in its place in grammatical case and gender. The original is "water of Barada."

[[Ḥaythu dhakara yuṣaffiqu]] because the meaning is "water of Barada." The phrase "*yajʿalūna*" has no place in the grammar, being a resumptive new sentence. For when He mentioned thunder and lightning, which indicate severity and terror, it is as if a questioner asked: "What is their state with such thunder?" So it was said: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾. Then he said: "What is their state with such lightning?" So it was said: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾. If you say: "The fingertip is what is put into the ear, so why not say 'their fingertips'?" I say: this is one of the broad usages of the language which no limiter can fully restrict, as in His saying ﴿wash your faces and your hands﴾ and ﴿cut off their hands﴾, meaning part of them, that which reaches to the elbow and that which reaches to the wrist. Also, mention of the fingers contains an emphasis absent from mention of the fingertips. If you say: "The finger with which the ear is blocked is a specific finger, so why was the general term mentioned rather than the specific?" I say: because the index finger is *fa'ālah* from *al-sabb* (cursing), so avoiding it is more fitting to the courtesy of the Qur'an. Do you not see that they found it abhorrent and so referred to it by *al-musabbiḥah* (the glorifying one), *al-sibāḥah* (the swimmer), *al-muhallilah* (the one that says "there is no god but God"), and *al-du'ā'ah* (the supplicating one)? If you say: "Why not mention some of these euphemisms?" I say: they are newly coined expressions that people had not commonly used in that era, and they were coined only later. His saying ﴿because of the thunderclaps﴾ is connected to *yajʿalūna*, meaning: because of the thunderclaps they put their fingers in their ears, like your saying "he gave him drink from *al-ʿayma*" (thirst for milk). It has been said *al-ʿayma* is intense craving for milk, and *Al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the lexicon) reports it. *Al-ṣā'iqah* is a crack of thunder that falls with a piece of fire. They say it is ignited from the cloud when its bodies collide, and it is a subtle, sharp fire that passes over nothing without consuming it, except that, despite its sharpness, it is quick to extinguish. It is related that it fell upon a palm tree and burned about half of it, and then went out. It is said: "The thunderbolt struck him" when it destroys him, so he *ṣa'iqa*, that is, died, either from the intensity of the sound or from the burning. From this is His saying ﴿and Moses fell down in a swoon﴾. Al-Ḥasan recited *min al-ṣawāqiʿ* (from the thunderbolts) and that is not a transposition of *al-ṣawāʿiq*, because both forms are equal in their usage, and when they are equal, each is a form in its own right. Do you not say: *ṣaqaʿahu ʿalā raʾsihi* (he struck him on his head), *ṣaqaʿa al-dīk* (the rooster crowed), and *khaṭīb miṣqaʿ* (an orator who makes his speech loud)? Its counterpart is *jabadha* alongside *jadhaba* (he pulled), which is not a transposition, because both are equal in usage. Its form is either an attribute of the thunderclap or of the thunder, and the *tā'* is for emphasis, as in *rāwiyah* (a great transmitter), or it is a verbal noun, like *al-kādhibah* and *al-ʿāfiyah*. Ibn Abi Layla recited *ḥadhara al-mawt* (fearing death), and it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, like the poet's saying:

*And I overlook the faults of the noble for the sake of storing them up,*
*and I turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity.*

[[And a crooked fault I have turned from, so it did not harm me,
and a crooked one whose bend I straightened, so it became straight.

And I overlook the faults of the noble for the sake of storing them up,
and I turn away from the abuse of the base, out of generosity.

These are by Hatim al-Ta'i. It is also said they belong to al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays. He says: "Many a fault, that is a blemish," I turned away from it so it did not harm me. "And many a one with a crookedness," that is, a bend, like a bent staff, I straightened and corrected by force, so it became straight. He divided the turning away into two parts, each with its specific cause, and said: "And I overlook the faults of the noble," that is, his blemish, because of storing it up for him. So *ādikhāruhu* is an object of purpose in the accusative governed by *aghfiru*, even though it is definite by annexation. "And I turn away from the abuse of the base out of generosity on my part, so that I do not become like him." It is also permissible that the meaning is: I turn away from punishing the base for his abuse of me, out of generosity on my part. Then *tukarruman* is an accusative object governed by *a'riḍu*. The claim that *tukarruman* is the cause for both *a'riḍu* and *aghfiru* is the claim of one who has not tasted the flavour of speech.]]

Death is the corruption of the animal's constitution. It has been said: an accident that prevents perception and is opposed to life. "*Iḥāṭat Allāh bi-al-kāfirīn*" (God's encompassing of the disbelievers) is metaphorical. The meaning is that they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses him in reality. This clause is parenthetical and has no grammatical place. *Al-khaṭf* is taking quickly. Mujahid recited *yakhṭifu* with a *kasrah* on the *ṭā'*, but the *fatḥah* is more eloquent and more elevated. From Ibn Mas'ud: *yakhtaṭif*. From al-Ḥasan: *yakhṭifu* with the *yā'* and *khā'* vowelled with *fatḥah*, and its origin is *yakhtaṭif*. Also from him: *yakhiṭu* with both vowelled with *kasrah*, making the *khā'* follow the *yā'*. From Zayd ibn ʿAlī: *yakhṭifu*, from *khaṭafa*. From Ubayy: *yatakhaṭṭafu*, from His saying ﴿they are snatched away from around them﴾.

*Kullamā aḍā'a lahum* (whenever it shines for them) is a third new sentence, as if it answered one who asks: "How do they act in the two states of the lightning's flashing and its dimness?" This is an illustration of how severe the matter is for the hypocrites, as it is severe for the people of the rain-cloud, and of their utmost bewilderment and ignorance about what they should do or leave undone. When they encounter a flash of lightning, while fearing it will snatch away their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few short steps. When it fades and its brightness weakens, they remain standing, restrained from movement. If God willed, He would intensify the crash of the thunder and deafen them, or the light of the lightning, and blind them. *Aḍā'a* may be transitive, meaning: whenever it lit up for them a path and a way, they took it, and its object is omitted. Or it may be intransitive, meaning: whenever it flashed for them, they walked in the place of its light and the spot where its brightness fell. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi ʿAblah: *kullamā ḍā'a lahum*. *Al-mashy* is the general class of a particular movement. When it intensifies it is *saʿy* (striving), and when it intensifies further it is *ʿadw* (running). If you say: "Why is *kullamā* used with illumination, and *idhā* with darkness?" I say: because they are eager for the existence of what their concern is bound to, namely the possibility and availability of walking. So whenever they encounter an opportunity, they seize it. This is not the case with stopping and being detained. *Aẓlama* may be intransitive, which is the apparent meaning, or transitive, transposed from *ẓalama al-layl* (the night was dark). This is confirmed by the reading of Yazid ibn Qutayb: *uẓlima*, in the passive. There occurs in the poetry of Ḥabīb ibn Aws:

*They two darkened my state, then they revealed*
*their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man.*

*Ḥaddidh*... [[Have you tried to guide me, when my intellect is my guide?
Or has the age of trouble disciplined me, when my era is my disciplinarian?

They two darkened my state, then they revealed
their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man.

Stuck in the throats of misfortunes, a bone that rises in the east and sets in the west.

These are by Abu Tammam. It is said they belong to Ḥabīb ibn Aws. *Ḥāwala al-shay'* means he desired it and circled around to obtain it. *Istāma al-shay'* means he aimed at it and traced its marks and recognised it by them. It is transmitted as: "Or has he longed for?" His saying "from the face of a beardless, grey-haired man" contains abstraction, meaning from the face of a man who is beardless, a metaphor for good character. "Grey-haired" is a metaphor for the sound judgment necessary for full manhood. The first is a metaphor for persisting on the paths of jest, and the second a metaphor for persisting on the paths of seriousness, which is why both are gathered together in one time. It is possible that he became grey despite being beardless, due to the abundance of the calamities of the age. *Al-shajī* is what lodges in the throat and neither rises nor descends. *Al-mushriq al-mughrib* means departing east and west, and the intended meaning is generality. *Al-tarhah* is a Persian loanword meaning a small path that is not a main road, and its plural is *tarahāt* and *tarārī*. Then it was used metaphorically for falsehood and became its name. The meaning: if you want a guide, it is my intellect, or a disciplinarian, it is my age. The interrogative is thus used with the sense of a condition, figuratively. It is possible that it is reproachful, and the *fā'* is causal for an omitted clause, meaning: it is not right to desire my guidance or my discipline, for my age and my intellect have undertaken that. He explains this by saying "they two darkened," and using *aẓlama* transitively is a poor usage. *Ḥālī* is the object. Darkening is a metaphor for the troubling of life and the clouding of the mind. *Ajlayā* means they removed and uncovered their darkness. *Al-ẓalāmayn* is a metaphor for turbidity and disturbance. His saying *shajī* is an apposition for "beardless," meaning "like one who is stuck." He likened the calamities to animals that have throats, by way of metonymy, and "throats" is an imaginative depiction of that. The meaning is that the calamities no longer affect him, and his resolve has carried him through all paths of jest just as it carried him through paths of seriousness. Between *mushriq* and *mughrib* is an antithetical contrast.]] Although he is a later poet whose verses are not cited as evidence in the language, he is among the scholars of Arabic, so consider what he says as equivalent to what he transmits. Do you not see the saying of the scholars: "The proof for it is the verse of *al-Ḥamāsah*," and they are satisfied with that because of their trust in its transmission and mastery. The meaning of *qāmū* is they stood and stayed firm in their place. From this: *qāmati al-sūq* (the market became stagnant) when it went slack, and *qāma al-mā'* (the water became still) when it froze. The object of *shā'a* is omitted, because the answer indicates it. The meaning: if God willed to take away their hearing and sight, He would take them away. This omission of the object with *shā'a* and *arāda* is very frequent. They rarely express the object except in something surprising, as in the poet's saying:

*If I wished to weep blood, I would have wept it,*
*but the courtyard of patience is wider.*

*Mulaktu dumū'a al-ʿayni ḥīna radadtuhā*
*ilā nāẓirī wa-al-ʿaynu ka-al-qalbi tadmaʿu*

*Wa-law shi'tu an abkiya daman labakaytuhu*
*ʿalayhi walākin sāḥatu al-ṣabri awsaʿu*

These are by Ibn Yaʿqūb, Isḥāq ibn Ḥassān al-Khudhaymī, lamenting Abu al-Haythām ʿĀmir ibn ʿAmmār, commander of the Arabs of Syria. He says: my eyes' tears overpowered me, and I was able to hold them back when I turned them back to their place. It is transmitted as "then I turned them back," and the eye, while weeping tears like the heart in redness and burning, or weeping tears in a subordinate way to the heart. It is transmitted as "the eye is in the heart," an exaggeration of his thought and his hidden grief within it. Mentioning the object of the will, though in their usage it has become forgotten, is good here because it is something surprising. *Abkā* is given the meaning of *adma'a* (to shed tears), so it governs "blood," although it only governs the one wept over. He likened patience to a generous person, or to a house with a courtyard, by metonymy. The meaning is that he abandons anxiety and turns to patience, so he is characterised by it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence﴾ [21:17], ﴿If God had wished to take a son﴾ [39:4].

Meaning: if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing with the crash of thunder and their sight with the flashing of lightning. Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited *la-adhhaba bi-asmāʿihim* with an added *bā'*, like His saying ﴿and do not cast your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [2:195]. *Al-shay'* is that which is valid to be known and spoken of. Sibawayh, in the chapter headed "The Course of the Final Endings of Words in Arabic," says: "Femininity is only derived from masculinity. Do you not see that *shay'* applies to everything spoken of before one knows whether it is male or female?" *Shay'* is masculine, and it is the most general of the general, just as God is the most specific of the specific. It applies to substance, accident, and the eternal. You say: "a thing unlike other things," meaning known, unlike other known things, and it applies to the non-existent and the impossible. If you say: "How is it said ﴿God is competent over all things﴾ when among things there is that to which the competent has no relation, such as the impossible, and the act of another competent being?" I say: the commentator (al-Zamakhsharī) said: "Among things there is that to which the competent has no relation, such as the impossible..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: What he has raised here is an error both according to the root and the branch. As for the root, the Sunnis hold that *shay'* only applies to the existent. As for the branch, even if we branch from the view of the Qadariyyah, for whom *shay'* applies to the existent and to the non-existent that can exist, and so does not apply to the impossible, then on that branching it is not a correct refutation on either doctrine. As for what is decided between two competent beings, it is a predicament which only the Qadariyyah are driven into, those who believe that what the servant's power is related to cannot be related to the Lord's power, since the servant's power is creative, so the act is independent of another creator's power—exalted is God above what they associate. As for the Sunnis, the competent creator is one, namely God, the One, the Unique, so His power relates to the act, and He creates it, and the servant's power relates to it by concomitance, not by effecting. For this reason, on this interpretation, what is decided between two competent beings is not created. The commentator (al-Zamakhsharī) has in the folds of this discourse denied and rejected the eternal power, and made God competent through His essence rather than through power. He concealed this under his saying "in what there is no relation to the essence of the competent," and did not say "to the power of the competent." So beware of its hidden meanings. How many errors he has smuggled into this doctrine. And God is the Granter of success. If it is said: "O Ash'arites, if the thing according to you is the existent, what is the meaning of power over it after its existence and its continuance, when God says, and He is the truest of speakers: ﴿Indeed, God is competent over all things﴾?" We say: power relates to its object and brings it into existence, and then it is a thing. Since what power relates to necessarily becomes a thing, it is correct to apply the name "thing" to it. This is of the kind of: "Whoever kills a slain man, to him is his spoil." When they name a thing by the name of what it generally becomes, then what it necessarily becomes is more fitting.

Then if you say: "*Qadīr* (competent) is derived from what?" I say: from *taqdīr* (measuring out), because he brings about his act in accordance with the measure of his strength and capacity, and what distinguishes him from the incapable.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 21:

When God the Exalted enumerated the categories of accountable people (mukallafun): the believers, the disbelievers, and the hypocrites; mentioned their attributes, their conditions, and the destinations of their affairs; and what each category was singled out for, of that which makes it happy or wretched, and that which brings it favour with God or ruin, He turned to them in address. This is the *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) mentioned at His words ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. It is a sublime style of speech in which there is stirring and motivation for the listener. Just as when you say to your companion, relating about a third person who is with you both: "So-and-so, his story is such and such," and you recount to him what befell him from him, then you turn your address to the third person and say: "O so-and-so, it is incumbent upon you to adhere to the praiseworthy way in the courses of your affairs, and to keep to the straight road in your departures and your arrivals." By your turning towards him you have alerted him with the greatest alerting, and you have demanded his attention to your guidance with greater demand, and you have produced in him, by moving from the third person to direct address, a stirring of his nature that he would not find if you had persisted in the third-person form. Likewise is the variation in speech and its movement from one kind to another: it opens the ears to listening and gladdens the souls to acceptance.

And we have been informed by a sound chain of transmission from Ibrahim, from ʿAlqamah: that everything in which ﴿O mankind﴾ was revealed is Meccan, and what has ﴿O you who believe﴾ is Madinan. [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, who said: "Waki' related to us from al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim with this." It was also narrated by al-Bazzar through the report of al-Aqyas ibn al-Rabiʿ from al-Aʿmash, connected with the mention of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud in it. He said: "We do not know of anyone who traced it back except Qays." He was contradicted by what al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dalail from him, and Ibn Mardawayh in the Tafsir of al-Hajj, all of them through the route of Waki' also, who said: "My father related to us from al-Aʿmash from Ibrahim from ʿAlqamah from ʿAbd Allah."

(Benefit) This is to be understood as meaning that what is "Meccan" is what was addressed to the people of Mecca, and what is "Madinan" is what was addressed to the people of Madinah, because the predominant condition of the people of Mecca was disbelief, so they were addressed with ﴿O mankind﴾, while the predominant condition of the people of Madinah was faith, so they were addressed with ﴿O you who believe﴾. This was stated by Shaykh Baha' al-Din ibn ʿAqil.]] Therefore His words ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ are addressed to the polytheists of Mecca.

"Ya" (the vocative particle) is, in its origin, a particle set for calling the distant; it is a sound by which a man calls out to the one he is summoning. As for calling the near, it has *ay* and the hamzah. Then it came to be used for calling one who is heedless and forgetful even if near, treating him as if he were distant. When the one who is near and attentive is called with it, that is for emphasis, indicating that the address which follows is of great concern. If you say: then what about the supplicant who says in his entreaty: "O Lord" [[His words "says in his entreaty: O Lord": in al-Sihah, *jaʾara al-thawr yajʾaru*, meaning he bellowed. *Jaʾara al-rajul ila Allah ʿazza wa-jall*, meaning he humbled himself in supplication. (ʿ)]] and "O Allah," while He is nearer to him than his jugular vein, and hears and sees him? I say: it is his own pronouncement of himself as lacking, and his deeming himself remote from the places of nearness and from what brings him close to the pleasure of God and the stations of those brought near; this is humbling himself and acknowledging his own shortcoming in regard to God, together with his intense eagerness for his supplication to be answered and his call and imploring to be heard.

*Ayy* serves as a connective to call that which has the definite article *al-*, just as *dhu* and *alladhi* serve as connectives for describing generic nouns with attributes and for describing definite nouns with clauses. It is an ambiguous noun, requiring something that clarifies it and removes its ambiguity; so it must be followed by a generic noun or something that takes its place, which it is qualified by, so that the intended object of the call is valid. Thus the element governed by the vocative particle is *ayy*, and the noun that follows it is its attribute, as when you say: "Ya Zayd al-Zarif." Except that *ayya* does not stand on its own the way *Zayd* does, so it is never without the attribute. In this progression from ambiguity to clarification there is a kind of emphasis and intensification. The particle of alerting (*kalimat al-tanbih*), inserted between the attribute and what it qualifies, serves two purposes: it supports the vocative particle and reinforces its meaning with emphasis, and it stands in as a substitute for what *ayy* deserves of the annexation (*idafah*).

If you ask: why has calling in this manner been frequent in the Book of God, more than in other speech? I say: because it has independent features of emphasis and causes of intensity. For everything to which God calls His servants, of His commands and prohibitions, His admonitions and warnings, His promises and threats, the narration of the histories of the nations that came upon them, and other matters which His Book has spoken, are weighty affairs and grave calamities, and meanings that they must be awake to and incline their hearts and insight towards, while they are heedless of them. Therefore the situation required that they be called with the most emphatic and eloquent form.

If you say: the command to worship cannot but be directed either to the believers and disbelievers together, or to the disbelievers of Mecca specifically, as is related from ʿAlqamah and al-Hasan. The believers worship their Lord, so how are they commanded with what they are already engaged in? Is this not like the saying of the poet:

"Had I done it, I would have been like one who asks Him,
while He is standing, to stand up."

[[God's blessing upon you, I do not ask God for another blessing joined to it, apart from its enduring, whether it be this blessing, or you, or both of you.

Had I done so... as one who asks him
while he is standing that he stand.

*Al-niʿmah* with a kasrah and *al-niʿmah* with a dammah, and likewise *al-naʿmaʾ* with a fathah, have the same meaning. He says: God's blessing upon us in you is sufficient; we do not ask God for another blessing added to it, except that it endure, either it or you or the two of you. Had I—by transposition for the metre—done so, that is, asked God for other than it, my situation with God would be like your situation with one whom you ask to stand while he is standing. This is a compound simile; otherwise he is the asker and the one asked is asked. He means that the request would be a seeking of what is already obtained, since there is no blessing other than it that is greater than it in his estimation. In this there is an exaggeration of its magnification.]]

As for the disbelievers, they do not know God, nor do they affirm Him; so how do they worship Him? I say: what is meant by the worship of the believers is their increase in it, their turning to it, and their steadfastness upon it. As for the worship of the disbelievers, what is conditioned upon it is that which it cannot do without, namely affirmation (*iqrar*). Just as the one commanded to pray is required to fulfil its conditions, such as ablution, intention, and others, and what the act cannot do without, it is included under the command to it even if not mentioned, since it is not performed except with them and they are among its necessities. Moreover, the polytheists of Mecca used to know God and acknowledge Him: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: God﴾.

If you say: you have made His words ﴿worship﴾ comprise two things together: the command to worship and the command to increase it. I say: increase in worship is worship, and not another thing. If you say: what is meant by ﴿your Lord﴾?

I say: the polytheists held two lordships: the lordship of God and the lordship of their gods. If the address is restricted to them, then what is meant is a name shared by the Lord of the heavens and the earth and the gods which they called lords; and His words ﴿who created you﴾ are a clarifying, distinguishing attribute. If the address is to all the categories, then what is meant by ﴿your Lord﴾ is in its literal sense, and ﴿who created you﴾ is an attribute applied to Him in the manner of praise and magnification. This interpretation is not excluded in the address to the disbelievers specifically, though the first is clearer and more correct.

*Khalq* (creation) is bringing a thing into existence according to a measure and proportion; it is said: *khalaqa al-naʿl* (he made the sandal), when he measured it and shaped it by the standard. Abu ʿAmr read ﴿khalaqakum﴾ with assimilation (*idgham*). Abu al-Sumayqaʿ read ﴿wa-khalaqa min qablikum﴾. In the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAli it is ﴿wa-alladhina min qablikum﴾, and this reading is problematic; its explanation, in spite of its difficulty, is that the second relative pronoun has been inserted between the first and its relative clause for emphasis, just as Jarir inserted it in his saying:

"O Taym, Taym of ʿAdi, may you have no father,
do not let ʿUmar's disgrace bring you down.

Taym confronted me in ignorance so that I might satirise it,
as the anus of the farting one confronts the stone."

[[Jarir; ʿUmar ibn Lajaʾ, or Ibn Lijam al-Tamimi, confronted him with satire, so he addressed his tribe with it. Omitting the genitive complement while the annexed noun keeps its state of annexation is common when it is accompanied by mention of its like to indicate it; otherwise it is an item of transmission (*sama'i*). For this kind of construction, the first word may be given a *damma*, in which case it is indefinite and the second is annexed to what follows; or it may be given a *fatha*, treating it as annexed to the mentioned item, or to an omitted similar item, or treating them as two parts forming one compound noun annexed to what follows. Thus here Taym the first is annexed to ʿAdi, and the second, inserted between them, is annexed to ʿAdi, which is omitted according to Sibawayh, or annexed to the mentioned item; the first is annexed to an omitted item like the mentioned one according to al-Mubarrad, and Ibn Malik followed him; or both are a compound like *khamsata ʿashara* (fifteen), annexed to ʿAdi according to al-Farra', and al-Aʿlam followed him. If the second were an appositive, an explanatory noun, or an emphatic, and the first were indefinite, the first would be given a *damma*, since they are not the Taym of Quraysh. Their saying *la abā lahu* is a supplication for his having no father; it has been said it is also open to dispraise, meaning "I do not consider him rightly guided; rather he is the son of fornication," and it is open to praise, meaning "he does not need a father; rather his glories are inherent in himself." But what is here is the first. *Lakum* is the predicate of *la* according to Ibn al-Hajib; its predicate is omitted according to others, and *lakum* is attached to an omitted item functioning as an attribute. Or the *lam* is superfluous and the pronoun is the genitive complement. As for the first view, it is built on an assumed fatha, its tanwin removed for construction; on the second view it is in the accusative by an assumed fatha, its tanwin removed for resemblance to annexation; on the third it is in the accusative by an assumed fatha, its tanwin removed for annexation. All this is according to the dialect that treats it as a shortened form like *fata* (youth). As for putting it in the accusative with an *alif* according to the dialect that inflects it with letters, it appears only in the third case, and there it is an issue that the annexed noun is definite while *la* governs only indefinites, unless it is said that the addition of the *lam* made it resemble an indefinite, so that *la* could govern it. *La yulqinannakum* is a prohibition against being cast into something disliked. It is reported with *fa'* instead of *qaf*, from *alfa*, "to find"; but it is reported as *la yuqiʿannakum* (does not bring you about), which supports the first.

The intention is the prohibition of ʿUmar's endorsement of his satire, which exposes them to disgrace, and that disgrace is Jarir's satire of them. The *lam* in *li-ahjuwhā* is the *lam* of consequence. He has compared himself—rather his mouth—to the anus of the farting one, meaning its rear; and he prepared for that comparison earlier by using the expression "disgrace." He has thus satirised himself without realising it. *Ist* (anus) is among the ten nouns whose initial letters they built on sukun, adding to them a hamzat al-wasl.]]

[The second *Taym* lies between the first and what is annexed to it], and as they inserted the *lam* of annexation between the annexed and the annexed-to in *la abālak* (may you have no father).

*La'alla* expresses hope or apprehension. You say: "Perhaps Zayd will honour me," and "Perhaps he will humiliate me." God the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ and ﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾. Do you not see His words ﴿Those who believe are apprehensive of it﴾? [La'alla] has come in the Qur'an in several places in the manner of raising hopes; but since it is the raising of hopes by one who is generous and merciful, when he raises hopes he does what he raises hopes for without fail, and his raising of hopes takes the place of his inevitable promise and his fulfilment of it. Some have said that *la'alla* means *kay* (in order that), but *la'alla* does not mean *kay*; the truth is what has been conveyed to you. Also, it is the custom of kings, and the established practice of their affairs and ceremonies, to restrict their promises, which they resolve to fulfil, to saying *ʿasā*, *laʿalla*, and similar words, or to hint at them; or one obtains from them a nod, a smile, or a pleasant glance, and when something of this kind is obtained from them, the seeker has no doubt about success and attaining what he seeks. Upon the like of this came the speech of the King of kings, the Possessor of might and majesty. Or it comes in the mode of raising hopes rather than certainty, lest the servants rely upon it, as in His words: ﴿O you who believe, turn to God in sincere repentance; perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds﴾. If you ask: what is the meaning of *la'alla* in the verse, and what is its position? I say: it is not of the kind we have mentioned at all, because His words ﴿who created you﴾ and ﴿that you may be mindful of God﴾ cannot be taken to mean that God hopes they will be mindful; hope is not admissible concerning the Knower of the unseen and the seen. Nor is it correct to understand it as meaning that He created them hoping they would be mindful. Rather, *la'alla* in the verse is used figuratively, not literally, because God the Mighty and Majestic created His servants to worship Him through obligation; He placed in them intellects and appetites; He removed every excuse from their destinies and their empowerment, guided them to the two highways, and placed in their hands the reins of choice. He desired from them goodness and piety [[His words "and He desired from them goodness and piety" are based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah that God wills only goodness, even if the opposite occurs. The doctrine of the People of the Sunnah is that He wills both good and evil, and whatever He wills occurs, by the consensus (*ijma'*) of the early generation that what God willed came to pass and what He did not will did not come to pass. (ʿ)]]. So they are in the form of those from whom piety is hoped, so that their affair may tip the balance, since they are free to choose between obedience and disobedience, just as the state of one who is hoped for is balanced between his doing and not doing. Its confirmation is His mighty and majestic words: ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. Only one who does not know the outcomes tests and examines; but the testing is figurative, the basing of their affair upon their choice. If you ask: just as He created the addressees perhaps they would be mindful, so He created those before them for that same purpose; why did He restrict it to them and not to those before them? I say: He did not restrict it to them; rather, the addressees predominated over the absent ones in wording and meaning, because all are intended. If you ask: why not say *tabudūn* (you worship) instead of *uʿbudū* (worship)? Or *ittaqū* (be mindful) for the sake of *tattaqūn* (you are mindful), so that the two ends of the composition would correspond? [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said, may God have mercy on him: "If you ask, why not say *taʿbudūn*..." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said, may God have mercy on him: a good statement, except his words "created you" for the sake of attaining the furthest extent of worship, for it is based on that earlier impulse. The precise expression of this in line with the rule of the Sunnah is to say: "Worship your Lord who created you in a state in which you are obliged to attain the furthest extent of worship, which is piety, because of the intellects He placed in you and the incentives to piety He made clear to you; so it is fitting that you not leave any effort in piety undone."]] I say: piety is not other than worship, so as to lead to a disharmony in the composition. Piety is merely the utmost aim and the furthest effort of the worshipper. So when He says ﴿Worship your Lord who created you﴾, for the sake of reaching the furthest extent of worship, it is more apt to arouse worship, more binding upon it, and more firmly established in souls. Similarly, you might say to your servant: "Carry the box of books; I have only owned you for carrying heavy loads." If you said, "to carry boxes of books," it would not fall in his soul into that same position.

He (glory be to Him) mentioned first, among the things that necessitate His worship and that make the obligation of gratitude to Him binding, that He created them living and able, because it is the precedent and foundation of the blessings and the means by which worship, gratitude and other acts become possible. Then He created the earth, which is their place and their dwelling that they cannot do without, and it is like the open ground of a dwelling, its place of turning and its bed.
