Then He created the sky, which is like a raised dome and an extended tent over this abode. Then (He made) what He, mighty and majestic, arranged, which is like the marriage contract between the (fertile) earth and the (overshadowing) sky by sending down water from it upon her. And the bringing forth by it from her womb of the likenesses of the offspring produced by animals, of the various kinds of fruits, as provision for the children of Adam, so that this would be for them a thing to be considered, a ladder to reflection that leads to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) and to acknowledgment, and a blessing they recognise and so respond to with the obligation of gratitude. They reflect on the creation of themselves and on what is above them and below them, and that none of these created things is able to bring any of them into being. Thus they become certain that they must have a Creator who is unlike them, so that they do not make created things equals to Him while they know that these are not able to do anything like what He is able to do.

The relative pronoun with its clause is either in the accusative position as a qualifier, like ﴿the one who created you﴾, or in the sense of praise and glorification. Or it is in the nominative as a subject (of a new sentence), and in it is the same praise as in the accusative.

Yazid al-Shami read بساطا (basatan, "a spread carpet"). Talha read مهادا (mihadan, "a cradle/bed"). The meaning of making it a bed, a carpet and a cradle for the people is that they sit upon it, sleep and turn over on it, as one of them turns on his bed, his carpet and his cradle.

If you say: is there in this evidence that the earth is flat and not spherical? I say: there is nothing in it except that people spread themselves upon it as they do with bedding, and whether it is in the shape of a plane or the shape of a sphere, spreading out is neither objectionable nor rejected, because of the great size of the earth, the vastness of its body and the distance of its extremities. And if it is easy in the mountain, which is one of the pegs of the earth, then in the earth with its length and breadth it is easier.

Al-bina' (building) is a verbal noun used to name the thing built, whether it is a house, a dome, a tent or a pavilion. The "abniyat" of the Arabs are their tents, and from this comes the expression "banā 'alā imra'atihi" (he consummated the marriage with his wife), because when they married they would pitch a new tent over her.

If you say: what is the meaning of bringing forth fruits by water, when they came forth by His power and will? I say: the meaning is that He made water a means of their emergence and a material for them, like the male's water in the creation of the child. He is able to bring all kinds into being without causes or materials, just as He brought into being the very selves of the causes and materials. But in bringing things into being He has a gradual course for them, moving them from one state to another and from one rank to another, by wisdom and by means, through which He renews for His angels and for those among His servants who look with the eyes of insight, lessons and sound reflections, and increased tranquillity and calm in His great power and wondrous wisdom. This is not the case in bringing them into being suddenly, without gradation and order.

The "min" in مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ (min al-thamarat, "of the fruits") is partitive (li-l-tab'idh), as evidenced by His saying ﴿so We brought forth by it from all the fruits﴾ and His saying ﴿so We brought forth by it fruits﴾. And because the two indefinite nouns, "water" and "provision", are flanked by it.

By making the two nouns indefinite, the partitive sense was intended, as if it were said: "And We sent down some water from the sky, and by it brought forth some fruits, so that it would be some of your provision." This is what matches the soundness of the meaning, because not all the water was sent down from the sky, nor were all fruits brought forth by the rain, nor was all provision placed in fruits. It is also permissible that the "min" be explanatory (li-l-bayan), as in your saying: "I spent a thousand of the dirhams."

If you say: in what is رِزْقاً (rizqan, "provision") put in the accusative?

I say: if "min" is partitive, its accusative is as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). If it is explanatory, it is an object of akhraja (the direct object of "brought forth").

If you say: the fruit brought forth by the rain of the sky is abundant and plentiful, so why is it said الثَّمَراتِ (al-thamarat, "the fruits") rather than الثَّمَرَ (al-thamar) or الثِّمَارَ (al-thimar)?

I say: there are two aspects to this. The first is that by الثَّمَراتِ is intended the plural of the unit noun thamara, as in your saying: "So-and-so reached the fruit (thamara) of his garden," meaning its fruits. A parallel to this is the expression "kalimat al-Huwaydara" (the poem of al-Huwaydara), for his qasida, and their saying of the village "al-madara," while it is only a collection of clods of earth that are joined together. The second is that plural forms may take the place of one another, because they share the quality of plurality, as in His saying ﴿how many gardens they left behind﴾ and ﴿three periods﴾. The first aspect is supported by the reading of Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa'": "min al-thamarati" in the singular.

As for قَبْلِكُمْ (qablikum, "before you"), it is a qualifier following "provision" if the physical object is intended by it; if it is made a name for the abstract meaning, then it is an object, as if it were said: "provision for you."

If you say: with what is فَلا تَجْعَلُوا (fa-la taj'alu, "so do not make") connected?

I say: there are three aspects. First, that it is connected with the command, meaning: worship your Lord, so do not make for Him equals, because the root and foundation of worship is tawhid, and that nothing should be made a rival or partner to God. Second, that it is connected with la'alla (perhaps), so that taj'alu is in the accusative in the manner of "fa-atţali'" in His, mighty and majestic, saying ﴿Perhaps I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses﴾ in the reading of Hafs from 'Asim. That is, He created you so that you may guard yourselves and fear His punishment, so that you do not liken Him to His creatures. Third, that it is connected with the one who made for you, if you make it the subject of a new sentence, meaning: He is the one who singled you out with these great signs and luminous proofs witnessing to His oneness, so do not take partners for Him.

The nidd (equal) is the like. It is said only of an equal who opposes and contends. Jarir said:

"Do you make Taym equals to me?
But Taym is no equal to a man of noble lineage."

[The interrogative is one of denial. Taym is the name of a man and of a tribe, and it is the object placed before the verb. "Ila" is connected to "tajʿalun" by way of tadmin (implying a verb of attribution), meaning: "you attribute it to me," or "ila" is in the sense of "li" (to me). It is permissible for it to be connected to nidda, which is the second object. The waw is for circumstance, meaning: "while the state is that Taym is not an equal to a man of lineage and glories; how then could he be an equal to me?" It is also reported as: "Atayman taj'alun," so then it is the subject, and the meaning is what has preceded. "Ila" is connected to a suppressed verb, as a circumstantial phrase from Taym or from nidda. The nidd is the equal and the opposite.]

And nāddaytu al-rajul: I opposed him and contended with him, from nadda, yanuddu, nadan, when he fled. The meaning of their saying "there is no equal (nidd) or opposite (didd) to God" is the negation of what could fill His place, and the negation of what would oppose Him.

If you say: they used to name their idols with His name and exalt them with what He is exalted by of nearness, and they did not claim that these opposed God or contended with Him. I say: when they drew near to them, exalted them and named them gods, their state resembled the state of one who believes that they are gods like Him, capable of opposing and contending with Him. So this was said to them in the manner of mockery, just as they were mocked with the word nidd. It censured them and made their situation appear monstrous, in that they made many equals for One who cannot possibly have any equal at all.

Concerning this, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said when he parted from the religion of his people:

"One Lord, or a thousand lords?
I serve (Him) when affairs are divided.
I have left al-Lat and al-'Uzza together,
as the wise man does."

[These verses are by 'Amr ibn Zayd ibn Nufayl ibn Riyah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Qurt ibn Riza ibn Rabi'a. The hamza is for interrogation. In it there is a kind of wonder and a showing of the error of worshipping lords, and a censure of their worshippers. "Rabban" is the object. "Adin" means: I obey. By "alf" (thousand) is meant multiplicity, not that specific number. "When affairs are divided" means: when each group takes for itself a religion of the religions. His saying "al-Lat al-'Uzza" means: and other idols besides them, since there is no difference between them. "Al-Basir" means one who looks carefully into a matter.]

And Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' read: فلا تجعلوا للَّه ندا (fa-la taj'alu lillahi nidda, "so do not make for God an equal") in the singular.

If you say: what is the meaning of وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ (wa-antum ta'lamun, "while you know")?

I say: its meaning is: your state and attribute is that, by the soundness of your discernment between the true and the false, your knowledge of the subtleties of matters and the obscure aspects of conditions, your correctness in plans, your cunning and shrewdness, you stand at a rank from which you cannot be turned back.

Thus were the Arabs, especially the residents of the Haram from Quraysh and Kinana, whose fire could not be warmed at by [[The phrase "lā yuṣṭalā bi-nārihim" ("whose fire one does not warm himself at") is perhaps "yuṣṭalā" without "lā", or perhaps "lā yuṣṭalā illā bi-nārihim" with "illā" added; let it be checked. It is possible that what is meant is their exclusive possession of complete knowledge, and that others do not attain anything of what they have of that. (ʿ)]] in the firmness of knowledge of matters and the good comprehension of them. The object of "ta'lamun" is omitted, as if it were said: "and you are among the people of knowledge and understanding." The rebuke in it is more emphatic, meaning: you are the diviners who discern. Then, what you are upon in the matter of your religion, namely making idols equals to God, is the utmost ignorance and the final foolishness of intellect.

It is also permissible to estimate: "and you know that He is not like (them)"; or: "and you know the disparity between Him and them"; or: "and you know that they do not do the like of His acts," as in His saying ﴿Is there any among your partners who does anything of that?﴾

When he had argued against them with what establishes God's oneness and confirms it, and nullifies and demolishes associating partners with Him, and had taught them the way to establish and verify that, and had made them aware that whoever associates partners with God has defied his own intellect and covered over the faculty of knowledge and discernment that God bestowed upon him, he followed this with what serves as proof of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and what refutes the doubt about the Qur'an being a miracle. He showed them how they could recognize whether it is from God, as he claims, or from himself, as they claim, by guiding them to assess themselves and examine their own natures, for they are of his kind and his own people.

If you ask: Why is it said ﴿of what We have sent down﴾ with the verb *nazzala* (the intensive form, "to send down gradually") rather than *anzala* (to send down)?

I answer: Because what is meant is descent in stages and in installments (*tanjim*), and this is figurative (*majaz*) on account of the challenge (*tahaddi*, the challenge to produce its equal). That is because they used to say: If this were from God, unlike what comes from people, it would not have descended in this manner, piecemeal, surah after surah and verse after verse, according to the occurrences and the events that match them, and in the way that the orators and poets are accustomed to, where what issues from them comes scattered at times and piece by piece, according to the renewed circumstances and the needs that arise for them. A composer does not present the collection of his poetry all at once, nor does a speaker throw out the whole of his sermons or letters in one blow. So if God had sent it down, He would have sent it down contrary to this custom, all at once. God the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ [25:32]. So it was said:

If you doubt this, which has been sent down in this manner, gradually and by stages, then produce for yourselves one installment of its like, and come forward with a single part of its portions: a surah from the shortest surahs, or various verses of fabrications. This is the utmost rebuke and the furthest removal of excuses.

It has been read ﴿upon Our servants﴾, meaning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his community. The *surah* (chapter) is a portion of the Qur'an that is delimited and whose smallest length is three verses. If its *waw* is original, then it is either named after *sur* (the wall of a city), for it is a portion of the Qur'an bounded and enclosed on its own, like a walled town, or because it contains various branches of knowledge and kinds of benefits, just as the enclosure of a town contains what is within it. Or it is named after *surah* in the sense of rank. Al-Nabigha said:

*And to the tribe of Harrab, and Qadd, is a surah*
*in glory, whose crow is never driven away.*

*They are a people, when the clamour grows, you see them*
*deaf (*waqr*) and calm on the morning of terror and dispersal.*

This is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani. *Al-surah*, with a *damma*, means rank. He says: For the people of Harrab ibn Zuhayr and Qadd ibn Malik there is a lasting degree in nobility, perpetual in honour. *Harrab* is with a *ra'*, and it is narrated with a *za'*. *Qadd* is with an unpointed letter, and it is narrated with a pointed one. *Qadd* and *waqad* are two brothers. *Laysa ghurabuha bi-mutar* ("whose crow is never driven away") is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*) for their perpetual glory, or an implicit metaphor (*kinaya*) for it. Its origin is that when trees and vegetation are abundant, a crow stays there and nothing drives it away, out of love for fertility and the absence of drought. The more apt view is that *surah* originally means a sensory rank, and it was borrowed for a non-sensory one. Then implicit metaphor (*takniya*) operated in it, since it was likened to a place of fertility, and attributing the crow and its being driven away is an imaginative evocation (*takhyil*) of that comparison. Then he said: They are a people who, when the shouting in war grows, you see them *waqr*, that is, deaf; it derives from *waqr*, meaning heaviness of the ear, in the sense that the increase of shouting does not disturb them, as if they were deaf. It is also said that it derives from *waqar*, meaning dignity and composure. *Ghadat al-rawʿ wa'l-infar* means the morning of fear and alarm. It is also said that the origin of this is that a crow alights on the head of a camel to pick up its vermin, and does not move its head lest the crow be startled; so he likened their rank to the head of the camel by way of implicit metaphor. It is also said that, because of its height, the crow does not reach it so as to be harmed by what is above it. So the meaning is: there is no crow above it to be driven away.

Either of two meanings is intended, because the surahs are like dwellings and degrees in which the reader ascends; and they are also graded in themselves: long, medium and short. Or it is because of the elevation of their status and the greatness of their place in the religion. If its *waw* is considered to be changed from a *hamza*, then it is because it is a piece and a portion of the Qur'an, like the *su'ra*, which is the remainder of a thing and its surplus.

If you ask: What is the benefit of dividing the Qur'an and cutting it into surahs?

I answer: The benefit in this is not single. For a reason, God sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and all else that He revealed to His prophets in this method, divided into surahs and with headings for the surahs. And the authors of every discipline have arranged their books into chapters adorned with headings. Among its benefits: when a kind (*jins*) contains various types and comprises various categories, it is better, nobler and more magnificent (*afkham*) than if it were a single statement. Among them: when the reader finishes a surah or a chapter of the book and then begins another, it is more invigorating for him, more inclined to his affection, and more conducive to study and acquisition than if he continued through the book in its entirety. Similarly the traveller, when he knows that he has covered a mile, or crossed a league, or reached the end of a postal stage, his soul is refreshed and he is energized for the journey. For this reason the reciters divided the Qur'an into sevens, parts, tens and fifths. Among them: when the memorizer masters a surah (*idha hadhaqa al-surah*, when he has perfected it), he believes that he has taken from the Book of God a portion that is independent in itself, having an opening and a closing, so what he has memorized becomes great in his sight, he holds it in esteem in his soul, and he rejoices in it.

From this is the hadith of Anas, may God be pleased with him: "When a man recited al-Baqarah and Ali Imran, he became great among us." [This is part of a hadith recorded by Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shaybah, who said: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us from Humayd, from Anas, may God be pleased with him: "A man who used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ) had recited al-Baqarah and Ali Imran, and when a man recited al-Baqarah and Ali Imran he became great among us (*jadda*, i.e. became great): the hadith." Ibn Hibban recorded it through this chain with the wording "a man of standing became prominent among us." Al-Jawhari also mentioned it in *al-Sihah* (his lexicon) from the hadith of Anas, may God be pleased with him, in the wording of the author. Its origin is in al-Bukhari, through the narration of Abd al-Aziz ibn Suhayb, and in Muslim through the narration of Thabit, both from Anas, without the portion the author restricted himself to. Al-Tibi was not correct in attributing it to the two Sahihs. Al-Zamakhshari also attributed it, in his commentary on the chapter of the Jinn, to a narration from Umar, may God be pleased with him, as will come.] And for this reason, reciting a complete surah in prayer is more excellent. Among them: division causes the forms and the analogous passages to be linked together, and some of them to suit others. By this the meanings are noticed and the composition resonates, along with other benefits and advantages.

﴿من مثله﴾ ("of its like") is connected to *surah* as its attribute, meaning a surah that is of its like. The pronoun refers to *what We have sent down* [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "The pronoun may refer back to *what We have sent down*..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: The meaning of this preference is that, in the more apt interpretation, the challenge is addressed to the whole body of addressees: that is, by gathering together and supporting one another, they are unable to produce a portion of it. As for the less preferred interpretation, they are addressed to designate one of their number who would oppose the challenger by bringing the like of what was brought, or a part of it. There is no doubt that the incapacity of all creatures together is more manifest than the incapacity of any one of them. The soundness of the first view is confirmed by the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants﴾ [17:88].] Or it refers to *Our servant*. It is permissible for it to be connected to His saying ﴿then produce﴾, with the pronoun referring to the servant.

If you ask: And what is its like, such that they could produce a surah of that like?

I answer: The meaning is: produce a surah of that which has the same qualities, in the strange eloquence of its exposition and the lofty rank of the beauty of its composition. Or: produce [a surah] from one who is in its condition, being a human, an Arab, an unlettered person who did not read books and did not take from the scholars, and who did not intend a likeness or equal there. It is rather like the saying of al-Qabthari to al-Hajjaj, when he said to him: "I will surely mount you on the dark-coloured horse." He replied: "Like the Amir's mounting the dark horse and the white one." He meant one who is of the same standing as the ruler, in authority, power and expansiveness of hand, and he did not intend anyone to be taken as a likeness of al-Hajjaj. Returning the pronoun to what was sent down is more appropriate, because of His saying ﴿then produce a surah of its like﴾, ﴿then produce ten surahs like it﴾ [11:13], ﴿upon producing the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like﴾ [17:88]. And because the Qur'an is worthy of sound arrangement and of falling upon the most correct styles, and the speech with the pronoun referring to what was sent down is better arranged.

That is because the discussion concerns what was sent down, not the one upon whom it was sent down. The discourse is directed toward it and tied to it, so it should not be detached from it by returning the pronoun to something else. Do you not see that the meaning is: "If you are in doubt that the Qur'an is sent down from God, then produce for yourselves a portion like it and of its kind"? The order would require, if the pronoun referred to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that it be said: "If you doubt that Muhammad has had it sent down to him, then produce a Qur'an of its like." Also, when they are addressed together, and they are a great multitude, to produce a small portion of the kind that one of them brought, it is more emphatic in the challenge than to say to them: "Let another one come with the like of what this one brought." Also, this interpretation is the one that suits His saying ﴿and call your witnesses﴾, and *shuhada'* (witnesses) is the plural of *shahid*, meaning present or one who bears witness. The meaning of *dun* (apart from, other than) is the nearest place to a thing; from it comes *al-shay' al-dun*, meaning the lowly, the base; and *dawwana al-kutub* (he compiled the books), when he gathered them, because gathering things is bringing some of them near to one another and reducing the distance between them. One says: "This is *dun* that," when it is slightly inferior to it. *Dunaka hadha* originally meant "take it from your nearest place," then it was abbreviated and borrowed for the difference in conditions and ranks, so one says: "Zayd is *dun* ʿAmr in nobility and knowledge." From this is the saying of one who said to his enemy, when he saw him praising him: "I am *dun* this that you say, and *fawq* what is in your soul." [This was recorded by al-Bazzar through the narration of Ali ibn Abi Rabi'a, who said: "A man came to Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and began praising him, and what reached him from him was the opposite of that. He said: 'I am beneath what you say, but I am above what is in your soul.'"] Then it was extended so that it is used for every transgression of a limit toward another limit, and overstepping one judgement toward another.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies apart from the believers﴾ [3:28], meaning: let them not go beyond the guardianship of the believers to the guardianship of the disbelievers. Umayya said:

*O soul, you have no protector apart from God,*
*nor any charmer against the stings of the daughters of time.*

This is by Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt. He says: O soul, there is no guardian for you apart from God, that is, going beyond God, or going beyond God in a manner that is transgressive, so it is a state either of the protector or of the soul. He borrowed "daughters" for events, by the joining of the constant attendance of each to its producer, by way of explicit metaphor (*tasrih*). Then he likened the events to vipers, by the joint quality of each harming another, by way of implicit metaphor, and the "sting" is an imaginative evocation. It is also permissible that he borrowed "sting" for striking, by way of explicit metaphor.

And *raqi* means the physician who treats the sting. *Min* is redundant in both places, for the emphasis of universality: meaning, you have no guardian except God, and no reliever for you except Him. The meaning is: if you exceed the protection of God and do not obtain it, no one else will protect you.

﴿من دون الله﴾ ("apart from God") is connected to *ud'u* (call) or to *shuhada'akum* (your witnesses). If you connect it to *shuhada'akum*, the meaning is: call those whom you have taken as gods apart from God and whom you claimed would bear witness for you on the Day of Resurrection that you are upon the truth. Or: call those who will bear witness for you before God, from the saying of al-A'sha:

*She shows you the dregs beyond her, while she is beyond them:*
*when one who has tasted her takes her, he smacks his lips.*

Al-A'sha said this in praise of al-Muhalliq, ʿAbd al-Rahim ibn Khaythama ibn Shaddad. *Al-kumayt* means the swift one. *Mada al-ʿazm* means swift in giving drink to people, even if they are many. *Al-ziyad*, with a *kasra* (as in *kirman*), is the froth of milk and the like. *Al-tarqraq* means the trickling and the pouring. *Tarqraq* originally was *tatarqraq*, from which one of the two *ta's* was dropped, meaning it moves. *Tuthri-ka*: that is, the *sahbaʾ*, which is wine, because it has the colour of *sahba* (reddish dun). *Al-qadhā* is what falls into a drink or an eye. *Duniha*: that is, she placed it as a barrier between it and you, while she is *duna-hu*, that is, he placed his barrier between her and you, when one who has tasted her, that is wine, has tasted it, *yatamattaq* means he makes a sound by opening his mouth and sucking his tongue and lips, or he closes and opens his mouth with pleasure in it so that it makes a sound. It is said that the pronoun in *tuthrika* refers to the glass, describing it as clear, so perhaps he applied the name *sahbaʾ* to it because it takes on the colour of the wine; and the pronoun in *dhāqahā* refers to it in the sense of the wine, so there is a double usage (*istikhdam*) in the speech. It is also narrated as *wa-hiya fawquhu* ("while she is above it") instead of *dunahu*, and in this there is some support for the pronoun referring to the wine.

That is: she shows you the dregs in front of her, while she is in front of the dregs, because of her fineness and clarity. In commanding them to seek the support of the inanimate object that does not speak, in opposing the Qur'an with its eloquence, there is the utmost mockery of them. ﴿And call your witnesses apart from God﴾, that is, apart from His friends and from the non-believers, to bear witness for you that you have brought its like. This is an indulgence, a loosening of the reins, and an indication that their witnesses, who are the pillars of the people and the leaders of the gatherings and the champions of the contests and disputes, are such that their natures refuse for them and their humanity and pride reject their agreeing to bear witness for the corruption that is manifestly corrupt to them, and to affirm the impossibility that is clear to their minds as impossible. Its linking to the call (*du'a'*) is permissible in this aspect. If you connect it to the call, the meaning is: call from apart from God your witnesses, that is, do not call God as a witness, and do not say: "God bears witness that what we claim is true," as one who is unable to establish proof of the soundness of his claim says; and call upon the witnesses from among the people, whose testimony is proof by which claims are validated before the judges. This is a challenge to them and a statement of their being cut off and abandoned, and that the argument has overwhelmed them and left them no hold except their saying: "God bears witness that we are truthful." This saying of theirs is a record they make against themselves of the extreme of incapacity and the fall of power.

It is reported of an Arab who was asked about his lineage, and he said: "A Qurashi, praise be to God." It was said to him: "Your saying 'praise be to God' in this position is suspicious." Or: call your witnesses apart from God, meaning: God is your witness, since He is nearer to you than your jugular vein [50:16], and He is between you and the necks of your mounts. The jinn and mankind are your witnesses. So call upon whoever witnesses for you and seek support from among the jinn and mankind, other than God the Exalted, for He alone is capable of bringing its like, unlike any witness among your witnesses. So this is in the sense of His saying: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn were to gather together...﴾ [17:88], to the end of the verse.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 24:

When He had guided them to the means by which they could recognize the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what he brought, so that they might arrive at its reality and its secret and distinguish his truth from falsehood, He said to them: "So if you do not produce a counterpart, and what you seek does not become easy for you, and it becomes clear to you that it is beyond your capacity, then the truth has become pure from its adulteration and belief is obligatory. So believe, and fear the punishment prepared for those who deny." In this there are two proofs for establishing prophethood: the soundness of the challenge (tahaddi) being something beyond human ability (i'jaz), and the报 information that they will never do it, which is an unseen matter that none knows except God. If you ask: the absence of their producing a surah is necessarily certain, so why was "idha" (if/since), which denotes certainty, not used instead of "in" (if), which denotes doubt? I answer: there are two aspects to this.

The first is that the statement is framed according to their own presumption and expectation, and that their inability to counter-argue was, before reflection, something doubtful to them, because of their reliance on their eloquence and their capacity for speech. The second is that it is said to them mockingly, as one who is endowed with strength and confident of victory over his opponent says: "If I overcome you, I will not spare you," while he knows that he will overcome him and is certain of it, mocking him. If you ask: why was the act expressed by the verb "ityan" (to produce/bring), and what is the benefit of leaving it for another verb? I answer: because it is an act among the acts. You say, "I came to so-and-so," and it is said to you, "What a fine thing you did." The benefit is that it functions as a metonymy (kinaya) which gives you brevity and concision, sparing you the lengthiness of what is referred to. Do you not see that a man says, "I struck Zayd in such-and-such a place in such-and-such a manner, and I insulted him and punished him," enumerating modes and acts, and you say, "Evil is what you did." If you had mentioned what he was referring to, it would have been lengthy for you; likewise, if the expression had not been shifted from "ityan" to "fi'l," it would have been lengthy to say: "So if you do not bring a surah like it."

"And you will never bring a surah like it." If you ask: what is the place (i'rab) of "wa lan taf'alu"? I answer: it has no place, because it is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tirada). If you ask: what is the real meaning of "lan" in the context of negation? I answer: "la" and "lan" are sisters in negating the future, except that in "lan" there is emphasis and intensification. You say to your companion, "I will not stand up tomorrow," and if he objects to you, you say: "I will certainly not stand up tomorrow," as you do in: "Ana muqim" and "inni muqim." According to al-Khalil, in one of two reports from him, its origin is "la an," and according to al-Farra', "la" whose alif was replaced with a nun. According to Sibawayh and one of the two reports from al-Khalil, it is a clipped particle (harf muqtadab) for emphasizing the negation of the future. If you ask: how do you know that it is a report of the unseen as it truly is, so that it would be a miracle? I answer: because if they had countered him with something, it would not have been impossible for people to describe it to one another and transmit it, since the concealment of such a thing in matters upon which customary practice is based is impossible, especially as those who opposed him were more numerous than those who defended him. When it was not transmitted, it became known that it was a report of the unseen as it truly is, and thus it was a miracle. If you ask: what is the meaning of making the absence of their producing a surah like it a condition for guarding against the Fire? I answer:

When they do not produce it and their inability to counter-argue becomes clear, the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) becomes established for them; and when his truthfulness has become established for them, and then they persist in obstinacy and do not submit or follow, they deserve punishment by the Fire. So it is said to them: "If you recognize the inability, then abandon obstinacy." The phrase "fa-ttaqu al-nar" (so guard against the Fire) is placed in its position, because guarding against the Fire is adjacent to and conjoined with abandoning obstinacy, in that it is one of its results, since whoever guards against the Fire abandons obstinacy. A parallel to this is a king saying to his retinue: "If you desire honor with me, then beware of my wrath," meaning: "Obey me and follow my command, and do what is the result of avoiding wrath." This is from the category of kinaya, which is a branch of the branches of eloquence. Its benefit is the brevity which is an ornament of the Qur'an, and the magnifying of the matter of obstinacy by placing the guarding against the Fire in its stead and displaying it in its form, accompanied by magnifying the description of the Fire and making its matter appear dreadful.

"Al-waqud" is that by which the fire is raised. As for the verbal noun (masdar), it is pronounced with a damma, though it has also come with a fatha. Sibawayh said: "We have heard from the Arabs one who says: 'The fire was kindled (waqadat al-nar) with a high kindling (waqudan 'aliyan).'" Then he said: "Al-wuqud (with damma) is more common, and al-wuqud (with damma) means firewood." 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Hamdani read it with a damma, as a naming by the verbal noun, as one says: "So-and-so is the pride of his people and the adornment of his land." It may also be like your saying: "The life of the lamp is the pure oil," meaning its life is nothing but by it, so that the essence of the oil is as if it were its life. If you ask: the relative clause of "alladhi" and "allati" must be a known matter to the addressee, so how did those people know that the Fire of the Hereafter is kindled with people and stones? I answer: it is not impossible that they had previously heard it from the People of the Book, or they heard it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or they heard before this verse the saying of God Most High in Surat al-Tahrim: "a Fire whose fuel is men and stones." If you ask: why did the Fire described by this sentence come indefinite in Surat al-Tahrim, while here it is definite? I answer: that verse was revealed in Mecca, so they knew from it a Fire described by this attribute. Then this verse was revealed in Medina, [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "This verse was revealed in Medina after the revelation of the verse of al-Tahrim in Mecca..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: he means by the verse the saying of God Most High: "Guard yourselves and your families against a Fire whose fuel is men and stones." However, I have not found any disagreement among the exegetes that Surat al-Tahrim is Medinan, and the well-known story it contains is the clearest witness to that. So it appears that al-Zamakhshari erred in his report that it is Meccan.]] referring by it to what they had known first.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying: "whose fuel is men and stones"? I answer: its meaning is that it is a fire distinguished from other fires, in that it is kindled only with men and stones, and that if other fires are used to burn men or to heat stones, they are first kindled with fuel and then what is to be burned or heated is cast into them; whereas that Fire—may God protect us from it by His vast mercy—is kindled by the very things that are burned and heated by fire. And because of its extreme heat and its intense ferocity, when it touches what no fire kindles from, it blazes and its flame rises. If you ask: is the whole of Hellfire kindled with men and stones, or are they various fires, one of which has this description? I answer: rather, they are various fires, among them a fire kindled with men and stones. This is indicated by its indefiniteness in His saying: "guard yourselves and your families against a Fire (naran)," and "So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes (talaza)." Perhaps the disbelieving jinn and their devils have a fire whose fuel is the devils, just as the disbelieving humans have a fire whose fuel is they themselves, as a requital to each kind with the punishment suited to it. If you ask: why were men paired with stones and the stones made fuel along with them? I answer: because they paired themselves with them in this world, when they carved them as idols and made them rivals to God, or worshipped them besides Him. God Most High said: "Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell (hasab Jahannam)." This verse explains what we are discussing.

So His saying: "You and what you worship besides God" has the meaning of "men and stones," and "fuel for Hell (hasab Jahannam)" has the meaning of "its fuel." Since the disbelievers believed that their stones worshipped besides God were intercessors and witnesses through whom they seek intercession and by whose standing they ward off harms from themselves, God made them their punishment, pairing them with them heated in the fire of Hell, for the sake of intensifying their pain and deepening their humiliation, similar to what He does with those who hoard gold and silver, making them a provision and a store, then withholding them stingily and refusing their dues, when they will be heated in the fire of Hell and their foreheads and sides will be branded with them. It has been said: they are stones of sulfur, but this is a specification without evidence and a neglect of the sound meaning which is attested by the meanings of the revelation. "U'iddat" means it was prepared for them and made a provision for their punishment. 'Abd Allah read "u'taddat," from al-i'tad, meaning readiness (al-ghudda).

Allah, the Exalted, has a habit in His Book of mentioning encouragement alongside warning, and of coupling good news with admonition, in order to stir the believer to acquire what brings him closer to Allah and to restrain him from committing what destroys him. When He mentioned the disbelievers, their deeds, and the threat of punishment for them, He followed this with good news for His servants who combined belief (taṣdīq) with righteous deeds, meaning the performance of acts of obedience and the abandonment of acts of disobedience, and who protected these deeds from being nullified (iḥbāṭ) by disbelief and from being outweighed by major sins, through reward.

If you ask: who is the one addressed by His words ﴿وَبَشِّرِ﴾ (And give good news)? I answer: it may be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it may be anyone. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Give good news to those who walk to the mosques in the darkness with the perfect light on the Day of Resurrection." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bazzar, through the chain of Isma'il ibn Sulayman from Abdullah ibn Aws from Buraydah. Al-Daraqutni said: Isma'il alone narrated it. It has a supporting narration from Thabit from Anas and Sahl ibn Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with them both, recorded by Ibn Majah and al-Hakim. Ibn Hibban recorded it from Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Tabarani recorded it from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Harithah, Abu Musa and Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with them, through weak chains. The hadith of Zayd is in Ibn Adi's al-Kamil. The hadith of Abu Musa is in al-Bazzar. Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat from the hadith of Aisha in the biography of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sadaqah, and said: Qatadah ibn al-Fadl alone narrated it from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Bayruti. Al-Tayalisi and Abu Ya'la narrated it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, and its chain is also weak. Umar ibn Shahin narrated it in his al-Targhib from the hadith of Haritha ibn Wahb al-Khuza'i.]] He did not command this of one specific person; rather, everyone is commanded with it. This second view is better and more eloquent, because it indicates that the matter, owing to its greatness and magnificence, deserves to be announced as good news by everyone who is able to announce it.

If you ask: upon what is this command conjoined, when no command or prohibition has preceded it to which it could be conjoined?
I answer: what is conjoined is not the command itself, so that one should seek for it some counterpart of command or prohibition to be conjoined to. Rather, what is conjoined is the sentence describing the reward of the believers, and it is conjoined to the sentence describing the punishment of the disbelievers. Just as you say: "Zayd is punished with shackles and distress, and give Amr good news of pardon and release."

You may also say that it is conjoined to His words ﴿فَاتَّقُوا﴾ (so beware). Just as you say: "O Banu Tamim, beware the punishment for what you have committed, and give good news, O so-and-so, to Banu Asad of my kindness to them." In the recitation of Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, it is read ﴿وَبُشِّرَ﴾ in the passive form, conjoined to ﴿أُعِدَّتْ﴾ (was prepared).

Al-bushārah (good news) is the report of something which manifests the joy of the one who reports it. For this reason the scholars said: if a man says to his slaves, "Whichever of you brings me the news of so-and-so's arrival will be free," and they bring him the news one by one, the first of them is freed, because he is the one who showed his joy at the news, to the exclusion of the others. But if he says, instead of "brings me the news" (bashsharanī), "informs me" (akhbaranī), then they are all freed, because they all informed him. From the same root is al-bashrah (the outer skin), and tabāshīr al-ṣubḥ (the first signs of the dawn light), which are what appears of its first light.

As for ﴿فَبَشِّرْهُمْ بِعَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ﴾ (so give them the news of a painful punishment), it is an inversion of the expression, used in speech intended for excessive mockery, to increase the anger of the one mocked and his pain and distress. As a man says to his enemy: "Be given good news of the killing of your offspring and the plundering of your wealth." From the same usage is the line:

"Tamim became angry that we should kill Amir... on the day of al-Nissar, so they were appeased with al-Sayqal."

This is by Bishr ibn Abi Hazim al-Asadi. Tamim and Amir are two tribes. Hal here is an interrogative of denial, meaning: the one who has tested affairs is not like the one who has not tested them. It is also possible that he commanded them to ask, because the one who asks and knows is not like the one who does not know. And "an naqtul" means "min an naqtul," that is, "because we kill."
It is also narrated as "yuqtal Amir" with the passive form. Al-Nissar is the name of a water source of Banu Amir. The meaning is that Tamim became angry with us for killing their allies, so it is as if they were rebuking us out of their weakness. So we appeased them (fa-a'taba-nāhum), that is, we removed their rebuke with al-Sayqal, which is the sword that cuts much, from ṣalama when he cuts. The response to them by fighting with the sword is likened to the response of one who removes the rebuke, by way of the explicit sarcastic metaphor (al-tasrīḥiyya al-tahakkumiyya, a metaphor stated explicitly and used for mockery), because the first is disliked and the second is loved.

And ﴿الصَّالِحَةُ﴾ (the righteous deeds) is like ﴿الْحَسَنَةِ﴾ in that it functions in the manner of a noun. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"How can I satirize when there continually comes to me a righteous (ṣāliḥa) [deed] from the family of Lam, in absence?"

Al-Hutay'ah, whose name was Jarwal ibn Aws ibn Hawmah ibn Makhdum ibn Malik al-Ghatafani, [composed this] when the Arabs came as a delegation to al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir. He brought great robes of honour and said: "I will put them on tomorrow on whomever you wish." When the next day came, Ibn Sa'di held back for fear that they would be put on someone else while he was present. So the king sought him and clothed him with the robes. The chiefs of the Arabs from his own people envied him, and they guaranteed al-Hutay'ah a hundred camels if he would satirize him. So he said: "How can I satirize him when a righteous deed continually comes to me from the family of Lam, while I am in a state of absence (bi-ẓahr al-ghayb)?" The meaning is: "...from the family of Lam, while I am clothed in the back of absence," or "while they are clothed in the back of absence." The word "back" (ẓahr) is inserted because the absent person is as if behind the back, or to strengthen the sense of absence, since when they want to strengthen something they attribute the back to it for its strength. And often they treat an attribute as a noun: either because there is no need to mention the noun, as in "ṣāliḥa," or because the attribute is sufficient to identify the qualified noun if it is needed.

And al-ṣāliḥāt (the righteous deeds) are everything from the deeds that is upright by the evidence of reason, the Book and the Sunnah. The lām here is the lām of the genus (lām al-jins).

If you ask: what is the difference between the lām of the genus entering on a singular noun and its entering on a plural? I answer: when it enters on a singular, it can be intended to refer to the genus as a whole until it is comprehended, and it can be intended to refer to a part of it, down to one individual of it. When it enters on a plural, it can be intended to refer to all of the genus, and it can be intended to refer to a part of it, but not down to one individual of it. This is because its equivalent in encompassing plurality within the genus is the equivalent of the singular in encompassing genericness, and plurality is in the aggregation of the genus, not in its unity.

If you ask: then what is meant by this plural with the lām? I answer: the totality of the sound, upright deeds in the religion, according to the state of the believer in the obligations of the religious duty.

And al-jannah (the garden) is an orchard of palm trees and trees, dense and shaded by the intertwining of its branches. Zuhayr said:

"Your companion has departed, and separation has parted us, and the heart has become attached to Asma, to what it became attached to.
And I parted from you with a pledge that has no redemption, on the day of farewell, so the pledge has become locked up.
As if my two eyes, on the western side of a slaughtered (camel) of the water-carrying camels, were watering a tall garden."

These are by Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. Al-khalīṭ is the companion, and al-bayn is separation and distance. Asmā is the name of his beloved; its root is from wasāma, which is the sign of beauty, and it is said its root is the plural of ism. "Alaqa" is in the passive. "Al-qalb" is the subject. "Mā 'alaqa" (what became attached) with the light form is its object, meaning what the heart became attached to from her, namely love, and grief and sorrow at her journey. He did not specify it, to indicate abundance and magnification, and because his heart was occupied with her; it is as if she had taken him away with her. For this reason he claimed that she had taken his heart as a pledge, by way of the explicit metaphor (isti'āra muṣarraḥa, a metaphor in which the comparison is stated outright), and he developed it with the phrase "has no redemption." The verb "ghalaqa" for a pledge, with a kasra, means that the creditor takes possession of it and its owner despairs of its return to him. Then he said: "As if my two eyes, from the intensity of weeping and the abundance of tears, were two eyes in two huge buckets full of water, carried by a slaughtered (ṣiqā) she-camel, a tamed camel accustomed to work, from the camels of the water-carrying type, which are used for drawing water, and that camel waters a tall garden." "Suḥuqā" with two dammas is the plural of saḥūq, meaning tall palm trees reaching towards the sky, or far from the place of water; they are thus continually going and returning. He addressed himself first as if he were informing it of Asma's departure, out of his excessive grief, then he turned as if complaining to the people in his words "as if my two eyes."

It means tall palm trees. The root of the word revolves around the meaning of covering, and as it is dense and shading, it was called "jannah" (garden), which is from the verbal noun of janna, when he covered it, as if it were one covering because of the intensity of its intertwining. The abode of reward was also called "jannah" because of the gardens (janān, hidden places) that are in it.

If you ask: is Paradise created or not? I answer: this has been disputed. The one who says it is created argues from the dwelling of Adam and Eve in Paradise, and from its mention in the Qur'an in the manner of dominant nouns that attach to proper names, like "the Prophet," "the Messenger," "the Book," and the like.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the plural of al-jannah and its being indefinite? I answer: al-jannah is the name of the whole abode of reward, and it contains many gardens arranged in ranks according to the deserts of those who do deeds, and for each class of them there are gardens from those gardens.

If you ask: is it not a condition for deserving reward through faith and righteous deeds that the responsible person does not nullify them by disbelief, or by committing major sins, and that he does not regret what he has done of obedience and the abandonment of disobedience? Why then was this condition not stipulated? I answer: since reward was made deserved through faith and righteous deeds, and the good news is specific to those who take hold of them, and since it is established in the intellects that a good deed merits its doer reward and praise only if it is not followed by something that corrupts it and removes its goodness, and that it does not remain a good deed in the presence of something that corrupts it; and since He informed His Prophet (ﷺ), who is the most noble and dear of people to Him, with His words: ﴿لَئِنْ أَشْرَكْتَ لَيَحْبَطَنَّ عَمَلُكَ﴾ (If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified), and said to the believers: ﴿وَلَا تَجْهَرُوا لَهُ بِالْقَوْلِ كَجَهْرِ بَعْضِكُمْ لِبَعْضٍ أَنْ تَحْبَطَ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾ (And do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds be nullified), the stipulation of protecting these two from nullification and regret was like something included within the mention.

If you ask: what is the form of the rivers flowing beneath them? I answer: as you see the trees growing on the banks of flowing rivers. It is narrated from Masruq that the rivers of Paradise flow without a ditch. The most delightful and noble of gardens in appearance are those whose trees are shaded and whose rivers flow amid them in streams. Were it not that flowing water is a great blessing and a supreme pleasure, and that gardens and meadows, though they are the most delightful and beautiful of things, do not please the eyes, nor gladden souls, nor bring about exhilaration and vigour until water flows through them, then the greatest delight would be missing and the fullest joy lacking, and they would be like statues with no spirits, and pictures with no life. So when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the gardens together with the mention of the flowing rivers beneath them, placed on one level like two things, one of which cannot be without the other, and preceded it before all their other descriptions.

Al-nahr (river) is the wide watercourse, above the small channel (jadwal) and below the sea. It is said of the Barada: the river of Damascus, and of the Nile: the river of Egypt. The high language has "al-nahr" with a fatha on the ha'. The root of the word revolves around breadth, and the attribution of flowing to the rivers is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī, attributing something to a thing other than its true agent), like their saying: "The road tramples them," and "Hunted upon him for two days."

If you ask: why are the gardens indefinite while the rivers are definite? I answer: as for the indefiniteness of the gardens, it has been mentioned. As for the definiteness of the rivers, it may be intended as the genus, as you say: "So-and-so has a garden in which there is flowing water, figs, grapes, and all kinds of fruits," pointing to the genera known to the addressee. Or it may be intended that the rivers are theirs, and the definite article replaces the definiteness of the annexation, like His words: ﴿وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا﴾ (and the head has blazed with grey hair). Or the lām may point to the rivers mentioned in His words: ﴿فِيهَا أَنْهَارٌ مِنْ مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ، وَأَنْهَارٌ مِنْ لَبَنٍ لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ﴾ (therein are rivers of water unchanging, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change), and so on, the verse.

His words ﴿كُلَّمَا رُزِقُوا﴾ (whenever they are provided with) either must be a second attribute of ﴿جَنَّاتٍ﴾ (gardens), or the predicate of an omitted subject, or a resumptive independent sentence. Since it was said that for them are gardens, it could not fail to occur to the mind of the hearer that the fruits of those gardens are like the fruits of the gardens of this world, or are other kinds that do not resemble these kinds. So it was said that their fruits are like the fruits of the gardens of this world, meaning their kinds are their kinds, though they differ to a degree known only to Allah.

If you ask: what is the position of ﴿مِنْ ثَمَرَةٍ﴾ (of a fruit)? I answer: it is like your saying: "Whenever I eat from your orchard some pomegranates, I thank you."

So the position of ﴿مِنْ ثَمَرَةٍ﴾ is the position of your saying "some pomegranates" (min al-rummān), as if it were said: whenever they are provided from the gardens with whatever fruit it is, whether of its apples, its pomegranates, its grapes, or other than that, a provision, they say that. So the first and the second ﴿مِنْ﴾ are both for the starting point (ibtidā' al-ghāya, the origin of the action), because the provision began from the gardens, and the provision from the gardens began from a fruit. Its application is like your saying: "So-and-so has provided me," and it is said to you: "From where?" and you say: "From his orchard," and it is said: "From what fruit did he provide you from his orchard?" and you say: "From pomegranates." Its explanation is that "ruziqū" (they were provided) was first made absolute, beginning from the pronoun of the gardens, then it was restricted by beginning from the pronoun of the gardens, beginning from a fruit. The meaning of the fruit here is not one apple or one pomegranate on this interpretation; rather, the meaning is a kind of fruits.

Another possibility: ﴿مِنْ ثَمَرَةٍ﴾ is an explanation (bayān) in the manner of your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning "you are a lion." On this view it is valid to intend by "fruit" the kind of fruits, and by "the gardens" the single garden.

If you ask: how is it said ﴿هَذَا الَّذِي رُزِقْنَا مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ (this is what we were provided with before), and how can the present thing in Paradise in their minds be the very thing they were provided with in the world? I answer: its meaning is "this is like what we were provided with before." [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Its meaning is: this is like what we were provided with before... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is simile without the particle (tashbīh bi-ghayr al-adāt), which is the most eloquent of the levels of simile, like their saying: "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifah."]] Its evidence is His words ﴿وَأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشَابِهًا﴾ (and they are given it in resemblance). This is like your saying: "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifah," meaning that because the resemblance is so firmly established, it is as if his essence were his essence.

If you ask: to what does the pronoun in His words ﴿وَأُتُوا بِهِ﴾ (and they are given it) refer? I answer: to the provision in both the world and the Hereafter together, because His words ﴿هَذَا الَّذِي رُزِقْنَا مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ comprised within them the mention of what they were provided with in both abodes. A parallel to this is His words, the Exalted: ﴿إِنْ يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًا فَاللَّهُ أَوْلَى بِهِمَا﴾ (If he is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them), meaning to both kinds, wealth and poverty, because His words "rich or poor" indicate both kinds. If the pronoun had referred to the one who spoke, it would have said ﴿أَوْلَى بِهِ﴾ in the singular.

If you ask: for what purpose do the fruits of this world resemble the fruits of Paradise, and why were the fruits of Paradise not other kinds? I answer: because a person is more at ease with what is familiar, and more inclined to what he knows. When he sees what he has not become accustomed to, his nature recoils from it and his soul dislikes it. And because when he obtains something of a kind that he has known before and has had an acquaintance with, and he sees in it a clear superiority and an evident excellence, and a considerable difference between it and what he knew, his delight and his gladness increase greatly, and his wonder and astonishment last long, and the essence of the blessing becomes clear to him, and the measure of his happiness with it is confirmed. But if it were a kind he had never known, however superior it was, he would suppose that this kind could only be like that, and so the position of the blessing would not become truly clear. So when they saw a pomegranate of the pomegranates of this world, and its limit in size, and that the largest of it does not exceed the size of a small watermelon, then they see a pomegranate of Paradise which satisfies the whole household; and a jujube (nabaq) of the jujubes of this world is the size of a spindle-whorl, then they see the jujubes of Paradise like the great jars of Hajar; just as they saw the shade of a tree of the trees of this world and the extent of its spread, then they see the tree in Paradise, in whose shade a rider travels a hundred years without crossing it, this was clearer for the excellence, more manifest for the superiority, more conducive to joy, and more increasing of wonder than being suddenly confronted with that pomegranate and that jujube without any previous acquaintance with their kinds. Their repeating this statement and uttering it at every fruit they are provided with is evidence of the extremity of the matter and the continuation of the state in the manifestation of superiority and the completion of excellence, and that this great difference is what excites their wonder and calls forth their exultation at every time.

It is narrated from Masruq: "The palm trees of Paradise are arranged in order from their roots to their branches, and their fruit is like great jars: whenever a fruit is plucked, another grows in its place, and their rivers flow without a ditch, and the bunch of grapes is twelve cubits long."

It is also permissible that the pronoun in ﴿أُتُوا بِهِ﴾ (they were given it) refers to the provision, just as ﴿هَذَا﴾ (this) is a reference to it, and the meaning would be: that what they are provided with of the fruits of Paradise comes to them homogeneous in itself, as is related from al-Hasan: one of them is brought a dish and eats from it, then another is brought, and he says: "This is what we were given before," and the king says: "Eat, for the colour is one and the taste is different." And from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, [it is narrated]: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad..."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 2 of 2):

"Indeed, a man among the people of Paradise reaches out for a fruit to eat it, but before it reaches his mouth, Allah replaces it with another like it." So when they see it, and its appearance is the same as the first, they say that. The first explanation is the same as this one.

If you ask: What is the place of His words ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾ within the structure of the speech? I answer: It is like your saying: "So-and-so is better than so-and-so, and what a good thing he did!" and "He saw an opinion of such-and-such, and it was correct." From the same type is the Exalted's words ﴿and they make the honored people of its city humiliated; and thus they do﴾, and similar sentences that are inserted into speech parenthetically for confirmation.

The meaning of purifying the spouses is that they are purified from what is specific to women, such as menstruation and irregular bleeding, and from what is not specific to them, such as filth and defilements. It is also permissible, since the expression is unrestricted, that it includes purification from the defilement of natures and the character traits of this world's women, which they acquire by themselves, which they inherit from evil stocks, bad origins and corrupting upbringings, and from all their other faults, blemishes, wickedness and cunning. If you ask: Why did the attribute not come in the plural, as the noun it describes is plural? I answer: They are two eloquent usages.

It is said: "al-nisa' fa'alna" (the women did), "hunna fa'ilat and fawa'il" (they are doers), and "al-nisa' fa'alat" (the women did), "hiya fa'ilah" (she is a doer). From the same usage is the verse from the Hamasa:

"When the virgins are veiled with smoke,
and hasten to set up the cooking pots, and they roast,
they distribute the provisions of the needy, with arrows of the gambling game,
from the humps of the she-camels, the fat ones."

It is attributed to Salma ibn Rabi'ah ibn Jafna al-Dabbi.

The comparison of the concealment of the virgins with smoke, or their blackness with it, is by way of explicit comparison (tasrih) with their concealment by the veil, or the comparison of smoke to it is by way of metaphor (makniyya). "Malat" means: she roasted the meat or bread by placing it on the coals so that it cooks. It is narrated as "darrat" instead of "darat", meaning that its giving became abundant. "Al-‘ufat" are those seeking provision. "Al-maghaliq" are the arrows of the gambling game that close off the prize and fix it for the winner. "Al-qama'" is cutting the humps, plural of qamah. "Al-‘ishar" are the she-camels whose pregnancy has passed ten months. "Al-jullah" are the fat, great-humped ones, plural of jalil, like sabiyyah, plural of sabiy; that is, when the time is barren, so that the virgins, despite their extreme shyness and guarding of themselves, approach the smoke and roast on the coals, and eat without waiting for the pots to cook because of hunger, they give to people abundantly. It is possible that the secluded women themselves attend to cooking the hospitality for the guests, and so they give it to them. The first is more eloquent. "Ra'ayt" means: I reformed. "Al-tha'a" means corruption, and "kafayt" means I dealt with whoever committed it. It is narrated as "janibaha" with a "b", meaning the small and great calamity. "Al-latya" is the diminutive of "allati" like other relative pronouns whose diminutive is heard, and an alif is added at its end in place of the diminutive vowel; it is with a fatha on the lam. Al-Akhfash said it is with a damma on the analogy of diminutives, although this is anomalous in indeclinable nouns as here. It dispenses with a relative clause because its meaning is shifted by diminution away from relative meaning, and "allati" is taken as modeled on it because, when it is mentioned in opposition to it, its meaning is the great calamity, so no intention to the relative meaning was made either. It is said that deleting the relative clause is permissible when there is an indicator, so here it is estimated: "al-latya" became small, and "allati" became great. Then this is among the proverbs in circulation. Its origin is that a man married a short woman, suffered hardships from her, then married a tall one, suffered twice that, so he divorced them both and said: "After al-latya and allati, I will never marry, ever."

And the meaning: "and a community of purified spouses." [Note: the phrase "and a community of purified spouses" — perhaps the waw is an addition by the copyist, or perhaps the original was "and for them therein is a community of spouses." (ʿ)]

Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿mutahharat﴾ (with a plural ending). ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿muṭahharah﴾, in the sense of "mutatahhirah" (purifying themselves). In the speech of some Arabs: "How I am in need of the House of Allah! So I purify myself with it, a purification," meaning: "so I purify myself with it, a thorough purification."

If you ask: Why was it not said ṭāhirah? I answer: In "muṭahharah" there is a majesty for their description that is not in ṭāhirah, and it signals that a Purifier purified them, and that is none other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who wills for His righteous servants that He endow them with every excellence in what He has prepared for them.

Al-khuld (eternity) is enduring permanence and lasting continuance that does not cease. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity. Then if you die, will they be the ones who remain forever?﴾ [21:34]. And Imru' al-Qays said:

"Ala, be well this morning, O ruined abode, decayed,
but can one who was in the bygone age be well?
None is well except a happy one granted eternity,
little in worries, who does not spend the night in fear."

These are by Imru' al-Qays. "Ala" is an introductory particle. "An'im sabahan" is the greeting of the Jahiliyyah, meaning: may your life be pleasant. It may be lightened to "amm," as narrated here; likewise "ya'manna" is narrated here too. "Na'ima yan'amu" like "daraba yadrubu," "na'ima yan'amu" like "sahula yashulu," and "na'ima yan'amu" like "alima ya'lamu," and "na'ima yan'amu" with both vowels in kasra, which is rare, meaning he became soft and tender. He specified the morning because it is the time of raids. "Al-talal" is what remains of the traces of dwellings. "Al-bali" is the perishing. The meaning is a greeting to the people of the ruin, then he mentions the error in their greeting, saying: whoever was in the past age does not enjoy himself, and today he is perished; so the interrogative is one of denial. "Al-mukhalladu" is one of long life such that he does not perish. "Al-awjal" is the plural of wajal, which is fear, and the ba' is for accompaniment. It is permissible that it is for location, by imagination.

This verse was revealed to show that what the ignorant, the foolish, and the stubborn disputers among the disbelievers denounced and found strange, namely that trivial things should be used as examples, is not a fitting matter for denunciation or astonishment. This is because a parable (tamthil) is resorted to only for the clarity of meaning it provides, the lifting of the veil from the intended purpose, and the bringing of the imagined closer to the observed. If the one being illustrated is great, the thing used as illustration is likewise great; and if it is lowly, the thing used is likewise lowly. Thus, greatness or lowliness in the thing used as an example is nothing but a matter demanded by the state of the one being illustrated, which draws it toward itself, so the one who coins the example acts according to that case. Do you not see that when the truth was clear, manifest and radiant, it was illustrated by light and luminosity, and when falsehood was of the opposite quality, it was illustrated by darkness? And since the state of the gods which the disbelievers made as rivals to God was no state lower or less contemptible than that, the spider's house was made its example in weakness and frailty, and they were made less than the fly and of lower rank, and the gnat was struck as an example for them, so whatever is below it is not denounced or deemed novel. No one said to the one who gave the example: "Be ashamed of illustrating them with a gnat," because he is correct in his illustration, right in his statement, driving the parable according to the case it strikes, and following the pattern of what it demands and calls for. And to show that the believers, whose custom is fairness, acting on justice and equity, and considering matters with the eye of reason, when they hear such an illustration, know that it is the truth against which doubt cannot pass, and the correct view around which error does not roam.

And that the disbelievers, whom ignorance has overcome in their minds, and whom usurpation has seized in their insight, so that they do not perceive or apply their minds, or who recognize that it is the truth but whose love of leadership, desire for familiarity and habit does not leave them to be fair, when they hear it they oppose and stubbornly deny it, judge it to be false, and confront it with rejection. And that this is the cause of the increase in the guidance of the believers and the immersion of the wicked in their error and misguidance. How strange of them that they denied this, when people have continually coined examples using animals, birds, creeping things, insects and vermin, and the proverbs of the Arabs are before them, circulating in their towns and deserts, in which they illustrated with the most contemptible things, saying: "More daring than an ant," "Bolder than a fly," "Hearing sharper than a tick," "Colder than a locust," "Weaker than a moth," and "More eating than a weevil." And about the gnat they said: "Weaker than a gnat," "More precious than the marrow of a gnat," and "You have burdened me with the marrow of a gnat." Examples were also coined in the Gospel with trivial things, such as darnel, bran, the mustard seed, the pebble, the termite, the worm, and the wasp. Illustration with these things and with things more contemptible than them is something whose soundness and correctness are not hidden from anyone with the least sense; but it is the habit of the one defeated and bewildered, who has no hold left on any proof, no clinging to any sign or persuasion, to resort, out of extreme confusion and inability to devise a stratagem, to rejecting the obvious and denying the straight, relying on obstinacy and sophistry when he finds nothing else to rely upon. It is narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah: when God mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book and struck them as examples for the polytheists, the Jews laughed and said: "This is not what the speech of God resembles."

So God, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse.

Modesty (al-haya') is a change and breaking that befalls a person from fear of what would be reproached and blamed. Its derivation is from life (hayah).

It is said: "Haya al-rajul," just as it is said: "nasiya," "hasha," and "shazhiya al-faras" (when these limbs become ailing), the living being being regarded, because of the breaking and change that overtakes him, as one whose strength is reversed and whose life is diminished, as they said: "So-and-so perished from modesty (haya') at such a thing," "he died of modesty," "I saw ruin in his face from the intensity of modesty," "he melted from modesty," and "he froze in his place from embarrassment." If you say: how is it permissible to describe the Eternal, glory be to Him, with it, while He cannot be characterized with change, fear or blame? This is in the hadith of Salman, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed God is Living and Generous; He is modest toward His servant when the servant raises his hands to Him, that He should return them empty until He places good in them." Say: it proceeds by way of illustration, like His leaving the servant disappointed, and that He does not return the hands of the one who asks empty of His gift, out of His generosity, by leaving aside what one who is ashamed would leave aside, namely the rejection of one in need, out of modesty before him. And likewise the meaning of His words: "Indeed God is not ashamed" (la yastahyi) means He does not abandon striking the example of the gnat, leaving it as one abandons something from which one who is ashamed would refrain because of its lowliness. It is also permissible that this expression occurs in the speech of the disbelievers, who said: "Is the Lord of Muhammad not ashamed to strike an example with the fly and the spider?" and so it came in the manner of counterpart and matching the answer to the question. This is a wonderful kind of their speech and a marvelous ornament, among which is the saying of Abu Tammam:

"Who will convey to all the offspring of Ya'rub
that I built the neighbor before the dwelling?"

And when a man testified before Shurayh, he said: "You are indeed loose in your testimony." The man said: "It has not been wrapped (lam tujaʿʿad) from me." He said: "May God keep your land," and accepted his testimony. So what permitted "building the neighbor" and "wrapping the testimony" is the observance of counterpart. Were it not for building the house, "building the neighbor" would not be correct, and were it not for the testimony being loose, its wrapping would be impossible. How marvelous is the Revelation and its encompassing of the arts of eloquence and their branches; you will hardly find any art strange in it without finding it in its most upright methods and most firmly paved paths. Modesty has also been used metaphorically for what does not properly bear it:

"When they feel shy of the water presenting itself,
they drink with a leather bucket in a vessel of roses."

And he read (yastahi) with one yā' according to Ibn Kathir in the narration of Shibl. There are two usages: transitivity with the preposition and transitivity directly. They say: "istahyitu minhu" and "istahyitu-hu," and both are possible here.

As for "darb al-mathal" (striking an example): it is its making and fashioning, from "darb al-labin" (forming bricks) and "darb al-khatim" (striking a ring). In the hadith: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, struck a ring of gold." And "ma" here is indefinite (ibhamiyyah), which is the one which, when attached to an indefinite noun, makes it vague and increases it in generality and comprehensiveness, as when you say: "Give me a book, any," meaning whatever book it may be; or it is superfluous for emphasis, like the one in His words: "for their breaking their covenant." As if it were said: "God is not ashamed to strike an example, truly or at all." This is when you put "baʿūḍatan" in the accusative. But if you put it in the nominative, then it is relative, its clause being the sentence, because the estimate is: "it is a gnat," and the first part of the sentence is omitted as in: "perfection upon the one who did well." Another good and beautiful aspect is that the "ma" carries the meaning of interrogation: when they recoiled from God's illustrating their idols with trivial things, He said: "Indeed God is not ashamed to strike for the rivals whatever things he wills as an example, trivial ones, let alone the gnat and what is above it," as one says: "So-and-so does not care what he gives: how much a dinar and two dinars." The meaning is: God may illustrate the rivals and the lowliness of their status by what has nothing smaller or less than it, such as the indivisible part, or by what only He, through His subtlety, can perceive because of its extreme tininess, or by the non-existent, as the Arabs say: "So-and-so is less than nothing in number." And the words of the Exalted touch on this: "Indeed God knows what they call upon besides Him of anything." This reading is attributed to Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj, the most chewing of the Arabs upon wormwood and southernwood, and the one attested to for eloquence; and they used to liken beauty to him. I do not think he took this reading except in this direction, which corresponds to his eloquence. "Ba'ūḍatan" is in the accusative either as an explanatory appositive to "mathalan," or as the object of "yadrib," with "mathalan" as a circumstantial accusative preceding it, or both are accusative objects, so that "darab" takes the course of "ja'ala." The derivation of "ba'ūḍ" is from "al-ba'ḍ," which means cutting, like "al-biḍʿ" and "al-ʿaḍb." It is said: "ba'aḍahu al-ba'ūḍ" (the gnat bit him). And he recited:

"How excellent is the house of Abu Dithar
when some of the people fear some of them."

The intended meaning of the house is the mosquito-net that protects from gnats during summer nights for those inside it; Abu Dithar is the name of a man, and "dithar" is what is worn over clothes. It is said: "when some of the people fear the gnat's bite, i.e., its cut and sting." It may also be that the meaning is: the best refuge and shelter is the house of Abu Dithar, from whose evil some people fear others. In it is double meaning (tawriyah), which is among the wonders of speech. Derived from it is "ba'ḍ al-shay'," because he cut it from it. "Ba'ūḍ" originally is an adjective on the pattern of "fa'ūl," like "quṭūʿ," but it became a noun by predominance.

وَكَذَلِكَ **الخَمُوش**[^1] ﴿فَمَا فَوْقَهَا﴾ فِيهِ مَعْنَيَانِ: أَحَدُهُمَا: فَمَا تَجَاوَزَهَا وَزَادَ عَلَيْهَا فِي الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي ضُرِبَتْ فِيهِ مَثَلًا، وَهُوَ الْقِلَّةُ وَالْحَقَارَةُ، نَحْوَ قَوْلِكَ لِمَنْ يَقُولُ: فُلَانٌ أَسْفَلُ النَّاسِ وَأَنْذَلُهُمْ: هُوَ فَوْقَ ذَاكَ، تُرِيدُ هُوَ أَبْلَغُ وَأَعْرَقُ فِيمَا وُصِفَ بِهِ مِنَ السَّفَالَةِ وَالنَّذَالَةِ. وَالثَّانِي: فَمَا زَادَ عَلَيْهَا فِي الْحَجْمِ، كَأَنَّهُ قَصَدَ بِذَلِكَ رَدَّ مَا اسْتَنْكَرُوهُ مِنْ ضَرْبِ الْمَثَلِ بِالذُّبَابِ وَالْعَنْكَبُوتِ، لِأَنَّهُمَا أَكْبَرُ مِنَ الْبَعُوضَةِ. كَمَا تَقُولُ لِصَاحِبِكَ، وَقَدْ ذَمَّ مَنْ عَرَفْتَهُ يَشِحُّ بِأَدْنَى شَيْءٍ، فَقَالَ: فُلَانٌ بَخِلَ بِالدِّرْهَمِ وَالدِّرْهَمَيْنِ: هُوَ لَا يُبَالِي أَنْ يَبْخَلَ بِنِصْفِ دِرْهَمٍ فَمَا فَوْقَهُ، تُرِيدُ بِمَا فَوْقَهُ مَا بَخِلَ فِيهِ وَهُوَ الدِّرْهَمُ وَالدِّرْهَمَانِ، كَأَنَّكَ قُلْتَ: فَضْلًا عَنِ الدِّرْهَمِ وَالدِّرْهَمَيْنِ. وَنَحْوُهُ فِي الِاحْتِمَالَيْنِ مَا سَمِعْنَاهُ فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ
