I say: it is permissible that entry into it be prevented in the manner of drawing near and honour, as the angels entered, while it is not prevented that he enter in the manner of whispering, as a trial for Adam and Eve.

It is said he used to draw near to the heaven and speak to them. It is said he stood at the gate and called out. It is reported that he wished to enter, but the guardians prevented him, so he entered into the mouth of the serpent until it entered with him while they were unaware. It is said (ihbiṭū) is addressed to Adam, Eve and Iblīs; and it is said [also to] the serpent. The correct view is that it is addressed to Adam and Eve, and what is meant is they and their offspring, since, as they were the origin of mankind and its branching-out, they were treated as if they were all of mankind. The proof for this is His saying: (He said: Go down from it, all of you, some of you enemies to others). This is further indicated by His saying: (Whoever follows My guidance, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve; and those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide forever). And this is nothing but a ruling that encompasses all people. The meaning of (some of you enemies to others) is the mutual enmity and oppression that people have, and their misleading one another. Al-habūṭ: descent to the earth. (Mustaqarr): a place of settling, or settling; (wa-matāʿ): enjoyment and taking pleasure in life (ilā ḥīn): that is, until the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: until death.

Prostration (sujud) to Allah, the Exalted, is an act of worship, while prostration to others is out of honour, as the angels prostrated to Adam. [Was it] "and Abu Yusuf and his brothers" (to him)? [The editor's note: the text "li-Adam wa-Abu Yusuf" is perhaps "li-Adam wa-abawai Yusuf" (to Adam and the two parents of Yusuf). (ʿAynī)] It is permissible that the states and times differ in this.

Abu Ja'far recited (lil-malā'ikati usjudū) with a ḍamma on the tā' by way of ittibāʿ (assimilation of the vowel). It is not permissible to suppress the grammatical vowel (ḥarakat al-iʿrāb) by the vowel of assimilation (ḥarakat al-ittibāʿ) except in a weak dialect, such as their saying (al-ḥamdu lillāh) [with the ḍamma on the lām]. Illā Iblīs is a muttaṣil (connected) exception, because he was a single jinn among a multitude of angels, overwhelmed by them; thus they were given precedence in His saying (fa-sajadū), and then one of them was excepted. It is also permissible to make it munqaṭiʿ (disconnected): abā, he refused what he was commanded, and istakbara, he was arrogant toward it, wa-kāna min al-kāfirīn, being of the kind of disbelieving jinn and their devils; thus he refused and was arrogant, like His saying: (He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord). Al-maskan (dwelling) is from al-sukūn, because it is a kind of staying and settling. Anta is an emphasis for the pronoun in (uskun), so that conjunction with it is valid.

Raghadan is a description of the verbal noun: that is, eat abundantly, wide and pleasant. Ḥaythu is for an indefinite place, that is: in any place of Paradise you wish.

He permitted them to eat from Paradise in a far-reaching manner that removes any pretext, when He did not forbid them some of the food nor some of the places gathering the foods of Paradise, so that no excuse remains for them in partaking from one tree among its many trees, which are too numerous to count. It is said the tree was the wheat, or the vine, or the fig. It was also read (wa-lā tiqrabā) with a kasra on the tā'. (Hādhihi) and (al-shajarah) with a kasra on the shīn, and (al-shīrah) with a kasra on the shīn and the yā'. It is reported from Abū ʿAmr that he disliked these readings, and said:

It is recited by the Berbers of Mecca and its blacks. (Min al-ẓālimīn): of those who wronged themselves by disobeying Allah. (Fa-takūnā) is jazm by conjunction with (taqrabā), or naṣb as an answer to the prohibition. The pronoun in (ʿanhā) refers to the tree; that is, the Satan caused them to slip because of it. Its precise sense: the Satan caused their slip to proceed from it. This "ʿan" is like its use in His saying: (And I did not do it of my own accord, ʿan amrī). And like the line:

(They forbid [people] from eating [a fat she-camel] and from drinking ...) describing a host who fed his guests to satiety; they walk and make a trace on the top of the mountain... The qunna (summit) of a mountain and its qulla is its highest point, while they are exceedingly fat, a fatness arising from much eating and much drinking.

It is said: (fa-azallahumā ʿan al-janna) means: He removed them from it and distanced them, as you say: zalla ʿan martabatihi (he slipped from his rank), and zalla ʿannī dhāka (that departed from me), and zalla min al-shahri kadhā (such-and-such departed from the month). It was also read: (fa-azālahumā). (Mimmā kānā fīhi): from the bliss and honour they were in.

Or [it means] "from Paradise," if the pronoun in (ʿanhā) refers to the tree. ʿAbdullāh read: (fa-waswasa lahumā al-shayṭān ʿanhā), and this is evidence that the pronoun refers to the tree, since the meaning is that his whispering proceeded from it. It is also said: until death.

The meaning of "talaqqa" (to receive) is to take hold of the words, accept them, and act upon them once they are known. It is also recited with ādama in the accusative and "al-kalimāt" in the nominative, meaning that the words reached him and connected with him. If you ask, "What are they?", the answer is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves...﴾ to the end of the verse.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The most beloved speech to Allah is that which our father Adam said when he committed the sin: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name and exalted is Your majesty. There is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.'" [A mawquf report. Ibn Abi Shaybah related it at the beginning of the book of prayer, through Ibrahim al-Taymi from al-Harith ibn Suwayd, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: then he mentioned it, but did not say "what Adam said when he committed the sin."]

And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, if I repent and amend, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." [A mawquf report. Al-Hakim related it in the chapter on Adam, in the Virtues of the Prophets, through al-Minhal ibn 'Amr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him.]

He mentioned only the repentance of Adam and not the repentance of Hawwa', because she was a follower of him, just as the mention of women is omitted in most of the Qur'an and Sunnah for this reason. She is mentioned in His saying: ﴿They both said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves...﴾. ﴿Then He accepted his repentance﴾, meaning He turned to him with mercy and acceptance.

If you ask: why is ﴿We said: Go down﴾ repeated? The answer: for emphasis, and because of the addition attached to it, His saying: ﴿Then when guidance comes to you from Me...﴾. If you ask: what is the answer (jawab) to the first condition? The answer: the second condition together with its answer is like your saying: "If you come to me, then if you are able, I will do good to you." The meaning is: "Then if guidance comes to you from Me, by a messenger I send to you and a book I reveal to you," as shown by His saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾ in contrast to His saying: ﴿Whoever follows My guidance﴾. If you ask: why is the word of doubt (kalimat al-shakk) used, when the coming of guidance is certain to occur? The answer: to signal that faith in Allah and His unity does not depend on the sending of messengers and the revelation of books; and that if He had not sent a messenger nor revealed a book, faith in Him and His unity would still be obligatory, because of the intellects He placed in them, the proofs He set up for them, and the capacity for reflection and inference He granted them. [His saying "obligatory because of what was placed in them" is the view of the Mu'tazilah. As for the Ahl al-Sunnah, there is no ruling before the Sharia. (Ghuzzi / editor's note)]

If you ask: the sin for which Adam was made to descend from the Garden, if it was a major sin, then major sins are not permissible for prophets; and if it was a minor sin, why did there befall him because of it what befell him, such as the removal of his garment, his expulsion from the Garden, and his descent from heaven, as was done to Iblis, and why is he ascribed to error, disobedience, forgetting the covenant, lack of resolve, and the need for repentance? The answer: it was only a minor sin, submerged by the deeds of his heart, such as sincerity and righteous thoughts, which are the most excellent deeds and the greatest acts of obedience. What befell him was only to magnify the sin, to make its matter grave and terrifying, so that this would be a kindness to him and to his offspring in avoiding transgressions and guarding against sins, and as a warning that he was expelled from the Garden for one sin, so how could one with many sins enter it. It is recited: "fa-man tabi'a hudāya" in the dialect of Hudhayl, "fa-lā khawf," with fatḥah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 40–41:

"Isrā'īl" (Israel) is the epithet of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. In their language it means "the chosen one of Allah" (ṣafwat Allāh), and it is also said to mean "the servant of Allah" (ʿabd Allāh). It has the same form as Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl and is diptote (ghayr munṣarif) like them, due to the presence of proper-name status (ʿalamiyya) and foreignness (ʿujma). It has also been read as Isrā'il and Isrā'illa. Their being reminded of the blessing means that they should not neglect its thanks, that they should count it as a favour, magnify it, and obey its bestower. By it he meant what Allah bestowed upon their forefathers, which He enumerated for them: the deliverance from Pharaoh and his torment, and from drowning; and the pardon for taking the calf and the accepting of their repentance, and other things; and what He bestowed upon them by letting them reach the time of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, who was foretold in the Torah and the Gospel.

The word "covenant" (ʿahd) may be attributed to both the one who makes the covenant and the one with whom it is made. One says "I fulfilled my covenant" (awfaytu bi-ʿahdī), meaning "with what I covenanted upon," as in His saying: ﴿And who fulfils his covenant more than Allah?﴾ [9:111], and "I fulfilled your covenant" (awfaytu bi-ʿahdika), meaning "with what I covenanted you upon." The meaning of ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ is: fulfil what you covenanted Me upon of faith in Me and obedience to Me, as in His saying: ﴿And who fulfils what he covenanted Allah upon?﴾ [48:10], ﴿Among them are those who have covenanted with Allah﴾ [33:23], ﴿Men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [33:23]. ﴿I will fulfil your covenant﴾ means: with what I promised you of goodly reward for your good deeds. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ means: do not break My covenant.

This is from your saying: "I feared Zayd" (zaydan rahibtuhu). It is more emphatic in conveying exclusivity than ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [1:5].

It is read as "awaffi" with the doubled letter (tashdīd), meaning: I will be thorough in fulfilling your covenant, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it﴾ [27:89].

It is permissible that by His saying ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ He means what they covenanted upon and promised Him of faith in the Prophet of mercy and the miraculous Book. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ — "the first to disbelieve in it," or "the first group or company to disbelieve in it," or "let not each one of you be the first to disbelieve in it," like your saying "he clothed us a garment" (kasānā ḥullatan), meaning each one of us. This is an allusion that they should have been the first to believe in him, given their knowledge of him and his attributes, and because they were the ones who gave glad tidings of the time of the one to whom revelation was sent, and who sought victory over those who disbelieved in him, and they used to consider following him to be the foremost of all people. But when he was sent, their situation was the reverse, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to depart until there came to them clear evidence﴾ [98:1], up to His saying ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after clear evidence came to them﴾ [98:4], ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [2:89].

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "do not be like the first disbeliever in it," meaning those among the people of Makkah who associated others with Allah. That is: do not be, while you recognise him as described and mentioned in the Torah, like one who did not recognise him and is a polytheist with no book.

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihi" refers to "what is with you," because when they disbelieve in what confirms it, they have disbelieved in it.

"Purchase" (ishtirāʾ) is used as a metaphor for exchange, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿They have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [2:16], and the poet's line:

"As the Muslim bought, when he became a Christian" [[The explanation of this evidence has passed on page 69 of this part, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

and his line:

"Indeed I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance" [[Asmāʾ thought that I do not love her, so I said: Yes, but my preoccupation prevents me from it... I repaid you double the affection, were it not that you complained of it... and no one before me has repaid you double... so if you accuse me of being ignorant among you... then I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance.

By Abū Dhu'ayb al-Hudhalī. "Zaʿamat" means: she thought, as a fact and a matter, that I do not love her; so I said to her: Yes, I love you, were it not that my preoccupation contends with me: that is, were it not that my preoccupation contends with me and turns me from your affection; or: had my preoccupation not contended with me I would have loved you. "I repaid you double the affection": that is, I loved you the usual measure twice, or twice your love; "were it not that you complained of it": that is, were it not that I got tired of you and became weary, or: had you not complained of it I would have doubled and increased it. Here "lawlā" may be a single word, so that "an" (the verbal particle) is understood after it, or it may be two words meaning "if not"; but this is a rare usage. In the second "lawlā" it is permissible that it is a particle of urging and rebuke, like "halā," meaning that the one more deserving of complaint was the abundance of affection which causes suspicion, not the abundance of desertion. "Mā" is negating, and "in" and "min" are superfluous. "Ajhalu" is a present-tense verb in the nominative case. It has also been said that it is an elative in the accusative. "Fīkum": that is, because of you, or among your tribe. He used the masculine plural pronoun to show respect. "Fa-innī sharaytu" is the answer of the condition. "Ishtarā al-shay'" means he took it for a price, and "sharāhu" means he sold it for that price; so the meaning here is: I exchanged reason after your departure for ignorance, which is a metonymy whose relation is generality. The meaning is that he excused his failure to return her love by his preoccupation, her complaining, and his reason.]]

meaning: "do not exchange My signs for a small price" — otherwise the price is that for which one buys. The "small price" was the leadership they held among their people, which they feared losing if they became followers of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, so they exchanged it — a small substitute and a trifling enjoyment — for the signs of Allah and the truth, to which every great thing is small and every big thing is insignificant; so what of a small and insignificant thing? It has also been said that most of them used to give their rabbis part of their crops and fruits, present them with gifts, and offer them bribes in return for distorting the words and making easy for them what was hard among the laws. Their kings used to shower them with wealth so that they would conceal or distort.

One says "I fulfilled my covenant" (awfaytu bi-ʿahdī), meaning "with what I covenanted upon," as in His saying: ﴿And who fulfils his covenant more than Allah?﴾ [9:111], and "I fulfilled your covenant" (awfaytu bi-ʿahdika), meaning "with what I covenanted you upon." The meaning of ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ is: fulfil what you covenanted Me upon of faith in Me and obedience to Me, as in His saying: ﴿And who fulfils what he covenanted Allah upon?﴾ [48:10], ﴿Among them are those who have covenanted with Allah﴾ [33:23], ﴿Men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [33:23]. ﴿I will fulfil your covenant﴾ means: with what I promised you of goodly reward for your good deeds. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ means: do not break My covenant.

This is from your saying: "I feared Zayd" (zaydan rahibtuhu). It is more emphatic in conveying exclusivity than ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [1:5].

It is read as "awaffi" with the doubled letter (tashdīd), meaning: I will be thorough in fulfilling your covenant, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it﴾ [27:89].

It is permissible that by His saying ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ He means what they covenanted upon and promised Him of faith in the Prophet of mercy and the miraculous Book. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ — "the first to disbelieve in it," or "the first group or company to disbelieve in it," or "let not each one of you be the first to disbelieve in it," like your saying "he clothed us a garment" (kasānā ḥullatan), meaning each one of us. This is an allusion that they should have been the first to believe in him, given their knowledge of him and his attributes, and because they were the ones who gave glad tidings of the time of the one to whom revelation was sent, and who sought victory over those who disbelieved in him, and they used to consider following him to be the foremost of all people. But when he was sent, their situation was the reverse, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to depart until there came to them clear evidence﴾ [98:1], up to His saying ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after clear evidence came to them﴾ [98:4], ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [2:89].

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "do not be like the first disbeliever in it," meaning those among the people of Makkah who associated others with Allah. That is: do not be, while you recognise him as described and mentioned in the Torah, like one who did not recognise him and is a polytheist with no book.

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihi" refers to "what is with you," because when they disbelieve in what confirms it, they have disbelieved in it.

"Purchase" (ishtirāʾ) is used as a metaphor for exchange, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿They have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [2:16], and the poet's line:

"As the Muslim bought, when he became a Christian" [[The explanation of this evidence has passed on page 69 of this part, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

and his line:

"Indeed I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance" [[Asmāʾ thought that I do not love her, so I said: Yes, but my preoccupation prevents me from it... I repaid you double the affection, were it not that you complained of it... and no one before me has repaid you double... so if you accuse me of being ignorant among you... then I have bought forbearance after you with ignorance.

"Zaʿamat" means: she thought, as a fact and a matter, that I do not love her; so I said to her: Yes, I love you, were it not that my preoccupation contends with me: that is, were it not that my preoccupation contends with me and turns me from your affection; or: had my preoccupation not contended with me I would have loved you. meaning: "do not exchange My signs for a small price" — otherwise the price is that for which one buys. The "small price" was the leadership they held among their people, which they feared losing if they became followers of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, so they exchanged it — a small substitute and a trifling enjoyment — for the signs of Allah and the truth, to which every great thing is small and every big thing is insignificant; so what of a small and insignificant thing? It has also been said that most of them used to give their rabbis part of their crops and fruits, present them with gifts, and offer them bribes in return for distorting the words and making easy for them what was hard among the laws. Their kings used to shower them with wealth so that they would conceal or distort.

The ba' in "bil-batil" (بِالْباطِلِ): if it is a connecting particle (صلة), like its use in your saying "labistu al-shay' bil-shay'" (I mixed the thing with the thing), then the meaning is: "And do not write into the Torah what is not from it, so that the revealed truth becomes mixed with the falsehood that you have written, until its truth cannot be distinguished from your falsehood." If it is the ba' of instrumentality (باء الاستعانة), like the one in your saying "katabtu bil-qalam" (I wrote with the pen), then the meaning is: "Do not make the truth confused and mingled with your falsehood which you write."

"Wa-taktumu" (وَتَكْتُمُوا) is in the jussive mood and falls under the scope of the prohibition, meaning: "and do not conceal." Or it is in the subjunctive, governed by an implied "an" (أن), with the waw meaning joining together, i.e., "do not combine the confusing of the truth with falsehood and the concealing of the truth," like your saying: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk." If you say: their confusing and their concealing are not two distinct acts, so that they are forbidden to combine, because when they confuse the truth with falsehood they have concealed the truth, [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him: "If you say their confusing and their concealing are not two distinct acts... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: The objection is not well-directed, for it claims there is no distinction between the two acts. Then we do not grant that combining them in the prohibition is impossible; rather, prohibiting one of them under this assumption entails prohibiting the other, even if it is not stated explicitly.]] I say: rather, they are distinct. It may also be an command to pray along with those who pray, that is, in congregation, as if it were said: "And establish the prayer and pray it with those who pray, not alone."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 44–46:

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people﴾: The hamzah (the interrogative particle *alif-hamzah*, *al-hamzah*) here expresses affirmation accompanied by rebuke, and an expression of wonder at their condition. *Al-birr* (righteousness) means the breadth of good and what is recognised as good.

From the same root is *al-birr* (dutifulness), because of its breadth, and it encompasses every good. From it is their saying: "You have spoken truthfully and dutifully (*barrarta*)."

The rabbis (*al-ahbar*) used to command those relatives and others who advised them in private to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), but they themselves did not follow him. It was also said that they used to enjoin charity while not giving charity themselves, and when they brought charitable donations to distribute, they would embezzle from them.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Wasi': "It has reached me that some people of Paradise looked down upon some people of the Fire and said to them: 'You used to command us to do things, and we did them, so we entered Paradise.' They said: 'We used to command you to them, but we would oppose them and turn to other things.'"

﴿and you forget yourselves﴾: And you leave yourselves, abandoning them from righteousness, as though they were forgotten.

﴿while you recite the Book﴾: This is a rebuke, like His saying ﴿while you know﴾. It means: while you recite the Torah, in which there is a description of Muhammad (ﷺ), or in which there is the threat against embezzlement, abandonment of righteousness, and the contradiction between speech and action.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾: A severe rebuke, meaning: will you not perceive the ugliness of what you have undertaken, so that its being recognised as ugly would restrain you from committing it? It is as though you were deprived of your intellects, because the intellects reject it and repel it. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God! Will you not then use your reason?﴾.

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: That is, by combining the two, and that you should pray while being patient in bearing the obligations of prayer, enduring its hardships and what is required within it: sincerity of heart, guarding the intentions, repelling whisperings, observing its etiquette, guarding against what is disliked, with fear and humility, and bringing to mind the knowledge that one is standing before the Tyrant of the heavens, to ask for the release of necks from His wrath and punishment.

From the same is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer, and be steadfast in it﴾.

Or: seek help in calamities and misfortunes by being patient through them, and by turning to prayer when they occur.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "When a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer." [[Al-Tabari recorded it in his tafsir from the hadith of Hudhayfah with this wording. Abu Dawud and Ahmad recorded it from the narration of 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Hudhayfah, from Hudhayfah with the wording "When a matter distressed him, he would pray." Al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Dala'il in the story of the Trench at length.]]

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when news of the death of his brother Qutham reached him while he was on a journey, he said "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un," turned aside from the road, and prayed two units (*rak'ahs*), prolonging the sitting in them. Then he rose and walked to his mount, saying: "Seek help through patience and prayer." [[Mawquf (a report ending with a Companion). Recorded by Sa'id ibn Mansur. Al-Tabari recorded it through the route of 'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from his father, that Ibn 'Abbas ... and he mentioned it. Al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Shu'ab through this route.]]

It was also said: *al-sabr* (patience) here means fasting, because one is restrained from things that break it. From this, the month of Ramadan was called "the month of patience."

It is permissible that by prayer is meant supplication (*al-du'a'*), and that one seek help against trials through patience, and resort to supplication, and entreat God, exalted is He, to repel them.

﴿And indeed it is﴾: The pronoun refers either to prayer or to seeking help.

It is permissible that it refers to all the matters that the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from His saying: ﴿Remember My favour﴾ up to ﴿and seek help﴾.

﴿is indeed difficult﴾: heavy and burdensome, from your saying: "This matter was difficult (*kabura*) for me," as in His saying: ﴿Hard for the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾.

If you say: why is it not heavy for the humble ones (*al-khashi'in*), while humility in itself is something that is burdensome?

I say: because they expect what has been stored up for those who are patient with its hardships, so it becomes easy for them. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who suppose that they will meet their Lord﴾, that is, who expect to meet His reward and attain what is with Him, and aspire to it. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), the reading is "those who know" (*ya'lamun*). Its meaning is: they know that there must be a meeting with the recompense, so they act accordingly. For this reason "suppose" (*yazunnun*) has been explained as "are certain" (*yatayaqqanun*).

As for one who does not believe with certainty in recompense and does not hope for reward, he has only pure hardship, so it is heavy upon him, like the hypocrites and those who show off with their deeds. An example of this is one who is promised an additional wage for some works or crafts beyond the measure of his labour: you see him undertaking it with desire, energy, an open heart, and joking with those present, as though he takes pleasure in undertaking it, unlike the state of a worker whom some oppressors compel to labour.

For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bazzar from the hadith of Anas, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." It will come in Al 'Imran.]] And he used to say: "O Bilal, give us rest (*rawwihna*)." [[Recorded by Abu Dawud through the narration of Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: A man from Khuza'ah said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "O Bilal, establish the prayer and give us rest by it." Its narrators are trustworthy, but it was reported with considerable variation from Salim. Al-Daraqutni mentioned it in al-'Ilal. Ahmad recorded it through the narration of the aforementioned Salim from a man of Aslam. Ahmad and Abu Dawud also recorded it from another route, from Salim, that Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: "I entered with my father upon a relative of ours from the Ansar. The prayer became due, and he mentioned a story, and in it: 'Stand up, O Bilal, and give us rest with the prayer.'" Al-Daraqutni recorded it in al-'Ilal through the narration of Salim from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. He said: Abu Khalid al-Qurashi alone reported it from al-Thawri in this way, and through the route of Hamzah al-Thumali from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah from Bilal. Ibrahim al-Harbi recorded it from the narration of Salim from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah as a mursal (a report with a missing Companion). He said: its meaning is: we pray and return to our homes. It is not from rest from burdens, for otherwise he would have said "give us rest from it." (End of quotation.) Based on this, it becomes clear that in the narration of Ahmad, the Ansari said: "O girl, bring me my ablution water, that perhaps I may pray and be at rest."]]

*Al-khushu'* (humility) means submission and lowering. *Al-khushu'* also means the lowered, flattened sand-dune. As for *al-khudu'* (submission), it means softness and compliance. From it: "She softened (*khada'at*) her speech when she made it gentle."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 44–46:

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people﴾: The hamzah (the interrogative particle *alif-hamzah*, *al-hamzah*) here expresses affirmation accompanied by rebuke, and an expression of wonder at their condition. *Al-birr* (righteousness) means the breadth of good and what is recognised as good.

From the same root is *al-birr* (dutifulness), because of its breadth, and it encompasses every good. From it is their saying: "You have spoken truthfully and dutifully (*barrarta*)."

The rabbis (*al-ahbar*) used to command those relatives and others who advised them in private to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), but they themselves did not follow him. It was also said that they used to enjoin charity while not giving charity themselves, and when they brought charitable donations to distribute, they would embezzle from them.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Wasi': "It has reached me that some people of Paradise looked down upon some people of the Fire and said to them: 'You used to command us to do things, and we did them, so we entered Paradise.' They said: 'We used to command you to them, but we would oppose them and turn to other things.'"

﴿and you forget yourselves﴾: And you leave yourselves, abandoning them from righteousness, as though they were forgotten.

﴿while you recite the Book﴾: This is a rebuke, like His saying ﴿while you know﴾. It means: while you recite the Torah, in which there is a description of Muhammad (ﷺ), or in which there is the threat against embezzlement, abandonment of righteousness, and the contradiction between speech and action.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾: A severe rebuke, meaning: will you not perceive the ugliness of what you have undertaken, so that its being recognised as ugly would restrain you from committing it? It is as though you were deprived of your intellects, because the intellects reject it and repel it. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God! Will you not then use your reason?﴾.

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: That is, by combining the two, and that you should pray while being patient in bearing the obligations of prayer, enduring its hardships and what is required within it: sincerity of heart, guarding the intentions, repelling whisperings, observing its etiquette, guarding against what is disliked, with fear and humility, and bringing to mind the knowledge that one is standing before the Tyrant of the heavens, to ask for the release of necks from His wrath and punishment.

From the same is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer, and be steadfast in it﴾.

Or: seek help in calamities and misfortunes by being patient through them, and by turning to prayer when they occur.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "When a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer." [[Al-Tabari recorded it in his tafsir from the hadith of Hudhayfah with this wording. Abu Dawud and Ahmad recorded it from the narration of 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Hudhayfah, from Hudhayfah with the wording "When a matter distressed him, he would pray." Al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Dala'il in the story of the Trench at length.]]

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when news of the death of his brother Qutham reached him while he was on a journey, he said "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un," turned aside from the road, and prayed two units (*rak'ahs*), prolonging the sitting in them. Then he rose and walked to his mount, saying: "Seek help through patience and prayer." [[Mawquf (a report ending with a Companion). Recorded by Sa'id ibn Mansur. Al-Tabari recorded it through the route of 'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from his father, that Ibn 'Abbas ... and he mentioned it. Al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Shu'ab through this route.]]

It was also said: *al-sabr* (patience) here means fasting, because one is restrained from things that break it. From this, the month of Ramadan was called "the month of patience."

It is permissible that by prayer is meant supplication (*al-du'a'*), and that one seek help against trials through patience, and resort to supplication, and entreat God, exalted is He, to repel them.

﴿And indeed it is﴾: The pronoun refers either to prayer or to seeking help.

It is permissible that it refers to all the matters that the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from His saying: ﴿Remember My favour﴾ up to ﴿and seek help﴾.

﴿is indeed difficult﴾: heavy and burdensome, from your saying: "This matter was difficult (*kabura*) for me," as in His saying: ﴿Hard for the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾.

If you say: why is it not heavy for the humble ones (*al-khashi'in*), while humility in itself is something that is burdensome?

I say: because they expect what has been stored up for those who are patient with its hardships, so it becomes easy for them. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who suppose that they will meet their Lord﴾, that is, who expect to meet His reward and attain what is with Him, and aspire to it. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), the reading is "those who know" (*ya'lamun*). Its meaning is: they know that there must be a meeting with the recompense, so they act accordingly. For this reason "suppose" (*yazunnun*) has been explained as "are certain" (*yatayaqqanun*).

As for one who does not believe with certainty in recompense and does not hope for reward, he has only pure hardship, so it is heavy upon him, like the hypocrites and those who show off with their deeds. An example of this is one who is promised an additional wage for some works or crafts beyond the measure of his labour: you see him undertaking it with desire, energy, an open heart, and joking with those present, as though he takes pleasure in undertaking it, unlike the state of a worker whom some oppressors compel to labour.

For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bazzar from the hadith of Anas, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." It will come in Al 'Imran.]] And he used to say: "O Bilal, give us rest (*rawwihna*)." [[Recorded by Abu Dawud through the narration of Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: A man from Khuza'ah said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "O Bilal, establish the prayer and give us rest by it." Its narrators are trustworthy, but it was reported with considerable variation from Salim. Al-Daraqutni mentioned it in al-'Ilal. Ahmad recorded it through the narration of the aforementioned Salim from a man of Aslam. Ahmad and Abu Dawud also recorded it from another route, from Salim, that Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: "I entered with my father upon a relative of ours from the Ansar. The prayer became due, and he mentioned a story, and in it: 'Stand up, O Bilal, and give us rest with the prayer.'" Al-Daraqutni recorded it in al-'Ilal through the narration of Salim from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. He said: Abu Khalid al-Qurashi alone reported it from al-Thawri in this way, and through the route of Hamzah al-Thumali from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah from Bilal. Ibrahim al-Harbi recorded it from the narration of Salim from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah as a mursal (a report with a missing Companion). He said: its meaning is: we pray and return to our homes. It is not from rest from burdens, for otherwise he would have said "give us rest from it." (End of quotation.) Based on this, it becomes clear that in the narration of Ahmad, the Ansari said: "O girl, bring me my ablution water, that perhaps I may pray and be at rest."]]

*Al-khushu'* (humility) means submission and lowering. *Al-khushu'* also means the lowered, flattened sand-dune. As for *al-khudu'* (submission), it means softness and compliance. From it: "She softened (*khada'at*) her speech when she made it gentle."

And that I preferred you over the worlds (ʿalamin), [this is] in conjunction (ʿatf) with "My favour" (niʿmati) — meaning: remember My favour and My preferring you over the worlds, that is, over the great multitude of people, as in His saying: ﴿We blessed therein for the worlds﴾. It is said: "I saw a ʿalam of people," meaning a great number.

A day (yawman) — meaning the Day of Resurrection.

No soul will avail (lā tajzī) — that is, will not settle on its behalf any of the rights (ḥuqūq).

From this is the hadith concerning Jadhʿa ibn Niyar: "It will suffice for you, but it will not suffice for anyone after you." [[Agreed upon (muttafaqun ʿalayhi) from the hadith of al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "My maternal uncle, called Abu Burda ibn Niyar, sacrificed..." — and he mentioned the hadith.]]

Shayʾan (anything) is the object (mafʿul bihi). It may also be in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "a little of recompense," as in His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged in the least (shayʾan)﴾.

As for the one who reads (lā tujziʾ) — from ajza'a ʿanhu, meaning "to suffice for him" — then in his reading it can only mean "anything of sufficiency." Abu al-Sarrar al-Ghanawi read: "No soul will suffice for another soul in anything."

This clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier (ṣifah) of "a day." If you ask: "Where is the returning pronoun (ʿaʾid) from it to the qualified noun?" I say: it is omitted, its estimated form being: "No soul will suffice in it." Similar to this is what Abu ʿAli recited:

*Tarawwahi ajdaru an taqīlī*
*Tarawwahi, O best of the palm-pollinated (ghasīl)...*
*Tarawwahi ajdaru an taqīlī*
*ghadan bi-janbī bāridun ẓalīl*

This is by Abu ʿAli Uhayha ibn al-Jullah. He says to his she-camel: "Hurry in the afternoon (bikrī bi-l-rawāḥ), or make the journey quick in it." Al-ghasīl: the best of the palms (ṣinwān al-nakhl). He likened his she-camel to the chosen one among them for her nobility in generosity and her height. He repeated the command for emphasis. It is also said: "tarawwaḥa al-nabt" when the plant grows tall.

*Fatarawwahi*: that is, extend and rise. The address is to the pollen-bearing palm (ʿanʿār al-nakhl), not to the she-camel — so said al-ʿAyni, differing from all the commentators on this rajaz. What confirms this is that instead of the first "tarawwahi" it is reported as "ta'abbari," and ta'bir is placing the male flower of the palm onto the females so their fruit grows. It may be said that this is a reinforcement of the simile. It appears that he moved from one rajaz to another by Uhayha, for it is reported from him:

*Ta'abbari yā khayrata al-ghasīl*
*Ta'abbari min ḥanadhin fashūlī*
*idh ḍanna ahl al-nakhl bi-l-fuḥūl*

This is the address to the ghasil. Hanadh (with a vowel on the first letter) is a place near Medina; it is said to be a village, and it is said to be a water. The meaning: the east wind blows from its direction, carrying the male flower from it to the females, sufficing them from artificial pollination. Shūlī: rise and extend, i.e., pollinate yourself, since the palm-owners have been stingy with the male flowers that fertilize the females. Ajdar: an accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning "and come to a place more worthy and more deserving that you may rest there and be relieved from travel." It may be accusative by taqīlī, implying the sense of "seek," so the preposition is dropped and the word "fīhi" is omitted for its being known. Ghadan is accusative by taqīlī; bi-janbī means "in my side," so it is a substitute (badal) for the omitted "fīhi": "in my two sides there is cool, shaded water," i.e., shaded by trees, or in my side a place of shade with no heat. Then the meaning is "more worthy that you rest by its side," and the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun to show the attribute of the place. The bare comparative (afʿal al-tafḍīl), if "min" is not attached to it verbally, is attached to it in estimation, on the condition that this applies when preference over a specific party is intended. Apparently, ajdar here is not of this kind, so there is no need to estimate it. It may also be that ajdar is a past verb, meaning "it entered into worthiness and rightfulness," "an taqīlī," i.e., your noon rest became right and obligatory, so there is no omission at all.

Al-ʿAyni said: it is possible that "bārid ẓalīl" is with the conjunction omitted out of necessity, meaning "beside a cool one and beside a shaded one."

That is, water more worthy that you rest in it. Some interpret it as "it is widened in it" (ittasaʿa fīhi), treating it as the direct object, so the preposition is dropped, then the pronoun is dropped, as in His saying: ﴿am māl aṣābū﴾. The meaning of the indefiniteness (tankīr) is that no soul of the souls will suffice for another soul any of anything; it is total despair, cutting off all hopes.

Likewise His saying: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾, that is, ransom (fidya), because ʿadl is equivalent to what is ransomed.

From this is the hadith: "No repentance (ṣarf) nor ransom (ʿadl) will be accepted from him." [[Agreed upon from the hadith of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Medina is a sanctuary between ʿAir and such-and-such. Whoever commits an innovation or shelters an innovator, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels and all people. No repentance nor ransom will be accepted from him — the hadith." ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated it and said at its end: "al-ṣarf and al-ʿadl: the voluntary and the obligatory." Both agreed upon it from the hadith of Anas similarly. Muslim has from the hadith of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, traced: "In Medina is a sanctuary, whoever commits..." — and he mentioned it. Al-Tibi overlooked and attributed it to Abu Dawud from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording "Whoever learns eloquent speech to captivate people's hearts, Allah will not accept from him on the Day of Resurrection any ṣarf or ʿadl."]] That is, repentance nor ransom.

Qatada read: "wa lā yuqbalu minhā shafāʿatun," with the verb in the active voice, its subject being Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and "shafāʿa" in the accusative.

It is said: the Jews used to claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them, so they were refuted.

If you ask: Is there in this a proof that intercession is not accepted for the disobedient? [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Is there in this a proof that intercession is not accepted for the sinners...?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: As for one who denies intercession, he is deserving of not attaining it. As for one who believes in it and affirms it — and they are the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah — they hope for the mercy of Allah. Their belief is that it reaches the sinful believers, and it has only been stored up for them. There is no proof in the verse for its deniers, because his saying "a day" (yawman) is indefinite, and there is no doubt that the Resurrection has stages, and its day is reckoned as fifty thousand years; some of its times are not a time for intercession, and some of it is the promised time, in which is the praiseworthy station of the master of mankind, upon him be the best prayers and peace. Many verses have come guiding to the multiplicity of its days and the variation of its times. Among them His saying: ﴿so there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾, together with His saying: ﴿and some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾. It is therefore necessary to read the two verses as referring to two different days, differing: one in which there is questioning, and another in which there is none. Likewise intercession, and the proofs for its establishment are too numerous to count. May Allah grant us intercession and gather us in the company of the people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah.]]? I say: Yes, because He negated that a soul could settle on behalf of another soul any right it had neglected, whether by action or omission; then He negated that the intercession of an intercessor be accepted from it, so it is known that it is not accepted for the disobedient. The meaning of "no intercession is accepted from it" is: if it comes with the intercession of an intercessor, it will not be accepted from it.

It may also refer to the first soul, on the basis that if it were to intercede for it, its intercession would not be accepted, just as nothing would suffice for it, and if it gave a compensation in its place, it would not be taken from it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 49:

The original form of Āl (family, people) is Ahl, which is why its diminutive is Uhayl; its hamza-less form was changed so that the h became an alif. Its use is restricted to matters of great importance and rank, such as kings and their like, so one does not say "Āl al-Iskāf" (the family of the cobbler) or "Āl al-Hajjām" (the family of the cupper). Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is a proper name for the ruler of the Amalekites, like Caesar for the king of the Romans and Khosrow for the king of the Persians. Because of the arrogance of the Pharaohs they derived the verb: tafarʿana Fulān, meaning that so-and-so acted with insolence and tyranny. In a satirical verse, one of them said:

"He was come at by the one who wounds (al-Mūsā al-Kalūm), and so he increased in the furthest extent of his tafarʿun and the excess of his ʿarām."

[The pronoun refers to the boy. It is also said to refer to his male organ. Al-Mūsā is the instrument of shaving and circumcision, from awsā his head, meaning he shaved it. Al-Farrāʾ and others said it is faʿlā and takes the feminine. One says: rajul māsa, like māl, meaning light-headed and flighty. It is also said that it is mafʿal. This is a metaphor for his circumcision with it, since it brings about growth and vigor. It is also said that it refers to shaving the pubic area, since that is the time of reaching full strength. Al-Saʿd preferred the first interpretation because it is more suitable to the context. Al-Kalūm: one who has many wounds, i.e., injuries. Al-Tafarʿun: insolence and tyranny, derived from Fir'awn because of his fame for transgression, wrongdoing and arrogance. Al-ʿArām, like ghurāb: intensity, sharpness and wickedness. It is possible that it derives from al-fariʿ (the branch), because of its height and its elevation over others.]

It is recited as anjaynākum and najjaytukum. Yasūmūnakum comes from sāmahu khasfan, meaning he subjected him to injustice. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:

"When the king subjects the people to humiliation, we refuse to let humiliation settle among us."

[From the mu'allaqa of ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm. The mā here is redundant. Al-Mulk with a sukūn is a dialectal variant of it. One says sāmahu dhullan, meaning he imposed it on him and attached it to him. It is also said: when he obliged him to what contains humiliation and compelled him to it. Al-khasf, with a fatḥa or ḍamma on the kh, means humiliation. He says: when humiliation is attached to the people, we prevent the acceptance of humiliation among us, and we do not submit to it as other people do, because of our courage over all others besides us.]

Its origin is from sāma al-silʿa, when he sought the commodity. As if it means: they desire for you the worst torment and want you to it.

Al-sūʾ is the verbal noun of the adjective sayyiʾ. One says: aʿūdhu billāh min sūʾ al-khuluq wa sūʾ al-fiʿl, meaning their ugliness is intended. The meaning of sūʾ al-ʿadhāb, though all torment is evil, is its most severe and atrocious kind, as if he described it as ugly in comparison with the rest of it.

Yudhabbiḥūn: an explanation of the statement yasūmūnakum. For this reason the conjunction is omitted, as in His words: yuḍāhiʾūna qawla alladhīna kafarū. Al-Zuhrī recited (yudhabbiḥūn) with the light form, as when you say: qaṭaʿtu al-thiyāb and qaṭaʿtuhā.

ʿAbd Allāh recited: yaqtulūn. They did this to them because the soothsayers warned Pharaoh that a boy would be born who would bring about his destruction at his hand, just as Nimrod had been warned. Their diligence in guarding against it did not avail them, and what Allah willed came to pass.

Al-balāʾ is a trial, if "dhalikum" refers to the act of Pharaoh. And it is a blessing, if it refers to the deliverance.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 50:

*Faraqna* means: We separated [the sea] into parts, so that there were paths in it for you. It is also read *farraqna*, with the same meaning as *fassalna*. One says *faraqa bayn al-shay'ayn* (he separated between two things) and *farraqa bayn al-ashya'* (he separated between many things). The paths were twelve, according to the number of the tribes (*asbat*).

If you ask, "What is the meaning of *bikum*?" I answer that it has several possible senses:

1. It may mean that they were traversing it, and the water divided as they passed through it, so it was as though they had divided it, just as one separates two things by placing something between them. [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is possible that they were traversing it..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: On this reading the *ba'* is for instrument, like its use in *katabtu bi-l-qalam* (I wrote with the pen).]]

2. It may mean: We divided it because of you and because of your deliverance. [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is also possible that the intended meaning is: We divided it because of you." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: On this reading the *ba'* expresses cause, as when you say *akramtuka bi-ihsanika ila* (I honoured you because of your kindness to me).]]

3. It may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: We divided it while you were in it. [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is also possible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: On this reading the *ba'* expresses accompaniment, like its use in *asnadtu zahri bi-l-ha'it* (I leaned my back against the wall). The first reading is weak, because its implication is that the division of the sea was caused by the Children of Israel. What is transmitted, indeed what is explicitly stated in the Mighty Book, is that the sea was split only by the staff of Moses. This is confirmed by the words of God Most High: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ (26:63). So the instrument of division is the staff, not the Children of Israel.]]

The meaning is therefore: We divided it while you were within it, as in the verse of the poet:

*"Kanna khuyulana kanat qadiman / tusqa fi quhufihim al-halibа"*
*"Fa-marrat ghayra nafiratin 'alayhim / tadusu bina al-jamajima wa-l-taribā"*

Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi said:

*"It was as if our horses had long ago / been watering in their skulls the milk.*
*So they passed over them, not startled, / trampling beneath us the skulls and the dust."*

*Tusqa* is read with doubled consonant (*tuqqa* form, meaning given to drink). *Quhuf* is the plural of *qahf*, with a vowel that is read with *kasra* and also *damma*; it is the bone above the brain, and also a small wooden vessel. *Halib* is milk that has been milked. The meaning is that the horses had long been accustomed to them, so they passed over them calmly. *Tadus jamajimahum* means: they trample their heads, while we ride upon them. *Tarib* is a dialectal form of *turab* (dust). The meaning is: the horses trample them while we are riding them.

It is related that the Children of Israel said to Moses: "Where are our companions? We do not see them." He said: "Proceed, for they are on a path like your path." They said: "We will not be content until we see them." So he said: "O God, help me against their evil character." Then it was revealed to him: "Say with your staff, like this." So he struck the walls with it, and openings (*kuwa*) appeared in them. Thus they called to one another and heard each other's speech, ﴿while you were looking on﴾ (2:50) at that and witnessing it, with no doubt about it.

When the Children of Israel entered Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, they had no book to turn to. God promised Moses that He would send down the Torah to him, and He appointed for him a fixed time: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. It was also said "forty nights," because the months are made up of nights.

It was read as "wa'adna" (We made a promise), because God promised him the revelation, and He promised his coming at the appointed time to Mount Sinai. "From after him" means from after his departure to Mount Sinai. "And you were wrongdoers" by your associating partners with God. "Then We pardoned you after that" when you repented, "after your committing the great matter," which is your taking the calf (as a god). "So that perhaps you would give thanks" means in the sense of "in the hope that you would give thanks." The bounty lies in pardoning you.

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is 'in the sense of wishing that you would give thanks.'" Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: He erred in interpreting "la'alla" as "wishing," because the will of God Most High is bound to occur without doubt. If He willed thanks from them, they would certainly have given thanks. Al-Zamakhshari applied it to his own principle, which is corrupt, in the belief that the will of the Lord is like the will of the servant, some of which takes effect and some of which is frustrated—exalted is God above that. What God wills comes to pass, and what He does not will does not come to pass. The correct interpretation of "la'alla" is the one that Sibawayh (may God have mercy on him) set down in his explanation of His words, "perhaps he will remember or fear" (Qur'an 20:44). Sibawayh said: "The hope is directed toward the addressee, as if he said: 'Be in your hope regarding his remembrance and his fear.' And likewise this verse means: 'So that you may be in the hope of giving thanks to God, Mighty and Majestic, and His favors,' so the hope is directed toward them, and God Most High is exalted above it."]] the bounty in pardoning you.

**al-Kitab wal-Furqan**: he means the one that combines being a revealed Book and a Furqan that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This refers to the Torah. It is like your saying, "I saw *al-ghayth* and *al-layth*," meaning a man who combines generosity (*al-judud*) and boldness (*al-jur'a*). A similar example is the Most High's saying, ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Furqan, and a light and a reminder﴾ (21:48). He means the Book that combines being a Furqan, a light, and a reminder, or the Torah. *Al-Burhan* is that which separates disbelief from faith, such as the staff, the hand, and other signs. Or it is the Law (*al-shar'*) that separates the lawful from the unlawful. It has also been said that *al-Furqan* is the splitting of the sea. It has also been said that it is the victory by which He distinguished between them and their enemy, as in the Most High's saying, ﴿the Day of the Furqan﴾ (8:41), by which he means the Day of Badr.

As for His saying, ﴿So kill yourselves﴾, it is taken in its apparent sense, which is *al-bakh'* (the one who destroys himself out of grief). In *al-Sihah*: "He *bakha'a* himself, *bakhan*, meaning he killed it out of grief." (Gh.)

It has also been said that the meaning is that some of them kill others. It has also been said that those who did not worship the calf were commanded to kill the worshippers. It is narrated that a man would see his child, his parent, his neighbour, and his relative, but they could not proceed to carry out God's command. So God sent a mist and a black cloud beneath which they could not see one another. They were ordered to sit on their knees in the courtyards of their houses, and those who had not worshipped the calf took up their swords. They were told: "Be patient. God curses whoever raises his eye, or loosens his sitting posture, or shields himself with a hand or a foot." They would say, "Amen," and they killed them until evening. Then Moses and Aaron prayed and said, "O Lord, the children of Israel are destroyed! The remnant, the remnant!" So the cloud was lifted and repentance was sent down. The blades then fell from their hands, and the slain numbered seventy thousand.

If you ask: what is the difference between the *fa's*? I answer: the first *fa'* is for causation only, because wrongdoing is the cause of repentance. The second is for sequence (*ta'qib*), because the meaning is: "resolve upon repentance, then kill yourselves," since God made their repentance the killing of themselves. It is also permissible that the killing be the completion of their repentance, so the meaning becomes: "Repent, then follow the repentance with killing as the completion of your repentance." The third *fa'* is connected to an elided element. It must either be included in Moses' statement to them, so it is connected to an elided condition, as if he had said, "If you do it, then He has accepted your repentance." Or it is an address from God Most High to them following the method of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), so the implied meaning is: "They did what Moses commanded them, so your Creator accepted their repentance."

If you ask: from where does this place specifically mention *al-Bari'* (the Originator)? I answer: *al-Bari'* is the One who created creation free from disparity, ﴿You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ (67:3), and distinguished some of it from others by different shapes and varying forms. So there is in it a rebuke for their abandoning the worship of the Wise World-Creator, who originated them with the subtlety of His wisdom in different forms, free from disparity and discord, in favour of worshipping a cow, which is a proverb for dullness and stupidity. In the proverbs of the Arabs: "*Abladu min thawr*" (more dull than a bull). This led them to expose themselves to God's wrath and to the descent of His command that He undo what He had assembled of their creation and scatter what He had arranged of their forms and shapes, since they did not give thanks for that blessing and disdained it by worshipping one who has no power over any of it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 55–57:

It is said: the ones who said it were the seventy who were struck senseless. And it is said that ten thousand of them said it, "openly," face to face (ʿiyanan).

Jahratan is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from your saying: "he recited aloud (jahara bi-l-qirāʾa) and supplicated aloud (jahara bi-l-duʿāʾ)." It is as if the one who sees with the eye is "openly" declaring the seeing, and the one who sees with the heart is speaking it in a low voice. It is in the accusative as a maṣdar, because it is a kind of seeing, so it is governed by its verb, just as qurfuṣāʾ is governed by the verb "to sit." Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), in the sense of "visibly, openly." It has been read as jahratan with a fatḥa on the hāʾ, and it is either a maṣdar like al-ghalaba, or a plural of jāhir. In this statement there is evidence that Musa (peace be upon him) rejected their claim and made them understand that seeing one who may not be located in a direction is impossible [[His saying "that He be located in a direction is impossible" is the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. Those who permit seeing Him are the People of the Sunna, and direction is not a condition of seeing according to them, so it does not follow that He is one of the bodies or the accidents, as is explained in the science of tawhid. (ʿ)]] and that whoever permits seeing God has made Him one of the bodies [[Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "In this there is evidence that Musa (peace be upon him) rejected their claim and made them understand that the seeing of one who may not be..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari has seized upon what he believed to be an opportunity from this verse, in which, upon close examination, he has no real hope of finding support. He built the matter on the basis that the punishment was caused by the request to see what is not permissible for God Most High, according to his supposition. How could he claim that, when there is a clear cause for the punishment other than what he asserts as the whole cause? For when Musa (peace be upon him) knew that seeing Him was permissible, he requested it in the Surah of al-Aʿraf in this world, and God Most High informed him that He would not be seen in this world. This became, for him and for the Children of Israel, an established principle, just as it is for us, the People of the Sunna, that God Most High is not seen in this world, because He informed us that He is not seen, and the report must be true. Just as He informed that He is not seen in this abode, the Truthful Promise, Mighty and Majestic, has promised that He will be seen in the Hereafter, and this is specified for the believers. After this belief was established, the Children of Israel asked to see Him in this world, out of obstinacy or doubt about the report, so God Most High sent down that punishment upon them. How did al-Zamakhshari and his followers imagine that Musa (peace be upon him) asked God for what is not permissible for Him? And if the matter were as he imagined, would he not be like the Children of Israel? God forbid! He has cleared him of that, and he was honored in the sight of God. As for the rational proofs for the permissibility of seeing Him, Exalted, by reason, and the revealed proofs for its occurrence in the Hereafter, they are too many to count, and they are fully set out in the discipline of kalam. Our purpose in this section is only to discuss al-Zamakhshari and refute him, from the angle by which he clings to his supposition and by which he has led some people astray. And God is the Granter of success.]] or the accidents. So they rejected him after the proof was explained and the evidence was clear, and they persisted, and they were in disbelief like the worshippers of the calf. So God imposed upon them the thunderbolt, just as He imposed killing upon those, as an equalizing between the two disbeliefs and as an indication of their magnitude through the magnitude of the trial.

Al-Ṣāʿiqa is that which struck them, that is, caused them to die. It was said: a fire that fell from the sky and burned them. It was said: a shout that came from the sky. It was said: God sent hosts whose sound they heard, and they fell down, struck dead, for a day and a night. As for Musa (peace be upon him), his being struck was not death but a swoon, as is shown by His saying: "then, when he recovered" (fa-lammā afāq). The apparent meaning is that what they were looking at befell them, according to His saying: "while you were looking" (wa-antum tanẓurūn). ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, read: "so the thunderbolt seized you" (fa-akhadhatkum al-ṣāʿiqa).

"Perhaps you will be grateful" (laʿallakum tashkurūn): for the blessing of resurrection after death, or for God's blessing after you had denied it, when you see the might of God in His striking you with the thunderbolt and making you taste death. "And We shaded you with clouds" (wa-ẓallalnā): We made the cloud shade you. This was in the wilderness (al-tīh): God subjected the clouds for them, moving with their journey, shading them from the sun, and at night a pillar of fire descended, by whose light they traveled; their garments did not become soiled or wear out. "And We sent down upon them the manna" (al-manna), which is terangbīn (honey-like sap), like snow, from the break of dawn until sunrise, a ṣāʿ for each person. God would send the south wind, which would gather for them the quails (al-salwā), which are the samāna (a kind of quail), and a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him. "Eat" (kulū) is on the assumption of a saying (qawl) being implied. "And they did not wrong Us" (wa-mā ẓalamūnā): meaning, they wronged themselves by denying these blessings; "and they did not wrong Us" — the speech is abbreviated by omitting the first clause, because "and they did not wrong Us" indicates it.
