This was in the wilderness (al-tīh): God subjected the clouds for them, moving with their journey, shading them from the sun, and at night a pillar of fire descended, by whose light they traveled; their garments did not become soiled or wear out. "And We sent down upon them the manna" (al-manna), which is terangbīn (honey-like sap), like snow, from the break of dawn until sunrise, a ṣāʿ for each person. God would send the south wind, which would gather for them the quails (al-salwā), which are the samāna (a kind of quail), and a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him. "Eat" (kulū) is on the assumption of a saying (qawl) being implied. "And they did not wrong Us" (wa-mā ẓalamūnā): meaning, they wronged themselves by denying these blessings; "and they did not wrong Us" — the speech is abbreviated by omitting the first clause, because "and they did not wrong Us" indicates it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 55–57:

It is said: the ones who said it were the seventy who were struck senseless. And it is said that ten thousand of them said it, "openly," face to face (ʿiyanan).

Jahratan is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from your saying: "he recited aloud (jahara bi-l-qirāʾa) and supplicated aloud (jahara bi-l-duʿāʾ)." It is as if the one who sees with the eye is "openly" declaring the seeing, and the one who sees with the heart is speaking it in a low voice. It is in the accusative as a maṣdar, because it is a kind of seeing, so it is governed by its verb, just as qurfuṣāʾ is governed by the verb "to sit." Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), in the sense of "visibly, openly." It has been read as jahratan with a fatḥa on the hāʾ, and it is either a maṣdar like al-ghalaba, or a plural of jāhir. In this statement there is evidence that Musa (peace be upon him) rejected their claim and made them understand that seeing one who may not be located in a direction is impossible [[His saying "that He be located in a direction is impossible" is the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. Those who permit seeing Him are the People of the Sunna, and direction is not a condition of seeing according to them, so it does not follow that He is one of the bodies or the accidents, as is explained in the science of tawhid. (ʿ)]] and that whoever permits seeing God has made Him one of the bodies [[Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "In this there is evidence that Musa (peace be upon him) rejected their claim and made them understand that the seeing of one who may not be..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari has seized upon what he believed to be an opportunity from this verse, in which, upon close examination, he has no real hope of finding support. He built the matter on the basis that the punishment was caused by the request to see what is not permissible for God Most High, according to his supposition. How could he claim that, when there is a clear cause for the punishment other than what he asserts as the whole cause? For when Musa (peace be upon him) knew that seeing Him was permissible, he requested it in the Surah of al-Aʿraf in this world, and God Most High informed him that He would not be seen in this world. This became, for him and for the Children of Israel, an established principle, just as it is for us, the People of the Sunna, that God Most High is not seen in this world, because He informed us that He is not seen, and the report must be true. Just as He informed that He is not seen in this abode, the Truthful Promise, Mighty and Majestic, has promised that He will be seen in the Hereafter, and this is specified for the believers. After this belief was established, the Children of Israel asked to see Him in this world, out of obstinacy or doubt about the report, so God Most High sent down that punishment upon them. How did al-Zamakhshari and his followers imagine that Musa (peace be upon him) asked God for what is not permissible for Him? And if the matter were as he imagined, would he not be like the Children of Israel? God forbid! He has cleared him of that, and he was honored in the sight of God. As for the rational proofs for the permissibility of seeing Him, Exalted, by reason, and the revealed proofs for its occurrence in the Hereafter, they are too many to count, and they are fully set out in the discipline of kalam. Our purpose in this section is only to discuss al-Zamakhshari and refute him, from the angle by which he clings to his supposition and by which he has led some people astray. And God is the Granter of success.]] or the accidents. So they rejected him after the proof was explained and the evidence was clear, and they persisted, and they were in disbelief like the worshippers of the calf. So God imposed upon them the thunderbolt, just as He imposed killing upon those, as an equalizing between the two disbeliefs and as an indication of their magnitude through the magnitude of the trial.

Al-Ṣāʿiqa is that which struck them, that is, caused them to die. It was said: a fire that fell from the sky and burned them. It was said: a shout that came from the sky. It was said: God sent hosts whose sound they heard, and they fell down, struck dead, for a day and a night. As for Musa (peace be upon him), his being struck was not death but a swoon, as is shown by His saying: "then, when he recovered" (fa-lammā afāq). The apparent meaning is that what they were looking at befell them, according to His saying: "while you were looking" (wa-antum tanẓurūn). ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, read: "so the thunderbolt seized you" (fa-akhadhatkum al-ṣāʿiqa).

"Perhaps you will be grateful" (laʿallakum tashkurūn): for the blessing of resurrection after death, or for God's blessing after you had denied it, when you see the might of God in His striking you with the thunderbolt and making you taste death. "And We shaded you with clouds" (wa-ẓallalnā): We made the cloud shade you. This was in the wilderness (al-tīh): God subjected the clouds for them, moving with their journey, shading them from the sun, and at night a pillar of fire descended, by whose light they traveled; their garments did not become soiled or wear out. "And We sent down upon them the manna" (al-manna), which is terangbīn (honey-like sap), like snow, from the break of dawn until sunrise, a ṣāʿ for each person. God would send the south wind, which would gather for them the quails (al-salwā), which are the samāna (a kind of quail), and a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him. "Eat" (kulū) is on the assumption of a saying (qawl) being implied. "And they did not wrong Us" (wa-mā ẓalamūnā): meaning, they wronged themselves by denying these blessings; "and they did not wrong Us" — the speech is abbreviated by omitting the first clause, because "and they did not wrong Us" indicates it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 2, verses 58–59:

﴿الْقَرْيَةَ﴾ refers to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is also said to be Jericho (Ariha), one of the villages of al-Sham (Greater Syria), which they were commanded to enter after the wandering (al-tih).

﴿الْبَابَ﴾ means the gate of the town. It is also said to be the gate of the dome (al-qubba) to which they used to pray, since they had not yet entered Bayt al-Maqdis during the lifetime of Musa, peace be upon him. They were commanded to prostrate (al-sujud) upon reaching the gate, in thanks to Allah and in humility.

It is also said that "prostration" means that they should bow and lower themselves as they entered, so that their entry would be with humility and submissiveness (al-ikhbat). It is also said:

They were told to lower the gate so that they would bow their heads, but they did not lower them, and they entered crawling on their buttocks.

﴿حِطَّةٌ﴾ is on the pattern fi'la, derived from al-hatt (lowering), like al-jilsa (the sitting) and al-rukba (the kneeling). It is the predicate (khabar) of an elided subject (mubtada'), meaning: our matter is ḥiṭṭa, or your command is ḥiṭṭa.

The original form is in the accusative (al-nasb), meaning: "Remove our sins from us, as a removal." It was put in the nominative (al-raf') in order to convey the sense of permanence, as in the verse of the poet:

*He complained to me, my camel, of the length of the night journey: "Patience, good patience, for we are both tested."*

He says: My camel complained of its fatigue from the long night journey. *Ṣabran* (patience) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) standing in place of its verb, meaning "be patient, O camel, with good patience"; there is here a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person. Or the implied meaning is: "I said to him, 'Be patient, a patience,' for each of us is afflicted by trial." Or: "each of us is being tested, whether he will endure the hardships of travel or not." It is also transmitted as *ṣabrun jamīl*, meaning "our patience is more fitting," with the predicate elided. Or the meaning is "our affair is patience," in which case it is one of the places where the subject must be elided because the predicate has taken the place of the verb. Good patience (al-ṣabr al-jamīl) is that in which there is no complaint made to creatures.

The original is *ṣabran*, from "be patient, a patience." Ibn Abi Ablah recited it in the accusative, according to the original form. It is also said that its meaning is: "Our command is ḥiṭṭa," that is, that we should settle down and remain in this town.

If you ask: Is it permissible to put ﴿حِطَّةٌ﴾ in the accusative, in the recitation of one who reads it in the accusative, governed by ﴿قُولُوا﴾ (say), with the meaning "say this word"? I say: It is not far-fetched. But the better view is that it is accusative by means of an implied verb (idmar fi'lihā), and the place of that implied verb is governed by ﴿قُولُوا﴾.

It was also recited as ﴿يُغْفَرْ لَكُمْ﴾ in the passive voice, with the yā' and the tā'.

﴿وَسَنَزِيدُ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ means: whoever among you was a good-doer, that word was a cause for increasing his reward; and whoever was a wrongdoer, for him it was a repentance and forgiveness.

﴿فَبَدَّلَ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ means: they put in place of ḥiṭṭa ﴿قَوْلًا غَيْرَهَا﴾ (another word). The meaning is that they were commanded to say a word whose meaning is repentance and seeking forgiveness, but they departed from it to a word whose meaning is not the meaning of what they were commanded, and they did not obey Allah's command. The point is not that they were commanded a particular wording, namely the word ḥiṭṭa, and that they came with a different wording; for if they had come with a different wording that independently conveyed the meaning of what they were commanded, they would not have been held accountable for it.

It is like if they had said, in place of ḥiṭṭa: "We seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance," or "O Allah, pardon us," and the like. It is also said:

They said, in place of ḥiṭṭa: ḥinṭa (wheat). It is also said they said in Nabataean: "ḥaṭā samqātha," meaning "red wheat," mocking what had been said to them, and turning away from seeking what is with Allah to seeking what they desired of the worldly aims.

The repetition of ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ (those who did wrong) is an increase in denouncing their conduct.

[[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The repetition of (those who did wrong) is an increase in denouncing ... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In it is a magnification of their wrongdoing, in that the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, and this serves that purpose, for it is a form of making this particular group known while it could have been abbreviated by a pronoun.]]

It also indicates that the sending down of the punishment upon them was because of their wrongdoing. In Surat al-A'raf it comes as ﴿فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (So We sent upon them), with a pronoun. The *rijz* means punishment. It was also recited with a *ḍamma* on the rā'. It is narrated that there died of them in one hour, from plague (al-ṭā'ūn), twenty-four thousand. It is also said: seventy thousand.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 60:

They became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tīh), so Musa (Moses) prayed for them to be given water. He was told: ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾. The definite article in "al-ḥajar" (the rock) may be for prior reference (ʿahd), pointing to a known rock. It is related that it was a rock from Mount Sinai (Ṭūr) which he carried with him. It was a square rock with four faces, and from each face three springs gushed forth, one for each tribe (sibṭ). Each spring flowed in a channel to the tribe that was commanded to drink from it. They numbered six hundred thousand, and the camp was twelve miles across.

It is also said that Adam brought it down from Paradise, and it was inherited until it reached Shuʿayb (Jethro), who gave it to Musa along with the staff. It is also said that it was the rock on which he placed his garment when he bathed, when they accused him of having a defect (al-adra) and he fled with it. Then Jibril (Gabriel) said to him: "Allah the Exalted says to you: Lift this rock, for in it is My power and for you in it is a miracle." So he carried it in his wallet.

The article may also be generic (lil-jins), meaning: strike the thing called a rock. It is reported from al-Ḥasan that He did not command him to strike a specific rock. He said: "This is more evident as proof and clearer as a demonstration of power." It is related that they said: "What will become of us if we arrive at a land with no stones?" So he carried a rock in his wallet, and wherever they camped he set it down.

It is also said that he would strike it with his staff and it would burst forth, and when he struck it with the staff it would dry up. They said: "If Musa loses his staff, we will die of thirst." So He revealed to him: "Do not strike the stones; speak to them and they will obey you, so that they may take heed."

It is also said that it was of marble, one cubit by one cubit. It is said it was the size of a human head. It is said it was from the myrtle (ās) of Paradise, its length ten cubits in proportion to Musa's height, with two prongs that shone in the dark, and it was carried on a donkey.

﴿So it gushed forth﴾: the fā' (fa') is connected to an implied element, meaning: so he struck, and it gushed forth. Or: if you strike, then it has gushed forth, as we mentioned in His saying ﴿so He turned to you in forgiveness﴾. On this reading the fa' is the eloquent fa' (fāʾ faṣīḥa), which occurs only in eloquent speech.

It is read as "ʿasharah" with a kasra and with a fatḥa on the shīn, both being dialects. ﴿Every people (kullu unās)﴾, i.e., every tribe (sibṭ), ﴿knew its drinking place﴾, i.e., the spring from which they drink. ﴿Eat﴾ is understood as with the implied "saying": ﴿from the provision of Allah﴾, that which He has provided you of food, namely the manna and the quail, and of the water of the springs. It is also said that the water causes crops and fruits to grow, so it is a provision from which one eats and drinks.

Al-ʿathiyy means the worst corruption. So it was said to them: ﴿Do not persist in corruption﴾, in your state of corruption, because they were persistent in it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 61:

They were farmers, so they yearned for their lentils (ʿakarihim) and rejected (fa-ajamū) what they had been given of blessing; their souls craved the lowly things. "Over one kind of food" (ʿalā ṭaʿāmin wāḥid): they meant the manna and quails they had been provided with in the wilderness (al-tīh). [[His words "fa-ajamū mā kānū fīhi" mean they disliked (karihū). Reported by al-Sihah (al-Jawhari). (ʿ)]] If you say: "They are two kinds of food, so why did they say 'one kind of food'?" I reply: by "one" they meant that which does not vary and does not change. Even if a man's table has several dishes which he persists in eating every day without changing them, it is said: "So-and-so eats only one kind of food," where the oneness is meant to negate change and variation. It is also permissible that they meant they are one type, since both are from the food of people of luxury and affluence, whereas we are a people of farming, people of cultivation, so we want only what we are accustomed to and have grown used to, from varied things such as grains and vegetables and the like. The meaning of "yukhrij lana" ("bring forth for us") is: make appear for us and cause to be found. "Al-baql" (vegetables) is what the earth produces of greens, and what is meant by it is the choice vegetables that people eat, such as mint, celery, leeks and their like. It has been read as "wa-qithāʾihā" with a ḍamma. "Al-fūm" is wheat; from it comes "fawwimū lanā," i.e., bake for us. It is also said to mean garlic (al-thūm), and this is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "wa-thūmihā." It goes well with lentils and onions. "Alladhī huwa adnā" means: which is closer in rank and lower in value. Nearness and closeness are used to express small quantity, so one says: "he is near in place" and "close in rank," just as distance is used for the opposite, so one says: "he is distant in place" and "distant in aspiration," meaning elevation and loftiness. Zuhayr al-Furqubi read "adna'" with a hamza, from "dana'a" (baseness). "Ihbitū miṣran" and it has been read "ihbitū" with a ḍamma: i.e., go down to it from the wilderness. It is said: "habaṭa al-wādī" when he descended into it, and "habaṭa minhu" when he came out of it. The land of the wilderness is what lies between Bayt al-Maqdis and Qinnasrin, and it is twelve farsakhs by eight farsakhs. It may be intended as a proper name; its being diptotic despite the two causes combined in it, namely definiteness and femininity, is because its middle is quiescent, like His saying: "Nūḥan wa-Lūṭan." Both are non-Arabic and definite. If the city is meant, then it has only one cause. It may also mean any of the cities (amṣār). In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh, and as read by al-Aʿmash: "ihbitū Miṣr" without tanwīn, like His saying: "udkhulū Miṣr." It has also been said it is "Miṣrāʾīm," which was arabicized. "Wa-ḍuribat ʿalayhimu al-dhilla" means: humiliation was made to encompass them and surround them, so they are within it as one is within a dome upon which it has been struck. Or it was affixed to them until it clung to them, like a clinging blow, as clay is thrown onto a wall and adheres to it. So the Jews are abased and humiliated, people of poverty and destitution. [[His words "ahl maskanah wa-madqa'ah" mean: dust-covered. Reported by al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] Whether this is literal, or it is their self-abasement and pretended poverty out of fear that the poll tax would be doubled upon them. "Wa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin min Allāh": from your saying "bāʾa fulān bi-fulān," when someone is worthy of being killed for another, due to equality and retaliation; i.e., they became deserving of His wrath. "Dhālika" refers to what preceded: the striking of humiliation, poverty, and deserving wrath. That is, this is because of their disbelief and their killing of the prophets. The Jews, may they be cursed, killed Shaʿyāʾ, Zakariyyā, Yahyā, and others. If you say: "The killing of prophets can only be without right, so what is the benefit of mentioning it?" I reply: the meaning is that they killed them without right in their own view, since they had not killed anyone nor committed corruption on earth such that they would be killed. Rather, they advised them and called them to what benefited them, and they killed them. Had they been asked and been fair to themselves, they would not have mentioned any reason by which they could deserve killing in their view. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read "wa-yaqtulūna" with the intensive form. "Dhālika" is a repetition of the reference: "bi-mā ʿaṣaw", because of their committing various sins and transgressing the limits of Allah in everything, together with their disbelief in the signs of Allah and their killing of the prophets. It has been said: it is their transgression on the Sabbath. It is also permissible that "dhālika" refers to the disbelief and the killing of the prophets, in the sense that this was because of their disobedience and transgression, since they immersed themselves in both and went to extremes, until their hearts hardened, so they dared to deny the signs and kill the prophets. Or that disbelief and killing, along with what they disobeyed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 62:

Inna alladhina amanu bi-alsinatihim min ghayri mawata'at al-qulub, wa-hum al-munafiqun. Wa-alladhina hadu wa-alladhina tahawwadu. It is said: hada, Yahud (to be Jewish; to repent). Tahawwada means he entered Judaism; the active participle is ha'id, and the plural is hud. Wa-al-nasara, which is the plural of nasran. It is said: rajul nasran (a Christian man) and imra'a nasrana (a Christian woman). He said: "A Christian woman who has not turned away from the faith." The yaa' in nasrani (Nasrani, the singular relative form) is for emphasis, like the one in ahmari (reddish). They were named so because they supported (nasarū) the Messiah. Wa-al-sabi'in, which is from sabi'a, meaning he left the religion. They are a people who deviated from the religion of Judaism and Christianity and worshipped the angels. Man amana min ha'ulai al-kafara iman-an khalisan wa-dakhala fi millat al-Islam dukhulan asilan wa-'amila salihan fa-lahum ajruhum alladhi yastawjibunahu bi-imanihim wa-'amalihim.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of man amana? I answer: it is in the nominative case if you make it the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is (fa-lahum ajruhum). It is in the accusative case if you make it a substitute (badal) for the noun of inna and the word coordinated with it. So the predicate of inna in the first case is the whole clause as it is, and in the second case it is fa-lahum ajruhum. The fa' (fa-) is there because man (whoever) includes the meaning of a conditional.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 67–73 (part 1 of 2):

There was a wealthy old man among the Children of Israel, and his nephews killed his son in order to inherit from him. They threw the body at the gate of a city and then came demanding the blood-money (diyah). God commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the body with a piece of it, so that he would come back to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said: "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾ That is, "Do you make us an object of mockery," or "people of mockery," or "one who is mocked," or "mockery itself," because of the extreme degree of mocking. ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because mockery in such a matter is a form of ignorance and foolishness.

It is also read as "huzu'an" with two damma (u-vowels), and as "huz'an" with a sukun on the zay, like "kufu'an" and "kufan". Hafs reads "huzuwan" with two damma and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan". Al-ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and al-liyadh (clinging for protection) come from one root.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): "Ask your Lord for us, what is it?" This is a question about its condition and description. They were amazed at a dead cow being struck with a piece of a dead man, and then he came back to life. So they asked about the description of that cow, which was extraordinary in its nature and different from ordinary cows.

Al-fariḍ means the old cow (al-musinnah), and it is said "faraḍat furuḍan, fa-hiya fāriḍ" (she became old). Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

*"By my life, you gave your guest an old she-camel,*
*led to him, which cannot stand on one leg."*

[[Khufaf ibn Nadbah, satirizing al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas for stinginess. Al-fāriḍ is an old she-camel that is led to him, meaning she is not ridden but needs someone to strike her and drive her from behind. "Cannot stand on one leg" means she has no strong leg to rely on for standing.]]

It seems she was called fāriḍ because she had reached the end of her age, having "cut off" (faraḍat) her teeth and reached their final stage. Al-bikr means the young one.

Al-ʿawān means the middle-aged one. The poet said:

*"Graceful ones among virgins and matrons."*

[[*"Caravans of women I used to know long ago,*
*and they, when dwelling, were not dark-skinned,*
*chaste in the faces, high-lying in the veils,*
*graceful, between virgins and matrons."*
By al-Ṭirmāḥ. Al-ẓaʿāʾin are women in howdahs. Al-ḍaʿāʾin (with ḍād) are mounts. Al-ḍaghāʾin (with ghayn) are plural of ḍaghīnah, meaning hatred, inclination, or crookedness; ḍaghanahu means you took him into your embrace. A ḍāghin horse is one that does not give its speed. A ḍāt ḍaghn she-camel is one longing for her homeland. A ḍāt ḍaghn woman loves someone other than her husband. Al-juun (with a ḍamma) is the plural of jawāʾ, meaning black.
Al-ḥaṣān (with a fatḥa) is the chaste one. Al-naqb is the plural of niqāb, like kutub and kitāb. Al-ʿawn originally has a ḍamma on the waw, as the plural of ʿawān, which means the middle, that is, the middle of women and animals, and it was lightened by a sukun. He says: those women are "ẓaʿāʾin," meaning travelers, the journey changed their color, and I used to know them long ago, when they were at home, not dark, chaste in their faces, and when they are protected they are all protected by habit. Al-aʿāli is an adjective for al-naqb or al-mawāḍiʿ, and this applies only to women, as you see. Some narrators reported "ḍaghāʾin" instead of "ẓaʿāʾin," but it is probably a distortion. They are graceful, moving among young virgins and middle-aged women.]]

It is said that "ʿawwanat" (she became middle-aged) is used. [[Al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) says: one says of her "ʿawwanat al-mar'ah taʿwīnan, wa ʿānat taʿūnu ʿawnan." (ʿ)]]

If you say: "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, how is it permitted to be followed by "dhālika" (that)? I say: because it has the sense of two things, since it refers to what was mentioned, the old cow and the young one. If you say: how is it permitted to refer with it to two feminine things, when it is only used to point to a single masculine thing? I say: this is permitted by interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned and what preceded, for brevity in speech, just as they used "faʿala" as a substitute for many actions mentioned before it. You say to a man: "How good what you did was!", and he has mentioned many actions and a long story, just as you say to him: "How good that is!" The pronoun may also be used in the same way as a demonstrative. Abu ʿUbaydah said: I said to Ruʾbah about his verse:

*"In it are lines of black and white,*
*as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy."*

[[Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj describes a wild cow, and it was said a horse, and it was said horses, in which is the color black and the color white, and it is narrated as "min bayāḍ wa bāq." Perhaps the white is white mixed with dust, as if it is "the mentioned one or the combination of both," like the pattern of leprosy on the skin. Or it means while being on the skin, the pattern of leprosy, that is, its marking of white mixed with dullness arising from leprosy, a disease by which the color of the skin changes. It is related that Abu ʿUbaydah said to him: if you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā"; if you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā." He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," (as if that). So he made the pronoun behave like a demonstrative in the correctness of pointing with the singular to the plural, by interpreting it as the thing mentioned or similar.]]

If you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā" (as if they). If you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā" (as if they two). He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," you fool! What makes it good is that the demonstratives in their dual, plural and feminine forms are not literal, and the same is true for relative pronouns. That is why "alladhī" was used to mean the plural, as in ﴿what you are commanded (mā tu'maruna)﴾, that is, what you are commanded to do, meaning "tu'maruna bihi" (you are commanded with it), from the saying: ﴿I commanded you the good (amartuka al-khayr)﴾ or ﴿their command (amruhum)﴾, meaning "ma'murukum" (what is commanded to you), calling the object by the verbal noun, like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the striking of the ruler).

Al-fuqūʿ is the most intense yellow and its purest. It is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqiʿ wa wāris" (intensely yellow and dark yellow), just as one says "aswad ḥālik wa ḥānik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqiq wa lahiq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānī wa dhurayqī" (intensely red), "akhḍar nāḍir wa mudhāmmim" (intensely green), "awraq khaṭbānī wa azmak rudānī" (grayish-green). If you say: "fāqiʿ" here is a predicate of the color, so it is not an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," I say: it is not a predicate of the color; it is an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," except that the color is raised by it like the subject, and the color belongs to it and is connected to it, so there is no difference between your saying "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa" and "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿ lawnuhā" (its color is intensely yellow). If you say: why not say "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa," and what is the benefit of mentioning the color? I say: the benefit is emphasis, because "lawn" is a name for the form, and it is yellowness. So it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow is its yellowness," like your saying "jadda jadduhu" (his grandfather is truly his grandfather) and "junūnuka majnūn" (your madness is madness).

It is related from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you that the light of the sun comes out of its skin. Joy is a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining a benefit or expecting it. It is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever wears yellow sandals, his anxiety decreases." [[It is a statement attributed to ʿAlī (mawqūf) which I have not found. But al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Khaṭīb reported it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Whoever wears yellow sandals will not cease to be in joy as long as he wears them." Ibn Abi Hatim said: I asked my father about it, and he said: it is a lie, fabricated.]] because of the statement of God Most High: ﴿it pleases the observers (tasurru al-nāẓirīn)﴾. It is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā" (yellow, intensely its color), he said: "black, intensely black." Perhaps it is borrowed from the description of camels, because their blackness is overlaid with yellowness. By this was explained the verse: ﴿camels, yellow (jimālatun ṣufrun)﴾. Al-Aʿshā said:

*"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*

[[*"Qays, the best of deeds, father of*
*Abu al-Ashʿath, whose echoes have become dispersed in the roads.*
*Every year he gives me generously from his camels*
*at the time of the birth of the sheep or the noble camel.*
*Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*
By al-Aʿshā, about Abu al-Ashʿath ibn Qays. Al-fiʿāl (with a fatḥa) means good deeds. Al-aṣdāʾ is the plural of ṣadā, which is the male owl. The Arabs used to claim that the bones of a slain person's head turn into an owl that cries "Avenge me!" until his blood is avenged. Shuʿūb is the name for death, and it is possible it is the plural of shiʿb meaning road, that is, they became scattered on the roads, which is a metaphor for his killing. The plural is for honor or is considered as such. Al-juumūm is the plural of jamm (with a triple vowel on the first letter), meaning many. Al-najīb is the noble one among horses and camels. Al-rikāb are mounts. "Hunna" (they) refers to the mounts; "ṣufr" is the plural of aṣfar or ṣafrāʾ; "their offspring like raisins" means their dark color predominates. The yellowness here means blackness overlaid with yellowness, because this is the most prized color of camels among them.]]

﴿What is it (mā hiya)?﴾ is a second repetition of the question about its condition and description, and an additional inquiry, so that they might gain more clarity regarding its description.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had taken any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they were strict, so God was strict with them, and excessive questioning is a bad omen." [[Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Abi Hatim all from the chain of al-Ḥasan, from Abu Rafiʿ, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain contains ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr, who is weak. Al-Ṭabarī has it as a statement of Ibn ʿAbbās (mawqūf), and from a statement of Abu al-ʿĀliyah, except the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen," which is not in the raised or the stopped version. I say: the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen" is from the statement of al-Zamakhsharī.]]

And it is related from one of the caliphs that he wrote to his agent to go to a people and cut down their trees and demolish their houses. He wrote back: "With which of them should I begin?" He said: "If I told you to cut down the trees, you would ask me: 'With which type of them should I begin?'" And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "If I order you to give so-and-so a sheep, you ask me: 'Is it a ewe or a goat?' If I clarify, you say: 'Male or female?' If I inform you, you say: 'Black or white?' So when I order you to do something, do not argue with me."

It is said in a hadith: "The greatest of people in sin is the one who asks about something that was not forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking." [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him.]]

﴿Indeed the cows have become similar to us (inna al-baqara tashābaha ʿalaynā)﴾, that is, the cow described with the color and yellowness is numerous, so it became confused for us which one to slaughter. It is read "tashābah" meaning "tatashābah," by dropping the taa and assimilating it into the shin, and also "tashābahat," "mutashābihah," and "mutashābih." Muhammad dhū al-Shāmah read: ﴿inna al-bāqara yushābihu﴾, with a yaa and a shaddah. It has come in a hadith: "If they had not made the exception, I would not have made clear to them the last of eternity," meaning, if they had not said "if God wills." [[I say: Ibn Jarir reported it through Ibn Jurayj, raised. It is mu'dal (a chain with two or more consecutive omissions).]] The meaning is: we are indeed guided to the cow intended for slaughter, or to what was hidden from us regarding the matter of the killer.

﴿Not a tamed one (lā dhalūl)﴾ is an adjective of "baqara" in the sense of "a cow that is not tame," meaning it has not been trained for plowing and tilling the land, nor is it one of the water-carrying camels by which irrigation for the fields is done. The first "lā" is for negation, and the second is redundant to emphasize the first, because the meaning is: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." The two verbs are attributes of "dhalūl," as if it were said: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read: "lā dhalūl," meaning "lā dhalūl hunāka," that is, there, where she is, and it is a negation of her being tame and of her being described as tame, so one says: "She is tame." A similar expression is your saying: "I passed by people who are not stingy or cowardly," meaning among them, or where they are.

"Tusqā" is read with a ḍamma on the tā, from "asqā" (to water). [[*"Or a camel left aside, whose back is bare, its offspring show her (its) saddle-cloth,*
*her owner has neither made the pilgrimage in the world nor performed the minor pilgrimage."* Sibawayh recited it. It is said: "aʿbarat al-shāh fa-hiya muʿabbarah" when the sheep's wool has grown much because it was left a year without shearing. So the "back left aside" is the one left from shearing, so its wool grows much, or because it has no wool, so it is not sheared. Perhaps the meaning here is the one left from being loaded upon. It is said: "al-munjarid al-shaʿr" (smooth-haired). "Nabā ʿanhu yanbū" means he deviated. "Anbaytuhu" means I made him deviate and I drove him away. So what is here means it prevents others from riding its saddle-cloth. And the apparent statement of some: it is said "nabā yanbī," like "ramā yarmī," when it deviates, and what is here is from it, that is, it shies away from its saddle-cloth, because it is what lies beside the hide. "Rabbuhu" with the vowel shortened for meter means "its owner." The meaning is: it is a camel left from work, so it is wild, shying away from the rider, because it has never traveled at all, so that its owner has not made the pilgrimage nor the minor pilgrimage. And the apparent statement of some is that "rabbuhu" is the "rabb" which is a preposition, making it govern the pronoun without a specifier, because its referent is anticipated, and indicating the confirmation of the negation metaphorically for the sense of multiplicity, and it is a parenthetical between the two conjoined items. The attribution of the two verbs to the pronoun of the camel is a rational metaphor, because it is one of the instruments of pilgrimage and the minor pilgrimage. The one who said this explained it as meaning that it is bare-backed, shying away from its saddle-cloth because of the sores from many journeys, that it did not travel for pilgrimage nor for the minor pilgrimage, but traveled to enemies. If its meaning is as stated above, it would be permissible. So the meaning is that it is a wild camel that has not been ridden and has not traveled at all, so that it did not travel for pilgrimage or the minor pilgrimage, and this is evident.]]

Or "musallamah" (sound), meaning "saved by God from defects," or "free from work," which its owners left alone. Or "mukhlisat al-lawn," from "sallama lahu kadhā" (it was pure for him) when it was pure for him, with no other color mixed into its yellowness, so it is yellow all over, including its horns and hooves. Originally, "shiyah" is a verbal noun: "shāhā yashūhā shiyatan" when he mixed its color with another color, and from it comes "thawr mūshā al-qawāʾim" (a bull with marked legs).

﴿You have now brought the truth (jiʾta bi-al-ḥaqq)﴾, that is, you have brought the reality of the description of the cow, and no difficulty remained regarding its matter. ﴿So they slaughtered her (fadhbaḥūhā)﴾, meaning they obtained the cow that combined all these attributes and slaughtered her. His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it (wa mā kādū yafʿalūn)﴾ is a rebuke for their extreme questioning and a reproach for their delay, and that because of their excessive lengthening and abundant investigation, they almost did not slaughter it, and their questions almost never ended, and the thread of their elaboration and their deep probing almost never broke. It is said: they almost did not slaughter it because of its high price. It is said: because of fear of exposure when the killer was revealed.

It is related that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. The calf grew and became one of the most beautiful and fattest cows. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for its hide filled with gold. At that time the cow was worth three dinars, and they had been searching for the described cow for forty years. [[The word "al-ghīḍah" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ means the thicket, the reed-bed where water gathers and trees grow. (ʿ)]]

If you say: the cow that was addressed by the command was a cow of the general kind, without being specified, and then it became specified by a color and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one. What then of the first command? I say: it was abrogated (mansūkhan) because the ruling shifted to the specified cow, and abrogation before the act is permissible. Moreover, the address, because of its vagueness, included this described cow just as it included others. And if the slaughter had fallen upon it by the ruling of the address before specification, it would have been compliance with it, so likewise if it falls upon it after specification.

﴿And when you killed a soul (wa idh qataltum nafsan)﴾: the group was addressed because the killing was among them. ﴿Then you disputed about it (fa-idāraʾtum fīhā)﴾, meaning you differed and quarreled regarding its matter, because those who dispute push one another away (yadraʾu), that is, they repel and crowd one another. Or you pushed one another, meaning the throwing of the slain man was cast by some of you upon others, so the one upon whom it was cast pushed back the one who cast it. Or because throwing in itself is a push. Or one of you pushed the other away from innocence and accused him.

﴿And God is the one who brings out (mukhrijun) what you were hiding﴾, that is, He will certainly reveal what you concealed of the matter of the killing and will not leave it hidden. If you say: how can "mukhrij" govern when it has the sense of the past? I say: the past tense has been narrated to indicate the time of the dispute, just as the present tense was narrated in His saying: ﴿stretching out his two forearms (bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi)﴾. This sentence is a parenthesis between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which are ﴿then you disputed﴾ and ﴿so We said﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿strike him (iḍribūhu)﴾ refers either to the soul, and the masculine is used with the interpretation of "person" and "human," or it refers to the slain man, because of what is indicated by His saying: ﴿what you were hiding﴾.

﴿With part of it (biba'ḍihā)﴾: with part of the cow. There is disagreement about the part with which he was struck. It was said: its tongue. It was said: its right thigh. It was said: its tail-bone (ʿajb). It was said: the bone that adjoins the cartilage, which is the root of the ear. It was said: the ear. It was said: the piece between the shoulders. The meaning is: they struck him, so he came to life, and that was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿thus God gives life to the dead﴾.

It is related that when they struck him, he stood up by God's permission, his veins gushing blood, and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his nephews. Then he fell dead. The two were seized and killed, and no killer inherited anything after that.

﴿Thus God gives life to the dead (kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā)﴾: this may be an address to those who witnessed the living of the slain man, meaning "We said to them: thus God will give life to the dead on the Day of Resurrection." ﴿And He shows you His signs (wa yurīkum āyātihi)﴾, that is, His proofs that He is capable of everything, ﴿so that you may understand (la'allakum taʿqilūn)﴾.

...ye (you) reason according to the dictates of your intellects. [Indeed,] whoever is able to give life to one soul is able to give life to all souls, since there is no specificity [in that power], so that you do not deny the Resurrection. Alternatively, it may be an address to the deniers in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If you say: "Why did He not give him life immediately, and why did He make the slaughtering of the cow and striking [the corpse] with a part of it a condition for his revival?" I say: There are wisdoms and benefits in causes and conditions. This condition was imposed because of the nearness to God (taqarrub) and the performance of obligations (taklif) and the gaining of reward in slaughtering the cow, and because of the indication of the excellence of placing an act of devotion before the request, and because of the kindness (lutf) to them in the severity imposed on them for their severity [in questioning]; and for others, [it teaches] avoiding severity and hastening to comply with the commands of God Exalted, and carrying them out immediately without investigation and excessive questioning; and [it benefits] the orphan through profitable trade; and it shows the blessing of goodness to parents, and compassion for children; and [it shows] the ignorance of the one who mocks at what he does not know the reality of and does not comprehend its truth, from the words of the wise; and it clarifies that it is the right of one who draws near to his Lord to be meticulous (yatanawwaq) in choosing what he draws near with, and to choose [an animal that is] young in age, not aged or weak, of good color, free from defects, pleasing to the one who looks at it, and that its price be expensive. This is as is narrated about ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) that he sacrificed a noble she-camel (najībah) for three hundred dinars.[[Abu Dawud related it from the narration of al-Jahm ibn al-Jarud, from Salim, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) gifted a noble she-camel, and was offered for it three hundred dinars. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I sell it and buy with its price a sacrificial camel?' He said: 'No, slaughter it as it is.'"]] And [it shows] that an addition to the address is an abrogation (naskh) of it, and that abrogation before the act is permissible, even though it is not permissible before the time of the act and its possibility, since that would lead to a change of mind (bada'). And so that it may be known, by what was commanded of touching the dead with the dead and the life occurring after it, that the effective cause is the Causer, not the means, because it is not conceivable that life could be generated from the two deaths present in the two bodies.

If you say: "Why was the story not related in its order? It would have been proper for the mention of the slain man and the striking with a part of the cow to precede the command to slaughter it, and to say: 'And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it'?" I say: Every story of the Children of Israel was related only to enumerate the transgressions that occurred from them, and to rebuke them for them, and for the great signs that were renewed among them. These are two stories, each of which is independent with a kind of rebuke, even though they are connected and unified. The first is to rebuke them for mockery and for not hastening to comply and what follows from that. The second is to rebuke them for killing a forbidden soul and what follows from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man only because, if it were done in reverse, it would have been one single story, and the purpose of doubling the rebuke would have been lost. And a subtle point was observed: after the second was begun as a separate story, it was connected to the first, indicating their unity by the pronoun referring to the cow, not by its explicit name, in His saying: ﴿strike him with a part of it﴾, so that it becomes clear that they are two stories as regards the rebuke and its doubling, by presenting the second as a fresh beginning while delaying it, and that they are one story by the pronoun referring back to the cow.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 67–73 (part 1 of 2):

There was a wealthy old man among the Children of Israel, and his nephews killed his son in order to inherit from him. They threw the body at the gate of a city and then came demanding the blood-money (diyah). God commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the body with a piece of it, so that he would come back to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said: "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾ That is, "Do you make us an object of mockery," or "people of mockery," or "one who is mocked," or "mockery itself," because of the extreme degree of mocking. ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because mockery in such a matter is a form of ignorance and foolishness.

It is also read as "huzu'an" with two damma (u-vowels), and as "huz'an" with a sukun on the zay, like "kufu'an" and "kufan". Hafs reads "huzuwan" with two damma and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan". Al-ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and al-liyadh (clinging for protection) come from one root.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): "Ask your Lord for us, what is it?" This is a question about its condition and description. They were amazed at a dead cow being struck with a piece of a dead man, and then he came back to life. So they asked about the description of that cow, which was extraordinary in its nature and different from ordinary cows.

Al-fariḍ means the old cow (al-musinnah), and it is said "faraḍat furuḍan, fa-hiya fāriḍ" (she became old). Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

*"By my life, you gave your guest an old she-camel,*
*led to him, which cannot stand on one leg."*

[[Khufaf ibn Nadbah, satirizing al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas for stinginess. Al-fāriḍ is an old she-camel that is led to him, meaning she is not ridden but needs someone to strike her and drive her from behind. "Cannot stand on one leg" means she has no strong leg to rely on for standing.]]

It seems she was called fāriḍ because she had reached the end of her age, having "cut off" (faraḍat) her teeth and reached their final stage. Al-bikr means the young one.

Al-ʿawān means the middle-aged one. The poet said:

*"Graceful ones among virgins and matrons."*

[[*"Caravans of women I used to know long ago,*
*and they, when dwelling, were not dark-skinned,*
*chaste in the faces, high-lying in the veils,*
*graceful, between virgins and matrons."*
By al-Ṭirmāḥ. Al-ẓaʿāʾin are women in howdahs. Al-ḍaʿāʾin (with ḍād) are mounts. Al-ḍaghāʾin (with ghayn) are plural of ḍaghīnah, meaning hatred, inclination, or crookedness; ḍaghanahu means you took him into your embrace. A ḍāghin horse is one that does not give its speed. A ḍāt ḍaghn she-camel is one longing for her homeland. A ḍāt ḍaghn woman loves someone other than her husband. Al-juun (with a ḍamma) is the plural of jawāʾ, meaning black.
Al-ḥaṣān (with a fatḥa) is the chaste one. Al-naqb is the plural of niqāb, like kutub and kitāb. Al-ʿawn originally has a ḍamma on the waw, as the plural of ʿawān, which means the middle, that is, the middle of women and animals, and it was lightened by a sukun. He says: those women are "ẓaʿāʾin," meaning travelers, the journey changed their color, and I used to know them long ago, when they were at home, not dark, chaste in their faces, and when they are protected they are all protected by habit. Al-aʿāli is an adjective for al-naqb or al-mawāḍiʿ, and this applies only to women, as you see. Some narrators reported "ḍaghāʾin" instead of "ẓaʿāʾin," but it is probably a distortion. They are graceful, moving among young virgins and middle-aged women.]]

It is said that "ʿawwanat" (she became middle-aged) is used. [[Al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) says: one says of her "ʿawwanat al-mar'ah taʿwīnan, wa ʿānat taʿūnu ʿawnan." (ʿ)]]

If you say: "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, how is it permitted to be followed by "dhālika" (that)? I say: because it has the sense of two things, since it refers to what was mentioned, the old cow and the young one. If you say: how is it permitted to refer with it to two feminine things, when it is only used to point to a single masculine thing? I say: this is permitted by interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned and what preceded, for brevity in speech, just as they used "faʿala" as a substitute for many actions mentioned before it. You say to a man: "How good what you did was!", and he has mentioned many actions and a long story, just as you say to him: "How good that is!" The pronoun may also be used in the same way as a demonstrative. Abu ʿUbaydah said: I said to Ruʾbah about his verse:

*"In it are lines of black and white,*
*as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy."*

[[Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj describes a wild cow, and it was said a horse, and it was said horses, in which is the color black and the color white, and it is narrated as "min bayāḍ wa bāq." Perhaps the white is white mixed with dust, as if it is "the mentioned one or the combination of both," like the pattern of leprosy on the skin. Or it means while being on the skin, the pattern of leprosy, that is, its marking of white mixed with dullness arising from leprosy, a disease by which the color of the skin changes. It is related that Abu ʿUbaydah said to him: if you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā"; if you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā." He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," (as if that). So he made the pronoun behave like a demonstrative in the correctness of pointing with the singular to the plural, by interpreting it as the thing mentioned or similar.]]

If you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā" (as if they). If you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā" (as if they two). He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," you fool! What makes it good is that the demonstratives in their dual, plural and feminine forms are not literal, and the same is true for relative pronouns. That is why "alladhī" was used to mean the plural, as in ﴿what you are commanded (mā tu'maruna)﴾, that is, what you are commanded to do, meaning "tu'maruna bihi" (you are commanded with it), from the saying: ﴿I commanded you the good (amartuka al-khayr)﴾ or ﴿their command (amruhum)﴾, meaning "ma'murukum" (what is commanded to you), calling the object by the verbal noun, like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the striking of the ruler).

Al-fuqūʿ is the most intense yellow and its purest. It is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqiʿ wa wāris" (intensely yellow and dark yellow), just as one says "aswad ḥālik wa ḥānik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqiq wa lahiq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānī wa dhurayqī" (intensely red), "akhḍar nāḍir wa mudhāmmim" (intensely green), "awraq khaṭbānī wa azmak rudānī" (grayish-green). If you say: "fāqiʿ" here is a predicate of the color, so it is not an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," I say: it is not a predicate of the color; it is an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," except that the color is raised by it like the subject, and the color belongs to it and is connected to it, so there is no difference between your saying "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa" and "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿ lawnuhā" (its color is intensely yellow). If you say: why not say "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa," and what is the benefit of mentioning the color? I say: the benefit is emphasis, because "lawn" is a name for the form, and it is yellowness. So it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow is its yellowness," like your saying "jadda jadduhu" (his grandfather is truly his grandfather) and "junūnuka majnūn" (your madness is madness).

It is related from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you that the light of the sun comes out of its skin. Joy is a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining a benefit or expecting it. It is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever wears yellow sandals, his anxiety decreases." [[It is a statement attributed to ʿAlī (mawqūf) which I have not found. But al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Khaṭīb reported it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Whoever wears yellow sandals will not cease to be in joy as long as he wears them." Ibn Abi Hatim said: I asked my father about it, and he said: it is a lie, fabricated.]] because of the statement of God Most High: ﴿it pleases the observers (tasurru al-nāẓirīn)﴾. It is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā" (yellow, intensely its color), he said: "black, intensely black." Perhaps it is borrowed from the description of camels, because their blackness is overlaid with yellowness. By this was explained the verse: ﴿camels, yellow (jimālatun ṣufrun)﴾. Al-Aʿshā said:

*"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*

[[*"Qays, the best of deeds, father of*
*Abu al-Ashʿath, whose echoes have become dispersed in the roads.*
*Every year he gives me generously from his camels*
*at the time of the birth of the sheep or the noble camel.*
*Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*
By al-Aʿshā, about Abu al-Ashʿath ibn Qays. Al-fiʿāl (with a fatḥa) means good deeds. Al-aṣdāʾ is the plural of ṣadā, which is the male owl. The Arabs used to claim that the bones of a slain person's head turn into an owl that cries "Avenge me!" until his blood is avenged. Shuʿūb is the name for death, and it is possible it is the plural of shiʿb meaning road, that is, they became scattered on the roads, which is a metaphor for his killing. The plural is for honor or is considered as such. Al-juumūm is the plural of jamm (with a triple vowel on the first letter), meaning many. Al-najīb is the noble one among horses and camels. Al-rikāb are mounts. "Hunna" (they) refers to the mounts; "ṣufr" is the plural of aṣfar or ṣafrāʾ; "their offspring like raisins" means their dark color predominates. The yellowness here means blackness overlaid with yellowness, because this is the most prized color of camels among them.]]

﴿What is it (mā hiya)?﴾ is a second repetition of the question about its condition and description, and an additional inquiry, so that they might gain more clarity regarding its description.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had taken any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they were strict, so God was strict with them, and excessive questioning is a bad omen." [[Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Abi Hatim all from the chain of al-Ḥasan, from Abu Rafiʿ, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain contains ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr, who is weak. Al-Ṭabarī has it as a statement of Ibn ʿAbbās (mawqūf), and from a statement of Abu al-ʿĀliyah, except the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen," which is not in the raised or the stopped version. I say: the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen" is from the statement of al-Zamakhsharī.]]

And it is related from one of the caliphs that he wrote to his agent to go to a people and cut down their trees and demolish their houses. He wrote back: "With which of them should I begin?" He said: "If I told you to cut down the trees, you would ask me: 'With which type of them should I begin?'" And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "If I order you to give so-and-so a sheep, you ask me: 'Is it a ewe or a goat?' If I clarify, you say: 'Male or female?' If I inform you, you say: 'Black or white?' So when I order you to do something, do not argue with me."

It is said in a hadith: "The greatest of people in sin is the one who asks about something that was not forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking." [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him.]]

﴿Indeed the cows have become similar to us (inna al-baqara tashābaha ʿalaynā)﴾, that is, the cow described with the color and yellowness is numerous, so it became confused for us which one to slaughter. It is read "tashābah" meaning "tatashābah," by dropping the taa and assimilating it into the shin, and also "tashābahat," "mutashābihah," and "mutashābih." Muhammad dhū al-Shāmah read: ﴿inna al-bāqara yushābihu﴾, with a yaa and a shaddah. It has come in a hadith: "If they had not made the exception, I would not have made clear to them the last of eternity," meaning, if they had not said "if God wills." [[I say: Ibn Jarir reported it through Ibn Jurayj, raised. It is mu'dal (a chain with two or more consecutive omissions).]] The meaning is: we are indeed guided to the cow intended for slaughter, or to what was hidden from us regarding the matter of the killer.

﴿Not a tamed one (lā dhalūl)﴾ is an adjective of "baqara" in the sense of "a cow that is not tame," meaning it has not been trained for plowing and tilling the land, nor is it one of the water-carrying camels by which irrigation for the fields is done. The first "lā" is for negation, and the second is redundant to emphasize the first, because the meaning is: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." The two verbs are attributes of "dhalūl," as if it were said: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read: "lā dhalūl," meaning "lā dhalūl hunāka," that is, there, where she is, and it is a negation of her being tame and of her being described as tame, so one says: "She is tame." A similar expression is your saying: "I passed by people who are not stingy or cowardly," meaning among them, or where they are.

"Tusqā" is read with a ḍamma on the tā, from "asqā" (to water). [[*"Or a camel left aside, whose back is bare, its offspring show her (its) saddle-cloth,*
*her owner has neither made the pilgrimage in the world nor performed the minor pilgrimage."* Sibawayh recited it. It is said: "aʿbarat al-shāh fa-hiya muʿabbarah" when the sheep's wool has grown much because it was left a year without shearing. So the "back left aside" is the one left from shearing, so its wool grows much, or because it has no wool, so it is not sheared. Perhaps the meaning here is the one left from being loaded upon. It is said: "al-munjarid al-shaʿr" (smooth-haired). "Nabā ʿanhu yanbū" means he deviated. "Anbaytuhu" means I made him deviate and I drove him away. So what is here means it prevents others from riding its saddle-cloth. And the apparent statement of some: it is said "nabā yanbī," like "ramā yarmī," when it deviates, and what is here is from it, that is, it shies away from its saddle-cloth, because it is what lies beside the hide. "Rabbuhu" with the vowel shortened for meter means "its owner." The meaning is: it is a camel left from work, so it is wild, shying away from the rider, because it has never traveled at all, so that its owner has not made the pilgrimage nor the minor pilgrimage. And the apparent statement of some is that "rabbuhu" is the "rabb" which is a preposition, making it govern the pronoun without a specifier, because its referent is anticipated, and indicating the confirmation of the negation metaphorically for the sense of multiplicity, and it is a parenthetical between the two conjoined items. The attribution of the two verbs to the pronoun of the camel is a rational metaphor, because it is one of the instruments of pilgrimage and the minor pilgrimage. The one who said this explained it as meaning that it is bare-backed, shying away from its saddle-cloth because of the sores from many journeys, that it did not travel for pilgrimage nor for the minor pilgrimage, but traveled to enemies. If its meaning is as stated above, it would be permissible. So the meaning is that it is a wild camel that has not been ridden and has not traveled at all, so that it did not travel for pilgrimage or the minor pilgrimage, and this is evident.]]

Or "musallamah" (sound), meaning "saved by God from defects," or "free from work," which its owners left alone. Or "mukhlisat al-lawn," from "sallama lahu kadhā" (it was pure for him) when it was pure for him, with no other color mixed into its yellowness, so it is yellow all over, including its horns and hooves. Originally, "shiyah" is a verbal noun: "shāhā yashūhā shiyatan" when he mixed its color with another color, and from it comes "thawr mūshā al-qawāʾim" (a bull with marked legs).

﴿You have now brought the truth (jiʾta bi-al-ḥaqq)﴾, that is, you have brought the reality of the description of the cow, and no difficulty remained regarding its matter. ﴿So they slaughtered her (fadhbaḥūhā)﴾, meaning they obtained the cow that combined all these attributes and slaughtered her. His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it (wa mā kādū yafʿalūn)﴾ is a rebuke for their extreme questioning and a reproach for their delay, and that because of their excessive lengthening and abundant investigation, they almost did not slaughter it, and their questions almost never ended, and the thread of their elaboration and their deep probing almost never broke. It is said: they almost did not slaughter it because of its high price. It is said: because of fear of exposure when the killer was revealed.

It is related that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. The calf grew and became one of the most beautiful and fattest cows. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for its hide filled with gold. At that time the cow was worth three dinars, and they had been searching for the described cow for forty years. [[The word "al-ghīḍah" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ means the thicket, the reed-bed where water gathers and trees grow. (ʿ)]]

If you say: the cow that was addressed by the command was a cow of the general kind, without being specified, and then it became specified by a color and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one. What then of the first command? I say: it was abrogated (mansūkhan) because the ruling shifted to the specified cow, and abrogation before the act is permissible. Moreover, the address, because of its vagueness, included this described cow just as it included others. And if the slaughter had fallen upon it by the ruling of the address before specification, it would have been compliance with it, so likewise if it falls upon it after specification.

﴿And when you killed a soul (wa idh qataltum nafsan)﴾: the group was addressed because the killing was among them. ﴿Then you disputed about it (fa-idāraʾtum fīhā)﴾, meaning you differed and quarreled regarding its matter, because those who dispute push one another away (yadraʾu), that is, they repel and crowd one another. Or you pushed one another, meaning the throwing of the slain man was cast by some of you upon others, so the one upon whom it was cast pushed back the one who cast it. Or because throwing in itself is a push. Or one of you pushed the other away from innocence and accused him.

﴿And God is the one who brings out (mukhrijun) what you were hiding﴾, that is, He will certainly reveal what you concealed of the matter of the killing and will not leave it hidden. If you say: how can "mukhrij" govern when it has the sense of the past? I say: the past tense has been narrated to indicate the time of the dispute, just as the present tense was narrated in His saying: ﴿stretching out his two forearms (bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi)﴾. This sentence is a parenthesis between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which are ﴿then you disputed﴾ and ﴿so We said﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿strike him (iḍribūhu)﴾ refers either to the soul, and the masculine is used with the interpretation of "person" and "human," or it refers to the slain man, because of what is indicated by His saying: ﴿what you were hiding﴾.

﴿With part of it (biba'ḍihā)﴾: with part of the cow. There is disagreement about the part with which he was struck. It was said: its tongue. It was said: its right thigh. It was said: its tail-bone (ʿajb). It was said: the bone that adjoins the cartilage, which is the root of the ear. It was said: the ear. It was said: the piece between the shoulders. The meaning is: they struck him, so he came to life, and that was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿thus God gives life to the dead﴾.

It is related that when they struck him, he stood up by God's permission, his veins gushing blood, and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his nephews. Then he fell dead. The two were seized and killed, and no killer inherited anything after that.

﴿Thus God gives life to the dead (kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā)﴾: this may be an address to those who witnessed the living of the slain man, meaning "We said to them: thus God will give life to the dead on the Day of Resurrection." ﴿And He shows you His signs (wa yurīkum āyātihi)﴾, that is, His proofs that He is capable of everything, ﴿so that you may understand (la'allakum taʿqilūn)﴾.

...ye (you) reason according to the dictates of your intellects. [Indeed,] whoever is able to give life to one soul is able to give life to all souls, since there is no specificity [in that power], so that you do not deny the Resurrection. Alternatively, it may be an address to the deniers in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If you say: "Why did He not give him life immediately, and why did He make the slaughtering of the cow and striking [the corpse] with a part of it a condition for his revival?" I say: There are wisdoms and benefits in causes and conditions. This condition was imposed because of the nearness to God (taqarrub) and the performance of obligations (taklif) and the gaining of reward in slaughtering the cow, and because of the indication of the excellence of placing an act of devotion before the request, and because of the kindness (lutf) to them in the severity imposed on them for their severity [in questioning]; and for others, [it teaches] avoiding severity and hastening to comply with the commands of God Exalted, and carrying them out immediately without investigation and excessive questioning; and [it benefits] the orphan through profitable trade; and it shows the blessing of goodness to parents, and compassion for children; and [it shows] the ignorance of the one who mocks at what he does not know the reality of and does not comprehend its truth, from the words of the wise; and it clarifies that it is the right of one who draws near to his Lord to be meticulous (yatanawwaq) in choosing what he draws near with, and to choose [an animal that is] young in age, not aged or weak, of good color, free from defects, pleasing to the one who looks at it, and that its price be expensive. This is as is narrated about ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) that he sacrificed a noble she-camel (najībah) for three hundred dinars.[[Abu Dawud related it from the narration of al-Jahm ibn al-Jarud, from Salim, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) gifted a noble she-camel, and was offered for it three hundred dinars. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I sell it and buy with its price a sacrificial camel?' He said: 'No, slaughter it as it is.'"]] And [it shows] that an addition to the address is an abrogation (naskh) of it, and that abrogation before the act is permissible, even though it is not permissible before the time of the act and its possibility, since that would lead to a change of mind (bada'). And so that it may be known, by what was commanded of touching the dead with the dead and the life occurring after it, that the effective cause is the Causer, not the means, because it is not conceivable that life could be generated from the two deaths present in the two bodies.

If you say: "Why was the story not related in its order? It would have been proper for the mention of the slain man and the striking with a part of the cow to precede the command to slaughter it, and to say: 'And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it'?" I say: Every story of the Children of Israel was related only to enumerate the transgressions that occurred from them, and to rebuke them for them, and for the great signs that were renewed among them. These are two stories, each of which is independent with a kind of rebuke, even though they are connected and unified. The first is to rebuke them for mockery and for not hastening to comply and what follows from that. The second is to rebuke them for killing a forbidden soul and what follows from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man only because, if it were done in reverse, it would have been one single story, and the purpose of doubling the rebuke would have been lost. And a subtle point was observed: after the second was begun as a separate story, it was connected to the first, indicating their unity by the pronoun referring to the cow, not by its explicit name, in His saying: ﴿strike him with a part of it﴾, so that it becomes clear that they are two stories as regards the rebuke and its doubling, by presenting the second as a fresh beginning while delaying it, and that they are one story by the pronoun referring back to the cow.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 67–73 (part 1 of 2):

There was a wealthy old man among the Children of Israel, and his nephews killed his son in order to inherit from him. They threw the body at the gate of a city and then came demanding the blood-money (diyah). God commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the body with a piece of it, so that he would come back to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said: "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾ That is, "Do you make us an object of mockery," or "people of mockery," or "one who is mocked," or "mockery itself," because of the extreme degree of mocking. ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because mockery in such a matter is a form of ignorance and foolishness.

It is also read as "huzu'an" with two damma (u-vowels), and as "huz'an" with a sukun on the zay, like "kufu'an" and "kufan". Hafs reads "huzuwan" with two damma and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan". Al-ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and al-liyadh (clinging for protection) come from one root.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): "Ask your Lord for us, what is it?" This is a question about its condition and description. They were amazed at a dead cow being struck with a piece of a dead man, and then he came back to life. So they asked about the description of that cow, which was extraordinary in its nature and different from ordinary cows.

Al-fariḍ means the old cow (al-musinnah), and it is said "faraḍat furuḍan, fa-hiya fāriḍ" (she became old). Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

*"By my life, you gave your guest an old she-camel,*
*led to him, which cannot stand on one leg."*

[[Khufaf ibn Nadbah, satirizing al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas for stinginess. Al-fāriḍ is an old she-camel that is led to him, meaning she is not ridden but needs someone to strike her and drive her from behind. "Cannot stand on one leg" means she has no strong leg to rely on for standing.]]

It seems she was called fāriḍ because she had reached the end of her age, having "cut off" (faraḍat) her teeth and reached their final stage. Al-bikr means the young one.

Al-ʿawān means the middle-aged one. The poet said:

*"Graceful ones among virgins and matrons."*

[[*"Caravans of women I used to know long ago,*
*and they, when dwelling, were not dark-skinned,*
*chaste in the faces, high-lying in the veils,*
*graceful, between virgins and matrons."*
By al-Ṭirmāḥ. Al-ẓaʿāʾin are women in howdahs. Al-ḍaʿāʾin (with ḍād) are mounts. Al-ḍaghāʾin (with ghayn) are plural of ḍaghīnah, meaning hatred, inclination, or crookedness; ḍaghanahu means you took him into your embrace. A ḍāghin horse is one that does not give its speed. A ḍāt ḍaghn she-camel is one longing for her homeland. A ḍāt ḍaghn woman loves someone other than her husband. Al-juun (with a ḍamma) is the plural of jawāʾ, meaning black.
Al-ḥaṣān (with a fatḥa) is the chaste one. Al-naqb is the plural of niqāb, like kutub and kitāb. Al-ʿawn originally has a ḍamma on the waw, as the plural of ʿawān, which means the middle, that is, the middle of women and animals, and it was lightened by a sukun. He says: those women are "ẓaʿāʾin," meaning travelers, the journey changed their color, and I used to know them long ago, when they were at home, not dark, chaste in their faces, and when they are protected they are all protected by habit. Al-aʿāli is an adjective for al-naqb or al-mawāḍiʿ, and this applies only to women, as you see. Some narrators reported "ḍaghāʾin" instead of "ẓaʿāʾin," but it is probably a distortion. They are graceful, moving among young virgins and middle-aged women.]]

It is said that "ʿawwanat" (she became middle-aged) is used. [[Al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) says: one says of her "ʿawwanat al-mar'ah taʿwīnan, wa ʿānat taʿūnu ʿawnan." (ʿ)]]

If you say: "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, how is it permitted to be followed by "dhālika" (that)? I say: because it has the sense of two things, since it refers to what was mentioned, the old cow and the young one. If you say: how is it permitted to refer with it to two feminine things, when it is only used to point to a single masculine thing? I say: this is permitted by interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned and what preceded, for brevity in speech, just as they used "faʿala" as a substitute for many actions mentioned before it. You say to a man: "How good what you did was!", and he has mentioned many actions and a long story, just as you say to him: "How good that is!" The pronoun may also be used in the same way as a demonstrative. Abu ʿUbaydah said: I said to Ruʾbah about his verse:

*"In it are lines of black and white,*
*as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy."*

[[Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj describes a wild cow, and it was said a horse, and it was said horses, in which is the color black and the color white, and it is narrated as "min bayāḍ wa bāq." Perhaps the white is white mixed with dust, as if it is "the mentioned one or the combination of both," like the pattern of leprosy on the skin. Or it means while being on the skin, the pattern of leprosy, that is, its marking of white mixed with dullness arising from leprosy, a disease by which the color of the skin changes. It is related that Abu ʿUbaydah said to him: if you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā"; if you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā." He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," (as if that). So he made the pronoun behave like a demonstrative in the correctness of pointing with the singular to the plural, by interpreting it as the thing mentioned or similar.]]

If you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā" (as if they). If you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā" (as if they two). He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," you fool! What makes it good is that the demonstratives in their dual, plural and feminine forms are not literal, and the same is true for relative pronouns. That is why "alladhī" was used to mean the plural, as in ﴿what you are commanded (mā tu'maruna)﴾, that is, what you are commanded to do, meaning "tu'maruna bihi" (you are commanded with it), from the saying: ﴿I commanded you the good (amartuka al-khayr)﴾ or ﴿their command (amruhum)﴾, meaning "ma'murukum" (what is commanded to you), calling the object by the verbal noun, like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the striking of the ruler).

Al-fuqūʿ is the most intense yellow and its purest. It is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqiʿ wa wāris" (intensely yellow and dark yellow), just as one says "aswad ḥālik wa ḥānik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqiq wa lahiq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānī wa dhurayqī" (intensely red), "akhḍar nāḍir wa mudhāmmim" (intensely green), "awraq khaṭbānī wa azmak rudānī" (grayish-green). If you say: "fāqiʿ" here is a predicate of the color, so it is not an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," I say: it is not a predicate of the color; it is an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," except that the color is raised by it like the subject, and the color belongs to it and is connected to it, so there is no difference between your saying "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa" and "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿ lawnuhā" (its color is intensely yellow). If you say: why not say "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa," and what is the benefit of mentioning the color? I say: the benefit is emphasis, because "lawn" is a name for the form, and it is yellowness. So it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow is its yellowness," like your saying "jadda jadduhu" (his grandfather is truly his grandfather) and "junūnuka majnūn" (your madness is madness).

It is related from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you that the light of the sun comes out of its skin. Joy is a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining a benefit or expecting it. It is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever wears yellow sandals, his anxiety decreases." [[It is a statement attributed to ʿAlī (mawqūf) which I have not found.
