﴿Not a tamed one (lā dhalūl)﴾ is an adjective of "baqara" in the sense of "a cow that is not tame," meaning it has not been trained for plowing and tilling the land, nor is it one of the water-carrying camels by which irrigation for the fields is done. The first "lā" is for negation, and the second is redundant to emphasize the first, because the meaning is: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." The two verbs are attributes of "dhalūl," as if it were said: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read: "lā dhalūl," meaning "lā dhalūl hunāka," that is, there, where she is, and it is a negation of her being tame and of her being described as tame, so one says: "She is tame." A similar expression is your saying: "I passed by people who are not stingy or cowardly," meaning among them, or where they are.

"Tusqā" is read with a ḍamma on the tā, from "asqā" (to water). [[*"Or a camel left aside, whose back is bare, its offspring show her (its) saddle-cloth,*
*her owner has neither made the pilgrimage in the world nor performed the minor pilgrimage."* Sibawayh recited it. It is said: "aʿbarat al-shāh fa-hiya muʿabbarah" when the sheep's wool has grown much because it was left a year without shearing. So the "back left aside" is the one left from shearing, so its wool grows much, or because it has no wool, so it is not sheared. Perhaps the meaning here is the one left from being loaded upon. It is said: "al-munjarid al-shaʿr" (smooth-haired). "Nabā ʿanhu yanbū" means he deviated. "Anbaytuhu" means I made him deviate and I drove him away. So what is here means it prevents others from riding its saddle-cloth. And the apparent statement of some: it is said "nabā yanbī," like "ramā yarmī," when it deviates, and what is here is from it, that is, it shies away from its saddle-cloth, because it is what lies beside the hide. "Rabbuhu" with the vowel shortened for meter means "its owner." The meaning is: it is a camel left from work, so it is wild, shying away from the rider, because it has never traveled at all, so that its owner has not made the pilgrimage nor the minor pilgrimage. And the apparent statement of some is that "rabbuhu" is the "rabb" which is a preposition, making it govern the pronoun without a specifier, because its referent is anticipated, and indicating the confirmation of the negation metaphorically for the sense of multiplicity, and it is a parenthetical between the two conjoined items. The attribution of the two verbs to the pronoun of the camel is a rational metaphor, because it is one of the instruments of pilgrimage and the minor pilgrimage. The one who said this explained it as meaning that it is bare-backed, shying away from its saddle-cloth because of the sores from many journeys, that it did not travel for pilgrimage nor for the minor pilgrimage, but traveled to enemies. If its meaning is as stated above, it would be permissible. So the meaning is that it is a wild camel that has not been ridden and has not traveled at all, so that it did not travel for pilgrimage or the minor pilgrimage, and this is evident.]]

Or "musallamah" (sound), meaning "saved by God from defects," or "free from work," which its owners left alone. Or "mukhlisat al-lawn," from "sallama lahu kadhā" (it was pure for him) when it was pure for him, with no other color mixed into its yellowness, so it is yellow all over, including its horns and hooves. Originally, "shiyah" is a verbal noun: "shāhā yashūhā shiyatan" when he mixed its color with another color, and from it comes "thawr mūshā al-qawāʾim" (a bull with marked legs).

﴿You have now brought the truth (jiʾta bi-al-ḥaqq)﴾, that is, you have brought the reality of the description of the cow, and no difficulty remained regarding its matter. ﴿So they slaughtered her (fadhbaḥūhā)﴾, meaning they obtained the cow that combined all these attributes and slaughtered her. His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it (wa mā kādū yafʿalūn)﴾ is a rebuke for their extreme questioning and a reproach for their delay, and that because of their excessive lengthening and abundant investigation, they almost did not slaughter it, and their questions almost never ended, and the thread of their elaboration and their deep probing almost never broke. It is said: they almost did not slaughter it because of its high price. It is said: because of fear of exposure when the killer was revealed.

It is related that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. The calf grew and became one of the most beautiful and fattest cows. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for its hide filled with gold. At that time the cow was worth three dinars, and they had been searching for the described cow for forty years. [[The word "al-ghīḍah" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ means the thicket, the reed-bed where water gathers and trees grow. (ʿ)]]

If you say: the cow that was addressed by the command was a cow of the general kind, without being specified, and then it became specified by a color and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one. What then of the first command? I say: it was abrogated (mansūkhan) because the ruling shifted to the specified cow, and abrogation before the act is permissible. Moreover, the address, because of its vagueness, included this described cow just as it included others. And if the slaughter had fallen upon it by the ruling of the address before specification, it would have been compliance with it, so likewise if it falls upon it after specification.

﴿And when you killed a soul (wa idh qataltum nafsan)﴾: the group was addressed because the killing was among them. ﴿Then you disputed about it (fa-idāraʾtum fīhā)﴾, meaning you differed and quarreled regarding its matter, because those who dispute push one another away (yadraʾu), that is, they repel and crowd one another. Or you pushed one another, meaning the throwing of the slain man was cast by some of you upon others, so the one upon whom it was cast pushed back the one who cast it. Or because throwing in itself is a push. Or one of you pushed the other away from innocence and accused him.

﴿And God is the one who brings out (mukhrijun) what you were hiding﴾, that is, He will certainly reveal what you concealed of the matter of the killing and will not leave it hidden. If you say: how can "mukhrij" govern when it has the sense of the past? I say: the past tense has been narrated to indicate the time of the dispute, just as the present tense was narrated in His saying: ﴿stretching out his two forearms (bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi)﴾. This sentence is a parenthesis between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which are ﴿then you disputed﴾ and ﴿so We said﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿strike him (iḍribūhu)﴾ refers either to the soul, and the masculine is used with the interpretation of "person" and "human," or it refers to the slain man, because of what is indicated by His saying: ﴿what you were hiding﴾.

﴿With part of it (biba'ḍihā)﴾: with part of the cow. There is disagreement about the part with which he was struck. It was said: its tongue. It was said: its right thigh. It was said: its tail-bone (ʿajb). It was said: the bone that adjoins the cartilage, which is the root of the ear. It was said: the ear. It was said: the piece between the shoulders. The meaning is: they struck him, so he came to life, and that was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿thus God gives life to the dead﴾.

It is related that when they struck him, he stood up by God's permission, his veins gushing blood, and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his nephews. Then he fell dead. The two were seized and killed, and no killer inherited anything after that.

﴿Thus God gives life to the dead (kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā)﴾: this may be an address to those who witnessed the living of the slain man, meaning "We said to them: thus God will give life to the dead on the Day of Resurrection." ﴿And He shows you His signs (wa yurīkum āyātihi)﴾, that is, His proofs that He is capable of everything, ﴿so that you may understand (la'allakum taʿqilūn)﴾.

...ye (you) reason according to the dictates of your intellects. [Indeed,] whoever is able to give life to one soul is able to give life to all souls, since there is no specificity [in that power], so that you do not deny the Resurrection. Alternatively, it may be an address to the deniers in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If you say: "Why did He not give him life immediately, and why did He make the slaughtering of the cow and striking [the corpse] with a part of it a condition for his revival?" I say: There are wisdoms and benefits in causes and conditions. This condition was imposed because of the nearness to God (taqarrub) and the performance of obligations (taklif) and the gaining of reward in slaughtering the cow, and because of the indication of the excellence of placing an act of devotion before the request, and because of the kindness (lutf) to them in the severity imposed on them for their severity [in questioning]; and for others, [it teaches] avoiding severity and hastening to comply with the commands of God Exalted, and carrying them out immediately without investigation and excessive questioning; and [it benefits] the orphan through profitable trade; and it shows the blessing of goodness to parents, and compassion for children; and [it shows] the ignorance of the one who mocks at what he does not know the reality of and does not comprehend its truth, from the words of the wise; and it clarifies that it is the right of one who draws near to his Lord to be meticulous (yatanawwaq) in choosing what he draws near with, and to choose [an animal that is] young in age, not aged or weak, of good color, free from defects, pleasing to the one who looks at it, and that its price be expensive. This is as is narrated about ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) that he sacrificed a noble she-camel (najībah) for three hundred dinars.[[Abu Dawud related it from the narration of al-Jahm ibn al-Jarud, from Salim, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) gifted a noble she-camel, and was offered for it three hundred dinars. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I sell it and buy with its price a sacrificial camel?' He said: 'No, slaughter it as it is.'"]] And [it shows] that an addition to the address is an abrogation (naskh) of it, and that abrogation before the act is permissible, even though it is not permissible before the time of the act and its possibility, since that would lead to a change of mind (bada'). And so that it may be known, by what was commanded of touching the dead with the dead and the life occurring after it, that the effective cause is the Causer, not the means, because it is not conceivable that life could be generated from the two deaths present in the two bodies.

If you say: "Why was the story not related in its order? It would have been proper for the mention of the slain man and the striking with a part of the cow to precede the command to slaughter it, and to say: 'And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it'?" I say: Every story of the Children of Israel was related only to enumerate the transgressions that occurred from them, and to rebuke them for them, and for the great signs that were renewed among them. These are two stories, each of which is independent with a kind of rebuke, even though they are connected and unified. The first is to rebuke them for mockery and for not hastening to comply and what follows from that. The second is to rebuke them for killing a forbidden soul and what follows from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man only because, if it were done in reverse, it would have been one single story, and the purpose of doubling the rebuke would have been lost. And a subtle point was observed: after the second was begun as a separate story, it was connected to the first, indicating their unity by the pronoun referring to the cow, not by its explicit name, in His saying: ﴿strike him with a part of it﴾, so that it becomes clear that they are two stories as regards the rebuke and its doubling, by presenting the second as a fresh beginning while delaying it, and that they are one story by the pronoun referring back to the cow.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 67–73 (part 1 of 2):

There was a wealthy old man among the Children of Israel, and his nephews killed his son in order to inherit from him. They threw the body at the gate of a city and then came demanding the blood-money (diyah). God commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike the body with a piece of it, so that he would come back to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said: "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾ That is, "Do you make us an object of mockery," or "people of mockery," or "one who is mocked," or "mockery itself," because of the extreme degree of mocking. ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because mockery in such a matter is a form of ignorance and foolishness.

It is also read as "huzu'an" with two damma (u-vowels), and as "huz'an" with a sukun on the zay, like "kufu'an" and "kufan". Hafs reads "huzuwan" with two damma and a waw, and likewise "kufuwan". Al-ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and al-liyadh (clinging for protection) come from one root.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): "Ask your Lord for us, what is it?" This is a question about its condition and description. They were amazed at a dead cow being struck with a piece of a dead man, and then he came back to life. So they asked about the description of that cow, which was extraordinary in its nature and different from ordinary cows.

Al-fariḍ means the old cow (al-musinnah), and it is said "faraḍat furuḍan, fa-hiya fāriḍ" (she became old). Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

*"By my life, you gave your guest an old she-camel,*
*led to him, which cannot stand on one leg."*

[[Khufaf ibn Nadbah, satirizing al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas for stinginess. Al-fāriḍ is an old she-camel that is led to him, meaning she is not ridden but needs someone to strike her and drive her from behind. "Cannot stand on one leg" means she has no strong leg to rely on for standing.]]

It seems she was called fāriḍ because she had reached the end of her age, having "cut off" (faraḍat) her teeth and reached their final stage. Al-bikr means the young one.

Al-ʿawān means the middle-aged one. The poet said:

*"Graceful ones among virgins and matrons."*

[[*"Caravans of women I used to know long ago,*
*and they, when dwelling, were not dark-skinned,*
*chaste in the faces, high-lying in the veils,*
*graceful, between virgins and matrons."*
By al-Ṭirmāḥ. Al-ẓaʿāʾin are women in howdahs. Al-ḍaʿāʾin (with ḍād) are mounts. Al-ḍaghāʾin (with ghayn) are plural of ḍaghīnah, meaning hatred, inclination, or crookedness; ḍaghanahu means you took him into your embrace. A ḍāghin horse is one that does not give its speed. A ḍāt ḍaghn she-camel is one longing for her homeland. A ḍāt ḍaghn woman loves someone other than her husband. Al-juun (with a ḍamma) is the plural of jawāʾ, meaning black.
Al-ḥaṣān (with a fatḥa) is the chaste one. Al-naqb is the plural of niqāb, like kutub and kitāb. Al-ʿawn originally has a ḍamma on the waw, as the plural of ʿawān, which means the middle, that is, the middle of women and animals, and it was lightened by a sukun. He says: those women are "ẓaʿāʾin," meaning travelers, the journey changed their color, and I used to know them long ago, when they were at home, not dark, chaste in their faces, and when they are protected they are all protected by habit. Al-aʿāli is an adjective for al-naqb or al-mawāḍiʿ, and this applies only to women, as you see. Some narrators reported "ḍaghāʾin" instead of "ẓaʿāʾin," but it is probably a distortion. They are graceful, moving among young virgins and middle-aged women.]]

It is said that "ʿawwanat" (she became middle-aged) is used. [[Al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon by al-Jawharī) says: one says of her "ʿawwanat al-mar'ah taʿwīnan, wa ʿānat taʿūnu ʿawnan." (ʿ)]]

If you say: "bayn" (between) requires two things or more, how is it permitted to be followed by "dhālika" (that)? I say: because it has the sense of two things, since it refers to what was mentioned, the old cow and the young one. If you say: how is it permitted to refer with it to two feminine things, when it is only used to point to a single masculine thing? I say: this is permitted by interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned and what preceded, for brevity in speech, just as they used "faʿala" as a substitute for many actions mentioned before it. You say to a man: "How good what you did was!", and he has mentioned many actions and a long story, just as you say to him: "How good that is!" The pronoun may also be used in the same way as a demonstrative. Abu ʿUbaydah said: I said to Ruʾbah about his verse:

*"In it are lines of black and white,*
*as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy."*

[[Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj describes a wild cow, and it was said a horse, and it was said horses, in which is the color black and the color white, and it is narrated as "min bayāḍ wa bāq." Perhaps the white is white mixed with dust, as if it is "the mentioned one or the combination of both," like the pattern of leprosy on the skin. Or it means while being on the skin, the pattern of leprosy, that is, its marking of white mixed with dullness arising from leprosy, a disease by which the color of the skin changes. It is related that Abu ʿUbaydah said to him: if you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā"; if you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā." He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," (as if that). So he made the pronoun behave like a demonstrative in the correctness of pointing with the singular to the plural, by interpreting it as the thing mentioned or similar.]]

If you mean the lines, say "kaʾannahā" (as if they). If you mean the black and the white, say "kaʾannahumā" (as if they two). He said: I meant "kaʾanna dhāk," you fool! What makes it good is that the demonstratives in their dual, plural and feminine forms are not literal, and the same is true for relative pronouns. That is why "alladhī" was used to mean the plural, as in ﴿what you are commanded (mā tu'maruna)﴾, that is, what you are commanded to do, meaning "tu'maruna bihi" (you are commanded with it), from the saying: ﴿I commanded you the good (amartuka al-khayr)﴾ or ﴿their command (amruhum)﴾, meaning "ma'murukum" (what is commanded to you), calling the object by the verbal noun, like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the striking of the ruler).

Al-fuqūʿ is the most intense yellow and its purest. It is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqiʿ wa wāris" (intensely yellow and dark yellow), just as one says "aswad ḥālik wa ḥānik" (intensely black), "abyaḍ yaqiq wa lahiq" (intensely white), "aḥmar qānī wa dhurayqī" (intensely red), "akhḍar nāḍir wa mudhāmmim" (intensely green), "awraq khaṭbānī wa azmak rudānī" (grayish-green). If you say: "fāqiʿ" here is a predicate of the color, so it is not an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," I say: it is not a predicate of the color; it is an emphasis of "ṣafrāʾ," except that the color is raised by it like the subject, and the color belongs to it and is connected to it, so there is no difference between your saying "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa" and "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿ lawnuhā" (its color is intensely yellow). If you say: why not say "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿa," and what is the benefit of mentioning the color? I say: the benefit is emphasis, because "lawn" is a name for the form, and it is yellowness. So it is as if it were said: "intensely yellow is its yellowness," like your saying "jadda jadduhu" (his grandfather is truly his grandfather) and "junūnuka majnūn" (your madness is madness).

It is related from Wahb: when you look at it, it appears to you that the light of the sun comes out of its skin. Joy is a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining a benefit or expecting it. It is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever wears yellow sandals, his anxiety decreases." [[It is a statement attributed to ʿAlī (mawqūf) which I have not found. But al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Khaṭīb reported it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Whoever wears yellow sandals will not cease to be in joy as long as he wears them." Ibn Abi Hatim said: I asked my father about it, and he said: it is a lie, fabricated.]] because of the statement of God Most High: ﴿it pleases the observers (tasurru al-nāẓirīn)﴾. It is related from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā" (yellow, intensely its color), he said: "black, intensely black." Perhaps it is borrowed from the description of camels, because their blackness is overlaid with yellowness. By this was explained the verse: ﴿camels, yellow (jimālatun ṣufrun)﴾. Al-Aʿshā said:

*"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*

[[*"Qays, the best of deeds, father of*
*Abu al-Ashʿath, whose echoes have become dispersed in the roads.*
*Every year he gives me generously from his camels*
*at the time of the birth of the sheep or the noble camel.*
*Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,*
*they are yellow, their offspring like raisins."*
By al-Aʿshā, about Abu al-Ashʿath ibn Qays. Al-fiʿāl (with a fatḥa) means good deeds. Al-aṣdāʾ is the plural of ṣadā, which is the male owl. The Arabs used to claim that the bones of a slain person's head turn into an owl that cries "Avenge me!" until his blood is avenged. Shuʿūb is the name for death, and it is possible it is the plural of shiʿb meaning road, that is, they became scattered on the roads, which is a metaphor for his killing. The plural is for honor or is considered as such. Al-juumūm is the plural of jamm (with a triple vowel on the first letter), meaning many. Al-najīb is the noble one among horses and camels. Al-rikāb are mounts. "Hunna" (they) refers to the mounts; "ṣufr" is the plural of aṣfar or ṣafrāʾ; "their offspring like raisins" means their dark color predominates. The yellowness here means blackness overlaid with yellowness, because this is the most prized color of camels among them.]]

﴿What is it (mā hiya)?﴾ is a second repetition of the question about its condition and description, and an additional inquiry, so that they might gain more clarity regarding its description.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had taken any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they were strict, so God was strict with them, and excessive questioning is a bad omen." [[Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Abi Hatim all from the chain of al-Ḥasan, from Abu Rafiʿ, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). Its chain contains ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr, who is weak. Al-Ṭabarī has it as a statement of Ibn ʿAbbās (mawqūf), and from a statement of Abu al-ʿĀliyah, except the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen," which is not in the raised or the stopped version. I say: the phrase "excessive questioning is a bad omen" is from the statement of al-Zamakhsharī.]]

And it is related from one of the caliphs that he wrote to his agent to go to a people and cut down their trees and demolish their houses. He wrote back: "With which of them should I begin?" He said: "If I told you to cut down the trees, you would ask me: 'With which type of them should I begin?'" And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: "If I order you to give so-and-so a sheep, you ask me: 'Is it a ewe or a goat?' If I clarify, you say: 'Male or female?' If I inform you, you say: 'Black or white?' So when I order you to do something, do not argue with me."

It is said in a hadith: "The greatest of people in sin is the one who asks about something that was not forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking." [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him.]]

﴿Indeed the cows have become similar to us (inna al-baqara tashābaha ʿalaynā)﴾, that is, the cow described with the color and yellowness is numerous, so it became confused for us which one to slaughter. It is read "tashābah" meaning "tatashābah," by dropping the taa and assimilating it into the shin, and also "tashābahat," "mutashābihah," and "mutashābih." Muhammad dhū al-Shāmah read: ﴿inna al-bāqara yushābihu﴾, with a yaa and a shaddah. It has come in a hadith: "If they had not made the exception, I would not have made clear to them the last of eternity," meaning, if they had not said "if God wills." [[I say: Ibn Jarir reported it through Ibn Jurayj, raised. It is mu'dal (a chain with two or more consecutive omissions).]] The meaning is: we are indeed guided to the cow intended for slaughter, or to what was hidden from us regarding the matter of the killer.

﴿Not a tamed one (lā dhalūl)﴾ is an adjective of "baqara" in the sense of "a cow that is not tame," meaning it has not been trained for plowing and tilling the land, nor is it one of the water-carrying camels by which irrigation for the fields is done. The first "lā" is for negation, and the second is redundant to emphasize the first, because the meaning is: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." The two verbs are attributes of "dhalūl," as if it were said: "not tame, plowing and irrigating." Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read: "lā dhalūl," meaning "lā dhalūl hunāka," that is, there, where she is, and it is a negation of her being tame and of her being described as tame, so one says: "She is tame." A similar expression is your saying: "I passed by people who are not stingy or cowardly," meaning among them, or where they are.

"Tusqā" is read with a ḍamma on the tā, from "asqā" (to water). [[*"Or a camel left aside, whose back is bare, its offspring show her (its) saddle-cloth,*
*her owner has neither made the pilgrimage in the world nor performed the minor pilgrimage."* Sibawayh recited it. It is said: "aʿbarat al-shāh fa-hiya muʿabbarah" when the sheep's wool has grown much because it was left a year without shearing. So the "back left aside" is the one left from shearing, so its wool grows much, or because it has no wool, so it is not sheared. Perhaps the meaning here is the one left from being loaded upon. It is said: "al-munjarid al-shaʿr" (smooth-haired). "Nabā ʿanhu yanbū" means he deviated. "Anbaytuhu" means I made him deviate and I drove him away. So what is here means it prevents others from riding its saddle-cloth. And the apparent statement of some: it is said "nabā yanbī," like "ramā yarmī," when it deviates, and what is here is from it, that is, it shies away from its saddle-cloth, because it is what lies beside the hide. "Rabbuhu" with the vowel shortened for meter means "its owner." The meaning is: it is a camel left from work, so it is wild, shying away from the rider, because it has never traveled at all, so that its owner has not made the pilgrimage nor the minor pilgrimage. And the apparent statement of some is that "rabbuhu" is the "rabb" which is a preposition, making it govern the pronoun without a specifier, because its referent is anticipated, and indicating the confirmation of the negation metaphorically for the sense of multiplicity, and it is a parenthetical between the two conjoined items. The attribution of the two verbs to the pronoun of the camel is a rational metaphor, because it is one of the instruments of pilgrimage and the minor pilgrimage. The one who said this explained it as meaning that it is bare-backed, shying away from its saddle-cloth because of the sores from many journeys, that it did not travel for pilgrimage nor for the minor pilgrimage, but traveled to enemies. If its meaning is as stated above, it would be permissible. So the meaning is that it is a wild camel that has not been ridden and has not traveled at all, so that it did not travel for pilgrimage or the minor pilgrimage, and this is evident.]]

Or "musallamah" (sound), meaning "saved by God from defects," or "free from work," which its owners left alone. Or "mukhlisat al-lawn," from "sallama lahu kadhā" (it was pure for him) when it was pure for him, with no other color mixed into its yellowness, so it is yellow all over, including its horns and hooves. Originally, "shiyah" is a verbal noun: "shāhā yashūhā shiyatan" when he mixed its color with another color, and from it comes "thawr mūshā al-qawāʾim" (a bull with marked legs).

﴿You have now brought the truth (jiʾta bi-al-ḥaqq)﴾, that is, you have brought the reality of the description of the cow, and no difficulty remained regarding its matter. ﴿So they slaughtered her (fadhbaḥūhā)﴾, meaning they obtained the cow that combined all these attributes and slaughtered her. His saying ﴿and they almost did not do it (wa mā kādū yafʿalūn)﴾ is a rebuke for their extreme questioning and a reproach for their delay, and that because of their excessive lengthening and abundant investigation, they almost did not slaughter it, and their questions almost never ended, and the thread of their elaboration and their deep probing almost never broke. It is said: they almost did not slaughter it because of its high price. It is said: because of fear of exposure when the killer was revealed.

It is related that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. The calf grew and became one of the most beautiful and fattest cows. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for its hide filled with gold. At that time the cow was worth three dinars, and they had been searching for the described cow for forty years. [[The word "al-ghīḍah" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ means the thicket, the reed-bed where water gathers and trees grow. (ʿ)]]

If you say: the cow that was addressed by the command was a cow of the general kind, without being specified, and then it became specified by a color and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one. What then of the first command? I say: it was abrogated (mansūkhan) because the ruling shifted to the specified cow, and abrogation before the act is permissible. Moreover, the address, because of its vagueness, included this described cow just as it included others. And if the slaughter had fallen upon it by the ruling of the address before specification, it would have been compliance with it, so likewise if it falls upon it after specification.

﴿And when you killed a soul (wa idh qataltum nafsan)﴾: the group was addressed because the killing was among them. ﴿Then you disputed about it (fa-idāraʾtum fīhā)﴾, meaning you differed and quarreled regarding its matter, because those who dispute push one another away (yadraʾu), that is, they repel and crowd one another. Or you pushed one another, meaning the throwing of the slain man was cast by some of you upon others, so the one upon whom it was cast pushed back the one who cast it. Or because throwing in itself is a push. Or one of you pushed the other away from innocence and accused him.

﴿And God is the one who brings out (mukhrijun) what you were hiding﴾, that is, He will certainly reveal what you concealed of the matter of the killing and will not leave it hidden. If you say: how can "mukhrij" govern when it has the sense of the past? I say: the past tense has been narrated to indicate the time of the dispute, just as the present tense was narrated in His saying: ﴿stretching out his two forearms (bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi)﴾. This sentence is a parenthesis between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which are ﴿then you disputed﴾ and ﴿so We said﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿strike him (iḍribūhu)﴾ refers either to the soul, and the masculine is used with the interpretation of "person" and "human," or it refers to the slain man, because of what is indicated by His saying: ﴿what you were hiding﴾.

﴿With part of it (biba'ḍihā)﴾: with part of the cow. There is disagreement about the part with which he was struck. It was said: its tongue. It was said: its right thigh. It was said: its tail-bone (ʿajb). It was said: the bone that adjoins the cartilage, which is the root of the ear. It was said: the ear. It was said: the piece between the shoulders. The meaning is: they struck him, so he came to life, and that was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿thus God gives life to the dead﴾.

It is related that when they struck him, he stood up by God's permission, his veins gushing blood, and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his nephews. Then he fell dead. The two were seized and killed, and no killer inherited anything after that.

﴿Thus God gives life to the dead (kadhālika yuḥyī Allāhu al-mawtā)﴾: this may be an address to those who witnessed the living of the slain man, meaning "We said to them: thus God will give life to the dead on the Day of Resurrection." ﴿And He shows you His signs (wa yurīkum āyātihi)﴾, that is, His proofs that He is capable of everything, ﴿so that you may understand (la'allakum taʿqilūn)﴾.

...ye (you) reason according to the dictates of your intellects. [Indeed,] whoever is able to give life to one soul is able to give life to all souls, since there is no specificity [in that power], so that you do not deny the Resurrection. Alternatively, it may be an address to the deniers in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If you say: "Why did He not give him life immediately, and why did He make the slaughtering of the cow and striking [the corpse] with a part of it a condition for his revival?" I say: There are wisdoms and benefits in causes and conditions. This condition was imposed because of the nearness to God (taqarrub) and the performance of obligations (taklif) and the gaining of reward in slaughtering the cow, and because of the indication of the excellence of placing an act of devotion before the request, and because of the kindness (lutf) to them in the severity imposed on them for their severity [in questioning]; and for others, [it teaches] avoiding severity and hastening to comply with the commands of God Exalted, and carrying them out immediately without investigation and excessive questioning; and [it benefits] the orphan through profitable trade; and it shows the blessing of goodness to parents, and compassion for children; and [it shows] the ignorance of the one who mocks at what he does not know the reality of and does not comprehend its truth, from the words of the wise; and it clarifies that it is the right of one who draws near to his Lord to be meticulous (yatanawwaq) in choosing what he draws near with, and to choose [an animal that is] young in age, not aged or weak, of good color, free from defects, pleasing to the one who looks at it, and that its price be expensive. This is as is narrated about ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) that he sacrificed a noble she-camel (najībah) for three hundred dinars.[[Abu Dawud related it from the narration of al-Jahm ibn al-Jarud, from Salim, from his father, who said: "ʿUmar (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) gifted a noble she-camel, and was offered for it three hundred dinars. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I sell it and buy with its price a sacrificial camel?' He said: 'No, slaughter it as it is.'"]] And [it shows] that an addition to the address is an abrogation (naskh) of it, and that abrogation before the act is permissible, even though it is not permissible before the time of the act and its possibility, since that would lead to a change of mind (bada'). And so that it may be known, by what was commanded of touching the dead with the dead and the life occurring after it, that the effective cause is the Causer, not the means, because it is not conceivable that life could be generated from the two deaths present in the two bodies.

If you say: "Why was the story not related in its order? It would have been proper for the mention of the slain man and the striking with a part of the cow to precede the command to slaughter it, and to say: 'And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it'?" I say: Every story of the Children of Israel was related only to enumerate the transgressions that occurred from them, and to rebuke them for them, and for the great signs that were renewed among them. These are two stories, each of which is independent with a kind of rebuke, even though they are connected and unified. The first is to rebuke them for mockery and for not hastening to comply and what follows from that. The second is to rebuke them for killing a forbidden soul and what follows from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man only because, if it were done in reverse, it would have been one single story, and the purpose of doubling the rebuke would have been lost. And a subtle point was observed: after the second was begun as a separate story, it was connected to the first, indicating their unity by the pronoun referring to the cow, not by its explicit name, in His saying: ﴿strike him with a part of it﴾, so that it becomes clear that they are two stories as regards the rebuke and its doubling, by presenting the second as a fresh beginning while delaying it, and that they are one story by the pronoun referring back to the cow.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 74:

The meaning of "thumma qasat" (then their hearts hardened) is the remoteness of hardness after what has been mentioned, which necessitates the softening and tenderness of hearts, and the like.

﴿Then you still doubt.﴾ Describing the hearts with hardness and harshness is a metaphor for their being barren of reflection and for admonitions having no effect upon them. ﴿That﴾ refers to the reviving of the slain man, or to all the signs mentioned earlier. ﴿So they are like stones﴾ meaning they are, in their hardness, like stones, ﴿or even harder﴾. "Ashadd" (harder) is conjoined to the kaf (like), either on the meaning of "or like something harder," so the modified noun is omitted and the modifier put in its place. The reading of al-A'mash with the dal in the accusative, conjoining it to "al-hijara" (the stones), supports this. Or it is conjoined to "aw hiya" (or they themselves): "or they are themselves harder in hardness."

The meaning is: whoever knows their state likens them to stones, or to a substance harder than stones, namely iron for example. Or whoever knows them likens them to stones, or says: they are harder than stones. If you ask: why was it said "harder in hardness" (ashadd qaswa), when the verb of hardness (qasa) is one from which the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) and the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub) are derived? I answer: because it is clearer and more indicative of the extreme degree of hardness. There is another aspect: that one does not intend the meaning of "harder" (aqsa) but intends to describe hardness with intensity, as if it were said: the hardness of stones has intensified, and their hearts are harder in hardness. It has also been read as "qasawa." The mention of the second party of comparison has been omitted, because there is no ambiguity, as when you say: Zayd is generous and 'Amr is more generous.

His saying ﴿And indeed among the stones﴾ is an explanation of the superiority of their hearts over stones in intensity of hardness, and a confirmation of His saying "or even harder." It has been read "wa-in" with the light pronunciation, and this is the "in" lightened from the heavy one, which is followed by the distinguishing lam. Among examples of it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed all of them, when gathered together...﴾. The "tafajjur" (gushing forth) is opening up with breadth and abundance. Malik ibn Dinar read "yanfajir" with the nun.

"Yashshaqqaq" means "it splits." It was also read by al-A'mash. The meaning is that among stones there are those with wide holes from which abundant, copious water pours forth, and among them are those that split open lengthwise or widthwise, so water also gushes forth from them. ﴿And some of them fall down﴾ means they hurl themselves down from the top of the mountain. It has been read with a dammed ba'. The "khashya" (fear, awe) is a metaphor for their submission to God's command, and that they do not resist what He wills concerning them; but the hearts of these people do not submit nor do they do what they were commanded. It has been read "ya'malun" (they do) with the ya' and with the ta', and this is a warning.

Addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers: ﴿Do you then hope that they will believe in you?﴾ That is, will they newly come to faith because of your call and respond to you? Like His saying, ﴿Lot believed in him﴾. "They" refers to the Jews. ﴿And there was a group among them﴾, meaning a faction of their predecessors, ﴿who heard the words of Allah﴾, which is what they recited of the Tawrah (Torah), ﴿then distorted it﴾, as they distorted the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning. It has also been said that some of the seventy chosen men heard the words of Allah when He spoke to Musa at the Tur (Mount Sinai), and what He commanded and forbade. Then they said: "We heard Allah say at the end of it: If you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish, do not do them, and there is no harm." It has been read as "Kallama Allah" (Allah spoke). ﴿After they had understood it﴾, after they had grasped and retained it with their intellects, and no doubt remained for them about its authenticity. ﴿And they knew﴾ that they were liars and fabricators. The meaning is: if these people disbelieved and distorted, they have a precedent in that.

﴿And when they meet﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿they say﴾. Their hypocrites say: [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him: "Their hypocrites... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is sound for the pronoun in the wording to return to one direction while the referent differs, because they are two categories included in the first. A parallel is His saying, ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾. The first pronoun refers to the husbands, and the second to the guardians, and it returns to one direction, namely the direction of the addressees, since it includes both categories. And Allah knows best.]] "We believe that you are upon the truth, and that Muhammad is the Messenger foretold." ﴿And when some of them are alone with some﴾, those who did not become hypocrites with those who became hypocrites, ﴿they say﴾, rebuking them: ﴿Do you tell them what Allah has opened up to you﴾, that is, what He has made clear to you in the Tawrah about the description of Muhammad. Or the hypocrites said to their companions, who regarded them as firm in their religion: "Do you tell them?", denouncing them for disclosing to them anything from their Book, so that they would become hypocrites toward the believers and toward the Jews. ﴿That they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, that they may use as proof against you what your Lord has revealed in His Book. They made their argument with it, and their saying "it is in your Book like this" is an argument before Allah. Do you not see that you say, "It is in the Book of Allah like this," and "It is with Allah like this," with the same meaning? ﴿Does He not know what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ Among that is their concealing of disbelief and their displaying of belief.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 78–79:

"And among them are unlettered folk who do not know the Book, but only wishful fancies, and they only conjecture." Those who cannot read or write do not study the Torah to verify what is in it. They know not the Book, the Torah, except for wishful fancies: except what they hold of their own wishes, that Allah pardons them, shows them mercy, and does not take them to account for their sins; that their forefathers, the prophets, will intercede for them; and what their rabbis wish for them, that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days. It is also said: except for various falsehoods they heard from their scholars, which they accepted by way of blind imitation (taqlid, following without evidence). A Bedouin said to Ibn Da'b concerning something he had related: "Is this something you narrated, or wished for, or fabricated?" [[The phrase "أم تمنيته أم اختلفته" (or wished for it, or fabricated it): perhaps he means "or ... etc." (ʿ)]] It is also said: except what they recite from the verse:

"Tamanna kitaba Allahi awwala laylatin ... tamanna Dawudu al-Zabura ʿala rislin"

by Hassan ibn Thabit, in his elegy for Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with them both. He says: "He wished for the Book of Allah," i.e., he recited it and continued reciting it, like Dawud's (peace be upon him) wishing for the Zabur, i.e., like his reciting the Zabur "ʿala rislin" (with the kasra), i.e., with deliberation and tranquility. And it is narrated with the second half replaced by:

"wa-ākhiruhā lāqā ḥamāma al-maqādir"

Al-ḥamām means death, because it is decreed, from ḥamma Allah al-shayʾ, meaning he decreed it.

The derivation is from tamanna (to wish) when it means to estimate, because the one who wishes estimates within himself and conjectures what he wishes for; likewise the fabricator and the reader estimate that such a word comes after such a word. The phrase "illā amānī" is a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). It is also read "amānī" with lightening of the yāʾ. The scholars who obstinately distorted the text despite knowledge and certainty are mentioned, then the common people who followed them, and it is pointed out that both are equal in misguidance, for the scholar must act upon his knowledge, and the layman must not be content with imitation and conjecture while he is able to acquire knowledge.

"yaktubūna al-kitāba" (they write the Book): the distorted book "bi-aydīhim" (with their own hands). [[Maḥmūd said: "If you say: what is the benefit of his saying bi-aydīhim...?" Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari often said regarding such things that its benefit is to depict the state in the soul as it occurred, so that the hearer almost becomes a witness to the situation.]] is an emphasis, and it is from the figurative use of emphasis, just as you say to someone who denies knowing what he wrote: "Sir, you wrote it with this right hand of yours." "Mimmā yaksibūna" (of what they earn): from bribery.

The Arabic passage quoted from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf on 2:80–82 is as follows.

**"Except for a number of days" (illa ayyaman ma'dudatan):** forty days, the number of days of worshipping the calf.

It is related from Mujahid that they used to say: "The duration of this world is seven thousand years, and we will be punished for one day in place of each thousand years."

**"Allah will not break His promise" (fa-lan yukhlifa Allahu):** this is connected to an omitted element, the sense being: "If you have taken a covenant with Allah, then Allah will not break His covenant."

**"Or" (am):** it may be a connecting particle (mu'adala), meaning "which of the two matters is the case," as an affirmation, since knowledge of the occurrence of one of them is certain. It may also be a disconnecting particle (munqati'a).

**"Yes" (bala):** an affirmation of what follows the negative particle, which is His saying: "The Fire will not touch us" (lan tamassana al-nar). That is: "Yes, indeed, it will touch you forever," as evidenced by His saying: "They will abide therein forever" (hum fiha khalidun).

**"Whoever earns an evil deed" (man kasaba sayyi'atan):** from among the evil deeds, meaning a major sin (kabira) from among the major sins.[[His saying "meaning a major sin" is his explanation so that the verse conforms to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, which holds that the perpetrator of a major sin abides eternally in the Fire, whereas the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna is that only the disbeliever abides eternally therein. They interpreted the sin (khati'a) as polytheism (shirk). In al-Khazin it is related that Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is polytheism, with which its possessor dies," end quote. It is that which encompasses its doer and closes the doors of salvation before him from every direction. (Ta'liq)]] **"And his sin has encompassed him" (wa ahatat bihi khati'atuhu):** that is, it has overcome him and taken possession of him, as an enemy surrounds someone, and he did not get free of it through repentance.[[His saying "and he did not get free of it" means: he did not free himself. (Ta'liq)]]

It is also read as *khatayahu* and *khati'atuhu* (plural forms). Regarding the "encompassing," it has been said: his sin outweighed his obedience.

A man asked al-Hasan about the *khati'a*, and he said: "Glory be to Allah! Do I see you with a beard and you do not know what the *khati'a* is? Look into the Mushaf: every verse in which Allah forbids something and informs you that whoever does it He will cause to enter the Fire, that is the encompassing *khati'a*."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 83:

�´لا تَعْبُدُونَﹼ is a report (ikhbar) carrying the sense of a prohibition (nahy) [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "﻿لا تعبدون﻿ is a report carrying the sense of a prohibition... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The proof from it is that if the first clause did not carry the sense of a prohibition, it would not be good to conjoin the command to it, because of the incompatibility between a command and a pure report. This is not so with command and prohibition, since they meet in the sense of demand.]], just as you say: "You go to so-and-so and tell him such-and-such," meaning a command. This is more eloquent than an explicit command or prohibition, because it is as if the addressee has hastened to comply and desist, so it is reported about him. The reading of Abd Allah and Ubayy supports it: "lā taʿbudū" (you shall not worship). The intention of saying must be assumed, and this is also indicated by His saying: ﴿وَقُولُوا﴾ (and speak).

As for His saying ﴿وَبِالْوالِدَيْنِ إِحْساناً﴾ (and to parents, good treatment), it may be construed as: "and you shall show kindness to parents" (taqdir: wa-tuhsinūna bi-l-wālidayni iḥsānan), or "and be good to parents" (wa-aḥsinū). It was also said that it is the answer to His saying ﴿أَخَذْنا مِيثاقَ بَنِي إِسْرائِيلَ﴾ (We took the covenant of the Children of Israel), treated as if it were an oath, as though it were said: "And when We made them swear, [saying], you shall not worship except Allah." It was also said that its meaning is "that you not worship," and when "an" (that) was deleted, the verb was put in the nominative, as in the verse:

﻿أَلَا أَيُّهذَا الزّاجِرِى أَحْضُرَ الوَغَى﻿
﻿وَأَنْ أَشْهَدَ اللَّذَاتِ هَلْ أَنْتَ مُخْلِدِى﻿

[[These are from the Mu'allaqa of Tarafa ibn al-Abd. "Ala" is an interjection of opening, the vocative particle is omitted, "ayyu" is the vocative noun, and the demonstrative is its attribute. "Al-zajir" is an attribute of the demonstrative, annexed to the first person pronoun ya' as an annexation of a description to its object. In another version, "al-lā'imī" (the one blaming) is narrated instead. "Uhdura" is narrated in the accusative by the hidden "an," and in the nominative by its being disregarded, and its omission is justified by mention of it afterward. He says: O you who rebuke me from attending the war and witnessing the delights of victory, conquest and booty, or witnessing the delights of drink and courting women who call for the squandering of wealth, you would not make me immortal even if I obeyed you. The interrogation is one of denial.]]

The reading of Abd Allah supports it: "an lā taʿbudū" (that you not worship). It may be that "in" in it is explanatory (mufassira), or that "an" with the verb is a substitute for the covenant, as if it were said: "We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: that they worship none but Allah." It is read with the tā' (you), as a narration of what they were addressed with, and with the yā' (they), since they are third person.

﴿حُسْناً﴾ (good) a speech that is good in itself [[Mahmud said: "That is, a speech that is good in itself... etc." Ahmad said: In it there is emphasis and specification of the excellence of dealing with people, in that he placed the masdar in the position of the noun. This is used only for intensifying the description, as in "a just man" (rajul ʿadl) and "fasting and breaking the fast" (ṣawm wa-faṭr). It is also read as ḥasanan, which on this basis is one of the attributive adjectives of the similar-to-active-participle form (al-ṣifāt al-mushabbaha).]] because of its extreme goodness. It is also read as ḥasanan and ḥusnā, as a verbal noun, like bushrā.

﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ﴾ (then you turned away) is in the manner of iltifat (shift of address), meaning: you turned away from the covenant and rejected it. ﴿إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْكُمْ﴾ (except a few of you): it was said they are those among them who embraced Islam. ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾ (while you are averse): and you are a people whose habit is turning away from covenants and turning back.

**Verse 84–86 of Surah al-Baqarah, from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf**

﴿You shall not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes.﴾ This means: one of you should not do this to another. He made the other man his own self when he was connected to him by kinship or religion. It is also said: whoever kills another has killed himself, because he will be subjected to retaliation (qisas).

﴿Then you acknowledged the covenant, and you bore witness.﴾ You acknowledged and admitted against yourselves that it was binding, and you were witnesses against yourselves, as when you say: so-and-so has acknowledged against himself such-and-such, and is a witness against himself. It is also said: "and you bear witness" means: today, O assembly of Jews, you bear witness to the acknowledgment of your forefathers of this covenant.

﴿Yet here you are﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at what is attributed to them, namely killing, expulsion and transgression after the covenant was taken from them, and after their acknowledgment and testimony. The meaning is: then after that you are these witnesses, meaning that you are other people, different from those who acknowledged, by a change of attribute that is treated as a change of essence, just as you say: "I returned by a different way from the one I went out by."

﴿You kill﴾ is an explanation of ﴿Yet here you are﴾. It is also said that "ha'ula'" (these) is a relative pronoun in the sense of "alladhi" (who).

It was read as "tazahiruna" with the ta' deleted and assimilated (idgham, the merging of one letter into the next), and as "tatazahiruna" with it retained, and as "tazhiruna," in the sense of "tatazahiruna": that is, you cooperate against them. It was also read "tufadu-hum" and "tufadiruhum," and "asra" and "asara." ﴿And it﴾ is a pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and it may be ambiguous, with its explanation being ﴿their expulsion﴾.

﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ That is, believe in the ransom and disbelieve in the fighting and expulsion. The reason is that the Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and the Nadir were allies of the Khazraj. Each party fought alongside its allies, and when they prevailed they destroyed their homes and expelled them. When a man from either party was taken captive, they gathered to ransom him. The Arabs reproached them, saying: "How can you fight them and then ransom them?" They replied: "We were commanded to ransom them, and fighting them was forbidden to us, but we are ashamed to let our allies be humiliated."

The disgrace (khizy) was the killing and captivity of the Banu Qurayza and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. It is also said that it was the jizya (poll tax).

He returned those among them who did this to the most severe punishment, because their disobedience is greater. It was read "yuraddun" and "ya'malun," with the ya' and the ta'. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ in this world by reducing the jizya, ﴿nor will anyone help them by warding it off﴾. Likewise is the punishment of the Hereafter.

**al-Kitab** (the Scripture): the Torah, which He gave to him all at once.

It is said: *qaffāhu* (he followed him up), when he follows him from the *qafā* (back of the neck), like *dhanabahu* (he followed his tail), from *dhanab* (tail). And *qaffāhu bihi* means he made him follow it, i.e., "And We sent after his trail many messengers," like His saying ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. They were Joshua, Samuel, Shimon, David, Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Ezekiel, Elijah, Elisha, Jonah, Zechariah, John, and others.

It is said that **ʿĪsā** (Jesus) in Syriac is *Īshūʿ*. And **Maryam** means "servant." It is also said: *al-maryam* in Arabic means a woman who is fond of men, as *al-zīr* means a man who is fond of women. [[His saying "like *al-zīr* among men": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, *al-zīr* is one who loves conversing with women and sitting with them. (ʿ)]] By this interpretation is explained the verse of Ruʾba:

*I said to a zīr whom his maryam did not reach:*
*"The misguided one of the desires of youth regrets him."*

[[Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj, rebuking Abū Jaʿfar al-Dawānīqī for idleness and dallying with women. He was so named because during his caliphate he increased the land tax by dawāniq (small coins). So it is in al-Kashshāf. The *zīr* is one who frequently shows affection to women and visits them, and the *maryam* is one who frequently shows affection to men and visits them.

Abū ʿAmr said: *rāma* with *raym*, meaning "remained" or "departed." And *rīmat al-saḥāba tarīman* means the cloud persisted, because of its persistence in affection, or because it left its house. *Al-ḍalīl* is one who often goes astray. *Al-ṣibā* is inclination toward ignorance and youthful folly. *Tandimuhu* means the same as *yandimuhu* (makes him regret), and it is a verbal noun in the nominative as the subject of *ḍalīl*. Perhaps its meaning is that his regret is lost and wandering in the desires of youth. It is also reported as *mundimuhu*, in the form of the active participle. *Ḍalīl* is nominative as the subject, and *mundimuhu* is its predicate. Perhaps its meaning is that the man who often goes astray, meaning himself, is the one who makes him regret and makes him remorseful, i.e., commands him to regret. ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm al-Bayḍāwī, quoting al-Kashshāf, said: that is, I said to him: whoever's error is great, his own self makes him remorseful and places him in regret. The *lām* in His saying *li-zīr* indicates cause, i.e., I said that statement for his sake. This is the explanation of what was said about it. If you made *ḍalīl* an adjective of *zīr* according to the first explanation, and *tandimuhu* an imperative verb being the quoted speech, vowelled with a *ḍamma* because it meets a silent letter with the *hāʾ al-sakt*, and for the rhyme's consistency, it would be permissible: that is, "I said to him: regret and repent." But this has an anomalous artificiality.]]

The grammarians hold that the measure of *Maryam* is *mafʿal*, because *faʿīl* with a *fatḥa* on the *fāʾ* is not established among the patterns, as *ʿuthayr* and *ʿulayb* are. [[His saying "*ʿuthayr* and *ʿulayb*": *al-ʿuthayr* is dust. *ʿUlayb* is the name of a valley. (ʿ)]]

**al-Bayyināt** (the clear signs): the manifest miracles and proofs, such as raising the dead, healing the blind-born and the leper, and informing of unseen matters.

It is read: *wa-ayyadnāhu* (and We strengthened him). From the same root comes *ājadahu* with a *jīm* when he strengthened him. It is said: "Praise be to Allah who strengthened me (*ājadanī*) after weakness, and granted me (*awjadanī*) after poverty." [[His saying "and from it *ājadahu* with a *jīm*": its origin is what is said: a *nāqa ajad*, i.e., a strong camel of firm build. (Al-Ṣiḥāḥ.) (ʿ)]]

**bi-rūḥ al-qudus** (with the Holy Spirit): with the holy spirit, as you say *Ḥātim al-jūd* (Ḥātim of generosity) and *rajul ṣidq* (a man of truth). Its description with holiness is like His saying ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾, describing it with particularity and closeness for honour. It is said: because it was not contained in the loins nor the wombs of menstruating women. It is said: it is Gabriel. It is said: it is the Gospel, as He said of the Qur'an ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾. It is said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, by whose mention he would bring the dead to life.

The meaning: And We certainly gave, O Children of Israel, your prophets what We gave them. ﴿Is it not that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you waxed proud?﴾ You were arrogant regarding belief in him. The interrogative *hamza* of rebuke and wonder at their condition is placed between the *fāʾ* and what it is connected with. It is also permissible that the intention is: "We certainly gave them what We gave them, and then they did what they did." Then He rebuked them for that. The *fāʾ* enters because it is conjoined to what is implied.

If you say: Why was it not said *wa-farīqan qataltum* (and a group you killed)? [[Al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, why was it not said 'and a group you killed' ..." etc. Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: The expression in the present tense conveys this, not the past tense, like His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, where He expressed it in the past, then said ﴿so the earth becomes green﴾, turning from it to the present tense to depict the greening in the mind. And on this is the saying of Ibn Maʿdīkarib depicting his bravery and daring:

*For I have met the opponent, striding*
*in a plain smooth as a page, level.*

*So I seize him and strike him, and he falls,*
*prostrate, on his hands and his jaw.* ]]

I say: It is in two ways: that the past state is intended, because the matter is grave, so it is intended to be brought to mind and depicted in hearts. And that it is intended: "and a group you will kill afterward," because you were circling around killing Muḥammad (ﷺ), were it not that I protect him from you. For that reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said at his death: "The morsel of Khaybar has continued to afflict me; now is the time my aorta has been cut." [[Narrated by al-Bazzār, Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Ṭibb*, and Ibn ʿAdī in *al-Kāmil*, through Saʿīd ibn Muḥammad al-Warrāq, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him). Saʿīd is weak, but al-Ḥākim narrated it through Ḥammād ibn Salama from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr with the same chain, that a Jewish woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a roasted sheep—he mentioned the story—and in it: that this sheep is poisoned, and that Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ died from it, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed her. Abū Dāwūd narrated this portion from the narration of Khālid al-Ṭaḥḥān from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr from Abū Salama as a *mursal*. al-Ṭabarī narrated it from the hadith of Burayda, who said: "We went out to Khaybar"—he mentioned the story—he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) settled—meaning at Khaybar—Zaynab bint al-Ḥārith sent him a sheep"—he mentioned the story in it and said: "O Umm Bishr, the morsel of Khaybar which you ate with your son has continued to afflict me. Now is the time my aorta has been cut." I say: the words "When he settled, etc." are not in the hadith of Burayda; they are from the speech of al-Ṭabarī. It is in the *Maghāzī* of Ibn Isḥāq with this first wording. In it Ibn Isḥāq said: Marwān ibn ʿUthmān narrated to me from Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umm Bishr, when she had entered upon him: "O Umm Bishr, this is indeed the time I found the cutting of my aorta"—the hadith. Likewise al-Ṭabarānī and Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Dalāʾil* narrated it from the narration of Abū al-Aswad from ʿUrwa, abridged. al-Wāqidī mentioned it in *al-Maghāzī* at length without a chain. Ibn Saʿd mentioned it in *al-Ṭabaqāt* from him with chains, and in it: "and she was handed over to the guardians of Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ, and they killed her." Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ḥarbī in their books on rare words narrated from the hadith of Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir something close to the first, as a *mursal*. al-Aṣmaʿī said: *tuʿādinnī* is from *al-ʿadād*, which is a thing that comes at a time and not at another time. al-Bukhārī mentioned it in suspended form from the narration of Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna from Yūnus from al-Zuhrī from ʿUrwa from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), and al-Bazzār and al-Ḥākim linked it through this route. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) agreed upon the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that "a Jewish woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a poisoned sheep, and he ate from it"—the hadith—and in it: "He said: I have continued to know its taste in the throat of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim narrated from the hadith of al-Zuhrī from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik from his father from Umm Bishr who said: "I entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during his illness in which he died, and I said: 'Do you not suspect yourself? If you say: Why was it not said *wa-farīqan qataltum* (and a group you killed)? [[Al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, why was it not said 'and a group you killed' ..." etc. Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: The expression in the present tense conveys this, not the past tense, like His saying ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, where He expressed it in the past, then said ﴿so the earth becomes green﴾, turning from it to the present tense to depict the greening in the mind. *For I have met the opponent, striding*
*in a plain smooth as a page, level.*

*So I seize him and strike him, and he falls,*
*prostrate, on his hands and his jaw.* ]]

I say: It is in two ways: that the past state is intended, because the matter is grave, so it is intended to be brought to mind and depicted in hearts. And that it is intended: "and a group you will kill afterward," because you were circling around killing Muḥammad (ﷺ), were it not that I protect him from you. For that reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said at his death: "The morsel of Khaybar has continued to afflict me; now is the time my aorta has been cut." Saʿīd is weak, but al-Ḥākim narrated it through Ḥammād ibn Salama from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr with the same chain, that a Jewish woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a roasted sheep—he mentioned the story—and in it: that this sheep is poisoned, and that Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ died from it, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed her. It is in the *Maghāzī* of Ibn Isḥāq with this first wording. In it Ibn Isḥāq said: Marwān ibn ʿUthmān narrated to me from Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umm Bishr, when she had entered upon him: "O Umm Bishr, this is indeed the time I found the cutting of my aorta"—the hadith. Likewise al-Ṭabarānī and Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Dalāʾil* narrated it from the narration of Abū al-Aswad from ʿUrwa, abridged. al-Wāqidī mentioned it in *al-Maghāzī* at length without a chain. Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim narrated from the hadith of al-Zuhrī from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik from his father from Umm Bishr who said: "I entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during his illness in which he died, and I said: 'Do you not suspect yourself? He said: I continued to find, from the morsel which I ate from the sheep on the day of Khaybar, a recurrence, until this was the time of the cutting of my aorta." Abū Dāwūd narrated from the narration of al-Zuhrī from Jābir likewise. al-Ṭabarānī and al-Dāraquṭnī narrated from the narration of Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Labība from his father from his grandfather Labība al-Anṣārī (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "A Jewish woman sent to the Prophet (ﷺ) a roasted poisoned sheep. When Bishr died from that morsel, he killed her in retaliation.]]

**Ghulf** is the plural of *aghlaf* (uncircumcised), meaning: they are of a creation and nature covered with coverings through which what Muḥammad (ﷺ) brought cannot reach, nor can they comprehend it. It is used figuratively from the *aghlaf* who is uncircumcised, like their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to﴾. Then Allah refuted that their hearts were created [[Al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Then Allah refuted that their hearts were created ..." etc. Aḥmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is among the errors of al-Zamakhsharī in applying the verses to their false beliefs. How could he do that in the Glorious Book, to which falsehood does not come from before it or behind it? Do you not see how he took from Allah's refutation of this group, that their hearts were created in disbelief, that disbelief and refusal to accept the truth were created by themselves for themselves, paving the way for his corrupt principle regarding the creation of acts. The way to refute him is:

That Allah, exalted is He, only denied them and refuted them in their claim of inability to believe, and of lacking capacity, and they gave as reason that their hearts are *ghulf*. Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth that He created them upon the natural disposition and the capacity to believe, and the ability and facility for it. They themselves chose disbelief over belief, so their choice of disbelief coincided with Allah's creation of it in their hearts after He originated them upon the natural disposition, through the establishment of Allah's proof against them: that He created them capable of belief, not compelled to disbelief. That does not contradict the Sunni understanding in the belief that Allah is the creator of that in their hearts in accordance with their choice. This is the clear truth and the radiant path, and Allah is the granter of success. As for al-Zamakhsharī's statement that their disbelief was created by themselves, due to the prevention of Allah's graces which the believers caused to come to them, and which were a cause for them to create belief in their hearts: all of this is a concealment of polytheism and a belief in gods other than Allah who create for themselves whatever they wish of belief and disbelief. Exalted is Allah above what they associate, a great exaltation.]] in the same way, because they were created upon the natural disposition and capacity to accept the truth. Rather, Allah cursed and abandoned them because of their disbelief. They are the ones who covered their hearts with the disbelief that deviated from the natural disposition, and by that caused the withholding of the graces which would be for those expected to believe and for the believers.

﴿So little is it that they believe﴾: so their belief is little, and they believe. *Mā* is extra (*zāʾida*), and it is their belief in some of the Book. It is also permissible that *qilla* means *ʿadam* (non-existence). It is said that *ghulf* is a lightened form of *ghulf*, the plural of *ghilāf* (sheath), meaning: our hearts are containers of knowledge, so we are sufficient with what we have from other than it. It is reported from Abū ʿAmr: *qulūbunā ghulf* with two *ḍammas*.

﴿A Book from Allah﴾: the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with them﴾ from their Scripture, not contradicting it. It is read *muṣaddiqan* in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). If you ask: How is it permissible for it to be in the accusative from an indefinite noun? I say: when an indefinite noun is described, it becomes specified, so the accusative of state from it is valid. And *kitāb* has been described by His saying ﴿from Allah﴾. The response to *lammā* is omitted, and it is like: they denied it, and treated its coming with contempt, and what resembles that.

﴿They were seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾: they sought victory over the polytheists. When they fought them they said: "O Allah, give us victory through the Prophet sent at the end of time, whose description and attributes we find in the Torah." And they would say to their enemies among the polytheists: "The time of a prophet who will come out confirming what we say has drawn near, and we will kill you with him, a killing like that of ʿĀd and Iram." It is said that the meaning of *yastaftiḥūna* is that they open (the way) against them and make them know that a prophet who will be sent from among them is near in time. The *sīn* is for emphasis, meaning they ask themselves for victory over them, like the *sīn* in *istaʿjaba* and *istasakhara*. Or some of them ask others to give them victory.

﴿But when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ out of envy, rebelliousness, and greed for leadership. ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾: that is, upon them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to show that the curse reached them because of their disbelief. The *lām* is for the known (*ʿahd*). It is also permissible that it is for the genus (*jins*), and they enter into it at the first level.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 90–91:

Bi'sama (what an evil thing) is an indefinite accusative, explaining the subject of bi'sa (an evil thing), meaning "bi'sa shay'an" (an evil thing). In "ishtaraw bihi anfusahum" (for which they sold their souls), and the object of blame is "an yakfuru" (that they disbelieve). Ishtaraw here means "baa'u" (they sold). Baghyan (out of envy and seeking what is not theirs) is the cause (ʿilla) of ishtaraw. "An yunazzila" (that Allah should send down) means "li-anna yunazzila" (because He sends down) or "ʿala an yunazzila" (in that He sends down); that is, they envied him because Allah sends down "min fadlihi" (of His bounty), which is the revelation, "ʿala man yashaʾu" (upon whomever He wills), and His wisdom requires that He send it. "Fa-baaw bi-ghadabin ʿala ghadabin" (so they earned wrath upon wrath): they became deserving of repeated wrath, because they disbelieved in the Prophet of truth and rebelled against him. It is said they disbelieved in Muhammad after Jesus; and it is said after their saying, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and their saying, "the hand of Allah is chained," and other kinds of their disbelief. "Bi-ma anzala Allah" (in what Allah has sent down) is unrestricted, covering whatever Allah sent down in every Book. "Qalu nu'minu bi-ma unzila ʿalayna" (they say: we believe in what was sent down to us) is restricted to the Torah. "Wa-yakfuruna bi-ma waraahu" (and they disbelieve in what is beyond it): that is, they said that while in fact they disbelieve in what lies beyond the Torah. "Wa-huwa al-haqq" (and it is the truth), "musaddiqan li-ma maʿahum" (confirming what is with them), not contradicting it. In this there is a refutation of their claim, because when they disbelieve in what agrees with the Torah, they have disbelieved in it [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "That when they disbelieve in what agrees with the Torah... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This very point is what makes the Qadariyya disbelievers according to one of the two opinions of Malik, al-Shafiʿi and al-Qadi, may Allah be pleased with them, for sound Sunni beliefs are interrelated and harmonious, confirming one another; so denying one of them is disbelief in it, and then disbelief in all of them. We ask Allah the Exalted for protection.]] Then he objected to them with their killing of the prophets, despite their claim to believe in the Torah, while the Torah does not permit the killing of prophets.
