**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 92–93:**

"And you are wrongdoers" (وَأَنْتُمْ ظالِمُونَ) may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: you worshipped the calf while you were placing worship in other than its proper place. It may also be a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ), meaning: you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing.

He repeated the raising of the Mount (rafʿ al-ṭūr) because it was connected to it with an addition not present in the first mention, together with the emphasis it carries.

"And listen" (وَاسْمَعُوا), to what you were commanded in the Torah. They said: "We hear your word and we disobey your command" (قالُوا سَمِعْنا قولك وَعَصَيْنا أمرك).

If you ask: how does their answer correspond to what was said to them? I say: it corresponds in that He said to them, "Listen," and let your listening be the listening of acceptance and obedience, so they said, "We hear," but not the listening of obedience.

"And the calf was made to sink into their hearts" (وَأُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ), meaning: its love and eagerness to worship it permeated them, just as dye permeates cloth. His words "in their hearts" (فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ) explain the place of the soaking, like His words: "They only eat fire into their bellies" (إِنَّما يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ ناراً).

"Because of their disbelief" (بِكُفْرِهِمْ), meaning: because of their unbelief.

"Wretched is what your faith commands you" (بِئْسَما يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمانُكُمْ), namely your faith in the Torah, since there is no worship of calves in the Torah. Attributing the command to their faith is mockery, as the people of Shu'ayb said: "Does your prayer command you?" (أَصَلاتُكَ تَأْمُرُكَ). Likewise the attribution of faith to them.

His words "if you are believers" (إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) cast doubt on their faith and cast aspersions on the soundness of their claim to it.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 92–93:**

"And you are wrongdoers" (وَأَنْتُمْ ظالِمُونَ) may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: you worshipped the calf while you were placing worship in other than its proper place. It may also be a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ), meaning: you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing.

He repeated the raising of the Mount (rafʿ al-ṭūr) because it was connected to it with an addition not present in the first mention, together with the emphasis it carries.

"And listen" (وَاسْمَعُوا), to what you were commanded in the Torah. They said: "We hear your word and we disobey your command" (قالُوا سَمِعْنا قولك وَعَصَيْنا أمرك).

If you ask: how does their answer correspond to what was said to them? I say: it corresponds in that He said to them, "Listen," and let your listening be the listening of acceptance and obedience, so they said, "We hear," but not the listening of obedience.

"And the calf was made to sink into their hearts" (وَأُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ), meaning: its love and eagerness to worship it permeated them, just as dye permeates cloth. His words "in their hearts" (فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ) explain the place of the soaking, like His words: "They only eat fire into their bellies" (إِنَّما يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ ناراً).

"Because of their disbelief" (بِكُفْرِهِمْ), meaning: because of their unbelief.

"Wretched is what your faith commands you" (بِئْسَما يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمانُكُمْ), namely your faith in the Torah, since there is no worship of calves in the Torah. Attributing the command to their faith is mockery, as the people of Shu'ayb said: "Does your prayer command you?" (أَصَلاتُكَ تَأْمُرُكَ). Likewise the attribution of faith to them.

His words "if you are believers" (إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) cast doubt on their faith and cast aspersions on the soundness of their claim to it.

Khālisatan is a accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) referring to al-Dār al-Ākhirah. What is meant is Paradise: pure for you, belonging exclusively to you, with no one else having any right to it. The meaning is: if your claim is true that none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews (hūdan).

Al-nās is generic (li-l-jins), and it is said that it refers to a specific group (li-l-ʿahd), namely the Muslims. Fatamannaw al-mawt: because whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise longs for it and desires to reach bliss quickly and to be freed from the abode full of impurities, as has been transmitted about those given the glad tidings of Paradise.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) used to walk between the two lines (of battle) wearing a light shirt, and his son al-Ḥasan said to him: "This is not the garb of warriors." He said: "O my son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him."

It is reported from Ḥudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to wish for death, and when he was on his deathbed he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty; he who regrets does not prosper."¹ That is, in the sense of longing.

ʿAmmār said at Ṣiffīn: "Now I shall meet the beloved, Muḥammad and his party."²

Each one of the ten (Companions promised Paradise) used to love death and yearn for it. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had wished for death, every person would have choked on his saliva and died in his place, and there would not remain a Jew on the face of the earth."

Bimā qaddamat aydīhim: by what their hands have sent forward, i.e., what has preceded them of the causes of the Fire: disbelief in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought, altering the Book of Allah, and all other kinds of disbelief and disobedience.

His saying wa-lan yatamannawhu abadan is among the miracles, because it is a report of the unseen, and it happened as it was reported, like His saying: "But you will never do it" (wa-lan tafʿalū).

If you say: How do you know that they did not wish for it? I say: Because if they had wished for it, that would have been transmitted as all other events were transmitted, and its transmitters would have been from the People of the Book and others, who would have been the most eager to raise objections against Islam, more than the ants (dharr). Yet none of them transmitted that.

If you say: Wishing is an action of the heart, a secret that no one can perceive, so how do you know they did not wish? I say: Wishing is not an action of the heart; rather it is a person's saying with his tongue: "Would that I had such-and-such." When he says it, they say: "He wished." And "layta" (would that) is the word of wishing. It is impossible for a challenge to be made regarding what is in minds and hearts. Had the wishing been in their hearts and they had wished, they would have said: "We have wished for death in our hearts." But it is not transmitted that they said that.

If you say: They did not say it because they knew they would not be believed. I say: How many things have been related of them, which they uttered against the Muslims, such as slander against Allah, altering His Book, and other things, which they knew they would not be believed in, and which had no interpretation except pure falsehood, yet they did not care. So how could they refrain from saying that wishing is an action of the heart and that they had done it, when it was possible that they were truthful in their statement and in their report about their inner selves? A man would report about himself that he had faith, and he would be believed, though it was possible he was lying, because it is a hidden matter with no way to access it.

Wa-llāhu ʿalīmun bi-l-ẓālimīn: a threat to them.

Wa-latajidannahum: here wajada is in the sense of ʿalima (to know), transitive to two objects, as in the saying "wajadtu Zaydan dhā l-ḥifāẓ" (I found Zayd to be possessed of pride).³ Its two objects are "hum aḥraṣ" (they are most eager).

If you say: Why did He say ʿalā ḥayāhin with indefiniteness? I say: Because He meant a particular kind of life, namely a long life. For this reason, the reading with it is more effective than Ubayy's reading ʿalā l-ḥayāh.

Wa-min alladhīna ashrakū is taken as referring to the sense: since the meaning of "aḥraṣ al-nās" is "more eager than people." If you say: Did those who associated partners not enter under "people"? I say: Yes, but they were singled out for mention because their eagerness is intense. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "and more eager than those who associated partners," the object being omitted because "aḥraṣ al-nās" indicates it.

In this there is great reproach, because those who associated partners do not believe in a final consequence and know nothing but the life of this world; so their eagerness for it is not surprising, since it is their paradise. When one who has a Book, and who acknowledges recompense, exceeds them in eagerness, he deserves the greatest reproach.

If you say: Why did their eagerness exceed the eagerness of the polytheists? I say: Because they knew, from knowing their own state, that they would inevitably go to the Fire, whereas the polytheists do not know that.

It is said that by "those who associated partners" he meant the Magians, for they used to say to their kings: "Live a thousand Nawrūz and a thousand Mihrjān." And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is the saying of the non-Arabs: "Zī hizār sāl" (live a thousand years).⁴

It is said that wa-min alladhīna ashrakū is a new sentence, meaning "and among them are people," the object being omitted, as in His saying: "And there is none of us but has a known station" (Q. 37:164). Those who associated partners, on this view, refers to the Jews, because they said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah."

The pronoun in wa-mā huwa li-aḥadihim is for "aḥadihim," and an-yuʿammara is the subject of bi-muzaḥzihi, meaning: and none of them is one whom his being granted a long life removes from the Fire. It is said that the pronoun refers to what is indicated by yuʿammar, from its verbal noun, and an-yuʿammara is a substitute for it. It is also permissible that huwa be a pronoun of ambiguity (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), with an-yuʿammara as its clarifying element.

Al-zaḥzaḥah means removing far away and withdrawing.

If you say: What is the position of yawaddu aḥadahum? I say: It is an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, given as a fresh sentence (istiʾnāf).

If you say: How is law yuʿammar connected to yawaddu aḥadahum? I say: It is a quotation of their wish. Law here carries the sense of wishing; the analogical form would have been law uʿammar, but it follows the third-person form because of His saying yawaddu aḥadahum, like your saying: "He swore by Allah that he would certainly do it."

³ Al-Zamakhsharī's remark in the text: in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, it is said that he is possessed of pride (dhū ḥifāẓ) when he has a sense of honour.
⁴ Zī is Persian for "live," hizār means "thousand," and sāl means "year."

Khālisatan is a accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) referring to al-Dār al-Ākhirah. What is meant is Paradise: pure for you, belonging exclusively to you, with no one else having any right to it. The meaning is: if your claim is true that none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews (hūdan).

Al-nās is generic (li-l-jins), and it is said that it refers to a specific group (li-l-ʿahd), namely the Muslims. Fatamannaw al-mawt: because whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise longs for it and desires to reach bliss quickly and to be freed from the abode full of impurities, as has been transmitted about those given the glad tidings of Paradise.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) used to walk between the two lines (of battle) wearing a light shirt, and his son al-Ḥasan said to him: "This is not the garb of warriors." He said: "O my son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him."

It is reported from Ḥudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him) that he used to wish for death, and when he was on his deathbed he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty; he who regrets does not prosper."¹ That is, in the sense of longing.

ʿAmmār said at Ṣiffīn: "Now I shall meet the beloved, Muḥammad and his party."²

Each one of the ten (Companions promised Paradise) used to love death and yearn for it. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had wished for death, every person would have choked on his saliva and died in his place, and there would not remain a Jew on the face of the earth."

Bimā qaddamat aydīhim: by what their hands have sent forward, i.e., what has preceded them of the causes of the Fire: disbelief in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought, altering the Book of Allah, and all other kinds of disbelief and disobedience.

His saying wa-lan yatamannawhu abadan is among the miracles, because it is a report of the unseen, and it happened as it was reported, like His saying: "But you will never do it" (wa-lan tafʿalū).

If you say: How do you know that they did not wish for it? I say: Because if they had wished for it, that would have been transmitted as all other events were transmitted, and its transmitters would have been from the People of the Book and others, who would have been the most eager to raise objections against Islam, more than the ants (dharr). Yet none of them transmitted that.

If you say: Wishing is an action of the heart, a secret that no one can perceive, so how do you know they did not wish? I say: Wishing is not an action of the heart; rather it is a person's saying with his tongue: "Would that I had such-and-such." When he says it, they say: "He wished." And "layta" (would that) is the word of wishing. It is impossible for a challenge to be made regarding what is in minds and hearts. Had the wishing been in their hearts and they had wished, they would have said: "We have wished for death in our hearts." But it is not transmitted that they said that.

If you say: They did not say it because they knew they would not be believed. I say: How many things have been related of them, which they uttered against the Muslims, such as slander against Allah, altering His Book, and other things, which they knew they would not be believed in, and which had no interpretation except pure falsehood, yet they did not care. So how could they refrain from saying that wishing is an action of the heart and that they had done it, when it was possible that they were truthful in their statement and in their report about their inner selves? A man would report about himself that he had faith, and he would be believed, though it was possible he was lying, because it is a hidden matter with no way to access it.

Wa-llāhu ʿalīmun bi-l-ẓālimīn: a threat to them.

Wa-latajidannahum: here wajada is in the sense of ʿalima (to know), transitive to two objects, as in the saying "wajadtu Zaydan dhā l-ḥifāẓ" (I found Zayd to be possessed of pride).³ Its two objects are "hum aḥraṣ" (they are most eager).

If you say: Why did He say ʿalā ḥayāhin with indefiniteness? I say: Because He meant a particular kind of life, namely a long life. For this reason, the reading with it is more effective than Ubayy's reading ʿalā l-ḥayāh.

Wa-min alladhīna ashrakū is taken as referring to the sense: since the meaning of "aḥraṣ al-nās" is "more eager than people." If you say: Did those who associated partners not enter under "people"? I say: Yes, but they were singled out for mention because their eagerness is intense. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "and more eager than those who associated partners," the object being omitted because "aḥraṣ al-nās" indicates it.

In this there is great reproach, because those who associated partners do not believe in a final consequence and know nothing but the life of this world; so their eagerness for it is not surprising, since it is their paradise. When one who has a Book, and who acknowledges recompense, exceeds them in eagerness, he deserves the greatest reproach.

If you say: Why did their eagerness exceed the eagerness of the polytheists? I say: Because they knew, from knowing their own state, that they would inevitably go to the Fire, whereas the polytheists do not know that.

It is said that by "those who associated partners" he meant the Magians, for they used to say to their kings: "Live a thousand Nawrūz and a thousand Mihrjān." And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is the saying of the non-Arabs: "Zī hizār sāl" (live a thousand years).⁴

It is said that wa-min alladhīna ashrakū is a new sentence, meaning "and among them are people," the object being omitted, as in His saying: "And there is none of us but has a known station" (Q. 37:164). Those who associated partners, on this view, refers to the Jews, because they said: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah."

The pronoun in wa-mā huwa li-aḥadihim is for "aḥadihim," and an-yuʿammara is the subject of bi-muzaḥzihi, meaning: and none of them is one whom his being granted a long life removes from the Fire. It is said that the pronoun refers to what is indicated by yuʿammar, from its verbal noun, and an-yuʿammara is a substitute for it. It is also permissible that huwa be a pronoun of ambiguity (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), with an-yuʿammara as its clarifying element.

Al-zaḥzaḥah means removing far away and withdrawing.

If you say: What is the position of yawaddu aḥadahum? I say: It is an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, given as a fresh sentence (istiʾnāf).

If you say: How is law yuʿammar connected to yawaddu aḥadahum? I say: It is a quotation of their wish. Law here carries the sense of wishing; the analogical form would have been law uʿammar, but it follows the third-person form because of His saying yawaddu aḥadahum, like your saying: "He swore by Allah that he would certainly do it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 97–98:

It is related that Abdullah ibn Suriya, one of the rabbis of Fadak, argued with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about the one who descends to him with revelation. He said: "Jibril." He said: "That is our enemy. Had it been someone else, we would have believed in you. He has been hostile to us many times, and the most severe of it is that he revealed to our Prophet that Bayt al-Maqdis would be destroyed by Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar). So we sent someone to kill him, and he met him in Babylon as a poor boy, and Jibril repelled him and said: 'If your Lord commanded you to destroy them, He will not give you power over him; and if it was not Him, then on what right do you kill him?'" [[Thus it was mentioned by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, who said: Ibn Abbas related that "a rabbi of the Jews from Fadak, called Abdullah ibn Suriya," and so on. I have not found a chain of narration for it. It is perhaps from the tafsir of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from him.]] It is also said: Allah commanded him to place prophethood among us, but he placed it among others.

It is related that Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) had land in the upper part of Madinah, and his route passed by the schools of the Jews. He would sit with them and listen to their talk. They said: "O Umar, we love you, and we hope for you." He said: "By Allah, I do not come to you out of your love, nor do I ask you because I am in doubt about my religion. I only enter upon you to increase my insight into the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and to see his traces in your book." Then he asked them about Jibril. They said: "That is our enemy; he informs Muhammad of our secrets, and he is the bringer of every collapse and punishment, whereas Mika'il brings fertility and peace." He said to them: "What is their rank with Allah, the Exalted?" They said: "The nearest rank: Jibril is on His right and Mika'il on His left."

"And Mika'il is an enemy of Jibril." Umar said: "If they are as you say, then they are not enemies. You are more disbelieving than donkeys! Whoever is an enemy of one of them is an enemy of the other, and whoever is an enemy of them both is an enemy of Allah." Then Umar returned and found that Jibril had preceded him with the revelation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your Lord has agreed with you, O Umar."

Umar said: "Afterwards I found myself in the religion of Allah harder than stone." [[Al-Wahidi related it in al-Asbab from the narration of Dawud ibn Abi Hind from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Umar had..." and so on in the same wording. al-Tabari related it through Asbat from al-Suddi, who said regarding His saying (Say: whoever is an enemy of Jibril) the verse: "Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) had land in the upper part of Madinah" – to its end – except that he said: "Umar said: 'By He who sent you with the truth, I came to you and I only wanted to inform you.'"]] It is also read: Jibril, on the pattern of qafshalil [[His words "on the pattern of qafshalil": in al-Sihah, al-qafshalil is a ladle, a Persian word arabicized. (Ghayn)]], Jibril with the hamza dropped, Jibril with the ya dropped, Jibril on the pattern of qandil, Jabrall with a heavy lam, Jibra'il on the pattern of jabra'il, and Jabra'il on the pattern of jabra'l. Its diptotic state (ghayr munsarif) is due to definiteness and foreignness. It is also said its meaning is "servant of Allah." The pronoun in nazzalahu refers to the Qur'an. This kind of reference to what has not been previously mentioned contains grandeur for the one referred to, since by its great fame it is as if it indicates itself, and one is satisfied with some of its attributes instead of its explicit name. ʿALA QALBIKA: that is, His preserving you and granting you understanding of it, BI-IDhNI ALLAH: by His facilitating and easing it. If you say: The proper form of speech would have been "upon my heart"? [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say: the proper form of speech would have been 'upon my heart'... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Reported speech sometimes keeps the wording, and sometimes is by meaning without following the wording. Perhaps the matter in this verse was directed to the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he should relate the meaning of Allah's words to him (Whoever is an enemy of Jibril, then he has indeed sent it down upon your heart) in the first-person form. A parallel to this is His saying: "And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them, who made the earth for you as a cradle..." up to: "and who sent down water from the sky in measure, and We revived by it a dead land." Look at what occurs after the attributed saying, which is understood as the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not as a report of their words, for they do not say "fa-ansharna" but say "fa-anshara" in the third person. Rather the speech came as a report according to meaning, since the meaning of their saying "fa-anshara Allah" is the meaning of Allah's saying about Himself "fa-ansharna," and it is not right to make this an instance of shifting from the third person to the first person called iltifat, for in this there is additional matter. And of it is His saying, reporting Musa, peace be upon him: "He said: its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets, the One who made the earth for you" up to: "and We brought forth by it pairs of various plants." The beginning of the speech is understood as the saying of Musa, and its end as the saying of Allah the Exalted. The unifying way in this is what I have established, and Allah knows best.]] I say: It came as a report of Allah's speech as He spoke it, as if it were said: Say what you have spoken of my word: whoever is an enemy of Jibril, then he has sent it down upon your heart. If you say: how does His saying "then He has sent it down" stand as the response to the condition? [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say how does His saying 'then He has sent it down' stand as the answer of the condition... etc.?" Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The entry of the fa' into the response in this way is justified by two reasons: one, that it is a nominal sentence; and the other, that it is a plain past verb.]]? I say: There are two aspects. The first: if any of the People of the Book is hostile to Jibril, there is no basis for his hostility, since he brought down a Book confirming the books before it. Had they been fair, they would have loved him and thanked him for his deed in bringing down what benefits them and confirms the scripture revealed to them. The second: if anyone is hostile to him, the cause of their enmity is that he sent down to you the Qur'an confirming their scripture and agreeing with it, while they dislike the Qur'an and its agreement with their scripture; for this reason they used to distort it and deny its agreement with it. It is like your saying: if so-and-so is hostile to you, then he has harmed you and done you wrong. The two angels are singled out for mention because of their excellence, as if they were of another kind; and this is among what is mentioned, that difference in attribute is treated as difference in essence. It is read: Mika'il, on the pattern of qintar; and Mika'il like Mika'il (Mi-ka'-il); Mika'il like Mika'l; Mika'il like Mik'l; Mika'il like Mik'il. Ibn Jinni said: when the Arabs speak a foreign word, they mix it up. "Enemy of the disbelievers": he meant "enemy of them," but he brought the apparent noun to indicate that Allah opposes them only because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief; and if enmity toward the prophets is disbelief, then what of the angels, who are more noble? [[His words "then what of the angels, who are more noble?" – this is according to the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, the prophets are more noble. (Ghayn)]] The meaning: whoever is hostile to them, Allah is hostile to him and will punish him with the most severe punishment.

[[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say how does His saying 'then He has sent it down' stand as the answer of the condition... etc.?" Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The entry of the fa' into the response in this way is justified by two reasons: one, that it is a nominal sentence; and the other, that it is a plain past verb.]]? I say: There are two aspects. The first: if any of the People of the Book is hostile to Jibril, there is no basis for his hostility, since he brought down a Book confirming the books before it. Had they been fair, they would have loved him and thanked him for his deed in bringing down what benefits them and confirms the scripture revealed to them. The second: if anyone is hostile to him, the cause of their enmity is that he sent down to you the Qur'an confirming their scripture and agreeing with it, while they dislike the Qur'an and its agreement with their scripture; for this reason they used to distort it and deny its agreement with it. It is like your saying: if so-and-so is hostile to you, then he has harmed you and done you wrong. The two angels are singled out for mention because of their excellence, as if they were of another kind; and this is among what is mentioned, that difference in attribute is treated as difference in essence. It is read: Mika'il, on the pattern of qintar; and Mika'il like Mika'il (Mi-ka'-il); Mika'il like Mika'l; Mika'il like Mik'l; Mika'il like Mik'il. Ibn Jinni said: when the Arabs speak a foreign word, they mix it up. "Enemy of the disbelievers": he meant "enemy of them," but he brought the apparent noun to indicate that Allah opposes them only because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief; and if enmity toward the prophets is disbelief, then what of the angels, who are more noble? [[His words "then what of the angels, who are more noble?" – this is according to the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, the prophets are more noble. (Ghayn)]] The meaning: whoever is hostile to them, Allah is hostile to him and will punish him with the most severe punishment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 99–101:

﴿Except the defiantly disobedient﴾ (al-fasiqun): that is, the stubborn rebels among the disbelievers. It is related from al-Hasan: when fisq (defiant transgression, moral corruption) is used for a category of sins, it applies to the gravest member of that category, whether it be disbelief or something else. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: Ibn Suriya said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You have brought us nothing that we recognise, and no sign has been sent down to you that we would follow you in." [[Related by al-Tabari through Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, Saʿid ibn Jubayr narrated to me from him, with this wording."]] So this was revealed. The lam in ﴿al-fasiqun﴾ is for the genus, and the better reading is that it refers to the People of the Book.

﴿而 kullama﴾ (awa kullama): the waw is a conjunction linking to an implied clause, meaning: "Did they disbelieve in the clear signs, and whenever they made a covenant...?" Abu al-Sammal read the waw with a sukun, so that al-Fasiqun means "those who transgressed," as if it were said: "None disbelieves in them except those who transgressed, or who broke Allah's covenant many times." It is also read ʿawahadu and ʿahadu. The Jews are marked for treachery and breaking covenants. How many times did Allah take their covenant, from them and from their fathers, and they broke it? And how many times did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) make covenants with them, and they did not keep them? ﴿Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant each time﴾. Nabadha means to throw away with disregard and to reject it. ʿAbd Allah read naqadahu. ﴿A group of them﴾ and ﴿a group of them said﴾, because some of them did not break it. ﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾ in the Torah, and they have nothing to do with the religion, so they do not regard breaking covenants as a sin and are not concerned by it. ﴿The Book of Allah﴾, meaning the Torah, because by their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah, who confirms what is with them, they disbelieve in it and reject it. It has also been said: the Book of Allah is the Qur'an, which they cast away after it had become binding on them to receive it with acceptance. ﴿As if they did not know that it is the Book of Allah﴾, which no doubt enters into their knowledge. That is, their knowledge of this is firm, but they were obstinate, opposed, and cast it behind their backs. The image is of their abandonment of it and their turning away from it, like a thing thrown behind the back out of indifference and lack of regard for it. It is related from al-Shaʿbi: "It is before them, they recite it, but they have cast aside acting upon it." It is related from Sufyan: "They wrapped it in silk and brocade and adorned it with gold, but they did not make lawful what it makes lawful, nor forbid what it forbids."

And they followed what the devils recited (تتلو) during the reign of Sulayman (ملك سليمان). That is, they abandoned the Book of Allah and followed the books of magic and sorcery that the devils used to recite over the kingdom of Sulayman, meaning in his time and during his rule. This was because the devils used to eavesdrop (يسترقون السمع), then add to what they overheard lies they fabricated, and convey them to the soothsayers (الكهنة). They wrote these down in books which they read and taught to people. This spread in the time of Sulayman, peace be upon him, until they said: "The jinn know the unseen," and they would say, "This is the knowledge of Sulayman, and his kingdom was only established through this knowledge, and by it the men and jinn and the wind that runs at his command were subjected to him."

﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾: a refutation of the devils and a rebuttal of what they falsely accused Sulayman of, namely believing in magic and practising it, and he called that disbelief. ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾: they are the ones who disbelieved by practising magic and writing it down, ﴿teaching people magic﴾, intending by it to lead them astray and misguide them.

﴿And what was sent down to the two angels﴾ is coordinated with "magic," meaning: and they taught them what was sent down to the two angels. It was also said that it is coordinated with "what they recited," meaning: and they followed what was sent down, ﴿Harut and Marut﴾, an explanatory apposition to "the two angels," being their names. What was sent down to them was the knowledge of magic, as a trial from Allah for people. Whoever learned it from them and acted upon it was a disbeliever, and whoever avoided it, or learned it not in order to act upon it but in order to guard against it and so as not to be deceived by it, was a believer:

*"I came to know evil, not for the sake of evil, but in order to guard against it;
For whoever does not know evil among people will fall into it."*

This is by Abu Nuwas. The "lakin" here is for a transitional turn (al-idrab al-intiqali). One might suppose from his saying "not for the sake of evil" that he did not know evil at all in regard to any of its aspects, so this supposition is dispelled by his saying, "but I knew it in order to guard against it." So it is for correction (al-istidrak), meaning he knew it for the sake of protecting himself from it. "Among people" is an explanatory specification of "whoever," emphasizing generality, and the verb in the answer of the condition is jussive: whoever is ignorant of evil falls into it, like a traveller who, not knowing the covered well on his path, falls into it. They took this as evidence for the permissibility of learning sorcery of this kind in order to be able to avoid it. It is also permissible that "from people" is an attribute of "evil," with "min" being explanatory or inceptive. It is narrated as "from good," meaning: whoever does not distinguish evil from good falls into evil.

As the people of Talut were tested with the river: *"Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it, he is of me."*

Al-Hasan read "ʿala al-malakayn" with a kasra on the lam, on the basis that the two who were sent down with the knowledge of magic were two kings in Babylon. The two angels did not teach anyone until they had warned him, advised him, and said to him: ﴿We are only a trial﴾, that is, a test and a choice from Allah, ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾, that is, do not learn it believing it to be true, lest you disbelieve. ﴿And they learn﴾: the pronoun refers to what is indicated by "anyone."

That is, people learn from the two angels what ﴿they use to cause separation between a man and his wife﴾, that is, the knowledge of magic which is a cause of separation between spouses through trickery and deception, such as blowing into the knot and similar things by which Allah causes hatred, ill-temper and discord, as a trial from Him, not because magic has any power in itself. The proof is His saying, ﴿and they cannot harm anyone by it except by Allah's permission﴾, because He may create by it one of His actions, and He may not. ﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾, because they intend evil by it. In this is the implication that avoiding it is better, like learning philosophy, which one cannot be sure will not lead to error.

These Jews knew well that whoever bought (ishtara), that is, exchanged for, what the devils recited instead of the Book of Allah, ﴿has no share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no portion. ﴿And how evil is what they sold themselves for﴾, that is, what they sold them for.

Al-Hasan read "al-shayatun" (الشياطون). It is narrated from some Arabs: "Bustan fulan hawlahu basatun" (بساتون). Its reasoning will be mentioned later. Al-Zuhri read "Harut and Marut" in the nominative, as "they are Harut and Marut," and these are two foreign names, as evidenced by their being diptotic; had they been derived from "al-hart" and "al-mart," meaning breaking, as some claim, they would have been declinable. Talha read "wa ma yuʿallimani" from "aʿlama." "Bayn al-marʾ" was read with a damma and a kasra on the mim, with hamza. "Al-marr" with shadda, on the assumption of the lightened form and pausal pronunciation, like their saying "faraj," and treating connected speech as pause. Al-Aʿmash read "wa ma hum bidarrin," dropping the nun and making it a genitive construction with "ahad," with the separation between them by the adverbial complement. If you ask: how can it be made a genitive construction with "ahad" when it is governed by "min"? I answer: the particle is treated as part of the genitive noun (as in "la abaka," where the particle is part of the construction). If you ask: how did He first affirm knowledge for them in His saying "And they certainly knew," as an emphatic oath, and then negate it from them in His saying "If only they knew"? I answer: its meaning is "if only they acted upon their knowledge," treating them, when they did not act upon it, as though they had departed from it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 103–105:

﴿Had they believed in Allah's Messenger and the Qur'an, and been mindful of Allah, and abandoned what they were engaged in of rejecting the Book of Allah and following the books of the devils, then a reward from Allah would have been better for them.﴾ It is also read as "لَمَثُوبَةٌ" and "مَثُوبَةٌ" like "مَشُورَةٌ" and "مَشُورَةٌ" (two readings of the same word, with the same pattern as "mashūrah" and "mashwarah"). ﴿Had they known﴾ that Allah's reward is better than what they are in. They did know it, but their ignorance lay in not acting on what they knew.

If you ask: Why was the nominal sentence preferred over the verbal sentence as the response to "لَوْ" (law, "if")? I answer: because it indicates the permanence and stability of the reward, just as the case is changed from the accusative to the nominative in "سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ" for this reason. If you ask: Why not say "لِمَثُوبَةِ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ" (the reward of Allah is better)? I answer: because the meaning is "for them, some reward is better."

It is permissible that His saying ﴿Had they believed﴾ is a wish (tamanni, expressing a desire for something unlikely or impossible), used metaphorically (majāz, figurative use) for Allah's will for their faith, meaning "Allah wishes them to believe," as if it were said: "Would that they believed," and then it begins: "a reward from Allah is better." [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It is permissible that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Had they believed﴾ is a wish... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The wish is a metaphor for Allah's will for their faith and piety, of the same kind as his explaining 'la'alla' (perhaps) by will, and the response to it in the manner of 'thumma' (then)."] Their faith is used metaphorically for Allah's will that they have faith and choose it.

The Muslims used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he presented them with some knowledge: "Ra'ina, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: "Be attentive to us, wait for us, and be patient with us until we understand and memorize it." The Jews had a word they used to abuse one another, in Hebrew or Syriac, which was "ra'ina." When they heard the believers say "Ra'ina," they seized the opportunity and addressed the Messenger (ﷺ) with it, intending by it that insult. So Allah forbade the believers from it and commanded them with what has its meaning, which is "unẓurna" (look at us), from "naẓara" (to look at, to wait for someone). Ubayy read "anẓirna" from "al-nazra" (a respite), meaning: "Give us time until we memorize." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read "rā'ūnā," on the basis that they addressed him with the plural form out of reverence. Al-Hasan read "rā'inan" with tanwin (nunation), from "al-ra'n," which is foolishness, meaning: "Do not say a statement that is 'ra'inan,' attributed to al-ra'n in the sense of 'foolish,' like 'dāri'' (armored) and 'laban' (milky)." Because it resembled their saying "ra'īnā," and it was the cause of the abuse, it was described as foolish.

﴿And listen﴾: listen well to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) speaks to you and the questions he puts to you, with attentive ears and present minds, so that you do not need to ask for help or request consideration. Or it means: listen with acceptance and obedience, and let your hearing not be like the hearing of the Jews, who said: "We hear and we disobey." Or it means: listen to what you have been commanded with earnestness, so that you do not return to what you have been forbidden, emphasizing for them the abandonment of that word.

It is reported that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them and said: "O enemies of Allah, may the curse of Allah be upon you! By Him in whose hand my soul is, if I hear any of you say it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I will strike off his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" Then it was revealed. [Abu Nu'aym reported it in al-Dala'il, from the narration of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾: "'Ra'ina' in the language of the Jews is a vile insult. The Jews used to say it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) secretly. When his companions heard it, they made it public and used to say it, laughing at it. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them." He mentioned the rest. Al-Suddi, this younger one, is abandoned (matrūk, rejected as a narrator), and so is his teacher.]

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾: the Jews who treated the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with contempt and insulted him, ﴿there is a painful punishment.﴾ The first "min" (from) is for specification, because "those who disbelieved" is a genus under which there are two kinds: the People of the Book and the polytheists, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists...﴾. The second "min" is added for emphasis on the generality of good, and the third "min" indicates the starting point.

The "good" here is revelation, and likewise mercy, as in His saying: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾. The meaning is that they consider themselves more deserving that revelation be sent to them, so they envy you, and they do not want any revelation to be sent down to you. ﴿And Allah chooses for prophethood whom He wills﴾, and He wills only what wisdom requires. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾: an indication that bestowing prophethood is great bounty, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, His bounty upon you has been great.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 103–105:

They did know it, but their ignorance lay in not acting on what they knew.

If you ask: Why was the nominal sentence preferred over the verbal sentence as the response to "لَوْ" (law, "if")? I answer: because it indicates the permanence and stability of the reward, just as the case is changed from the accusative to the nominative in "سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ" for this reason. If you ask: Why not say "لِمَثُوبَةِ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ" (the reward of Allah is better)? I answer: because the meaning is "for them, some reward is better."

It is permissible that His saying ﴿Had they believed﴾ is a wish (tamanni, expressing a desire for something unlikely or impossible), used metaphorically (majāz, figurative use) for Allah's will for their faith, meaning "Allah wishes them to believe," as if it were said: "Would that they believed," and then it begins: "a reward from Allah is better." [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It is permissible that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Had they believed﴾ is a wish... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The wish is a metaphor for Allah's will for their faith and piety, of the same kind as his explaining 'la'alla' (perhaps) by will, and the response to it in the manner of 'thumma' (then)."] Their faith is used metaphorically for Allah's will that they have faith and choose it.

The Muslims used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he presented them with some knowledge: "Ra'ina, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: "Be attentive to us, wait for us, and be patient with us until we understand and memorize it." The Jews had a word they used to abuse one another, in Hebrew or Syriac, which was "ra'ina." When they heard the believers say "Ra'ina," they seized the opportunity and addressed the Messenger (ﷺ) with it, intending by it that insult. So Allah forbade the believers from it and commanded them with what has its meaning, which is "unẓurna" (look at us), from "naẓara" (to look at, to wait for someone). Ubayy read "anẓirna" from "al-nazra" (a respite), meaning: "Give us time until we memorize." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read "rā'ūnā," on the basis that they addressed him with the plural form out of reverence. Al-Hasan read "rā'inan" with tanwin (nunation), from "al-ra'n," which is foolishness, meaning: "Do not say a statement that is 'ra'inan,' attributed to al-ra'n in the sense of 'foolish,' like 'dāri'' (armored) and 'laban' (milky)." Because it resembled their saying "ra'īnā," and it was the cause of the abuse, it was described as foolish.

﴿And listen﴾: listen well to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) speaks to you and the questions he puts to you, with attentive ears and present minds, so that you do not need to ask for help or request consideration. Or it means: listen with acceptance and obedience, and let your hearing not be like the hearing of the Jews, who said: "We hear and we disobey." Or it means: listen to what you have been commanded with earnestness, so that you do not return to what you have been forbidden, emphasizing for them the abandonment of that word.

It is reported that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them and said: "O enemies of Allah, may the curse of Allah be upon you! By Him in whose hand my soul is, if I hear any of you say it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I will strike off his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" Then it was revealed. [Abu Nu'aym reported it in al-Dala'il, from the narration of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾: "'Ra'ina' in the language of the Jews is a vile insult. The Jews used to say it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) secretly. When his companions heard it, they made it public and used to say it, laughing at it. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them." He mentioned the rest. Al-Suddi, this younger one, is abandoned (matrūk, rejected as a narrator), and so is his teacher.]

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾: the Jews who treated the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with contempt and insulted him, ﴿there is a painful punishment.﴾ The first "min" (from) is for specification, because "those who disbelieved" is a genus under which there are two kinds: the People of the Book and the polytheists, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists...﴾. The second "min" is added for emphasis on the generality of good, and the third "min" indicates the starting point.

The "good" here is revelation, and likewise mercy, as in His saying: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾. The meaning is that they consider themselves more deserving that revelation be sent to them, so they envy you, and they do not want any revelation to be sent down to you. ﴿And Allah chooses for prophethood whom He wills﴾, and He wills only what wisdom requires. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾: an indication that bestowing prophethood is great bounty, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, His bounty upon you has been great.﴾

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 2, verses 106–110:**

It is narrated that they (the Jews) criticized abrogation (*naskh*, the replacing or cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation) and said: "Do you not see that Muhammad orders his companions to do something, then forbids them from it, orders them to do the opposite, and says one thing today and retracts it tomorrow?" So this was revealed.

It was recited as ﴿ma nansakh min ayatin aw nansaha﴾ with a *damma* on the *nun* of *nansakh*, from *ansakha*, or as ﴿aw nunsa'uha﴾. It was also recited as ﴿nunsiha﴾ and as ﴿nansaha﴾ with *tashdid* (doubling), and as ﴿tunsaha﴾ and ﴿tunsaha﴾, addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited ﴿ma nunsika min ayatin aw nansakha﴾. Hudhayfah recited ﴿ma nansakh min ayatin aw nansakiha﴾. The abrogation of a verse (*naskh al-ayah*) is its removal by replacing it with another in its place, and its *insākh* (copying out or causing it to be removed).

The command to abrogate it is that Jibril (peace be upon him) is ordered to make it abrogated, by informing [the Prophet] of its abrogation.

Its *nasʾ* (postponement) means delaying it and removing it, without a replacement. Its *ināsāʾ* means that it is removed from the hearts' memory. The meaning is that every verse is taken away as wisdom requires, by removing its wording and its ruling together, or by removing one of them, with or without a replacement. ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, that is, a verse whose practice brings more reward or one equal to it in that respect. ﴿Allah has power over all things﴾: He is able to do the good and what is better than it, and what is equal to it in goodness. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: He owns your affairs, manages them, and directs them in the way that is good for you. ﴿And He knows best what He imposes on you of abrogation and other things.﴾ When He had shown them that He is the owner of their affairs and their manager according to their interests, through the abrogation of verses and other things, and had established this for them by saying ﴿Do you not know﴾, He wished to instruct them to trust Him in what is best for them of what He imposes on them and reveals to them, and not to demand of their Messenger what the fathers of the Jews demanded of Musa (peace be upon him), such things as had dire consequences for them, like their saying: "Make for us a god," and "Show us Allah plainly," and other things.

﴿Whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾: whoever abandons trust in the revealed verses, doubts them, and demands others in their place, ﴿has indeed strayed from the right way.﴾

It is narrated that Finhas ibn ʿAzura, Zayd ibn Qays, and a group of Jews said to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and ʿAmmar ibn Yasir after the Battle of Uhud: "Did you not see what befell you? If you were upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better and more excellent for you, and we are more rightly guided than you." ʿAmmar said: "How is the covenant broken among you?" They said: "Severely." He said: "Then I have vowed never to disbelieve in Muhammad as long as I live." The Jews said: "As for this one, he has apostatized." Hudhayfah said: "As for me, I am content with Allah as Lord, Muhammad as Prophet, Islam as religion, the Qur'an as leader, the Kaʿbah as qibla, and the believers as brothers." Then the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "You have done well and you have prospered." [[I have not found it with a chain of transmission. It is in the Tafsir of al-Thaʿlabi likewise, without any chain or narrator.]] So this was revealed.

If you say: With what does the phrase ﴿from themselves﴾ connect? [[Mahmud (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "If you say: With what does the phrase 'from themselves' connect ... ?" Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The second possibility is made remote by the presence of 'from', and the first is strengthened by the Exalted's saying: "These are their wishful thoughts."]] I say: There are two possibilities. The first is that it connects with *wadda* (they wish), meaning that they wished you would turn away from your religion, and this wishing was from themselves and from their own desires, not from religious conviction and inclination toward the truth. For they wished this after it had become clear to them that you were upon the truth. So how could their wishing come from the truth?

The second is that it connects with *hasadan* (out of envy), meaning intense envy arising from the very core of their selves. ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾: follow the way of pardon and forgiveness toward what comes from them of ignorance and enmity, ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, which is the killing of the Banu Qurayzah, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, and their humiliation by imposing the *jizyah* (poll tax) upon them. ﴿Indeed Allah has power over all things﴾: He is able to take vengeance upon them. ﴿Whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾, such as a good deed, prayer, charity, or other things, ﴿you will find it with Allah﴾: you will find its reward with Allah. ﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: knowing, so that the deed of any doer is not lost in His sight.

The command to abrogate it is that Jibril (peace be upon him) is ordered to make it abrogated, by informing [the Prophet] of its abrogation.

Its *nasʾ* (postponement) means delaying it and removing it, without a replacement. Its *ināsāʾ* means that it is removed from the hearts' memory. The meaning is that every verse is taken away as wisdom requires, by removing its wording and its ruling together, or by removing one of them, with or without a replacement. ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, that is, a verse whose practice brings more reward or one equal to it in that respect. ﴿Allah has power over all things﴾: He is able to do the good and what is better than it, and what is equal to it in goodness. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: He owns your affairs, manages them, and directs them in the way that is good for you. ﴿And He knows best what He imposes on you of abrogation and other things.﴾ When He had shown them that He is the owner of their affairs and their manager according to their interests, through the abrogation of verses and other things, and had established this for them by saying ﴿Do you not know﴾, He wished to instruct them to trust Him in what is best for them of what He imposes on them and reveals to them, and not to demand of their Messenger what the fathers of the Jews demanded of Musa (peace be upon him), such things as had dire consequences for them, like their saying: "Make for us a god," and "Show us Allah plainly," and other things.

﴿Whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾: whoever abandons trust in the revealed verses, doubts them, and demands others in their place, ﴿has indeed strayed from the right way.﴾

It is narrated that Finhas ibn ʿAzura, Zayd ibn Qays, and a group of Jews said to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and ʿAmmar ibn Yasir after the Battle of Uhud: "Did you not see what befell you? If you were upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better and more excellent for you, and we are more rightly guided than you." ʿAmmar said: "How is the covenant broken among you?" They said: "Severely." He said: "Then I have vowed never to disbelieve in Muhammad as long as I live." The Jews said: "As for this one, he has apostatized." Hudhayfah said: "As for me, I am content with Allah as Lord, Muhammad as Prophet, Islam as religion, the Qur'an as leader, the Kaʿbah as qibla, and the believers as brothers." Then the two of them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "You have done well and you have prospered." [[I have not found it with a chain of transmission. It is in the Tafsir of al-Thaʿlabi likewise, without any chain or narrator.]] So this was revealed.

If you say: With what does the phrase ﴿from themselves﴾ connect? [[Mahmud (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "If you say: With what does the phrase 'from themselves' connect ... ?" Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The second possibility is made remote by the presence of 'from', and the first is strengthened by the Exalted's saying: "These are their wishful thoughts."]] I say: There are two possibilities. The first is that it connects with *wadda* (they wish), meaning that they wished you would turn away from your religion, and this wishing was from themselves and from their own desires, not from religious conviction and inclination toward the truth. For they wished this after it had become clear to them that you were upon the truth. So how could their wishing come from the truth?

The second is that it connects with *hasadan* (out of envy), meaning intense envy arising from the very core of their selves. ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾: follow the way of pardon and forgiveness toward what comes from them of ignorance and enmity, ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, which is the killing of the Banu Qurayzah, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, and their humiliation by imposing the *jizyah* (poll tax) upon them. ﴿Indeed Allah has power over all things﴾: He is able to take vengeance upon them. ﴿Whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾, such as a good deed, prayer, charity, or other things, ﴿you will find it with Allah﴾: you will find its reward with Allah. ﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: knowing, so that the deed of any doer is not lost in His sight.

The pronoun in ﴿وَقالُوا﴾ refers to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. The meaning is: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews (hud)," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Christians (nasara)." He combined the two statements, trusting that the listener would assign each statement to its own group, and that there was no risk of confusion because the enmity between the two groups and each one's condemnation of the other were well known. A similar construction is ﴿وَقالُوا كُونُوا هُوداً أَوْ نَصارى تَهْتَدُوا﴾.

"Hud" is the plural of "ha'id" (one who repents and returns), like "a'idh" and "'uudh," and "bazil" and "buzl." If you ask, "Why does it say ﴿كان هوداً﴾ with a singular subject and a plural predicate?" The answer: the subject is treated according to the wording of "man" (whoever), and the predicate according to its meaning. This is like al-Hasan's reading ﴿إلا من هو صالوا الجحيم﴾, and like ﴿فَإِنَّ لَهُ نارَ جَهَنَّمَ خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read ﴿إلا من كان يهوديا أو نصرانيا﴾.

If you ask, "Why does it say ﴿تِلْكَ أَمانِيُّهُمْ﴾ (those are their wishes), when their statement ﴿لَنْ يَدْخُلَ الْجَنَّةَ﴾ is one wish?" [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him: "If you ask, why does it say 'those are their wishes' when their statement 'none will enter Paradise' is one wish... etc.?"]]

Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: This answer is weakened by God's words that follow it: ﴿قُلْ هاتُوا بُرْهانَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ، بَلى مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِ وَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾. The proof demanded of them here concerns only the validity of their claim that no one but them will enter Paradise. This is confirmed by ﴿بَلى مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِ﴾, since it means Paradise and its bliss, as a rebuttal of their claim that others are excluded from it. This is clear evidence that the wishes referred to are nothing other than what they were asked to prove, and that is one wish. God knows best. The closer answer is that, because of the intensity of their desire for this wish, their repeated return to it, and its firm hold on their hearts, it was put in the plural. The plural conveys that it is firmly fixed in their hearts and that they have reached the utmost of it. The plural conveys this even though its implication is one. A parallel is their saying "ma'an jiya'" (together, hungry), where the attribute is pluralized though its meaning is singular, because its subject is singular, to emphasize the establishment and firmness of the attribute. This is one of the things reported about God's words ﴿إِنَّ هؤُلاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ﴾, where "qalilun" (few) is plural, though the original form would have been singular, as in "shirdhimah qalilah." Compare ﴿كَمْ مِنْ فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ﴾, where it is singular. Pluralizing it was intended to emphasize the meaning of fewness. The way the plural serves emphasis in such cases is that the plural, by its form, adds to the number of units, so it is transferred to emphasize the singular. This is a wonderful metaphorical transfer, since the singular refuses to be increased beyond its peers. Reflect on this passage, for it is one of the precious gems of the art of rhetoric (balagha). God grants success.

I say: By "those" he refers to the wishes mentioned, namely their wish that no good be sent down to the believers from their Lord, their wish that they be returned to disbelief, and their wish that no one but them enter Paradise. In other words, those are their vain wishes. God's words ﴿قُلْ هاتُوا بُرْهانَكُمْ﴾ are connected to their statement, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." And "those are their wishes" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ). Alternatively, the meaning is "the likes of those wishes are their wishes," by omitting the mudaf (the governing noun) and putting the mudaf ilayhi (the noun in the genitive) in its place. He means that all their wishes are as false as this wish of theirs. "Umniyyah" (wish) is on the pattern "uf'ulah," like "uḍḥukah" (a laughingstock) and "a'jubah" (a marvel).

﴿هاتُوا بُرْهانَكُمْ﴾: bring here your proof, your argument for your exclusive entry into Paradise, ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾: if you are truthful in your claim. This is the most devastating thing against the doctrine of the muqallidun (those who follow others blindly, without evidence). Every statement without evidence is false and unestablished.

"Hat" is a sound that functions as "hā'," meaning "bring here." ﴿بَلى﴾ affirms what they denied, namely that others enter Paradise. ﴿مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ﴾: whoever submits himself wholly to God, sincerely devoting himself to Him without associating anything with Him. ﴿وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ﴾: and he does good in his deeds. ﴿فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ﴾: he has his reward, which he deserves.

If you ask, "What is the grammatical position of ﴿مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ﴾?" The answer: it is permissible for ﴿بَلى﴾ to be a reply to their statement, and then ﴿مَنْ أَسْلَمَ﴾ begins a new sentence, with ﴿مَنْ﴾ carrying the meaning of a conditional, its response being ﴿فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ﴾. It is also permissible for ﴿مَنْ أَسْلَمَ﴾ to be the subject of an omitted verb, meaning "yes, whoever has submitted will enter it," and ﴿فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ﴾ is then a sentence conjoined to "whoever has submitted will enter it."

"on something" — that is, on something that is valid and counts. This is a great exaggeration, for the impossible and the non-existent are also described by the name "thing." [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him: "This is a great exaggeration, for the impossible and the non-existent are also described by the name 'thing'... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir, may God have mercy on him) said: His explanation of "thing" differs from both the Sunni and the innovator (Mu'tazili) positions. For the Sunnis it is restricted to the existent, whereas for the Mu'tazila it applies to the existent and to the non-existent that is capable of existing, so that according to both of them it does not in any way include the impossible. He had already given a similar explanation earlier.] So when the application of the name "thing" to them is negated, the disregard for them has been exaggerated to a point beyond which there is nothing. ["His words 'to a point beyond which there is nothing' probably mean: to a limit beyond which there is no limit. (Ibn al-Munayyir?)"] This is like their saying: "Less than nothing."

"And they recite the Book" — the waw here indicates a circumstantial clause, and "the Book" is generic. That is, they said this while their state was that they were people of knowledge and of reciting the scriptures. Whoever carries the Torah, the Gospel, or other books of God and believes in it has no right to disbelieve in the rest, because each of the two Books confirms the other and testifies to its authenticity; likewise, all the books of God corroborate one another.

"So too" — that is, in the same manner as what you have heard, on that same course — "said those who have no knowledge": the ignorant who have neither knowledge nor scripture, such as the idol-worshippers, the deniers of God, and their like. They said to the adherents of every religion: "You are not on anything." This is a severe rebuke to them, since they placed themselves, despite their knowledge, in the same category as those who have no knowledge.

It is related that when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the rabbis of the Jews came to them, and they debated until their voices rose. The Jews said: "You are not on anything of the religion," and they disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel. The Christians said the like to them, and they disbelieved in Moses and the Torah. [Al-Tabari related it through Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad told me, Sa'id or Ikrimah told me, from Ibn 'Abbas," and in it the name of the Jewish speaker is Rafi' ibn Huraymala.]

"So God will judge between the Jews and the Christians on the Day of Resurrection" — by apportioning to each group the punishment it deserves. It is related from al-Hasan: God's judgment between them is that He will declare them liars and cause them to enter the Fire.

"That mention of His name should be prevented" — the second object of "prevent" (man'a). For you say: "I prevented him from such-and-such." Similar is: "And what prevented us from sending..." and "And what prevented people from believing..." It is permissible to delete the preposition with "that" (an), and you may treat it in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning "for fear that His name be mentioned." This is a general ruling covering the category of God's mosques, and that whoever prevents them from the remembrance of God is excessively unjust. The reason for it is that the Christians used to throw filth into Jerusalem's sanctuary and prevent people from praying in it, and the Romans invaded its people, destroyed it, burned the Torah, and killed and enslaved. It was also said that the intended reference is the prevention by the polytheists of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from entering the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. If you ask: how is it said "God's mosques" when the prevention and destruction befell only one mosque, namely Jerusalem's or the Sacred Mosque? I reply: there is nothing wrong with a ruling coming in general terms even though its cause is specific, just as you say to one who harmed a single righteous person: "And who is more unjust than one who harms the righteous?" And as God, exalted is He, said: "Woe to every slanderer, defamer" — and the one referred to was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

"And who strives to ruin them" — by cutting off remembrance, or by destroying the buildings. It is fitting that "whoever" ("man") be understood in the sense of generality, just as "God's mosques" is, and that it not be restricted to those specific Christians or polytheists who did the preventing.

"Those — it was not for them to enter them except in fear." That is, it was not proper for them to enter God's mosques, except in a state of dread and trembling, fearing that the believers would seize them. How much more so that they should take possession of them, defile them, and prevent the believers from them. The meaning is: the right and obligation was nothing but this, were it not for the wrongdoing and insolence of the disbelievers. It was also said: "It was not for them under God's decree," meaning that God had decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet that He would grant victory to the believers and empower them, so that they would not enter them except in fear. It is related that no Christian would enter Jerusalem except disguised, secretly.

Qatadah said: No Christian is found in Jerusalem except that he is beaten severely and subjected to the utmost punishment. It was also said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) proclaimed: "Let no polytheist perform the pilgrimage after this year, and let no one circumambulate the House naked." [Agreed upon, from the narration of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.]

'Abd Allah recited: "illa khifan" (except fearfully), which is like "siyam" (plural of sa'im, fasting), [In al-Sihah: "qawm sawm and siyam."]

The jurists have differed on the entry of a disbeliever into the mosque: Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, permitted it; Malik did not permit it; and al-Shafi'i distinguished between the Sacred Mosque and others. It was also said: the meaning is a prohibition on enabling them to enter and on leaving them free to access it, as in His saying: "And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of God."

"Disgrace" — killing and captivity, or humiliation through the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax). It was also said: the conquest of their cities, Constantinople, Rome, and Amorion.
