If you ask: how is it said "God's mosques" when the prevention and destruction befell only one mosque, namely Jerusalem's or the Sacred Mosque? I reply: there is nothing wrong with a ruling coming in general terms even though its cause is specific, just as you say to one who harmed a single righteous person: "And who is more unjust than one who harms the righteous?" And as God, exalted is He, said: "Woe to every slanderer, defamer" — and the one referred to was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

"And who strives to ruin them" — by cutting off remembrance, or by destroying the buildings. It is fitting that "whoever" ("man") be understood in the sense of generality, just as "God's mosques" is, and that it not be restricted to those specific Christians or polytheists who did the preventing.

"Those — it was not for them to enter them except in fear." That is, it was not proper for them to enter God's mosques, except in a state of dread and trembling, fearing that the believers would seize them. How much more so that they should take possession of them, defile them, and prevent the believers from them. The meaning is: the right and obligation was nothing but this, were it not for the wrongdoing and insolence of the disbelievers. It was also said: "It was not for them under God's decree," meaning that God had decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet that He would grant victory to the believers and empower them, so that they would not enter them except in fear. It is related that no Christian would enter Jerusalem except disguised, secretly.

Qatadah said: No Christian is found in Jerusalem except that he is beaten severely and subjected to the utmost punishment. It was also said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) proclaimed: "Let no polytheist perform the pilgrimage after this year, and let no one circumambulate the House naked." [Agreed upon, from the narration of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.]

'Abd Allah recited: "illa khifan" (except fearfully), which is like "siyam" (plural of sa'im, fasting), [In al-Sihah: "qawm sawm and siyam."]

The jurists have differed on the entry of a disbeliever into the mosque: Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, permitted it; Malik did not permit it; and al-Shafi'i distinguished between the Sacred Mosque and others. It was also said: the meaning is a prohibition on enabling them to enter and on leaving them free to access it, as in His saying: "And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of God."

"Disgrace" — killing and captivity, or humiliation through the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax). It was also said: the conquest of their cities, Constantinople, Rome, and Amorion.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿To Allah belong the East and the West.﴾ That is, the lands of the East and the West, and the whole earth, belong to Allah; He is their Owner and their Lord. ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.﴾ That is, in whatever place you make your turning, meaning the turning of your faces toward the qibla, as is shown by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [2:144]. ﴿Then there is the Face of Allah﴾, that is, His direction, which He commanded and approved. The meaning is that if you are prevented from praying in the Sacred Mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis, then the earth has been made a mosque for you, so pray in whatever spot of its places you wish, and make the turning there, for turning is possible in every place; its settlement is not restricted to one mosque over another nor to one place over another. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: He desires to widen things for His servants and to ease them, and He is All-Knowing of their welfare. It is narrated from Ibn Umar: it was revealed concerning the prayer of the traveler on his mount, wherever it faces. It is narrated from Ata': the qibla was obscured for a people, so they prayed toward different directions; when they woke up, they realized their error and were excused. It was said: its meaning is, wherever you turn for supplication and remembrance, and it does not refer to prayer. al-Hasan recited: ﴿fa-aynama tuwallu﴾ with a fatha on the ta', from the tawalli (turning), meaning: wherever they face the qibla.

And they say (a variant reads it without the waw): those who said "the Messiah is the son of God," "Uzayr is the son of God," and "the angels are the daughters of God." Glory be to Him (subhanahu): a declaration of His transcendence above that, and a removal of Him far from it. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth: He is their Creator and their Owner, and among them are the angels, Uzayr and the Messiah. All of them are devoutly obedient (qanitun) to Him, submissive, and no part of them can resist His bringing into being, His decree, or His will. Whoever has this attribute is not of a like nature with Him, and it is required of a child that it be of the same kind as its father. The tanwin in "kullun" (all) is a substitute for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all that is in the heavens and the earth. It is also permissible that what is meant is: all of those whom they made a son of God are obedient (qanitun), worshipping, acknowledging lordship, and rejecting what they attributed to them. If you ask: how does He use "ma" (which is for non-rational beings) together with "qanitun" (which applies to rational beings)? I answer: it is like His saying, "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" (sabhana ma sakhkhara lana). It seems He used "ma" rather than "man" to belittle them and diminish their status, as in His saying: "And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship" (wa ja'alu baynahu wa bayna al-jinnati nasaban).

The verb *bada'a al-shay'* means "he originated the thing," so he is *badi'*, as you say *bazaa al-rajul* ("the man was unique") and he is *bazii'*. The phrase *Badi' al-samawat* ("the Originator of the heavens") is an annexation of the *sifa mushabbaha* (the adjective of resemblance, an attributive form) to its agent, meaning *badi' samawatihi wa ardihi* ("the one who originated its heavens and its earth"). It has also been said that *al-badi'* means *al-mubdi'* (the Originator), just as *al-sami'* in the verse of 'Amr means *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear), though this view is open to question.

﴿Kun fa-yakun﴾ ("Be, and it is") is from *kana al-tamma* (the complete *kāna*, meaning "to come into being"). That is, "He brings into being, and so it comes into being." This is a figure of speech and an illustration, and there is no actual saying, just as there is no saying in the verse of Abu al-Najm al-'Ajali:

*"When the girths said to the belly, 'Tighten up!' ... so it rose up like a stallion made proud and enraged."*

The girths (*al-anса'*, sing. *nis'*) are wide straps tied around the middle of the animal's body and the covering of the howdah (*hawdaj*). *Hiqq* is an imperative verb, meaning "stick, O belly, to the back and draw in." *Qadaman* is in the accusative as a verbal noun governed by a hidden verb or by what precedes it, or as an object of purpose. *Aada ya'iidu* also means *ada yaisu* ("to become, to turn into"), meaning that the she-camel became like the stallion. Another reading is *fa-ahnaqat*, meaning she became resentful and enraged, originally with a kasra on the *ha'*, which was softened to a sukun, as noted before in *dajar* and *dabr*. *Al-fanīq* is a pampered, honoured stallion, and one says *afnaqahu* when he pampers him. A *jariyya fanqa* is a pampered girl. *Al-muhnaq* is the one angered, from *al-hanq*, meaning resentment and rage. It is also reported as *idh qalat* instead of *idha qalat*. *Al-hiqq* is pronounced with a connected or cut hamza. *Al-muhnaq* with a sukun on the *ha'* would make the line belong to *rajaz* rather than *tawil*. *Qadama qadaman* (like *nasara nasran*) means he went forward. The apparent view is that this report is the correct one, given how much of Abu al-Najm's verse is in *rajaz*. Attributing speech to the girths and having them address the belly is a figure of speech. The meaning is that he fastened the travelling gear on her, and she grew extremely angry, like a noble stallion whose pride has been offended by another.

The meaning intended is that whatever He decrees among affairs and wills to exist comes into being and enters existence without resistance or hesitation, just as an obedient subordinate who is commanded complies without delay, refusal or defiance.

By this, He emphasises the improbability of birth, because one who has this degree of power is in a state utterly different from the states of bodies in their reproduction.

﴿Badi' al-samawat﴾ is read in the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *lahu*. Al-Mansur read it in the accusative as an expression of praise.

And those who do not know said: "Why does Allah not speak to us directly?" — meaning the ignorant among the polytheists, and it is said, among the People of the Book. He denied them knowledge because they did not act upon it. "Or a sign should come to us" — meaning, why would not Allah speak to us as He speaks to the angels and spoke to Musa? This was out of arrogance and insolence. "Or a sign should come to us" — denying (that what came to them from the signs of Allah are signs), and belittling them. "Their hearts have become alike" — that is, the hearts of these people and of those before them are alike in blindness, as in His saying: ﴿Did they charge one another with this?﴾ "We have indeed made the signs clear for a people who are certain" — who are fair-minded, so that they are certain that these are signs which must be acknowledged, submitted to, and sufficed by, in place of anything else.

We have sent you (O Muhammad) only to give good news and to warn, not to compel them to faith. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a solace for him, because he would grieve and his chest would tighten at their persistence and determination in disbelief. "And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire" — that is, you will not be asked what has become of them for not believing, after you have conveyed the message and exerted your utmost effort in calling them. This is like His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and upon Us is the reckoning.﴾ It is also recited as "وَلا تُسْئَلُ" (wa-la tus'al), in the prohibitive mood (on the nahy form), meaning "and do not ask." It is related that he said: "I wish I knew what my two parents have done," and so he was forbidden to ask about the conditions of the disbelievers and to concern himself with the enemies of Allah.

It was also said that the meaning is to magnify the punishment into which the disbelievers have fallen, as one says: "How is so-and-so?" asking about someone who has fallen into a calamity, and it is told to you: "Do not ask about him." The reason for the magnification is that the one inquiring recoils from having what he is in put into words because of its dreadfulness, so you should not ask him nor burden him with what would distress him; or, you, O inquirer, cannot bear to hear his report because it would horrify and distress the listener, so do not ask.

The first reading is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "وَلَنْ تُسْئَلَ" (and you will never be asked), and the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): "وَما تُسْئَلُ" (and you are not asked).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 120:

It is as if they had said: "We will never be pleased with you, however much you seek our pleasure, until you follow our religion" — they said this in order to dishearten the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from their entering Islam. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, related their words, and for this reason He said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance."﴾ This is in the manner of answering them concerning their statement, meaning: the guidance of Allah, which is Islam, is the guidance in truth, and the one that may rightly be called guidance; it is all guidance, with nothing beyond it being guidance. What you call them to follow is not guidance at all; it is merely desire (hawa). Do you not see His saying: ﴿And if you followed their desires﴾, that is, their statements which are desires and innovations, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, that is, from the religion whose soundness is known through sound proofs?

Those whom We gave the Book, they are believers: the People of the Book who recite it as it should be recited, neither distorting it nor altering what it contains of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Those believe in their Book, unlike the distorters. And whoever disbelieves in it, from among the distorters, then those are the losers, since they have bartered guidance for misguidance.

Those whom We gave the Book, they are believers: the People of the Book who recite it as it should be recited, neither distorting it nor altering what it contains of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Those believe in their Book, unlike the distorters. And whoever disbelieves in it, from among the distorters, then those are the losers, since they have bartered guidance for misguidance.

Those whom We gave the Book, they are believers: the People of the Book who recite it as it should be recited, neither distorting it nor altering what it contains of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Those believe in their Book, unlike the distorters. And whoever disbelieves in it, from among the distorters, then those are the losers, since they have bartered guidance for misguidance.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 124–125:

Abraham was tested by his Lord with words (﴿ibtalā Ibrāhīma rabbuhu bi-kalimāt﴾). He tested him with commands and prohibitions. God's testing of His servant is a figurative usage (majāz) for enabling him to choose between one of two things: what God wills and what the servant desires, as though He were examining what he would do in order to repay him according to that. Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, and Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, read (﴿Ibrāhīmu rabbahu﴾) with Ibrahim in the nominative and rabbahu in the accusative. The meaning is that he (Abraham) called upon Him with words of supplication, as one who tests whether He will answer them or not. If you say: in the well-known reading, the subject comes immediately before the verb in the underlying structure, so attaching the pronoun to it would be a pronoun referring back to something not yet mentioned (iḍmār qabl al-dhikr). I say: a pronoun referring back before mention is when one says "ibtalā rabbahu Ibrāhīm" (his Lord tested Abraham). As for "ibtalā Ibrāhīma rabbuhu" or "ibtalā rabbuhu Ibrāhīm," neither of them is a pronoun before mention. The first, the possessor of the pronoun has been mentioned explicitly before the pronoun. As for the second, Ibrahim is placed first in meaning, which is not the case in "ibtalā rabbuhu Ibrāhīm," since there the pronoun has come before its referent both in wording and in meaning, so there is no way to make it correct.

The hidden pronoun in (﴿fa-atammahunna﴾) in one of the two readings refers to Ibrahim, meaning: he fulfilled them, performed them their due, and discharged them in the best manner without neglect or slackness. Similar to this is (﴿wa-Ibrāhīma alladhī waffā﴾, "and Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]"). In the other reading it refers to God, the Exalted, meaning: He gave him what he asked for, without diminishing anything of it. This is supported by what is reported from Muqatil, that he interpreted the words as what Abraham asked his Lord in His saying: (﴿Rabbi ij'al hādhā baladan āminan﴾, "My Lord, make this a secure city"), (﴿wa-j'alnā muslimayni laka﴾, "and make us submissive to You"), (﴿wa-ib'ath fīhim rasūlan minhum﴾, "and raise among them a messenger from among them"), and (﴿Rabbanā taqabbal minnā﴾, "Our Lord, accept from us"). If you say: what governs "idh"? I say: either a hidden verb such as "wa-dhkur idh ibtalā" ("and mention when He tested") or "wa-idhā ibtalāh kāna kayt wa-kayt" ("when He tested him, such and such occurred"); or it is (﴿qāla innī jā'iluka﴾, "He said: I am making you"). If you say: what is the position of "qāla"? I say: according to the first, it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), as though it were said: "What did his Lord say to him when he had fulfilled the words?" And it was said: "He said: I am making you an imam for the people." According to the second, it is a clause conjoined to what precedes it. It is also permissible for it to be an explanation (bayān) of (﴿ibtalā﴾) and an elucidation of it, so that by "the words" is meant what He mentioned of the imamate, the purification of the House, and the raising of its foundations. Islam (submission) precedes that in His saying: (﴿idh qāla lahu rabbuhu aslim﴾, "when his Lord said to him: Submit"). It has been said regarding the "words": they are five in the head: parting the hair, trimming the moustache, using the siwak (tooth-stick), rinsing the mouth, and istinshāq (sniffing water into the nose). And five in the body: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, istinjā' (cleansing after excretion), cutting the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. It has also been said that He tested him with the laws of Islam in thirty portions: ten in Bara'a (the Repentance surah) (﴿al-tā'ibūna al-'ābidūn﴾, "those who repent, who worship"), ten in al-Aḥzāb (﴿inna al-muslimīna wa-al-muslimāt﴾, "indeed the submitting men and submitting women"), and ten in al-Mu'minūn, and a questioner asked up to His saying (﴿wa-alladhīna hum 'alā ṣalawātihim yuḥāfiẓūn﴾, "and those who are maintaining their prayers"). It has also been said that they are the rites of the Hajj, such as the tawaf, the sa'y, the stoning, the ihram, the standing at 'Arafat, and others. It has also been said: He tested him with the star, the moon, the sun, circumcision, the sacrifice of his son, the fire, and the migration.

Imam is a noun for one who is followed, on the pattern of an instrument, like izār for that with which one wraps oneself, meaning: they will follow you in their religion. (﴿wa-min dhurriyyatī﴾, "and of my offspring") is conjoined to the kāf (the "you" in "innī jā'iluka"), as though he said: "and making some of my offspring [imams]," just as one says to you: "I will honour you," and you reply: "and Zayd." (﴿lā yanālu 'ahdī al-ẓālimīn﴾, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers"). It is also read (﴿al-ẓālimūn﴾, with ḍamma), meaning: whoever among your offspring is a wrongdoer. It does not reach him, My succession, or My covenant to him of the imamate; it reaches only the one who is just and free from wrongdoing.

They said: in this is evidence that a sinner (fāsiq) is not fit for the imamate. How can one be fit for it when his ruling and testimony are not valid, his obedience is not obligatory, his report is not accepted, and he may not lead the prayer? Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, used to issue a fatwa privately requiring support for Zayd ibn 'Alī, may God be pleased with both of them, bringing money to him, and going out with him against the usurper who seized power and called himself imam and caliph, such as al-Dawaniqi and his like. A woman said to him: "You advised my son to go out with Ibrahim and Muhammad, the two sons of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan, until he was killed." He said: "I wish I were in your son's place." He used to say about al-Mansur and his partisans: "If they wanted to build a mosque and asked me to count its bricks, I would not do it." It is reported from Ibn 'Uyayna: "A wrongdoer never becomes an imam at all." How is it permissible to appoint a wrongdoer to the imamate, when the imam is only for restraining wrongdoers? When one who is a wrongdoer in himself is appointed, the well-known proverb applies: "Whoever entrusts the wolf with the flock has been wronged."

(﴿al-Bayt﴾, "the House") is the name predominantly applied to the Ka'ba, like "al-najm" (the star) for the Pleiades. (﴿mathābatan lil-nās﴾, "a place of return for the people"): a resort and a place of return for the pilgrims and visitors; they disperse from it and then return to it, meaning that the notable ones among those who visit it, or their like, return to it. (﴿wa-amnan﴾, "and a sanctuary"): a place of safety, like His saying: (﴿ḥaraman āminan wa-yutakhaṭṭafu al-nāsu min ḥawlihim﴾, "a sacred, secure sanctuary, while people are snatched away from around them"). And because the offender takes refuge in it, so he is not touched until he leaves.

It is also read (﴿mathābāt﴾, in the plural), because it is a resort for all people, not specific to any one of them (﴿sawā'an al-'ākifu fīhi wa-al-bād﴾, "equal for the one who dwells there and the one from outside"). (﴿wa-ittakhidhū﴾, "and take"): this is on the intention of a saying, meaning: and We said: take from it a place of prayer where you pray. This is by way of choice and recommendation, not obligation. It is reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that "he took Umar by the hand and said: This is the Station of Abraham. Umar said: Should we not take it as a place of prayer?" He meant: should we not prefer it, because of its merit in praying there, seeking blessing by it and taking blessing from the place where Abraham's foot treaded. He said: "I have not been commanded to do that." Then the sun had not set before it was revealed. [This was narrated by Abu Nu'aym from the transmission of Mujahid from Ibn Umar: "that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, took Umar by the hand, and he passed by the Station and said to him: O Prophet of God, is this the Station of Abraham? He said: Yes. He said: Should we not take it as a place of prayer? So God revealed (﴿wa-ittakhidhū min maqāmi Ibrāhīma muṣallā﴾, "and take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer") – the verse." He said: it is strange from the transmission of Mujahid; it was transmitted alone by Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Madā'inī from his father from Harun al-A'war from Aban ibn Taghlib from al-Hakam from Mujahid. In the two Sahihs from Anas, may God be pleased with him, he said: Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "My Lord agreed with me in three [matters]," and he mentioned the hadith, and in it: "I said: O Messenger of God, if only we took the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer, and then it was revealed."] And from Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, kissed the Black Stone, performed ramal (quick pacing) for three circuits and walked for four; when he finished he went to the Station of Abraham, prayed two rak'ahs behind it, and recited (﴿wa-ittakhidhū min maqāmi Ibrāhīma muṣallā﴾)." [This is how he mentioned it. What is in Sahih Muslim in the long hadith on the description of the Hajj is: "that he recited the verse when he finished the tawaf, then prayed."]

It has been said: (﴿muṣallā﴾) is a place of du'a (supplication). The Station of Abraham is the stone which has the mark of his two feet, and the place where the stone was when he placed his feet upon it, which is the place called the Station of Abraham. It is reported from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he asked al-Muṭallib ibn Abī Wadā'a: "Do you know where its first place was?" He said: "Yes," and showed him its place today. It is reported from 'Ata' that (﴿maqāmi Ibrāhīm﴾) refers to 'Arafat, Muzdalifa, and the jamarat, because he stood in these places and supplicated in them. It is reported from al-Nakha'i: "the whole Sanctuary is the Station of Abraham." It is also read (﴿wa-ittakhadha﴾, in the past tense), conjoined to (﴿ja'alnā﴾, "We made"), meaning: and the people took from the place of Abraham, which was marked for him because of his concern with it and the settlement of his offspring beside it, a qibla which they face in prayer.

(﴿'ahidnā﴾, "We charged"), meaning: We commanded them (Abraham and Ishmael) (﴿an ṭahhirā baytiya﴾, "to purify My House"), either by making it pure, or meaning "that you two purify." The meaning is: purify it from idols, impurities, and the tawaf of one in major impurity (junub), of a menstruating woman, and of all abominations; or make it sincere for these (worshippers), so that no one else approaches it. (﴿wa-al-'ākifīn﴾, "and those who dwell there"): those who stay near it, who remain and do not depart, or those who are secluded in retreat (i'tikāf). It is permissible that by "al-'ākifīn" he means those standing, namely those standing in prayer, as He said: (﴿lil-ṭā'ifīna wa-al-qā'imīna wa-al-rukka' al-sujūd﴾, "for those who circumambulate, those who stand, and those who bow and prostrate"), and the meaning is: for those who circumambulate and those who pray, because standing, bowing, and prostration are the forms of the one who prays.

If you say: what is the position of "qāla"? I say: according to the first, it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), as though it were said: "What did his Lord say to him when he had fulfilled the words?" And it was said: "He said: I am making you an imam for the people." According to the second, it is a clause conjoined to what precedes it. It is also permissible for it to be an explanation (bayān) of (﴿ibtalā﴾) and an elucidation of it, so that by "the words" is meant what He mentioned of the imamate, the purification of the House, and the raising of its foundations. Islam (submission) precedes that in His saying: (﴿idh qāla lahu rabbuhu aslim﴾, "when his Lord said to him: Submit"). It has been said regarding the "words": they are five in the head: parting the hair, trimming the moustache, using the siwak (tooth-stick), rinsing the mouth, and istinshāq (sniffing water into the nose). And five in the body: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, istinjā' (cleansing after excretion), cutting the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. It has also been said that He tested him with the laws of Islam in thirty portions: ten in Bara'a (the Repentance surah) (﴿al-tā'ibūna al-'ābidūn﴾, "those who repent, who worship"), ten in al-Aḥzāb (﴿inna al-muslimīna wa-al-muslimāt﴾, "indeed the submitting men and submitting women"), and ten in al-Mu'minūn, and a questioner asked up to His saying (﴿wa-alladhīna hum 'alā ṣalawātihim yuḥāfiẓūn﴾, "and those who are maintaining their prayers"). It has also been said that they are the rites of the Hajj, such as the tawaf, the sa'y, the stoning, the ihram, the standing at 'Arafat, and others. It has also been said: He tested him with the star, the moon, the sun, circumcision, the sacrifice of his son, the fire, and the migration.

Imam is a noun for one who is followed, on the pattern of an instrument, like izār for that with which one wraps oneself, meaning: they will follow you in their religion. (﴿wa-min dhurriyyatī﴾, "and of my offspring") is conjoined to the kāf (the "you" in "innī jā'iluka"), as though he said: "and making some of my offspring [imams]," just as one says to you: "I will honour you," and you reply: "and Zayd." (﴿lā yanālu 'ahdī al-ẓālimīn﴾, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers"). It is also read (﴿al-ẓālimūn﴾, with ḍamma), meaning: whoever among your offspring is a wrongdoer. It does not reach him, My succession, or My covenant to him of the imamate; it reaches only the one who is just and free from wrongdoing.

They said: in this is evidence that a sinner (fāsiq) is not fit for the imamate. How can one be fit for it when his ruling and testimony are not valid, his obedience is not obligatory, his report is not accepted, and he may not lead the prayer? Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, used to issue a fatwa privately requiring support for Zayd ibn 'Alī, may God be pleased with both of them, bringing money to him, and going out with him against the usurper who seized power and called himself imam and caliph, such as al-Dawaniqi and his like. A woman said to him: "You advised my son to go out with Ibrahim and Muhammad, the two sons of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan, until he was killed." He said: "I wish I were in your son's place." He used to say about al-Mansur and his partisans: "If they wanted to build a mosque and asked me to count its bricks, I would not do it." It is reported from Ibn 'Uyayna: "A wrongdoer never becomes an imam at all." How is it permissible to appoint a wrongdoer to the imamate, when the imam is only for restraining wrongdoers? When one who is a wrongdoer in himself is appointed, the well-known proverb applies: "Whoever entrusts the wolf with the flock has been wronged."

(﴿al-Bayt﴾, "the House") is the name predominantly applied to the Ka'ba, like "al-najm" (the star) for the Pleiades. (﴿mathābatan lil-nās﴾, "a place of return for the people"): a resort and a place of return for the pilgrims and visitors; they disperse from it and then return to it, meaning that the notable ones among those who visit it, or their like, return to it. (﴿wa-amnan﴾, "and a sanctuary"): a place of safety, like His saying: (﴿ḥaraman āminan wa-yutakhaṭṭafu al-nāsu min ḥawlihim﴾, "a sacred, secure sanctuary, while people are snatched away from around them"). And because the offender takes refuge in it, so he is not touched until he leaves.

It is also read (﴿mathābāt﴾, in the plural), because it is a resort for all people, not specific to any one of them (﴿sawā'an al-'ākifu fīhi wa-al-bād﴾, "equal for the one who dwells there and the one from outside"). (﴿wa-ittakhidhū﴾, "and take"): this is on the intention of a saying, meaning: and We said: take from it a place of prayer where you pray. This is by way of choice and recommendation, not obligation. It is reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that "he took Umar by the hand and said: This is the Station of Abraham. Umar said: Should we not take it as a place of prayer?" He meant: should we not prefer it, because of its merit in praying there, seeking blessing by it and taking blessing from the place where Abraham's foot treaded. He said: "I have not been commanded to do that." Then the sun had not set before it was revealed. [This was narrated by Abu Nu'aym from the transmission of Mujahid from Ibn Umar: "that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, took Umar by the hand, and he passed by the Station and said to him: O Prophet of God, is this the Station of Abraham? He said: Yes. He said: Should we not take it as a place of prayer? So God revealed (﴿wa-ittakhidhū min maqāmi Ibrāhīma muṣallā﴾, "and take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer") – the verse." He said: it is strange from the transmission of Mujahid; it was transmitted alone by Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Madā'inī from his father from Harun al-A'war from Aban ibn Taghlib from al-Hakam from Mujahid. In the two Sahihs from Anas, may God be pleased with him, he said: Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "My Lord agreed with me in three [matters]," and he mentioned the hadith, and in it: "I said: O Messenger of God, if only we took the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer, and then it was revealed."] And from Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, kissed the Black Stone, performed ramal (quick pacing) for three circuits and walked for four; when he finished he went to the Station of Abraham, prayed two rak'ahs behind it, and recited (﴿wa-ittakhidhū min maqāmi Ibrāhīma muṣallā﴾)." [This is how he mentioned it. What is in Sahih Muslim in the long hadith on the description of the Hajj is: "that he recited the verse when he finished the tawaf, then prayed."]

It has been said: (﴿muṣallā﴾) is a place of du'a (supplication). The Station of Abraham is the stone which has the mark of his two feet, and the place where the stone was when he placed his feet upon it, which is the place called the Station of Abraham. It is reported from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he asked al-Muṭallib ibn Abī Wadā'a: "Do you know where its first place was?" He said: "Yes," and showed him its place today. It is reported from 'Ata' that (﴿maqāmi Ibrāhīm﴾) refers to 'Arafat, Muzdalifa, and the jamarat, because he stood in these places and supplicated in them. It is reported from al-Nakha'i: "the whole Sanctuary is the Station of Abraham." It is also read (﴿wa-ittakhadha﴾, in the past tense), conjoined to (﴿ja'alnā﴾, "We made"), meaning: and the people took from the place of Abraham, which was marked for him because of his concern with it and the settlement of his offspring beside it, a qibla which they face in prayer.

(﴿'ahidnā﴾, "We charged"), meaning: We commanded them (Abraham and Ishmael) (﴿an ṭahhirā baytiya﴾, "to purify My House"), either by making it pure, or meaning "that you two purify." The meaning is: purify it from idols, impurities, and the tawaf of one in major impurity (junub), of a menstruating woman, and of all abominations; or make it sincere for these (worshippers), so that no one else approaches it. (﴿wa-al-'ākifīn﴾, "and those who dwell there"): those who stay near it, who remain and do not depart, or those who are secluded in retreat (i'tikāf). It is permissible that by "al-'ākifīn" he means those standing, namely those standing in prayer, as He said: (﴿lil-ṭā'ifīna wa-al-qā'imīna wa-al-rukka' al-sujūd﴾, "for those who circumambulate, those who stand, and those who bow and prostrate"), and the meaning is: for those who circumambulate and those who pray, because standing, bowing, and prostration are the forms of the one who prays.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 126:

Meaning: make this land, or this place, a secure land, possessing security, as in His saying ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:21). Or [make it] secure for its inhabitants, as in the expression "a sleeping night." ﴿And whoever believes among them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "its people," meaning: provide sustenance to the believers among its people specifically. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ is conjoined to "whoever believes," just as ﴿and from my offspring﴾ is conjoined to the kaf in "making you" (jā'iluka). If you ask: why did Abraham, peace be upon him, specify the believers, so that he was answered [with a rebuff]? I say: he analogized provision to the imamate, and so he made clear the difference between them, because the act of appointing someone as successor (istikhlaf) is an entrusting of guardianship, which is restricted to one who gives sincere counsel to those under his care, and the people furthest from sincere counsel are the wrongdoers. Provision, by contrast, may be a gradual leading-on (istidraj) for the one provided for and a strengthening of the proof against him. The meaning is:

"And I will provide for whoever disbelieves, and I will let him enjoy [it] briefly."

It is permissible for ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾ to be a subject (mubtada') containing the meaning of a conditional, and His saying ﴿then I will let him enjoy [it]﴾ to be the response of the condition, meaning: "and whoever disbelieves, then I will let him enjoy [it]." It was also read as "fa-umatti'uhu fa-adtarruhu" [[The reading in the text: thumma adtarruhu (ʿ)]], meaning: "then I will drive him forcefully (alzzahu) to the punishment of the Fire, the forcing of one who has no power to refuse what he is compelled to." Ubayy read: "fa-numatti'uhu qalilan thumma nadtarruhu."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read: "fa-idtarruhu," with a kasra on the hamza. Ibn 'Abbas read: "fa-umatti'uhu qalilan thumma idtarruhu," in the imperative form. The intended meaning is a supplication from Abraham, who asked his Lord for this. If you ask: how is the sentence to be construed on this reading? I say: in "[He] said" there is a pronoun referring to Abraham, meaning: Abraham said, after his request that the believers be specially provided for: "And whoever disbelieves, let him enjoy [it] briefly, then drive him forcefully." Ibn Muhaysin read: "fa-attarhu," with the dad assimilated into the ta', as they say "itjaʿ" for "idtajaʿ," but this is a despised dialect, because the dad is one of the five letters into which neighboring letters are assimilated while it itself is not assimilated into what is adjacent to it; these letters are those gathered in the phrase "ḍamm shafar" (ḍ, m, sh, f, r).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 127–129:

[The verb] *yarfa'u* (raises) narrates a past situation (*hikayat hal madiya*, a narrated past circumstance). *Al-qawa'id* is the plural of *qa'ida*, which means the foundation and base of what is above it. It has become a predominant adjective, and its meaning is "that which is firmly established." From the same root comes *qa'adaka Allah*, meaning "I ask God to make you sit (qa'ada), that is, to make you firm." *Raf' al-asas* (raising the foundation) means building upon it, because when a building is erected on a foundation, it is transferred from a state of lowness to a state of height, and what was low becomes tall. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the *sawafat* (courses) of the building [[The author's phrase "al-muradu biha sawafat al-bina'" (the intended meaning is the courses of the building): the word "sawafat" is from Abu al-Su'ud's expression. Al-Fakhr has "saqat" with a qaf instead of a fa'. The correct reading is with fa', as in al-Sihah, in the chapter on the letter fa': "al-saf: every vein of a wall." (Ed.)]], because every *saf* is a base for what is built upon it and placed above it. The meaning of raising the foundations is raising them by building, because when one places a course upon a course, one has raised the courses.

It may also be that the meaning is: "When Abraham raises what sat (*qa'ada*), that is, what was settled, of the House," meaning that he makes its state, the settled and established base, high and lofty by building. It is narrated that it had a foundation before Abraham, and he built upon the foundation. It is also narrated that God Most High sent down the House as a ruby of the rubies of Paradise, having two doors of emerald, eastern and western, and He said to Adam, peace be upon him: "I have sent down to you that which is to be circumambulated, just as my Throne is circumambulated." So Adam set out from the land of India toward it on foot, and the angels met him and said: "May your pilgrimage be accepted, O Adam! We performed pilgrimage to this House two thousand years before you" [[Al-Fakihi narrated it in the book *Makka*, through the chain of al-Dahhak, who is Ibn Muzahim. He said: Hudhayfa and Salman al-Farisi said: "We heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: God sent down the House from a red ruby, and the angels descended with Adam with it. It landed in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and Adam landed in India, on a mountain called Washib in the land of India. Iblis landed in the Sacred Precinct, so God transferred Iblis to the land of India and transferred Adam to the Sacred Precinct." The hadith. Its chain has weakness and a break. He also narrated it through the chain of Ibn Idris, from his father, from Ata', that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, asked Ka'b and said: "Inform me about the building of this House, what was its matter?" He said: "This House, God sent it down from the sky as a red hollow ruby with Adam." In the narration of al-Nahhas ibn Qahm: I heard Ata' say: "Adam said: 'O Lord, where do You direct me?' He said: 'Build for Me in Tihama a House on the side facing the sea, which is circumambulated, just as the angels circumambulate My Throne, and it is prayed at, just as the angels pray at My Throne.' So he came toward the House, on the side facing al-Safa, and circumambulated the House and prayed there." Al-Nahhas said: "Aqil Ali ibn Sufyan narrated to me: Ata' narrated to us from Abdullah ibn Amr with the like of this." Al-Fakihi also said in the book *Makka*: "Ibn Amr narrated to us."

Sufyan narrated to us from Ibn Abi Labid, who said: "Adam performed the pilgrimage, and the angels met him and said: 'May your rites be accepted, for we performed pilgrimage to this House two thousand years before you.'" This is thus in the *Jami'* of Sufyan ibn Uyayna.]] Adam performed the pilgrimage forty times from the land of India to Makka on foot, and he continued in this until God raised it during the days of the Flood to the fourth heaven, and it is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur).

Then God Most High commanded Abraham to build it, and Gabriel showed him its place. It was said that God sent a cloud which shaded it, and it was called out: "Build upon its shade, neither adding nor subtracting." It was also said: he built it from five mountains: Mount Sinai (Tur Sina), Tur Zaytun, Lebanon, al-Judi, and he laid its foundation from Hira'. Gabriel brought him the Black Stone from heaven. It was also said: Abu Qubays split open and it [the Stone] came out of it; it had been hidden in it during the days of the Flood, and it was a white ruby from Paradise, but when the menstruating women touched it in the pre-Islamic period, it turned black.

It was also said that Abraham was building and Isma'il was handing him the stones. ﴿Our Lord﴾: that is, they both said, "Our Lord." This verb is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the main action), and Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] made it explicit in his recitation (*qira'a*, a canonical variant reading). Its meaning: they raise them, saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the All-Hearing of our supplication, the All-Knowing of our inner thoughts and intentions.﴾

If you say: Why was it not said "the foundations of the House"? What is the difference between the two expressions? I say: in leaving the foundations indefinite and then specifying them after the indefiniteness, there is something not present in their being put in construct form (*idafa*), because clarification after vagueness conveys an exaltation of the status of what is clarified.

﴿Two who submit to You﴾, devoted to You, sincerely directing our faces to You, from the saying (*Aslama wajhahu li-Allah*): ﴿He submitted his face to God﴾; or ﴿submitting ourselves to You﴾. One says *aslama lahu*, *sallama*, and *istaslama*, when one humbles oneself and yields. The meaning: increase us in sincerity or submission to You. It was recited as *Muslimin* in the plural, as if they meant themselves and Hajar, or they applied the dual to the rule of the plural because it derives from it.

﴿And from our offspring﴾: ﴿make from our offspring a community submitting to You﴾. The *min* (from) is either partitive (*li-l-tab'id*) or explicative (*li-l-tabyin*), like His saying: ﴿God has promised those of you who believe﴾.

If you say: Why did they specify their offspring in the supplication? I say: because they are most deserving of compassion and sincere counsel, ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾. And because when the children of prophets are righteous, others are made righteous through them and follow them in goodness. Do you not see that when the leading scholars and the great men are upright, how they bring about the uprightness of those who come after them?

It was also said: by "the community" they meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And show us﴾: it is derived from *ra'a*, meaning "to see" or "to know." That is why it did not exceed two objects. The meaning: "Let us see our acts of worship in the pilgrimage," or "Let us know them." It was also said: "our slaughtering places."

It was recited as *wa-arna* with a sukun on the ra' (*ra'* sakin), by analogy with *fakhdh* becoming *fakhd*. But this has been considered weak, because the kasra was transferred from the dropped hamza, which indicates it, so dropping it is an unjustified reduction. Abu Amr recited with *ishmam* of the kasra (a rounding of the vowel, partial sign of the kasra). Abdullah recited: *wa-arihim manasikahum* (and show them their rites).

﴿And accept our repentance﴾: "what has been committed by us" [[The author's phrase "wa-tub 'alayna ma faraṭa minna": perhaps "tub" is here meant to include the sense of "ghfir" (forgive). (Ed.)]] of minor sins; or they asked God to accept repentance for their offspring.

﴿And raise among them﴾: among the community that submits, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾: from among themselves.

It is narrated that it was said to him: "Your supplication has been answered, and it is at the end of time." So God sent among them Muhammad (ﷺ). He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, the good news of my brother Jesus, and the vision of my mother" [[Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim narrated it from the hadith of al-Irbad ibn Sariya: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "I am the servant of God and the Seal of the Prophets, and Adam was lying prostrate in his clay, and I will inform you of that: the supplication of my father Abraham, the good tidings of Jesus, and the vision of my mother which she saw..." (the hadith). And Ahmad has, from the hadith of Abu Umama, may God be pleased with him: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, what was the beginning of your matter?' He said: 'The supplication of my father Abraham, the good tidings of Jesus, and my mother saw that a light came out of her by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.'" Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in *al-Shu'ab*, then said: "As for the supplication of Abraham, it is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. As for the good tidings of Jesus, it is the saying of God Most High: ﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾." He said: "As for the vision of his mother, Ibn Ishaq mentioned in the *Sira* that he said: 'Amina bint Wahb, the mother of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), used to narrate that she was visited...'" And Abu Ya'la narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, raising it: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, the good news of my brother Jesus son of Mary, and my mother saw in a dream a light. She said: 'I began to follow the light with my sight, and the light outran my sight until it illuminated for me the eastern and western parts of the earth.'" And al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* narrated through the chain of Ibn Ishaq, from Thawr ibn Yazid, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "They said: 'O Messenger of God, inform us about yourself.' He said: 'The supplication of my father Abraham, the good tidings of Jesus, and my mother saw that a light came out of her by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.'"]]

﴿Who recites to them Your verses﴾: he reads to them and conveys what is revealed to him of the proofs of Your oneness and the truthfulness of Your prophets. ﴿And teaches them the Book﴾: the Qur'an. ﴿And wisdom﴾: the sacred law and the explanation of rulings. ﴿And purifies them﴾: he cleanses them from polytheism and all other impurities, like His saying: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the wicked things﴾.

﴿Two who submit to You﴾, devoted to You, sincerely directing our faces to You, from the saying (*Aslama wajhahu li-Allah*): ﴿He submitted his face to God﴾; or ﴿submitting ourselves to You﴾. One says *aslama lahu*, *sallama*, and *istaslama*, when one humbles oneself and yields. The meaning: increase us in sincerity or submission to You. It was recited as *Muslimin* in the plural, as if they meant themselves and Hajar, or they applied the dual to the rule of the plural because it derives from it.

﴿And from our offspring﴾: ﴿make from our offspring a community submitting to You﴾. The *min* (from) is either partitive (*li-l-tab'id*) or explicative (*li-l-tabyin*), like His saying: ﴿God has promised those of you who believe﴾.

If you say: Why did they specify their offspring in the supplication? I say: because they are most deserving of compassion and sincere counsel, ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾. And because when the children of prophets are righteous, others are made righteous through them and follow them in goodness. Do you not see that when the leading scholars and the great men are upright, how they bring about the uprightness of those who come after them?

It was also said: by "the community" they meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And show us﴾: it is derived from *ra'a*, meaning "to see" or "to know." That is why it did not exceed two objects. The meaning: "Let us see our acts of worship in the pilgrimage," or "Let us know them." It was also said: "our slaughtering places."

It was recited as *wa-arna* with a sukun on the ra' (*ra'* sakin), by analogy with *fakhdh* becoming *fakhd*. But this has been considered weak, because the kasra was transferred from the dropped hamza, which indicates it, so dropping it is an unjustified reduction. Abu Amr recited with *ishmam* of the kasra (a rounding of the vowel, partial sign of the kasra). Abdullah recited: *wa-arihim manasikahum* (and show them their rites).

﴿And accept our repentance﴾: "what has been committed by us" [[The author's phrase "wa-tub 'alayna ma faraṭa minna": perhaps "tub" is here meant to include the sense of "ghfir" (forgive). (Ed.)]] of minor sins; or they asked God to accept repentance for their offspring.

﴿And raise among them﴾: among the community that submits, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾: from among themselves.

It is narrated that it was said to him: "Your supplication has been answered, and it is at the end of time." So God sent among them Muhammad (ﷺ). He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, the good news of my brother Jesus, and the vision of my mother" [[Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim narrated it from the hadith of al-Irbad ibn Sariya: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "I am the servant of God and the Seal of the Prophets, and Adam was lying prostrate in his clay, and I will inform you of that: the supplication of my father Abraham, the good tidings of Jesus, and the vision of my mother which she saw..." (the hadith). And Ahmad has, from the hadith of Abu Umama, may God be pleased with him: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, what was the beginning of your matter?' He said: 'The supplication of my father Abraham, the good tidings of Jesus, and my mother saw that a light came out of her by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.'" Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in *al-Shu'ab*, then said: "As for the supplication of Abraham, it is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them﴾. As for the good tidings of Jesus, it is the saying of God Most High: ﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾." ﴿Who recites to them Your verses﴾: he reads to them and conveys what is revealed to him of the proofs of Your oneness and the truthfulness of Your prophets. ﴿And teaches them the Book﴾: the Qur'an. ﴿And wisdom﴾: the sacred law and the explanation of rulings. ﴿And purifies them﴾: he cleanses them from polytheism and all other impurities, like His saying: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the wicked things﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 127–129:

[The verb] *yarfa'u* (raises) narrates a past situation (*hikayat hal madiya*, a narrated past circumstance). *Al-qawa'id* is the plural of *qa'ida*, which means the foundation and base of what is above it. It has become a predominant adjective, and its meaning is "that which is firmly established." From the same root comes *qa'adaka Allah*, meaning "I ask God to make you sit (qa'ada), that is, to make you firm." *Raf' al-asas* (raising the foundation) means building upon it, because when a building is erected on a foundation, it is transferred from a state of lowness to a state of height, and what was low becomes tall. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the *sawafat* (courses) of the building [[The author's phrase "al-muradu biha sawafat al-bina'" (the intended meaning is the courses of the building): the word "sawafat" is from Abu al-Su'ud's expression. Al-Fakhr has "saqat" with a qaf instead of a fa'. The correct reading is with fa', as in al-Sihah, in the chapter on the letter fa': "al-saf: every vein of a wall." (Ed.)]], because every *saf* is a base for what is built upon it and placed above it. The meaning of raising the foundations is raising them by building, because when one places a course upon a course, one has raised the courses.

It may also be that the meaning is: "When Abraham raises what sat (*qa'ada*), that is, what was settled, of the House," meaning that he makes its state, the settled and established base, high and lofty by building. It is narrated that it had a foundation before Abraham, and he built upon the foundation. It is also narrated that God Most High sent down the House as a ruby of the rubies of Paradise, having two doors of emerald, eastern and western, and He said to Adam, peace be upon him: "I have sent down to you that which is to be circumambulated, just as my Throne is circumambulated." So Adam set out from the land of India toward it on foot, and the angels met him and said: "May your pilgrimage be accepted, O Adam! We performed pilgrimage to this House two thousand years before you" [[Al-Fakihi narrated it in the book *Makka*, through the chain of al-Dahhak, who is Ibn Muzahim. He said: Hudhayfa and Salman al-Farisi said: "We heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: God sent down the House from a red ruby, and the angels descended with Adam with it. It landed in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and Adam landed in India, on a mountain called Washib in the land of India. Iblis landed in the Sacred Precinct, so God transferred Iblis to the land of India and transferred Adam to the Sacred Precinct." The hadith. Its chain has weakness and a break. He also narrated it through the chain of Ibn Idris, from his father, from Ata', that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, asked Ka'b and said: "Inform me about the building of this House, what was its matter?" He said: "This House, God sent it down from the sky as a red hollow ruby with Adam." In the narration of al-Nahhas ibn Qahm: I heard Ata' say: "Adam said: 'O Lord, where do You direct me?' He said: 'Build for Me in Tihama a House on the side facing the sea, which is circumambulated, just as the angels circumambulate My Throne, and it is prayed at, just as the angels pray at My Throne.' So he came toward the House, on the side facing al-Safa, and circumambulated the House and prayed there." Al-Nahhas said: "Aqil Ali ibn Sufyan narrated to me: Ata' narrated to us from Abdullah ibn Amr with the like of this." Al-Fakihi also said in the book *Makka*: "Ibn Amr narrated to us."

Sufyan narrated to us from Ibn Abi Labid, who said: "Adam performed the pilgrimage, and the angels met him and said: 'May your rites be accepted, for we performed pilgrimage to this House two thousand years before you.'" This is thus in the *Jami'* of Sufyan ibn Uyayna.]] Adam performed the pilgrimage forty times from the land of India to Makka on foot, and he continued in this until God raised it during the days of the Flood to the fourth heaven, and it is the Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur).

Then God Most High commanded Abraham to build it, and Gabriel showed him its place. It was said that God sent a cloud which shaded it, and it was called out: "Build upon its shade, neither adding nor subtracting." It was also said: he built it from five mountains: Mount Sinai (Tur Sina), Tur Zaytun, Lebanon, al-Judi, and he laid its foundation from Hira'. Gabriel brought him the Black Stone from heaven. It was also said: Abu Qubays split open and it [the Stone] came out of it; it had been hidden in it during the days of the Flood, and it was a white ruby from Paradise, but when the menstruating women touched it in the pre-Islamic period, it turned black.

It was also said that Abraham was building and Isma'il was handing him the stones. ﴿Our Lord﴾: that is, they both said, "Our Lord." Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 130–131:

﴿وَمَنْ يَرْغَبُ﴾: an expression of denial and disbelief, that anyone among the sensible would turn away from the clear truth, which is the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham). ﴿وَمَنْ سَفِهَ﴾ is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal, apposition) for the pronoun in ﴿يَرْغَبُ﴾. The substitution is valid because ﴿مَنْ يَرْغَبُ﴾ is in a non-affirmative context, like your saying: "Has anyone come to you except Zayd?" ﴿سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ means he degraded it, made it contemptible, and belittled it.

The root meaning of safah (folly, lightness) is lightness, and from it comes "a safih rein" (a loose, unrestrained bridle). It has also been said that ﴿نَفْسَهُ﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz, distinguishing noun), as in "his opinion was cheated" (ghabana ra'yuhu) and "his head was pained" (alama ra'suhu). It is also permissible that it is a specification with a definite noun, which is an irregularity (shudhudh), as in the verse:

"Neither is my people the Tha'laba ibn Sa'd,
nor the Fazara, the hairy-necked ones (ash-shu'r ar-riqab)."

"And my people, if you ask, are the sons of Lu'ayy,
in Makkah they taught Mudar the right course."

This is by al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Murri, who claimed to be from Quraysh, saying that his mother took him out to Murra when he was young, and so he was ascribed to them. Tha'laba, Fazara and Mudar are names of tribes. Tha'laba is described as "son of" (ibn) her, because it is the ancestral name of the tribe's founder. Ash-shu'r is the plural of ash'ar, like hamr and ahmar. Ar-riqab is a definite specification according to the opinion of the Kufans. Ash'ar ar-raqaba is used for the lion, and for the back of the neck, which is the intended meaning here. He says: "My people are not these base ones; I am from the sons of Lu'ayy." "If you ask" is an interjection between the subject and its predicate. "Mudar" and "as-sawab" (the right course) are two objects of "alamu" (they taught).

Ajabb az-zahr laysa lahu sanam (a back cut off, with no hump):

"If Abu Qabus perishes, then perish
the spring of the people and the sacred month.
And after him we take hold of the thin remnant of life,
a back cut off, with no hump."

This is by an-Nabigha adh-Dhubyani, lamenting an-Nu'man al-Ma'afi ibn al-Harith al-Asghar, king of the Arabs. It has been said that it was said about Jarir, but that is not correct. He means: if the death of an-Nu'man becomes certain, the death of the spring of the people becomes certain. He likened him to the spring, which is rain, or a river, or the season of spring, or fertility, in that each of them benefits all the people. He likened him to the sacred month in that each is security for the people from wars and fears. It is also narrated: "and the sacred land" (al-balad al-haram), meaning Makkah, likening him to it also in security.

It is also possible that the meaning is: if he perishes, his generosity and his standing, which are like the spring and the sacred month in benefit and security, perish after him. All of this is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). It is also possible that he used to guard their spring from others' pasturing and the sanctity of their month from violation, by defending them in it, so there is a metaphor only in the perishing of the month. It is narrated as "nata'khudh" with the three vowel endings. Likewise every imperfect verb coordinated with the answer of a conditional: jazm (apocopation) is by coordination, raf' (nominative) is by resumption (isti'naf), and nasb (accusative) is by an implied "an" because the conditional resembles negation, but this is rare. Adh-dhanab (with a kasra) is the tail of a camel or horse, and the end of everything. The hard, narrow, deficient life is likened to a emaciated camel by way of implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya). Adh-dhanab, az-zahr, and as-sanam (with a fatha) are an imaginative image (takhyil). "Ajabb az-zahr" means one whose back is cut off, i.e. "we hold on after him to a remnant of life, narrow and little, like a camel whose back is cut off," and he explained this by saying: "it has no hump." "Ajabb" is a qualitative adjective (sifa mushabbaha), not declined, so it takes a fatha in the genitive as an adjective of "'aysh" (life). It has also been said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is narrated in the nominative as predicate of an omitted subject, and "az-zahr" is narrated in the nominative as the subject of the adjective, or as a substitute for the pronoun in it. The grammarians pronounced it with a fatha, and in the accusative as resembling an object or a specification according to the view of those who allow definite specification, which they considered weak. In the genitive by annexation of "ajabb" to it, so "ajabb" takes a kasra, and they considered this good.

It has also been said that its meaning is: "he degraded himself," with the preposition omitted, as in the saying "Zayd is present in my opinion" (zanni), meaning "in my opinion." The first explanation is the better one. It is sufficient evidence for it what has come in the hadith:

Al-Bazzar narrated it through Ibn Ishaq from Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Umar: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that a man prepares food and people gather around him, or that he wears a clean shirt?" He said: "That is not pride. Pride is to belittle the truth and to despise people." And he mentioned a story in it. He said: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it from Amr from Ibn Umar except Ibn Ishaq."

At-Tabarani narrated it through Ibn Ishaq from Amr ibn Dinar from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that I wear a good garment? He said: No. I said: Then what is pride? and he mentioned it." Al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, through as-Sa'b ibn Zuhayr from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "We do not know it except from Ata ibn Yasar from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: 'A man came and said: O Messenger of Allah, is pride that one of us has a garment that he wears? He said: No... the hadith.'" He also narrated it through Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad, and al-Bazzar narrated it through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Sabra. Ahmad narrated it in az-Zuhd through Hisham ibn Sa'd, all of them from Zayd with the same. Abd ibn Humayd said in his Musnad: "Abdullah ibn Musa informed us from Musa ibn Ubayda from Zayd ibn Aslam from Jabir," and mentioned a hadith in which: Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that one of us has a mount that he rides, or sandals, or clothes that he wears, or food around which his companions gather?" He said: "No. But pride is to belittle the truth and to despise the believers." Musa is weak.

In at-Tabarani, through Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, from Imarah ibn Ghaziyya, from Fatima bint al-Husayn, from her father, that Abdullah ibn Amr said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that I wear a fine robe? The hadith." At-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat and Musnad ash-Shamiyyin from Ata al-Khurasani from Nafi from Ibn Umar, similarly. On the topic there is also from Abu Hurayra, narrated by Ibn Hibban and "wa akhikum" (your brother) through Ibn Sirin from him; from Ibn Mas'ud, narrated by Ishaq, Abu Ya'la and al-Hakim: that Malik ibn Murara ar-Rahawi said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have of beauty what you see, and I do not like anyone to surpass me with two shirak (sandals/shoe straps?) or more. Is this from transgression?" He said: "No. The hadith." And from Abu Rayhana, narrated by Ahmad and at-Tabarani. From Thabit ibn Qays, narrated by ad-Darimi and at-Tabarani.

And from Sawda ibn Amr and al-Husayn ibn Ali, both narrated by at-Tabarani. From Ibn Abbas, narrated by Abd ibn Humayd. From Uqba ibn Amir, narrated by Abu Muslim in al-Jami' from his Sunan.

"Pride is that you belittle the truth and despise people." [Note: "wa tughammis an-nas" means: you belittle them and find fault with them. Explained by as-Sihah (Ibn Hammad/al-Jawhari).]

This is because when one turns away from what no sensible person ever turns away from, he has gone to great lengths in degrading his soul [i.e., "idhalat nafsihi" means humiliating it, explained by as-Sihah] and making it powerless, since he has opposed with it every soul in its outcome.

﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ﴾: an explanation of the error of the one who turns away from his religion, because whoever has gathered honour with Allah in both abodes, by being His choice and best in this world, and being witnessed to be steadfast in good in the next, no one is more deserving of following his way than he.

﴿إِذْ قَالَ﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) of "we chose him," meaning: We chose him at that time. Or it is in the accusative by an implied "udhkur" (remember), as evidence for what has been mentioned of his condition, as if it were said: remember that time, so that you know that he is the chosen, righteous one, who does not turn away from the religion of one like him. The meaning of "He said to him: Submit" is that it brought to his mind the consideration of the proofs leading to knowledge and Islam. ﴿قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ﴾: meaning he reflected and came to know.

It has also been said: "Aslim" means: submit and obey. It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salama and Muhajir, to Islam, and said to them: "We know that Allah the Exalted said in the Torah: I will send from the offspring of Isma'il a prophet named Ahmad. Whoever believes in him has been guided and rightly guided, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed." So Salama embraced Islam, but Muhajir refused to embrace it, and then the verse was revealed.
