in Makkah they taught Mudar the right course."

This is by al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Murri, who claimed to be from Quraysh, saying that his mother took him out to Murra when he was young, and so he was ascribed to them. Tha'laba, Fazara and Mudar are names of tribes. Tha'laba is described as "son of" (ibn) her, because it is the ancestral name of the tribe's founder. Ash-shu'r is the plural of ash'ar, like hamr and ahmar. Ar-riqab is a definite specification according to the opinion of the Kufans. Ash'ar ar-raqaba is used for the lion, and for the back of the neck, which is the intended meaning here. He says: "My people are not these base ones; I am from the sons of Lu'ayy." "If you ask" is an interjection between the subject and its predicate. "Mudar" and "as-sawab" (the right course) are two objects of "alamu" (they taught).

Ajabb az-zahr laysa lahu sanam (a back cut off, with no hump):

"If Abu Qabus perishes, then perish
the spring of the people and the sacred month.
And after him we take hold of the thin remnant of life,
a back cut off, with no hump."

This is by an-Nabigha adh-Dhubyani, lamenting an-Nu'man al-Ma'afi ibn al-Harith al-Asghar, king of the Arabs. It has been said that it was said about Jarir, but that is not correct. He means: if the death of an-Nu'man becomes certain, the death of the spring of the people becomes certain. He likened him to the spring, which is rain, or a river, or the season of spring, or fertility, in that each of them benefits all the people. He likened him to the sacred month in that each is security for the people from wars and fears. It is also narrated: "and the sacred land" (al-balad al-haram), meaning Makkah, likening him to it also in security.

It is also possible that the meaning is: if he perishes, his generosity and his standing, which are like the spring and the sacred month in benefit and security, perish after him. All of this is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). It is also possible that he used to guard their spring from others' pasturing and the sanctity of their month from violation, by defending them in it, so there is a metaphor only in the perishing of the month. It is narrated as "nata'khudh" with the three vowel endings. Likewise every imperfect verb coordinated with the answer of a conditional: jazm (apocopation) is by coordination, raf' (nominative) is by resumption (isti'naf), and nasb (accusative) is by an implied "an" because the conditional resembles negation, but this is rare. Adh-dhanab (with a kasra) is the tail of a camel or horse, and the end of everything. The hard, narrow, deficient life is likened to a emaciated camel by way of implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya). Adh-dhanab, az-zahr, and as-sanam (with a fatha) are an imaginative image (takhyil). "Ajabb az-zahr" means one whose back is cut off, i.e. "we hold on after him to a remnant of life, narrow and little, like a camel whose back is cut off," and he explained this by saying: "it has no hump." "Ajabb" is a qualitative adjective (sifa mushabbaha), not declined, so it takes a fatha in the genitive as an adjective of "'aysh" (life). It has also been said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is narrated in the nominative as predicate of an omitted subject, and "az-zahr" is narrated in the nominative as the subject of the adjective, or as a substitute for the pronoun in it. The grammarians pronounced it with a fatha, and in the accusative as resembling an object or a specification according to the view of those who allow definite specification, which they considered weak. In the genitive by annexation of "ajabb" to it, so "ajabb" takes a kasra, and they considered this good.

It has also been said that its meaning is: "he degraded himself," with the preposition omitted, as in the saying "Zayd is present in my opinion" (zanni), meaning "in my opinion." The first explanation is the better one. It is sufficient evidence for it what has come in the hadith:

Al-Bazzar narrated it through Ibn Ishaq from Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Umar: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that a man prepares food and people gather around him, or that he wears a clean shirt?" He said: "That is not pride. Pride is to belittle the truth and to despise people." And he mentioned a story in it. He said: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it from Amr from Ibn Umar except Ibn Ishaq."

At-Tabarani narrated it through Ibn Ishaq from Amr ibn Dinar from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that I wear a good garment? He said: No. I said: Then what is pride? and he mentioned it." Al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, through as-Sa'b ibn Zuhayr from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "We do not know it except from Ata ibn Yasar from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: 'A man came and said: O Messenger of Allah, is pride that one of us has a garment that he wears? He said: No... the hadith.'" He also narrated it through Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad, and al-Bazzar narrated it through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Sabra. Ahmad narrated it in az-Zuhd through Hisham ibn Sa'd, all of them from Zayd with the same. Abd ibn Humayd said in his Musnad: "Abdullah ibn Musa informed us from Musa ibn Ubayda from Zayd ibn Aslam from Jabir," and mentioned a hadith in which: Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that one of us has a mount that he rides, or sandals, or clothes that he wears, or food around which his companions gather?" He said: "No. But pride is to belittle the truth and to despise the believers." Musa is weak.

In at-Tabarani, through Abd al-Hamid ibn Sulayman, from Imarah ibn Ghaziyya, from Fatima bint al-Husayn, from her father, that Abdullah ibn Amr said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it pride that I wear a fine robe? The hadith." At-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat and Musnad ash-Shamiyyin from Ata al-Khurasani from Nafi from Ibn Umar, similarly. On the topic there is also from Abu Hurayra, narrated by Ibn Hibban and "wa akhikum" (your brother) through Ibn Sirin from him; from Ibn Mas'ud, narrated by Ishaq, Abu Ya'la and al-Hakim: that Malik ibn Murara ar-Rahawi said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have of beauty what you see, and I do not like anyone to surpass me with two shirak (sandals/shoe straps?) or more. Is this from transgression?" He said: "No. The hadith." And from Abu Rayhana, narrated by Ahmad and at-Tabarani. From Thabit ibn Qays, narrated by ad-Darimi and at-Tabarani.

And from Sawda ibn Amr and al-Husayn ibn Ali, both narrated by at-Tabarani. From Ibn Abbas, narrated by Abd ibn Humayd. From Uqba ibn Amir, narrated by Abu Muslim in al-Jami' from his Sunan.

"Pride is that you belittle the truth and despise people." [Note: "wa tughammis an-nas" means: you belittle them and find fault with them. Explained by as-Sihah (Ibn Hammad/al-Jawhari).]

This is because when one turns away from what no sensible person ever turns away from, he has gone to great lengths in degrading his soul [i.e., "idhalat nafsihi" means humiliating it, explained by as-Sihah] and making it powerless, since he has opposed with it every soul in its outcome.

﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ﴾: an explanation of the error of the one who turns away from his religion, because whoever has gathered honour with Allah in both abodes, by being His choice and best in this world, and being witnessed to be steadfast in good in the next, no one is more deserving of following his way than he.

﴿إِذْ قَالَ﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) of "we chose him," meaning: We chose him at that time. Or it is in the accusative by an implied "udhkur" (remember), as evidence for what has been mentioned of his condition, as if it were said: remember that time, so that you know that he is the chosen, righteous one, who does not turn away from the religion of one like him. The meaning of "He said to him: Submit" is that it brought to his mind the consideration of the proofs leading to knowledge and Islam. ﴿قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ﴾: meaning he reflected and came to know.

It has also been said: "Aslim" means: submit and obey. It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salama and Muhajir, to Islam, and said to them: "We know that Allah the Exalted said in the Torah: I will send from the offspring of Isma'il a prophet named Ahmad. Whoever believes in him has been guided and rightly guided, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed." So Salama embraced Islam, but Muhajir refused to embrace it, and then the verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 132:

It is recited as "wa-awsa" (and he enjoined), and this is the reading in the codices of the people of the Hijaz and Syria. The pronoun in "bihā" (by it) refers to the statement "aslamtu li-rabb al-ʿalamīn" (I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds), interpreted as a word and a sentence. Similar to this is the return of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾ [43:28] to His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who originated me﴾ [43:26–27]. And His saying "kalimatan bāqiyatan" (a lasting word) is evidence that the feminine form is in accordance with the interpretation of "word." "Yaʿqūb" is conjoined to Ibrahim and falls under his ruling. The meaning is: Yaʿqub also enjoined it upon his sons.

It is also recited as "wa-Yaʿqūba" (in the accusative), conjoined to "banīhi" (his sons). Its meaning: Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons and upon his grandson Yaʿqub, "yā baniyya" (O my sons), with the verb of saying implied according to the Basrans. According to the Kufans, it is connected to "wa-awsā," because it carries the sense of saying.

Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"Two men of Dabba informed us... that we saw a naked man"
[Note: "rajulān" is with a sukun for lightness and metre, as "ʿaḍd" is also made sukun. "Ḍabba" is the name of a tribe. It is also narrated with "min Makka" instead of it. The verb "akhbarā" carries the sense of saying, which is why "inna" is kasra after it, by way of direct quotation, i.e., they said that statement to us, which is: "innā raʾaynā" (we saw). The view of the Kufans is that the quoted clause is in the place of accusative by the mentioned verb. The view of the Basrans is that it is by an implied saying. Some of them said: the apparent meaning is that it is explanatory, so it has no place in i'rab, and it is narrated with fatha by omitting the preposition, i.e., "bi-annā raʾaynā" (that we saw).]

With kasra on the hamza: it is, according to us, by an implied "qāla" (he said), and according to them, it is connected to the verb of informing. In the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud: "anna yā banayya, iṣṭafā lakumu l-dīn" (that, O my sons, He has chosen for you the religion), i.e., He has given you the religion, which is the choicest of religions, and it is the religion of Islam, and He has guided you to adopt it.

"Fa-lā tamūtunna" (so do not die except...): its meaning is: let your death be only in a state in which you are steadfast upon Islam. So the prohibition is in reality against their being in a condition contrary to the state of Islam when they die, like your saying: "Do not pray except while humble," where you are not forbidding prayer but forbidding the abandonment of humility in the state of prayer. If you ask: what is the point of attaching the particle of prohibition to prayer when it is not something prohibited? I say: its point is to show that a prayer without humility is as no prayer at all, as if he said: "I forbid you from it if you do not pray it in this state." Do you not see the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no prayer for the neighbour of the mosque except in the mosque" [[narrated by al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim from the narration of Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, in which is Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Yamani, who is weak; and al-Daraqutni, Ibn ʿAdi and al-ʿUqayli from a hadith of Jabir, in which is Muhammad ibn Miskin, who is weak; and Ibn Hibban mentioned it in al-Duʿafāʾ in the biography of ʿUmar ibn Rashid, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha, and said: ʿUmar ibn Rashid used to fabricate hadith. It is authentically reported as a statement of ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba]], for it is like an explicit statement to the neighbour of the mosque: "Do not pray except in the mosque."

Likewise, the meaning in the verse is to show that their dying in a state other than steadfastness upon Islam is a death with no good in it, that it is not the death of the blessed, and that it is fitting that such a death should not befall them. You also say in the imperative: "Die while you are a martyr." You do not mean commanding death, but commanding being in the attribute of the martyrs when one dies; you only commanded him to die out of your high regard for his death and to show its superiority over others, and that it is worthy of being urged upon.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 133:

﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ — "أم" here is "al-munqati'a" (the disjunctive "am"), and the explanation of it is "bal" and the hamza. (ʿA.) The meaning of the hamza in it is denial (al-inkar). "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid", in the sense of "present": that is, you were not present with Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, when death attended him, i.e. at the time he was dying, and the address is to the believers, in the sense: you did not witness that. [Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "The address in it is to the believers, in the sense that you did not witness ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may God have mercy on him, said: He only chose, according to this interpretation, that it be connected (muttasila), because if he had made it disjunctive as in the first case, the content of the speech would be a negation of the witnessing of the addressees, who are the Jews, according to this second interpretation, of the death of Yaʿqub and his charge concerning Islam; and then that would be like establishing their proof against their denial of Islam and their rejection that the prophets were Muslims, whereas the purpose is the opposite of that. The speech only required negation in that case because a question from God, exalted is He, is not taken at its apparent meaning, so it is necessarily diverted to denial, since the context requires it. For this reason it was a negation of the witnessing of the Muslims of Yaʿqub's death and his charge according to the first interpretation, especially since the usual practice is to address the contemporary Jews of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with what is addressed to their forebears, treating their knowledge and their approval as their presence and participation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ and ﴿And when you said, O Musa﴾, and similar to that. So if "am" is connected and the address is to the Jews, the matter in addressing them proceeds as usual; and if it is disjunctive, the matter is reversed.] Rather, knowledge of it came to you only through revelation. It has also been said that the address is to the Jews, because they used to say: No prophet died except upon Judaism. However, had they witnessed it and heard what he said to his sons and what they said, the zeal of his adherence to the religion of Islam would have become apparent to them, and they would not have claimed Judaism for him. So the verse contradicts their claim; how then can it be said to them: "Or were you witnesses?" But the better view is that "am" is connected, on the basis that something omitted is presumed before it, as if it were said: Do you attribute Judaism to the prophets? Or were you witnesses when Yaʿqub was attended by death? That is, your forefathers from the Children of Israel were witnesses to him when he charged his sons with monotheism and the religion of Islam, and you know that; so what is the matter with you that you attribute to the prophets what they are innocent of?

And it was read "ḥaḍara" with a kasra on the ḍad, and it is a dialect form.

﴿What do you worship﴾: "ma" here means "what thing do you worship?" The "ma" is general for everything; so when the one who knows is distinguished, one says "man" (who), and what is sufficient as evidence for you is the saying of the scholars: "man" is for the one who has reason. Had it been said "man taʿbudun" (who do you worship), it would not have been general except for those possessing knowledge alone. It is also permissible to say that ﴿mā taʿbudūn﴾ is a question about the attribute of the worshipped, as you say: "Mā Zayd?" meaning: is he a jurist, or a physician, or other attributes?

﴿Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ are an explanatory appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to "your fathers". Isma'il, who was his paternal uncle, was counted among his fathers, because the paternal uncle is a father and the maternal aunt is a mother, since they are joined in one category, which is brotherhood, with no difference between them. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father" [agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, concerning the story of al-ʿAbbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid and Ibn Jamil when they refused to give the zakat], meaning there is no difference between them, just as there is no difference between the two shoots of a palm. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, said concerning al-ʿAbbas: "This is the remnant [of my fathers]" [narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba: Ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us from Dawud ibn Sabur from Mujahid, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Guard me in regard to al-ʿAbbas, for he is the remnant of my fathers, and the paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father." It was also narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat from the narration of Musa ibn ʿAbdullah ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan from his father from his grandfather from al-Hasan from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: "Guard me," and he mentioned the like of it; and it was narrated in al-Kabir from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas by two routes.] "my fathers", and he said: "Return my father to me, for I fear that Quraysh will do to him what Thaqif did to ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud" [Ibn Abi Shayba said in his Maghazi in his Musannaf: Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us from Ayyub, from ʿIkrima, who said: "When the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, made a truce with the people of Makkah..." to his saying: "al-ʿAbbas went and mounted the Messenger of God's mule, al-Shahba', and set off to Quraysh to invite them to God, but he was delayed. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Return my father to me, for the paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father. I fear that Quraysh will do to him what Thaqif did to ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud, who invited them to God, and they killed him. By God, if they mount it, it would be more harmful to them in fire."]

And Ubayy read: ﴿wa-ilaha ibrahima wa-isma'ila wa-ishaqa﴾ with the omission of "your fathers" [ʿAbāʾika]. And it was read "abīka" (your father, singular). In it there are two possibilities: that it be singular, and Ibrahim alone is the explanatory appositive to it; or that it be plural with the sound masculine plural (wāw and nūn). A poet said:

*"Fa-lammā tabayyana aṣwātanā... bakayna wa-fadaynanā bil-ābīnā"*
[When our voices became distinct (to them in war)... they wept and ransomed us with the fathers.]

He says: when the women recognised our voices in war and knew them, they wept out of compassion for us and mercy toward us, and "fadaynanā" means each one would say: "My father is your ransom," or she would say to her companion: "My father is your ransom." "Al-ābīnā" is the plural of "ab", declined as a sound plural.

﴿ilaha wahidan﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "ilah ābā'ika", like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾, or it is in the sense of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: by "the God of your fathers" we intend one God. ﴿And we are to Him Muslims﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "naʿbudu", or from its object, since the pronoun returns to it in "lahu". It is also permissible that it be a clause conjoined to "naʿbudu", and that it be a parenthetical emphatic clause, meaning: and of our state is that we are to Him Muslims, sincere in monotheism, or submissive.

That is a reference to the community mentioned, namely Abraham, Jacob and their descendants, the monotheists. The meaning is: no one benefits from the deeds of another, whether he came earlier or later. Just as those people benefit only from what they themselves earned, so too you benefit only from what you yourselves earn. This is because they took pride in their forefathers. A similar statement is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Banu Hashim, people will not come to me with their deeds while you come to me with your lineages." [[I have not found it.]] ﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾, and you will not be held accountable for their misdeeds, just as their good deeds will not benefit you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 135:

﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾ (*bal milata Ibrahim*): the meaning is "rather, let there be the religion of Ibrahim," i.e., the people of his religion (*ahl millatih*), as in the saying of ʿAdi ibn Hatim: "I am from the religion (*din*)" [[Ibn Saʿd transmitted it through Ibn Sirin from Abu ʿUbayda ibn Hudhayfa. He said: ʿAdi ibn Hatim said, and then he mentioned the story of his conversion. In it, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O ʿAdi, submit (*aslim*) and you will be safe." He said: "I am from a religion." He (ﷺ) said: "I know your religion better than you do."]], meaning: "from among the people of a religion." It was also said: "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim."

It is also recited as *millatu Ibrahima* with a *raf* (nominative) vowel, meaning: his religion is our religion, or our affair is his religion, or we are his religion in the sense of the people of his religion.

﴿Hanifan﴾ (*hanifan*) is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier, indicating the state of the subject at the time of the action) of the *mudaf ilayhi* (the genitive complement of the construct phrase), as in your saying: "I saw the face of Hind, facing (*qaʾimatan*)."

The *hanif* is one who inclines away from every false religion toward the religion of truth. The *hanf* is inward turning of the feet, and *tahannafa* means he inclined. The poet said:

*"But we were created, when we were created, / inclining (hanifan), our religion turning away from every religion."*

[[The *hanf* and *tahannuf* mean inclination. The *hanif* is one who inclines away from falsehood toward truth. He says: we were created in a state in which we were inclining, our religion turning away from all false religions toward the religion of our father Ibrahim, because the Arabs agreed that it is true; and that is from the time of the beginning of our creation. So "idha" (when) is a *zarf* (adverbial of time) for the first creation, after being qualified by the *hal* that follows it.]]

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ (*wa ma kana min al-mushrikin*): this is an allusion (*taʿrid*) directed at the People of the Book and others, because each of them claims to follow Ibrahim while being on polytheism.

﴿Say﴾ (*qulu*): this is addressed to the believers. It is also permissible that it is addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: say it so that you may be upon the truth, otherwise you are upon falsehood. Likewise his saying ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾ may be understood as: "rather, you follow the religion of Ibrahim," or "become the people of his religion."

Al-sibt: the grandson (al-hafid). Al-Hasan and al-Husayn were the two grandsons of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Al-asbat" are the descendants of Ya'qub's (Jacob's) children, the offspring of his twelve sons. "We make no distinction between any of them": we do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. The word "ahad" (any one) carries the sense of a group. [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Ahad, in the sense of a group..." etc. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is evidence that an indefinite noun appearing in a negative context denotes generality verbally, so that the singular in it is treated like the plural in encompassing the individuals by direct implication, not as some of the usulis believed, that its signification by direct implication in negation is like its signification in affirmation. That signification is the reference to the quiddity (mahiyya). Generality is necessarily entailed in it because negating the quiddity requires negating the individuals, since, between the more general and the more specific, there is a mutual entailment on the side of negation: negating the more general is more specific than negating the less specific, so it entails it. Thus, if a word did not by its imposition indicate plurality and generality, it would not be permissible for "bayn" (between) to be attached to it.]]

For this reason it is correct for "bayn" to be attached to it, in "in the likeness of what you believed in," as a rebuke, because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾. So there is no other religion that resembles the religion of Islam in being true, such that if they believed in that resembling religion they would be guided. It was said: "If they believe" is an expression of doubt, used on the basis of supposition and assumption, meaning: if they attain another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and correctness, then they have been guided. In this there is the point that their religion, which they hold, and every religion other than it, differ from it and are not like it, because it is truth and guidance, and what is other than it is falsehood and misguidance. A similar example is your saying to a man whom you advise: "This is the correct opinion; if you have an opinion more correct than it, act upon it. You know that no opinion is more correct than yours." But you intend to rebuke your companion and to make him realize that what he has seen has no opinion beyond it.

It is also permissible that the "ba'" is not superfluous (sila), but is the "ba'" of instrumentality (isti'ana), as in your saying: "I wrote with the pen," and "I worked with the adze." That is: if they enter into faith with a testimony like your testimony by which you believed. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read: "bima amantum bihi" (by what you believed in), and Ubayy read: "bil-ladhi amantum bihi" (by that which you believed in). "And if they turn away": from what you say to them, and they do not act justly, "then they are only in dissension," i.e., in opposition and obstinacy, "and they are not in pursuit of the truth at all." Or: "And if they turn away" from the testimony and from entering into faith in it, "then Allah will suffice you against them," a guarantee from Allah for the manifestation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over them; and He fulfilled His promise by killing the Banu Qurayzah and taking their women and children captive, and by expelling the Banu al-Nadir. The meaning of the "sin" (in "sayakfikahum") is that this is certain to happen without doubt, even if it is delayed for a time. "And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing": a threat to them, i.e., He hears what they utter and knows what they conceal of envy and rancor, and He will requite them for it. Or it is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: He hears what you supplicate with and knows your intention and what you desire of manifesting the religion of truth, and He answers you and brings you to your aim.

Al-sibt: the grandson (al-hafid). Al-Hasan and al-Husayn were the two grandsons of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Al-asbat" are the descendants of Ya'qub's (Jacob's) children, the offspring of his twelve sons. "We make no distinction between any of them": we do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. The word "ahad" (any one) carries the sense of a group. [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Ahad, in the sense of a group..." etc. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is evidence that an indefinite noun appearing in a negative context denotes generality verbally, so that the singular in it is treated like the plural in encompassing the individuals by direct implication, not as some of the usulis believed, that its signification by direct implication in negation is like its signification in affirmation. That signification is the reference to the quiddity (mahiyya). Generality is necessarily entailed in it because negating the quiddity requires negating the individuals, since, between the more general and the more specific, there is a mutual entailment on the side of negation: negating the more general is more specific than negating the less specific, so it entails it. Thus, if a word did not by its imposition indicate plurality and generality, it would not be permissible for "bayn" (between) to be attached to it.]]

For this reason it is correct for "bayn" to be attached to it, in "in the likeness of what you believed in," as a rebuke, because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾. So there is no other religion that resembles the religion of Islam in being true, such that if they believed in that resembling religion they would be guided. It was said: "If they believe" is an expression of doubt, used on the basis of supposition and assumption, meaning: if they attain another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and correctness, then they have been guided. In this there is the point that their religion, which they hold, and every religion other than it, differ from it and are not like it, because it is truth and guidance, and what is other than it is falsehood and misguidance. A similar example is your saying to a man whom you advise: "This is the correct opinion; if you have an opinion more correct than it, act upon it. You know that no opinion is more correct than yours." But you intend to rebuke your companion and to make him realize that what he has seen has no opinion beyond it.

It is also permissible that the "ba'" is not superfluous (sila), but is the "ba'" of instrumentality (isti'ana), as in your saying: "I wrote with the pen," and "I worked with the adze." That is: if they enter into faith with a testimony like your testimony by which you believed. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read: "bima amantum bihi" (by what you believed in), and Ubayy read: "bil-ladhi amantum bihi" (by that which you believed in). "And if they turn away": from what you say to them, and they do not act justly, "then they are only in dissension," i.e., in opposition and obstinacy, "and they are not in pursuit of the truth at all." Or: "And if they turn away" from the testimony and from entering into faith in it, "then Allah will suffice you against them," a guarantee from Allah for the manifestation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over them; and He fulfilled His promise by killing the Banu Qurayzah and taking their women and children captive, and by expelling the Banu al-Nadir. The meaning of the "sin" (in "sayakfikahum") is that this is certain to happen without doubt, even if it is delayed for a time. "And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing": a threat to them, i.e., He hears what they utter and knows what they conceal of envy and rancor, and He will requite them for it. Or it is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: He hears what you supplicate with and knows your intention and what you desire of manifesting the religion of truth, and He answers you and brings you to your aim.

Ṣibghata Allāh (the dye of God): a emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu’akkad) in the accusative, governed by His saying, "We believe in God" (āmannā billāh), just as "the promise of God" (waʿd Allāh) is in the accusative by what precedes it. It is on the pattern fiʿla from ṣabagha, like jilsa from jalasa, and denotes the state in which dyeing takes place. The meaning is: the purification of God, because faith purifies souls.

The background to this is that the Christians used to immerse their children in a yellow water which they called the maʿmūdiyya (baptism), and they would say, "It is a purification for them." When one of them did this to his child, he would say, "Now he has truly become a Christian." So the Muslims were commanded to say to them: "Say: We believe in God, and God has dyed us with faith, a dye unlike your dye, and has purified us with it, a purification unlike your purification." Or the Muslims would say: "God has dyed us with faith, His dye, and we did not dye ourselves with your dye."

The word ṣibgha was used by way of mushākala (matching of expression), as when you say to someone who plants trees, "Plant as so-and-so plants," meaning a man who cultivates vineyards. "And who is better than God in dyeing (ṣibgha)?" means that He dyes His servants with faith and purifies them with it from the filth of disbelief, so there is no dye better than His dye.

His saying, "And we are worshippers of Him" (wa naḥnu lahu ʿābidūn), is a conjunction upon "We believe in God." This conjunction refutes the view of those who claimed that "the dye of God" is a substitute for "the religion of Abraham" or an accusative governed by an incitement (al-ighrā’) meaning: "Upon you is the dye of God," because that disrupts the arrangement of the discourse and removes it from its coherence and connection, [[The saying "wa-ittisāquh" in the Ṣiḥāḥ: al-ittisāq is al-intiẓām (orderliness). And also in it: al-tansīq is al-tanẓīm (organisation). (ʿ)]] and its being in the accusative as a emphatic verbal noun is what Sībawayh mentioned. "And the saying is what Ḥidhām said."

Zayd ibn Thabit recited ﴿atuḥājjūnā﴾ (the Arabic reading "a-tuḥājjūnanā," meaning "Do you dispute with us?") with *idgham* (assimilation of the nun into the following letter). The meaning is: Do you dispute with us about God and His choosing of the Prophet from among the Arabs rather than from among you? You say, "If God had sent down revelation to anyone, He would have sent it down to us," and you consider yourselves more deserving of prophethood than us. ﴿He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: we share together in being His servants, and He is our Lord. ﴿He bestows His mercy and honour on whom He wills among His servants﴾. They have no say in this, and no non-Arab is excluded from it over an Arab if he is worthy of honour. ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾: that is, deeds are the foundation of the matter and the basis of judgement. Just as you have deeds which God takes into account in granting or withholding honour, so do we. Then He said, ﴿and we are sincere to Him﴾, mentioning what is the cause of honour. That is: we profess His unity (*tawhid*) and make Him sincere through faith, so do not find it unlikely that the people of His sincerity should be qualified for His honour of prophethood. They used to say, "We are more deserving that prophethood should be among us, because we are People of the Book, while the Arabs are idol-worshippers."

﴿Or do you say...﴾: in the case of the one who read with the *ta'* (second person), *am* may be a connective (*mu'adilah*) corresponding to the *hamzah* in "a-tuḥājjūnanā," meaning: which of the two things do you do, dispute concerning God's wisdom, or claim that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, were Jews or Christians? The intent of questioning about both is to deny both together. It may also be disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), meaning "Rather, do you say...?" with the *hamzah* also expressing denial. For the one who read with the *ya'* (third person), it can only be disjunctive. ﴿Say: "Are you more knowing, or is God?"﴾ That is, God testified on their behalf to the religion of Islam in His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a *hanif*, a Muslim﴾. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony from God which he has?﴾ That is, who conceals the testimony of God which is with him, that He testified to it, and it is His testimony to Abraham's *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheism). There are two possible meanings. The first: no one is more unjust than the People of the Book, because they concealed this testimony while knowing it. The second: if we were to conceal this testimony, no one would be more unjust than we are, so we shall not conceal it. In it is an allusion to their concealment of God's testimony to Muhammad (ﷺ) as a prophet in their books, and other testimonies. The *min* in ﴿a testimony from God which he has﴾ is like it in your saying, "This is a testimony from me to so-and-so," when you testify on his behalf, and similarly ﴿a declaration of disavowal from God and His Messenger﴾.

The foolish ones (al-sufaha’), the light-minded, will say, and they are the Jews, out of their dislike of turning toward the Kaaba, and because they do not accept abrogation (naskh, the replacing of one ruling by a later one). It has also been said that they are the hypocrites, out of their eagerness to find fault and to mock. And it has been said that they are the polytheists, who said: "He has turned away from the qibla of his fathers and then returned to it. By Allah, he will return to their religion."

If you ask: what is the benefit of reporting their saying before it occurs? I answer: its benefit is that the shock of an unwanted event is greater, while knowing of it before it happens lessens the disturbance when it does occur, because of the preparation of the soul that precedes it. Also, a ready answer given before there is need for it is more decisive against the opponent and more effective in repelling his clamor. This is like "before shooting, the arrow is fletched."

﴿The foolish will say: what has turned them away from their qibla?﴾ The qibla here is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿To Allah belong the East and the West.﴾ That is, the lands of the East and the West, and the whole earth. ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ of its people ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is what wisdom and benefit require, by directing them at one time to Bayt al-Maqdis and at another to the Kaaba.

﴿And thus We have made you﴾, that is, by a similar wondrous making, ﴿a middle community (ummah wasatan)﴾, that is, the best. It is a description by the noun that means the middle of a thing, which is why the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine are all the same in it.

A similar saying is the Prophet’s (ﷺ) words: "Give the thabjah," where the thabjah is the middle one between the fat and the lean, described by thabj, which is the middle of the back. But he added the feminine ta’ marbuta in observance of the description. It has also been said that the best is called "middle" (wasat), because the extremities are where defects quickly appear, while the middles are protected and enclosed. From this is the verse of al-Ta’i:

"She was the protected middle, but calamities surrounded her
until she became an extremity."

These are lines of Abu Tammam addressing al-Mu’tasim. The ghayda is a place where water gathers, then drains away, and plants grow in it. Here it means the site of the army. The Bidh is the name of a fortress of Babak al-Khurrami. The ‘armarim is a large army. Khurud al-ard are its paths. The mu’tasif is one who deviates from the road because of its crowds. He compared that place to a ghayda by way of mockery of its occupants, since such places are attributed to water, and he attributed it to death. He compared the army in its obedience to camels, in the figure of the metaphor (al-makniyya), and "guided" is an imaginative image. He referred to the middle by what cannot be reached by defect, because it is protected by its extremities, so the calamities surrounded it, meaning the armies of al-Mu’tasim, until that ghayda became an extremity and the defects and hardships of the army reached it.

I once hired in Mecca an Arab's camel for the pilgrimage, and he said: "Give me of their sataat," meaning of the best dinars.

Or it means "just" (‘udulan), because the middle is a balance between the extremities, not closer to one of them than to the other. ﴿So that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. It is related that "on the Day of Resurrection the nations will deny that the prophets conveyed the message. Allah will then ask the prophets for proof that they had conveyed it, though He knows best. The community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and will testify. The nations will say: ‘How do you know?’ They will say: ‘We know it through the information of Allah in His Book, the speaking one, upon the tongue of His truthful Prophet.’ Then Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the state of his community. He will vouch for them and bear witness after doubt."

[Report: transmitted by al-Tabari from Zayd ibn Aslam as a statement of a Companion (mawquf). It is also reported in the Tafsir of al-Nasa’i as a statement of al-Suddi.

In al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Sa’id al-Khudri: "Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say: ‘At your service, O Lord.’ He will be asked: ‘Did you convey?’ He will say: ‘Yes.’ His people will be asked: ‘Did he convey to you?’ They will say: ‘No warner came to us.’ He will be asked: ‘Who will bear witness for you?’ He will say: ‘Muhammad and his community.’ They will bear witness that he conveyed." Then he recited: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi related in al-Ba’th wa al-Nushur, through Abu Mu’awiya from al-A’mash from Abu Salih from Abu Sa’id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A Prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection with three or four or two men with him, and a Prophet will come with no one with him. Then the community of Muhammad will be called, and they will testify that they conveyed. It will be said to them: ‘How do you know that they conveyed?’ They will say: ‘Our Messenger came to us with a Book, which informed us that they had conveyed, so we believed him.’ It will be said: ‘You have spoken truly.’" That is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community﴾.]

That is the Almighty’s saying: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ If you ask: why was it not said "a witness for you," since his testimony is for them and not against them? I answer: because the witness is like the watcher and the guardian over the one to whom testimony is given, the preposition "over" (‘ala) was used. From this is the saying of Allah: ﴿And Allah is witness over all things﴾, and ﴿You were the watcher over them, and You are witness over all things.﴾

It has been said: that you may be witnesses over the people in this world, in matters that are valid only by the testimony of upright and righteous men. ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾, purifying you and knowing of your uprightness.

If you ask: why was the complement of "witness" placed first in the first case and last in the second? I answer: because the favor is upon them in both cases. In the first it establishes that they are witnesses, and in the second that they are those for whom the witness is given, by the vouching of this exalted Messenger in particular. If "witness" had been placed first, the point would shift to bestowing favor upon the Prophet (ﷺ) by making him a witness, and the context of the address to them and the favor upon them would reject that. Al-Zamakhshari derived the exclusivity from the fronting because it indicates importance and attention, and he often draws on this kind of thing in his discourse. But there is room for examination in this.

If you ask: why was the first case aimed at establishing their testimony over the nations, while the second aimed at their being singled out by the Messenger being a witness over them? I answer: that is what it is.

﴿The qibla which you used to face﴾ is not an attribute of the qibla. It is rather the second object of "made". The meaning is: We did not make the qibla the direction that you were facing, which is the Kaaba, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray in Mecca toward the Kaaba. Then after the Hijra he was commanded to pray toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, to win the hearts of the Jews. Then he was turned back to the Kaaba. So the meaning is: We did not make the qibla which you must face the direction you faced at first in Mecca. That is, We did not return you to it except as a test for people and an ordeal, ﴿that We might know﴾ the one who is steadfast in Islam and truthful in it, from the one who is ﴿on the edge, who turns back on his heels﴾ because of his instability, so he apostatizes. It is like the saying: ﴿And We did not make their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾, and so on.

It may also be an explanation of the wisdom in making Bayt al-Maqdis the qibla. That is, the original command for you was to face the Kaaba, and your facing Bayt al-Maqdis was an incidental matter for a purpose. We made the qibla the direction you were facing before this time, which is Bayt al-Maqdis, only so that We might test people and see who follows the Messenger and who does not follow him and turns away from him.

It is related from Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the qibla of the Prophet in Mecca was Bayt al-Maqdis, except that he would place the Kaaba between himself and it. [Reported by Ishaq, Ibn Sa’d, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani from the narration of Mujahid from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray in Mecca toward Bayt al-Maqdis, with the Kaaba before him, and after he migrated to Medina, for sixteen months." Al-Bazzar said: "No one is known to have related this except al-A’mash from him, and from him only Abu ‘Awana."]

If you ask: how does He say "that We might know," when He has always known that? I answer: its meaning is "that We might know it as knowledge on which the reward depends," namely that He knows it as existing and realized. Similar is the saying: ﴿And Allah has not yet known those of you who strove, nor known the patient﴾. It has also been said: "that the Messenger of Allah and the believers might know." The knowledge of them was attributed to His own Essence, because they are His elect and those brought near to Him. It has also been said that the meaning is "to distinguish the follower from the one who turns back," as He says: ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. So "knowledge" is put in the place of "distinction," because by knowing it the distinction is made.

﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾: here "in" is the light form (mukhaffafa) of "inna," which requires the distinguishing lam. The pronoun in "was" refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you used to face﴾, namely the turning back, or the change, or the making. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the qibla, so that the meaning is ﴿a great thing﴾, heavy and difficult, ﴿except for those whom Allah has guided﴾, that is, except for the steadfast and truthful in following the Messenger, whom Allah has favored and who were worthy of His favor.

﴿And Allah would never make your faith be lost﴾, that is, your steadfastness in faith, and that you did not waver or doubt, but rather He thanks your action and prepares for you a great reward. It is also permissible to mean: Allah would not leave your change of direction, knowing that leaving it would be a corruption and a loss of your faith. It has been said: whoever prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis before the change, his prayer is not lost. [Reported by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, and authenticated by al-Hakim, from the narration of Simak from ‘Ikrima from him.]

From Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was directed to the Kaaba, they said: "What about those of our brothers who died before the change?" Then it was revealed. [This is in the report that follows.] ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful﴾, who does not lose their rewards and does not leave what would benefit them.

It is related that al-Hajjaj said to al-Hasan: "What is your opinion of Abu Turab?" Al-Hasan recited the saying: ﴿except for those whom Allah has guided﴾, and then said: "And ‘Ali is among them. He was the cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his son-in-law through his daughter, the nearest of people to him, and the most beloved of them."

It was read: "illa li-ya‘lam" with the verb in the passive. The meaning of "knowledge" here is "recognition." It is also permissible that "min" includes the meaning of interrogation, with the knowledge suspended before it, as in your saying: "I knew whether Zayd is in the house or ‘Amr." Ibn Abi Ishaq read ‘ala ‘aqibayhi with the qaf unvoweled. Al-Yazidi read "la-kabira" with the nominative. Its justification is that "kana" is extra (zaida), as in the verse:

"And neighbors of ours who were noble."

[This is by al-Farazdaq: "How then when you pass by the dwelling of a people, and neighbors of ours who were noble?" He means: how will the situation be when you pass by the dwelling of a people and our noble neighbors? "Kanu" is extra, to indicate the past, and that the neighbors existed and then passed away. "Kiram," in the genitive, is an attribute of "jiran."]

The original is: "wa-in hiya la-kabira," as in your saying "in Zayd la-munṭaliq." Then "in kanat la-kabira." It was also read "li-yudiya‘" with the doubled letter.

The foolish ones (al-sufaha’), the light-minded, will say, and they are the Jews, out of their dislike of turning toward the Kaaba, and because they do not accept abrogation (naskh, the replacing of one ruling by a later one). It has also been said that they are the hypocrites, out of their eagerness to find fault and to mock. And it has been said that they are the polytheists, who said: "He has turned away from the qibla of his fathers and then returned to it. By Allah, he will return to their religion."

If you ask: what is the benefit of reporting their saying before it occurs? I answer: its benefit is that the shock of an unwanted event is greater, while knowing of it before it happens lessens the disturbance when it does occur, because of the preparation of the soul that precedes it. Also, a ready answer given before there is need for it is more decisive against the opponent and more effective in repelling his clamor. This is like "before shooting, the arrow is fletched."

﴿The foolish will say: what has turned them away from their qibla?﴾ The qibla here is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). ﴿To Allah belong the East and the West.﴾ That is, the lands of the East and the West, and the whole earth. ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ of its people ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is what wisdom and benefit require, by directing them at one time to Bayt al-Maqdis and at another to the Kaaba.

﴿And thus We have made you﴾, that is, by a similar wondrous making, ﴿a middle community (ummah wasatan)﴾, that is, the best. It is a description by the noun that means the middle of a thing, which is why the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine are all the same in it.

A similar saying is the Prophet’s (ﷺ) words: "Give the thabjah," where the thabjah is the middle one between the fat and the lean, described by thabj, which is the middle of the back. But he added the feminine ta’ marbuta in observance of the description. It has also been said that the best is called "middle" (wasat), because the extremities are where defects quickly appear, while the middles are protected and enclosed. From this is the verse of al-Ta’i:

"She was the protected middle, but calamities surrounded her
until she became an extremity."

These are lines of Abu Tammam addressing al-Mu’tasim. The ghayda is a place where water gathers, then drains away, and plants grow in it. Here it means the site of the army. The Bidh is the name of a fortress of Babak al-Khurrami. The ‘armarim is a large army. Khurud al-ard are its paths. The mu’tasif is one who deviates from the road because of its crowds. He compared that place to a ghayda by way of mockery of its occupants, since such places are attributed to water, and he attributed it to death. He compared the army in its obedience to camels, in the figure of the metaphor (al-makniyya), and "guided" is an imaginative image. He referred to the middle by what cannot be reached by defect, because it is protected by its extremities, so the calamities surrounded it, meaning the armies of al-Mu’tasim, until that ghayda became an extremity and the defects and hardships of the army reached it.

I once hired in Mecca an Arab's camel for the pilgrimage, and he said: "Give me of their sataat," meaning of the best dinars.

Or it means "just" (‘udulan), because the middle is a balance between the extremities, not closer to one of them than to the other. ﴿So that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. It is related that "on the Day of Resurrection the nations will deny that the prophets conveyed the message. Allah will then ask the prophets for proof that they had conveyed it, though He knows best. The community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and will testify. The nations will say: ‘How do you know?’ They will say: ‘We know it through the information of Allah in His Book, the speaking one, upon the tongue of His truthful Prophet.’ Then Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the state of his community. He will vouch for them and bear witness after doubt."

[Report: transmitted by al-Tabari from Zayd ibn Aslam as a statement of a Companion (mawquf). It is also reported in the Tafsir of al-Nasa’i as a statement of al-Suddi.

In al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Sa’id al-Khudri: "Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say: ‘At your service, O Lord.’ He will be asked: ‘Did you convey?’ He will say: ‘Yes.’ His people will be asked: ‘Did he convey to you?’ They will say: ‘No warner came to us.’ He will be asked: ‘Who will bear witness for you?’ He will say: ‘Muhammad and his community.’ They will bear witness that he conveyed." Then he recited: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi related in al-Ba’th wa al-Nushur, through Abu Mu’awiya from al-A’mash from Abu Salih from Abu Sa’id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A Prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection with three or four or two men with him, and a Prophet will come with no one with him. Then the community of Muhammad will be called, and they will testify that they conveyed. It will be said to them: ‘How do you know that they conveyed?’ They will say: ‘Our Messenger came to us with a Book, which informed us that they had conveyed, so we believed him.’ It will be said: ‘You have spoken truly.’" That is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community﴾.]

That is the Almighty’s saying: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ If you ask: why was it not said "a witness for you," since his testimony is for them and not against them? I answer: because the witness is like the watcher and the guardian over the one to whom testimony is given, the preposition "over" (‘ala) was used. From this is the saying of Allah: ﴿And Allah is witness over all things﴾, and ﴿You were the watcher over them, and You are witness over all things.﴾

It has been said: that you may be witnesses over the people in this world, in matters that are valid only by the testimony of upright and righteous men. ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾, purifying you and knowing of your uprightness.

If you ask: why was the complement of "witness" placed first in the first case and last in the second? I answer: because the favor is upon them in both cases. In the first it establishes that they are witnesses, and in the second that they are those for whom the witness is given, by the vouching of this exalted Messenger in particular. If "witness" had been placed first, the point would shift to bestowing favor upon the Prophet (ﷺ) by making him a witness, and the context of the address to them and the favor upon them would reject that. Al-Zamakhshari derived the exclusivity from the fronting because it indicates importance and attention, and he often draws on this kind of thing in his discourse. But there is room for examination in this.

If you ask: why was the first case aimed at establishing their testimony over the nations, while the second aimed at their being singled out by the Messenger being a witness over them? I answer: that is what it is.

﴿The qibla which you used to face﴾ is not an attribute of the qibla. It is rather the second object of "made". The meaning is: We did not make the qibla the direction that you were facing, which is the Kaaba, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray in Mecca toward the Kaaba. Then after the Hijra he was commanded to pray toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, to win the hearts of the Jews. Then he was turned back to the Kaaba. So the meaning is: We did not make the qibla which you must face the direction you faced at first in Mecca. That is, We did not return you to it except as a test for people and an ordeal, ﴿that We might know﴾ the one who is steadfast in Islam and truthful in it, from the one who is ﴿on the edge, who turns back on his heels﴾ because of his instability, so he apostatizes. It is like the saying: ﴿And We did not make their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾, and so on.

It may also be an explanation of the wisdom in making Bayt al-Maqdis the qibla. That is, the original command for you was to face the Kaaba, and your facing Bayt al-Maqdis was an incidental matter for a purpose. We made the qibla the direction you were facing before this time, which is Bayt al-Maqdis, only so that We might test people and see who follows the Messenger and who does not follow him and turns away from him.

It is related from Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the qibla of the Prophet in Mecca was Bayt al-Maqdis, except that he would place the Kaaba between himself and it. [Reported by Ishaq, Ibn Sa’d, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani from the narration of Mujahid from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray in Mecca toward Bayt al-Maqdis, with the Kaaba before him, and after he migrated to Medina, for sixteen months." Al-Bazzar said: "No one is known to have related this except al-A’mash from him, and from him only Abu ‘Awana."]

If you ask: how does He say "that We might know," when He has always known that? I answer: its meaning is "that We might know it as knowledge on which the reward depends," namely that He knows it as existing and realized. Similar is the saying: ﴿And Allah has not yet known those of you who strove, nor known the patient﴾. It has also been said: "that the Messenger of Allah and the believers might know." The knowledge of them was attributed to His own Essence, because they are His elect and those brought near to Him. It has also been said that the meaning is "to distinguish the follower from the one who turns back," as He says: ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. So "knowledge" is put in the place of "distinction," because by knowing it the distinction is made.

﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾: here "in" is the light form (mukhaffafa) of "inna," which requires the distinguishing lam. The pronoun in "was" refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you used to face﴾, namely the turning back, or the change, or the making. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the qibla, so that the meaning is ﴿a great thing﴾, heavy and difficult, ﴿except for those whom Allah has guided﴾, that is, except for the steadfast and truthful in following the Messenger, whom Allah has favored and who were worthy of His favor.

﴿And Allah would never make your faith be lost﴾, that is, your steadfastness in faith, and that you did not waver or doubt, but rather He thanks your action and prepares for you a great reward. It is also permissible to mean: Allah would not leave your change of direction, knowing that leaving it would be a corruption and a loss of your faith. It has been said: whoever prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis before the change, his prayer is not lost. [Reported by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, and authenticated by al-Hakim, from the narration of Simak from ‘Ikrima from him.]

From Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was directed to the Kaaba, they said: "What about those of our brothers who died before the change?" Then it was revealed. [This is in the report that follows.] ﴿Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful﴾, who does not lose their rewards and does not leave what would benefit them.

It is related that al-Hajjaj said to al-Hasan: "What is your opinion of Abu Turab?" Al-Hasan recited the saying: ﴿except for those whom Allah has guided﴾, and then said: "And ‘Ali is among them. He was the cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his son-in-law through his daughter, the nearest of people to him, and the most beloved of them."

It was read: "illa li-ya‘lam" with the verb in the passive. The meaning of "knowledge" here is "recognition." It is also permissible that "min" includes the meaning of interrogation, with the knowledge suspended before it, as in your saying: "I knew whether Zayd is in the house or ‘Amr." Ibn Abi Ishaq read ‘ala ‘aqibayhi with the qaf unvoweled. Al-Yazidi read "la-kabira" with the nominative. Its justification is that "kana" is extra (zaida), as in the verse:

"And neighbors of ours who were noble."

[This is by al-Farazdaq: "How then when you pass by the dwelling of a people, and neighbors of ours who were noble?" He means: how will the situation be when you pass by the dwelling of a people and our noble neighbors? "Kanu" is extra, to indicate the past, and that the neighbors existed and then passed away. "Kiram," in the genitive, is an attribute of "jiran."]

The original is: "wa-in hiya la-kabira," as in your saying "in Zayd la-munṭaliq." Then "in kanat la-kabira." It was also read "li-yudiya‘" with the doubled letter.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 2, verses 144–145**

﴿Indeed We see﴾ (qad naraa) means "often We see" (rubbama naraa), and its meaning is frequency of seeing. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari), may God have mercy on him, said: "Its meaning is frequency of seeing..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may God have mercy on him, said: This is one of the places where the Arabs go to great lengths in expressing a meaning by its opposite. From this is ﴿Often will those who disbelieve wish﴾, where what is meant is their frequent wish to have been Muslims on the Day of Resurrection and when they witness its reward and recompense. Likewise is ﴿And you know that I am the Messenger of God to you﴾, where the intent is to show their obstinacy: their knowledge of his message is certain and firmly established, and yet they still disbelieve in it.] Like the saying of the poet:

*"Often I leave the opponent with fingertips gone pale,
as if his garments were stained with mulberry juice,
or I drag him, while the forelocks of the horses are marked,
with a spear whose shaft is behind them, thrust with force."*

This is attributed to al-Hudhali, and it is also attributed to ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras. *Qad* here indicates frequency, and *tark* (leaving) is in the sense of *tasyir* (making [him] into something).

The paling of the fingertips is a metaphor for death. *Al-Farsad* is mulberry juice, which is red. *Al-Ayjar* means to give someone to drink by force. *Nawasi al-khayl* are the hair of the horses' heads. *Al-Mu'allamah* means "well known by marks." *Al-Samra'* is the spear-shaft. *ʿAmiluha* originally refers to the part of it that is next to the spearhead, and he used it figuratively for what comes after, as an intensification. It is said: *na'adathu al-dahiyah nadan*, when calamity struck him severely and reached him fully. The *nad* here is lightened by changing the hamzah into an alif, meaning: often I leave my peer in courage as a corpse, his garments smeared with his blood; I made him drink a spear, its shaft behind them, from the intensity of my blows. It is also transmitted as *thadi*, with the letter *tha'*. *Al-Thad* (with a hamzah, though it may be lightened) is dew and rain, while *al-thadi* as an active participle is the cloud that rains heavily; that is, I gave him to drink while the forelocks of the horses were marked by a spear whose shaft was behind them from the force of my blow, which resembles dew or cloud, and that suits brevity.

It is also transmitted as *samar* (like *hamr*), which is then a second predicate. *A'miluha* is the present tense, and *nad* is an object. *Jarrat* (dragged) and in it there is a kind of mockery. It is transmitted that Zuhayr completed the first line with his words:

*"He sways upon the spear, swaying like one who draws water, from the stinking stagnant water."*

That is, *asin*, meaning foul. It is said: *asana al-ma'* (the water became *asin*), *fa-huwa asin*, with or without the extended vowel, when it becomes foul.

﴿The turning of your face﴾ means the repeated turning and the directing of your gaze towards the direction of the sky. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to expect from his Lord that He would turn him towards the Kaʿbah, because it was the qiblah (direction of prayer) of his father Ibrahim (Abraham), and because it would more readily draw the Arabs to faith, since it was their pride, their place of visitation, and their place of circumambulation, and in order to oppose the Jews. So he would watch for the descent of Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, and for the revelation concerning the change. ﴿So We will surely turn you﴾ means: We will certainly give you, and enable you to face it, from your saying *wallaytuhu kadha* (I made him so), when you make him a governor over it; or: We will surely cause you to face its direction rather than the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), ﴿which you like﴾, meaning you love it and incline towards it for your sound purposes which you harboured, and which agreed with the will of God and His wisdom, ﴿towards the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning towards it. He said:

*"And I travel with the people towards the kings."*

Ubayy read: *"in the direction of the Sacred Mosque."* On the authority of al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, came to Madinah and prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months, then he was turned towards the Kaʿbah. [Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) through the chain of Abu Ishaq from him. In it: "He liked that his qiblah should be towards the House," and in a narration of Ibn Hibban: "He loved that he be turned towards the House."] It is also said: that happened in Rajab, after the sun had passed its zenith, two months before the battle of Badr, while the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was in the mosque of Banu Salamah, and he had prayed two rak'ahs of the noon prayer with his companions. He turned during the prayer and faced the spout (of the roof), and the men were moved to the place of the women and the women to the place of the men. So the mosque was named the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. [Al-Waqidi transmitted it in his Maghazi, quoting from Ibn Saʿd, then Abu al-Fath al-Yaʿmuri.] And ﴿the direction of the Sacred Mosque﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning: make the turning of your face towards the Mosque, that is, in its direction and its bearing. [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "The *shatr* is the direction and the bearing..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Our Maliki companions have transmitted a disagreement within the school concerning what is obligatory: it is said to be the general direction, and it is said to be the exact point, and this is when one is at a distance. As for when the Kaʿbah is visible within the Sacred Mosque, whoever deviates from the bearing and whose prayer is then not valid is so by unanimous opinion. Then each of the two views has its difficulty. As for the view of the exact point, it follows that the prayer of a straight, elongated row is not valid beyond facing the Kaʿbah (may God honour it), because we know necessarily, even if we do not witness it, that some of them pray towards other than its exact point, since its bearing does not cover that on this assumption. Yet permissibility in such a case when at a distance is agreed upon. As for the view of the general direction, it follows that one permits the prayer of a person in the north, for example, towards all three directions, because they are all directions of the Kaʿbah, and bearing is not observed on this school's view. This confusion arose only from failing to distinguish between observing the general direction and observing the bearing, and Abu Hamid distinguished them with a geometric example in the book *Ihya'*, so there is no need to lengthen it here. The verified position for legal ruling is that when one is at a distance, what is required is the general direction, not the bearing.] Because facing the exact point of the qiblah entails great hardship for the one who is far away. Mentioning the Sacred Mosque rather than the Kaʿbah is evidence that what is obligatory is observing the general direction, not the exact point.

﴿That they may know that it is the truth﴾, meaning that the turning towards the Kaʿbah is the truth, because it was in the good news of their prophets concerning the Messenger of God, that he would pray towards the two qiblahs. ﴿They do work﴾ is read with the *ya'* and with the *ta'*. ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah.﴾ The phrase ﴿they would not follow﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and it stands in the place of the answer to the conditional clause. ﴿Every sign﴾ means every decisive proof that the turning towards the Kaʿbah is the truth. ﴿They would not follow your qiblah﴾, because their refusal to follow you is not due to a doubt that you could remove by presenting the argument, but is rather out of arrogance and obstinacy, despite their knowledge of what is in their books concerning your description, that you are upon the truth. ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾: this is a decisive cutting-off of their hopes, since they had been in turmoil over this matter and said: "If he remains upon our qiblah, we hope that he is the one we are awaiting," and they hoped for his return to their qiblah. It is also read *"bi-tabiʿin qiblatahum"* with an idafah (construction). ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qiblah of others﴾, meaning: although they agree in opposing you, they differ about the matter of the qiblah, and their agreement is not to be expected, just as their agreement with you is not to be expected. That is because the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, while the Christians face the rising of the sun. He, mighty and majestic, informed of the firm adherence of each party to what it is upon and its steadfastness in it: the one among them who is right does not slip from his school because he holds to the proof, and the one who is in error does not desist from his falsehood because of the strength of his obstinacy. And His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, after the clear statement of his true condition, known to Him, in His saying ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾, is a statement given as a supposition and hypothesis, meaning: if you were to follow them, for example, after the clarity of the proof and the full grasp of the reality of the matter, ﴿then you would indeed be, at that time, among the wrongdoers﴾, those committing gross injustice. In this there is kindness to the listeners and an added warning, and an expression of the monstrousness of the state of one who abandons the proof after its illumination and follows his desires, and an incitement and inspiration to steadfastness upon the truth.

If you say: How did He say ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾ [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: why did it come in the singular, when there are two qiblahs...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Similar to this is what was answered concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food﴾, although it is multiple, namely the manna and the quails. It was said that they meant that both are foods of luxury, and they preferred the food of the farmers and the rustics. So when the two foods mentioned were united in being luxuries, they made them one food. This meaning is more emphatic in the denial of the food, because they did not suffice in their denial with their saying ﴿We will not be patient with food﴾, but they reinforced it with their saying ﴿one﴾. Al-Zamakhshari has another answer to this which has passed in its place.]: ﴿their qiblah﴾, when they have two qiblahs, one for the Jews and one for the Christians? I say: Both qiblahs are false, opposed to the qiblah of truth, so by the judgment of their unity in falsehood they were one qiblah.
