The verified position for legal ruling is that when one is at a distance, what is required is the general direction, not the bearing.] Because facing the exact point of the qiblah entails great hardship for the one who is far away. Mentioning the Sacred Mosque rather than the Kaʿbah is evidence that what is obligatory is observing the general direction, not the exact point.

﴿That they may know that it is the truth﴾, meaning that the turning towards the Kaʿbah is the truth, because it was in the good news of their prophets concerning the Messenger of God, that he would pray towards the two qiblahs. ﴿They do work﴾ is read with the *ya'* and with the *ta'*. ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah.﴾ The phrase ﴿they would not follow﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and it stands in the place of the answer to the conditional clause. ﴿Every sign﴾ means every decisive proof that the turning towards the Kaʿbah is the truth. ﴿They would not follow your qiblah﴾, because their refusal to follow you is not due to a doubt that you could remove by presenting the argument, but is rather out of arrogance and obstinacy, despite their knowledge of what is in their books concerning your description, that you are upon the truth. ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾: this is a decisive cutting-off of their hopes, since they had been in turmoil over this matter and said: "If he remains upon our qiblah, we hope that he is the one we are awaiting," and they hoped for his return to their qiblah. It is also read *"bi-tabiʿin qiblatahum"* with an idafah (construction). ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qiblah of others﴾, meaning: although they agree in opposing you, they differ about the matter of the qiblah, and their agreement is not to be expected, just as their agreement with you is not to be expected. That is because the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, while the Christians face the rising of the sun. He, mighty and majestic, informed of the firm adherence of each party to what it is upon and its steadfastness in it: the one among them who is right does not slip from his school because he holds to the proof, and the one who is in error does not desist from his falsehood because of the strength of his obstinacy. And His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, after the clear statement of his true condition, known to Him, in His saying ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾, is a statement given as a supposition and hypothesis, meaning: if you were to follow them, for example, after the clarity of the proof and the full grasp of the reality of the matter, ﴿then you would indeed be, at that time, among the wrongdoers﴾, those committing gross injustice. In this there is kindness to the listeners and an added warning, and an expression of the monstrousness of the state of one who abandons the proof after its illumination and follows his desires, and an incitement and inspiration to steadfastness upon the truth.

If you say: How did He say ﴿And you are not one who will follow their qiblah﴾ [Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: why did it come in the singular, when there are two qiblahs...?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Similar to this is what was answered concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food﴾, although it is multiple, namely the manna and the quails. It was said that they meant that both are foods of luxury, and they preferred the food of the farmers and the rustics. So when the two foods mentioned were united in being luxuries, they made them one food. This meaning is more emphatic in the denial of the food, because they did not suffice in their denial with their saying ﴿We will not be patient with food﴾, but they reinforced it with their saying ﴿one﴾. Al-Zamakhshari has another answer to this which has passed in its place.]: ﴿their qiblah﴾, when they have two qiblahs, one for the Jews and one for the Christians? I say: Both qiblahs are false, opposed to the qiblah of truth, so by the judgment of their unity in falsehood they were one qiblah.

(يَعْرِفُونَهُ) They know him [the Messenger of Allah ﷺ] with a clear knowledge, distinguishing him from others by his specific, individual description, ﴿as they know their own sons﴾, so that their sons are not confused for them or the sons of others.

It is related from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I know him better than I know my own son." He said: "Why?" He replied: "Because I have no doubt about Muhammad that he is a prophet. As for my son, perhaps his mother betrayed [him]." So ʿUmar kissed his head.

The pronoun is permitted even though no prior mention of it has been made, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the listener. Such a pronoun carries an element of magnification and an indication that, because of his fame and being a well-known, recognized figure, he needs no introduction. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the [Prophet's] knowledge (ʿilm), or to the Qur'an, or to the change of the qibla. His saying ﴿as they know their own sons﴾ bears witness to the first view and supports it, and so does the narration from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam.

If you say: why was "sons" singled out? I say: because males are more famous and better known, and they are more bound to the companionship of their fathers and more closely attached to their hearts. [Note: al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask, why did he single out sons and not say children...?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: He based this statement on the view that females are not included in the term "sons" as they are included in the term "children" (awlad). The matter is not so; rather, both terms are equal in including females, and for that reason they are included in the term of one who endows (waqf) for his sons and his sons' sons, just as they are included in the term "children." This is the view of Imam Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.]

Some of them (﴿فَرِيقٌ مِنْهُمْ﴾) — this is an exception for those among them who believed, or for their ignorant ones who were said of: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Book﴾.

﴿الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ — "the truth is from your Lord" may be read with al-Haqq as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the truth." Or it may be the subject, with its predicate being ﴿from your Lord﴾. In this there are two possibilities: that the lam is for prior reference (ʿahd), pointing to the truth which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) holds, or to the truth mentioned in His saying ﴿they conceal the truth﴾ — that is: this which they conceal is the truth from your Lord; or that the lam is for the genus, in the sense of "the truth from Allah, not from other than Him." That is, the truth is what is established as being from Allah, like what you are upon, and what is not established as being from Allah, like what the People of the Book hold, is falsehood. If you ask: when you make al-Haqq the predicate of a subject, what is the position of ﴿from your Lord﴾? I say: it may be a predicate after a predicate, and it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "al-Haqqu min rabbika" (the truth from your Lord), as a substitution (badal) for the first: they conceal the truth — the truth from your Lord. ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, those who doubt their concealment of the truth while knowing it, or doubt that it is from your Lord.

﴿لِكُلٍّ﴾ — for each of the followers of different religions there is ﴿وِجْهَةٌ﴾, a direction (qibla). In Ubayy's reading: "wa li-kulli qiblatun." ﴿هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا﴾ — "he turns himself toward it," so one of the two objects is omitted. It has been said that the subject is Allah, Exalted: Allah turns them toward it. It is also read: ﴿لِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ﴾ with the idafa construction, meaning: "every direction, Allah is the one who turns it," and the lam is added because the object precedes the verb, like your saying: "to Zayd I struck" and "to Zayd his father I struck." Ibn ʿAmir read: "huwa mawlaha," meaning: he is the lord of that direction and has turned to it. The meaning: for every community there is a qibla they face, whether you or others. ﴿So race to the good works﴾ — you, and outpace others in the matter of the qibla and other things.

Another meaning: it may be intended, "for each of you, O community of Muhammad, there is a direction — whether southern, northern, eastern, or western — toward which he prays; so race to the good works." ﴿Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together﴾ for the reckoning, whether agreeing or disagreeing; you cannot escape Him. It is also possible that the meaning is: "So race to the most excellent directions, which are those facing the Kaʿba even if they differ; wherever you are among the different directions, Allah will bring you all together, joining your prayers as if they were toward one direction, as though you were praying in the presence of the Sacred Mosque."

And from wherever you set out (ومن حيث خرجت), i.e., from whatever city you go out to travel, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque (شطر المسجد الحرام) when you pray. And indeed it (وإنه), that is, this command that has been enjoined, [is the truth from your Lord]. And it was read as "ya'malūna" with both the ta' and the ya' (وقرئ يعملون بالتاء والياء). This repetition is to emphasize and reinforce the matter of the qibla, because abrogation (naskh) is a source of trial, doubt, and the whisperings of Satan, and there is a need to distinguish it from badā' (change of mind in God's knowledge). So it was repeated for them so that they would be steadfast, resolve, and exert themselves. Also, each one (of the repetitions) is tied to something not tied to the other, so their benefits differ.

Except those who did wrong among them (إلا الذين ظلموا منهم): this is an exception from "the people," and its meaning is that there should be no argument for any of the Jews, except the obstinate among them, who say: "He did not abandon our qibla for the Ka'ba except out of inclination toward the religion of his people and love for his city; had he been upon the truth, he would have followed the qibla of the prophets." If you say: What argument would there have been for the fair-minded among them had he not changed (the qibla), such that he guarded against that argument and did not heed the argument of the obstinate? I say: They would have said, "Why does he not turn toward the qibla of his father Ibrahim, as is mentioned in his description in the Torah?" If you say: How is the term "argument" applied to the saying of the obstinate? I say: Because they put it in the form of an argument.

It is also permissible that the meaning be: so that the Arabs would have no argument or objection against you in your abandoning facing the Ka'ba, which is the qibla of Ibrahim and Isma'il, the fathers of the Arabs, except those of them who did wrong, namely the people of Makkah, who say: "It has become apparent to him, so he returned to the qibla of his fathers, and he is about to return to their religion."

Zayd ibn 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with them both) read: "Alā (ألا) alladhīna ẓalamū minhum," where "alā" is for alerting, and he paused on "ḥujja," then resumed with an alert: 

So do not fear them (فلا تخشوهم), i.e., do not fear their criticisms regarding your qibla, for they cannot harm you. And fear Me (واخشوني), i.e., do not oppose My command or what I have seen as beneficial for you.

The object of the lām is omitted; its meaning is: "And for My completion of favor upon you and My desire for your guidance, I have commanded you with that," or it is conjoined with an implied cause, as if it were said: "And fear Me, so that I may grant you success and complete My favor upon you." It was also said: it is conjoined to "so that there should not be" (لئلا يكون).

In a hadith: "The completion of favor is entry into Paradise" [narrated by Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Bazzār from the hadith of Mu'ādh, and it will come in Surat al-Raḥmān]. And from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): "The completion of favor is dying upon Islam."

As (كما) We sent: either it relates to what precedes it, i.e., "and that I may complete My favor upon you in the Hereafter by reward, as I completed it upon you in this world by sending the Messenger," or to what follows it: i.e., "as I mentioned you by sending a Messenger, so remember Me (فاذكروني) through obedience, and I will remember you (أذكركم) through reward; and be grateful to Me (واشكروا لي) for what I have bestowed upon you, and do not be ungrateful (ولا تكفرون) and do not deny My blessings."

Do not say of those slain in the way of Allah that they are dead (أموات); rather, they are alive (بل أحياء), but you do not perceive (ولكن لا تشعرون) their condition in their life.

From Mujāhid: They are provided with the fruit of Paradise and they find its fragrance, though they are not in it.

They said: It is possible for Allah to gather from the parts of a martyr a whole and revive it, and deliver bliss to it, even if it is the size of an atom. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 155–157:**

*"And We will surely test you": We will afflict you with something that resembles the conduct of one who tests your states: whether you will be patient and steadfast in the obedience you are upon, and submit to Allah's command and His judgment, or not. "With something of": a little of each of these afflictions, and a portion of it. "And give good tidings to the patient": those who say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (istirja', the statement "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return") at the time of affliction, because istirja' is submission and acceptance.*

*It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says istirja' at the time of calamity, Allah will repair his calamity, grant him a better outcome, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with."* [[Related by al-Tabari, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, through the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding His saying ﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them...﴾: Indeed the believer, when he submits to Allah's command and says istirja' at the time of calamity, secures three kinds of good: the blessings (salah) from Allah, mercy, and the attainment of the path of guidance. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says istirja' ..." and then he mentioned it.]]

*It is also reported that the lamp of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, and he said, "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un." It was asked: "Is that a calamity?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him."* [[Related by Abu Dawud in al-Marasil, from the hadith of Imran al-Qasir, who said: The lamp of the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and he said istirja'. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "It is only a lamp." He said: "Everything that distresses the believer is a calamity."]]

*The reduction in "with something" (bi-shay') is mentioned to indicate that every affliction that befalls a person, however great, has something beyond it that is less than it, and to lighten the matter for them and show them that His mercy is with them in every state and never leaves them. He promised them this before it occurred so that they would prepare their souls for it.*

*"And loss (naqs)" is conjoined either to "with something" or to "fear," meaning: and some loss of wealth.*

*The address in "give good tidings" is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to anyone capable of giving good tidings.*

*It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the fear: it is the fear of Allah; the hunger is the fasting of the month of Ramadan; the loss of wealth is the zakat and charities; the loss of souls is illness; and the loss of fruits is the death of children.* [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: The fear is the fear of Allah, the hunger is the fasting of Ramadan, the loss of wealth is the zakat, the loss of souls is illness, and the loss of fruits is the death of children." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: There is room for scrutiny in this interpretation, because this trial is promised for the future and mentioned before it occurs so that they may prepare themselves for it when it happens. Perhaps every affliction mentioned had already preceded them before the revelation of the verse, since the fear of Allah the Exalted has never ceased to fill the hearts of the believers. It is also unlikely that charity be described as a loss, when the Law has named it zakat, which means growth, the opposite of loss, and it is reported: "No wealth decreases through charity." It may be said that it is a loss in a sensory sense, but it was called zakat in view of what the act of giving leads to, namely growth. The reward hoped for from Allah's generosity is a replacement. So when Allah the Exalted mentioned it in the context of the promised trial, He expressed it as zakat to facilitate its payment by the one obligated, for when he perceives the compensation from Allah the Exalted and the growth of his wealth through it, giving it becomes easy for him and his soul consents to it.]]

*It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when a servant's child dies, Allah the Exalted says to the angels: "Have you seized the child of My servant?" They say: "Yes." He says: "Have you seized the fruit of his heart?" They say: "Yes." Allah the Exalted says: "What did My servant say?" They say: "He praised You and said istirja'." Allah the Exalted says: "Build for My servant a house in Paradise and name it the House of Praise."* [[Related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: Hasan gharib. Ahmad and others also related it from a hadith. Ibn Hibban authenticated it. Al-Bayhaqi related it in Shu'ab al-Iman both as marfu' and mawquf.]]

*Salah (blessings): tenderness and compassion. It is placed in the position of ra'fah (kindness), and it is combined with mercy, as in His saying ﴿compassion and mercy﴾ and ﴿Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾. The meaning is: upon them is kindness after kindness, and mercy of every kind.*

*"And those are the guided ones" to the path of right conduct, since they said istirja' and submitted to Allah's command.*

"And give good tidings to the patient": those who say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (istirja', the statement "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return") at the time of affliction, because istirja' is submission and acceptance.*

*It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says istirja' at the time of calamity, Allah will repair his calamity, grant him a better outcome, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with."* [[Related by al-Tabari, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, through the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding His saying ﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them...﴾: Indeed the believer, when he submits to Allah's command and says istirja' at the time of calamity, secures three kinds of good: the blessings (salah) from Allah, mercy, and the attainment of the path of guidance. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says istirja' ..." and then he mentioned it.]]

*It is also reported that the lamp of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, and he said, "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un." It was asked: "Is that a calamity?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him."* [[Related by Abu Dawud in al-Marasil, from the hadith of Imran al-Qasir, who said: The lamp of the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and he said istirja'. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "It is only a lamp." He said: "Everything that distresses the believer is a calamity."]]

*The reduction in "with something" (bi-shay') is mentioned to indicate that every affliction that befalls a person, however great, has something beyond it that is less than it, and to lighten the matter for them and show them that His mercy is with them in every state and never leaves them. He promised them this before it occurred so that they would prepare their souls for it.*

*"And loss (naqs)" is conjoined either to "with something" or to "fear," meaning: and some loss of wealth.*

*The address in "give good tidings" is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to anyone capable of giving good tidings.*

*It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding the fear: it is the fear of Allah; the hunger is the fasting of the month of Ramadan; the loss of wealth is the zakat and charities; the loss of souls is illness; and the loss of fruits is the death of children.* [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: The fear is the fear of Allah, the hunger is the fasting of Ramadan, the loss of wealth is the zakat, the loss of souls is illness, and the loss of fruits is the death of children." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: There is room for scrutiny in this interpretation, because this trial is promised for the future and mentioned before it occurs so that they may prepare themselves for it when it happens. Perhaps every affliction mentioned had already preceded them before the revelation of the verse, since the fear of Allah the Exalted has never ceased to fill the hearts of the believers. It is also unlikely that charity be described as a loss, when the Law has named it zakat, which means growth, the opposite of loss, and it is reported: "No wealth decreases through charity." It may be said that it is a loss in a sensory sense, but it was called zakat in view of what the act of giving leads to, namely growth. The reward hoped for from Allah's generosity is a replacement. So when Allah the Exalted mentioned it in the context of the promised trial, He expressed it as zakat to facilitate its payment by the one obligated, for when he perceives the compensation from Allah the Exalted and the growth of his wealth through it, giving it becomes easy for him and his soul consents to it.]]

*It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when a servant's child dies, Allah the Exalted says to the angels: "Have you seized the child of My servant?" They say: "Yes." He says: "Have you seized the fruit of his heart?" They say: "Yes." Allah the Exalted says: "What did My servant say?" They say: "He praised You and said istirja'." Allah the Exalted says: "Build for My servant a house in Paradise and name it the House of Praise."* [[Related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: Hasan gharib. Ahmad and others also related it from a hadith. Ibn Hibban authenticated it. Al-Bayhaqi related it in Shu'ab al-Iman both as marfu' and mawquf.]]

*Salah (blessings): tenderness and compassion. It is placed in the position of ra'fah (kindness), and it is combined with mercy, as in His saying ﴿compassion and mercy﴾ and ﴿Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾. The meaning is: upon them is kindness after kindness, and mercy of every kind.*

*"And those are the guided ones" to the path of right conduct, since they said istirja' and submitted to Allah's command.*

Safa and Marwa: they are proper names for the two hills, like al-Sammân and al-Muqattam. *Sha'a'ir* is the plural of *sha'ira*, which means a sign. That is, they are among the markers of its rites and acts of worship. *Hajj* (pilgrimage) means intention, and *i'tamar* (umrah, the lesser pilgrimage) means visiting. The two terms became specific to intending the House and visiting it for the two well-known rites. In meaning they are like "the star" and "the house" in their concrete referents. The original form of *yattawwaf* is *yatatawwaf*, which was assimilated. It is also read as *an yatawwafa*, from *tāfa*.

If you say: how can it be said that they are among the signs of Allah, and then it is said, "there is no blame upon him for going around them"? I say: on Safa there was Isaf, and on Marwa there was Na'ila, and they were two idols. It is narrated that they were a man and a woman who committed fornication in the Ka'ba. They were transformed into two stones, which were placed on them as a lesson to be taken from them. When the period grew long, they were worshipped besides Allah. So when the people of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam) performed the sa'y (the walking between the two hills), they would touch them. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked going around between them because of the act of the Jahiliyya, and so that there would be no blame upon them in doing so. Therefore the blame was lifted from them.

Scholars differed about the sa'y. Some said it is a voluntary act, based on the lifting of blame and the choice it contains between doing and leaving it, as in Allah's words: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they return to one another﴾ and other such verses. It is also based on His words: ﴿whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, like His words: ﴿whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. This view is narrated from Anas, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports it: "there is no blame upon him that he not go around them." From Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, it is reported that it is obligatory but not a pillar, and whoever leaves it must offer a sacrifice. According to the earlier group, there is nothing upon him. According to Malik and al-Shafi'i, it is a pillar, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Run, for Allah has prescribed for you the running (sa'y)."

[The hadith is narrated by al-Tabarani from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked in the year of his hajj about the ramal (the hurried walk), and he mentioned it. It was related by al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, and al-Hakim, through the narration of Abdullah ibn al-Mu'ammil, from Umar ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Mukhayyis, from Ata ibn Abi Rabah, from Hubayba bint Abi Tajra, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) going around between Safa and Marwa, with the people before him, and he was behind them, running until I could see his knees from the intensity of the running, and he was saying: 'Run, for Allah has prescribed for you the running.'" And Ubaydullah is weak. Al-Hakim also narrated it by another route, from Abdullah ibn Shayba, from his grandmother Safiyya bint Shayba, from Hubayba bint Abi Tajra, who said: "I looked out early in the morning between Safa and Marwa and saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) running, and he was saying to his companions: 'Run, for Allah has prescribed for you the running.'" Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi also narrated it through Ibn Uyayna, from al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah, from al-Mughira ibn Hakim, from Safiyya, from Tamlak al-Abdariyya, who said: "I looked at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while I was in my upper room between Safa and Marwa, and he was saying: 'O people, Allah has prescribed for you the running, so run.'" Al-Muthanna is weak. Al-Tabarani narrated it through Hamid ibn Abd al-Rahman, from al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabbah, but he did not mention Tamlak.]

It is also read as *wa man yattawwa'* meaning *wa man yatatawwa'*, which was assimilated.

In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "and whoever volunteers good."

Indeed, those who conceal, from among the rabbis of the Jews, what We sent down (in the Torah) of the clear proofs (min al-bayyinat), meaning the verses that testify to the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the guidance (wal-huda), meaning the guidance that directs to following him and believing in him, after We had made it clear and summarized it for the people in the Book (in the Torah), leaving in it no point of difficulty or confusion for any of them, yet they deliberately turned to that clarified and summarized matter, concealed it, and confused the people about it: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah curses, and the cursers curse them﴾. The cursers are those from whom cursing can proceed against them, namely the angels and the believers among both jinn and humankind.

And reform what they had corrupted of their affairs, and make good what they had neglected. "And make clear what Allah had made clear in their Scripture, which they had concealed." Or: make clear to the people what they had newly undertaken of repentance, so that the mark of disbelief might be erased from them, and they might be known by the opposite of what they had been known by, and others among the corrupters might follow their example.

Indeed, those who disbelieve (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا): he means those among these concealers who died without repenting. He mentioned their being cursed while alive, then their being cursed after death.

Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) read ﴿والملائكة والناس أجمعون﴾ with the nominative (bi-l-raf') as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the place (maḥall) of the word Allah (ism Allah), because it is the agent (fa'il) in the implied sense, as when you say: "I was amazed at the striking of Zayd and ʿAmr," meaning "at the fact that Zayd and ʿAmr struck," as if it were said: "Those, upon them is that Allah curses them and the angels."

If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿وَالنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ while among people are both the Muslim and the disbeliever? I say: by "people" He means those whose cursing is counted, and they are the believers. It was also said: on the Day of Resurrection some of them will curse others.

﴿خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا﴾ means: remaining in the curse. It was also said: remaining in the Fire, except that it was left implicit to magnify its matter and to make it awesome.

﴿وَلَا هُمْ يُنْظَرُونَ﴾ from al-inẓār, meaning: they will not be given respite, nor will their term be extended, or they will not be waited for so that they may make excuses. And He will not look upon them with a look of mercy.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 163:

"Your God is one God" (ﷻ, ﴿وَإِلهُكُمْ إِلهٌ وَاحِدٌ﴾): One, unique in divinity, with no partner in it, and it is not valid to name anything other than Him a god. "There is no god but He" (﴿لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ﴾) is an affirmation of His oneness through the negation of anything else and the affirmation of Him alone. "The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" (﴿الرَّحْمَٰنُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾): the Patron of all blessings, both their roots and their branches, and nothing other than Him has this attribute, for everything besides Him is either a blessing or one upon whom a blessing is bestowed.

It is said that there were three hundred and sixty idols around the Kaaba for the polytheists. When they heard this verse, they were amazed and said: "If you are truthful, then bring a sign by which we may know your truthfulness." So this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 164:

Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation (ikhtilaf) of the night and the day, and their succession (i'taqab), because each of them follows the other, like His saying: ﴿He made the night and the day to succeed each other﴾ [25:62], and in the ships that run in the sea with what benefits mankind, with that which benefits them of what is carried in them, or benefits people. So if you say: Is His saying ﴿and He scattered in it every kind of creature﴾ coordinated (ma'tuf) with "sent down" or with "gave life"? I say: The apparent meaning is that it is coordinated with "sent down," falling under the governance of the relative clause (silah), because His saying ﴿and gave life thereby to the earth﴾ is coordinated with "sent down," so it is joined to it and both become like one thing, as if it were said: "what He sent down from the sky of water, and what He scattered in the earth of every creature."

It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "gave life," in the sense of ﴿He gave life by the rain to the earth and scattered in it every creature﴾, because they (the creatures) flourish through abundance and live by the rain (al-hayā) [[His saying "wa-ya'īshūna bil-hayā" (and they live by al-hayā): in al-Sihah, al-hayā, with a short vowel, means rain and abundance. (ʿayn)]]. And the turning of the winds in their directions: the north wind (qabūl), the south wind (dabūr), the south (janūb), and the north (shamāl); and in their conditions: hot, cold, violent, gentle, barren, and fertilizing. It is said that they are sometimes a mercy and sometimes a punishment. And the clouds made subservient, subjected to the winds, which turn them about in the sky by the will of God, raining wherever He wills. ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who use their reason﴾: they look with the eyes of their intellects and take heed, because they are indications of great power and dazzling wisdom. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), "Woe to him who recites this verse and passes over it (majja bihā)," meaning he does not reflect upon it and does not take heed of it. And it is recited as "wal-falak" with two dammas. And "taṣrīf al-riḥ" in the singular.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 165–167:

*Andādan* (rivals, equals) means idols. It has also been said that it refers to the leaders whom they followed, obeyed, and acted upon in their commands and prohibitions. He cites in support His saying: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. The meaning of *yuḥibbūnahum* (they love them) is: they venerate them and submit to them with the veneration of one who is loved, ﴿as they love God﴾, that is, as the veneration of God and submission to Him. [[Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "They love them as they love God: they venerate them as God is venerated..." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: the verbal noun here is, on this reading, annexed to its object, as in the first case; but this agent is named and its verb is in the active form when it is unpacked from the construction.]] Here the verb is "as God is loved," meaning the verbal noun is derived from the passive form. He dispensed with mentioning who loves them because it is not ambiguous. It has also been said: "as they love God," meaning they equate Him with them in their love, because they used to acknowledge God and draw near to Him. Yet when they board ships they call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, because they do not turn away from Him to anything else, unlike the polytheists, who turn from their rivals to God in times of distress, seek refuge in Him, submit to Him, and make their rivals intermediaries between themselves and Him, saying, "These are our intercessors with God." They worship an idol for a time and then abandon it for another, or they eat it, as the tribe of Bahila ate their god made of dates and butter during a year of famine.

﴿Those who have done wrong﴾ refers to those who take rivals. That is: if these people who committed the great wrong of association could know that all power belongs to God over everything, both punishment and reward, and not to their rivals, and if they knew the severity of His punishment for wrongdoers when they witness the torment on the Day of Resurrection, then there would befall them what cannot be described of remorse, regret, and the certainty of their wrong and error. The answer is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand﴾, and the saying: "If only you had seen so-and-so while the whips were taking him."

It is read *wa-law tarā* with the *tā'* (you), addressed to the Messenger or to every addressee, meaning: "If you saw that, you would see a tremendous matter." It is also read *idh yarawna* in the passive. The *idh* here refers to the future, as in His saying: ﴿and the companions of the Garden will call out﴾.

﴿When those who were followed disown﴾ is a substitution for ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, meaning the followed, who are the leaders, disown their followers. Mujahid read the first verb in the active and the second in the passive. That is, the followers disown the leaders. ﴿and they see the punishment﴾: the *wāw* is for the circumstantial clause, meaning they disown one another while seeing the punishment. ﴿and the bonds are severed﴾ is coordinated with "disown." *Al-asbāb* (the bonds) are the connections that existed between them: agreement upon one religion, kinship, affection, following, and being followed, as in His saying: ﴿Surely your bonds have been cut﴾.

*Law* here has the sense of wishing (*tamannī*). That is why it is answered with *fa-* (then), which is how a wish is answered, as if it were said: "If only we had a return, so that we might disown them." ﴿Thus﴾, like that dreadful sight, ﴿God will show them their deeds as regrets and anguish.﴾ *Ḥasarāt* means remorse and anguish. It is the third object of *arā* (to show). The meaning is that their deeds turn into anguish upon them, so they see nothing but anguish in place of their deeds. ﴿And they will not come out of the Fire.﴾ *Hum* here is like its use in His saying:

*hum yafrishūna al-libda kulla ṭimirratin* (they spread the felt-cloth for every swift horse).

[[Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "*Hum* here has the same function as in His saying, *hum yafrishūn*..." Aḥmad said, may God have mercy on him: I will reveal what is most hidden in these words, for the speaker of such words has a heart that is constricted, and he breathes out the strangling of concealment in some moments. The matter becomes clear when it is said: when he sensed that the verse provides evidence for the People of the Sunna that only the disbeliever will abide forever in the Fire, whereas the sinner, even if he persists in major sins, his monotheism will bring him out of it, and this is necessarily fulfilled by the promise. The way the verse indicates this is that it begins the sentence with a pronoun of the subject, and such a construction, linguistically, implies exclusivity and restriction. There will pass through al-Zamakhshari places where he derives restriction from this construction; he says in His saying, *Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?*, that its meaning is that none raises the dead except them, and that what is denounced against them is what follows from restricting divinity to them. Likewise he says regarding such phrases as *and they are certain of the Hereafter*, that its meaning is restriction: that none is certain of the Hereafter except them. When the matter is built upon this, it follows that the restriction of the negation of exit from the Fire applies to these disbelievers, not to other monotheists. But al-Zamakhshari rejects that, and so he treats the conflict with this meaning by adopting another meaning that fits his principle: he makes the mentioned pronoun emphasize the attribution of eternity to them because it is specific to them, and they hold that rank in his view, since sinners, though they abide in his view, the disbelievers are more worthy of abiding and more deserving of it than they are. Glory be to Him who tested him with this trial, revealing his skill and acuteness. And God is the Granter of success.]] in its indication of the strength of their matter in what is ascribed to them, not in exclusivity.

*Andādan* (rivals, equals) means idols. It has also been said that it refers to the leaders whom they followed, obeyed, and acted upon in their commands and prohibitions. He cites in support His saying: ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. The meaning of *yuḥibbūnahum* (they love them) is: they venerate them and submit to them with the veneration of one who is loved, ﴿as they love God﴾, that is, as the veneration of God and submission to Him. [[Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "They love them as they love God: they venerate them as God is venerated..." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: the verbal noun here is, on this reading, annexed to its object, as in the first case; but this agent is named and its verb is in the active form when it is unpacked from the construction.]] Here the verb is "as God is loved," meaning the verbal noun is derived from the passive form. He dispensed with mentioning who loves them because it is not ambiguous. It has also been said: "as they love God," meaning they equate Him with them in their love, because they used to acknowledge God and draw near to Him. Yet when they board ships they call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion. ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, because they do not turn away from Him to anything else, unlike the polytheists, who turn from their rivals to God in times of distress, seek refuge in Him, submit to Him, and make their rivals intermediaries between themselves and Him, saying, "These are our intercessors with God." They worship an idol for a time and then abandon it for another, or they eat it, as the tribe of Bahila ate their god made of dates and butter during a year of famine.

﴿Those who have done wrong﴾ refers to those who take rivals. That is: if these people who committed the great wrong of association could know that all power belongs to God over everything, both punishment and reward, and not to their rivals, and if they knew the severity of His punishment for wrongdoers when they witness the torment on the Day of Resurrection, then there would befall them what cannot be described of remorse, regret, and the certainty of their wrong and error. The answer is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand﴾, and the saying: "If only you had seen so-and-so while the whips were taking him."

It is read *wa-law tarā* with the *tā'* (you), addressed to the Messenger or to every addressee, meaning: "If you saw that, you would see a tremendous matter." It is also read *idh yarawna* in the passive. The *idh* here refers to the future, as in His saying: ﴿and the companions of the Garden will call out﴾.

﴿When those who were followed disown﴾ is a substitution for ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, meaning the followed, who are the leaders, disown their followers. Mujahid read the first verb in the active and the second in the passive. That is, the followers disown the leaders. ﴿and they see the punishment﴾: the *wāw* is for the circumstantial clause, meaning they disown one another while seeing the punishment. ﴿and the bonds are severed﴾ is coordinated with "disown." *Al-asbāb* (the bonds) are the connections that existed between them: agreement upon one religion, kinship, affection, following, and being followed, as in His saying: ﴿Surely your bonds have been cut﴾.

*Law* here has the sense of wishing (*tamannī*). That is why it is answered with *fa-* (then), which is how a wish is answered, as if it were said: "If only we had a return, so that we might disown them." ﴿Thus﴾, like that dreadful sight, ﴿God will show them their deeds as regrets and anguish.﴾ *Ḥasarāt* means remorse and anguish. It is the third object of *arā* (to show). The meaning is that their deeds turn into anguish upon them, so they see nothing but anguish in place of their deeds. ﴿And they will not come out of the Fire.﴾ *Hum* here is like its use in His saying:

*hum yafrishūna al-libda kulla ṭimirratin* (they spread the felt-cloth for every swift horse).

[[Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "*Hum* here has the same function as in His saying, *hum yafrishūn*..." Aḥmad said, may God have mercy on him: I will reveal what is most hidden in these words, for the speaker of such words has a heart that is constricted, and he breathes out the strangling of concealment in some moments. The matter becomes clear when it is said: when he sensed that the verse provides evidence for the People of the Sunna that only the disbeliever will abide forever in the Fire, whereas the sinner, even if he persists in major sins, his monotheism will bring him out of it, and this is necessarily fulfilled by the promise. The way the verse indicates this is that it begins the sentence with a pronoun of the subject, and such a construction, linguistically, implies exclusivity and restriction. There will pass through al-Zamakhshari places where he derives restriction from this construction; he says in His saying, *Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?*, that its meaning is that none raises the dead except them, and that what is denounced against them is what follows from restricting divinity to them. Likewise he says regarding such phrases as *and they are certain of the Hereafter*, that its meaning is restriction: that none is certain of the Hereafter except them. When the matter is built upon this, it follows that the restriction of the negation of exit from the Fire applies to these disbelievers, not to other monotheists. But al-Zamakhshari rejects that, and so he treats the conflict with this meaning by adopting another meaning that fits his principle: he makes the mentioned pronoun emphasize the attribution of eternity to them because it is specific to them, and they hold that rank in his view, since sinners, though they abide in his view, the disbelievers are more worthy of abiding and more deserving of it than they are. Glory be to Him who tested him with this trial, revealing his skill and acuteness. And God is the Granter of success.]] in its indication of the strength of their matter in what is ascribed to them, not in exclusivity.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 168–169:

ḥalālan (ḥalāl) is a direct object (maf'ūl) of kulū (eat), or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of mā fi al-arḍ (what is on the earth). ṭayyiban (ṭayyib) means pure, free from every doubt (shubha). Wa lā tattabi'ū khuṭuwāti al-shayṭān (﴿and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾), so that you would fall into what is forbidden (ḥarām), or into doubtful matters (shubha), or into forbidding what is lawful (ḥalāl) or permitting what is forbidden (ḥarām). The "min" (from) here is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), because not everything on the earth is edible.

Khuṭuwāt is recited in several ways: khuṭuwāt with two ḍammas; khuṭuwāt with a ḍamma and a sukūn; khuṭu'āt with two ḍammas and a hamza, where the ḍamma on the ṭā' is treated as if it were on the wāw; khuṭuwāt with two fatḥas; and khuṭuwāt with a fatḥa and a sukūn. The khaṭwa (step) is a single instance of khaṭw (stepping). The khaṭwa is also the distance between the two feet of the one who walks. These two forms are like ghurfa and ghurfa (a handful of water scooped up), and qabḍa and qabḍa (a handful). It is said: "He followed his footsteps" and "he stepped on his heels," meaning he took him as a model and followed his way.

Mubīn (manifest) means clearly hostile, with nothing hidden about it.

Innamā yaʾmurukum (﴿He only commands you﴾) is an explanation of the obligation to refrain from following him and of the clarity of his enmity. That is, he never commands you to anything good at all. Innamā yaʾmurukum bi-l-sūʾ (﴿only to evil﴾), that is, to what is ugly, and al-faḥshāʾ (﴿and immorality﴾), meaning the great sins that exceed the limit in ugliness. It is also said that sūʾ is what has no prescribed punishment (ḥadd), and faḥshāʾ is what requires a prescribed punishment. Wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāh mā lā taʿlamūn (﴿and that you say about God what you do not know﴾), which is your saying: "This is lawful and this is forbidden," without knowledge. It includes everything attributed to God Most High that is not permissible for Him.

If you ask: how could Satan be a commander, given the verse "You have no authority over them" (Q. 15:42)?

I answer: his adorning of evil and urging you toward it is likened to the command of one who commands, just as you say, "My soul commanded me to do such-and-such." There is an implication in this that you are, with respect to him, in the position of those commanded, because of your obedience to him and your acceptance of his whisperings. For this reason He said: ﴿and I will surely command them, and they will surely cut the ears of the cattle, and I will surely command them, and they will surely alter the creation of God﴾ (Q. 4:119). And God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, the soul is certainly inclined to evil﴾ (Q. 12:53), since a person obeys it and gives it what it desires.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 170:**

"Lahum" (to them): the pronoun refers to the people. The address is turned away from them, in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of address), to call out to their misguidance, because there is no one more astray than the blind follower (*muqallid*). It is as if he were saying to people of intellect: "Look at these fools, see what they say." It has been said: they are the polytheists. And it has been said: they are a group of Jews whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited to Islam, and they said:

﴿Nay, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers.﴾ *Alfayna* means *wajadna* (we found), as shown by the verse: ﴿Nay, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers.﴾ "Even though their fathers..." The *waw* is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the *hamza* carries the sense of rebuttal and wonder. The meaning is: would they follow them even though their fathers understood nothing of the religion and were not guided to what is right?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 171:

It is necessary to supply an omitted genitive-annexed noun, its sense being: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in calling them (to faith), is like the likeness of him who shouts to (cattle) that which hears nothing but a call and a cry." Or: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of the cattle of him who shouts." The meaning is: the likeness of their caller to faith, in that they hear from the call nothing but the jingle of the tune and the echo of the voice, without any attentive reception of minds or insight, is like the likeness of one who shouts at cattle, which hear nothing but the shouting and calling of the one who shouts, which is only a vocal sound directed at them and a rebuke to them; they understand nothing else and do not comprehend, as rational people understand and comprehend. It is also permissible that what is meant by "that which does not hear" is the deaf and dumb one, who, when someone raises his voice in speech to him, hears nothing but the call and the sound, without understanding the letters. It has also been said that the meaning is: their likeness in following their fathers and imitating them is like the likeness of cattle that hear only the outward sound and do not understand what lies beneath it; so likewise these people follow them according to their outward condition and do not comprehend whether they are upon truth or falsehood. It has also been said that the meaning is: their likeness in calling upon idols is like the likeness of one who shouts at that which does not hear, except that His saying ﴿but a call and a cry﴾ does not support this, because idols hear nothing at all. And al-Na'iq means: the vocal sound. It is said: "na'aqa al-mu'adhdhin" (the muezzin cried out), and "na'aqa al-ra'i bi'l-dha'n" (the shepherd called to the sheep). Al-Akhtal said:

So call to your sheep, O Jarir, for indeed
your soul has deluded you in the empty wilderness with error.

[[From al-Akhtal. Na'aqa, yan'aqu, na'iqan, with the unpointed ʿayn, means when one calls to his flock. Naghaqa al-ghurab, nighaqan, with the dotted ghayn, means when the crow caws.

That is: call out to your sheep, O Jarir, and be content with that instead of boasting, for you are not of its people; you are only a shepherd of sheep. "Mannatka": your soul spoke to you, promised you, and beautified for you, in the empty wilderness free of people, error and falsehood, not guidance and truth as you claim. Jarir censured him by saying:

And the Taghlibi, when he clears his throat for hospitality,
scratches his backside and recites proverbs.

Al-Akhtal answered him by saying:

A people who, when their guests call their dog to bark (to find them), say to their mother: "Piss on the fire!"]]

As for "naghaqa al-ghurab," with the dotted ghayn, it is: "ṣummun hum ṣum" (deaf, dumb, they are deaf), and it is in the nominative case, as a censure.

from the good things of what We have provided you with, meaning what is delicious to them, because everything Allah provides is necessarily lawful [[His statement "everything Allah provides is necessarily lawful" is the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school of theology). As for the Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna, the mainstream Sunni theologians), what Allah provides may be unlawful, as explained in its proper place. (ع)]]. And give thanks to Allah, who provided them to you, if you truly worship Him, if it is true that you single Him out for worship.

And you acknowledge that He is the Master of blessings. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah the Exalted says: 'Indeed, I, and the jinn and mankind, are in a great matter: I create and am worshipped other than Me, I provide and am thanked other than Me'" [[Al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated it through Baqiyya, who said: Safwan ibn Amr told us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr told me, and Shurayh ibn Ubayd (narrated) from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Indeed, I, and the jinn and mankind...'" and he mentioned it the same.]].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 173:

It is read as ḥarrama (حَرَّم) with the active voice, and as ḥurrima (حُرِّم) with the passive voice, and as ḥaruma (حَرُم) on the pattern of karuma. ﴿That which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾: that is, the voice was raised over it for an idol (ṣanam), and this is the saying of the people of the Jahiliyyah: "In the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza." ﴿Neither desiring nor transgressing﴾: not transgressing against another person in necessity by monopolizing it over him, ﴿nor exceeding﴾: exceeding the limit of satisfying hunger.

If you ask: among carrion (al-maytatat) there is something lawful, namely fish and locusts. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us." [[Narrated by Ahmad and al-Shafi'i, and by Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]

I say: the intended meaning is what people understand and commonly recognize by custom. Do you not see that when the speaker says, "So-and-so ate carrion," the mind does not leap to fish and locusts, just as if he said, "He ate blood," the mind does not leap to the liver and spleen. And on the basis of custom and common usage, they said: whoever swears he will not eat meat and then eats fish does not break his oath, even though in reality it is meat. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿that you may eat from it fresh meat﴾. And they likened this to one who swears he will not ride an animal and then rides an unbeliever, and does not break his oath, even though Allah the Exalted called him an animal in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the worst of animals in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾.

If you ask: why was only the flesh of swine mentioned and not its fat? I say: because the fat is included in the mention of the flesh, being subordinate to it and a quality within it, as evidenced by their saying "fatty meat" (laḥm samīn), meaning that it is fat.

in their bellies: meaning, filling their bellies. It is said: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "he ate in part of his belly." [They eat] only the Fire (﴿only the Fire﴾), because what they consume is something that pertains to the Fire, since it is a punishment upon them, so it is as if they had eaten the Fire. From this is the saying: "So-and-so ate blood," meaning he took the blood-money (diyah), which is a substitute for it. [A poet] said:

"I have consumed blood, if I do not terrify you with a co-wife,
Far from the place where the earring falls, pleasant in fragrance."

[The verse is said to be] about a Bedouin who married a woman who did not suit him, so it was said to him: "The fever of Damascus is swift in causing the death of women." So he brought her to it and said that to her. He had alighted at Damascus, a city in al-Sham, as if it were a rational being, and so he addressed it. Apparently this assigning [of rational qualities] is a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyah), and the calling out (al-nida') is an imaginative representation (takhyil). Likewise the command to "know" [in the verse]. The word "al-murur" means walking. Attributing it to "the night" is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli) of attribution to time, and in reality it belongs to the bearers of the bier. Or it may mean "passing," in which case it is literal, and the bi' (ba') indicates association, and it is a kinayah (allusion) for her death. The "'awdan" are the two ends of the bier. He made that night like the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) in his view, because of the intensity of his longing for it, his desire for it, and his yearning for it. Then he turned to address her and invoked a curse upon himself by saying: "I have eaten blood," meaning blood-money (diyah), since it is the substitute for blood, and taking it is a disgrace among the Arabs, because it indicates cowardice and love of wealth rather than vengeance. "Wa in lam arru'ki" [And if I do not terrify you]: from "ra'ahu yarou'uhu," meaning he frightened him. The intended meaning is that he will enrage her by marrying a co-wife over her, beautiful and long-necked. "Fa-ba'ida mahwa al-qurt" [far from the place where the earring falls] is a kinayah for that. "Al-qurt" is an ear ornament, and "mahwa" is its place of falling from the shoulder. "Al-nashr" is a pleasant scent. It is also possible that he invoked a curse upon himself with drought, so that he would need to bleed the she-camels and eat their blood, as the Jahiliyyah used to do in times of drought. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: "I have drunk blood," in which case it is a conditional clause (ta'liq) on what is impossible for him, indicating the certainty of his marriage, because it reverts to the fact that not marrying is impossible, just as drinking blood is impossible. A parallel to this is what Abu Iyas recited:

"Are you, O 'Amr, only a serpent?
If she does not kill you, you will live the rest of your life."

"Thirty years, I see no ease from you,
For, by your lips, you are lasting in the life of this world."

"Damascus, take her, do not release her, a few [pieces]...
She passes by the two ends of her bier on the Night of Power."

"If she escapes from 'Amr, a difficult [wife], safe,
She will be among the women of people, to me, an egg of barrenness."

Perhaps "al-'Umr" in the first rhyme means "the age (al-dahr)." "Lahunnaka" [for by your lips], the hamzah (ha') is a substitution for the hamzah of "inna" according to the Basrans, while according to others its origin is: "Lillahi innaka" [by God, indeed you]. "Bayd al-'aqr" [egg of barrenness]: they claim it is the egg of the rooster, which never lays another in its lifetime. It has been said it is a proverb for what has no existence at all.

So the meaning is: he marries a beautiful woman and no other, or he does not marry at all. "Sa'bah" is his wife.

And [another poet] said:

"Indeed we have lean donkeys
That eat every night a pack-saddle."

Al-ahmirah: the donkeys. Al-'ijaf: the emaciated ones. Al-akaf: the saddle-pad (barda'ah). The intended meaning is: they eat every night fodder purchased with the price of a pack-saddle, by selling the pack-saddle and then buying with its price fodder for them. So the eating is attributed to the pack-saddle through two intermediaries. Perhaps the selling of their saddle-pads is due to their weakness for work. It is also possible that it is simply a case of anteposition (taqdim), and the pack-saddle was specified because it is specific to donkeys.

﴿every night a pack-saddle﴾ [Note: the poet's line] "kull laylatin ikafa" is what is placed on the back of the donkey when it is ridden or loaded. This is stated by al-Sihah (the Sihah dictionary). (ʿ)

He intended the price of the pack-saddle, and called it "ikaf" because of its association with being its price.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾: a reference to their deprivation of the state of the people of Paradise, in which Allah honors them by speaking to them and purifies them by praising them. It has also been said: the negation of speech is an expression of His anger toward them, like one who is angry with his companion and so shuns him and cuts off speech with him. It has also been said: He will not speak to them with what they love, but with something like His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein, and do not speak to Me﴾.

﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ It is an expression of wonder at their state in being involved in things that necessitate the Fire without any concern on their part, just as you say to one who exposes himself to what would incur the wrath of the ruler: "How patient you are with the shackles and the prison!", meaning that no one exposes himself to that except one who is extremely patient under punishment. It has also been said: "fa-ma asbarahum," meaning: "What is it that has made them patient?" One says: "asbarahu 'ala kadhā" and "sabarahu," with the same meaning.

This is the original meaning of the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub). What is related from al-Kisa'i is that he said: The judge of Yemen in Mecca said to me:

"Two men from the Arabs disputed before me, and one of them swore to the right of his companion, so he said to him: 'How patient you are with Allah!'" meaning: "How patient you are with the punishment of Allah."

﴿That is because Allah sent down﴾: that is, that punishment is due to the fact that Allah sent down the Books with the truth. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning the Books of Allah, saying of some of it "true" and of some of it "false," and they are the People of the Book, are surely in extreme opposition (shiqaq ba'id)﴾, far from the truth. The word "al-kitab" is for the genus.

Or [it is said]: their disbelief is due to the fact that Allah sent down the Qur'an with the truth as they know, and indeed those who differed concerning it from among the polytheists, some of them saying "magic," some "poetry," some "fables," are surely in extreme opposition. The meaning is that if those [earlier ones] had not differed and not opposed one another, these [later ones] would not have dared to disbelieve.

"Wa in lam arru'ki" [And if I do not terrify you]: from "ra'ahu yarou'uhu," meaning he frightened him. "Fa-ba'ida mahwa al-qurt" [far from the place where the earring falls] is a kinayah for that. "Al-qurt" is an ear ornament, and "mahwa" is its place of falling from the shoulder. "Al-nashr" is a pleasant scent. It is also possible that he invoked a curse upon himself with drought, so that he would need to bleed the she-camels and eat their blood, as the Jahiliyyah used to do in times of drought. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: "I have drunk blood," in which case it is a conditional clause (ta'liq) on what is impossible for him, indicating the certainty of his marriage, because it reverts to the fact that not marrying is impossible, just as drinking blood is impossible. A parallel to this is what Abu Iyas recited:

"Are you, O 'Amr, only a serpent?
If she does not kill you, you will live the rest of your life."

"Thirty years, I see no ease from you,
For, by your lips, you are lasting in the life of this world."

"Damascus, take her, do not release her, a few [pieces]...
She passes by the two ends of her bier on the Night of Power."

"If she escapes from 'Amr, a difficult [wife], safe,
She will be among the women of people, to me, an egg of barrenness."

Perhaps "al-'Umr" in the first rhyme means "the age (al-dahr)." "Lahunnaka" [for by your lips], the hamzah (ha') is a substitution for the hamzah of "inna" according to the Basrans, while according to others its origin is: "Lillahi innaka" [by God, indeed you]. "Bayd al-'aqr" [egg of barrenness]: they claim it is the egg of the rooster, which never lays another in its lifetime. It has been said it is a proverb for what has no existence at all.

So the meaning is: he marries a beautiful woman and no other, or he does not marry at all. "Sa'bah" is his wife.

And [another poet] said:

"Indeed we have lean donkeys
That eat every night a pack-saddle."

Al-ahmirah: the donkeys. Al-'ijaf: the emaciated ones. Al-akaf: the saddle-pad (barda'ah). The intended meaning is: they eat every night fodder purchased with the price of a pack-saddle, by selling the pack-saddle and then buying with its price fodder for them. So the eating is attributed to the pack-saddle through two intermediaries. Perhaps the selling of their saddle-pads is due to their weakness for work. It is also possible that it is simply a case of anteposition (taqdim), and the pack-saddle was specified because it is specific to donkeys.

﴿every night a pack-saddle﴾ [Note: the poet's line] "kull laylatin ikafa" is what is placed on the back of the donkey when it is ridden or loaded. This is stated by al-Sihah (the Sihah dictionary). (ʿ)

He intended the price of the pack-saddle, and called it "ikaf" because of its association with being its price.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾: a reference to their deprivation of the state of the people of Paradise, in which Allah honors them by speaking to them and purifies them by praising them. It has also been said: the negation of speech is an expression of His anger toward them, like one who is angry with his companion and so shuns him and cuts off speech with him. It has also been said: He will not speak to them with what they love, but with something like His saying: ﴿Be driven away therein, and do not speak to Me﴾.

﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ It is an expression of wonder at their state in being involved in things that necessitate the Fire without any concern on their part, just as you say to one who exposes himself to what would incur the wrath of the ruler: "How patient you are with the shackles and the prison!", meaning that no one exposes himself to that except one who is extremely patient under punishment. It has also been said: "fa-ma asbarahum," meaning: "What is it that has made them patient?" One says: "asbarahu 'ala kadhā" and "sabarahu," with the same meaning.

This is the original meaning of the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub). What is related from al-Kisa'i is that he said: The judge of Yemen in Mecca said to me:

"Two men from the Arabs disputed before me, and one of them swore to the right of his companion, so he said to him: 'How patient you are with Allah!'" meaning: "How patient you are with the punishment of Allah."

﴿That is because Allah sent down﴾: that is, that punishment is due to the fact that Allah sent down the Books with the truth. ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning the Books of Allah, saying of some of it "true" and of some of it "false," and they are the People of the Book, are surely in extreme opposition (shiqaq ba'id)﴾, far from the truth. The word "al-kitab" is for the genus.

Or [it is said]: their disbelief is due to the fact that Allah sent down the Qur'an with the truth as they know, and indeed those who differed concerning it from among the polytheists, some of them saying "magic," some "poetry," some "fables," are surely in extreme opposition. The meaning is that if those [earlier ones] had not differed and not opposed one another, these [later ones] would not have dared to disbelieve.

in their bellies: meaning, filling their bellies. It is said: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "he ate in part of his belly." [They eat] only the Fire (﴿only the Fire﴾), because what they consume is something that pertains to the Fire, since it is a punishment upon them, so it is as if they had eaten the Fire. From this is the saying: "So-and-so ate blood," meaning he took the blood-money (diyah), which is a substitute for it. [A poet] said:

"I have consumed blood, if I do not terrify you with a co-wife,
Far from the place where the earring falls, pleasant in fragrance."

[The verse is said to be] about a Bedouin who married a woman who did not suit him, so it was said to him: "The fever of Damascus is swift in causing the death of women." So he brought her to it and said that to her. He had alighted at Damascus, a city in al-Sham, as if it were a rational being, and so he addressed it. Apparently this assigning [of rational qualities] is a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyah), and the calling out (al-nida') is an imaginative representation (takhyil). Likewise the command to "know" [in the verse]. The word "al-murur" means walking. Attributing it to "the night" is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli) of attribution to time, and in reality it belongs to the bearers of the bier. Or it may mean "passing," in which case it is literal, and the bi' (ba') indicates association, and it is a kinayah (allusion) for her death. The "'awdan" are the two ends of the bier. He made that night like the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) in his view, because of the intensity of his longing for it, his desire for it, and his yearning for it. Then he turned to address her and invoked a curse upon himself by saying: "I have eaten blood," meaning blood-money (diyah), since it is the substitute for blood, and taking it is a disgrace among the Arabs, because it indicates cowardice and love of wealth rather than vengeance.
