Righteousness (al-birr) is a name for goodness and for every pleasing act. ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾. The address is to the People of the Book.

[[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The address in it is to the Jews and the Christians... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is transmitted from al-Mubarrad, struck down by the arrows of refutation. It implies that the variant readings are left to ijtihad (independent reasoning), and that whatever the analogy of the language requires, it is permissible to recite with it, for one who is deemed qualified for ijtihad in Arabic and language. This is pure error, for the readings (qira'at) are a followed tradition (sunnah) in which there is no room for personal opinion. Moreover, what he said, and supposed to be the more correct, does not reach the peak of the eloquence of the verse, except in the widely transmitted readings, because the speech begins by mentioning al-birr, which is the verbal noun, unanimously. So if it were changed to mention al-birr as a descriptive (adjective), it would break the correspondence and the coherence of the composition. For this reason, the interpretation of the verse by deleting the genitive complement (mudaf) of the second term, with the sense "the righteousness of one who believes," is more correct, better, and more consistent with the context. Whoever thinks that he can keep pace with the dust (of the eloquent) or cling to the skirts of the eloquence of the inimitable Qur'an in front of the eloquent, his soul has adorned for him the impossible, and his wish has led him to error.]]

This is because the Jews pray facing the west toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and the Christians face the east. That is because they engaged excessively in discussion about the qibla (direction of prayer) when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned toward the Ka'ba, and each of the two groups claimed that righteousness was facing their own qibla. So (Allah) refuted them.

It was said: "Righteousness is not in what you are upon, for it is abrogated (mansukh) and has gone out of righteousness; rather, righteousness is what We shall explain."

It was said: "The discussion of the Muslims and the People of the Book about the qibla increased, so it was said: 'The great righteousness that you must be astonished by, to the neglect of all other kinds of righteousness, is not the matter of the qibla, but the righteousness that must be attended to and to which the resolve should be directed is the righteousness of one who believes and performs these deeds.'"

It was recited: "Wa-laysa al-birru" (with the accusative, "and righteousness is not"), with the predicate placed first. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: "bi-an tuwallu" (with a preposition before the predicate), for emphasis, like your saying: laysa al-muntaliqu bi-Zayd (the one who departs is not Zayd). ﴿But righteousness is that of one who believes in Allah﴾, with the interpretation of deleting the genitive complement, meaning "the righteousness of one who believes." Or al-birr is interpreted to mean "one possessing righteousness," or as the poet said:

*Fa-innama hiya iqbalun wa-idbaru*

[[Her camel-colt is a calf, around which a hide-skin is circling, for her there are two cries, one low and one high.

Do not grow weary of her through the ages, whenever she is mentioned, for she is nothing but approach and retreat.

One day more grieved than I, when he parted from me, Sakhr; and for fate there is sweetness and bitterness.]]

By al-Khansa', lamenting her brother Sakhr. The 'ajul is the she-camel that has aborted her fetus before two months were complete, or one who lost her young by slaughter or death. The bu' is a hide stuffed with straw, for whose sake the she-camel is milked. It was also said: the she-camel's colt. The verb tatif means to circle around it (tafa bihi), and to approach it (tāfa ʿalayhi yatīfu tayfan), when it turns toward it. Each may be used in place of the other, that is, "she is passionate for it." Another version reads: "tahinnu lahu" (she yearns for it).

"Ihsar wa-ikbar" (low and high): a substitution (badal) for hanInan (two cries). Another version reads: "i'lan wa-israr" (open and secret). The meaning is the same, except that there is an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir).

Or "al-ihsar" is the yearning for a young calf, and "al-ikbar" for a grown one, so it was said, but the best explanation is what has been transmitted.

"Al-dahr" (the age/fate) is the object of "tasʾam" (grow weary): meaning, do not tire throughout the ages of what has been mentioned, namely the yearning and its return to the hide-skin; the eloquence of the meaning rejects this. It may be returned to the "tayf" (phantom/circling) known from "tatif." Another version replaces this half-line with: "tar'a ma ra'at hatta idha adkarat" (she grazes as long as she grazes, until she remembers), whose original is "adhtakarat," meaning "tadhakkarat" (she remembered). Another version reads: "tar'a ma ghafalat hatta idha dhakarat" (she grazes during the period of her unawareness of him, until when she remembers him). Then she is "dhat iqbal wa-dhat idbar" (one of approach and one of retreat), or "muqbila wa-mudbira" (approaching and retreating), or she is the very approach and retreat for emphasis: that is, she turns one moment in front of her and one moment behind, and distracts herself from grazing. It was said that the meaning is the approach of the day and the retreat of the night, or the reverse. It is possible that its aspect is the short duration: that is, the span of the ages is nothing but approach and retreat revolving between night and day. The pronoun returns to a known referent from the context, but this does not appear in the second version.

"Yawman" (one day): the accusative, governed by "awjad" (more grieved), and it was permissible for it to precede the comparative (af'al al-tafdil), because it is an adverb of time; and likewise, as an indication that by "day" is meant time in general, mostly. "Bi-awjad" is the predicate of 'ajul. Another version reads "bi-awja'" (more painful): meaning "she is not more grieved one day than I am when my brother departed from me." "Hina" is also in the accusative governed by "awjad." Its explanation is that it has the sense of two governing elements: that is, "her grief one day is not greater than my grief at the time of parting." So the first governs the first, and the second the second. Then she consoled herself with her words: "wa-li-l-dahri ihla'un wa-imrar" (and for fate there is sweetness and bitterness). It is said: "ahla al-shay'" and "amura" meaning it became sweet and became bitter. It is also permissible that both are transitive.

The meaning is that fate sometimes makes life pleasant and sometimes makes it miserable. Thus "ihla'" (sweetening) and "imrar" (embittering) are metaphors for that.]]

﴿And he gives wealth, though he loves it﴾ (with love for the wealth and stinginess toward it), as Ibn Mas'ud said: "That you give it while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty, and you do not delay until, when the throat rattles, you say: 'For so-and-so is such-and-such, and for so-and-so is such-and-such.'"

[[Halted (mawquf, a saying of a Companion). Abd al-Razzaq transmitted it thus, from al-Thawri, from Zubayd, from Murra, from him. He said, regarding His words (Exalted is He): ﴿And gave wealth, despite love of it, to the near of kin﴾, "That you give it..." and mentioned it up to his words "and fear poverty," but did not mention what follows. Through this chain, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim transmitted it, and Abu Nu'aym mentioned it in al-Hilya, in the biography of Mis'ar, and transmitted it through him from Zubayd. He said: "Thus Mis'ar and the people narrated it, from Zubayd, halted. Makhlad ibn Yazid narrated it from al-Thawri as marfu' (traced to the Prophet), and he alone narrated it as marfu', then he cited it." Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it from the narration of Shu'ba from Zubayd, halted, and through Salam ibn Salim al-Mada'ini from Muhammad ibn Talha from Zubayd, as marfu'. Salam is weak. Al-Tabari transmitted it from three chains from Zubayd, halted. None of them mentioned "and do not delay," but it is in the hadith of Abu Hurayra. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) agreed upon it with the wording: "A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Messenger of Allah, which charity is best?' He said: 'That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty, and you do not delay until, when the throat rattles, you say: For so-and-so is such-and-such, and for so-and-so is such-and-such, and it has already become for so-and-so.'"]]

It was said: "on His love," meaning Allah's love. It was said: "on the love of giving," meaning he gives while he is content with giving. He mentioned "the near of kin" first because they have the greater right. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity given to a poor person is one charity; but to a relative it is two: it is charity and a bond of kinship."

[[Transmitted by al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba, and al-Darimi, all from the hadith of Salman ibn Amir, with the wording: "Charity to the poor is a good deed" (al-Tirmidhi). On this topic there are also reports from Ibn Talha and Abu Umama. Al-Tabarani transmitted it.]]

And he (ﷺ) said: [[Transmitted by Abd al-Razzaq, al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Tabarani, from the narration of Ibn Uyayna from al-Zuhri, from Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, from his mother Umm Kulthum bint Uqba. Abu Ubayd transmitted it in Kitab al-Amwal from the narration of Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Makki from al-Zuhri from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib from Abu Hurayra. He also transmitted it through 'Aqil from al-Zuhri as mursal (lacking the Companion's name), without mentioning Abu Hurayra. Ahmad transmitted it from the narration of Sufyan ibn Husayn from al-Zuhri from Ayyub ibn Bashir from Hakim ibn Hizam; and he and Ishaq and al-Tabarani also transmitted it through al-Hajjaj ibn Arta, from him, from Hakim ibn Bashir, from Abu Ayyub. All these chains revolve around al-Zuhri, with differences upon him, and the most retentive of them is Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, though 'Aqil is more retentive than him, and his narration is more similar to the correct.]]: "The best charity is to a near relative who is hostile to you."

[[His words "dhi al-rahm al-kashih": in al-Sihah (Lexicon of al-Jawhari): one says "tawa fulan 'an kashihi" when he has cut you off. The kashih is one who harbors enmity toward you. (Gloss by the editor.)]]

And "dhawi al-qurba" (the near of kin), "al-yatama" (the orphans), and the poor are mentioned absolutely, and what is meant by them is the poor among them, to avoid ambiguity. "Al-miskin" (the needy) is one who constantly keeps still toward people, because he has nothing, like "al-mishkir" for one who constantly is drunk. "Ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer) is the traveler who has been cut off. He is called the son of the road because of his constant association with it, as one says of a highway robber: "son of the road." It was said: he is the guest, because the road brings him forth (yarʿafu bihi), that is, presents him and displays him to the residents, as the nose bleeds with the blood of a nosebleed (al-ruʿaf).

[[His words "li'anna al-sabil yarʿafu bihi": that is, he goes forward with him and displays him to the residents, as the nose bleeds with a nosebleed. Recorded in al-Sihah. (Editor's gloss.)]]

And "al-sa'ilin" (those who ask): those who seek sustenance. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on the back of a horse."

[[Transmitted by Abu Dawud from the narration of Fatima bint al-Husayn ibn Ali, from her father, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), and from the narration of al-Husayn ibn Ali without mention of his father. In their chains is Yahya ibn Abi Ya'la, or it is said Ya'la ibn Abi Yahya, who is unknown. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh transmitted it through him and made it from the narration of Fatima bint al-Husayn from Fatima. Al-Tabarani transmitted it from the hadith of al-Hurmas ibn Ziyad, in which is Uthman ibn Fayid, who is weak. Malik said in the Muwatta': "Zayd ibn Aslam informed us: Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)..." and he mentioned it. Ibn Adi also transmitted it connected through Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra; and Abd Allah is weak. He also transmitted it through Umar ibn Yazid al-Mada'ini, from Ata', from Abu Hurayra; and Umar is weak.]]

And "fi al-riqab" (in the necks/slaves): in aiding the mukatabin (slaves contracted to buy their freedom) until they free their necks. It was said: in buying and freeing slaves. It was said: in ransoming captives.

If you say: the giving of wealth has been mentioned in these categories, then it was followed by "the giving of zakat," so does that indicate that there is a right in wealth other than zakat? I say: this is possible. It was reported from al-Sha'bi that there is a right in wealth other than zakat, and he recited this verse. It is possible that this is an explanation of the categories of zakat, or that it is an urging toward voluntary charities and acts of goodness.

In a hadith: "Zakat has abrogated every charity" [[Transmitted by al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). Its chain is weak. Abd al-Razzaq transmitted it as a saying of Ali, halted.]], meaning its obligation. And it was narrated: "There is no right in wealth other than zakat" [[Transmitted by Ibn Majah from the narration of Abu Hamza, from al-Sha'bi, from Fatima bint Qays, with this wording. He titled it "Chapter: whoever pays its zakat, it is not a treasure." Al-Bayhaqi said: "What our companions narrate in the hanging chains (ta'aliq) is 'There is no right in wealth other than zakat'; I do not know a chain for it. Al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, and al-Tabarani transmitted it through this route with the wording: 'Indeed in wealth there is a right other than zakat.' Al-Tirmidhi said: its chain is not of that standard. Bayan and Isma'il transmitted it from al-Sha'bi, and this is more correct."]].

﴿And those who fulfill﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "man amana" (one who believes).

﴿And the steadfast﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (ikhtisas) and praise, to show the excellence of patience in hardships and the battlefields over all other deeds. It was recited: "wa-l-sabirun" (nominative). It was recited: "wa-l-muwfin" and "wa-l-sabirin" (genitive/accusative variants).

﴿Distress﴾ is poverty and hardship, and ﴿adversity﴾ is illness and affliction. ﴿Those are the ones who have been truthful﴾: they are those who were sincere and earnest in religion.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 178–179:

It is related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, al-Hasan al-Basri, ʿAtaʾ, and ʿIkrima, and it is the position of Malik and al-Shafiʿi [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The position of Malik and al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that a free person is not killed for a slave, and a male is not killed for a female..." etc. Ahmad (al-Iskandari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an error by al-Zamakhshari concerning the two imams, for they both hold that a male is subject to retaliation for killing a female, without any disagreement from them. As for the free person and the slave, according to them, this is the point on which al-Zamakhshari erred concerning them.]], may Allah have mercy on them, that a free person is not killed for a slave, and a male is not killed for a female, adopting this verse as evidence. They say:

It explains what was left general in His words ﴿the life for the life﴾, and because that verse reports what was prescribed in the Torah for its people, whereas this verse is addressed to the Muslims and what is in it was prescribed for them.

They cite the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafaʾu dimaʾuhum) [[Related by Abu Dawud, al-Nasai, and al-Hakim, through the route of Qays ibn ʿUbad from ʿAli, in a story. Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah also related it through ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, and he added: "The least of them may give protection on their behalf, and the farthest of them may be compelled to fulfil their obligations, and they are a hand against whoever is other than them." On this topic there is also a report from ʿAʾisha, related by al-Bukhari in his History and by al-Daraqutni. And from Ibn ʿAbbas and Maʿqil ibn Yasar in Ibn Majah, and from Jabir in the al-Mujam al-Awsat of al-Tabarani.]]." They also argue that superiority is not considered in lives, as evidence by the fact that if a group kills one person, they are all killed for him. It is related that: "Between two tribes of the Arabs there was bloodshed in the pre-Islamic period, and one of the two had superiority over the other. They swore: 'We will certainly kill the free man among you for the slave among us, the male for the female, and two for one.' They brought their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when Allah brought Islam, and the verse was revealed, and he ordered them to settle it [[I have not found it.]]."

﴿But whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾: its meaning is: whoever is pardoned something from the side of his brother [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The meaning of the verse is: whoever is pardoned something by his brother..." etc. Ahmad (al-Iskandari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is strengthened by the view that the obligation for intentional killing is one of two things, either retaliation or blood money, and the choice belongs to the guardian. This is one of the two opinions in the school of Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, and the more well-known of them. For if we made the obligation for intentional killing retaliation alone, according to the other opinion, that would be a constraint upon the guardian. The verse indicates facilitation and ease. The verse may bear another interpretation, namely that both pronouns refer to the guardian. They said that on this reading, pardon means giving a substitute, as if he had said: "whoever gives something to his brother," meaning a substitute from his brother. And "min" would be like it in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made among you angels in the earth succeeding one another﴾. Its parallel in the use of pardon to mean giving, in my view, is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿except that they pardon, or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie should pardon﴾, when the one in whose hand is the tie is taken to be the husband. This is the position of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions say: his pardon is one of two forms: either the return of the half that is due if he had paid the whole dower, or the payment of the other half which he was excused from if he had not paid it. So the pardon, on this reading, is used in the sense of giving. This reading is strengthened, as regards there being no retaliation, by His words: ﴿then pursuit in a fair manner﴾, because the one addressed with pursuing in a fair manner is only the guardian. If we make both pronouns refer to him, the speech runs in one consistent direction and the meaning becomes: whoever among the guardians gives a substitute for his brother, let him pursue it fairly in seeking what he has given. And when the guardian opposed litigation, the killer is addressed with good payment, so the speech is coherent, directed to one direction. But on the reading that al-Zamakhshari established, both pronouns refer back to the killer, and the sense of the speech is: whoever among the killers is pardoned something of the pardon for his crime, then let the guardian pursue this pardoned killer in a fair manner. Thus the addressee at the beginning of the verse is the killer and at the end the guardian, unlike the reading I have established, and Allah knows best. Both readings are good and sound.]] of pardon. As if you were to say: "Travel with Zayd part of the journey and a portion of the journey." It is not valid for shayʾ (something) to be in the sense of the direct object, because ʿafa (to pardon) does not take a direct object except through an intermediary. His brother here is the guardian of the one killed. It is said he is called his brother because he is connected to him, since he is the guardian of the blood and the one who demands it, just as you say to a man: "Tell your companion such-and-such," to one with whom he has a slight connection, or by mentioning him with the term brotherhood, so that one may incline toward the other by mentioning what is firmly established between them of kinship and Islam. If you ask: since ʿafa is transitive with ʿan and not with li, what is the reason for His words ﴿whoever is pardoned (ʿufiya lahu)﴾? I say: it is transitive with ʿan to the offender and to the offence, so one says: "I pardoned so-and-so and his offence." Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has pardoned you﴾ and He said: ﴿Allah has pardoned it﴾. When it is transitive to both the offence and the offender together, one says: "I pardoned so-and-so for what he committed," just as you say: "I forgave him his sin and overlooked it for him." Upon this is what is in the verse, as if it had been said: "whoever is pardoned for his crime, so he is excused from mention of the crime." If you ask: why not explain ʿafa as "to leave," so that shayʾ would have the sense of the direct object? I say: because ʿafa al-shayʾ in the sense of leaving it is not established; rather it is aʿfah. From this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let the beards grow (wa-aʿfu al-lihā)" [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. I say: that is an unsettled expression in its place, while pardon in the domain of offences is a widely circulated and well-known expression in the Book, the Sunnah, and the usage of people, so one does not turn from it to another unsettled expression, foreign to its place. And you will see many who busy themselves with this discipline, when a problem is difficult for them, presume, in deriving an interpretation for the difficulty in the speech of Allah, to invent a language and to claim of the Arabs what they do not know. This is an audacity from which one seeks refuge in Allah. If you ask: why was it said "something of the pardon"? I say:

To indicate that if a portion of the pardon is granted to him, and some of it, such as when some of the blood is pardoned, or some of the heirs pardon him, the pardon is complete, retaliation falls away, and only the blood money becomes obligatory. ﴿then pursuit in a fair manner﴾: let there be pursuit. Or the command is pursuit. This is an admonition to both the one pardoned and the one who pardons together. That is, let the guardian pursue the killer in a fair manner, without harassing him and demanding only in a gracious way, and let the killer render the blood compensation to him with goodness, without delaying or diminishing it. ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾: this ruling mentioned, of pardon and blood money. Because the people of the Torah were prescribed retaliation absolutely and pardon and taking blood money were forbidden to them, and the people of the Gospel were prescribed pardon and retaliation and blood money were forbidden to them, whereas this community was given the choice among the three: retaliation, blood money, and pardon, as a widening upon them and facilitation.

﴿But whoever transgresses after that﴾ the lightening, by going beyond what was legislated for him, by killing someone other than the killer [[His words "by killing someone other than the killer" are an explanation of the transgression and aggression. (ʿ)]], or killing after taking the blood money. It is related from Qatada: "the painful punishment is that he be killed without doubt, and no blood money be accepted from him," because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will not spare anyone who kills after taking the blood money."

﴿And for you in retaliation is life﴾: an eloquent expression because of its strangeness [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "an eloquent expression because of its strangeness..." etc. Ahmad (al-Iskandari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: His statement that he made one of two opposites a locus for the other is either a mistake he has made or a loose expression, because the condition for the opposition of life and death is their coexistence in one locus in a presumptive sense, and there is no opposition between the life of the one not subjected to retaliation and the death of the one subjected to it. This is an address that has a special excellence, directed to the rulers.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 180–182:

﴿When death approaches any one of you, if he leaves wealth﴾ (khayran): that is, when death draws near to him and its signs appear, [if he leaves] much wealth.

It is narrated from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man wished to make a bequest. He had dependents and four hundred dinars, and she said: "I do not see any surplus in it." [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from al-Thawri from Mansur ibn Safiyya, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr told us that ʿĀʾisha was asked about a man who died leaving four hundred dinars and a number of children. ʿĀʾisha said: "There is no surplus in this over his children." Also from Ibn Jurayj, from Mansur ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from his mother, from ʿĀʾisha, the like of this, and he added: "She rebuked him and said: 'Indeed that is little.'" I say: Mansur ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman is the son of Safiyya. It seems he heard it from his mother and from ʿAbd Allah, both of them from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her.]]

Another man wished to make a bequest, so she asked him: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependents do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "Allah only said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and this thing is small, so leave it for your dependents." [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba: Abu Muʿawiya told us, from Muhammad ibn Sharik, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from ʿĀʾisha, that a man said to her: "I wish to make a bequest," and he mentioned the rest.]] And it is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that a client of his wished to make a bequest and he had seven hundred [dirhams], and ʿAlī forbade him. [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq: Maʿmar informed us, from Hisham, from his father, who said: "ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon a client of his who was dying, and he said: 'Shall I not make a bequest?' ʿAlī said to him: 'Allah the Exalted only said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and you do not have much wealth.' He said: 'He had seven hundred dirhams.'" It was also transmitted by Ibn Abi Shayba from Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, from Hisham, with the same wording.]]

He said: Allah the Exalted said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and khayr is wealth, and you have no wealth. The verb of al-wasiyya (the bequest) is feminine, while the verb is masculine, because the word is a separator, and because it has the sense of "that he should bequeath." For this reason the pronoun referring back is masculine in His saying ﴿and whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. The bequest to the heir was at the beginning of Islam, and it was abrogated (naskh, meaning abrogation, the annulment of one ruling by a later one) by the verses of inheritance, and by his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right; no bequest is to an heir." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (sound), and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Abu Umama. Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and graded it sahih (authentic). Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Kharija, and Ibn Majah from the narration of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Saʿid ibn Abi Saʿid, that he told him from Anas ibn Malik, with the same.]] And by the community's acceptance of it, so that it reached the level of the mutawatir (widely transmitted reports), even though it is a single report (ahad), because they only accept with acceptance what is firmly established in its transmission. It was also said: it was not abrogated, and the heir combines the bequest and the inheritance by the ruling of the two verses. It was also said: it does not contradict the verse of inheritance.

Its meaning: ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, that is, what Allah bequeathed concerning the inheritance of the parents and the relatives, from His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾; or it means: it is prescribed upon the dying person that he make a bequest to the parents and relatives, by fulfilling what Allah has bequeathed to them upon them, and that he not reduce their shares. ﴿In a fair manner﴾, that is, with justice, which is that he not bequeath to the rich and leave out the poor, and not exceed one-third. ﴿A duty﴾ is an emphatic infinitive; that is, this is a duty as a duty. ﴿So whoever alters it﴾: that is, alters the bequest from its proper course, if it accords with the Sharia, whether by the executors or the witnesses, ﴿after he has heard it﴾ and known it. ﴿Then its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾: so the sin of the altered bequest, or of the alteration, is only upon those who alter it, and not upon others, whether the testator or the legatee, because they are both free of wrongdoing. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: a warning to the one who alters. ﴿But whoever fears﴾: whoever anticipates and knows. This is common in their speech; they say: "I fear that the sky will send rain," meaning anticipation and strong supposition that functions as knowledge. ﴿Deviation﴾: a turning away from the truth through error in the bequest, ﴿or sin﴾: or deliberately wronging. ﴿Then reconciles between them﴾: between the legatees, who are the parents and relatives, by directing them to the path of the Sharia. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ at that time, because his alteration is an alteration from falsehood to truth. He mentioned the one who alters for falsehood, then the one who alters for truth, so that it may be known that not every alteration is sinful. [[His saying "that every alteration is not sinful" perhaps means that not every alteration is sinful. (ʿ)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 180–182:

﴿When death approaches any one of you, if he leaves wealth﴾ (khayran): that is, when death draws near to him and its signs appear, [if he leaves] much wealth.

It is narrated from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that a man wished to make a bequest. He had dependents and four hundred dinars, and she said: "I do not see any surplus in it." [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from al-Thawri from Mansur ibn Safiyya, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr told us that ʿĀʾisha was asked about a man who died leaving four hundred dinars and a number of children. ʿĀʾisha said: "There is no surplus in this over his children." Also from Ibn Jurayj, from Mansur ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from his mother, from ʿĀʾisha, the like of this, and he added: "She rebuked him and said: 'Indeed that is little.'" I say: Mansur ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman is the son of Safiyya. It seems he heard it from his mother and from ʿAbd Allah, both of them from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her.]]

Another man wished to make a bequest, so she asked him: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependents do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "Allah only said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and this thing is small, so leave it for your dependents." [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba: Abu Muʿawiya told us, from Muhammad ibn Sharik, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from ʿĀʾisha, that a man said to her: "I wish to make a bequest," and he mentioned the rest.]] And it is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that a client of his wished to make a bequest and he had seven hundred [dirhams], and ʿAlī forbade him. [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq: Maʿmar informed us, from Hisham, from his father, who said: "ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon a client of his who was dying, and he said: 'Shall I not make a bequest?' ʿAlī said to him: 'Allah the Exalted only said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and you do not have much wealth.' He said: 'He had seven hundred dirhams.'" It was also transmitted by Ibn Abi Shayba from Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, from Hisham, with the same wording.]]

He said: Allah the Exalted said ﴿if he leaves khayr﴾, and khayr is wealth, and you have no wealth. The verb of al-wasiyya (the bequest) is feminine, while the verb is masculine, because the word is a separator, and because it has the sense of "that he should bequeath." For this reason the pronoun referring back is masculine in His saying ﴿and whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. The bequest to the heir was at the beginning of Islam, and it was abrogated (naskh, meaning abrogation, the annulment of one ruling by a later one) by the verses of inheritance, and by his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right; no bequest is to an heir." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (sound), and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Abu Umama. Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and graded it sahih (authentic). Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Kharija, and Ibn Majah from the narration of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Saʿid ibn Abi Saʿid, that he told him from Anas ibn Malik, with the same.]] And by the community's acceptance of it, so that it reached the level of the mutawatir (widely transmitted reports), even though it is a single report (ahad), because they only accept with acceptance what is firmly established in its transmission. It was also said: it was not abrogated, and the heir combines the bequest and the inheritance by the ruling of the two verses. It was also said: it does not contradict the verse of inheritance.

Its meaning: ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, that is, what Allah bequeathed concerning the inheritance of the parents and the relatives, from His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾; or it means: it is prescribed upon the dying person that he make a bequest to the parents and relatives, by fulfilling what Allah has bequeathed to them upon them, and that he not reduce their shares. ﴿In a fair manner﴾, that is, with justice, which is that he not bequeath to the rich and leave out the poor, and not exceed one-third. ﴿A duty﴾ is an emphatic infinitive; that is, this is a duty as a duty. ﴿So whoever alters it﴾: that is, alters the bequest from its proper course, if it accords with the Sharia, whether by the executors or the witnesses, ﴿after he has heard it﴾ and known it. ﴿Then its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾: so the sin of the altered bequest, or of the alteration, is only upon those who alter it, and not upon others, whether the testator or the legatee, because they are both free of wrongdoing. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: a warning to the one who alters. ﴿But whoever fears﴾: whoever anticipates and knows. This is common in their speech; they say: "I fear that the sky will send rain," meaning anticipation and strong supposition that functions as knowledge. ﴿Deviation﴾: a turning away from the truth through error in the bequest, ﴿or sin﴾: or deliberately wronging. ﴿Then reconciles between them﴾: between the legatees, who are the parents and relatives, by directing them to the path of the Sharia. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ at that time, because his alteration is an alteration from falsehood to truth. He mentioned the one who alters for falsehood, then the one who alters for truth, so that it may be known that not every alteration is sinful. [[His saying "that every alteration is not sinful" perhaps means that not every alteration is sinful. (ʿ)]]

As in ﴿those before you were prescribed it﴾, upon the prophets and the nations from the time of Adam until your own era. Allah has never left any community without its being prescribed for them, and He did not prescribe it for you alone. ﴿So that you may be mindful of Allah﴾, by preserving it and honouring it because of its origin and antiquity. Or ﴿so that you may be mindful of Allah﴾ means so that you may refrain from sins, since the fasting person restrains himself [[The phrase "li-anna al-sa'im azlaf li-nafsihi" (because the fasting person is more restrained for his soul): in al-Sihah, "zalafa nafsahu 'an al-shay'" means he restrained his soul from it, and "zalaftu nafsi 'an kadha," with the kasra vowel, means I was restrained from it.]] and is more effective in deterring it from committing evil. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for fasting is a shield for him" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. Or ﴿so that you may be mindful of Allah﴾ means so that you may be counted among the God-fearing, since fasting is their emblem.

It has also been said that the meaning is that your fasting resembles theirs in the number of days, which is the month of Ramadan. It was prescribed for the People of the Gospel, but a plague struck them, so they added ten days before it and ten days after it, making it fifty days.

It has also been said that it fell in severe cold and severe heat, which was hard for them during their travels and livelihoods, so they moved it to between winter and spring, and added twenty days as expiation for shifting it from its time.

It has also been said that the "numbered days" (ayyaman ma'dudat) are the day of 'Ashura' and three days of every month. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was prescribed to fast them when he emigrated. Then they were abrogated (nusikhat) by the month of Ramadan.

It has also been said: "It was prescribed for you as it was prescribed for them, that you should abstain from eating after the night prayer and after sleeping." Then this was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of the fast﴾ ... to the end of the verse.

The meaning of ma'dudat is limited, fixed by a known number, or few in number, as in His saying: ﴿for a few dirhams﴾. Its origin is that a small amount of wealth is measured by counting and is treated carefully, whereas a large amount is poured out in handfuls and scattered. The accusative of ayyaman is governed by al-siyam (the fast), as when you say: "I intended to leave on Friday." ﴿Whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾, or one who is travelling, then ﴿a number of other days﴾, meaning he must fast a number of days. It was read in the accusative, meaning: let him fast a number of days, and this is by way of concession.

It has also been said: it is prescribed for both of them that they break the fast and make up a number of other days. Scholars differed about the illness that permits breaking the fast. Some say any illness, because Allah Most High did not single out one illness over another, just as He did not single out one journey over another. Just as every traveller may break the fast, so every sick person may do likewise. It is related from Ibn Sirin that he came to him during Ramadan while he was eating, and he gave as his excuse a pain in his finger. Malik was asked about a man who suffers a severe eye inflammation or a harmful headache, and who is not ill to the point of being bedridden. He said: "He has latitude to break the fast."

Others say it is an illness with which fasting becomes difficult and aggravates the condition, based on His saying: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾. It is related from al-Shafi'i: "One does not break the fast until the hardship becomes unbearable."

Scholars also differed about making up the days. The majority of scholars allow a choice (in the manner of making them up). It is related from Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "Allah did not grant you a concession in breaking the fast while He intends to make its making up difficult for you. If you wish, make them up consecutively, and if you wish, make them up separately" [[Mawquf (a statement of a Companion): al-Daraqutni transmitted it through his narration.]]. It is related from Ali, Ibn Umar, al-Sha'bi and others that it must be made up in the same way it was missed, consecutively [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq from them both, who said: "He makes it up in succession."]]. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿a number of other days, consecutive﴾.

If you ask: why was it said ﴿a number (fa-'iddatun)﴾ in indefinite form, and not "its number" (fa-'iddatuha), meaning the number of the numbered days? I answer: when it was said ﴿fa-'iddatun﴾, and 'iddah means the counted thing, He commanded that he fast a number of days in their place. It is therefore understood that no number other than their number is acceptable. Thus the definite form by annexation is unnecessary.

﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾, meaning for those capable of fasting who have no excuse if they break the fast, ﴿there is a ransom: feeding a poor person﴾, which is half a sa' of wheat or a sa' of something else according to the people of Iraq, while according to the people of the Hijaz it is a mudd. This was at the beginning of Islam. The fast was prescribed for them, but they were not accustomed to it, so it weighed heavily upon them, and they were granted a concession to break the fast and pay the ransom.

Ibn 'Abbas read: yuṭawwiqūnahu, a form of tafi'il from the tawq, which means either capacity (ṭāqa) or a necklace. That is, they burden themselves with it or put it around their necks. And it is said to them: "Fast." It is also related from him: yatatawwaqūnahu, meaning they bear it with effort or wear it as a necklace. And yaṭawwaqūnahu, with the ta assimilated into the ta' (idgham). And yaṭīqūnahu and yuṭīqūnahu, meaning yatatawwaqūnahu. Their original forms were yaṭīwiqūnahu and yatatayawwiqūnahu, from fay'il and tafi'il of tawq. The ya' was assimilated into the waw after being changed to ya', as in the saying "tadīra al-makān wa-mā bihā diyār" [[A grammatical example: the original form is "tadayyara," with the ya' assimilated and converted.]]. In this there are two meanings. The first is close in meaning to yuṭīqūnahu. The second is that they burden themselves with it, or force themselves to it, with great effort and difficulty. These are the old men and old women, and their ruling is breaking the fast and paying the ransom. On this interpretation the ruling stands and is not abrogated.

It may also be that this is the meaning of yuṭīqūnahu, namely that they fast with all their effort, capacity and utmost ability. ﴿Whoever volunteers good﴾, meaning whoever gives more than the amount of the ransom, ﴿it is better for him﴾, so the voluntary act is better for him, or the good is better. It is read: fa-man yaṭawwa', meaning yatatawwa'. ﴿And that you fast﴾, O you who are able or who make the effort, and who exert yourselves and strain your capacity, ﴿is better for you﴾ than the ransom and voluntary good deeds. It is also permissible that the address includes the sick and the traveller.

In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿And fasting is better for you﴾.

Ramadan: a verbal noun from ramida, meaning to be scorched, from ar-ramda' (hot sand). The month was given this name and made a proper noun. It is not declined (diptotic) because of its definiteness and the alif and nun, just as it is said "Ibn Dayah" for the crow, by idafa of "son" to "the nurse of the camel," because it frequently lands on her when she is sore-backed. If you ask: why was it called Shahr Ramadan? I answer: fasting in it is an ancient act of worship, so they named it thus because of their being scorched (irtimada) in it by the heat of hunger and enduring its severity, just as they called (the month) Natiq, because it used to disturb (yanti'uhum) them, that is, distress them with its severity upon them. It was also said that when they transmitted the names of the months from the old language, they named them after the seasons in which they fell, and this month coincided with the days of intense heat (ramd al-harr). If you ask: since the naming applies to the construct phrase (al-mudaf and al-mudaf ilayhi) together, what is the point of what has come in the hadiths, such as the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward" [agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him], and "Whoever lives to see Ramadan and is not forgiven"? [Al-Tirmidhi related it from the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqburi from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "May he be humiliated, a man upon whom Ramadan entered and departed before he was forgiven" – the hadith. I say: this does not match the wording of the author. What matches it is what Ibn Hibban related.] I say: it is an instance of ellipsis for the sake of safety from ambiguity, as the poet said:

"Whether you have a desire for what I [can do] ... I am a seer of what defeated the skilled physician Hudhaym"

He says: Do you have a desire for what is attributed to me of soundness of opinion, for I am perceptive in resolving difficult matters. He expressed this by saying "what defeated the skilled physician Hudhaym," and he is a highly skilled, clever physician. Hudhaym, with a kasra and then a sukun, is meant as Ibn Hudhaym, because it is his kunya, so part of the name was dropped for safety from confusion. Al-Nitasi is a nisba to al-Nitas, on the pattern of al-Qirtas, and in the language of the Romans it means one skilled and adept in medicine. Its lightening here is either a usage of the Arabs or for the sake of the metre. It was also said its meaning is: Do you have an opinion and insight in what returns benefit to me? Then he turned away from consulting them by saying: "for I know and recognise more than you what defeated the physician." It is not hidden that the fa' has no proper place then, unless the meaning is that he is asking them for a bribe.

[It is] what Ibn Hudhaym meant. Its being raised (marfu') is either because it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "the one in which the Qur'an was sent down," or because it is an apposition (badal) of "fasting" in His saying "Fasting has been prescribed for you," or because it is the predicate of an elided subject. It is also read in the accusative (nasb), meaning: fast the month of Ramadan; or by substitution of "numbered days"; or as the object of "and that you fast." The meaning of "in which the Qur'an was sent down" is that its revelation began in it, and that was on the Night of Decree. It was also said: it was sent down entirely to the lowest heaven, then it descended to the earth in parts. It was also said: the Qur'an was sent down concerning its affair, namely His saying "Fasting has been prescribed for you," just as you say "such-and-such was revealed concerning Umar" or "concerning Ali." From the Prophet (ﷺ): "The scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down six nights in, the Gospel thirteen nights in, and the Qur'an twenty-four nights in." [Ahmad and al-Tabarani related it from the hadith of Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' raised to the Prophet; there is a parallel in Abu Dawud. al-Tha'labi related it in his tafsir. From Jabir, Abu Ya'la related it.] "A guidance for mankind and clear proofs" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: it was sent down while being guidance for people to the truth, and it consists of clear, manifest signs which guide to the truth and distinguish between truth and falsehood. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "and clear proofs of the guidance" after "a guidance for mankind"? I answer: He first mentioned that it is guidance, then mentioned that it is clear proofs from among what Allah guided by, and by which He distinguishes truth from falsehood, from His revelation and His heavenly scriptures, which guide and distinguish between guidance and error.

"So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it": whoever is present, that is, resident and not travelling in the month, let him fast in it and not break the fast. "The month" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time (zarf), and likewise the pronoun in "let him fast it"; it cannot be a direct object, as in your saying "I witnessed Friday," because both resident and traveller are witnesses of the month. "Allah desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you." He has removed from you hardship in religion and commanded you the easy, tolerant monotheism which has no burden in it. The sum of that is what He permitted for you: allowance to break the fast during travel and illness. Some people have made breaking the fast obligatory for the sick and the traveller, to the extent that they claim whoever fasts in these two states must repeat it. It is read: al-yusr and al-'usr, with two dammas.

The causative verb is elided, indicated by what precedes it, its estimated form being: [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The causative verb is elided; its estimate is: He legislated that ..." etc. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its special term in the art of rhetoric is "returning the ends of speech to its beginning" (radd a'jaz al-kalam ila sudurih). Al-Zamakhshari has excelled in investigating it, and it is counted among his good works.] "and that you complete the prescribed period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and that perhaps you will be thankful." He legislated that, meaning the whole of what was mentioned: the command to the witness to fast the month, the command to the one granted dispensation to observe the number of days he broke the fast, and the dispensation to permit breaking the fast. So His saying "that you complete" is the cause of the command to observe the number; "and that you glorify" is the cause of what is known of the manner of making up and discharging the obligation of breaking the fast; "and that perhaps you will be thankful" is the cause of the dispensation and ease. This is a kind of subtle interweaving (laff) whose course is hardly perceived except by the modern scholars of rhetoric (al-nuqqab al-muhdath min 'ulama' al-bayan). The verb "glorify" was made transitive by the particle of elevation (huruf al-isti'la') because it implies the meaning of praise, as if it were said: "that you glorify Allah, praising Him for what He guided you to."

The meaning of "perhaps you will be thankful" is "and the intention that you be thankful." "That you complete" is also read with tashdid (intensive). If you ask: could "and that you complete" be conjoined to an estimated cause, as if it were said: "that you do what you know, and that you complete the number"; or to "ease," as if it were said: "Allah desires ease for you, and desires for you that you complete," like His saying "They desire to extinguish"? I answer: that is not far-fetched, but the first is more apt. If you ask: what is meant by glorifying? I answer: magnifying Allah and praising Him. It was also said: it is the takbir of the day of breaking the fast (Eid al-Fitr). It was also said: it is the takbir at the beginning of the pilgrimage rites [his words "at the beginning" (al-ihlal) meaning entering into the state of ihram for the rite of pilgrimage, as stated in al-Sihah].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 186:

﴿Then indeed I am near﴾ is an image (tamthil) depicting His state: how easily He answers the one who calls upon Him, and how swiftly He grants the request of the one who asks Him, by the likeness of one whose place is near. So when one calls, his response comes quickly. Similar to this is ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾, and the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "He is with you, and closer to you than the necks of your riding animals." [Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a military campaign. When we turned back and came close to Madinah, the people raised their voices in takbir. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your Lord is not deaf nor absent; He is with you, and closer to you than the heads of your riding animals.'" It was also narrated by al-Tirmidhi.]

It is related that a Bedouin (a'rabi) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?" [Narrated by al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif, through the narration of al-Salt ibn Hakim ibn Mu'awiya ibn Haydah from his father from his grandfather, that "a Bedouin" — and he mentioned it — and added after "so that we must call out to Him": "So he remained silent about him" (fasakata 'anhu).] So the verse was revealed: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾, i.e., when I call them to faith and obedience, just as I respond to them when they call upon Me for their needs. And it is read yarshudun and yurshidun, with the shin vowelled with fatha and with kasra.

It used to be that when a man entered the evening, eating and drinking became lawful for him, [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari), may God have mercy on him: "It used to be that when a man entered the evening, eating and drinking became lawful for him... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may God have mercy on him, said: What confirms the soundness of this answer is that when the permission in this matter was established, He said: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾, and so He used for it the euphemism customary in the Mighty Book. It may be challenged by His saying: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the Hajj﴾, for this expression was used there and nothing was transmitted about the Hajj of what was transmitted about the fast regarding the occasion of the revelation of the verse, namely intercourse that was disliked. This may be answered: what was forbidden in the verse about the Hajj was meant as a deterrent for them, so that they would not fall into it, so it was expressed by something repulsive, because that would repel them from becoming entangled in it.]] and intercourse, until he prays the night prayer (ʿishāʾ) or sleeps. If he has prayed it or slept without having broken his fast, then food, drink and women became forbidden to him until the next night. Then ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, had relations with his wife after the night prayer. When he had washed, he began to weep and blame himself, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, I apologise to God and to you for this sinful self of mine," and he informed him of what he had done. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You were not worthy of that, O ʿUmar." [[Narrated by al-Tabari through ʿAṭiyya, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go to your wives﴾, the verse. He said: When people first embraced Islam, when they fasted they would eat food between the time of water (i.e. drinking) and the ʿatama (night prayer). When they had prayed the ʿatama, food was forbidden to them until they reached the evening of the next night. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, while he was asleep, was tempted by his self and went to his wife and told her about it. It does not contain "Then men stood up and confessed." Al-Tabari also transmitted through al-Suddi, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, had relations with a slave-girl of his among some Muslim men who could not control themselves, and he came to the Prophet ﷺ.]] Then some men stood up and confessed what they had done after the night prayer, and so this was revealed. It is recited: "Ahilla lakum laylata al-ṣiyām al-rafathu" [read as "it was made lawful" in the active form], meaning God made it lawful. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) read: al-rafūth. Rafath is plain speech about what should be euphemised, like the word "nīk" (coition), and one says "arfatha al-rajul" (the man spoke obscenely). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, that he recited while in a state of ihram:

"And they walk with us in a gentle pace... If the bird speaks truly, we will have intercourse with Lamis"

[[Ibn ʿAbbas recited this during the Hajj, and Abu al-ʿAliya said to him: "Do you speak obscenely while in ihram?" He said: "Obscenity is only what is said in front of women."

Some of them said: Husayn ibn Qays said: Ibn ʿAbbas took hold of the tail of his camel, turning it, while he was driving it on and saying: "And they..." the verse.

I said to him: "Do you speak obscenely while in ihram?" He said: "Obscenity is only what is said in front of women." "They" (hunna), i.e. the she-camels, "walk with us," i.e. with us. Al-hamis is a kind of walk with no sound, accusative after "yamshīna." "If the bird speaks truly" means the bird by which we take omens, flying to the right; he likened the bird to a informer by way of metaphor, and "speaking truly" is imaginative. It is also related: "If the omen speaks truly," and the verb after it is the answer to the condition. The word "nīk" is the literal term for inserting the male organ into the vagina; whatever else, such as wati' (intercourse), jimāʿ (coition) and mulāmasa (touching), is figurative in origin or euphemistic, and that is why it is ugly to speak it rather than other terms. "Lamis" is a woman's name, and perhaps Ibn ʿAbbas was using it as an example of attaining what he intended.]]

So he was asked: "Did you speak obscenely?" He said: "Obscenity is only what is said in front of women." [[Al-Hakim transmitted it in al-Mustadrak through Ziyad ibn al-Husayn from Abu al-ʿAliya: "Do you speak obscenely while in ihram?" He said: "Obscenity is only what is addressed to women." Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tabari also transmitted it by this route. Al-hamis: with a fatha on the ha and an unpointed letter at the end, a kind of walk that makes no sound. Mentioned by Thabit al-Sarqusti.]] God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness,﴾ and by it He referred to intercourse, because it is hardly free of some of these things. If you ask: why did He here use the word rafath, which indicates ugliness, unlike His other expressions: ﴿And one of you has gone in to the other﴾, ﴿When he covered her﴾, ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾, ﴿Or you have touched women﴾, ﴿You have consummated with them﴾, ﴿Then come to your tillage﴾, ﴿before you touch them﴾, ﴿so for what you have enjoyed of them﴾, ﴿and do not approach them﴾? I say: to express disapproval of what they did before the permission, just as He called it betrayal of themselves. If you ask: why was rafath followed by ilā? I say: because it is included in the sense of ifḍāʾ (going in to). Since a man and a woman embrace and each wraps the other in his embrace, one is likened to a garment that envelops the other. Al-Ju'di said:

"When the bedfellow turns her side, she turns and becomes a garment over him"

[[By al-Nabigha al-Ju'di. "Ma" is superfluous. ḍajīʿ: the bedfellow. ʿaṭf (with kasra): the side. Tathannat: she bent, in eagerness for embracing; she became wrapped around him like a garment, so it is an eloquent simile. It is also related: "thanā jīdahā," i.e. her neck.]]

If you ask: what is the position of His saying: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾? I say: it is a resumed sentence, serving as an explanation for the cause of the permission: since between you and them there is such close contact and enveloping, your patience with them diminishes and avoiding them becomes hard for you, so you were granted permission to have relations with them. ﴿You were betraying yourselves﴾: wronging them and depriving them of their share of good. Ikhtiyān is from khiyāna (betrayal), like iktisāb from kasb, with added intensity. ﴿So He relented toward you﴾ when you repented of what you had committed of the forbidden. ﴿And seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, i.e. seek what God has allotted and recorded for you of offspring through intercourse; that is, do not have intercourse merely to satisfy desire, but to seek what God established marriage for, namely procreation. It has been said: this is a prohibition of ʿazl (coitus interruptus), because it concerns free women. It has been said: and seek the place that God prescribed for you and made lawful, apart from the forbidden place that He did not prescribe for you. From Qatada: seek what God prescribed for you of permission after the prohibition. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-ittabiʿū" and al-Aʿmash read "wa-ātū." It has been said that its meaning is: seek the Night of Power and what God prescribed for you of reward if you attain it and stand in prayer during it; this is close to the strange interpretations. ﴿The white thread﴾ is the first thing that appears of the dawn, spreading across the horizon like a stretched thread. ﴿The black thread﴾ is what extends with it of the darkness of the night; they are likened to two threads, white and black. Abu Dawud [[The text says "Abu Dawud," perhaps "Dawud." (Editor)]] said:

"When the dawn-light shone for us, and a thread of morning appeared and shone"

[[By Abu Dawud. Ḍaʾa and anāra both come intransitive and transitive, as here. Al-sadfa is the whiteness of dawn mixed with a little darkness; in the dialect of Najd it means darkness. Asdafat al-mar'a al-qināʿ means she let loose her veil. Asdafa al-layl means the night grew dark. According to others it is brightness and morning; asdafa al-ṣubḥ means the morning shone; asdafa al-bāb means he opened the door. The whiteness of part of the dawn is likened to a thread in its extension. It is permissible that "min" is explanatory, and the clause anāra is a description of the thread, and the answer of the condition is in what follows.]]

His saying: ﴿of the dawn﴾ explains the white thread, and it suffices as an explanation so that the black thread need not be explained, because explaining one of them explains the other. It is permissible that "min" be partitive, since it is a part of the dawn and its beginning. If you ask: is this metaphor or simile? I say: His saying ﴿of the dawn﴾ takes it out of the category of metaphor, just as your saying "I saw a lion" is a metaphor; when you add "min fulān" (of so-and-so), it becomes a simile. If you ask: why was ﴿of the dawn﴾ added so that it became a simile? Why not limit it to metaphor, which is more eloquent than simile and more fitting to eloquence? I say: because a condition of the metaphorical term is that the context or speech should indicate it; had ﴿of the dawn﴾ not been mentioned, it would not be known that the two threads are used metaphorically. So ﴿of the dawn﴾ was added, and it became an eloquent simile and left the category of metaphor.

If you ask: how was ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim confused despite this explanation, so that he said: "I took two cords, a white one and a black one, and put them under my pillow, and I would get up at night and look at them, but the white was not distinguishable to me from the black. When I woke up I went to the Messenger of God ﷺ and told him, and he laughed and said: 'If your pillow is indeed wide... ' and it is related: 'You have a broad nape. That is only the whiteness of day and the blackness of night'"? I say: he was inattentive to the explanation, and so the Messenger of God ﷺ alluded to his nape, because it is something by which the foolishness and dullness of a man is inferred. Some Bedouin women recited to me a verse by a Bedouin:

"Broad of nape, his scales are on his left; his moustache has receded from the many carats..."

[[It describes a man as dull-witted by way of allusion. "Broad of nape" is a metaphor for stupidity. His scales being on his left is a metaphor for foolishness. Infaṣṣa: his moustache receded from much biting his lip at a reckoning, a metaphor for dullness.]]

If you ask: what do you say about what is related from Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Saʿidi [[Agreed upon, from a narration of Abu Hazim from him.]] that it was revealed without "of the dawn," and men who wanted to fast would tie a white thread and a black thread to their legs, and would not stop eating and drinking until the two became distinct to them, and then "of the dawn" was revealed afterward, so they knew that He meant the night and the day? And how is delaying the explanation permissible when it resembles futility, since the intended meaning is not understood from it, as it is not a metaphor for lack of indication, nor a simile before mention of dawn, so nothing is understood from it except the literal meaning, which is not intended? I say: as for those who do not permit delaying explanation—most jurists and theologians, and this is the view of Abu ʿAli and Abu Hashim—this hadith is not sound according to them. As for those who permit it, they say it is not futile, because the addressee benefits from it, the obligation of the address, and resolves to act upon it once the intended meaning is clarified. Then ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. They said: this is evidence for the permissibility of making the intention during the day in the fast of Ramadan, for the permissibility of delaying the bath until dawn, and for denying continuous fasting (wiṣāl). [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him: "They said it is evidence... etc." Ahmad: The way they derive the first ruling from the verse is unsound, because joining the intention to the beginning of the fast is not considered by consensus, while making it from the night and carrying it forward is considered by consensus. So there is no conflict between eating and drinking until dawn and the intention to fast from the night. Its occurring at night, preceding the fast, is established from another proof. The argument from the verse for requiring intention during the day would have been complete only if eating and drinking at night until dawn conflicted with the validity of carrying the intention; and the verse's permitting eating and drinking until dawn would prevent intention from night to dawn, though it is necessary, so intention would have to occur after dawn on that reading. That reading, as you know, is agreed to be invalid. As for deriving the other two rulings from it, that is sound and well founded, and God knows best. Al-Zamakhshari, noticing the invalidity of deriving the stated ruling from the verse, took the route of attributing it to them, saying "They said," which is used only for such an opinion, and he could not afford to point out the invalidity of the derivation because it accords with his school.]]

﴿While you are devoted to worship in the mosques﴾: staying in them. Iʿtikāf is confining oneself to the mosque for worship. The "mubāshara" here means intercourse, as preceded in His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go to your wives﴾, ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾. It has been said that its meaning is: do not touch them with desire; intercourse invalidates iʿtikāf, and likewise touching or kissing that leads to ejaculation. From Qatada: when a man was in iʿtikāf he would go out, have relations with his wife, and then return to the mosque, so God forbade them that. They said: this is evidence that iʿtikāf is only in a mosque, and that it is not restricted to one particular mosque. It has been said: it is valid only in the mosque of a prophet, which is one of the three mosques. It has been said: in a congregational (jāmiʿ) mosque. The common view is that it is in a mosque where congregational prayer is held. Mujahid recited: "fī al-masjid."

﴿These are the limits of God; so do not approach them﴾, i.e. do not come near them. If you ask: how is ﴿do not approach them﴾ said alongside His saying: ﴿So do not transgress them, and whoever transgresses the limits of God﴾? I say: whoever is in obedience to God and acts by His laws is operating within the sphere of truth, so he was forbidden to transgress it, because whoever transgresses it falls into the sphere of falsehood. Then the matter was intensified, and he was forbidden to approach the boundary, which is the barrier between the spheres of truth and falsehood, lest he draw near to falsehood and, being in the middle, keep far from the edge, let alone cross it. As the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every king has a protected preserve, and God's preserve is His prohibitions; whoever grazes around the preserve will soon fall into it." So grazing around the preserve and approaching its sphere are one and the same. It is also permissible that by the limits of God He means specifically His prohibitions and what He forbade, because of His saying: ﴿and do not have relations with them﴾, which is a limit not to be approached.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 188:

"And do not consume one another's wealth by false means" — in a manner that Allah has not permitted and has not prescribed. "And do not present it [as a bribe] to the rulers, nor cast its matter and its adjudication before the judges" — "so that you may consume a portion (fariq, a party) of people's wealth" — a part of the wealth of people, "sinfully," by means of false testimony, or by a false oath, or by a settlement, while knowing that the one in whose favour the judgment is given is a wrongdoer.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to the two disputants: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes before me. Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than the other, so I judge in his favour according to what I hear from him. Whoever I give, by my judgment, something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for what I give him is a piece of Fire." Then they both wept, and each of them said: "My right belongs to my companion." He said: "Go, and seek what is right (tawakhkha, i.e., be careful and deliberate), then draw lots (istahmil, i.e., cast lots), then let each of you absolve the other."

[[Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Abu Ya'la, all from the narration of Usama ibn Zayd from Abdullah ibn Rafi', freedman of Umm Salamah, from Umm Salamah. Its origin is in the two Sahihs without the addition.]]

It is also said that "and present it" means: cast part of it to the rulers of evil, by way of bribery. "And present" (tudlu) is a jussive verb falling under the prohibition, or a subjunctive governed by an implied "an," as in His words: "and conceal the truth" (wa taktumu al-haqq). "And you know" that you are upon falsehood; committing a sin while knowing its ugliness is uglier, and its doer is more deserving of reproach.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 189:

It is related that Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanm al-Ansari said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the matter with the crescent moon? It appears thin like a thread, then it increases until it becomes full and complete, then it keeps decreasing until it returns as it first appeared, never remaining in one state?" So it was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are signs marking times for people and for the pilgrimage.﴾ [[Al-Wahidi, in Asbab al-Nuzul, attributed it to Ibn al-Kalbi in abridged form, and al-Sha'bi also mentioned it, as the author mentioned.]] *Mawaqit* (times, markers) are landmarks by which people fix the times of their planting and trading, the due dates of their debts, their fasting and breaking of the fast, the number of their wives' waiting periods, the days of their menstruation, the periods of their pregnancies, and other matters, and they are markers for the Hajj by which its time is known. Some of the Ansar, when they entered the state of ihram, would not enter a garden, a house or a tent through its door. If a man was of the town-dwellers, he would make a breach in the back of his house through which he would enter and leave, or he would take a ladder to climb up. If he was of the dwellers of wool tents, he would exit from behind the tent. So they were told: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs; but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. So enter houses through their doors.﴾ ... wait, the verse reads: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah, and enter houses through their doors﴾ — and the sense of what is forbidden by Allah is the point of the verse.

If you ask: what is the connection of this with what precedes it? I answer: it is as if they were told, when they asked about the new moons and the wisdom in their waning — and its completion is known — that everything Allah, mighty and majestic, does is nothing but perfect wisdom and benefit for His servants. So leave off asking about it, and consider instead one practice you yourselves perform, which has nothing to do with righteousness, while you think it to be righteousness. It is also permissible that this be taken as a digression, since it was mentioned that the moons are markers for the Hajj, and this was among their practices in the Hajj. It may also be that this is a reproof of their inverting their question, and that their case in it is like the case of one who leaves the door of a house and enters it from its back. The meaning is: righteousness and what you ought to be upon is not that you invert your questions, but righteousness is the righteousness of one who fears this and avoids it and does not dare to do the like. Then He said: ﴿And come to houses through their doors﴾, that is: and undertake matters from the ways in which they must be undertaken, and do not invert them. What is meant is the obligation to settle the souls and bind the hearts to the belief that all of Allah's acts are wise and right, without the stirring of doubt or the objection of suspicion concerning that, so that one does not ask about it, since asking involves the ambiguity of committing doubt: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾

The fighting in the way of Allah: this is jihad (striving) to raise the word of Allah and to strengthen the religion. **Those who fight you**: those who engage you in actual combat, not those who withdraw from fighting. On this reading the verse is abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by His words: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾. It is narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that this was the first verse revealed about fighting in Medina, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fight whoever fought him and refrain from whoever refrained.

Or, "those who fight you" means those who set themselves against you in battle, excluding those who are not among the people of hostility: the elderly, the children, the monks, and the women. Or, "the disbelievers" all of them, because they are all opposed to the Muslims and intend to fight them, so they are in the status of combatants, whether they fight or not.
