[[Abū Dāwūd, Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Ḥākim narrated it through al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib: Abū Umāmah al-Taymī narrated to us, who said: "I used to hire out (my camel) on this route, and a people would say: 'You have no Hajj.' So I met Ibn ʿUmar, and he said: 'Are you not in the state of iḥrām? But—' the hadith..."]]

It is also related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked: "Did you used to dislike trade during the Hajj?" He said: "Was our livelihood anything but trade during the Hajj?" [[al-Ṭabarī narrated it through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muhājir from Abū Ṣāliḥ, the client of ʿUmar, who said: "I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful...' and he mentioned it." In its chain is Mandal ibn ʿAlī, who is weak.]]

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: ﴿fadlan min rabbikum fī mawāsim al-ḥajj﴾ (a gift from your Lord during the seasons of the Hajj). ﴿in tabtaghū﴾ (in that you seek) ﴿an tabtaghū﴾ [[The words "an tabtaghū" should have been placed before the explanation of His words, ﴿fadlan min rabbikum﴾. (ʿ)]] ﴿afaḍtum﴾: you pressed on in large numbers (dafaʿtum bi-kathrah). It is from the pouring of water, which is pouring abundantly. Its original form was afaḍtum anfusakum (you poured yourselves forth), and the object was omitted, as it is omitted in dafaʿū min mawḍiʿ kadhā (they pushed from such-and-such a place) and ṣabbū (they poured).

In the hadith of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him [[I have not found it. What is in al-Gharāʾib by Abū ʿUbayd al-Jurmī. In Musnad al-Shāfiʿī and Ṭabaqāt Ibn Saʿd, all from the hadith of Ibn ʿUyaynah from Ibn al-Munkadir, and from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Saʿīd ibn Yarbūʿ from Jubayr ibn al-Ḥuwayrith who said: "I saw Abū Bakr on Qaza', and he was urging his camel with his staff." Al-Jurmī added from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah from Ibn ʿUyaynah: "As if I were looking at his thigh, and it had become uncovered."]]: "He poured forth (ṣabba) at Dafrān, and he was urging (yakhrush) his camel with his staff." [[In some copies it is "Dhafrān," with the letter dhāl and fāʾ. Perhaps the first is with dāl and fāʾ, from al-dafar meaning stench only. Al-dhafar, with dhāl and fāʾ and a vowel, means the sharpness of a smell, whether pleasant or foul, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. As for al-daqar with dāl and qāf, it means harshness, lying, obscenity and slander. This is from al-Ṣiḥāḥ, and in it: al-khirsh is like al-khadsh. (ʿ)]]

They say: "They plunged into the talk (afāḍū fī al-ḥadīth) and burst out with it (ḥaḍabū fīhi)." [[In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-haḍbah is a downpour, and haḍaba al-qawm and ihtaḍabū fī al-ḥadīth means they poured into it. (ʿ)]]

﴿ʿArafāt﴾ is a name for the place of standing, named with a plural form like Adhruʿāt. If you say: "Why is it not made diptote (ghayr munṣarif), when it has two causes (of diptotic inflection): the definite form and the feminine?" I say: It cannot be free of the feminine. Either it is with the tāʾ that is in its wording, or with an implied tāʾ, as in Suʿād. The tāʾ in its wording is not a feminine marker. Rather, it is, together with the alif before it, the sign of the feminine plural. The tāʾ cannot be implied in it, because this tāʾ, by being specific to the feminine plural, prevents its being implied, just as the tāʾ of the feminine cannot be implied in bint (daughter), since the tāʾ which replaces the wāw, by being specific to the feminine like the tāʾ of the feminine, refuses to be implied.

They said: It was named so because it was described to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and when he saw it, he recognized it (ʿarafahā). It was said that when Jibrīl was taking him around the holy places, he showed it to him and said: "You have recognized it (qad ʿarafta)." It was said: Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ met there and recognized one another (taʿārafā). It was said: Because people recognize one another there. Allah knows the reality of that best. It is one of the names that were coined (murtajalah), because ʿarafah is not known among the names of kinds, except to be the plural of ʿārif (one who knows).

It was said: In it there is evidence that standing at ʿArafah is obligatory, because the outpouring (ifāḍah) cannot occur except after it. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "Hajj is ʿArafah; whoever attains ʿArafah has attained the Hajj." [[Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan and al-Ḥākim, and the wording is from al-Nasāʾī, who added: "before the dawn rises." All of them from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿmar al-Dīlī, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

﴿fa-dhkurū Allāh﴾ (so remember Allah): with the talbiyah, the tahlīl, the takbīr, praise and supplications. It was said: with the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers. ﴿al-mash ʿar al-ḥarām﴾ is Quzaḥ, the mountain on which the Imam stands, and on which there is a fire-beacon (al-mīqadah). It was said: the Mashʿar al-Ḥarām is what lies between the mountain of Muzdalifah, from the two narrow passes of ʿArafah [[His words "from the two narrow passes of ʿArafah": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-maʾzam is the narrow passage, and also the place of battle. (ʿ)]] to the valley of Muḥassir. Neither the two passes nor the valley of Muḥassir is part of the Mashʿar al-Ḥarām. The correct view is that it is the mountain, because of what Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, related: that when the Prophet ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah in the darkness, he mounted his she-camel and came to the Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, and he supplicated, glorified (kabbara) and declared the unity of Allah (hallala), and he remained standing until it became light. [[Narrated by Muslim in the chapter on the description of the Hajj, in the long hadith.]]

His words ﴿ʿinda al-mash ʿar al-ḥarām﴾ mean: in the direction of the Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, near to it, for the sake of its merit, like being near the Mountain of Mercy. Otherwise, all of Muzdalifah is a place of standing except the valley of Muḥassir. Or the ʿaqāb (rear parts) of Muzdalifah were made to be the Mashʿar, since they have the ruling of the Mashʿar and are joined to it, near the Mashʿar. The mashʿar means the sign, because it is the sign of worship.

It is described as al-ḥarām because of its sanctity. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that he looked at the people on the night of Jamʿ and said: "I have seen people this night who do not sleep." It was said: Muzdalifah was called Jamʿ because Ādam, peace be upon him, gathered there with Ḥawwāʾ, and he drew near to her (izdalafa ilayhā), meaning he approached her. It is related from Qatādah: because the two prayers are combined there (yujmaʿu). It is permissible to say: it is described by the act of its people, because they draw near (yazdalifūn) to Allah, that is, they seek nearness by standing there.

﴿kamā hadākum﴾: here mā is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah) or a preventive particle (kāffah). The meaning: remember Him with a good remembrance, as He guided you with good guidance; and remember Him as He taught you how to remember Him, and do not deviate from it. ﴿wa-in kuntum min qablihi﴾ (though before it you were): before the guidance, ﴿la-mina al-ḍāllīn﴾ (certainly among those who were astray), the ignorant, who did not know how to remember Him and worship Him. Here in is the lightened form of the heavy in (inna), and the lām is the distinguishing lām.

﴿thumma afīḍū﴾ (then pour forth): then let your outpouring be ﴿min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nās﴾ (from where the people poured forth), and do not be from Muzdalifah. This is because of what the Ḥums (Quraysh and their allies) were upon of arrogance over the people and haughtiness over them, and their exalting themselves above standing with the others. And their saying: "We are the people of Allah and the dwellers of His sanctuary, so we will not leave it," and so they stand at Jamʿ while all other people stand at ʿArafāt. [[Maḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "Al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him: 'That is because of what the Ḥums were upon of arrogance over the people...' (etc.)." Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The verse includes two points. First: the coordination of the two outpourings, one upon the other, with a single referent, which is the outpouring commanded. Someone might suppose it is coordination of a thing with itself, and this supposition is removed by the fact that between them there is the difference that exists between the general and the specific: the first statement is the outpouring in its unrestricted form, and the second command is the outpouring restricted by equality with the people. Second: after clarifying the soundness of the coordination, its being introduced by the particle thumma (then), which implies delay in addition to difference, while there is no delay between the absolute and the restricted addition. The answer: delay may be in terms of time, and it may also be in terms of the elevation of rank and the distance in height relative to others, and this is what he answered with after further vigor and clarification.]]

Then you asked: "What is the position of thumma?" I say: Its position is like its position in your saying: "Be kind to people, then do not be kind to other than the noble," where you use thumma to indicate the difference between being kind to the noble and being kind to others, and the distance between them. Likewise, when He commanded them to remember Him at the outpouring from ʿArafāt, He said: "Then pour forth," to show the difference between the two outpourings, and that one of them is correct and the other is mistaken.

It was said: "Then pour forth from where the people poured forth" means the Ḥums, that is, from Muzdalifah to Minā after the outpouring from ʿArafāt. It was read: "min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsī" with a kasrah on the sīn, that is, al-nāsī, who is Ādam, from His words: ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Ādam before, but he forgot (fa-nasiya)﴾. It means that the outpouring from ʿArafāt is an ancient law, so do not oppose it.

﴿wa-istaghfirū Allāh﴾ (and ask Allah for forgiveness): for your opposition in the standing place and similar matters of your ignorance. ﴿fa-idhā qaḍaytum manāsikakum﴾ (so when you have completed your rites): that is, when you have finished your acts of worship of Hajj and have departed. ﴿fa-dhkurū Allāh kadhikrikum ābāʾakum﴾ (then remember Allah as you remember your fathers): so increase the remembrance of Allah and go to extremes in it, as you do in remembering your fathers, their glories and their days. When they had completed their rites, they would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, enumerating the virtues of their fathers and mentioning the good qualities of their days.

﴿aw ashadda dhikran﴾ (or with a greater remembrance): in a position of genitive (jarr) by coordination with what the remembrance is attached to in His words ﴿kadhikrikum﴾, as you say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance." Or in an accusative position by coordination with ābāʾakum, meaning: or more intense in remembrance than your fathers, on the basis that dhikran is the tamyīz (specification) of the one who remembers. [[Mahmūd, may Allah have mercy on him: "Ashadd is coordinated with what the remembrance is attached to..." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: On the first view, ashadd refers to the thing remembered as the object. An example of the first: two people strike Zayd as an example, and one asks: "Which of them is more intense in striking Zayd?" and he refers it to the striker. An example of the second: Zayd strikes two people as an example, and you say: "Which of them is more intense in striking?" and you refer it to the one struck. On the first view, the preference is for the agent, which is the analogical form. On the second, the preference is for the object, which is contrary to analogy. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned in his Mufaṣṣal that it is irregular, with their saying: "Atasabbalu mirʾat al-taḥsīn wa-anā asarru minka" (in these examples he enumerated). I wonder how he applied the verse to it, when another path was available. In both views there is an escape from coordinating ashadd with the first remembrance, lest it refer to the remembrance while the remembrance has been put in the accusative as a tamyīz from it, so the remembrance would be remembering itself, which is impossible. But Abū al-Fatḥ (Ibn Jinnī) corrected this view and linked it to the pattern of their saying: "shaʿara shāʿir" and "janna junūnuh," and similar expressions in which the Arabs went to extremes, making an attribute have an attribute like itself, to establish its existence. It is clarified that the accusative of the remembrance as tamyīz requires that ashadd not refer to it, and determines that it is excluded from it, either by its referring to the remembering body by interpreting it as making it a remembering agent, as Abū al-Fatḥ arrived at: if you say "Zayd akram abā," then Zayd would be among the sons; and if you say "Zayd akram ab," he would be among the fathers. It is possible to coordinate it with the remembrance, meaning another way besides what Abū al-Fatḥ went to, namely the matter Sībawayh mentioned: "They say: 'He is ashaḥḥ al-nās rajulan (most miserly of people in a man), and hum khayr al-nās rajulan (they are the best of people in a man), and hum khayr al-nās ithnayn (they are the best of people in two).'" Here the genitive is in the position of the tanwīn, and rajul and ithnayn are accusative, just as wajh is accusative in your saying "huwa aḥsanu minhu wajhan." It is not except indefinite, just as the ḥāl (circumstantial) is not except indefinite. The rajul is the subject of the beginning. He meant by this that this is not like "huwa ashjaʿu al-nās ghulāman," for this may be that ghulām is the subject of the beginning, as in the first example, and it may be other than it. The verse in this way that I have clarified is placed on the first example, so the accusative mention refers to ashadd just as rajul (in the accusative) referred to ashaḥḥ. It is as if he said: "or the most intense of remembrances in remembrance." These are four ways, all of which have been trodden, except this way which I added, for my reflection has made that clear. ﴿ka-khashyati Allāh aw ashadda khashyah﴾ (like the fear of Allah or more intense fear). I did not come across al-Zamakhsharī's words on it after that.]]

﴿fa-minā al-nās man yaqūlu﴾ (among people is he who says): its meaning is: increase the remembrance and supplication of Allah, for people are divided between one who seeks through the remembrance of Allah nothing but the goods of this world, and one who seeks the good of both abodes. So be among the ones who increase. ﴿rabbanā ātinā fī al-dunyā﴾ (Our Lord, give us in this world): make our giving, that is, our provision, in this world only. ﴿wa-mā lahu fī al-ākhirati min khalāq﴾ (and he has no portion in the Hereafter): that is, whoever seeks my portion (khalāqī), which is share. Or: this caller has no share in the Hereafter, because his concern is limited to this world.

The two good things (al-ḥasanatān) are what the righteous seek in this world: health, sufficiency, and success in good; and what they seek in the Hereafter: reward. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "The good in this world is a righteous wife, and in the Hereafter the maiden of paradise (ḥawrāʾ). The punishment of the Fire is an evil wife." ﴿ulāʾika al-dāʿūna bi-al-ḥasanatayni lahum naṣībun mimmā kasabū﴾ (those are the ones who ask for the two good things; for them is a share of what they earned): that is, a share of the same kind as what they earned of good deeds, which is the reward, the good benefits. Or: from the sake of what they earned, as in His words: ﴿mimmā khaṭīʾātihim ughriqū﴾ (because of their sins they were drowned). Or: they have a share of what they asked for, and We will give them what they deserve according to their interests in this world and their merit in the Hereafter. Supplication was called earning because it is one of the deeds, and deeds are described as earned: ﴿bimā kasabat aydīkum﴾ (by what your hands have earned). It is permissible that ﴿ulāʾika﴾ refers to both groups together, and that each group has a share of the kind of what they earned.

﴿wa-Allāhu sarīʿu al-ḥisāb﴾ (and Allah is swift in reckoning): He is about to establish the Resurrection and call the servants to account. So hasten to increase the remembrance and to seek the Hereafter. Or: He described Himself as swift in reckoning the creatures despite their great number and the abundance of their deeds, to show the perfection of His power and the necessity of being wary of Him.

It is related that He reckons all creation in the time it takes to milk a sheep. It is related: in the time between two milkings of a she-camel. It is related: in the time of a single blink.

فَضْلًا مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ ﴿fadlan min rabbikum﴾: an enrichment and a gift from Him, and it means profit and gain through trade. Some of the Arabs considered it sinful to trade during the days of the Hajj. When the ten days began, they refrained from buying and selling, so no market was held for them. They called anyone who went out to trade al-Dāj, and they would say: "These are the dāj, and they are not the ḥājj (pilgrims)." It was said that ʿUkāz, Majannah and Dhū al-Majāz were their markets in the Jahiliyyah, where they traded during the season, and their livelihood came from them. When Islam came, they regarded it as sinful, so Allah lifted the blame from them in this matter and permitted it for them. Trade is permitted only so long as it does not distract from worship.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "We are a people who hire out our camels on this route, and some people claim that we have no Hajj." He said: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what you have asked, and he did not answer him, until ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ was revealed. Then he called for him and said: 'You are pilgrims.'" [[Abū Dāwūd, Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Ḥākim narrated it through al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib: Abū Umāmah al-Taymī narrated to us, who said: "I used to hire out (my camel) on this route, and a people would say: 'You have no Hajj.' So I met Ibn ʿUmar, and he said: 'Are you not in the state of iḥrām? But—' the hadith..."]]

It is also related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked: "Did you used to dislike trade during the Hajj?" He said: "Was our livelihood anything but trade during the Hajj?" [[al-Ṭabarī narrated it through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muhājir from Abū Ṣāliḥ, the client of ʿUmar, who said: "I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful...' and he mentioned it." In its chain is Mandal ibn ʿAlī, who is weak.]]

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited: ﴿fadlan min rabbikum fī mawāsim al-ḥajj﴾ (a gift from your Lord during the seasons of the Hajj). ﴿in tabtaghū﴾ (in that you seek) ﴿an tabtaghū﴾ [[The words "an tabtaghū" should have been placed before the explanation of His words, ﴿fadlan min rabbikum﴾. (ʿ)]] ﴿afaḍtum﴾: you pressed on in large numbers (dafaʿtum bi-kathrah). It is from the pouring of water, which is pouring abundantly. Its original form was afaḍtum anfusakum (you poured yourselves forth), and the object was omitted, as it is omitted in dafaʿū min mawḍiʿ kadhā (they pushed from such-and-such a place) and ṣabbū (they poured).

In the hadith of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him [[I have not found it. What is in al-Gharāʾib by Abū ʿUbayd al-Jurmī. This is from al-Ṣiḥāḥ, and in it: al-khirsh is like al-khadsh. (ʿ)]]

They say: "They plunged into the talk (afāḍū fī al-ḥadīth) and burst out with it (ḥaḍabū fīhi)." [[In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-haḍbah is a downpour, and haḍaba al-qawm and ihtaḍabū fī al-ḥadīth means they poured into it. (ʿ)]]

It is permissible to say: it is described by the act of its people, because they draw near (yazdalifūn) to Allah, that is, they seek nearness by standing there.

﴿kamā hadākum﴾: here mā is either a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah) or a preventive particle (kāffah). The meaning: remember Him with a good remembrance, as He guided you with good guidance; and remember Him as He taught you how to remember Him, and do not deviate from it. ﴿wa-in kuntum min qablihi﴾ (though before it you were): before the guidance, ﴿la-mina al-ḍāllīn﴾ (certainly among those who were astray), the ignorant, who did not know how to remember Him and worship Him. Here in is the lightened form of the heavy in (inna), and the lām is the distinguishing lām.

﴿thumma afīḍū﴾ (then pour forth): then let your outpouring be ﴿min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nās﴾ (from where the people poured forth), and do not be from Muzdalifah. This is because of what the Ḥums (Quraysh and their allies) were upon of arrogance over the people and haughtiness over them, and their exalting themselves above standing with the others. And their saying: "We are the people of Allah and the dwellers of His sanctuary, so we will not leave it," and so they stand at Jamʿ while all other people stand at ʿArafāt. [[Maḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "Al-Zamakhsharī, may Allah have mercy on him: 'That is because of what the Ḥums were upon of arrogance over the people...' (etc.)." Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The verse includes two points. First: the coordination of the two outpourings, one upon the other, with a single referent, which is the outpouring commanded. Someone might suppose it is coordination of a thing with itself, and this supposition is removed by the fact that between them there is the difference that exists between the general and the specific: the first statement is the outpouring in its unrestricted form, and the second command is the outpouring restricted by equality with the people. Second: after clarifying the soundness of the coordination, its being introduced by the particle thumma (then), which implies delay in addition to difference, while there is no delay between the absolute and the restricted addition. The answer: delay may be in terms of time, and it may also be in terms of the elevation of rank and the distance in height relative to others, and this is what he answered with after further vigor and clarification.]]

Then you asked: "What is the position of thumma?" I say: Its position is like its position in your saying: "Be kind to people, then do not be kind to other than the noble," where you use thumma to indicate the difference between being kind to the noble and being kind to others, and the distance between them. Likewise, when He commanded them to remember Him at the outpouring from ʿArafāt, He said: "Then pour forth," to show the difference between the two outpourings, and that one of them is correct and the other is mistaken.

It was said: "Then pour forth from where the people poured forth" means the Ḥums, that is, from Muzdalifah to Minā after the outpouring from ʿArafāt. It was read: "min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsī" with a kasrah on the sīn, that is, al-nāsī, who is Ādam, from His words: ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Ādam before, but he forgot (fa-nasiya)﴾. It means that the outpouring from ʿArafāt is an ancient law, so do not oppose it.

﴿wa-istaghfirū Allāh﴾ (and ask Allah for forgiveness): for your opposition in the standing place and similar matters of your ignorance. ﴿fa-idhā qaḍaytum manāsikakum﴾ (so when you have completed your rites): that is, when you have finished your acts of worship of Hajj and have departed. ﴿fa-dhkurū Allāh kadhikrikum ābāʾakum﴾ (then remember Allah as you remember your fathers): so increase the remembrance of Allah and go to extremes in it, as you do in remembering your fathers, their glories and their days. When they had completed their rites, they would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, enumerating the virtues of their fathers and mentioning the good qualities of their days.

﴿aw ashadda dhikran﴾ (or with a greater remembrance): in a position of genitive (jarr) by coordination with what the remembrance is attached to in His words ﴿kadhikrikum﴾, as you say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance." Or in an accusative position by coordination with ābāʾakum, meaning: or more intense in remembrance than your fathers, on the basis that dhikran is the tamyīz (specification) of the one who remembers. [[Mahmūd, may Allah have mercy on him: "Ashadd is coordinated with what the remembrance is attached to..." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: On the first view, ashadd refers to the thing remembered as the object. An example of the first: two people strike Zayd as an example, and one asks: "Which of them is more intense in striking Zayd?" and he refers it to the striker. An example of the second: Zayd strikes two people as an example, and you say: "Which of them is more intense in striking?" and you refer it to the one struck. On the first view, the preference is for the agent, which is the analogical form. On the second, the preference is for the object, which is contrary to analogy. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned in his Mufaṣṣal that it is irregular, with their saying: "Atasabbalu mirʾat al-taḥsīn wa-anā asarru minka" (in these examples he enumerated). I wonder how he applied the verse to it, when another path was available. In both views there is an escape from coordinating ashadd with the first remembrance, lest it refer to the remembrance while the remembrance has been put in the accusative as a tamyīz from it, so the remembrance would be remembering itself, which is impossible. But Abū al-Fatḥ (Ibn Jinnī) corrected this view and linked it to the pattern of their saying: "shaʿara shāʿir" and "janna junūnuh," and similar expressions in which the Arabs went to extremes, making an attribute have an attribute like itself, to establish its existence. It is clarified that the accusative of the remembrance as tamyīz requires that ashadd not refer to it, and determines that it is excluded from it, either by its referring to the remembering body by interpreting it as making it a remembering agent, as Abū al-Fatḥ arrived at: if you say "Zayd akram abā," then Zayd would be among the sons; and if you say "Zayd akram ab," he would be among the fathers. It is possible to coordinate it with the remembrance, meaning another way besides what Abū al-Fatḥ went to, namely the matter Sībawayh mentioned: "They say: 'He is ashaḥḥ al-nās rajulan (most miserly of people in a man), and hum khayr al-nās rajulan (they are the best of people in a man), and hum khayr al-nās ithnayn (they are the best of people in two).'" Here the genitive is in the position of the tanwīn, and rajul and ithnayn are accusative, just as wajh is accusative in your saying "huwa aḥsanu minhu wajhan." It is not except indefinite, just as the ḥāl (circumstantial) is not except indefinite. The rajul is the subject of the beginning. He meant by this that this is not like "huwa ashjaʿu al-nās ghulāman," for this may be that ghulām is the subject of the beginning, as in the first example, and it may be other than it. The verse in this way that I have clarified is placed on the first example, so the accusative mention refers to ashadd just as rajul (in the accusative) referred to ashaḥḥ. It is as if he said: "or the most intense of remembrances in remembrance." These are four ways, all of which have been trodden, except this way which I added, for my reflection has made that clear. ﴿ka-khashyati Allāh aw ashadda khashyah﴾ (like the fear of Allah or more intense fear). I did not come across al-Zamakhsharī's words on it after that.]]

﴿fa-minā al-nās man yaqūlu﴾ (among people is he who says): its meaning is: increase the remembrance and supplication of Allah, for people are divided between one who seeks through the remembrance of Allah nothing but the goods of this world, and one who seeks the good of both abodes. So be among the ones who increase. ﴿rabbanā ātinā fī al-dunyā﴾ (Our Lord, give us in this world): make our giving, that is, our provision, in this world only. ﴿wa-mā lahu fī al-ākhirati min khalāq﴾ (and he has no portion in the Hereafter): that is, whoever seeks my portion (khalāqī), which is share. Or: this caller has no share in the Hereafter, because his concern is limited to this world.

The two good things (al-ḥasanatān) are what the righteous seek in this world: health, sufficiency, and success in good; and what they seek in the Hereafter: reward. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "The good in this world is a righteous wife, and in the Hereafter the maiden of paradise (ḥawrāʾ). The punishment of the Fire is an evil wife." ﴿ulāʾika al-dāʿūna bi-al-ḥasanatayni lahum naṣībun mimmā kasabū﴾ (those are the ones who ask for the two good things; for them is a share of what they earned): that is, a share of the same kind as what they earned of good deeds, which is the reward, the good benefits. Or: from the sake of what they earned, as in His words: ﴿mimmā khaṭīʾātihim ughriqū﴾ (because of their sins they were drowned). Or: they have a share of what they asked for, and We will give them what they deserve according to their interests in this world and their merit in the Hereafter. Supplication was called earning because it is one of the deeds, and deeds are described as earned: ﴿bimā kasabat aydīkum﴾ (by what your hands have earned). It is permissible that ﴿ulāʾika﴾ refers to both groups together, and that each group has a share of the kind of what they earned.

﴿wa-Allāhu sarīʿu al-ḥisāb﴾ (and Allah is swift in reckoning): He is about to establish the Resurrection and call the servants to account. So hasten to increase the remembrance and to seek the Hereafter. Or: He described Himself as swift in reckoning the creatures despite their great number and the abundance of their deeds, to show the perfection of His power and the necessity of being wary of Him.

It is related that He reckons all creation in the time it takes to milk a sheep. It is related: in the time between two milkings of a she-camel. It is related: in the time of a single blink.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 203:**

"The counted days" (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat): these are the days of tashriq, and the remembrance of Allah during them is the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") after the prayers and at the jamarat (the pillars stoned during the pilgrimage).

It is related from ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) that he would say the takbir in his tent at Mina, and those around him would say it too, until the people were saying it in the road and during the circumambulation (ṭawāf).

﴿Whoever hastens (taʿajjala)﴾: meaning, whoever hastens in the departure (al-nafr) or seeks to hasten the departure. *Taʿajjala* and *istaʿjala* both come as intransitive (muṭāwiʿ) forms meaning "to hasten" (ʿajjala). One says *taʿajjala fī al-amr* and *istaʿjala* (to hurry in the matter). They are also transitive (mutaʿaddī), so one says *taʿajjala al-dhahāb* and *istaʿjalahu* (to hasten the going). The intransitive sense (muṭāwaʿa) is more suited to His words ﴿and whoever delays﴾, as it is in the saying of the poet:

*Qad yudriku al-mutaʾanni baʿḍa ḥājatihi... wa qad yakūnu maʿa al-mustaʿjili al-zalalu*

*"The one who takes his time sometimes attains part of his need, and sometimes the hasty one faces a slip."*

[[*Wa al-nāsu man yulqi khayran qāʾilūna lahu... mā yashtahī wa li-umm al-mukhṭiʾ al-habalu*

*Qad yudriku al-mutaʾanni baʿḍa ḥājatihi... wa qad yakūnu maʿa al-mustaʿjili al-zalalu*

*Wa rubbamā fāta qawman jalla amruhum... min al-ta'annī wa kāna al-ra'yu law ʿajjalū*

*It is by al-Quṭāmī, and it is said to be by al-Aʿshā.* "Al-nās" is the subject (mubtada'). "Man yulqi" (whoever meets) "khayran" (good) is a conditional clause (shart) whose answer's first part is omitted, meaning "they are saying to him," and the clause is the predicate of the subject. "Mā yashtahī" means what he desires, namely a prayer for good or praise. It is also narrated as *mā tashtahī*, so its meaning may be: they say to him, "what you desire, O addressee." It is also permissible for "mā" to be interrogative, meaning "what is it that you desire, O you who have met good?" but the antithesis (muqābala) rules this out. "Habilat al-mar'ah habalan" (kataʿiba taʿaban) means the woman was bereaved of her child, lost him, and grieved over him. The meaning is: "and it is said to the mother of the one who errs, the bereaved one," which is a curse upon her for the death of her son. Then he said:

*Qad yudriku al-manhalu baʿḍa qaṣdihi... wa qad yakūnu maʿa al-mutaʿajjili al-khaṭaʾu*

*"The one who drinks (at the water) attains part of his aim, and sometimes the hasty one faces error."*

"Ajjalahu, fa-taʿajjala wa-istaʿjala," and both also take a direct object, so one says *taʿajjala al-amr* and *istaʿjalahu*. Then he said: "Sometimes the greater part of the aim of some people is lost because of their deliberation, when the correct opinion would have been to hasten." "Law" here is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. The meaning is that some needs call for deliberation and some for haste.

It is also permissible that "law ʿajjalū" be the noun (ism) of *kāna*, with "al-raʾy" in the accusative as its predicate. In place of it, *al-ḥazm* (resolve) is also narrated, and the meaning is close. In the verse there is a rhetorical device (badīʿ) called *al-ʿaks wa al-tabdīl* (reversal and substitution), which is bringing the opposite of the well-known meaning, as here: praise of deliberation is the well-known view, and praise of haste contradicts it. This was stated by al-Suyuti in his commentary on *ʿUqūd al-Jumān*.]]

﴿in two days﴾ after the day of sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr), the day of rest (yawm al-qarr) [[His saying "the day of sacrifice, the day of rest": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, it is because people rest in their dwellings. (ʿ)]]. This is the day that the people of Mecca call "the day of heads," and the day after it one departs once one has finished the stoning of the jamarat, as people do today. This is the school of al-Shafiʿi, and it is narrated from Qatada. According to Abu Ḥanifa and his companions, one departs before dawn [of the third day], and ﴿whoever delays until he has stoned on the third day﴾. Stoning on the third day may be brought forward before midday according to Abu Ḥanifa, but according to al-Shafiʿi it is not permissible.

If you ask: how does He say ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ regarding both hastening and delaying? I answer: it is an indication that hastening and delaying are both optional, as if it were said: "so hasten or delay." If you ask: is not delaying more excellent? I answer: indeed it is, but the option may be between the permissible and the more excellent, just as the traveler is given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast, although fasting is better. [[Maḥmūd (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "He negated sin on both sides only to show the choice between the two matters, the permissible and the more excellent, just as the traveler is given the choice between fasting and not fasting, although fasting is better." Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: his statement that the choice occurs between the permissible and the more excellent is not sound, for choice necessitates equality in the purpose of the one choosing, and conflicts with seeking one of the two sides and commanding it. How can what necessitates demand and preference be combined with what necessitates equality and choice? Something close to this happened to Imam al-Ḥaramayn, who distinguished obligation from recommendation by saying that recommendation involves a command together with the option of leaving, whereas obligation does not. The scholars of the field did not accept this. Al-Zamakhshari, in his commentary on the verse, erred, so he is bound by the objection raised against him. The lack of agreement between his commentary and the verse is that the verse's content negates sin on both sides together, and this shared aspect is common to recommendation, disapproval, and permissibility; but recommendation is distinguished by preferring the act over leaving it, while disapproval and permissibility are distinguished by the choice between them. Thus there is no conflict between recommending delay and that it is more excellent, and negating sin from the one who leaves it for hastening. Then the objection that was binding on him does not arise, and he answered it.]] It was also said: the people of the Jahiliyya were two groups: some held that the one who hastened was sinful, and others held that the one who delayed was sinful, so the Qur'an came with negating sin from both of them, meaning that this is the choice.

﴿for the one who fears Allah﴾: negating sin from the one who hastens and the one who delays is for the sake of the pilgrim who is mindful of Allah, so that nothing of either doubt enters his heart, and he does not suppose that one of them burdens the other with sins for acting upon it. Because the one who is mindful is cautious and guards against everything that troubles him, and because he is truly the pilgrim in the sight of Allah.

Then He said: ﴿and fear Allah, that you may be cared for by Him﴾ (liyuʿbaʾa bikum). It is also permissible that what is meant is that which has been mentioned of the rulings of the pilgrimage and other matters, for those who are mindful, because they alone benefit from it and not others, as in His words: ﴿That is better for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 204–206:

﴿And there is of the people one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you﴾: "yu'jibuka" means "yurūquka" (pleases you) and "yu'ẓimu fī qalbika" (is great in your heart). From it comes the expression "al-shay' al-'ajīb" (the wondrous thing), which is great in the soul.

He is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. He was a man sweet of speech: whenever he met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would soften his words to him, claim that he loved him and was a Muslim, and say: "Allah knows that I am truthful." It was also said: the verse is general, concerning the hypocrites, whose tongues were sweet while their hearts were more bitter than aloes.

If you ask: with what does the phrase ﴿in the life of this world﴾ connect? I answer: it connects with "speech," meaning: what he says concerning the affairs of this world pleases you, because his claim of love is false, sought thereby as a portion of the worldly portions, and he does not intend by it the Hereafter, as genuine faith and sincere love for the Messenger are intended. So his speech is then in this world, not in the Hereafter. It is also permissible for it to connect with "yu'jibuka" (pleases you), meaning: his speech is sweet and eloquent in this world, so it pleases you; but it will not please you in the Hereafter, because of the stammering and faltering that will overtake him at the Standing, or because he will not be permitted to speak, so he will not speak in a way that pleases you.

﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾: that is, he swears and says, "Allah is witness to what is in my heart of love for you and of Islam." It is recited as "wa-yashhadu Allah" and in the codex of Ubayy it is "wa-yastashhidu Allah" (and he asks Allah to witness).

﴿And he is the most contentious of opponents﴾: he is the most intense in disputation and enmity toward the Muslims. It was also said: there was a feud between him and Thaqif, so he attacked them by night, destroyed their livestock, and burned their crops. "Al-khiṣām" means mutual contention. The genitive construction of "alladd" is in the sense of "fī," as in their saying "thabata al-ghadr" (treachery is established). Or the contention is made "alladd" as an intensification. It was also said that "al-khiṣām" is the plural of "khaṣm," like "ṣa'b" and "ṣi'āb," meaning: he is the most intense of adversaries in contention.

﴿And when he turns away﴾: that is, departs from you after softening his speech and sweetening his discourse, ﴿he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein﴾, as he did to Thaqif. It was also said: "wa-idhā tawallā" means, when he becomes a ruler, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the earth by destroying the tilth and the progeny. It was also said: he displays injustice, so that Allah, because of the evil of his injustice, withholds the rain, and so the tilth and the progeny are destroyed. It is recited as "wa-yuhlika al-ḥarth wa-al-nasl" (and He destroys the tilth and the progeny), with the verb taking the tilth and progeny as subject; the nominative is then coordinated with "sa'ā" (strives). Al-Ḥasan read it with a fatḥa on the lām, which is a dialect form, like "abā yaʾbā" (he refused). And it is transmitted from him as "wa-yuhlaka" in the passive voice.

﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾: from your saying "akhadhtuhu bi-kadhā" (I took him with such-and-such), when you cause him to bear it and bind him to it. That is, the might within him and the zeal of the Jahiliyyah carry him toward the sin that is forbidden, and bind him to committing it, and not let him be freed from it out of harm and obstinacy. Or it means: in rejection of the words of the admonisher.

﴿And when he turns away﴾: that is, departs from you after softening his speech and sweetening his discourse, ﴿he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein﴾, as he did to Thaqif. It was also said: "wa-idhā tawallā" means, when he becomes a ruler, he does what the wicked rulers do of corruption in the earth by destroying the tilth and the progeny. It was also said: he displays injustice, so that Allah, because of the evil of his injustice, withholds the rain, and so the tilth and the progeny are destroyed. It is recited as "wa-yuhlika al-ḥarth wa-al-nasl" (and He destroys the tilth and the progeny), with the verb taking the tilth and progeny as subject; the nominative is then coordinated with "sa'ā" (strives). Al-Ḥasan read it with a fatḥa on the lām, which is a dialect form, like "abā yaʾbā" (he refused). And it is transmitted from him as "wa-yuhlaka" in the passive voice.

﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾: from your saying "akhadhtuhu bi-kadhā" (I took him with such-and-such), when you cause him to bear it and bind him to it. That is, the might within him and the zeal of the Jahiliyyah carry him toward the sin that is forbidden, and bind him to committing it, and not let him be freed from it out of harm and obstinacy. Or it means: in rejection of the words of the admonisher.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 207:

"yashri nafsahu" (﴿sells his soul﴾): meaning he sells it, i.e., expends it in jihad. It is also said: he enjoins good and forbids evil until he is killed. It is also said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan. The polytheists wanted to force him to abandon Islam, and they killed a group who were with him. So he said to them: "I am an old man. If I am with you, I will not benefit you, and if I am against you, I will not harm you. So leave me with what I am upon, and take my wealth." They accepted his wealth from him, and he went to Madinah.

"Wallahu ra'ufun bil-'ibad" (﴿And Allah is Compassionate to the servants﴾): in that He imposed jihad upon them and thereby exposed them to the reward of the martyrs.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 208–209:

Al-silm (السلم), with the sin vowelled both with a kasra and with a fatha. Al-A'mash read it with a fatha on the sin and the lam, and it means submission and obedience, i.e., submit to God and obey Him completely (كافة), so that none of you withdraws his hand from obedience to Him. It has also been said that it means Islam. The address is to the People of the Book, because they believed in their prophet and their scripture, or to the hypocrites, because they believed with their tongues.

It is permissible for kaffatan (كافة, "completely") to be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from al-silm, because it is feminine, just as ḥarb (war) is feminine. The poet said:

"Peace: take from it what pleases you,
and war will suffice you with a few of its breaths (jurʿ, sips)."

[[Abu Khurasha, as for you, if you are a man of a clan...
the Ḍabuʿ (hyena) has not devoured my people.

If you are a boulder of basr (flint stone), I will not grind it down,
I will kindle fire upon it and heat it, and it will split.

Peace: take from it what pleases you,
and war will suffice you with a few of its breaths (sips).

It is by al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas, addressing Khafaf ibn Nadba. As for "wa-amma anta" (وأما أنت): its origin is "li-anna kunta" (لأن كنت), where the lam of causation was deleted and kāna in its defective (nāqiṣa) function, so its pronoun became detached, and mā replaced it, and the verbal-noun "an" (أن) was assimilated into it. The Kufans said that "an" with a fatha can be conditional, as "kāna" with a kasra, and on this basis there is no need to posit a lam of causation, and the meaning is a conditional and its response. The ḍabuʿ (ضبع) is either a year of drought or the well-known animal.

The basr is stones that tend towards whiteness, singular basra. It has been said it has the same meaning as the previous. "Abbasahu tabʾīsan" (أبسه تأبيسا) means he humbled and broke it. He says: O Abu Khurasha, because you were the commander of an army and boasted over me, do not do that, for my people are present and numerous. He alluded to this by the hyena not devouring them. It may also be that there is an oblique allusion in it. Then he said: If you are like a rock of stone, I am unable to grind it down and break it because of its hardness, or I will kindle the fire of war upon it with the help of the horsemen for me, so I burn it and it cracks and breaks. Thus the kindling (al-īqād) is an explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya), and the heating (al-iḥmāʾ) is a supporting complement (tarshīḥ). Or, if I do not overcome you by the usual way, I will contrive until I overcome you, just as a stone is broken by fire through contrivance. He used the third person pronoun in view of the subject (khabar), and the raising of "uḥmīhi" (أحميه) and "yanṣadiʿ" (ينصدع) after a present-tense conditional is a rare and weak usage, especially with their being conjoined to a jussive verb, and perhaps he thought it was jussive.

Al-silm, with a fatha and with a kasra, means reconciliation. "Take from it" means take enough of it through the length of the period, or take from us because of it. As for war, a little of it will suffice you, so the indefiniteness of jurʿ (جرع) is for diminution. He likened war to a fire confined in a vessel with vents from which breaths escape, and he likened the breaths to water, by way of metonymy (al-makniyya). The "breaths" are an imaginative representation (takhyīl) for the first, and the "sips" are an imaginative representation for the second. There is in it a kind of mockery, in that he likened the hot to the cold, as if he gives it to drink from its breaths. It is narrated as "fī al-silm taʾkhudhu minnā mā raḍīta bihi" (في السلم تأخذ منا ما رضيت به), meaning: you take from us a great deal in a time of peace, and you can endure only little of our war. But this narration only indicates the feminine gender of al-silm, by way of contrast with ḥarb.]]

Because the believers were commanded to enter into all the acts of obedience, and not to enter into one act of obedience and leave another. Or into all the branches and laws of Islam, and not to neglect any of them. It is narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam that he asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to observe the Sabbath, and to read from the Torah in his night prayer.

[[ʿAbd al-Ghani ibn Saʿid al-Thaqafi narrated it in his tafsir, from Musa ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-San'ani, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAtaʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. That was because, when they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), they believed in his law and the law of Musa. So they venerated the Sabbath and disliked the flesh and milk of camels after they had become Muslims. The Muslims rebuked them for this, and they said: 'We are able to do this and that,' and they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'The Torah is the book of God, the Exalted; let us act by both of them.' [In another copy: 'Indeed the Torah is the book of God. Call us to act by it.'] So God, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace completely﴾." This is a fabricated report (nuskha mawḍūʿa). Al-Tabari has also related it through the narration of Hajjaj ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿIkrima. And a group of the Jews asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to observe the Sabbath and to stand in the night with the Torah. So God commanded them to uphold the rites of Islam and to desire nothing other than it. He said, then he mentioned the verse. This [explanation] is preferable. And Ibn Jurayj did not hear from ʿIkrima.]] and that he read from the Torah in his night prayer [[His words "in his night prayer" probably have a lacuna after them, with the estimated meaning: "so it was revealed." (ʿ)]]. Kāffa (كافة) is from the root kaffa (to restrain), as if they restrained themselves so that none of them would go out from their collective unity.

﴿But if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you﴾, i.e., after the proofs and the evidences that what you were called to enter is the truth, ﴿then know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾. ﴿Mighty﴾: dominant, whom the retribution against you cannot overpower. ﴿Wise﴾: He does not punish except with right.

It is narrated that a reciter recited "ghafūrun raḥīm" (forgiving, merciful), and a Bedouin heard him, rejected it, and did not recite the Qur'an, and said: "If this is the word of God, then the Wise would not say such a thing; He does not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping, for that would be an incitement to it." Abu al-Sammal read zallatum with a kasra on the lam, and they are two dialects, like ẓalla and ẓalla (ظللت وظللت).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 210:

"Coming of Allah" means the coming of His command and His punishment, like His saying: ﴿Or there come the command of your Lord﴾ (16:33), and ﴿...when Our punishment came to them﴾ (7:4 and similar). It is also permissible that the thing that comes be omitted, in the sense that Allah Himself comes to them with His might or His vengeance, the omission being indicated by His saying: ﴿...then surely Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ (2:209).

﴿In shadows﴾: the plural of ẓullah (ẓulla), which is that which shades you. It is also read ẓilāl, which is the plural of ẓulla, like qillah and qilāl, or the plural of ẓill (shade).

﴿And the angels﴾ is read in the nominative (wal-malā'ikatu), like His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them?﴾ (16:33). It is also read in the genitive, as a conjunction with ẓulal or with al-ghamām (the clouds).

If you ask: why would the punishment come in the clouds? I answer: because clouds are the place where mercy is expected. So when punishment descends from them, the matter is more dreadful and terrifying, for when evil comes from where one does not expect it, it is more grievous, just as when good comes from where one does not expect it, it is more joyful. How much more so when evil comes from where good is expected. For this reason the thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqah) is among the most dreadful forms of punishment, since it comes from where rain is anticipated. And for this reason the saying of the Exalted has weighed heavily upon those who reflect on the Book of Allah: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾ (39:47).

﴿And the matter is decided﴾: the affair of their destruction and annihilation is completed and finished. Mu'ādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) read it as wa-qaḍā'u l-amr (with qaḍā'), in the nominative as a verbal noun, conjoined to al-malā'ikah (the angels). It is also read turja'u and turja'a, in the active and passive voice, with the feminine and masculine forms in both.

Ask (sal) — an imperative addressed to the Messenger (peace be upon him), or to everyone. This question is one of reproach, just as the disbelievers will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection: "How many clear signs have We given them?" — that is, clear signs through the hands of their prophets, which are their miracles; or a sign in the scriptures testifying to the truth of the religion of Islam. "And whoever substitutes the blessing of Allah" — His signs, and they are the most excellent blessing from Allah, because they are the means of guidance and deliverance from misguidance. Their substitution of them: Allah manifested them so that they would be means of their guidance, but they made them means of their misguidance, as in His saying: "But it increased them in uncleanness to their uncleanness" (Qur'an 9:125). Or they distorted the verses of the scriptures [[His saying "or they distorted the verses of the scriptures" is perhaps a coordination with the meaning, i.e., that they made the miracles means of their misguidance, whereas Allah had made them means of their guidance. Or they distorted the verses of the scriptures ... etc. (Ghayth)]] which indicate the religion of Muhammad (peace be upon him). If you say: is "kam" interrogative or informative? I say: it may be either.

The meaning of interrogation in it is for affirmation (taqrir). If you say: what is the meaning of "after what has come to them"? I say: its meaning is "after they had become able to know it, or knew it," as in His saying: "Then they distort it after they had understood it" (Qur'an 2:75). For when a person is not able to know it, or does not know it, it is as though it were absent from him. And it has been read: "wa-man yubaddil" with the lightened (takhfif) form.

al-Mu'ayyin (the one who beautifies) is Satan. [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him: "al-Muzayyin huwa al-Shaytan... ila akhirihi." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, says: The attribution of beautifying (tazyin) to Allah the Exalted and its attribution to others occur in several places in the Noble Book. This verse admits both readings, but attribution to Allah's power is literal (haqiqah), while attribution to other than Him is figurative (majaz), according to the principles of the Sunnah. Al-Zamakhshari operates in the reverse of this: if he attributes an act to Allah's power, he makes it figurative, and if he attributes it to some of His creatures, he makes it literal. The cause of this inversion is following desire in corrupt principles.]] He beautified the life of this world for them and made it attractive in their eyes through his whisperings, and made it beloved to them, so they desire nothing other than it.

It is also permissible that Allah beautified it for them by forsaking them until they found it good and loved it, or that His granting respite to the one who beautifies it is itself a beautifying. What indicates this is the reading of one who recited (zuyyina lilladhina kafaru al-hayat al-dunya) with the verb in the active voice. "And those who disbelieve mock those who believe": the disbelievers used to mock the believers who had no share of this world, such as Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ammar, Suhayb and others, meaning they desire nothing other than it. They mock those who have no share in it, or those who seek something other than it. "But those who have feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection," because they are in 'Illiyyin of the heaven, while they are in Sijjin of the earth. [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him: "Li-annahum fi 'Illiyyin min al-sama', wa-hum fi Sijjin... ila akhirihi." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, says: This is placing an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun with another attribute, and its like is abundant in the Book of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment," and the original would have been "Indeed they..." So the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun with another attribute, and in it is included the mention of the attribute of wrongdoing following the attribute of loss. In al-Zamakhshari's words there is an inclination toward his principle of the obligation of threatening the sinners. Do you not see him saying: "to show you that none is made happy in His presence except the believing God-fearing one," an indication that the one who is not God-fearing, who persists in major sins, is certainly wretched, like those who mock the believers? Some of them strain to justify this by saying: because he made the believer the same as the God-fearing one. The requirement of his corrupt principle is that faith entails piety, so that no believer is assumed except a God-fearing one, since faith, as he explains it in this commentary and as the people of his innovation explain it in their books, is affirmation of correct belief and its utterance with righteous deeds, and whoever falls short in deeds, either by persisting in a major sin or by abandoning an important obligation, is a sinner, neither a believer nor a disbeliever. The consequence of this formulation, as you see, is that every believer is God-fearing; yet you have learned from his words on this verse what refutes and undermines that.]] Or their state is elevated above their state, because they are in honour and these are in humiliation. Or they are high over them, domineering over them, laughing at them as these people domineer over them in this world and consider themselves superior to them: "So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers." "And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning," without measure. He means that He widens provision for whom wisdom requires widening, as He widened it for Qarun and others. So this widening upon you is from God for the wisdom in it, which is your being led on gradually by blessing. Had it been an honour, His believing friends would have been more deserving of it than you. If you say: why did He say "from those who believe" and then say "those who have feared God"? I say: to show you that none is made happy in His presence except the believing God-fearing one, and to be an incitement to the believers toward piety when they hear that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 213:

"The people were one community" (kāna al-nāsu ummatan wāḥidatan), agreeing upon the religion of Islam (dīn al-Islām); "so Allah sent the prophets" — meaning: they differed, so Allah sent [the prophets]. It was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ (li-yaḥkuma baynal-nāsi fīmā ikhtalafū fīh). In the reading of ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd): "The people were one community, then they differed, so Allah sent [the prophets]." The evidence for it is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And the people were not but one community, then they differed﴾ [10:19]. It has also been said: "The people were one community in disbelief, so Allah sent the prophets, and they differed about them." The first is the more correct view. If you ask: when were the people one community agreeing upon the truth? I say: it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that between Adam and Noah there were ten centuries upon a law of truth, and then they differed.

It has also been said: they were Noah and those who were with him in the ark. ﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾ — meaning the category (of books), or with each one of them his own book; ﴿so that Allah might judge﴾, or the Book, or the prophet to whom it was sent down, ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾ — concerning the truth and the religion of Islam over which they differed after agreement. ﴿And none differed concerning it﴾ — concerning the truth — ﴿except those who had been given it﴾, except those who were given the Book sent down to remove the difference; that is, they increased in difference after the Book was sent down to them, and they made the descent of the Book a cause of intensifying and entrenching the difference. ﴿Out of mutual insolence﴾ — out of envy among themselves and injustice, due to their greed for worldly things and their lack of fairness. And ﴿of the truth﴾ is an explanation of what they differed about, meaning: Allah guided those who believed to the truth about which the one who differed had differed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 214:

Am is disjunctive (munqati'a), and the meaning of the hamza [[His saying "am munqati'a wa-ma'na al-hamza" is interpreted as meaning bal (rather) and the hamza. (A)]] in it is for affirmation (taqrir) and for denying and disapproving the supposition (inkar al-hisban wa-istib'aduhu).

When he mentioned what the nations had been like in terms of disagreement over the prophets after the clear signs had come, as encouragement for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers to stand firm and be patient alongside those who disagreed with him among the polytheists and the People of the Book, and their denial of His signs and their enmity towards him, He said to them, in the manner of iltifat (shift of address) which is more eloquent: "Am hasibtum" (Or did you suppose). Lamma (not yet) in it carries the sense of expectation (tawaqqu'), and in negation it is the counterpart of qad in affirmation. The meaning is that the occurrence of that is expected and awaited. "Mathalu alladhina khalaw" (The likeness of those who passed away), their condition, which is an example of severity.

"Massathumu" (touched them) is an explanation of the likeness, and it is a resumption (isti'naf), as if a questioner had asked: "How was that likeness?" So it was said: "Massathumu al-ba'sa'" (adversity touched them) and "wa-zulzilu" (they were shaken), and they were disturbed with a severe disturbance, resembling an earthquake, due to the calamities and terrors that befell them. "Hatta yaqula al-rasulu" (until the Messenger said), to the point at which the Messenger and those with him said: "Mata nasru Allah" (When is the help of Allah?). That is, their impatience reached such a degree that no patience remained for them until they said that. Its meaning is a request for patience and a wish for it, and the lengthening of the time of hardship. In this ultimate point there is evidence that the matter reached its extreme in severity and its intensity in magnitude, because the prophets' steadfastness, endurance and self-restraint cannot be measured; so when no patience remained for them until they cried out, that was the ultimate point of severity beyond which there is no aspiration.

"Ala inna nasra Allahi qarib" (Verily, the help of Allah is near), on the supposition of a saying, meaning: it was said to them thus, in response to their request for swift victory. It has been read "hatta yaqula" with the accusative (naṣb) by supposing an implicit "an", and the sense is the future, because "an" is a sign of it. And with the nominative (raf') it is in the sense of the state (hal), like your saying: "Shariba al-ibilu hatta yaji'a al-ba'iru yajurru batnahu" (The camels drank until the camel came dragging its belly), except that it is a past state being related.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 215:

If you say: how does the answer correspond to the question in His words, ﴿Say: whatever you spend of good is for parents and kinsfolk...﴾? They asked about what to spend, and they were answered by stating where it is to be spent. I say: His words ﴿whatever you spend of good﴾ include a statement of what they spend, which is every good thing, and the speech was built upon what is more important, which is the statement of where it goes, because spending is not counted as such unless it falls in its proper place. The poet says:

Indeed, a favour is not a favour ...
until the path of the place of making it is reached.

So when you make a favour, aim it ...
at God, or at the near kin, or leave it.

He means: a gift is not truly a gift until it is in its proper place. So he used reaching the path as a metaphor for delivering it to its destination, which is the one who deserves it. His words "fa'mad bihā" (aim it) mean "qṣid bihā" (intend it). He implied the meaning of "go with it" and so construed it with "li-" (for). It is also narrated as "li-dhawī al-qarā'ib" (to the kinsfolk), so its meaning may be "to the people of the kinship ties." His words "aw da'" mean "or leave it," because beyond these two there is only boasting.

And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man (himm) and had great wealth, came and said:

"What should we spend of our wealth, and where should we place it?" Then it was revealed.

And it is narrated from al-Suddi that it was abrogated by the obligation of zakat. And it is narrated from al-Hasan that it concerns voluntary charity.

This is the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 216.

And it is "disliked" (kurh) for you, from karahah (aversion). The evidence is His saying: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing﴾. Then it may be that it is in the sense of kurh (aversion), with the verbal noun placed in the position of the adjective for emphasis, as in her saying:

*"Fa-innama hiya iqbalun wa idbar"* [[This verse's witness is cited again on page 218 of this part, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

As if it, in itself, were the object of their intense aversion to it. Or it may be a verbal form in the sense of a passive participle, like *al-khubz* in the sense of *al-makhbuz* (the baked bread), meaning: "and it is disliked by you." Al-Sulami read it with a fatha, treating it as in the sense of *al-madmum* (that which is imposed), like *al-day'f* and *al-dz'f*. It may also be in the sense of *al-ikrah* (compulsion) by way of metaphor, as if they were compelled to it because of their great aversion to it and its hardship for them. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His mother bore him in weakness and gave birth to him in pain﴾ [[His saying "and she gave birth to him in pain" and His saying "And it may be that you dislike a thing" — all that they were charged with follows His saying: "And it may be that you dislike a thing..." etc., for souls dislike it though it is good for them, and love its opposite though it is evil for them. (Editor's note.)]], and in His saying: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing﴾, all that they were charged with, for souls dislike it and recoil from it and love its opposite. ﴿And Allah knows what is good for you, and you do not know﴾.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh on an expedition (*sariyya*, a raid led by a small detachment) in Jumada al-Akhira, two months before the battle of Badr, to lie in wait for a caravan of Quraysh. In it were 'Amr ibn Abdullah al-Hadrami and three others with him. They killed him, took two prisoners, and seized the caravan, which carried merchandise from al-Ta'if. That was the first day of Rajab, though they thought it was still Jumada al-Akhira. Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the frightened are safe and in which people disperse to their livelihoods." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) halted the caravan. This weighed heavily on the members of the expedition, and they said: "We will not move until our repentance is revealed." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned the caravan and the prisoners. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the spoils.

The meaning is: the disbelievers or the Muslims ask you about fighting in the sacred month. The words ﴿وَقِتَالٍ فِيهِ﴾ ("and fighting in it") are a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition, a substitute noun that is connected to the original by a broader relation) for "the sacred month." In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is ﴿عَنْ قِتَالٍ فِيهِ﴾, with the governing verb repeated, as in His saying ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا لِمَنْ آمَنَ مِنْهُمْ﴾. 'Ikrima recited ﴿قَتْلٍ فِيهِ قُلْ قَتْلٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ﴾, meaning that the sin is great. It is related from 'Ata' that he was asked about fighting in the sacred month, and he swore by Allah: "It is not lawful for people to raid in the Sacred Precinct or in the sacred month unless they are fighting in it." He said this was not abrogated.

Most of the opinions hold that it was abrogated (*mansukh*, superseded by a later ruling) by His saying ﴿فَاقْتُلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ ("So kill the polytheists wherever you find them").

﴿وَصَدٌّ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿أَكْبَرُ﴾ is its predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is that the grave offences of Quraysh were their barring people from the path of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque, their disbelief in Allah, and the expulsion of the people of the Sacred Mosque, who were the Messenger and the believers. These are ﴿أَكْبَرُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("greater in the sight of Allah") than what the expedition did, fighting in the sacred month by mistake and on the basis of assumption. ﴿وَالْفِتْنَةُ﴾ ("and persecution") means expulsion or shirk. ﴿وَالْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾, and it is not permissible to conjoin it to the pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("in it" / "with Him").

﴿وَلا يَزالُونَ يُقاتِلُونَكُمْ﴾ is information about the continuing enmity of the disbelievers toward the Muslims, and that they will not cease from it until they turn them back from their religion. ﴿حَتَّى﴾ ("until") here expresses purpose (*ta'lil*), as when you say: "So-and-so worships Allah until he enters Paradise," meaning: they fight you in order that they may turn you back. ﴿إِنِ اسْتَطاعُوا﴾ ("if they are able") is said to express improbability of their ability, like a man saying to his enemy: "If you overcome me, do not spare me," while he is confident that the enemy will not overcome him.

﴿وَمَنْ يَرْتَدِدْ مِنْكُمْ﴾ ("whoever of you turns back") means whoever returns from his religion to their religion and obeys them in turning him back, ﴿فَيَمُتْ﴾ ("and dies") in apostasy (*ridda*, abandonment of Islam). ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أَعْمالُهُمْ فِي الدُّنْيا وَالْآخِرَةِ﴾ ("those, their deeds are void in this world and the Hereafter") means that they lose, by causing apostasy, the fruits of Islam that Muslims have in this world, and by persisting in it and dying upon it, the reward of the Hereafter. Al-Shafi'i used this verse to argue that apostasy does not void deeds unless one dies in it. According to Abu Hanifa, it voids them even if one returns to Islam.

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَالَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا﴾ ("Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated"): It is related that when Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions killed al-Hadrami, some people thought that if they were safe from sin, they would have no reward. So it was revealed: ﴿أُولَئِكَ يَرْجُونَ رَحْمَتَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("those hope for the mercy of Allah"). It is related from Qatada: "These were the best of this community. Then Allah made them people of hope, as you hear." Indeed, whoever hopes seeks, and whoever fears flees.
