Revealed concerning wine were four verses; they were revealed in Mecca. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Four verses were revealed concerning wine; they were revealed in Mecca..." etc. Ahmad said: A secret appears to me, arising from what he mentioned on this point. The first question among the questions joined by "wa" (and) is the same as the first question among the questions without "wa." But its answer came first with the expenditure's destination, because that is the more important matter, even though what was asked about was the spender, not the place of expenditure. Then, since the first answer did not explicitly state what was asked about, the question was repeated so that they would be answered explicitly about what was asked, and it was said: "al-'afw," that is, the surplus of expenditure beyond what is obligatory for dependents, or something similar, as is reported in its exegesis. Therefore it was necessary for this question to be joined with "wa" in order to connect it to the first. It is also possible that when they were first answered by an explanation of the destination of expenditure, and were not told explicitly the answer as to what exactly the spender spends, they repeated the question so that they might receive its answer explicitly, so "wa" was necessary. As for the second question among the questions joined with "wa," it concerned their situation with orphans, and whether it is permissible for them to mix with them in food, clothing and dwelling, when they used to be scrupulous about this in the Jahiliyyah. Since it was appropriate to the question about expenditure, considering both the spender and the destination of expenditure, it was joined to it so as to complete for them the explanation of the legislation regarding expenditure and its religious etiquette in a thorough manner, since in their knowledge had gathered what they spend, on what they spend, and in what state they spend, whether by mixing with the orphan or by separating from him. As for the third question among them, which concerned menstruating women, it is reported that in the Jahiliyyah they used to keep away from menstruating women in eating and living together, following the Jews in this, so they asked the question mentioned, just as they used to keep away from orphans in living together and eating together out of Jahili scrupulosity. There was an affinity between these two questions as you see, so it was good to join the latter to what preceded it, as an alert to the resemblance between them. And Allah knows best. If you consider the questions without "wa," you will find no closeness or relevance between them at all, for the first of them concerns expenditure, the second concerns fighting in the sacred month, and the third concerns wine and gambling. Among these questions there is such disparity and disconnection as is not hidden, so they were mentioned thus, unjoined, connected by conjunction without being tied to one another. So be alert to this secret, for it is marvellous, and you will not find it observed except in the Noble Book, for it has mastery over the secrets of eloquence and the subtleties of fluency, and it is not derived except by probing into the craft of rhetoric and the science of language. The aforementioned answer of al-Zamakhshari contains a delusion which I wish to point out: he said: "The last three questions occurred at one time and were in the ruling of one question, so some of them were connected to others by 'wa'." This, as you see, requires that the second and third questions alone be joined by "wa" and not the first, since "wa" only connects what follows to what precedes; joining it to the first does not connect it to the second but to what is before it. According to this, the questions that occurred at one time would be four questions, not three specifically, while he said that the connected questions occurring at one time are the last three; so he is undoubtedly mistaken, and everyone's statement is taken and rejected except that of the Infallible.]] : (And from the fruits of the date palm and the grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision) — so the Muslims used to drink it, and it was lawful for them. Then Umar, Mu'adh and a group of the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling on wine, for it takes away the intellect and plunders wealth." So it was revealed: (In both there is great sin and benefits for people). Some drank it and others abandoned it. Then Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf invited a group of people, and they drank and became intoxicated; then one of them led the prayer and recited: "Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship," so it was revealed: "Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated," and few drank it after that. Then Utban ibn Malik invited a group including Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; when they became intoxicated they boasted and recited poetry to one another, until Sa'd recited a poem containing satire of the Ansar, so an Ansari struck him with a camel's jawbone and wounded his head, and he complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding wine," so it was revealed: (Indeed, wine and gambling...) up to His saying: (So will you not desist?). Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We have desisted, O Lord." [[Al-Tha'labi mentioned it thus in his tafsir without a chain, and its meaning will come in the tafsir of Surah al-Nisa' from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "If a drop fell into a well and a minaret were built on its place, I would not call the adhan upon it. And if it fell into the sea, then it dried up and grass grew in it, I would not graze in it." [[I have not found it from him.]] And from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "If I put my finger into it, it would not follow me." [[Ibn Abi Shaybah related it from Ibn al-Mubarak from al-Awza'i from Sulayman ibn Habib that Ibn Umar said: "If I put my finger into wine, I would not wish it to return to me."]] This is true faith, and they are those who fear Allah with the fear due to Him. Wine (khamr) is what has boiled, become strong and thrown up foam from grape juice, and it is forbidden; likewise the steeped infusion of raisins or dates that has not been cooked. If it is cooked until two-thirds of it has gone, then it boils and becomes strong, its impurity and the share of Satan have gone. According to Abu Hanifah, drinking what is less than intoxication is lawful if one does not intend by drinking it amusement and delight. It is reported from one of his companions: "That I say repeatedly that it is lawful is more beloved to me than that I say once that it is forbidden; and that I fall from the sky and be cut into pieces is more beloved to me than that I take a single drop of it." According to most jurists it is forbidden like wine, and likewise every intoxicant of every drink. It was named khamr because it covers the intellect and discernment, just as it was named sakar (intoxicant) because it intoxicates them, that is, it restrains them; and it seems it was named by the verbal noun of "khamarahu khamran" when he covered it, for emphasis. Maysir (gambling): gambling, a verbal noun from "yasara," like al-mawʿid and al-marjiʿ from their verbs. It is said: "yasartuhu," when I gambled with him, and its derivation is from yusr (ease), because one takes a man's wealth with ease and facility without toil or hardship; or from yasar (wealth), because it strips him of his wealth. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: a man in the Jahiliyyah would stake his family and his wealth. He said:

"I say to them at the mountain pass when they make me the stake of the game: Did you not despair that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?"

This is said by Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi. Al-Sh'ab: a place name. It is said: "yasarahu," when he defeated him in the game of maysir, which is gambling. Al-yas here means knowledge. Zahdam originally means the chick of a falcon, and the horse is named by it for its swiftness. That is: I say to them in this place, at the time when they defeated me in the maysir and struck me with its arrows: Did you not know that I am the son of the brave man, the knight of that horse? The interrogative is for affirmation and reproach. It is also narrated: "idh ya'sirūnī," meaning they take me as a captive among them. It may also mean: "Did you not despair and cut off your hopes of what you want from me, because I am the son of that famous knight?" so the interrogative is for rebuke and urging despair of that.

That is, they do to me what the players of maysir do to the stake. If you ask: what is the description of maysir? I say: they had ten arrows, namely: al-azlam, al-aqlam, al-fadh, al-tawam, al-raqib, al-hils, al-nafis, al-musbil, al-mu'alla, al-munih, al-safih, and al-wagh'. Each of them had a known share of a slaughtered camel, which they slaughtered and divided into ten parts. It is said: twenty-eight, except three, which are al-munih, al-safih and al-wagh'. One of them said:

"I have arrows in this world, none of which is a winner; and their names are al-wagh', al-safih and al-munih."

The three names of the maysir arrows that have no share of the camel are proper names; al-wagh' originally means the servant and the base man, and the pod of the eggplant; unlike the remaining seven, which have shares. The speech is by way of metaphor: his state in this world is likened to the state of one for whom those arrows came out in the maysir, for not attaining the desired aim. It is far-fetched that it is a figure for generosity, where one gives and does not take.

[[Instead of "wa-asamiyhinna" it is narrated "innama sahmi," meaning "my arrows," as evidenced by "sihām" before it.]] The fadh has one arrow; the tawam has two; the raqib has three; the hils has four; the nafis has five; the musbil has six; and the mu'alla has seven. They put them in the rabab, which is a bag, and place it on the hands of a just man; then he shakes it and puts his hand in and takes out for each man one arrow. Whoever has drawn one of the arrows with shares takes the share marked on that arrow; and whoever has drawn an arrow for which there is no share takes nothing and pays the full price of the whole camel. They used to give those shares to the poor and did not eat from them. They boasted of this and blamed whoever did not take part in it, calling him al-barm. Included in the ruling of maysir are kinds of gambling, such as backgammon, chess and others. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of these two ill-omened games, for they are of the gambling of the non-Arabs." [[Ibn Mardawayh related it from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub, and from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari similarly; Ahmad and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad related it through two routes from Abu al-Ahwas from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, with the wording "Beware of these two ill-omened games which are played with a roar, for they are of the gambling of the non-Arabs."]] From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: that backgammon and chess are of maysir. [[Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi and al-Tha'labi related it through Hatim ibn Isma'il from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father that Ali said about backgammon and chess: "They are of maysir." It is disconnected.]] From Ibn Sirin: everything in which there is a stake is of maysir.

The meaning: they ask you about what is in indulging in them, as evidenced by His saying: "Say: In both there is great sin," and their sin and the punishment for sin in indulging in them is greater than their benefit, which is the pleasure of drinking wine and gambling, delight in them, reaching through them to companionship and fellowship with young men, partaking of their food, drink and gifts, plundering wealth through gambling, and boasting over the barm. [[His saying "and boasting over the abram": abram is the plural of barm, with vowel, meaning one who does not enter into maysir with the people. Thus in al-Sihah. (Ed.)]] It was also read: "ithm kathir" with the thaʾ; and in the reading of Ubayy: "wa-ithmuhuma aqrab." The meaning of multiplicity is that those who drink and gamble commit sins in them in many ways. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 221:

﴿And do not marry﴾ (wa-la tankihu). It is also read with a ḍamma on the tā’ (tunkihu), meaning: do not marry them, or do not give them in marriage (lā tazawwijūhunna aw lā tuzawwijūhunna). ﴿Al-mushrikāt﴾ refers to the female polytheists who are at war (al-ḥarbiyyāt), and the verse is established (thābita). It has also been said that ﴿al-mushrikāt﴾ includes both the warring women and the women of the People of the Book (al-kitābiyyāt) together, because the People of the Book are among the people of shirk, based on the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews say, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"﴾, up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Glorified is He above what they associate with Him﴾. It is abrogated (mansūkha) by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And [lawful to you are] the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾. The whole of Surat al-Mā'ida is established, and nothing of it has ever been abrogated; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Awzāʿī.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Marthad ibn Abī Marthad al-Ghanawī to Makkah to bring out some Muslims from it. In the Jāhiliyya he had been attached to a woman named ʿAnāq. She came to him and said: "Shall we not be alone together?" He said:

"Woe to you! Islam has come between us." She said: "Then would you be willing to marry me?" He said: "Yes, but I will return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and seek his permission." So he sought his permission, and then this was revealed: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better﴾, and a believing free woman, whether free or a slave, and likewise ﴿and a believing slave is better﴾, because all people are the servants and bondmen of Allah. ﴿Even though she pleases you﴾, that is, even if the situation is that the polytheist woman pleases you and you love her, a believing woman is still better than her in spite of that. ﴿Those﴾ refers to the polytheist women and men, meaning they call to the Fire, so their due is that they should not be befriended, nor should marriage ties be made with them, and there should be nothing between them and the believers except enmity and fighting. ﴿But Allah calls to Paradise﴾, meaning: and the friends of Allah, who are the believers, call to Paradise ﴿and forgiveness﴾ and what leads to them. They are the ones whose friendship and intermarriage must be obligatory, and who must be preferred over others ﴿by His permission﴾, by Allah's facilitation and enabling of the deed by which Paradise and forgiveness are deserved. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿wal-maghfiratu bi-idhnihi﴾ with a ḍamma (raf‘) on the word "forgiveness," meaning: and forgiveness is attained by His facilitation.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 222–223:**

*al-maḥīḍ* (الْمَحِيضِ) is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is said: *ḥāḍat maḥīḍan* (حاضت محيضا), as in *jā'a majī'an* (جاء مجيئا) and *bāta mabītan* (بات مبيتا).

﴿Say: It is an injury﴾ (قُلْ هُوَ أَذىً): menstruation is a thing that is loathed and that harms whoever approaches it, through aversion to it and dislike of it.

﴿So keep away from women﴾ (فَاعْتَزِلُوا النِّساءَ): that is, avoid them, meaning avoid having intercourse with them.

It is related that the people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) would not eat with a woman when she was menstruating, would not drink with her, would not sit with her on the same bedding, and would not share a house with her, like the practice of the Jews and the Magians. When this verse was revealed, the Muslims took its apparent meaning of "keeping away" and expelled the women from their houses. Some of the Bedouins said: "O Messenger of Allah, the cold is severe and the garments are few. If we give the women the garments, the rest of the household will perish, and if we keep the garments for ourselves, the menstruating women will perish." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were only commanded to avoid intercourse with them when they menstruate, and He did not command you to expel them from the houses, as the non-Arabs do." [[I have not found it.]]

It is also said that the Christians would have intercourse with them without concern for menstruation, while the Jews would avoid them in everything. So Allah commanded a moderate course between the two positions.

There is disagreement among the jurists regarding *al-i'tizāl* (الاعتزال, keeping away). Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf require avoiding what lies under the wrapper (*izār*), while Muhammad ibn al-Hasan requires avoiding only the genitals (*al-farj*). Muhammad related the hadith of ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her): that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar asked her, "Does a man have contact with his wife while she is menstruating?" She said: "She should tighten her wrapper over her lower part, and then he may have contact with her if he wishes." [[It is in the Muwatta' through the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan: from Malik, from Nafi', "that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar sent to ʿĀʾisha asking her…" and so on. Likewise the transmitters of the Muwatta' from Malik, al-Shafiʿi and others have recorded it. ʿAbd al-Razzaq recorded it from Ibn Jurayj, from Sulayman ibn Musa, from Nafiʿ, similarly.]] Then he said: "This is the view of Abu Hanifa."

And what Zayd ibn Aslam related: that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), "What is lawful for me of my wife when she is menstruating?" He said: "Let her tighten her wrapper on herself, and then do as you wish with her upper part." [[Malik narrated it in the Muwatta' from him in this form as a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain). al-Tabarani connected it through al-Darawardi, from Zayd ibn Aslam and Safwan ibn Muslim, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasar, as a mursal. On this topic there is also a report from Hizam ibn Hakim, from his paternal uncle ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "What is lawful for me of my wife when she is menstruating?" He said: "What is above the wrapper is lawful for you." Abu Dawud recorded it. And from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) something similar," and added: "Abstaining from that is better." Its chain is weak.]]

Yet there is something more lenient than this from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "Let him avoid the place of blood, and everything else is permitted to him." [[al-Darimi recorded it through Ayyub, from a man, from ʿĀʾisha, that she said to a person: "Avoid the place of blood, and everything else is permitted to you."]]

*Yaṭṭahharna* (يطهرن) is read with a doubled *ṭāʾ* (*yaṭṭahharna*), meaning *yatatahharna* (يتطهرن, they purify themselves), as is shown by His words ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ (فَإِذا تَطَهَّرْنَ). Abdullah (ibn Masʿud) read ﴿until they purify themselves﴾ (حتى يتطهرن). It is also read *yaṭhurna* (يطهرن) with a single *ṭāʾ*. *Al-tatahhur* (التطهر) means washing with water (*al-ghusl*), and *al-ṭuhr* (الطهر) means the cessation of menstrual blood.

Both readings are binding in practice. Abu Hanifa held that the husband may approach her during most of the menstrual period once the bleeding has stopped, even if she has not yet bathed; but during the shortest part of the period he does not approach her until she bathes or until the time of a prayer passes over her. Al-Shafiʿi held that he does not approach her until she has both ceased bleeding (*tuhr*) and bathed (*taṭahhur*), thus combining the two matters. This is a clear view, and His words ﴿when they have purified themselves﴾ support it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 224–225:

Al-'Urḍah (the obstacle): it is a form (fa'lah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like al-qabḍah (the handful) and al-ghurfah (the scoop). It is the name of that which you place in front of a thing, from the phrase "ʿarraḍa al-ʿūd ʿalā al-inā'" (when a stick is laid across a vessel), so that it stands in the way and becomes a barrier and a hindrance to it. You say: "Fulān ʿurḍah dūna al-khayr" (so-and-so is an obstacle standing between people and goodness). Al-ʿUrḍah also means one who is exposed to a matter. A poet said:

*"Fa-lā tajʿalūnī ʿurḍatan lil-lawā'im"* [[*"Da'ūnī anūḥ wajdan kanawḥ al-ḥamā'im... wa-lā tajʿalūnī ʿurḍatan lil-lawā'im"*

It is said that this is by Abu Tammam. He means: leave me to lament, because of the passion that is in me and the burning of love, like the wailing of doves. It is also narrated as "li-nawḥ al-ḥamā'im" (for the wailing of doves), in which case it is a cause ('illah) joined to the thing caused. Al-ʿUrḍah is one who is exposed to a matter, i.e.: "and do not make me exposed to the blame of the blamers." Or the intended meaning of "al-lawā'im" is the various kinds of blame, as hyperbole, on the pattern of "jadda jaddahu" (he truly strove). This is because the blamer is, in reality, the one who performs the blame.]]

The meaning of the verse according to the first interpretation: a man would swear to avoid some good deeds, such as maintaining family ties, reconciling people, showing kindness to someone, or worship. Then he would say: "I fear Allah that I might break my oath," and so he would abandon righteousness out of a wish to keep his oath. It was therefore said to them: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾, i.e., a barrier against what you have sworn to do.

The object sworn upon is called an oath (yamīn) because it is bound up with the oath, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: "If you swear an oath and then see something else to be better than it, then do what is better and make expiation for your oath." [[Narrated by the five (imams) from the narration of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah.]] That is, upon something of what one swears about. His saying: ﴿that you do good, fear Allah, and make peace among people﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) for "your oaths", i.e., for the matters sworn about, which are righteousness, piety, and reconciliation between people. If you ask: with what is the lām in "li-aymānikum" connected? I answer: with the verb, i.e., "and do not make Allah a barrier and a hindrance for your oaths." It is also permissible for it to be connected to ʿurḍah, because it contains the meaning of obstruction, i.e., "do not make Him something that obstructs righteousness," as in "so-and-so obstructed me." It is also permissible for the lām to indicate causation, with "an tabarrū" connected to the verb or to ʿurḍah, i.e., "and do not make Allah, because of your oaths, an obstacle to your being righteous."

Its meaning according to the other interpretation: "and do not make Allah an object exposed to your oaths, so that you cheapen Him by frequent swearing by Him." For this reason, He censured the one about whom it was revealed: ﴿And do not obey every frequent swearer, contemptible﴾, describing him with the most vile faults and making frequent swearing their foremost. "An tabarrū" is the cause of the prohibition, i.e., "for the sake of your being righteous, pious, and reconciling," because the frequent swearer is bold against Allah and does not revere Him, so he will not be righteous or pious, and people will not trust him, so they will not include him in their mediations and reconciliation between themselves.

Al-laghw: that which is fallen and not taken into account, in speech and other things. For this reason, the young camels that are not counted in blood-money are called "laghw." The laghw of oaths is that which is fallen and not taken into account in oaths, namely the oath that has no intention (ʿaqd) with it. The proof is ﴿But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned, and for the oaths you have bound﴾ and ﴿for what your hearts have earned.﴾ The jurists differed regarding it. According to Abu Hanifah and his companions, it is to swear upon a thing believing it to be as he swore, and then its opposite becomes apparent. According to al-Shafiʿi, it is the saying of the Arabs: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," which they use to emphasize their speech, without the swearing occurring to their minds. If one of them were told: "I heard you swear today in the Sacred Mosque," he would deny it, and perhaps he had said "No, by Allah" a thousand times.

In it there are two meanings:

First: ﴿He will not call you to account﴾, i.e., He will not punish you for the laghw of oaths which one of you swears by supposition, but He will punish you for what your hearts have earned, i.e., the sin you committed by intending to lie in an oath, which is to swear to what one knows to be contrary to what he says, and this is the perjurious oath (al-yamīn al-ghamūs).

Second: ﴿He will not call you to account﴾, i.e., He does not make expiation obligatory upon you for the laghw of oaths in which there is no intention, but He makes expiation obligatory upon you for what your hearts have earned, i.e., for what your hearts intended and purposed of oaths, and which was not merely the earning of the tongue alone. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾, in that He did not hold you to account for laghw in your oaths.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 226–228:

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) recited ﴿āluu min nisā'ihim﴾ ("those who swear off from their wives"). Ibn Abbas recited ﴿yuqsimūna min nisā'ihim﴾ ("those who swear an oath concerning their wives"). If you ask: how is it that it is construed with *min* when it is construed with *'alā*? It is also possible that the return is with the women's consent, out of concern on their part for a nursing child (from the *ghīl*, i.e., intercourse with a nursing mother),¹ or for some other reason, for the sake of the return, which is like repentance. ﴿Wa-in 'azamū al-ṭalāqa﴾ ("and if they resolve upon divorce") means: then wait until the period has passed, ﴿fa-inna Allāha samī'un 'alīm﴾ ("indeed Allah is Hearing, Knowing"), a threat against their persistence and their abandonment of the return. According to al-Shafi'i, its meaning is: "if they return, and if they resolve," each of the two conditions occurring after the period has passed.²

If you ask: how does the *fā'* (then) fit when the return occurs before the waiting period ends? I answer: it fits correctly, because ﴿fa-in fā'ū﴾ and ﴿wa-in 'azamū﴾ are a detailed explanation of ﴿lilladhīna yu'lūna min nisā'ihim﴾ ("for those who swear off their wives"), and a detailed explanation follows what it details, as you say: "I am your guest this month; if you please me, I will stay with you until its end; and if not, I will stay only until I move away."

If you ask: what do you say about ﴿fa-inna Allāha samī'un 'alīm﴾ and their resolve on divorce being something known but not heard? I answer: usually the one who resolves on divorce and on abandoning the return and the harm does not avoid some muttering and murmuring (*damdama*),³ and he must speak to himself and confide in it, and that is a discourse that none hears except Allah, just as He hears the whisperings of Satan.

﴿Wa-al-muṭallaqāt﴾ ("and the divorced women") means: those who have been consummated with, from among those with menstrual periods (*dhawāt al-aqrā'*). If you ask: how is it permissible to restrict them specifically when the wording implies generality? I answer: rather, the wording is absolute in including the class, fit for the whole and for part of it, so it came to apply to one of what it is fit for, like a homonym (*ism mushtarak*).

If you ask: what is the meaning of the report about them with the waiting? I answer: it is a report with the meaning of a command. The original wording is: "let the divorced women wait." Expressing the command in the form of a report is an emphasis on the command and an indication that it is something to be received with haste in carrying it out, as though they had already complied with the command to wait, so He reports it as existing. Similar to it is the saying in supplication: "may Allah have mercy on you," phrased as a report out of confidence in being answered, as though mercy had already been found, so He reports it. Its construction on the subject (*mubtada'*) is also an added emphasis. Had it been said: "and let the divorced women wait," it would not have had this force.

If you ask: why was it not said, "they shall wait three *qurū'*," as it was said, "waiting of four months"? And what is the meaning of mentioning *anfus* (selves)? I answer: mentioning the selves stirs them to wait and adds incitement, because in it there is what they would disdain, which moves them to wait. The selves of women are inclined toward men, so they are commanded to restrain their selves, overcome their longing, and compel them to wait.

*Qurū'* is the plural of *qar'* or *qurū'*, and it means menstruation, as shown by the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Leave off prayer during the days of your *aqrā'*" (menstrual periods).⁴ And his saying: "The divorce of a slave-woman is two divorces, and her waiting period is two menstruations."⁵ And he did not say "two purities." And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-al-lā'ī yasna mina al-maḥīḍ min nisā'ikum in irtabtum fa-'iddatuhunna thalāthatu ashhur﴾ ("and those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months"), in which He put months in place of menstruation, not purities. Also, the essential purpose of the waiting period is to ascertain the womb's clearance (*istibra' al-raḥm*), and it is menstruation, not purity, by which the wombs are ascertained to be clear; that is why the ascertaining of a slave-woman is by a menstruation. It is said: "the woman *aqra'at*," when she menstruated, and "a woman *muqri'*." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "So-and-so gave his slave-girl to so-and-so to *tuqri'uhā*," that is, to keep her with her until she menstruates for ascertainment.

If you ask: what do you say about His saying: ﴿fa-ṭalliqūhunna li-'iddatihinna﴾ ("divorce them at their waiting period"), while lawful divorce is only during purity? I answer: its meaning is "in a state of facing their waiting period," as you say: "I met him three days before the end of the month," meaning facing three days, and their waiting period is three menstruations. If you ask: what do you say of the verse of al-A'sha:

*Afī kulli 'āmin anta jāshimu ghazwatin / tashuddu li-aqṣāhā 'azīmu 'azā'ikā*
*Mu'thilatan mālan wa-fī al-ḥayyi ri'fatun / limā ḍā'a fīhā min qurū'i nisā'ikā*

[Is it every year that you undertake a raid, / tightening for its farthest reach the resolve of your endurance? / Establishing wealth, and in the tribe a station, / for what was lost in it of the *qurū'* of your women.]

I answer: he meant: "for what was lost in it of the waiting of your women," because *qurū'* was well known among them in reckoning waiting periods. That is, from a long period like the period in which women observe the waiting, he deemed his absence from his family each year, because of his plunging into wars and raids, to be a long time; and that a span like the waiting period passes over his women in which they are not lain with. Or he meant the times of your women, since *qar'* and *qāri'* came with the meaning of "time," and he did not mean either menstruation or purity.⁶

If you ask: on what is ﴿thalātha qurū'﴾ ("three *qurū'*") in the accusative? I answer: it is the object of the verb, as you say: "the hoarder waits for high prices," meaning they wait for three *qurū'* to pass; or it is adverbial of time, meaning they wait for the duration of three *qurū'*. If you ask: why is the specifier in the plural of paucity (*jam' al-kathra*) and not in the plural of fewness (*jam' al-qilla*), which are *aqrā'*? I answer: they are liberal in this and use each of the two plurals in place of the other, since both share the sense of plurality. Do you not see His saying, ﴿bi-anfusihinna﴾ ("in their selves"), though they are only many selves? Perhaps *qurū'* was more commonly used as a plural of *qar'* than *aqrā'*, so the less commonly used one was preferred, treating the rarely used form as if it were absent, like their saying "thalāthat shusū'" (three shoes).⁷

Al-Zuhri recited *thalātha qurū* without a hamza.

﴿Mā khalaqa Allāhu fī arḥāmihinna﴾ ("what Allah created in their wombs") means: the child, or the blood of menstruation. This is when the woman wants to separate from her husband, so she conceals her pregnancy, so that he will not wait for her to give birth before divorcing her, and so that he will not feel pity for the child and leave off releasing her; or she conceals her menstruation and says, while she is menstruating, "I have become pure," hastening the divorce. It is also permissible that the meaning concerns those who wish to abort what is in their wombs of fetuses, and therefore do not acknowledge it and deny it; so concealing what is in their wombs is made a metaphor for aborting it.

﴿In kunna yu'minna bi-Allāhi wa-al-yawmi al-ākhir﴾ ("if they believe in Allah and the Last Day") is a magnification of their act, and that whoever believes in Allah and in His punishment does not dare to do the like of such great sins.

*Al-bu'ūla* is the plural of *ba'l* (husband), and the *tā'* is attached to mark the feminine of the plural, as in *al-ḥazūna* and *al-suhūla*. It is also permissible that *al-bu'ūla* be the verbal noun from your saying "ba'ala ḥasana al-bu'ūla" (he had a good marital life), meaning: "and the people of their marital relations (*ahl bu'ūlatihinna*) have more right to take them back (*bi-raddihinna*)," that is, by return (*raj'a*).⁸ In the recitation of Ubayy: *bi-raddatihinna*. ﴿Fī dhālika﴾ ("in that") means: during the period of that waiting.

If you ask: how are they made more entitled to the return, as though women had a right in it? I answer: the meaning is that if the man wants the return and the woman refuses, it is obligatory to prefer his word over hers, and he is more entitled than she is. However, she has a right in the return ﴿in arādū bi-al-raj'ati iṣlāḥan﴾ ("if they desire by return reconciliation") between them and them, and kindness to them, and they do not intend to harm them. ﴿Wa-lahunna mithlu alladhī 'alayhinna﴾ ("and they have rights similar to those which are upon them") means: there is due to them from men a right similar to that which is due to men from them. ﴿Bi-al-ma'rūf﴾ ("in kindness") means: in the manner that is not denied in the law and in people's customs, so they do not burden them with what is not theirs, nor do they burden them with what is not theirs, and neither spouse harasses the other. The intended meaning of equivalence is equivalence in the obligation as a good deed, not in the kind of act; so it is not obligatory on him, if she washes his clothes or bakes for him, to do likewise, but he responds with what befits men. ﴿Wa-lil-rijāli 'alayhinna darajatun﴾ ("and men have a degree over them") means: an increase in right and a superiority. It is said: the woman obtains from pleasure what the man obtains, and he has the superiority by his standing over her (*qiyāmihi 'alayhā*) and his spending on her interests.

¹ The text refers to *al-ghīl*: a man lying with a woman who is nursing, out of concern for the child.
² The commentator's editor notes that al-Shafi'i holds both conditions to apply after the period has passed.

⁴ Narrated by al-Tahawi and al-Daraqutni from the hadith of Fatima bint Abi Hubaysh.
⁵ Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim through Muzahir ibn Aslam, who is weak; also by Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni through 'Atiyya from Ibn 'Umar, in which 'Umar ibn Shabib is weak.

The talaq (divorce) here carries the sense of tatlīq (pronouncing divorce), as salām means taslīm (greeting). That is, the legally prescribed divorce is pronounced one pronouncement after another, separated and not combined or released all at once. By "twice" (al-marratān) he did not mean the dual, but repetition, as in His saying ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾ [67:4], meaning one glance after another, not exactly two glances. Similar to this are dual forms used to express repetition, such as the Arabs' saying *labbayka* (I answer Your call), *sa‘dayka* (I am at Your service), *ḥanānayka* (Your compassion), *hadhādhayka*, and *dawālayka* (again and again). His saying ﴿Then either retain them with kindness or release them with grace﴾ [2:229] is an option given to them after He taught them how to divorce: between keeping the women with good companionship and fulfilling their rights, or releasing them in the gracious manner He has taught them. It has been said that the meaning is: the revocable divorce is twice, because there is no revocation after the third. So "retain with kindness" means by taking her back (ruj‘a, revocation), and "release with grace" means by not taking her back until she is separated by the end of her waiting period ('iddah), or by not taking her back in a way that intends to prolong her waiting period and harm her.

It has also been said: it means that he divorces her a third time in the third purity (ṭuhr).

It is reported that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Where is the third?" He (ﷺ) said: "Or release with grace." [Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated it through ‘Abd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘ from Anas. In *al-‘Ilal* he said: Layth ibn Ḥammād erred in it, narrating it from ‘Abd al-Wāḥid. The preserved version is from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘ from Abū Razīn, as a mursal (a report lacking a companion). Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated it from Abū Mu‘āwiyah, and ‘Abd al-Razzāq from al-Thawrī, both from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘. Al-Dāraquṭnī also narrated it through Ḥammād ibn Salamah from Qatādah from Anas, who said: A man said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I hear Allah say: Divorce is twice, so where is the third?" He said: "Retaining with kindness or releasing with grace: that is the third."]

According to Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions, combining two pronouncements or three is an innovation (bid‘ah), and the Sunnah is that one pronounces only a single divorce, in a purity during which he has not had intercourse with her, based on what is related in the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "The Sunnah is that you await the purity in its proper time, then divorce her once for each menstrual cycle (qurū’)." [Al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it through Shu‘ayb ibn Ruzayq, that ‘Aṭā’ al-Khurāsānī told them from al-Ḥasan, who said: ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn ‘Umayr told us that he divorced his wife once while she was menstruating, then wanted to follow it with two more divorces at the two cycles. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "O Ibn ‘Umayr, this is not what Allah commanded you. You have erred from the Sunnah. The Sunnah is that you await the purity and then divorce for each cycle." So he commanded him to take her back. He said: "When she becomes pure, divorce her at that time, or retain her."]

According to al-Shāfi‘ī, there is no harm in pronouncing three at once, based on the hadith of al-‘Ajlānī, who performed li‘ān (mutual oath of condemnation) with his wife and then divorced her three times in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he did not reject it. [Agreed upon (by al-Bukhārī and Muslim) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa‘d, but it is said that his words "he divorced her three times before the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to divorce her" are from al-Zuhrī's narration from Sahl. Note: ‘Abd al-Ḥaqq said in *al-Aḥkām*: the wording with three has not been authentically established except in the hadith of the one who performed li‘ān. This is refuted by what is in Muslim from Fāṭimah bint Qays, who said: "My husband divorced me three times, so I disputed with him..." and so on.]

It is reported that Jamīlah bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās. She hated him, while he loved her. She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, neither I nor Thābit! Nothing can bring my head and his together. By Allah, I do not fault him in religion or character, but I hate to be ungrateful in Islam. I cannot bear him out of hatred. I lifted the side of the tent and saw him coming in a group, and he was the blackest of them, the shortest in stature, and the ugliest in face." So the verse was revealed. He had given her an orchard as her dower, so she returned it to him in exchange for her release, and it was the first khul‘ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) in Islam.

[Al-Ṭabarī narrated in his *Tafsīr*: Muḥammad ibn ‘Abd al-A‘lā told us, Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān told us, he said: I read to Fuḍayl from Abū Jarīr that he asked ‘Ikrimah: "Did khul‘ have a basis?" He said: Ibn ‘Abbās used to say: The first khul‘ in Islam was in the case of the sister of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned this, but did not name her. Al-Bukhārī named her, through Ḥammād ibn Zayd from Ayyūb from ‘Ikrimah: "that Jamīlah..." and so on. Ibn Mājah has, through another chain from ‘Ikrimah from Ibn ‘Abbās: "that Jamīlah bint Salūl..." Likewise ‘Abd al-Razzāq narrated it by another route: "that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and she was Jamīlah bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy." In al-Dāraquṭnī, through Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abū al-Zubayr informed us: "Thābit ibn Qays had Zaynab bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy as his wife. He had given her an orchard as dower, and she disliked him..." until the end. If this is preserved, it is possible that she had two names.]

The story has also been related about another woman. In the *Muwaṭṭa’*, from Yaḥyā ibn Sa‘īd, from ‘Amr, from Ḥabībah bint Sahl: "She was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out for the dawn prayer and found her at his door in the dimness. He said: 'Who is this?' She said: 'I am Ḥabībah bint Sahl.' He said: 'What is your matter?' She said: 'Neither I nor Thābit ibn Qays!'" It is also narrated from this route by Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī, and Aḥmad. Ibn Mājah has, from the narration of ‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb from his father from his grandfather: "Ḥabībah bint Sahl was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, and he was an ugly man. She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, were it not for fear of Allah, I would spit in his face.' He said: 'Will you return his orchard to him?' She said: 'Yes.' So she returned his orchard to him, and he separated them." Aḥmad has, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Abī Ḥathmah, who said: "The daughter of Sahl..." and so on.

If you say: To whom is the address in His saying ﴿It is not lawful for you to take﴾? If you say it is addressed to the husbands, then His saying ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ does not correspond to it. And if you say it is addressed to the rulers and judges, then they do not take from the women nor give to them?

I say:

Both are permissible: the beginning of the address may be to the husbands and its end to the rulers and judges. Such shifts are not rare in the Qur’an or elsewhere. Alternatively, the whole address may be to the rulers and judges, because they are the ones who command taking and giving when cases are brought before them. So they are regarded as the ones who take and give ﴿of what you have given them﴾, meaning of what you have given them of dowries, ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾, meaning unless the spouses fear that they will fail to keep the limits of Allah in the obligations of marriage, because of the wife's disobedience (nushūz) and bad character. ﴿Then there is no blame upon either of them﴾, meaning there is no blame on the husband for what he takes, nor on her for what she gives, ﴿for that by which she ransoms herself﴾, meaning for what she pays to ransom herself and obtains release by giving back what she received as dowry. Khul‘ in exchange for more than the dowry is disliked, though it is valid legally.

It is reported that a woman was disobedient to her husband and was brought before ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He let her spend three nights in the dung room, then called her and said: "How did you find your night's stay?" She said: "Since I have been with him, I have not spent nights more soothing to my eyes than these." He said to her husband: "Divorce her, even if it is for her earring." [Narrated by ‘Abd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Ṭabarī, and Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī in the end of his *Gharīb*, all through a narration from Ayyūb from Kathīr, the freedman of Samurah: "‘Umar was brought a disobedient woman..." and so on. Ibrāhīm said: al-nāshiz is the one who disobeys her husband.]

Qatādah said: he means with all her property. This applies when the disobedience comes from her. If it comes from him, it is disliked for him to take anything from her.

It was read as ﴿unless they both fear﴾ in the passive form, and the clause ﴿that they will not keep﴾ replaces the pronoun of the verb as a substitution of part (badal al-ishtimāl), like your saying: "Zayd was feared, [in respect of] his neglecting to keep the limits of Allah." Similar to it is ﴿and they conferred secretly, those who did wrong﴾ [21:3]. It is supported by ‘Abd Allāh's reading: ﴿unless you fear﴾. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿unless they suspect﴾. It is possible that "fear" here means "suspicion," as they say: "I fear that it is so," meaning "I think it is so." ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾, meaning the divorce described above as repeated in His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ and completing its quota, or if he divorces her a third time after the two, ﴿she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾, meaning after that pronouncement, ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾, meaning until she marries someone else. Marriage (nikāḥ) is attributed to the woman as it is to the man, as in tazawwaja (to marry).

It is said: "Fulānah nākiḥ fī Banī Fulān," meaning she is married among the tribe of so-and-so. Whoever restricts the legal (taḥlīl) effect to the contract alone, relying on its apparent sense, is Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyab. But the majority hold that consummation is required, based on what ‘Urwah related from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the wife of Rifā‘ah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Rifā‘ah divorced me, completing the third divorce. Then ‘Abd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Zubayr married me, but with him is only like the tassel of a garment, and he divorced me before he had touched me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you wish to return to Rifā‘ah? No, not until you taste his honey and he tastes yours." [Agreed upon through this route.]

It is also reported that she remained as long as Allah willed, then she returned and said: "He had touched me." He said to her: "You lied in your first statement, so I will not believe you in the latter." So she remained until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. [‘Abd al-Razzāq said: Ibn Jurayj informed us from Ibn Shihāb from ‘Urwah from ‘Ā’ishah, and he mentioned the hadith. In it: "She sat as long as Allah willed. Then she came to him and informed him that he had touched her, so he forbade her to return to her first husband, and said: 'O Allah, if it is a sin for her to become lawful for Rifā‘ah, then let her marriage to him never be completed a second time.' Then she came to Abū Bakr and ‘Umar in their caliphates, and they forbade her."]

Then she came to Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "May I return to my first husband?" He said: "You know what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to you when he said what he said, so do not return to him." When Abū Bakr passed away, she said the same to ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: "If you come to me after this time of yours, I will stone you," and he forbade her.

If you say: What do you say about a marriage contracted on the condition of tahlīl (intended to make her lawful to the first husband)? I say: Sufyān, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū ‘Ubayd, Mālik, and others held that it is not permissible. Abū Ḥanīfah held that it is permissible with disapproval. He also said that if they both intend tahlīl but do not state it explicitly, there is no disapproval.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): he cursed the muḥallil (one who makes her lawful) and the one for whom she is made lawful. [This is narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd, ‘Alī, Jābir, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir, Abū Hurayrah, and Ibn ‘Abbās. I say: he referred to its takhrīj in *al-Hidāyah*. The hadith of Ibn Mas‘ūd was narrated by al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā’ī, and Ibn Daqīq al-‘Īd declared it sound according to al-Bukhārī's condition. The hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās was narrated by Ibn Mājah. The hadith of ‘Alī was narrated by Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd. The hadith of Abū Hurayrah was narrated by Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī. The hadith of ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir was narrated by Ibn Mājah. The hadith of Jābir was mentioned by al-Tirmidhī.]

From ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I will not be brought a muḥallil or one for whom she is made lawful except that I will stone both of them." [Narrated by ‘Abd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Shaybah, through the narration of al-Musayyab ibn Rāfi‘ from Qabīṣah ibn Jābir from ‘Umar.]

From ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him: "No, except a marriage of desire, without deception." [I did not find it from ‘Uthmān, but found it from Ibn ‘Umar. Al-Ḥākim narrated it through ‘Umar ibn Nāfi‘ from his father, that he said: "A man came to Ibn ‘Umar and asked him about a man who divorced his wife three times, and then his brother married her, without his consent, in order to make her lawful for his brother. Is she lawful to the first?" He said: "No, except a marriage of desire. We used to count this as fornication during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It has also been related as a marfū‘ report (traced to the Prophet), narrated by al-Ṭabarānī from the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the muḥallil. He said: 'No, except a marriage of desire, without deception, and not one who mocks the Book of Allah, who has not tasted the honey.'" In its chain is Ibrāhīm ibn Ismā‘īl ibn Abī Ḥabībah, who is weak.]

Then if the second husband divorces her, ﴿there is no blame upon them both if they return to each other﴾, meaning that each of them returns to the other by marriage, ﴿if they think that they can keep the limits of Allah﴾, meaning if in their assumption they can maintain the rights of marriage. He did not say "if they know that they will keep them," because certainty is hidden from them and only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows it. Whoever interprets "think" (ẓann) here as "know" (‘ilm) has erred in both wording and meaning, because you do not say "I know that Zayd will stand" but "I know that he will stand," and because a person does not know what tomorrow holds; he only assumes by conjecture.

The talaq (divorce) here carries the sense of tatlīq (pronouncing divorce), as salām means taslīm (greeting). That is, the legally prescribed divorce is pronounced one pronouncement after another, separated and not combined or released all at once. By "twice" (al-marratān) he did not mean the dual, but repetition, as in His saying ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾ [67:4], meaning one glance after another, not exactly two glances. Similar to this are dual forms used to express repetition, such as the Arabs' saying *labbayka* (I answer Your call), *sa‘dayka* (I am at Your service), *ḥanānayka* (Your compassion), *hadhādhayka*, and *dawālayka* (again and again). His saying ﴿Then either retain them with kindness or release them with grace﴾ [2:229] is an option given to them after He taught them how to divorce: between keeping the women with good companionship and fulfilling their rights, or releasing them in the gracious manner He has taught them. It has been said that the meaning is: the revocable divorce is twice, because there is no revocation after the third. So "retain with kindness" means by taking her back (ruj‘a, revocation), and "release with grace" means by not taking her back until she is separated by the end of her waiting period ('iddah), or by not taking her back in a way that intends to prolong her waiting period and harm her.

It has also been said: it means that he divorces her a third time in the third purity (ṭuhr).

It is reported that a questioner asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Where is the third?" He (ﷺ) said: "Or release with grace." [Al-Dāraquṭnī narrated it through ‘Abd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘ from Anas. In *al-‘Ilal* he said: Layth ibn Ḥammād erred in it, narrating it from ‘Abd al-Wāḥid. The preserved version is from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘ from Abū Razīn, as a mursal (a report lacking a companion). Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated it from Abū Mu‘āwiyah, and ‘Abd al-Razzāq from al-Thawrī, both from Ismā‘īl ibn Sumay‘. Al-Dāraquṭnī also narrated it through Ḥammād ibn Salamah from Qatādah from Anas, who said: A man said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I hear Allah say: Divorce is twice, so where is the third?" He said: "Retaining with kindness or releasing with grace: that is the third."]

According to Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions, combining two pronouncements or three is an innovation (bid‘ah), and the Sunnah is that one pronounces only a single divorce, in a purity during which he has not had intercourse with her, based on what is related in the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "The Sunnah is that you await the purity in its proper time, then divorce her once for each menstrual cycle (qurū’)." [Al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it through Shu‘ayb ibn Ruzayq, that ‘Aṭā’ al-Khurāsānī told them from al-Ḥasan, who said: ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn ‘Umayr told us that he divorced his wife once while she was menstruating, then wanted to follow it with two more divorces at the two cycles. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "O Ibn ‘Umayr, this is not what Allah commanded you. You have erred from the Sunnah. The Sunnah is that you await the purity and then divorce for each cycle." So he commanded him to take her back. He said: "When she becomes pure, divorce her at that time, or retain her."]

According to al-Shāfi‘ī, there is no harm in pronouncing three at once, based on the hadith of al-‘Ajlānī, who performed li‘ān (mutual oath of condemnation) with his wife and then divorced her three times in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he did not reject it. [Agreed upon (by al-Bukhārī and Muslim) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa‘d, but it is said that his words "he divorced her three times before the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to divorce her" are from al-Zuhrī's narration from Sahl. Note: ‘Abd al-Ḥaqq said in *al-Aḥkām*: the wording with three has not been authentically established except in the hadith of the one who performed li‘ān. This is refuted by what is in Muslim from Fāṭimah bint Qays, who said: "My husband divorced me three times, so I disputed with him..." and so on.]

It is reported that Jamīlah bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās. She hated him, while he loved her. She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, neither I nor Thābit! Nothing can bring my head and his together. By Allah, I do not fault him in religion or character, but I hate to be ungrateful in Islam. I cannot bear him out of hatred. I lifted the side of the tent and saw him coming in a group, and he was the blackest of them, the shortest in stature, and the ugliest in face." So the verse was revealed. He had given her an orchard as her dower, so she returned it to him in exchange for her release, and it was the first khul‘ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) in Islam.

[Al-Ṭabarī narrated in his *Tafsīr*: Muḥammad ibn ‘Abd al-A‘lā told us, Mu‘tamir ibn Sulaymān told us, he said: I read to Fuḍayl from Abū Jarīr that he asked ‘Ikrimah: "Did khul‘ have a basis?" He said: Ibn ‘Abbās used to say: The first khul‘ in Islam was in the case of the sister of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned this, but did not name her. Al-Bukhārī named her, through Ḥammād ibn Zayd from Ayyūb from ‘Ikrimah: "that Jamīlah..." and so on. Ibn Mājah has, through another chain from ‘Ikrimah from Ibn ‘Abbās: "that Jamīlah bint Salūl..." Likewise ‘Abd al-Razzāq narrated it by another route: "that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and she was Jamīlah bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy." In al-Dāraquṭnī, through Ibn Jurayj, who said: Abū al-Zubayr informed us: "Thābit ibn Qays had Zaynab bint ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy as his wife. He had given her an orchard as dower, and she disliked him..." until the end. If this is preserved, it is possible that she had two names.]

The story has also been related about another woman. In the *Muwaṭṭa’*, from Yaḥyā ibn Sa‘īd, from ‘Amr, from Ḥabībah bint Sahl: "She was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out for the dawn prayer and found her at his door in the dimness. He said: 'Who is this?' She said: 'I am Ḥabībah bint Sahl.' He said: 'What is your matter?' She said: 'Neither I nor Thābit ibn Qays!'" It is also narrated from this route by Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī, and Aḥmad. Ibn Mājah has, from the narration of ‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb from his father from his grandfather: "Ḥabībah bint Sahl was married to Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, and he was an ugly man. She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, were it not for fear of Allah, I would spit in his face.' He said: 'Will you return his orchard to him?' She said: 'Yes.' So she returned his orchard to him, and he separated them." Aḥmad has, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Abī Ḥathmah, who said: "The daughter of Sahl..." and so on.

If you say: To whom is the address in His saying ﴿It is not lawful for you to take﴾? If you say it is addressed to the husbands, then His saying ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ does not correspond to it. And if you say it is addressed to the rulers and judges, then they do not take from the women nor give to them?

I say:

Both are permissible: the beginning of the address may be to the husbands and its end to the rulers and judges. Such shifts are not rare in the Qur’an or elsewhere. Alternatively, the whole address may be to the rulers and judges, because they are the ones who command taking and giving when cases are brought before them. So they are regarded as the ones who take and give ﴿of what you have given them﴾, meaning of what you have given them of dowries, ﴿unless they both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾, meaning unless the spouses fear that they will fail to keep the limits of Allah in the obligations of marriage, because of the wife's disobedience (nushūz) and bad character. ﴿Then there is no blame upon either of them﴾, meaning there is no blame on the husband for what he takes, nor on her for what she gives, ﴿for that by which she ransoms herself﴾, meaning for what she pays to ransom herself and obtains release by giving back what she received as dowry. Khul‘ in exchange for more than the dowry is disliked, though it is valid legally.

It is reported that a woman was disobedient to her husband and was brought before ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He let her spend three nights in the dung room, then called her and said: "How did you find your night's stay?" She said: "Since I have been with him, I have not spent nights more soothing to my eyes than these." He said to her husband: "Divorce her, even if it is for her earring." [Narrated by ‘Abd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Ṭabarī, and Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī in the end of his *Gharīb*, all through a narration from Ayyūb from Kathīr, the freedman of Samurah: "‘Umar was brought a disobedient woman..." and so on. Ibrāhīm said: al-nāshiz is the one who disobeys her husband.]

Qatādah said: he means with all her property. This applies when the disobedience comes from her. If it comes from him, it is disliked for him to take anything from her.

It was read as ﴿unless they both fear﴾ in the passive form, and the clause ﴿that they will not keep﴾ replaces the pronoun of the verb as a substitution of part (badal al-ishtimāl), like your saying: "Zayd was feared, [in respect of] his neglecting to keep the limits of Allah." Similar to it is ﴿and they conferred secretly, those who did wrong﴾ [21:3]. It is supported by ‘Abd Allāh's reading: ﴿unless you fear﴾. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿unless they suspect﴾. It is possible that "fear" here means "suspicion," as they say: "I fear that it is so," meaning "I think it is so." ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾, meaning the divorce described above as repeated in His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ and completing its quota, or if he divorces her a third time after the two, ﴿she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾, meaning after that pronouncement, ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾, meaning until she marries someone else. Marriage (nikāḥ) is attributed to the woman as it is to the man, as in tazawwaja (to marry).

It is said: "Fulānah nākiḥ fī Banī Fulān," meaning she is married among the tribe of so-and-so. Whoever restricts the legal (taḥlīl) effect to the contract alone, relying on its apparent sense, is Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyab. But the majority hold that consummation is required, based on what ‘Urwah related from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the wife of Rifā‘ah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Rifā‘ah divorced me, completing the third divorce. Then ‘Abd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Zubayr married me, but with him is only like the tassel of a garment, and he divorced me before he had touched me." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you wish to return to Rifā‘ah? No, not until you taste his honey and he tastes yours." [Agreed upon through this route.]

It is also reported that she remained as long as Allah willed, then she returned and said: "He had touched me." He said to her: "You lied in your first statement, so I will not believe you in the latter." So she remained until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. [‘Abd al-Razzāq said: Ibn Jurayj informed us from Ibn Shihāb from ‘Urwah from ‘Ā’ishah, and he mentioned the hadith. In it: "She sat as long as Allah willed. Then she came to him and informed him that he had touched her, so he forbade her to return to her first husband, and said: 'O Allah, if it is a sin for her to become lawful for Rifā‘ah, then let her marriage to him never be completed a second time.' Then she came to Abū Bakr and ‘Umar in their caliphates, and they forbade her."]

Then she came to Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "May I return to my first husband?" He said: "You know what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to you when he said what he said, so do not return to him." When Abū Bakr passed away, she said the same to ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: "If you come to me after this time of yours, I will stone you," and he forbade her.

If you say: What do you say about a marriage contracted on the condition of tahlīl (intended to make her lawful to the first husband)? I say: Sufyān, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū ‘Ubayd, Mālik, and others held that it is not permissible. Abū Ḥanīfah held that it is permissible with disapproval. He also said that if they both intend tahlīl but do not state it explicitly, there is no disapproval.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): he cursed the muḥallil (one who makes her lawful) and the one for whom she is made lawful. [This is narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd, ‘Alī, Jābir, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir, Abū Hurayrah, and Ibn ‘Abbās. I say: he referred to its takhrīj in *al-Hidāyah*. The hadith of Ibn Mas‘ūd was narrated by al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā’ī, and Ibn Daqīq al-‘Īd declared it sound according to al-Bukhārī's condition. The hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās was narrated by Ibn Mājah. The hadith of ‘Alī was narrated by Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd. The hadith of Abū Hurayrah was narrated by Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī. The hadith of ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir was narrated by Ibn Mājah. The hadith of Jābir was mentioned by al-Tirmidhī.]

From ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I will not be brought a muḥallil or one for whom she is made lawful except that I will stone both of them." [Narrated by ‘Abd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Shaybah, through the narration of al-Musayyab ibn Rāfi‘ from Qabīṣah ibn Jābir from ‘Umar.]

From ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him: "No, except a marriage of desire, without deception." [I did not find it from ‘Uthmān, but found it from Ibn ‘Umar. Al-Ḥākim narrated it through ‘Umar ibn Nāfi‘ from his father, that he said: "A man came to Ibn ‘Umar and asked him about a man who divorced his wife three times, and then his brother married her, without his consent, in order to make her lawful for his brother. Is she lawful to the first?" He said: "No, except a marriage of desire. We used to count this as fornication during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It has also been related as a marfū‘ report (traced to the Prophet), narrated by al-Ṭabarānī from the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the muḥallil. He said: 'No, except a marriage of desire, without deception, and not one who mocks the Book of Allah, who has not tasted the honey.'" In its chain is Ibrāhīm ibn Ismā‘īl ibn Abī Ḥabībah, who is weak.]

Then if the second husband divorces her, ﴿there is no blame upon them both if they return to each other﴾, meaning that each of them returns to the other by marriage, ﴿if they think that they can keep the limits of Allah﴾, meaning if in their assumption they can maintain the rights of marriage. He did not say "if they know that they will keep them," because certainty is hidden from them and only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows it. Whoever interprets "think" (ẓann) here as "know" (‘ilm) has erred in both wording and meaning, because you do not say "I know that Zayd will stand" but "I know that he will stand," and because a person does not know what tomorrow holds; he only assumes by conjecture.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 231–232:

﴿فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾ means: they reached the end of their waiting period (ʿidda) and were close to its termination. The word ajal (term, appointed time) applies to the whole duration and also to its last part. It is said of a person's lifespan that it is his ajal, and of the death by which it ends that it is his ajal. Likewise the words ghayah (goal, limit) and amad (term, span) are used. The grammarians say that "min" (from) denotes the beginning of a goal and "ila" (to, until) denotes the end of a goal. And a poet said:

Every living being will complete the duration of its life,
and will perish when its term comes to an end.

[[It is said: awda means he perished; awdaa bihi al-subul and the like mean it destroyed him and carried him off. Al-wadi, like al-ghana, means destruction. It is also narrated as "ajaluhu" (his term). Amad and ajal are used both for the whole duration of a thing and for its end, just as ghayah is used both for the whole distance and for its last part.

He says: every living being must complete the duration of its life and perish when its term is finished; and the sukun of "al-umr" is a dialectal form of it.]]

The word "balagha" is also used in a broader sense: one says "balagha al-balad" when one approaches a place and nears it. It is said "qad wasalat" (she has arrived), but she has not arrived; she has only drawn near. Because it is known that retaining (imsak) after the term has been fulfilled has no sense, since after its fulfilment she is no longer his wife, in no waiting period from him, so he has no authority over her. ﴿فَأَمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾: either he takes her back, without intending harm by the taking back; ﴿أَوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾: or he lets her go, so that her waiting period ends and she is separated, without harm. ﴿وَلا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِراراً﴾: a man would divorce a woman and leave her until her waiting period is nearly over, then take her back, not out of need, but in order to prolong the waiting period over her; this is retaining her by way of harm. ﴿لِتَعْتَدُوا﴾: so that you may wrong them. It is also said: so that you may force them to ransom themselves (iftida'). ﴿فَقَدْ ظَلَمَ نَفْسَهُ﴾: he has wronged himself by exposing himself to the punishment of God. ﴿وَلا تَتَّخِذُوا آياتِ اللَّهِ هُزُواً﴾: that is, strive in taking them up and acting upon what is in them, and observe them with their proper observance; otherwise you have taken them as a jest and a game.

It is said of one who does not strive in a matter: "You are only a player and a mocker." And it is said: "Be a Jew, or else do not play with the Torah."

It is also said: a man would divorce, free a slave, and marry, and say, "I was only joking." And from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Three things are serious whether one is in earnest or in jest: divorce, marriage, and taking back (a wife)." [[His saying "wa-hazluhunna jadd" (and their jest is earnest): in Abu al-Su'ud, marriage, divorce and manumission. (Gh.)]] [[Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra. Its chain contains weakness.]]

﴿وَاذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: by Islam and by the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿وَما أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِنَ الْكِتابِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ﴾: from the Qur'an and the Sunna. Mentioning them is to be matched with gratitude and with fulfilling their rights. ﴿يَعِظُكُمْ بِهِ﴾: by what was sent down to you. ﴿فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ فَلا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾: this may be addressed to the husbands who prevent their wives, after the end of the waiting period, through injustice and coercion, as was the custom of the Jahiliyya out of zeal, not letting them marry whomever they wish among the husbands. The meaning is that they should marry those husbands whom they desire and who are suitable for them. Or it may be addressed to the guardians (awliya') who prevent them from returning to their former husbands.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar, when he prevented his sister from returning to her first husband. It is also said: concerning Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, when he prevented a daughter of his paternal uncle. The more apt view is that it is an address to people in general, i.e. there should be no prevention among you, for if it occurs among them while they are content, they are in the position of those who prevent. Al-ʿadl means confinement and restriction. From it comes: "ʿadalat al-dajaja" when its egg is lodged and does not come out. And Ibn Harma recited:

"Indeed my odes to you, so make me your favourite:
noble maidens who have been prevented from marriage."

[[Al-ʿaqa'il: plural of ʿaqila, the women kept secluded in their curtained chambers. He says: my odes to you are like veiled women; so they are a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the odes or from the "ʿaqa'il". His saying "fastanaʿni" is a parenthetical phrase, meaning: take me as a eulogist and reward me for my praise of you with odes I do not praise anyone else with. Since he likened the odes to women, he gave a hint of this by the word "ʿadl", which is prevention from marriage, a term specific to women.]]

The reaching of the term is in its literal sense. It is narrated from al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him: the context of the two statements shows that the two reachings differ. ﴿إِذا تَراضَوْا﴾: when the addressees and the women are content with one another. ﴿بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾: in what is good according to religion and manliness, of the conditions; it is also said: with the proper dower (mahr al-mithl). According to the school of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, if she marries herself to someone for less than the proper dower of her equal, the guardians may object. If you ask: to whom is the address in His saying ﴿ذلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾? I answer: it may be to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to every individual. Similar is ﴿ذلِكَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾: ﴿أَزْكى لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾ means more purifying for you and cleaner from the filth of sins. It is also said that ﴿أَزْكى لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾ means more excellent and better. ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ﴾ what there is in that of growth and purity, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾; or: God knows what you are made upright by of rulings and laws, and you are ignorant of it.
