[[His saying "wa-hazluhunna jadd" (and their jest is earnest): in Abu al-Su'ud, marriage, divorce and manumission. (Gh.)]] [[Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra. Its chain contains weakness.]]

﴿وَاذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: by Islam and by the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿وَما أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِنَ الْكِتابِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ﴾: from the Qur'an and the Sunna. Mentioning them is to be matched with gratitude and with fulfilling their rights. ﴿يَعِظُكُمْ بِهِ﴾: by what was sent down to you. ﴿فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ فَلا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾: this may be addressed to the husbands who prevent their wives, after the end of the waiting period, through injustice and coercion, as was the custom of the Jahiliyya out of zeal, not letting them marry whomever they wish among the husbands. The meaning is that they should marry those husbands whom they desire and who are suitable for them. Or it may be addressed to the guardians (awliya') who prevent them from returning to their former husbands.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar, when he prevented his sister from returning to her first husband. It is also said: concerning Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, when he prevented a daughter of his paternal uncle. The more apt view is that it is an address to people in general, i.e. there should be no prevention among you, for if it occurs among them while they are content, they are in the position of those who prevent. Al-ʿadl means confinement and restriction. From it comes: "ʿadalat al-dajaja" when its egg is lodged and does not come out. And Ibn Harma recited:

"Indeed my odes to you, so make me your favourite:
noble maidens who have been prevented from marriage."

[[Al-ʿaqa'il: plural of ʿaqila, the women kept secluded in their curtained chambers. He says: my odes to you are like veiled women; so they are a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the odes or from the "ʿaqa'il". His saying "fastanaʿni" is a parenthetical phrase, meaning: take me as a eulogist and reward me for my praise of you with odes I do not praise anyone else with. Since he likened the odes to women, he gave a hint of this by the word "ʿadl", which is prevention from marriage, a term specific to women.]]

The reaching of the term is in its literal sense. It is narrated from al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him: the context of the two statements shows that the two reachings differ. ﴿إِذا تَراضَوْا﴾: when the addressees and the women are content with one another. ﴿بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾: in what is good according to religion and manliness, of the conditions; it is also said: with the proper dower (mahr al-mithl). According to the school of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, if she marries herself to someone for less than the proper dower of her equal, the guardians may object. If you ask: to whom is the address in His saying ﴿ذلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾? I answer: it may be to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to every individual. Similar is ﴿ذلِكَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾: ﴿أَزْكى لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾ means more purifying for you and cleaner from the filth of sins. It is also said that ﴿أَزْكى لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾ means more excellent and better. ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ﴾ what there is in that of growth and purity, ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾; or: God knows what you are made upright by of rulings and laws, and you are ignorant of it.

يُرْضِعْنَ (*yurḍi'na*, "they nurse") is like يتربصن (*yatarabbaṣna*, "they wait") in that it is a statement with the force of an emphatic command. كامِلَيْنِ (*kāmilayn*, "complete") is an emphasis (*tawkīd*), like the Qur'anic ﴿That makes ten complete﴾. This is because it is one of the things on which looseness is allowed. You say: "I stayed with so-and-so for two years," and you did not complete them.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: أن يكمل الرضاعة (*an yukmila al-raḍā'a*). It is also read الرِّضاعة with a kasra on the rā', and الرِّضعة, and وأن تتم الرضاعة and وأن يتم الرضاعة, with the verb in the nominative, likening أن (*an*) to ما (*mā*) because both are interpreted in the same way. If you ask: how is the phrase لِمَنْ أَرادَ (*liman arāda*, "for whoever wishes") connected to what precedes it? I say: it is an explanation of the person to whom the ruling is addressed, like the Qur'anic ﴿Come, [I am] for you﴾, where لك (*laka*, "for you") explains the one addressed by هَيْتَ (*hayta*). That is, this ruling is for whoever wishes to complete the nursing.

It is related from Qatada: "Two complete years," then Allah sent down ease and lightness and said: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. He meant that a shortfall is permitted. It is related from al-Hasan: "That is not a fixed term from which nothing may be reduced, provided that weaning does not harm the child."

It has also been said that the lām (ل) in لِمَنْ is connected to يرضعن (*yurḍi'na*), as you say: "So-and-so nursed a child for so-and-so," meaning: they nurse for two years for the fathers who wish to complete the nursing, because the father is obligated to provide nursing for the child, not the mother. He must hire a wet-nurse (*ẓi'r*) for him, unless the mother volunteers to nurse him. She is recommended to do so but cannot be compelled. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is not permitted to hire the mother as long as she is a wife or in her waiting period from a marriage. Al-Shafi'i held that it is permitted. Once her waiting period has ended, it is permitted by agreement.

If you ask: why are the mothers commanded to nurse their children? I say: either it is a command in the mode of recommendation (*nadb*), or it is in the mode of obligation if the infant will accept only his mother's breast, or no wet-nurse is available, or the father is unable to hire one.

It has also been said that it refers to divorced mothers, and that the maintenance and clothing are obligatory on account of the nursing.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾, that is, upon the one to whom a child is born, who is the father. لَهُ (*lahu*, "to him") is in the nominative position as the agent, like عَلَيْهِمْ (*'alayhim*) in ﴿those who have incurred anger﴾. If you ask: why is it said المَوْلُودِ لَهُ (*al-mawlūdi lahu*, "the one to whom [a child] is born") rather than "the father"? I say: so that it is known that the mothers only bore [children] for them, since children belong to fathers, and that is why they are attributed to them and not to the mothers.

And he recited for al-Ma'mun ibn al-Rashid:

*Indeed, the mothers of men are but vessels,*
*Receptacles that are entrusted; and to the fathers belong sons.*

[[Do not belittle a youth for having as his mother a Roman woman, or a black, foreign, mute one.

Indeed the mothers of men are vessels,
Receptacles entrusted; and to the fathers belong sons.

These are by al-Ma'mun ibn al-Rashid when his brother al-Amin wrote to him reproaching him for the caliphate without entitlement, and at the end of it: "The son of a slave-woman, how base he is!"

So he replied to him with this. وأزرى به (*wa-azrā bihi*) means: when he attacked him with a fault and hurled it at him. The nūn in the verb is for emphasis. It is also narrated as لا تزدرين فتى (*lā tazdarīna fatan*), addressing a feminine second person, as if he meant it to be heard by his brother. وزرى عليه (*wa-zarā 'alayhi*) means: when he found fault with him. والازدراء (*al-izdirā'*) is its derived form (*iftiʿāl*), meaning: do not find fault. The nūn is retained after the prohibition, which is an irregularity. العجماء (*al-'ajmā'*) is the one who does not speak clearly. He likened women to vessels in which things are deposited, a forceful metaphor, or in the manner of the explicit metaphor according to the opinion of al-Sa'd regarding every forceful metaphor.

It is also narrated: وللأبناء آباء (*wa-lil-abnā'i ābā'*, "and to the sons belong fathers"). The meaning is that nobility and baseness come from the fathers, not from the mothers, since mothers are like vessels for the sons. But this comparison is based on the outward sense.

Then al-Ma'mun also wrote in reply to his brother: "The pen by its edge, the sword by its blade, the man by his fortune, not by his father nor by his grandfather."]]

So it was incumbent upon them to provide for them and clothe them when they nurse their child, like wet-nurses. Do you not see that He mentioned him by the title of "father" where this meaning is not intended? That is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when no father will avail his child, nor will a child avail his father at all﴾.

بِالْمَعْرُوفِ (*bil-ma'rūf*, "in a fair manner") is explained by what follows it, which is that neither of them should be made to bear what is beyond their capacity, and that neither should cause harm to the other.

It is read لا تكلف (*lā tukallaf*) with a fatḥa on the tā', and لا نكلف (*lā nukallaf*) with the nūn. It is read لا تُضَارَّ (*lā tuḍārru*) with a ḍammah on the rā' as a report (*ikhbār*), and this allows it to be read as active or passive. The original form may be تضارر with a kasra on the rā', or تضارر with a fatḥa on it. Most readers read لا تُضَارَّ with a fatḥa. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra as a prohibition, and this also allows both readings. This is clarified by the reading لا تضارَرْ and لا تضارِرْ, with the jazm, and a fatḥa or kasra on the first rā'.

Abu Ja'far read لا تضارّ with a sukūn and shadda, intending a pause. It is related from al-A'raj: لا تضارْ with a sukūn and no shadda, from ḍārrahu, "to harm him." He intended a pause as Abu Ja'far did, or he silently dropped the ḍammah and the transmitter took it to be a sukūn. It is related from the scribe of Umar ibn al-Khattab: لا تضرر (*lā tuḍarrir*).

The meaning is: the mother should not harm the father on account of her child, by being harsh with him and demanding from him what is not just in provision and clothing, by preoccupying his heart with neglect of the child's affairs, or by saying, after the infant has grown attached to her: "Seek a wet-nurse for him," and the like. Nor should the father, the one to whom the child belongs, harm his wife on account of the child, by withholding from her any part of her provision and clothing that is due from him, or by taking the child from her while she wishes to nurse him, or by compelling her to nurse. Likewise, when it is read in the passive, it is a prohibition against harm coming to her from the husband, and against harm coming to him from her side on account of the child.

It is also permitted that تُضَارَّ (*tuḍārra*) means تضر (*tuḍurr*, "harm"), with the bā' being part of its complement, meaning: a mother should not harm her child by him, so she should not neglect his nourishment and care, nor fall short in what is due to him, nor hand him over to the father after he has grown attached to her. Nor should the father harm him by snatching him from her hands or by falling short in his rights, so that she in turn falls short in her rights concerning the child.

If you ask: why is it said بِوَلَدِها (*biwaladihā*, "by her child") and بِوَلَدِهِ (*biwaladihi*, "by his child")? I say: when the woman was forbidden from causing harm, the child was attributed to her in order to move her compassion towards him, and to show that he is not a stranger to her. It is her right to be compassionate towards him, and likewise the father.

وَعَلَى الْوارِثِ (*wa-'alā al-wārith*, "and upon the heir") is a conjunction with the phrase وَعَلَى الْمَوْلُودِ لَهُ رِزْقُهُنَّ وَكِسْوَتُهُنَّ (*wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna*, "and upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and clothing"), and what lies between them is an explanation of the fair manner, inserted between the conjunct and the thing conjoined. The meaning is: upon the heir of the one to whom the child belongs is the like of what was obligatory upon him of provision and clothing. That is, if the one to whom the child belongs dies, the one who inherits from him is bound to take his place in providing for her and clothing her, on the condition mentioned, which is fairness and avoidance of harm.

It has also been said: it refers to the heir of the child, that is, whoever would inherit from the child if the child died. The scholars differed: according to Ibn Abi Layla, it is everyone who inherits from him. According to Abu Hanifa, it is whoever is a close blood relative within the forbidden degrees. According to al-Shafi'i, there is no maintenance except for the lineal ascendants and descendants. It has also been said: it is whoever inherits from him among his agnatic relatives, such as the grandfather, the brother, the brother's son, the paternal uncle, and the paternal cousin.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is the heir of the father, who is the child himself. If his father dies and he inherits from him, the wages for his nursing become obligatory upon him from his own property, if he has property. If he has no property, the mother is compelled to nurse him.

It has also been said that عَلَى الْوارِثِ refers to the remaining two parents, from the saying: "and make him the heir among us" (the well-known transmission is "among us"). (ع)

﴿So if they both wish to wean, by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both﴾, whether they add to the two years or reduce from them. This is a widening of the allowance after the specified limit. It has also been said that it is a limit of two years which may not be exceeded. The mutual consent of both in weaning and their consultation is considered only because the father's consent is not in question, while as for the mother, she has the greater right to upbringing and knows the condition of the child best.

فَإنْ أرادَ (*fa-in arāda*, "if he wishes") is also read. استرضع (*istarḍa'a*, "to seek a wet-nurse") is derived from أرضع (*arḍa'a*, "to nurse"). One says: the woman nursed the child, and he sought a wet-nurse for the child (*istarḍa'tuhā al-ṣabiyy*), because it takes two objects. Just as you say: he fulfilled the need (*anjaḥa al-ḥāja*) and he sought the need to be fulfilled (*istanjaḥtahu al-ḥāja*).

The meaning is: that you seek wet-nurses for your children, so one of the two objects is omitted because it is not needed, just as you say: "I sought the need to be fulfilled" and do not mention the one from whom you sought it. The same ruling applies to any two objects where one is not a restatement of the first. ﴿When you hand over to the wet-nurses what you gave﴾, that is, what you intended to give. Compare the Qur'anic ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾. It is read ما أتيتم (*mā ataytum*), from أتى إليه إحسانا (*atā ilayhi iḥsānan*, "he did good to him") when he did it. From this is the Qur'anic ﴿Indeed His promise was ever to be fulfilled﴾, meaning: fulfilled (*maf'ūlan*). Shayban related from 'Asim: ما أوتيتم (*mā ūtītum*), meaning: what Allah has given you and empowered you to give of wages. Similar to it is the Qur'anic ﴿And spend from what He has made you successors over﴾.

Handing over is not a condition for permissibility or validity; it is only a recommendation toward what is better. It is permissible that it be an exhortation that what is given to the nurse should be the most pleasant of things, so that she is in good spirits and content. That would result in the improvement of the child's condition and a precaution regarding his affairs. Therefore we were commanded to give it promptly, hand to hand, as if it were said: when you pay them in cash, hand to hand, what you have given them.

بِالْمَعْرُوفِ (*bil-ma'rūf*) is connected to سلمتم (*sallamtum*, "you hand over"). They were commanded that, when handing over the wages, they should have cheerful faces, speak kind words, and comfort the hearts of the nurses as much as possible, so that their negligence is guarded against by removing their excuses.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 234–235:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ — on the assumption that a noun has been elided, the meaning is: "and the wives of those among you who die shall wait." It was also said that the meaning is: "they shall wait after them," like their saying: "Samn (ghee) is two manns for a dirham."

It is also read as ﴿يَتَوَفَّوْنَ﴾ with an open yā' [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) read it with an open yā' … etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: Perhaps the questioner of Abu al-Aswad was one of those from whom it was understood that for him there was no difference between the kasra and the fatḥa, and this is the apparent meaning; Abu al-Aswad answered him accordingly, so there is then no contradiction.]], meaning: "they complete their terms," and this is the reading of ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him). It is related that Abu al-Aswad al-Du'alī was walking behind a funeral bier, and a man said to him: "Man al-mutawaffā?" (with a kasra on the fāʾ), and he said: "God Almighty [i.e., the deceased is God's creature, so mutawaffā is the correct form with the fatḥa — the sense being that the reading with a kasra would make God the one who dies]." This was one of the causes that moved ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) to order him to compose a book on grammar. This reading contradicts His saying: ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْراً﴾ — they shall observe this period, which is four months and ten days. It was also said that ʿashran (ten) is used in reference to the nights, with the days included along with them, and they never use the masculine form for it when they intend the days.

You say: "I fasted ʿashran (ten)" [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "You say: I fasted ʿashran … etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: From this is the hadith, "Whoever fasts Ramadan and follows it with six (days) of Shawwal, it is as if he fasted the whole year," where the nights were given precedence, or fasting was not conceived of in them, to the point that they said: the condition of intention and its time is the night; therefore it was given a share in fasting and the nights were given precedence.]], and if you mention it (the feminine form), it falls outside their speech. Clear in this is His saying: ﴿إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا عَشْراً﴾ and then ﴿إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا يَوْماً﴾. ﴿فَإِذا بَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾ — when their term is completed, that is, when their waiting period is over, ﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ — there is no blame upon you, O rulers and the body of Muslims, ﴿فِيما فَعَلْنَ فِي أَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ — concerning what they do with themselves, such as exposing themselves to proposals, ﴿بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ — in a manner that the Sharia does not disapprove. The meaning is that if they did what is disapproved, it would be incumbent upon the rulers to restrain them.

And if they (the guardians) are negligent, the blame falls upon them. ﴿فِيما عَرَّضْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ is that a man says to her: "You are indeed beautiful, or righteous, or ... and it is my aim to marry, and God may make easy for me a righteous woman," and similar words that give the impression that he wants to marry her, so that she holds herself back for him if she is inclined to him, without explicitly stating the marriage: he does not say, "I want to marry you," or "I will marry you," or "I propose to you." Ibn al-Mubarak related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulayman, from his maternal aunt, who said:

Muhammad ibn ʿAli Abu Jaʿfar entered upon me while I was in my waiting period, and he said: "You know my kinship to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the right of my grandfather over me, and my precedence in Islam." I said: "May God forgive you! Do you propose to me during my waiting period while people take knowledge from you?" He said: "Did you really? I only informed you of my kinship to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and my standing. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon Umm Salama, who had been with her cousin Abu Salama, and he died leaving her. He kept mentioning to her his station with God while leaning on his hand, until the mat left a mark on his hand from the strength of his leaning on it. That was not a proposal." [[This is how it is in the Kitab al-Nikah of Ibn al-Mubarak; al-Daraqutni related it from the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Salt from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman — Ibn al-Ghasil — similarly in full.]]

If you ask: what is the difference between kināya and taʿrīḍ? I say:

Kināya (allusion/metonymy) is that you mention a thing by other than its proper word, as in your saying: "tall of the sword-belt and the shoulder-straps" for tall stature, and "abundant in ashes" for a generous host. Taʿrīḍ (indirect hinting) is that you mention something by which you indicate another thing you did not mention, as when a person in need says to the one he needs: "I came to greet you, and to look upon your noble face." That is why they said:

"And let it suffice you, from me, the greeting as a demand."

It is as if one inclines the speech toward an aim that indicates the purpose; it is called talwīḥ (hinting), because what he wants gleams from it. ﴿أَوْ أَكْنَنْتُمْ فِي أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ — or you conceal and harbor in your hearts, so you do not mention it with your tongues, neither by allusion nor by explicit statement. ﴿عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّكُمْ سَتَذْكُرُونَهُنَّ﴾ — God knows that you will certainly mention them, and you will not refrain from speaking of your desire for them and will not be patient about it. There is in it an element of reproach, like His saying: ﴿عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّكُمْ كُنْتُمْ تَخْتانُونَ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾.

If you ask: where is the object of the exception in His saying ﴿وَلكِنْ لا تُواعِدُوهُنَّ﴾? I say: it is elided, because ﴿ستذكرونهن﴾ indicates it; its estimated form is: "God knows that you will mention them, so mention them, but do not promise them in secret." The "secret" (sirr) has come as a metonym for marriage, which is the intercourse, because it is something kept secret. al-Aʿshā said:

"And do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so marry or keep away forever."

[[Wa-la tashkhar min ba'isin dhī ḍarāra… (the verse) by al-Aʿshā Maymun ibn Qays. Al-bāʾis: the poor, the needy. Al-ḍarāra: blindness. Attributing "al-ikhlād" (perpetuity) to wealth is a metaphor, as it is its cause in imagination. "Taqrab" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ means "tafʿal," so the min is extra; "jāra" is the object; with a ḍamma it means "tadnū" (draw near), so the min is original. It is also narrated: "wa-la tqarabanna jāratan" with a shadda on the nūn. In any case it is a metonym for prohibiting intercourse. Al-sirr: the opposite of al-jahr (openly), used here metaphorically for intercourse, either because it occurs in secret or because it is kept secret. Al-nikāh: the marriage contract. It is said: abada al-waḥshī yabūdu abūdan, and tabaddada tabaddudan: it shied away from companionship; its alif here is converted from the nūn of emphasis in pause, and the intended meaning is distance metaphorically; the addressee is not specific. He forbade him to draw near to her because that is more emphatic than forbidding her intercourse; then he said: marry or withdraw from women like the wild beasts.]]

Then he used it to refer to the marriage contract, which is the cause of it, just as the word nikāḥ was used. ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ — that is, that you allude and do not speak explicitly. If you ask: with what is the exceptive particle connected? I say: with "do not promise them," meaning: do not promise them any promise except a known promise, not a disapproved one. That is, do not promise them except by saying, that is, do not promise them except by allusion. It is not permissible for it to be a discontinuous exception from "secretly," since that would lead to your saying "do not promise them except by allusion." It was also said that its meaning is: do not promise them intercourse, which is that a man says to her, "If I marry you, such-and-such will happen," meaning what takes place between them beneath the blanket. ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ means without obscenity or indecency in speech. It was also said: "do not promise them in secret," meaning privately, with the promise in secret being an expression for a promise of what is disgraceful, because whispering to them is generally about what one would be ashamed to say openly. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) concerning ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ that it means: that they pledge to each other that she will not marry anyone else. ﴿وَلا تَعْزِمُوا عُقْدَةَ النِّكاحِ﴾ — from "ʿazm al-amr" (resolving upon a matter) and "ʿazama ʿalayhi." Mentioning resolve is for emphasis in forbidding the contracting of the marriage bond during the waiting period, because resolve upon an action precedes it; so when it is forbidden, the action is forbidden all the more. Its meaning is: do not resolve to contract the marriage bond. It was also said: its meaning is: do not sever the marriage bond; the true sense of ʿazm is "cutting off," by the evidence of his peace be upon him saying: "There is no fast for one who does not resolve the fast from the night," and it is narrated "for one who does not spend the night fasting" [[Related by the authors of the Sunan from the hadith of Ḥafṣa with the wording "for one who does not gather (the intention)"; and "for one who does not spend the night" is in al-Nasa'i.]].

﴿حَتَّى يَبْلُغَ الْكِتابُ أَجَلَهُ﴾ — meaning what was written and prescribed of the waiting period. ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ ما فِي أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ — of resolve upon what is not permitted, ﴿فَاحْذَرُوهُ﴾ — so beware of it, and do not resolve upon it. ﴿غَفُورٌ حَلِيمٌ﴾ — He does not hasten to punish you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 234–235:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ — on the assumption that a noun has been elided, the meaning is: "and the wives of those among you who die shall wait." It was also said that the meaning is: "they shall wait after them," like their saying: "Samn (ghee) is two manns for a dirham."

It is also read as ﴿يَتَوَفَّوْنَ﴾ with an open yā' [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) read it with an open yā' … etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: Perhaps the questioner of Abu al-Aswad was one of those from whom it was understood that for him there was no difference between the kasra and the fatḥa, and this is the apparent meaning; Abu al-Aswad answered him accordingly, so there is then no contradiction.]], meaning: "they complete their terms," and this is the reading of ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him). It is related that Abu al-Aswad al-Du'alī was walking behind a funeral bier, and a man said to him: "Man al-mutawaffā?" (with a kasra on the fāʾ), and he said: "God Almighty [i.e., the deceased is God's creature, so mutawaffā is the correct form with the fatḥa — the sense being that the reading with a kasra would make God the one who dies]." This was one of the causes that moved ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him) to order him to compose a book on grammar. This reading contradicts His saying: ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْراً﴾ — they shall observe this period, which is four months and ten days. It was also said that ʿashran (ten) is used in reference to the nights, with the days included along with them, and they never use the masculine form for it when they intend the days.

You say: "I fasted ʿashran (ten)" [[Mahmud (may God have mercy on him) said: "You say: I fasted ʿashran … etc." Ahmad (may God have mercy on him) said: From this is the hadith, "Whoever fasts Ramadan and follows it with six (days) of Shawwal, it is as if he fasted the whole year," where the nights were given precedence, or fasting was not conceived of in them, to the point that they said: the condition of intention and its time is the night; therefore it was given a share in fasting and the nights were given precedence.]], and if you mention it (the feminine form), it falls outside their speech. Clear in this is His saying: ﴿إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا عَشْراً﴾ and then ﴿إِنْ لَبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا يَوْماً﴾. ﴿فَإِذا بَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾ — when their term is completed, that is, when their waiting period is over, ﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ — there is no blame upon you, O rulers and the body of Muslims, ﴿فِيما فَعَلْنَ فِي أَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ — concerning what they do with themselves, such as exposing themselves to proposals, ﴿بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ — in a manner that the Sharia does not disapprove. The meaning is that if they did what is disapproved, it would be incumbent upon the rulers to restrain them.

And if they (the guardians) are negligent, the blame falls upon them. ﴿فِيما عَرَّضْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ is that a man says to her: "You are indeed beautiful, or righteous, or ... and it is my aim to marry, and God may make easy for me a righteous woman," and similar words that give the impression that he wants to marry her, so that she holds herself back for him if she is inclined to him, without explicitly stating the marriage: he does not say, "I want to marry you," or "I will marry you," or "I propose to you." Ibn al-Mubarak related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulayman, from his maternal aunt, who said:

Muhammad ibn ʿAli Abu Jaʿfar entered upon me while I was in my waiting period, and he said: "You know my kinship to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the right of my grandfather over me, and my precedence in Islam." I said: "May God forgive you! Do you propose to me during my waiting period while people take knowledge from you?" He said: "Did you really? I only informed you of my kinship to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and my standing. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon Umm Salama, who had been with her cousin Abu Salama, and he died leaving her. He kept mentioning to her his station with God while leaning on his hand, until the mat left a mark on his hand from the strength of his leaning on it. That was not a proposal." [[This is how it is in the Kitab al-Nikah of Ibn al-Mubarak; al-Daraqutni related it from the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Salt from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman — Ibn al-Ghasil — similarly in full.]]

If you ask: what is the difference between kināya and taʿrīḍ? I say:

Kināya (allusion/metonymy) is that you mention a thing by other than its proper word, as in your saying: "tall of the sword-belt and the shoulder-straps" for tall stature, and "abundant in ashes" for a generous host. Taʿrīḍ (indirect hinting) is that you mention something by which you indicate another thing you did not mention, as when a person in need says to the one he needs: "I came to greet you, and to look upon your noble face." That is why they said:

"And let it suffice you, from me, the greeting as a demand."

It is as if one inclines the speech toward an aim that indicates the purpose; it is called talwīḥ (hinting), because what he wants gleams from it. ﴿أَوْ أَكْنَنْتُمْ فِي أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ — or you conceal and harbor in your hearts, so you do not mention it with your tongues, neither by allusion nor by explicit statement. ﴿عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّكُمْ سَتَذْكُرُونَهُنَّ﴾ — God knows that you will certainly mention them, and you will not refrain from speaking of your desire for them and will not be patient about it. There is in it an element of reproach, like His saying: ﴿عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّكُمْ كُنْتُمْ تَخْتانُونَ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾.

If you ask: where is the object of the exception in His saying ﴿وَلكِنْ لا تُواعِدُوهُنَّ﴾? I say: it is elided, because ﴿ستذكرونهن﴾ indicates it; its estimated form is: "God knows that you will mention them, so mention them, but do not promise them in secret." The "secret" (sirr) has come as a metonym for marriage, which is the intercourse, because it is something kept secret. al-Aʿshā said:

"And do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so marry or keep away forever."

[[Wa-la tashkhar min ba'isin dhī ḍarāra… (the verse) by al-Aʿshā Maymun ibn Qays. Al-bāʾis: the poor, the needy. Al-ḍarāra: blindness. Attributing "al-ikhlād" (perpetuity) to wealth is a metaphor, as it is its cause in imagination. "Taqrab" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ means "tafʿal," so the min is extra; "jāra" is the object; with a ḍamma it means "tadnū" (draw near), so the min is original. It is also narrated: "wa-la tqarabanna jāratan" with a shadda on the nūn. In any case it is a metonym for prohibiting intercourse. Al-sirr: the opposite of al-jahr (openly), used here metaphorically for intercourse, either because it occurs in secret or because it is kept secret. Al-nikāh: the marriage contract. It is said: abada al-waḥshī yabūdu abūdan, and tabaddada tabaddudan: it shied away from companionship; its alif here is converted from the nūn of emphasis in pause, and the intended meaning is distance metaphorically; the addressee is not specific. He forbade him to draw near to her because that is more emphatic than forbidding her intercourse; then he said: marry or withdraw from women like the wild beasts.]]

Then he used it to refer to the marriage contract, which is the cause of it, just as the word nikāḥ was used. ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ — that is, that you allude and do not speak explicitly. If you ask: with what is the exceptive particle connected? I say: with "do not promise them," meaning: do not promise them any promise except a known promise, not a disapproved one. That is, do not promise them except by saying, that is, do not promise them except by allusion. It is not permissible for it to be a discontinuous exception from "secretly," since that would lead to your saying "do not promise them except by allusion." It was also said that its meaning is: do not promise them intercourse, which is that a man says to her, "If I marry you, such-and-such will happen," meaning what takes place between them beneath the blanket. ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ means without obscenity or indecency in speech. It was also said: "do not promise them in secret," meaning privately, with the promise in secret being an expression for a promise of what is disgraceful, because whispering to them is generally about what one would be ashamed to say openly. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) concerning ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تَقُولُوا قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفاً﴾ that it means: that they pledge to each other that she will not marry anyone else. ﴿وَلا تَعْزِمُوا عُقْدَةَ النِّكاحِ﴾ — from "ʿazm al-amr" (resolving upon a matter) and "ʿazama ʿalayhi." Mentioning resolve is for emphasis in forbidding the contracting of the marriage bond during the waiting period, because resolve upon an action precedes it; so when it is forbidden, the action is forbidden all the more. Its meaning is: do not resolve to contract the marriage bond. It was also said: its meaning is: do not sever the marriage bond; the true sense of ʿazm is "cutting off," by the evidence of his peace be upon him saying: "There is no fast for one who does not resolve the fast from the night," and it is narrated "for one who does not spend the night fasting" [[Related by the authors of the Sunan from the hadith of Ḥafṣa with the wording "for one who does not gather (the intention)"; and "for one who does not spend the night" is in al-Nasa'i.]].

﴿حَتَّى يَبْلُغَ الْكِتابُ أَجَلَهُ﴾ — meaning what was written and prescribed of the waiting period. ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ يَعْلَمُ ما فِي أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ — of resolve upon what is not permitted, ﴿فَاحْذَرُوهُ﴾ — so beware of it, and do not resolve upon it. ﴿غَفُورٌ حَلِيمٌ﴾ — He does not hasten to punish you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 236–237:

"There is no blame upon you" (لا جُناحَ عَلَيْكُمْ): there is no liability (تبعة) upon you for the imposition of a dower (مهر), "if you divorce women" (إِنْ طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ) "as long as you have not touched them" (ما لَمْ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ), i.e., not had intercourse with them, "or you have not specified for them a portion" (أَوْ تَفْرِضُوا لَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةً): "unless you have specified for them a portion," or "until you specify," and the imposition of the portion (فرض الفريضة) is the naming of the dower (تسمية المهر). This is because a woman divorced before consummation, if a dower was named for her, has half of the named amount; and if no dower was named for her, she has no half of the proper dower (مهر المثل) but rather the provision (المتعة). The proof that the blame refers to liability for the dower is His saying: "And if you divorce them" up to His saying: "then half of what you have specified" (فَنِصْفُ ما فَرَضْتُمْ). So His saying "then half of what you have specified" is an affirmation of the blame that was negated there.

The provision (المتعة) is a garment (درع), a wrap (ملحفة), and a head-cover (خمار), according to the circumstances, according to Abu Hanifa, except that if the proper dower of such a woman is less than that, then she has the lesser of half the proper dower and the provision, and it is not reduced below five dirhams, because the minimum dower is ten dirhams, so it is not reduced below half of it.

"The affluent" (الْمُوسِعِ) is the one who has means. "The straitened" (الْمُقْتِرِ) is the one of narrow circumstances. "According to his capacity" (وَقَدَّرَهُ): its measure, which he can bear, because what one can bear is what is specific to him. It is also read with a fatha on the dal (وَقَدَرَهُ), and qadr and qadar are two dialects.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to a man from the Ansar who had married a woman, not specifying a dower for her, and then divorced her before touching her: "Did you provide for her?" He said: "I had nothing." He said: "Provide for her with your cap [[I have not found it.]]."

According to our companions (the Hanafis), the provision is obligatory only for this one alone, and it is recommended for the rest of divorced women, and not obligatory.

"A provision" (مَتاعاً) is an emphatic object for "provide for them" (متعوهن), meaning provision (تمتيعاً). "According to what is fair" (بِالْمَعْرُوفِ): in the manner that is good in the Sharia and in manliness. "As a duty" (حَقًّا) is an attribute of "provision," i.e., a provision incumbent upon them. Or: "that is a right" (حق ذلك), "upon the doers of good" (عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ): upon those who do good to the divorced women by providing for them. He called them "doers of good" before the act, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils" [[It passed on page 35 of this part.]].

"Unless they forgo" (إِلَّا أَنْ يَعْفُونَ): it means the divorced women. If you say: what is the difference between your saying "the men forgo" (الرجال يعفون) and "the women forgo" (النساء يعفون)? I say: the waw in the first is their pronoun, and the nun is the sign of the nominative; the waw in the second is the verb's radical letter, and the nun is their pronoun, and the verb is indeclinable, having no trace in its wording of the governing particle, and it is in the place of the accusative. "Or that he forgo" (ويعفو) is conjoined to its place.

"And the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage" (والَّذِي بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ النِّكاحِ): the guardian (الولي). [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "And the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage is the guardian..." etc. Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: In this citation al-Zamakhshari erred, attributing it to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, for his school agrees with the school of Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, that the intended person is the husband.

He (al-Zamakhshari) went to the view that the intended person is the guardian, and Imam Malik, may God be pleased with him, held this; and al-Zamakhshari was right that it is an opinion of apparent soundness, bearing the radiance of truth and the sheen of correctness, for several reasons:

First: the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage, firmly and permanently, is the guardian. As for the husband, he has that only at the time of the earlier contract, specifically, and then after divorce, and the speech at that point has nothing to do with the bond of marriage at all. If it is said: it was applied to him after divorce by an interpretation of a hidden "was" (كان), then the fair-minded cannot fail to see what distance and departure from the normal application of speech and its original sense this involves.

Second: the first address is to the wives by agreement, by His saying "unless they forgo" (إِلَّا أَنْ يَعْفُونَ), and among them are those who have no power of forgoing at all, such as the slave-woman and the virgin. So unless the division is completed by turning the second to the guardian over his virgin daughter or his slave-woman, the speech would depart from the apparent generality of the first. And when the speech is taken to mean the guardian, the meaning becomes: "unless they forgo," meaning they are fit to forgo, or someone forgoes on their behalf if they are not fit. For this reason, the guardian who forgoes and whose forgoing is considered by Malik is the father over his virgin daughter, and the master over his slave-woman specifically.

Third: the Noble Book is worthy of the correspondence of divisions and the coherence of the parts of speech, and the matter in it, on this reading, is of this kind, for the verse then comprises address to the wives, then the guardians, then the husbands by His saying "and do not forget the bounty among you" (وَلا تَنْسَوُا الْفَضْلَ بَيْنَكُمْ), so on this aspect it is replete with benefits and gathers the aims.

Fourth: the forgoing ascribed to the possessor of the bond of marriage is like that ascribed to the wives, and forgoing (العفو) in lexical sense is dropping (الاسقاط), which is the meaning of the first by agreement, since what is ascribed to the wives is dropping without doubt. If the intended possessor of the bond were the husband, then forgoing would necessarily be understood as completing the dower and giving him what is not due upon him, and what matches this of names is bounty (التفضل). For this reason, in addressing the husbands He said "and do not forget the bounty among you," because what is given by him is not due upon him, so it is bounty, not forgoing.

And one should not say: perhaps the husband paid the dower in full before divorce, and then divorced, so it is obligatory to recover half, and he drops it and forgoes it, and then the forgoing on the husband's side remains in its apparent and literal sense. We say: it suffices, in rejecting this aspect, what it contains of strain and the assumption of what the original sense contradicts.

Fifth: the beginning of the verse is address to the husbands in His saying "and if you divorce them" up to His saying "you have specified," so if His saying "or he forgo, the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage" were meant as the husband, it would be a shift and a turn (التفات) from address to third-person, which is not among its places. For this reason, His saying "and do not forget the bounty among you" came in the form of address, because it means the husbands, since they were addressed first.

Sixth: His saying "unless they forgo" and what is conjoined to it is an exception from His saying "then half of what you have specified." The original sense: "then half of what you have specified is obligatory upon you, unless the wives forgo it, and then it is not obligatory upon you." When the speech is taken to mean the guardian, it stands: for if they complete the dower for them, then half is obligatory upon them and does not change and does not contradict the excepted case from which the exception is made, so the exception does not operate in its literal sense of contradiction between the first and second. Unless it is said: what His saying "then half of what you have specified" implies, that it is obligatory upon you, is that the other half is not delivered to them, since it is dropped from the husband; so if he forgoes in the sense of completing the dower, the other half has become delivered to them. In this interpretation there is strain enough to remove the burden of rejecting it.]] meaning: unless the divorced women forgo against their husbands, so they do not demand from them half the dower, and the woman says: he has not seen me, nor served him, nor enjoyed me, so how should I take anything from him? Or the guardian who has charge of their marriage contract forgoes; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. It was said that it is the husband, and his forgoing is that he sends the full dower to her; this is the view of Abu Hanifa, and the first is of apparent soundness. Calling the surplus over the right "forgoing" is open to scrutiny, unless it is said that it was customary among them that the husband sent the dower to her at the time of marriage, so when he divorces her he is entitled to demand from her half of what he sent, and when he leaves the demand he has forgone it. Or he called it forgoing by way of figurative correspondence (المشاكلة). It is related from Jubayr ibn Mut'im that he married a woman and divorced her before consummating, so he completed her dowry and said: "I have more right to forgoing." And it is related from him that he entered upon Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who offered him a daughter of his, so he married her; when he went out he divorced her and sent her the dowry in full. It was said to him: "Why did you marry her?" He said: "She was offered to me, and I disliked refusing her." It was said: "Why then did you send the dowry?" He said: "Then where is the bounty?" [[Al-Tabari related it through Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr from his grandfather Jubayr ibn Mut'im, the same.]]

"And the bounty" (والْفَضْلَ): the favour. I.e., "and do not forget that one of you should show favour to another, and be lenient, and do not insist strictly."

Al-Hasan read: "that the one should forgo" (أن يعفو الذي), with the waw silent. Silencing the waw and the ya in the accusative position is a likening of them to the alif, since they are its sisters. Abu Nahik read: "and that he forgo" (وأن يعفو) with the ya. It is also read: "and do not forget the bounty" (ولا تنسو الفضل) with the waw kasra.

"There is no blame upon you" (لا جُناحَ عَلَيْكُمْ): there is no liability (تبعة) upon you for the imposition of a dower (مهر), "if you divorce women" (إِنْ طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ) "as long as you have not touched them" (ما لَمْ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ), i.e., not had intercourse with them, "or you have not specified for them a portion" (أَوْ تَفْرِضُوا لَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةً): "unless you have specified for them a portion," or "until you specify," and the imposition of the portion (فرض الفريضة) is the naming of the dower (تسمية المهر). It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to a man from the Ansar who had married a woman, not specifying a dower for her, and then divorced her before touching her: "Did you provide for her?" He said: "I had nothing." He said: "Provide for her with your cap [[I have not found it.]]."

According to our companions (the Hanafis), the provision is obligatory only for this one alone, and it is recommended for the rest of divorced women, and not obligatory.

"A provision" (مَتاعاً) is an emphatic object for "provide for them" (متعوهن), meaning provision (تمتيعاً). "According to what is fair" (بِالْمَعْرُوفِ): in the manner that is good in the Sharia and in manliness. "As a duty" (حَقًّا) is an attribute of "provision," i.e., a provision incumbent upon them. Or: "that is a right" (حق ذلك), "upon the doers of good" (عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ): upon those who do good to the divorced women by providing for them. He called them "doers of good" before the act, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills an enemy, he has his spoils" [[It passed on page 35 of this part.]].

"Unless they forgo" (إِلَّا أَنْ يَعْفُونَ): it means the divorced women. If you say: what is the difference between your saying "the men forgo" (الرجال يعفون) and "the women forgo" (النساء يعفون)? I say: the waw in the first is their pronoun, and the nun is the sign of the nominative; the waw in the second is the verb's radical letter, and the nun is their pronoun, and the verb is indeclinable, having no trace in its wording of the governing particle, and it is in the place of the accusative. "Or that he forgo" (ويعفو) is conjoined to its place.

"And the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage" (والَّذِي بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ النِّكاحِ): the guardian (الولي). [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "And the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage is the guardian..." etc. Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: In this citation al-Zamakhshari erred, attributing it to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, for his school agrees with the school of Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, that the intended person is the husband.

He (al-Zamakhshari) went to the view that the intended person is the guardian, and Imam Malik, may God be pleased with him, held this; and al-Zamakhshari was right that it is an opinion of apparent soundness, bearing the radiance of truth and the sheen of correctness, for several reasons:

First: the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage, firmly and permanently, is the guardian. As for the husband, he has that only at the time of the earlier contract, specifically, and then after divorce, and the speech at that point has nothing to do with the bond of marriage at all. If it is said: it was applied to him after divorce by an interpretation of a hidden "was" (كان), then the fair-minded cannot fail to see what distance and departure from the normal application of speech and its original sense this involves.

Second: the first address is to the wives by agreement, by His saying "unless they forgo" (إِلَّا أَنْ يَعْفُونَ), and among them are those who have no power of forgoing at all, such as the slave-woman and the virgin. So unless the division is completed by turning the second to the guardian over his virgin daughter or his slave-woman, the speech would depart from the apparent generality of the first. And when the speech is taken to mean the guardian, the meaning becomes: "unless they forgo," meaning they are fit to forgo, or someone forgoes on their behalf if they are not fit. For this reason, the guardian who forgoes and whose forgoing is considered by Malik is the father over his virgin daughter, and the master over his slave-woman specifically.

Third: the Noble Book is worthy of the correspondence of divisions and the coherence of the parts of speech, and the matter in it, on this reading, is of this kind, for the verse then comprises address to the wives, then the guardians, then the husbands by His saying "and do not forget the bounty among you" (وَلا تَنْسَوُا الْفَضْلَ بَيْنَكُمْ), so on this aspect it is replete with benefits and gathers the aims.

Fourth: the forgoing ascribed to the possessor of the bond of marriage is like that ascribed to the wives, and forgoing (العفو) in lexical sense is dropping (الاسقاط), which is the meaning of the first by agreement, since what is ascribed to the wives is dropping without doubt. If the intended possessor of the bond were the husband, then forgoing would necessarily be understood as completing the dower and giving him what is not due upon him, and what matches this of names is bounty (التفضل). For this reason, in addressing the husbands He said "and do not forget the bounty among you," because what is given by him is not due upon him, so it is bounty, not forgoing.

And one should not say: perhaps the husband paid the dower in full before divorce, and then divorced, so it is obligatory to recover half, and he drops it and forgoes it, and then the forgoing on the husband's side remains in its apparent and literal sense. We say: it suffices, in rejecting this aspect, what it contains of strain and the assumption of what the original sense contradicts.

Fifth: the beginning of the verse is address to the husbands in His saying "and if you divorce them" up to His saying "you have specified," so if His saying "or he forgo, the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage" were meant as the husband, it would be a shift and a turn (التفات) from address to third-person, which is not among its places. For this reason, His saying "and do not forget the bounty among you" came in the form of address, because it means the husbands, since they were addressed first.

Sixth: His saying "unless they forgo" and what is conjoined to it is an exception from His saying "then half of what you have specified." The original sense: "then half of what you have specified is obligatory upon you, unless the wives forgo it, and then it is not obligatory upon you." When the speech is taken to mean the guardian, it stands: for if they complete the dower for them, then half is obligatory upon them and does not change and does not contradict the excepted case from which the exception is made, so the exception does not operate in its literal sense of contradiction between the first and second. Unless it is said: what His saying "then half of what you have specified" implies, that it is obligatory upon you, is that the other half is not delivered to them, since it is dropped from the husband; so if he forgoes in the sense of completing the dower, the other half has become delivered to them. In this interpretation there is strain enough to remove the burden of rejecting it.]] meaning: unless the divorced women forgo against their husbands, so they do not demand from them half the dower, and the woman says: he has not seen me, nor served him, nor enjoyed me, so how should I take anything from him? Or the guardian who has charge of their marriage contract forgoes; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. It was said that it is the husband, and his forgoing is that he sends the full dower to her; this is the view of Abu Hanifa, and the first is of apparent soundness. Calling the surplus over the right "forgoing" is open to scrutiny, unless it is said that it was customary among them that the husband sent the dower to her at the time of marriage, so when he divorces her he is entitled to demand from her half of what he sent, and when he leaves the demand he has forgone it. Or he called it forgoing by way of figurative correspondence (المشاكلة). It is related from Jubayr ibn Mut'im that he married a woman and divorced her before consummating, so he completed her dowry and said: "I have more right to forgoing." And it is related from him that he entered upon Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who offered him a daughter of his, so he married her; when he went out he divorced her and sent her the dowry in full. It was said to him: "Why did you marry her?" He said: "She was offered to me, and I disliked refusing her." It was said: "Why then did you send the dowry?" He said: "Then where is the bounty?" [[Al-Tabari related it through Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr from his grandfather Jubayr ibn Mut'im, the same.]]

"And the bounty" (والْفَضْلَ): the favour. I.e., "and do not forget that one of you should show favour to another, and be lenient, and do not insist strictly."

Al-Hasan read: "that the one should forgo" (أن يعفو الذي), with the waw silent. Silencing the waw and the ya in the accusative position is a likening of them to the alif, since they are its sisters. Abu Nahik read: "and that he forgo" (وأن يعفو) with the ya. It is also read: "and do not forget the bounty" (ولا تنسو الفضل) with the waw kasra.

The middle prayer (al-Salah al-Wusta): that is, the middle one among the prayers, or the most excellent one, from their saying of the most excellent thing: "al-awsat" (the middle).

It was singled out and conjoined to "the prayer" [[His words "and conjoined to the prayer": perhaps "to the prayers." (ʿ)]] because of its distinction, and it is the afternoon prayer (Salat al-ʿAsr). It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer. May God fill their houses and graves with fire." [[Muslim related it from the narration of Shutayr ibn Shakal from ʿAli. The hadith is in the six books, but the words "the afternoon prayer" are in Muslim alone. al-Bukhari related it in the chapters on the campaigns, on jihad, and on tafsir. On this subject, from Ibn Masʿud, traced to the Prophet: "The middle prayer is the afternoon prayer," related by al-Tirmidhi, and in his collection, from Samurah, something similar.]] He (peace be upon him) also said: "It is the prayer that Sulayman ibn Dawud (Solomon son of David) was distracted from until it was hidden behind the veil." [[Ibn ʿAdi related it in al-Kamil from ʿAli, traced to the Prophet: "The middle prayer is the afternoon prayer, which Sulayman ibn Dawud neglected until it was hidden behind the veil." In its chain is Muqatil ibn Sulayman, who is discarded (saqit). Ibn Abi Shaybah related it from the narration of Abu Ishaq from al-Harith ibn ʿAli, traced to the Prophet, and this is closer to correct. On this subject, from Ibn ʿAbbas as a statement of his companion (mawquf), in al-Tabari.]] And from Hafsah, that she said to the one who was writing the Mushaf for her: "When you reach this verse, do not write it until I dictate it to you as I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recite it." So she dictated to him: "And the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer." [[al-Tabari related it through Abu Bishr from Salim from Hafsah, that she commanded a man who wrote a Mushaf for her. She said: "When you reach this place, inform me." When he reached ﴿Guard against the prayers and the middle prayer﴾, she said: "Write: the afternoon prayer." In another narration of his, she said to him: "Write, for I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: Guard against the prayers and the middle prayer, which is the afternoon prayer." Thus it is in al-Tabari. The well-known report from Hafsah is that she dictated to the scribe: "Guard against the prayers and the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer." Likewise Malik related it in al-Muwatta from Zayd ibn Aslam from ʿAmr ibn Rafiʿ, who said: "I used to write a Mushaf for Hafsah," and he mentioned it. Ibn Hibban related it from the narration of Ibn Ishaq: "Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli and Nafiʿ ibn ʿAmr ibn Nafiʿ, freedman of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, related to me that he used to write the Mushafs in the time of the wives of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." He said: "Hafsah asked me to write a Mushaf for her and said: When you reach this verse of this surah, al-Baqarah, do not write it until you come to me with it, and I will dictate it to you as I memorized it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." He said: "When I reached it, I brought her the sheet on which I was writing, and she said to me: Write: Guard against the prayers and the middle prayer and the afternoon prayer." From this route Abu Yaʿla and al-Tahawi also related it. ʿAbd al-Razzaq related it from Ibn Jurayj from Nafiʿ from Hafsah in similar words, and likewise al-Tabari related it through ʿAbdallah ibn ʿUmar from Nafiʿ, that Hafsah commanded a freedman of hers. Ibn Abi Dawud in his Kitab al-Masahif related it through nearly twenty routes, all of which contain "and the afternoon prayer" with the conjunction "wa."]] And it is reported from ʿAʾishah and Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them, "and the middle prayer and the afternoon prayer" [[As for ʿAʾishah, Muslim related through Abu Yunus, the freedman of ʿAʾishah, who said: "ʿAʾishah commanded me to write a Mushaf for her, and she said: When you reach this verse, inform me. When I reached it, I informed her, and she dictated to me: Guard against the prayers and the middle prayer and the afternoon prayer." And she said: "I heard it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Likewise Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and Ahmad related it through this route. As for Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Dawud in al-Masahif related it through the narration of Abu Ishaq ʿUmar ibn Maryam from Ibn ʿAbbas, "that he used to recite it thus."]] with the conjunction "wa."

On this recitation, the specification then concerns two prayers: the first is the middle prayer, which is either the noon prayer (Salat al-Zuhr), or the dawn prayer (Salat al-Fajr), or the sunset prayer (Salat al-Maghrib), according to the differing reports on it; and the second is the afternoon prayer. It was said that its excellence is due to the people's preoccupation with their trades and livelihoods during its time. It is reported from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, that it is the noon prayer [[al-Tabari related it through the narration of Abu ʿAqil Zahrah ibn Maʿbad, that Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibrahim ibn Talhah asked Ibn ʿUmar about the middle prayer. He said: "It is the noon prayer."]], because it is in the middle of the day, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to pray it at the time of the midday heat (al-Hajirah), and no prayer was more difficult for his companions than it. It is reported from Mujahid that it is the dawn prayer, because it lies between the daytime prayers and the nighttime prayers. And it is reported from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb that it is the sunset prayer, because it is the odd-numbered prayer of the day, and it is not shortened during travel from three units. [[al-Tabari related it through the narration of Ishaq ibn Abi Farwah from Rahl from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, who said: "The middle prayer is the sunset prayer. Do you not see that it is neither the fewest nor the most in units, and it is not shortened during travel?" Ishaq is abandoned (matruk), and his shaykh is unknown.]]

And ʿAbdallah (ibn Masʿud) recited: "and upon the middle prayer." And ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, recited "wa-l-salat al-wusta" in the accusative, as praise and specification. And Nafiʿ recited "al-Wusta" with the letter sad (al-Wusta with ṣ).

﴿And stand before God in devotion﴾: standing in remembrance of God during your standing. And qunut is that you remember God while standing. It is reported from ʿIkrimah: "They used to speak during prayer, so they were forbidden." It is reported from Mujahid that it is stillness, restraining the hands and the gaze. And it is reported that when one of them stood for prayer, they were in awe of the Merciful, so that they would not extend their gaze, nor turn, nor move the pebbles, nor let their minds dwell on any matter of worldly affairs.

﴿But if you fear﴾: if there is fear from an enemy or other cause for you, then ﴿on foot﴾: pray on foot. It is the plural of "rajil" (one on foot), like "qa'im" and "qiyam," or of "rajl." It is said: "rajul rajul," meaning "rajil." It has been recited as "fa-rijalan" with a damma on the ra, "wa-rijalan" with a tashdid, and "wa-rajulan."

According to Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, they do not pray while walking or while fighting with swords as long as standing is possible. According to al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, they pray in every condition, and the rider makes gestures, and the requirement of facing the qiblah is waived for him.

﴿And when you are safe﴾: when your fear has passed, ﴿remember God as He taught you what you did not know﴾: of the prayer of security (salat al-amn); or, "when you are safe, give thanks to God for the security, and remember Him through worship, just as He has been good to you by teaching you the laws, and how you should pray in a state of fear and in a state of security."

Its interpretation (taqdir) according to the one who reads wasiyyatun in the nominative: "The bequest (wasiyyah) of those who die", or "The ruling (hukm) concerning those who die is a bequest for their wives", or "Those who die, (there is) a bequest for their wives" (taking alladhina as the subject with the bequest as predicate, meaning the ruling for them). According to the one who reads it in the accusative: "And those who die shall make a bequest (yuwsuna wasiyyatan)", like your saying: "You are only the mail-courier's journey (innama anta sayr al-barid)", with tasir implied; or "And adhere to (ilzam) those who die with a bequest."

The recitation of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "It is prescribed for you, the bequest for your wives, as provision until the year's end", in place of His words "And those of you who die and leave wives, a bequest for their wives, provision until the year's end." The recitation of Ubayy reads: "Provision (mata') for their wives, provision (matan)." It is also related from him: "So provision for their wives." The accusative matan is governed by the bequest (wasiyyah), except when you supply yuwsuna, in which case it is governed by the verb. On the recitation of Ubayy, matan is in the accusative governed by mata', since it carries the sense of providing (tamti'), like your saying: "Praise belongs to God, the praise of the thankful," and "The beating of Zayd by you, a severe beating, pleased me." Ghayra ikhraj is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid), like your saying: "This statement is not what you say." Or it is a substitute (badal) for matan, or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the wives, meaning "not expelling" (ghayr mukhrajat).

The meaning is that it is the right of those who die, leaving wives behind, to bequeath, before they are near death, that their wives be provided for after them for a full year, meaning that they be maintained from his estate and that they not leave their dwellings. This was at the beginning of Islam, then the period was abrogated by His words: "four months and ten (days)." It is said: what exceeds this measure was abrogated, and the maintenance was abrogated by inheritance, which is the quarter and the eighth. Scholars differed regarding residence: according to Abu Hanifa and his companions, they have no right to residence. "Without expulsion" (ghayra ikhraj) ... "Concerning what they do with themselves" (fi ma fa'alna fi anfusihinna) means adornment and exposing themselves to proposals, "of what is reasonable" (min ma'ruf), meaning what is not legally reprehensible.

If you ask: how could the earlier verse be abrogated by the later one? I answer: a verse may come earlier in the recited order (tilawah) while coming later in revelation (tanzil), like His words: "The foolish among the people will say" together with His words: "We have seen the turning of your face toward the heaven."

﴿And for divorced women there is provision﴾ (mut'ah), in that He makes the provision obligatory for all of them, after He had made it obligatory for one of them, namely the divorced woman who has not been consummated with. He said ﴿as a duty upon the God-conscious﴾, just as He said there ﴿as a duty upon the good-doers﴾. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zuhri that it is obligatory for every divorced woman. It is said that the word "provision" covers both the obligatory and the recommended provision together. It is also said that the intended meaning of "provision" is maintenance during the waiting period (nafaqat al-'iddah).

﴿And for divorced women there is provision﴾ (mut'ah), in that He makes the provision obligatory for all of them, after He had made it obligatory for one of them, namely the divorced woman who has not been consummated with. He said ﴿as a duty upon the God-conscious﴾, just as He said there ﴿as a duty upon the good-doers﴾. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zuhri that it is obligatory for every divorced woman. It is said that the word "provision" covers both the obligatory and the recommended provision together. It is also said that the intended meaning of "provision" is maintenance during the waiting period (nafaqat al-'iddah).

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 2, verses 243–244:

﴿Did you not see﴾ is a rebuke addressed to whoever has heard of their story from the People of the Book and the reports of earlier peoples, and an expression of wonder at their condition. It is also permissible to address this to someone who neither saw nor heard of them, because this statement functions as a proverb in the sense of expressing wonder. It is narrated that the people of Dawardan, a village before Wasit, were struck by plague, so they fled. Allah caused them to die and then brought them back to life, so that they would take heed and know that there is no escape from the decree and judgment of Allah.

It was also said that Hizqil (Ezekiel) passed by them after a long time, when their bones had been stripped bare and their joints scattered. He twisted his cheek and his fingers in astonishment at what he saw. Then it was revealed to him: "Call out to them that they should rise by Allah's permission." He called out, and he saw them standing, saying: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; there is no god but You."

It was also said that they were a group from the Children of Israel whose king called them to jihad, but they fled in fear of death. So Allah caused them to die for eight days and then brought them back to life. ﴿And they were thousands﴾ is evidence for large numbers. There is disagreement about this: it was said ten thousand, it was said thirty thousand, and it was said seventy thousand. As for the innovative (bid'ah) interpretations of tafsir (exegesis), some say that ﴿ulūf﴾ means "those who are bound together," as the plural of ﴿ālif﴾, like ﴿qā'id﴾ and ﴿qu'ūd﴾ (sitting, and those who sit).

If you say: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿Allah said to them: "Die"﴾? I say: Its meaning is "so He caused them to die." It was expressed in this way to indicate that they died a single death, as one man dies, by the command and will of Allah, and that is a death beyond the usual course. It is as if they were commanded to do something and they carried it out without refusal or hesitation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

This is an encouragement to the Muslims toward jihad and to seeking martyrdom, and that if death cannot be avoided and no escape from it is possible, then it is more fitting that it occur in the way of Allah. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, in that He shows them what they may take heed from and gain insight from, as He showed those (people), and as He has shown you by relating their story to you. Or, it means: He is full of bounty toward mankind in that He brought those people back to life so that they would take heed and thereby succeed; had He willed, He would have left them dead until the Day of Resurrection.

The evidence that He related this story as an incitement to jihad is what He followed it with, the command to fight in the way of Allah: ﴿And know that Allah is All-Hearing, hearing what those who stay behind and those who go forth say, and All-Knowing of what they conceal﴾, and He is beyond (the scope of) recompense.
