Lending to God: a metaphor for putting forward the deed by which one seeks its reward. "The good loan" is either striving (mujahada) itself, or spending in the way of God. "Many multiples": it was said, the single one is seven hundred. And on the authority of al-Suddi: "many, whose true extent none knows but God." "God withholds and extends" — He widens for His servants and restricts, so do not be stingy toward Him with what He has widened upon you; He will not exchange hardship for ease for you. "And to Him you will be returned," so that He may recompense you for what you have put forward.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 246:

﴿لِنَبِيٍّ لَهُمُ﴾: (to a prophet of theirs), who is Yusha' (Joshua), or Shim'un (Simeon), or Ishmu'il (Samuel). ﴿ابْعَثْ لَنا مَلِكاً﴾ (Send for us a king) who will rise up with us to fight, a commander whose opinion we follow in directing the war and whose command we obey. They asked their prophet for something like what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do in appointing commanders over the armies he equipped, and in ordering them to obey him and carry out his orders.

It is related that he ordered the people, when they travelled, to make one of them a commander over them.

﴿نُقاتِلْ﴾ (we fight) is read with the nun and with the jazm (short vowel), as a response (jawab) to the imperative. It is also read with the nun and the raf' (final damma), as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "Send him for us, as those who intend to fight." Or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if he had said to them: "What will you do with a king?" and they said: "We will fight." It is also read as yuqatil with the ya' and jazm as a response, and with raf' as an attribute (sifah) of malikan (a king).

The predicate of ʿasaytum (ʿasaytum) is ﴿أَلَّا تُقاتِلُوا﴾ (that you will not fight), and the conditional clause intervenes between them. The meaning: "Have you come close to not fighting?" That is, "Is the matter as I expect, that you will not fight?" He meant to say: "Perhaps you will not fight," in the sense of "I expect your cowardice in fighting," so he introduced "hal" (is it not that) as a question about what he expected and suspected. He intended by the interrogative the affirmation, and the establishment that what is expected is certain, and that he is correct in his expectation [[The phrase "and that he is correct in his expectation": in al-Sihah: sāba al-sahm al-qirtās yuṣībuhu, a dialect form of aṣābahu. (ʿ)]], like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ﴾ (Has there come upon man...), whose meaning is affirmation. It is also read ʿasītum with a kasra on the sin, but this is weak.

﴿وَما لَنا أَلَّا نُقاتِلَ﴾ (And what reason do we have not to fight), what cause do we have to abandon fighting, and what purpose do we have in it, ﴿وَقَدْ أُخْرِجْنا مِنْ دِيارِنا وَأَبْنائِنا﴾ (when we have been expelled from our homes and our children). That is because the people of Jalut (Goliath) lived on the coast of the Roman Sea between Egypt and Palestine, and they captured four hundred and forty of their sons ﴿إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ﴾ (except a few of them). It is said that the few among them were three hundred and thirteen, according to the number of the people of Badr. ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers) is a warning to them for their wrongdoing in holding back from fighting and abandoning jihad.

Ṭālūt is a non-Arabic (ʿajamī) name, like Jālūt and Dāwūd. It is not declined (ṣarf) because it is a proper name and non-Arabic. Some claimed that it derives from *al-ṭiwāl* (tallness), because he was described as having physical largeness. If its pattern were *fa'lūt* from *al-ṭūl*, its root would be *ṭawlūt*. But the fact that it is not declined rules out that derivation, unless one says that it is a Hebrew name that happened to match an Arabic word, as *Ḥanṭā* matched *ḥinṭah* (wheat), and *Bashmalā* matched *lahā*, and *Rakhmānā Rakhīmā* matched *bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm*. In that case it derives from *al-ṭūl* just as if it were Arabic, and one of its two reasons for not being declined is its foreignness, since it is Hebrew.

*Anná* (how, from where) here expresses denial of his kingship over them and considers it unlikely. If you ask: what is the difference between the two *wāws* in ﴿وَنَحْنُ أَحَقُّ﴾ and ﴿وَلَمْ يُؤْتَ﴾?

[[Al-Zamakhsharī, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say, what is the difference between the two *wāws*... etc." Aḥmad [Ibn al-Munayyir], may God have mercy on him, said: The summary of this is that the first *wāw* conveyed its clause as a circumstantial clause by itself, and the second clause also conveyed circumstance, but through the conjunctive *wāw*. This kind of analysis is "easy yet unattainable" (al-sahl al-mumtaniʿ).]]

I say: the first is the *wāw* of circumstance (ḥāl), and the second is the *wāw* of conjunction, joining a clause to a clause that is in circumstantial position. Both are governed together by the rule of the *wāw* of circumstance. The meaning is: how can he rule over us when he does not deserve kingship, since there is someone more entitled to it, and he is poor, and kingship needs wealth to support it? They said this because prophethood was in the tribe of Lāwī ibn Yaʿqūb, and kingship was in the tribe of Yahūdhā, and Ṭālūt was from neither of the two tribes. Also, he was a water-carrier or a tanner, and poor.

It is related that their prophet prayed to God, Exalted, when they asked him for a king, and a staff was brought with which the one who would rule over them would be measured, and only Ṭālūt matched it. ﴿Indeed God has chosen him over you﴾ means: God is the one who chose him over you, and He knows the interests better than you do, and there is no objection to God's judgment. Then he mentioned two qualities more beneficial than what they had mentioned about lineage and wealth, namely knowledge (*al-ʿilm al-mabsūṭ*, extensive knowledge) and bodily stature.

The apparent meaning of "knowledge" is knowing what they asked him for, namely matters of war. It is also permissible that he was knowledgeable in religion and in other matters. It was said: he had already received revelation and was a prophet. That is because a king must be among the people of knowledge, since the ignorant person is despised and not benefited from. And he must be large in body, filling the eye with prominence, because that is greater in souls and more awe-inspiring in hearts.

*Al-basṭah* means breadth and extension. It is related that a standing man could extend his hand and reach his head. ﴿He gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾: that is, kingship belongs to Him, with no one disputing it. So He gives it to whomever He wills, namely whomever He deems fit for kingship. ﴿And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: All-Encompassing in bounty and giving, who widens provision for those who lack means of wealth, and enriches them after poverty. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of whom He chooses for kingship.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 248:

The tabut (ark) is the chest of the Torah. When Musa (peace be upon him) went into battle, he would send it forward, and the hearts of the Children of Israel would be calmed, so they would not flee. As-sakinah (tranquility) means stillness and composure. It is also said that it was a figure of green stone (zabarjad) or ruby, having a head like the head of a cat, a tail like its tail, and two wings. It would hum, and the ark would advance toward the enemy while they walked with it. When it settled, they would stand firm, become calm, and victory would descend. It is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that it had a face like the face of a human being and within it was a gentle, fluttering wind. Baqiyyah means the fragments of the tablets, the staff of Musa, his garments, and some of the Torah. Allah raised it after Musa (peace be upon him), and the angels brought it down carrying it while they looked at it, and that was a sign of Allah's choosing Talut. It is also said that it was with Musa and with the prophets of the Children of Israel after him, who would seek victory through it. When the Children of Israel changed, the disbelievers overcame them and seized it, and it was in the land of Jalut. When Allah willed that Talut should rule, He afflicted them with calamity until five cities were destroyed. They said: "This is because of the ark among us," so they placed it on two oxen, and the angels drove them to Talut. It is also said that it was made of shimshar wood overlaid with gold, about three cubits by two cubits.

Ubayy and Zayd ibn Thabit read: al-tabut with a ha' (at-tabuh), and this is the dialect of the Ansar.

If you ask: What is the wazn (morphological pattern) of at-tabut? I answer: it is either fa'lawt or fa'awl. It cannot be fa'awl, because it is rare, like salas and qalaq, and because it is an unfamiliar construction, and it is not permissible to abandon the familiar for it. So it is, then, fa'lawt, from at-tawb, which means return, because it is a container in which things are placed and deposited, so whatever comes out of it keeps returning to it, and its owner returns to it for what he needs from his deposits.

As for the one who reads with a ha', its pattern is, in his view, fa'awl, except for those who make its ha' a substitute for the ta', because they share the quality of hams and both are among the letters of augmentation. For this reason it was substituted for the ta' of the feminine.

Abu al-Sammal read sakinah with a fatha on the sin and a shadda, and this is rare. It is also read yahmiluhu with the ya'.

If you ask: Who are the family (al) of Musa and the family of Harun? I answer: they are the prophets from the sons of Ya'qub after the two of them. For Imran is the son of Qahith, son of Lawi, son of Ya'qub, so the descendants of Ya'qub are their family. It is also permissible that what is meant is: what Musa and Harun left behind. The word al is inserted to magnify their status.

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 249:

*Fassala* ʿan mawdiʿi kadhā: idhā infasala ʿanhu wa-jāwazahu. Wa-aṣluhu: faṣala nafsahu, thumma kathura maḥdhūf al-mafʿūl ḥattā ṣāra fī ḥukm ghayr al-mutaʿaddī ka-*infasala*. Wa-qīla: faṣala ʿan al-balad fuṣūlan. Wa-yajūzu an yakūna: *faṣṣalahu faṣlan*, wa-*faṣala fuṣūlan* ka-*waqafa* wa-*ṣadda* wa-naḥwihimā.

Wa-l-maʿnā: *infaṣala ʿan baladihi bi-l-junūd*. Ruwiya annahu qāla li-qawmihi: "Lā yakhruju maʿiya rajulun banā bināʾan lam yafrugh minhu, wa-lā tājirun mushtaghilun bi-l-tijāra, wa-lā rajulun mutazawwijun bi-imra-atin lam yubni ʿalayhā, wa-lā abtaghī illā al-shābb al-nashīṭ al-fārigh." Fa-ijtamaʿa ilayhi mimmā ikhtārahu thamānūna alfan, wa-kāna al-waqtu qayḍan, wa-salakū mafāzatan, fa-saʾalū an yajriya Allāhu lahum nahran.

Fa-qāla: ﴿Inna Allāha mubtalīkum bi-nahr﴾ — bi-mā iqtarahtumūhu min al-nahr. ﴿Fa-man shariba minhu fa-laysa minnī﴾: fa-man ibtadaʾa shurbahu min al-nahr bi-an karaʿa fīhi, ﴿fa-laysa minnī﴾: fa-laysa bi-muttaṣil bī wa-muttaḥid maʿī, min qawlihim: *fulānun minnī*, ka-annahu baʿḍuhu li-ikhtilāṭihimā wa-ittiḥādihimā. Wa-yajūzu an yurāda: *fa-laysa min jumlatī wa-ashyāʿī*. ﴿Wa-man lam yaṭʿamhu﴾: wa-man lam yadhuqhu, min ṭaʿima al-shayʾ idhā dhāqahu. Wa-minhu *ṭaʿima al-shayʾ* li-madhāqihi. Qāla:

*Wa-in shi'ta lam aṭʿam naqākhan*
*wa-lā bardā*

[[Qawluhu "lam aṭʿam naqākhan" huwa al-māʾ al-ʿadhb alladhī yanqukhu al-fuʾād bi-bardihi. Wa-l-naqkh: al-naqf, wa-huwa kasr al-raʾs ʿan al-dimāgh. (ʿ)]] [[Fa-in shiʾta ḥarramta al-nisāʾa siwākum ... wa-in shiʾta lam aṭʿam naqākhan wa-lā bardā. Li-l-ʿarjī. Wa-tāʾ "shiʾta" yaḥtamilu annahā li-l-mutakallim, wa-annahā li-l-mukhāṭaba wa-huwa abλagh. Wa-khāṭaba al-wāḥida bi-lafẓ jamʿ al-mudhakkar taʿẓīman.

Wa-lam aṭʿam: ayy lam atanāwal. Wa-l-naqākh bi-l-qāf wa-l-khāʾ al-muʿjama: al-māʾ al-ʿadhb al-bārid. Wa-l-bard: al-nawm. Wa-ʿan baʿḍ al-ʿarab: "manaʿa al-bardu al-bard", wa-huwa min bāb al-jinās al-tāmm. Wa-l-ʿarjī: huwa ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, nisba li-ʿarj al-Ṭāʾif.]]

Alā tarā kayfa ʿuṭifa ʿalayhi al-bardu wa-huwa al-nawm. Wa-yuqālu: *mā dhuqtu ghammāḍan*. Wa-naḥwuhu min al-ibtilāʾ: mā ibtalā Allāhu bihi ahla Ayla min tark al-ṣayd maʿa ityān al-ḥītān sharʿan. Bal huwa ashaddu minhu wa-aṣʿab. Wa-innamā ʿarafa dhālika Ṭālūt bi-ikhbār min al-Nabī, wa-in kāna nabiyyan — kamā yurwā ʿan baʿḍihim — fa-bi-l-waḥy.

Wa-qurīʾa (bi-nahrin) bi-l-sukūn.

Fa-in qulta: mimma istathnā qawluhu ﴿illā man ightaraf﴾? Qultu: min qawlihi ﴿fa-man shariba minhu fa-laysa minnī﴾. [[Qāla Maḥmūd raḥimahu Allāh: "Mustathnan min qawlihi ﴿fa-man shariba minhu fa-laysa minnī﴾ ... al-kh." Qāla Aḥmad raḥimahu Allāh: Wa-fī hādhihi al-āya taqwiyatun li-man dhahaba ilā anna al-istithnāʾ al-mutaʿaqqib lil-jumal (the exception following a series of sentences) lā yataʿayyanu ʿawduhu ilā al-akhīra li-iḥtimāl ʿawdihi ilā mā qablahā.

Wa-rudda ʿalā man manaʿa dhālika muḥtajjan bi-imtināʿ al-faṣl bayn al-mustathnā wa-l-mustathnā minhu bi-ajnabī min al-istithnāʾ. Wa-li-dhālika ḥaqqaqa ʿawdahu ilā al-akhīra, wa-tawaqqafa fī inʿiṭāfihi ʿalā mā taqaddamahā, fa-yajūzu ʿindahu an yaʿūda ʿalā al-jamīʿ maʿa al-akhīra. Wa-ammā ʿawduhu ʿalā mā qabla al-akhīra dūnahā fa-mutaʿadhdhir ʿinda hādhā al-qāʾil, fa-lam yaṣif fī al-ʿawd ilā al-akhīra li-hādhihi al-shubha. Wa-qad bayyana al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr ṣalāḥiyyata ʿawdihi ilā mā qabla al-akhīra dūnahā radan ʿalā hādhā al-qāʾil, wa-istashhada bi-qawlihi taʿālā: ﴿Wa-law raddūhu ilā al-Rasūl wa-ilā ūlī al-amr minhum la-ʿalimahu alladhīna yastanbiṭūnahu minhum, wa-lā faḍlu Allāhi ʿalaykum wa-raḥmatuhu la-ittabaʿtum al-shayṭāna illā qalīlan﴾. Wa-wajhu istishhādihi: anna al-maʿnā yaʾbā inʿiṭāf hādhā al-istithnāʾ ilā al-jumla al-akhīra wa-yuʿayyinu ʿawdahu ilā mā qablahā, wa-sa-yaʾtī bayān dhālika ʿinda al-kalām ʿalā al-āya.]] Wa-l-jumla al-thāniya fī ḥukm al-mutaʾakhkhira, illā annahā quddimat lil-ʿināya, kamā quddima (wa-l-ṣābiʾūn) fī qawlihi: ﴿Inna alladhīna āmanū wa-alladhīna hādū wa-l-ṣābiʾūn﴾. Wa-maʿnāhu: al-rukhṣa fī ightirāf al-ghurfa bi-l-yad dūna al-kurūʿ. Wa-l-dalīl ʿalayhi qawluhu ﴿fa-sharibū minhu﴾, ayy fa-karaʿū fīhi, ﴿illā qalīlan minhum﴾.

Wa-quriʾa (ghurfa) bi-l-fatḥ bi-maʿnā al-maṣdar, wa-bi-l-ḍamm bi-maʿnā al-maghrūf. Wa-qaraʾa Ubayy wa-l-Aʿmash: "illā qalīlun", bi-l-rafʿ. Wa-hādhā min maylihim maʿa al-maʿnā wa-l-iʿrāḍ ʿan al-lafẓ jānibān, wa-huwa bāb jalīl min ʿilm al-ʿarabiyya.

Fa-lammā kāna maʿnā ﴿fa-sharibū minhu﴾ fī maʿnā "fa-lam yuṭīʿūhu", ḥumila ʿalayhi, ka-annahu qīla: "fa-lam yuṭīʿūhu illā qalīlun minhum."

Naḥwuhu qawlu al-Farazdaq:

*... lam yadaʿ*
*min al-māli illā musḥatun aw mujallafu*

[[Ilayka amīr al-muʾminīn ramat bina ... shuʿūb al-nawā wa-l-hawjal al-mutaʿassif
Wa-ʿaḍḍ zamānin yā ibna Marwān lam yadaʿ ... min al-māli illā musḥatun aw mujallafu

Lil-Farazdaq. Yaqūlu: yā amīr al-muʾminīn, qadhafatnā ilayka ṭuruq al-buʿd, lākin al-rāmī bihi fī al-ḥaqīqa dawāʿī al-nafs, fa-isnād al-ramy ilā al-shuʿūb majāz ʿaqlī (rational metaphor). Aw shabbaha al-ṭuruq bi-man yaṣiḥḥu minhu al-ramy ʿalā sabīl al-makniyya (metaphor of implicit comparison), wa-l-murād bi-l-ramy al-baʿth majāzan. Wa-l-hawjal: al-ṭawīl al-aḥmaq, ayy al-baʿīr al-mutaʿassif al-ḥāʾid ʿan sunan al-ṭarīq, aw al-ṭarīq al-ṭawīl al-muʿawwaj, fa-huwa ʿaṭf khāṣṣ ʿalā ʿāmm. Wa-shabbaha al-zamān al-mujdib bi-dhī nāb ʿalā ṭarīq al-makniyya, wa-isnād al-ʿaḍḍ lahu takhyīl (imaginative representation). Wa-l-musḥat: al-baqiyya al-qalīla min al-shayʾ, yuqālu saḥtahu wa-asḥatahu idhā istaʾṣalahu, wa-l-ūlā lughat al-Ḥijāz, wa-l-thāniya lughat Najd. Wa-l-mujalaf: al-munqariḍ min jawānibihi, yuqālu jalafahu ka-naṣarahu idhā qashshharahu aw qaṭaʿahu. Wa-l-jāʾifa abligh min al-jālifa. Wa-qīla: al-musḥat wa-l-mujalaf alladhī ukhidha minhu māluhu aw halaka minhu.

Wa-kāna al-wājib naṣb al-istithnāʾ li-annahu lā wajha li-l-rafʿ, lākin rūiʿiya fīhi maʿnā al-nafy fa-rufiʿa, ayy lam yabqa min al-māl illā humā. Wa-ruwiya: "illā musḥatan aw mujalfin", fa-rafaʿa al-thānī ʿaṭfan ʿalā al-maʿnā. Ruwiya annahu suʾila: limādhā khālafta baynahumā? Fa-qāla: "qultu dhālika li-tashqā bihi al-naḥwiyyūn." Wa-nidāʾ ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān fī al-mawḍiʿayn lil-taʿẓīm wa-l-istiʿṭāf.]]

Ka-annahu qāla: lam yabqa min al-māl illā musḥatun aw mujalaf.

Wa-qīla: lam yabqa maʿa Ṭālūt illā thalāthumiʾa wa-thalāthata ʿashara rajulan. ﴿Wa-alladhīna āmanū﴾, yaʿnī al-qalīl. ﴿Qāla alladhīna yaẓunnūna﴾, yaʿnī al-khawāṣṣ minhum alladhīna naṣabū bayna aʿyunihim liqāʾ Allāh wa-yaqqanūhu, aw alladhīna tayaqqanū annahum yastashhidūna ʿammā qarībin wa-yalqawna Allāh, wa-l-muʾminūn mukhtalifūn fī quwwat al-yaqīn wa-naṣūʿ al-baṣīra.

Wa-qīla: al-ḍamīr fī ﴿qālū lā ṭāqata lanā﴾ li-l-kathīrin alladhīna ikhtadhalū, wa-alladhīna yaẓunnūna hum al-qalīl alladhīna thabatū maʿahu, ka-annahum taqāwalū bi-dhālika wa-l-nahru baynahumā, yuẓhiru ūlāʾika ʿudhrahum fī al-ikhtidhāl, wa-yaruddu ʿalayhim hāʾulāʾ mā yaʿtadhirūna bihi.

Wa-ruwiya anna al-ghurfa kānat takfī al-rajul li-shurbihi wa-idāwatihi, wa-l-alladhīna sharibū minhu iswaddat shifāhuhum wa-ghalabahumu al-ʿaṭash.

Jalut (Goliath) was a giant tyrant from the Amalekites, descended from the sons of ʿImlīq ibn ʿĀd, and his coat of mail weighed three hundred raṭl.

﴿And make firm our feet, and grant us what will make us steadfast in the slippery places of battle﴾: that is, the strength of hearts and the casting of terror into the heart of the enemy, and similar means.

Ayshā, the father of Dāwūd, was in the army of Ṭālūt with six of his sons, and Dāwūd was the seventh of them, a young boy tending sheep. Then it was revealed to Ishmawīl that Dāwūd ibn Ayshā was the one who would kill Jālūt, so he asked for him from his father. He came, and on his way he had passed three stones, each of which called to him to take it, saying: "You will kill Jālūt with us." So he put them in his pouch and threw them at Jālūt, and killed him. Ṭālūt then married him to his daughter. It is also related that [Ṭālūt] envied him and wished to kill him, but then repented.

﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾: he was given sovereignty over the blessed land in its eastern and western regions, and the Children of Israel had never united under a single king before Dāwūd; ﴿and [Allah] taught him of what He willed﴾, such as the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds and beasts, and other things.

﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾: that is, were it not that Allah repels some people by others and restrains through them their corruption, the corrupters would prevail, the earth would be ruined, its benefits would cease and its interests would be disrupted, in tillage, in progeny, and in all that makes the earth flourish.

It is said: were it not that Allah grants victory to the Muslims over the disbelievers, the earth would be corrupted by the disbelievers' wrongdoing and the killing of the Muslims. Or, [the meaning is]: had He not repelled them by means of one another, disbelief would have spread, the wrath would have descended, and the people of the earth would have been utterly uprooted.

These are the signs of God, meaning the stories He has related: the account of the thousands who fled and were made to die and then were brought back to life, the installing of Talut (Saul) as king and his being shown to be so by the sign of the Ark (al-tabut) descending from heaven, and the overcoming of the tyrants at the hands of a youth. "In truth" means with certainty, a certainty that the People of the Book have no doubt about, because it is so in their scriptures. "And indeed you are among the messengers" means: in that you relate them without having learned them by reading any book or by hearing reports.

Those messengers: We have caused some of them to excel others. Among them are those whom Allah spoke to, and He raised some of them in rank.

This is a reference to the group of messengers whose stories were mentioned in the surah, or whose knowledge was established with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "We have caused some of them to excel others" because that required variation in their good deeds. "Among them are those whom Allah spoke to": among them is the one whom Allah favoured by speaking to him without an intermediary, and he is Musa (peace be upon him).

It is read "Kallama Allah" with the accusative (naṣb), and al-Yamani read "Kalama Allah" (from mukalama, "speaking with"). What confirms this is their saying "Kalim Allah," meaning one who speaks with Him. "And He raised some of them in rank": that is, among them is the one whom He raised above the rest of the prophets, so that, after their differing in excellence, he became superior to them by many degrees. The apparent meaning is that he intended Muhammad (ﷺ) [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The apparent meaning is that He intended Muhammad (peace be upon him)... etc." Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: I have included this passage from his words because of its beauty in wording and meaning, and seeking blessing by giving the Chosen One (peace be upon him) some of his due excellence. Al-Zamakhshari was right in his statement that the Prophet (peace be upon him) was given the lofty excellence above all that the prophets were given, upon all of them be blessings and peace. It is not as some people of our age say, about preferring the Prophet (peace be upon him) over every single one of the prophets individually. One should refrain from attributing that to him, for he is among the great scholars and pillars of the religion of Islam; the proper course is to attribute the error to those who transmitted it from him.]] because he is the one who was preferred over them, having been given signs that no one else was given, numbering in the many thousands of verses or more. Even if he had been given only the Qur'an, it would suffice as a unique excellence above all that the prophets were given, because it is the miracle that remains for the duration of time, unlike other miracles. In this vagueness there is an exaltation of his excellence and a raising of his station that is not hidden, for it contains a testimony that he is the knowledge that is not confused and the distinguished one who is not obscured. One says to a man, "Who did this?" and he replies, "One of you, or some of you," intending the one who is known and famous for such deeds; this is more majestic than explicitly naming him and more honouring to his companion. Al-Hutay'a was asked about the best poet of people, and he mentioned Zuhayr and al-Nabigha, then said: "If I wished, I would have mentioned the third," meaning himself. Had he said, "If I wished, I would have mentioned myself," he would not have exalted his matter.

It is also permissible that he intended Ibrahim, Muhammad, and others among the messengers of steadfast resolve (ulu al-'azm). From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): "We were in the mosque discussing the excellence of the prophets. We mentioned Nuh for the length of his worship, Ibrahim for his intimate friendship (khullah), Musa for Allah's speaking to him, and 'Isa for his being raised to heaven, and we said: The Messenger of Allah is superior to them; he was sent to all people, his past and future sins were forgiven, and he is the seal of the prophets." He (peace be upon him) entered and said, "What are you discussing?" We told him. He said, "It is not fitting for anyone to be better than Yahya ibn Zakariyya," and he mentioned that he never committed a sin nor even intended one [[Narrated by Ishaq ibn Rahawayh: Abu 'Asim al-'Abbadi informed us, from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, from him. Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Asim al-'Abbadi. It is weak, and its narrator is unknown.]].

If you ask, "Why were Musa and 'Isa singled out from among the prophets for mention?" I answer: because of the great signs and the striking miracles they were given. Allah has explained the basis of the preference, since He made speaking (with Allah) a form of excellence, and it is one of the signs. When these two prophets were given such great signs, they were singled out for mention in the context of preference. This is clear evidence that whoever is given more preference through signs among them has been preferred over others. Since our Prophet (peace be upon him) was given signs that no one else was given, in both quantity and greatness, he is the one acknowledged, undisputed, as having taken the prize of excellence. O Allah, grant us his intercession on the Day of Judgment.

"And if Allah had willed" a willing of compulsion and coercion [[His words "a willing of compulsion and coercion" mean that He willed non-fighting, but not a willing of coercion, which is why what was willed did not occur. This is the position of the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, there is no will whose object fails to occur; rather, whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur, as explained in its proper place. (ʿA)]], "they would not have fought one another, those who came after the messengers, because of their disagreement in religion, the divergence of their paths, and their declaring one another to be unbelievers. But they differed: some of them believed, by adhering to the religion of the prophets, and some of them disbelieved, by turning away from it. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought; He repeated it for emphasis [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "He repeated 'and if Allah had willed' for emphasis." Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Beyond emphasis there is a more specific secret, namely that when the Arabs build the beginning of their speech on one purpose, then another purpose intervenes and they wish to return to the first, they intend to mention it either with that same expression or something close to it. This is among them an accepted path of eloquence and a well-trodden way. My maternal grandfather Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Faris, the jurist and vizier, used to count in the Book of Allah several instances of this meaning, among them the verse: "Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief..." and among them the verse: "Were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur from them a hurt without knowledge..." up to His words "Had they been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved." This verse is of this pattern: the speech began by stating that their fighting was in accordance with the will, then the speech lengthened, or it was intended to explain that Allah's will, as it takes effect in this particular matter—the fighting of these people—so it takes effect in every act that occurs. This is the meaning expressed in His words "But Allah does what He wills." The mention of the will's relation to the fighting occurred, then the general relation of the will followed, to suit the speech and so that each is known in its proper form. This is a secret whose explanation opens the breast and eases the mind, and Allah is the granter of success. And what foothold can the Mu'tazila have against this? For it is a decisive circle cutting off their root, sufficient to refute their adherent and supporter. This is why al-Zamakhshari permitted it, since it is confined to his interpretation, and its firmness in textual evidence is among his stratagems and ruses.]] "But Allah does what He wills," of abandonment and protection.

"Spend of what We have provided you, before there comes a day in which there is no trade and no close friendship and no intercession." He intended obligatory spending, since the threat is connected to it. "Before there comes a day in which you cannot make up what you missed of spending, because there is no trade in it, so that you could buy what you spend, nor any close friendship, so that your friends would overlook it for you." According to the People of the Sunna, it may also be for lightening the punishment. (ʿA)]]. The Living, the Everlasting, to whom no path to extinction leads. [[On his words "The Living, the Everlasting, to whom no path to extinction leads, etc.": the Mu'tazilah shy away from affirming for God an existential attribute such as life that stands opposed to death, so they interpret "Living" as what he said. (ʿA)]] In the terminology of the theologians (mutakallimun, the scholars of kalam, speculative theology), it is that which can be known and can exercise power. Al-Qayyum is the One who constantly sustains the creation in its management and preservation. It has been read as al-qiyam and al-qayyim. Al-sinah is the languor that precedes sleep, called drowsiness (al-nuʿas). Ibn al-Raqqaʿ al-ʿAmili said:

*He is drowsy, sleep has overcome him, and languor has clouded in his eye, yet he is not asleep.* [[*Had it not been for shame, though my head has grown rough, with the whiteness of old age in it, I would have visited Umm al-Qasim.*

*As if between the women she had lent him her eyes, the blackest-eyed of the gazelle fawns of Jasim.*

*He is drowsy, sleep has overcome him, and languor has clouded in his eye, yet he is not asleep.*

These are by ʿAdi ibn al-Raqqaʿ, in amatory prelude (tashbib) to a eulogy of al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. It is also transmitted from al-Asmaʿi as belonging to Ahmad ibn al-Raqqaʿ. ʿAtha (yaʿtha) like saʿa (yasʿa), and ʿaatha (yaʿithu) like ʿasha (yaʿish): to go about in the manner of corruption. It is also narrated as ʿasa with a sin, meaning it appeared, spread and grew strong, so ʿasa here is a complete verb, not a defective one. Umm al-Qasim is the kunya of his beloved. "Between the women" means "apart from the women," and this is also narrated thus. "Ahwar" is the subject of "aʿaara," and al-hawar is the clearness of the whiteness and blackness of the eye. Al-jaʾadir is the plural of ju'dhar, the young of the gazelle. Jasim is a specific place. Wasnan is an adjective of ahwar. "Aqsadtu al-rajul" means: when you stab a man and do not miss his vital spot, that is, sleep struck him, and that is the languor and heedlessness that precede sleep. "Raniqa al-ma'" means it became turbid; tarannaqa means became turbid; and "raanaqahu" and "arnaqahu" mean he made it turbid. "Raniqa al-tair tarnīqan" means when the bird stands still in the air with its wings spread, intending to descend. The meaning, then, is: languor stood in his eye. It is also possible that the meaning is: languor clouded his eye, that is, made it turbid. "Fi" has been inserted because he made the eye a container for the clouding, and this suggests the comparison of the eye to water in extreme clarity. Al-sinah derives from wasan, so one says wasnan, and it is of the pattern of ʿidah. The cause of sleep is a wind that rises into the membranes of the brain; when it reaches the eye, the eye grows languid, and this is wasan. When it reaches the heart and settles there, perception by the senses ceases, and this is sleep. For this reason He negated sleep while affirming drowsiness.]]

That is, neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him. This is an emphasis on al-Qayyum, because whoever is subject to such a state cannot be sustaining.

From this is the hadith about Musa: he asked the angels, and this was among his people, in the manner of asking to see God: "Does our Lord sleep?" God revealed to them that they should wake Him three times and not let Him sleep. Then He said: "Take two bottles filled," and he took them. God cast sleep upon him, and he struck one against the other, and they broke. Then He revealed to him: "Tell these people: I hold up the heavens and the earth by My power; had sleep or drowsiness seized Me, they would both have ceased." [[I say: his words "and this was among his people, in the manner of asking to see God" are from the words of al-Zamakhshari, which he inserted into the report. ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated it in his tafsir from Maʿmar, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning God's words ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him﴾, that Musa asked the angels: "Does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sleep?" and he related the rest. It was also narrated by Abu Yaʿla, al-Tabari, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sifat, all through the chain of Ishaq ibn Abi Israʾil, from Hisham ibn Yusuf, from Umayyah ibn Sabal, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from ʿIkrimah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) relate from Musa (peace be upon him) that he said: "It occurred to Musa's mind: Does our Lord sleep? So He sent to him an angel who kept him awake, then gave him two bottles, one in each hand, and commanded him to guard them. He began to sleep, and his hands almost met, then he would wake and hold one back against the other, until he slept a sleep, and his hands struck together and the two bottles broke." He said: "Allah struck for him an example: if Allah were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not stay firm." Al-Bayhaqi narrated it as a statement of the Companion (mawquf) and said: "This is more likely." Al-Daraqutni said: "Al-Hakam alone transmitted it from ʿIkrimah and his mother, and Hisham transmitted it from Umayyah." Al-Khatib said: "Maʿmar narrated it from al-Hakam, from ʿIkrimah, as his own words, and did not mention Abu Hurayrah or the Prophet (ﷺ)." I say: the narration of ʿAbd al-Razzaq refutes him, but it is mawquf. Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-ʿIlal al-Mutanahiyah and said: "It seems that ʿIkrimah received it from the books of the People of the Book." He said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated in his Kitab al-Sunnah, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, that the Children of Israel said to Musa (peace be upon him): 'Does our Lord sleep?'" He said: "And this is the correct version."]] Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? This is a statement of His dominion and majesty, and that no one can speak on the Day of Resurrection except when permitted to speak, as in His words ﴿None shall speak except by the permission of the Most Merciful﴾. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, that is, what was before them and what will be after them. The pronoun refers to what is in the heavens and the earth, since among them are rational beings; or it refers to what is indicated by "who" (man dha), namely the angels and prophets. ﴿Of His knowledge﴾, that is, of His known things, ﴿except what He wills﴾, that is, except what He has willed to make known. Al-kursi is that upon which one sits, and it does not exceed the seat of the one sitting. Regarding His words ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ there are four interpretations. [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾, there are four interpretations, etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: his saying in the first interpretation that this is an imagery of greatness is bad manners in unrestricted expression and remote in its implication, for imagery is used only for falsehoods and for things that have no true reality. If what he said has a correct meaning, then he erred in expressing it with a misleading phrase that has no place in the legal etiquette, and similar expressions of his will come later, which etiquette requires one to avoid.]] The first is that His Kursi has not been too narrow for the heavens and the earth, because of its vastness and expanse; this is only a depiction of His greatness and an imagery, and there is no chair there, no sitting, and no one sitting, like His words ﴿They have not measured God with His true measure; the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾, without imagining a handful, folding, or a right hand; it is only an imagery of the greatness of His affair and a sensory illustration. Do you not see His words ﴿They have not measured God with His true measure﴾? The second: His knowledge is vast, and knowledge is called a kursi by naming it after its place, which is the kursi of the scholar. The third: His dominion is vast, named after its place, which is the kursi of rule. The fourth: it is narrated that He created a kursi that is before the Throne, beneath which are the heavens and the earth, and that it is, in relation to the Throne, like the smallest thing. It is narrated from al-Hasan that the Kursi is the Throne. ﴿And their preservation does not weary Him﴾, that is, it does not burden Him or make Him hard-pressed, the preservation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾, in dominion and power. If you say: how are the clauses of the Throne Verse arranged? [[He returned to his speech and said: "If you say: how are the clauses of the Throne Verse arranged, and why were they not joined with the conjunction 'wa'? I say: because they are all in the mode of explanation, and explanation is one with what is explained, so inserting a 'wa' between them, as the Arabs say, is like inserting something between the stick and its bark. The first is an explanation of His standing in the management of creation and His being the watcher over it, not heedless of it. The second is because He is the owner of His management. The third is because of the greatness of His majesty. The fourth is because of His encompassing the conditions of creation. The fifth is because of the vastness of His knowledge and its relation to all known things." Traditions have been transmitted concerning its excellence. Among them is his (ﷺ) saying: "This verse is not recited in a house but that the devils flee from it for thirty days, and no sorcerer or sorceress enters it for forty nights. O ʿAli, teach it to your children, your family, and your neighbours, for no verse greater than it has been revealed." From ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "I heard your Prophet on the pulpit steps say: 'Whoever recites the Throne Verse after every obligatory prayer, nothing will prevent him from entering Paradise except death; and none persists in it except a truthful one or a worshipper. Whoever recites it when he lies down on his bed, Allah will grant him security for himself, his neighbour, his neighbour's neighbour, and the houses around him.'" The Companions discussed the best of the Qur'an, and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said to them: "Where are you from the Throne Verse?" Then he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'O ʿAli, the lord of mankind is Adam, the lord of the Arabs is Muhammad, without boasting; the lord of the Persians is Salman, the lord of the Romans is Suhayb, the lord of the Abyssinians is Bilal, the lord of the mountains is Mount Sinai, the lord of days is Friday, the lord of speech is the Qur'an, the lord of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah, and the lord of al-Baqarah is the Throne Verse.'"]] I say: as Surat al-Ikhlas was preferred for what it comprises of God's unity, His exaltation, His glorification, and His supreme attributes, so this verse was preferred. [[Ahmad said: my grandfather, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: the Throne Verse comprises what no other verse comprises of the Names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for it contains seventeen places where the Name of Allah appears, explicit in some and implicit in others, and it appears to most counters as sixteen, except to a sharp-sighted observer with deep insight in extracting them. The first: Allah. The second: He (huwa). The third: al-Hayy. The fourth: al-Qayyum. The fifth: the pronoun in "la ta'khudhuhu." The sixth: the pronoun in "lahu." The seventh: the pronoun in "ʿindahu." The eighth: the pronoun in "illa bi-idhnihi." The ninth: the pronoun in "yaʿlamu." The tenth: the pronoun in "ʿilmihi." The eleventh: the pronoun in "shaʾa." The twelfth: the pronoun in "kursiyyuhu." The thirteenth: the pronoun in "wa la yaʾuduhu." The fourteenth: huwa. The fifteenth: al-ʿAli. The sixteenth: al-ʿAzim. These are the number of the manifest Names. As for the hidden one, it is the pronoun contained in the verbal noun in His words "ḥifẓuhuma," for it is a verbal noun annexed to its object, and the explicit pronoun is its object, and it necessarily has a subject, which is Allah; this appears when the verbal noun is unpacked, so one says: "wa la yaʾuduhu an yahfazahuma huwa" (and it does not burden Him that He preserve them). Shaykh Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi wished to increase this count when I told him what my grandfather, may Allah have mercy on him, said. He said: "It is possible to count the derived Names in the verse, each of them as two verses, because each derived name bears a pronoun by necessity of being derived, and that pronoun refers only to Allah, Exalted is He. As a manifest form it is a name, and it contains another concealed one. So the total on this reckoning is twenty-one names." I had proposed a subtle point against this increase, namely that a derived name does not bear a pronoun after becoming a proper name by designation, according to the more correct view. These attributes are all names of Allah, Exalted is He. Then, even if we assume that they bear pronouns after being named, by way of supposition, the derived name falls upon its described object only by virtue of bearing its pronoun. Do you not see that when you say "Zayd is generous" (karim), you find that "generous" falls on Zayd only because its pronoun is in it; even if you consider it in isolation, you do not find it restricted to Zayd, for you may apply it to every person described as generous. You find it restricted to Zayd only by its containing its pronoun. So the derived word is not independent in falling upon its described object except by joining the pronoun to it. It is therefore impossible to give it the ruling of independence from the pronoun while holding that it refers definitively to a specific referent. The aforementioned Shaykh was satisfied with this discussion, approved it, and Allah is the One who grants success in what is right.]] Those are the things mentioned about the Throne Verse, and they are sufficient. [[Ibn Aban]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 256:

Lā ikrāha fī al-dīn (﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾): that is, God has not ordained the matter of faith to be by compulsion and coercion, but by enablement (al-tamkīn) and choice (al-ikhtiyār). A similar statement is His, exalted be He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Then, would you compel the people until they become believers?﴾ That is, had He willed, He would have forced them to faith, but He did not do so, and He built the matter upon choice. ﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾: faith has been distinguished from disbelief by clear proofs. ﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-ṭāghūt﴾: whoever chooses disbelief in Satan or the idols, and belief in God. ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾: from a rope that is firm and secure, whose breaking (infiṣām) is guaranteed not to occur, that is, its being cut off. This is an illustration (tamthīl) of what is known through reflection, and of inference from what is observed and perceptible, so that the listener conceives of it as though he were looking at it with his own eye, and so his belief is firmly settled and he attains certainty concerning it. It has also been said: it is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, that is, do not compel one another in religion. Then some of them said: it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾. It was also said: it applies specifically to the People of the Book, because they secured themselves by paying the jizya (poll tax). It is narrated that there were two sons of an Ansari man from the Banu Salim ibn ʿAwf who had become Christians before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent. Then they came to Medina, and their father clung to them and said: "By God, I will not leave you until you become Muslims." They refused, so they brought their dispute to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Ansari said: "O Messenger of God, shall part of me enter the Fire while I look on?" So this was revealed, and he released them. [[Al-Wahidi reported it in his Asbab from the saying of Masruq, and likewise al-Baghawi. And al-Tabari has reported, from the narration of Abu Ishaq from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad from ʿIkrima or Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: It was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar from the Banu Salim ibn ʿAwf, called al-Husayn: he had two Christian sons, and he himself was a Muslim. He said: "O Messenger of God, should I not compel them?" So God, exalted be He, revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ ... the verse.]]

Allah is the Protector of those who believe: meaning, those who wished to believe, He shows them kindness until He brings them out, through His gentle favour and support, from disbelief into faith. And as for those who disbelieve: meaning, those who were resolute in disbelief, their affair is the opposite of that.

Or, Allah is the Protector of the believers: He brings them out of doubts in religion, should any arise for them, by guiding them to and enabling them to find the resolution of those doubts, until they come forth into the light of certainty. And as for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the devils, who bring them out of the light of the clear proofs that appear to them into the darkness of doubt and misgiving.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 258–259:

﴿Have you not considered?﴾ An expression of wonder at the disputation of Nimrod concerning Allah and his disbelief in Him. ﴿That Allah had given him the kingdom﴾ is connected to "disputed" (ḥājja), in two ways. [[Mahmud said: "That ātāhu (that He had given him) is connected to ḥājja (disputed), in two ways... etc." Aḥmad said: May Allah pardon him. The two ways are close in meaning, except that there is a grammatical (ṣinā'ī) difference between them: in the first he used the verbal noun as an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi), and in the second as an adverb of time (ẓarf).

Verbal nouns have indeed occurred as adverbs in expressions such as khufūq al-najm (the setting of the star) and muqaddam al-ḥājj (the arrival of the pilgrim), and similar things. His disputation occurred with this adverb because it contains the giving of kingship, which led him to insolence, or to placing the ingratitude in it in place of its thanks. These two meanings are exactly those mentioned in the first way, and therefore I pointed out that the difference between the two ways is grammatical, not semantic. And Allah is the one who grants success in understanding his words.]]

The first: he disputed because Allah had given him the kingdom, meaning that the giving of kingship made him insolent and bred pride and tyranny, so he disputed on account of that; or [[his saying "or" perhaps stands for "or in the sense that" (ʿ)]] he placed the disputation against his Lord in place of the thanks that was due from him for Allah having given him the kingdom. So it is as if the disputation was for that reason, as you say: "So-and-so opposed me because I did him a kindness," meaning that he reversed what should have been due from him by way of loyalty on account of the kindness. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾.

The second: he disputed at the time when Allah had given him the kingdom. If you say: how is it permissible for Allah to give the kingdom to an unbeliever? I say: there are two opinions on this. He gave him what he prevailed by and was empowered with, of wealth, servants and followers; but as for the domination and empowerment itself, no. And it has been said: He gave him kingship as a trial for His servants. [[Mahmud said: "If you say: how is it permissible for Allah to give the kingdom to an unbeliever? I say: that is on two ways. One: He gave him what he prevailed by and was empowered with, of wealth, servants and followers, but not the domination and empowerment. The second: that his kingship be a trial for His servants." Aḥmad said: The question, as it arises, is built on a corrupt premise, namely the belief that it is obligatory to observe what the Qadariyya imagine to be good or better for Allah, exalted is He, in His acts. All of this is among the principles of the Qadariyya which conclusive proof has uprooted, so they have no stability. As for the question being phrased as: "Why did Allah give him the kingdom while he is an unbeliever?" or "Did I not do such and such?", its answer is His unrestricted words: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned﴾, which the deaf and dumb would hear. And Allah is the guardian of success. (End of his words.) He said: the meaning of his saying "I give life and cause death" is: I pardon from killing and I kill. The objection was ready, but when Abraham, peace be upon him, heard his foolish answer, he did not dispute with him over it, but moved on to something on which he could not offer the like of that answer, to confound him at the very first. This is evidence for the permissibility of the disputant moving from one argument to another.]] Aḥmad said: Many scholars have maintained that what proceeded from the Friend (Abraham), upon him be blessings and peace, is not a transition from argument, but from example. As for the argument, it is his reasoning for the divinity of Allah by the reach of His power to what the power of a created being cannot reach. Then this has examples, among them the giving of life and causing death, and among them: bringing the sun from the east. And moving after the establishment of the argument and the laying down of the principle from one example to another example is not novel among the people of disputation. And Allah knows best.]] ﴿When Abraham said﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "disputed," or it is a substitute for "ātāhu" if "idh" is taken to mean "time." ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ He means: I pardon from killing and I kill. [[His saying "he means I pardon from killing" — in the Ṣiḥāḥ: "ʿafawtu ʿan dhanbihi" means I left him and did not punish him. And in it: "a'finī min al-khurūj maʿaka" meaning leave me from it. (ʿ)]] The objection was ready, but when Abraham heard his foolish answer, he did not dispute with him over it, but moved on to something on which the like of that answer could not be given, to confound him at the very first.

This is evidence for the permissibility of the disputant moving from one argument to another. It was read: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾, meaning: so Abraham overcame the unbeliever. Abū Ḥaywa read: "fabuhta," in the pattern of "qarib." And it has been said: this disputation was when he broke the idols, and Nimrod imprisoned him, then brought him out of the prison to burn him, and said to him: "Who is your Lord to whom you call?" He said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."

﴿Or like the one who passed by﴾ its meaning is: "Or have you not seen the like of the one who passed by..." [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is: or have you seen the like of the one who passed by... etc." Aḥmad said: In such a construction the verb of seeing is often omitted, as in his saying: "He said to her: 'Hurry, like today, sought and not seeking,'" meaning: "I have not seen like today," so the verb and the negative particle were omitted. The apparent reading of the verse is to take it in the first way, because its parallel exists. And Allah knows best.]] ﴿upon a town﴾ is elided because "Have you not considered" points to it, since both are an expression of wonder. It is permissible to take it according to meaning rather than wording, as if it were said: "Have you seen like the one who disputed with Abraham, or like the one who passed by a town?" The one who passed by was a disbeliever (in resurrection), and this is the apparent reading, since he is listed alongside Nimrod in one series, and because of the expression of improbability in "how will He give life." It has been said he was ʿUzayr or al-Khiḍr, wishing to witness the giving of life to the dead, to increase in insight, as Abraham had asked. His saying ﴿How will He give it life﴾ is an admission of inability to know the manner of giving life, and an exalting of the power of the one who gives life. The town: Jerusalem, when Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it. It has been said: it is the one from which thousands went out. ﴿And it was fallen upon its roofs﴾, its explanation comes later. ﴿A day or part of a day﴾ is based on conjecture.

It is narrated that he died in the forenoon and was raised after a hundred years before the sun set; so he said, before looking at the sun: "A day," then he turned and saw a remnant of the sun and said: "Or part of a day." And it is narrated that his food was figs and grapes, and his drink juice or milk; he found the figs and grapes as they were when plucked, and the drink unchanged. ﴿It has not changed﴾ meaning: it has not altered. The "hā'" is either original or the "hā' of pause." Its derivation is from "sana" (year) on both views, since its final radical is either hā' or wāw, because a thing changes with the passage of time. It has been said: its origin is "yatasannan," from "ḥama' masnūn" (malleable clay), and its nūn was changed into a letter of weakness, like "taqaḍḍā al-bāzī." It is permissible that the meaning of ﴿It has not changed﴾ is: the years that passed over it did not pass over it, meaning it remained as it was, as if he had not lingered a hundred years. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "Look at your food and this your drink, it has not changed." Ubayy read: "lam yasinhu," with the tā' assimilated into the sīn.

﴿And look at your donkey, how its bones were scattered and decayed﴾; he had a donkey which he had tied up. It is permissible that it means: look at it whole in its place, as you tied it, and that is among the greatest signs, that He let it live a hundred years without fodder or water, just as He preserved his food and drink from change. ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: We did that, meaning the reviving of him after death and the preservation of what was with him. It has been said: he came to his people riding his donkey and said: "I am ʿUzayr." They denied him, so he said: "Bring the Torah," and he began to recite it by heart rapidly while they looked in the book, and he did not miss a letter, so they said: "He is the son of Allah." No one had recited the Torah openly before ʿUzayr, so that was his being a sign. It has been said: he returned to his house and found his children old men while he was young; when he told them a story, they said: "A story of a hundred years."

﴿And look at the bones: how We raise them﴾, meaning: how We give them life. ʿAsim read... (The reading of al-Ḥasan: "nunshiruhā," from "nashara Allāh al-mawtā," meaning "ansharahum" so they rose. It was also read with the zāy, meaning: We move them and raise some of them to others, for assembling.)

The subject of ﴿it became clear﴾ is implied, its estimate being: "So when it became clear to him that Allah is powerful over all things, he said: 'I know that Allah is powerful over all things.'" The first is elided because the second points to it, as in their saying: "He struck me and I struck Zayd." It is permissible: "So when there became clear to him what had been unclear to him," meaning the matter of the giving of life to the dead. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "fa-lammā tubayyina lahu" in the passive. It was read: "qāla iʿlam" in the imperative form. ʿAbdullāh read: "qīla iʿlam" (it was said: know). If you say: if the passer-by was a disbeliever, how is it proper for Allah to speak to him? [[(His words continue) He said: "If you say: when the passer-by was a disbeliever..." Aḥmad said: This is a strange question, and the answer to it is stranger still. Who conceded to this questioner that Allah, exalted is He, may not speak to a disbeliever? Is this anything but speech without foundation?

Is not Iblis the head of disbelief and its source, and yet Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed...﴾ to the end of the verse, and He says to the disbelievers, while they are among its layers being tormented: ﴿Be driven into it, and do not speak to Me﴾. Moreover, the occurrence of this is certain, let alone its permissibility; the scholars interpret His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ as meaning He will not speak to them in a way that gladdens or benefits them. This is my objection to the question. As for the answer, I have already mentioned above its refutation, that this passer-by's faith, on the view that he was a disbeliever, occurred at the end of the story after the signs became clear to him. But Allah's speech is from the beginning of the story. I say: al-Zamakhshari has spared us the burden of this excess, question and answer alike. And Allah is the one sought for help.]] I say: the speech was after the resurrection, and at that time he was not a disbeliever.
