This is evidence for the permissibility of the disputant moving from one argument to another.]] Aḥmad said: Many scholars have maintained that what proceeded from the Friend (Abraham), upon him be blessings and peace, is not a transition from argument, but from example. As for the argument, it is his reasoning for the divinity of Allah by the reach of His power to what the power of a created being cannot reach. Then this has examples, among them the giving of life and causing death, and among them: bringing the sun from the east. And moving after the establishment of the argument and the laying down of the principle from one example to another example is not novel among the people of disputation. And Allah knows best.]] ﴿When Abraham said﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "disputed," or it is a substitute for "ātāhu" if "idh" is taken to mean "time." ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ He means: I pardon from killing and I kill. [[His saying "he means I pardon from killing" — in the Ṣiḥāḥ: "ʿafawtu ʿan dhanbihi" means I left him and did not punish him. And in it: "a'finī min al-khurūj maʿaka" meaning leave me from it. (ʿ)]] The objection was ready, but when Abraham heard his foolish answer, he did not dispute with him over it, but moved on to something on which the like of that answer could not be given, to confound him at the very first.

This is evidence for the permissibility of the disputant moving from one argument to another. It was read: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾, meaning: so Abraham overcame the unbeliever. Abū Ḥaywa read: "fabuhta," in the pattern of "qarib." And it has been said: this disputation was when he broke the idols, and Nimrod imprisoned him, then brought him out of the prison to burn him, and said to him: "Who is your Lord to whom you call?" He said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death."

﴿Or like the one who passed by﴾ its meaning is: "Or have you not seen the like of the one who passed by..." [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is: or have you seen the like of the one who passed by... etc." Aḥmad said: In such a construction the verb of seeing is often omitted, as in his saying: "He said to her: 'Hurry, like today, sought and not seeking,'" meaning: "I have not seen like today," so the verb and the negative particle were omitted. The apparent reading of the verse is to take it in the first way, because its parallel exists. And Allah knows best.]] ﴿upon a town﴾ is elided because "Have you not considered" points to it, since both are an expression of wonder. It is permissible to take it according to meaning rather than wording, as if it were said: "Have you seen like the one who disputed with Abraham, or like the one who passed by a town?" The one who passed by was a disbeliever (in resurrection), and this is the apparent reading, since he is listed alongside Nimrod in one series, and because of the expression of improbability in "how will He give life." It has been said he was ʿUzayr or al-Khiḍr, wishing to witness the giving of life to the dead, to increase in insight, as Abraham had asked. His saying ﴿How will He give it life﴾ is an admission of inability to know the manner of giving life, and an exalting of the power of the one who gives life. The town: Jerusalem, when Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it. It has been said: it is the one from which thousands went out. ﴿And it was fallen upon its roofs﴾, its explanation comes later. ﴿A day or part of a day﴾ is based on conjecture.

It is narrated that he died in the forenoon and was raised after a hundred years before the sun set; so he said, before looking at the sun: "A day," then he turned and saw a remnant of the sun and said: "Or part of a day." And it is narrated that his food was figs and grapes, and his drink juice or milk; he found the figs and grapes as they were when plucked, and the drink unchanged. ﴿It has not changed﴾ meaning: it has not altered. The "hā'" is either original or the "hā' of pause." Its derivation is from "sana" (year) on both views, since its final radical is either hā' or wāw, because a thing changes with the passage of time. It has been said: its origin is "yatasannan," from "ḥama' masnūn" (malleable clay), and its nūn was changed into a letter of weakness, like "taqaḍḍā al-bāzī." It is permissible that the meaning of ﴿It has not changed﴾ is: the years that passed over it did not pass over it, meaning it remained as it was, as if he had not lingered a hundred years. In the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "Look at your food and this your drink, it has not changed." Ubayy read: "lam yasinhu," with the tā' assimilated into the sīn.

﴿And look at your donkey, how its bones were scattered and decayed﴾; he had a donkey which he had tied up. It is permissible that it means: look at it whole in its place, as you tied it, and that is among the greatest signs, that He let it live a hundred years without fodder or water, just as He preserved his food and drink from change. ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: We did that, meaning the reviving of him after death and the preservation of what was with him. It has been said: he came to his people riding his donkey and said: "I am ʿUzayr." They denied him, so he said: "Bring the Torah," and he began to recite it by heart rapidly while they looked in the book, and he did not miss a letter, so they said: "He is the son of Allah." No one had recited the Torah openly before ʿUzayr, so that was his being a sign. It has been said: he returned to his house and found his children old men while he was young; when he told them a story, they said: "A story of a hundred years."

﴿And look at the bones: how We raise them﴾, meaning: how We give them life. ʿAsim read... (The reading of al-Ḥasan: "nunshiruhā," from "nashara Allāh al-mawtā," meaning "ansharahum" so they rose. It was also read with the zāy, meaning: We move them and raise some of them to others, for assembling.)

The subject of ﴿it became clear﴾ is implied, its estimate being: "So when it became clear to him that Allah is powerful over all things, he said: 'I know that Allah is powerful over all things.'" The first is elided because the second points to it, as in their saying: "He struck me and I struck Zayd." It is permissible: "So when there became clear to him what had been unclear to him," meaning the matter of the giving of life to the dead. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read: "fa-lammā tubayyina lahu" in the passive. It was read: "qāla iʿlam" in the imperative form. ʿAbdullāh read: "qīla iʿlam" (it was said: know). If you say: if the passer-by was a disbeliever, how is it proper for Allah to speak to him? [[(His words continue) He said: "If you say: when the passer-by was a disbeliever..." Aḥmad said: This is a strange question, and the answer to it is stranger still. Who conceded to this questioner that Allah, exalted is He, may not speak to a disbeliever? Is this anything but speech without foundation?

Is not Iblis the head of disbelief and its source, and yet Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed...﴾ to the end of the verse, and He says to the disbelievers, while they are among its layers being tormented: ﴿Be driven into it, and do not speak to Me﴾. Moreover, the occurrence of this is certain, let alone its permissibility; the scholars interpret His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ as meaning He will not speak to them in a way that gladdens or benefits them. This is my objection to the question. As for the answer, I have already mentioned above its refutation, that this passer-by's faith, on the view that he was a disbeliever, occurred at the end of the story after the signs became clear to him. But Allah's speech is from the beginning of the story. I say: al-Zamakhshari has spared us the burden of this excess, question and answer alike. And Allah is the one sought for help.]] I say: the speech was after the resurrection, and at that time he was not a disbeliever.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 260:**

أَرِنِي (*arini*), meaning "show me," here glossed as "make me see" (*baṣṣirni*). Now, if you ask: how did He say to him ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ when He knew that he was the most firmly believing of people?

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how did He say to him ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ when He knew ... etc."? Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The best approach to this verse is to mention in it the chosen interpretation from the *Mumtahina* (the *Mumtahana* surah), with the liberated thought and the clarifying insights of an intoxicated opinion. Whatever agrees with the author's words is from the praise of Allah, and whatever contradicts them, the truth is what we have stated. And Allah is the Granter of success.

So we say: As for the Friend's (Khalil's) question, peace be upon him, when he said to Him ﴿How will You give life to the dead?﴾, it was not out of doubt, God forbid, regarding Allah's power to give life. Rather, it was a question about the *how* of giving life. Faith does not require a complete grasp of its form, since this is only a request for knowledge on which faith does not depend. This is shown by the question being phrased with *kayfa* ("how"), whose function is to ask about a state. A parallel: someone says, "How does Zayd judge among the people?" He does not doubt that Zayd judges among them, but he asks about the manner of his judgment, not whether it happens.

If the imagination were to play with some thoughts, a doubt from this verse might reach Ibrahim. But the Prophet (ﷺ) cut off the root of this suspicion by saying: "We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim," meaning: we did not doubt, so Ibrahim not doubting is more fitting and more apt. If you say: if the question is directed to the *how*, which the inability to conceive or witness it does not harm faith or undermine it, then what is the place of His saying ﴿Have you not believed?﴾? I say: one of the skilled scholars has reached a subtle point on this, namely that this phrasing is outwardly used to ask about the manner, as already explained, but it may also be used to express incapacity. An example: a claimant says he can carry a certain heavy load, and you are certain of his inability to carry it, so you say to him: "Show me how you will carry this." Since this phrasing may take on this usage, and Allah, exalted is He, knew that Ibrahim was free of it, He intended by His words ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ that Ibrahim should say, "Yes, I have believed," to remove that verbal possibility in the first expression, so that his faith would be sincere, affirmed with a phrase that everyone who hears it understands without any doubt reaching it. If you say: the connection between the speech under the stated assumption has become clear to me, so what is the place of Ibrahim's saying ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾, which outwardly indicates that at the time of the question he lacked tranquility? I say: its meaning is: "but that the thought about the *how* of life may leave my heart, for when I witness it my heart will settle from wandering among its imagined forms, and it will be fixed in my mind through the witnessed depiction. The verse will then match his question, because he witnessed the image of the life of the dead. Its estimation: 'He who gives life and causes death.' This is the best that comes to me in interpreting this verse, and your Lord is the Opener, the All-Knowing."

As for al-Zamakhshari's saying: "Inferential knowledge is open to doubt, unlike necessary knowledge," this is a statement that did not proceed from an illuminating opinion or a liberated thought. That is because knowledge that is held by a cause cannot be conceived as subject to doubt, so long as its cause is present in the mind of the knower. What accepts doubt absolutely is belief (*i'tiqad*), even if it is correct, and its cause remains in mind. Through this, correct belief falls short of the summit of knowledge. But the earlier Qadariyya (the early determinist-theologians) had a long confusion in distinguishing knowledge from belief, to the point that Abu Hashim went to extremes and said: knowledge of a thing and ignorance of it are two equivalents. In truth this is ignorance even of the reality of ignorance. Al-Zamakhshari in his principles of doctrine follows the traces of this speaker wherever he goes, so perhaps from this he came to think that theoretical knowledge is open to doubt, as belief is open to it, since belief is sometimes ignorance and sometimes correct. And Allah is the Granter of success.]]

?I say: He commanded him to answer as he answered, because of the great benefit in it for the listeners. *Balā* (بلى) is an affirmation after a negation. Its meaning: "Yes, I have believed, but that my heart may be at rest," that is, that it may increase in tranquility and settledness by combining necessary knowledge with inferential knowledge. The coming together of proofs is more calming for hearts and more increasing for insight and certainty. Also, because inferential knowledge admits doubt, unlike necessary knowledge, by "the tranquility of the heart" he meant the knowledge in which there is no room for doubt.

If you ask: to what is the *lam* in ﴿li-yaṭma'inna﴾ (لِيَطْمَئِنَّ) attached? I say: it is attached to an omitted element, its estimate being: "But I asked for that, desiring the tranquility of the heart." ﴿Take four birds﴾: it was said they were a peacock, a rooster, a crow and a dove. ﴿Then make them incline toward you﴾: *ṣurhunna* (فَصُرْهُنَّ) is read with the *ṣād* either dammed or kasra-ed, meaning: gather them and draw them to you. The poet said:

*"But the points of spears incline them (taṣūruhā)"*

[[And the catching of necks among them is not by nature, / but the points of spears incline them." *Al-ṣayr* (الصير), with vowel, means the bending of the neck. It is said *ṣāra yaṣūru* and *yaṣīru*, meaning to incline or to cut off. That is: the inclining of necks is not their natural disposition, but the points of spears, because of their great number above their heads, incline their necks. The attributing of the inclining to the points is a rational metaphor (*majāz 'aqlī*) from attributing to the cause. It is also permissible that "among them" is a state (*ḥāl*) of the hunted, not of *jibla*, meaning: in the state of its being among them.]]

And he said:

*"And a branch that inclines the neck, dense and black, / as if on the nape are the clusters of the laden vines."*

[[*Ṣārahu yuṣīruhu* and *yuṣūruhu*: when he inclined it or cut it. It is narrated: "adorns the neck." *Al-jīd*: the neck. *Al-waḥf*: the dense black. *Al-layt*: the side of the neck. *Al-dawāliḥ*: those weighed down with load. He describes the hair of his beloved, that it inclines her neck because of its weight upon her, and he likened her locks on the side of her neck to clusters of laden vines.]]

And Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read *faṣurrahunna* with the *ṣād* dammed or kasra-ed and the *rā'* doubled, from *ṣarrahu yaṣurruhu* and *yaṣirruhu* meaning to gather it, like *ḍarrahu*, *yaḍurruhu* and *yaḍirruhu*. And from him also: *faṣurhunna*, from *al-taṣriya*, which is also gathering. ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾: meaning: divide them into parts and spread their parts over the mountains. The meaning: on every mountain of the mountains that are in your presence and in your land. It was said: there were four mountains. From al-Suddi: seven. ﴿Then call them﴾ and say to them: "Come by Allah's permission," ﴿they will come to you in haste﴾: hastening, swiftly, in their flight or in their walking on their feet. If you say: what is the meaning of His command to gather them to himself after taking them? I say:

so that he may contemplate them and know their forms, their shapes and their features [[His words "their shapes and their features": plural of *ḥilya* (with kasra), meaning their attributes. This is stated in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. (ʿ)]], lest they be confused for him after the revival, and he not imagine that they were other than those. For this reason He said: ﴿they will come to you in haste﴾. It is narrated that he was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, cut them up, separate their parts, mix their feathers, blood and flesh, and hold their heads. Then he was commanded to place their parts on the mountains, on every mountain a quarter of each bird. Then he would call to them: "Come by Allah's permission." So each part would fly to the other until they became bodies, and then they came and joined themselves to their heads, each body to its head.

It is also read *juz'a* with two damma-s, and *juzzā* with doubling. Its basis is that the hamza was dropped and then the consonant was doubled, as is done in pausal pronunciation, treating the continuous speech as if it were pause.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 261:

﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ There must be an omitted noun (mudaf mahdhuf), i.e., "the likeness of their spending is like a grain," or "their likeness is like the sower of a grain." The one who causes it to grow is Allah, but since the grain was the means, the growing is attributed to it, just as it is attributed to the earth and to the water. The meaning of its growing into seven ears is that it sends up a stalk from which seven branches diverge, each bearing one ear. This similitude is a depiction of multiplication, as if it were standing right before the eyes of the beholder. If you say: how is this comparison valid when the thing compared with is not existent? I say: rather, it exists in millet, sorghum and other grains, and the stalk of wheat sometimes sprouts in strong, fertile soil so that its grain reaches this extent. And even if it did not exist, it would be correct as a supposition and assumption. If you say: why was it not said "seven spikes" (sunbulat), in accordance with its proper form of distinction using the plural of paucity, as He said: ﴿وَسَبْعَ سُنْبُلاتٍ خُضْرٍ﴾ ("and seven green ears")? I say: this is because of what I mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿ثَلاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾ ("three periods"), namely that the forms of the plural alternate in their positions. ﴿وَاللَّهُ يُضاعِفُ لِمَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ ("And Allah multiplies for whom He wills"): that is, He multiplies in that manner for whom He wills, not for every spender, due to the differing states of the spenders. Or He multiplies the seven hundred and adds to it multiples of it for whoever deserves that.

Al-mann (reproach, or reminding the recipient of one's favour) is when a person considers himself superior to the one he has benefited with his kindness, and means that he has bestowed a favour upon him and imposed on him a right owed to himself. They used to say: "If you do a favour, forget it." And one of them said:

*"Verily, a man who conferred a favour upon me and reminded me of it once is base."*

[[He says: if a man gave me a gift and reminded me of it once, he is base, meaning extremely lowly in baseness and meanness.]]

In Nawabigh al-Kalim (a collection of striking sayings): *sinwan* [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "In Nawabigh al-Kalim: sinwan..." Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: "Thumma" (then), in its original usage, indicates that the element it introduces is separated in time from what precedes it and that the gap between them is considerable. Al-Zamakhshari interprets it as indicating a difference in rank and a distance between the two, since he cannot interpret it as temporal delay because the context in a verse like this one rejects that. The summary is that it has been borrowed from the distance of times to express the distance of rank. In my view there is another possibility that is admissible in this verse and similar ones: that it indicates the continuation of the action it introduces and the prolongation of its persistence. On this reading, it has not departed from the indication of temporal distance, but its original meaning is the delay in the time of the act's occurrence and its coming into being, while its extended meaning is the continuance of the act's existence and the delay in the time of its duration. On this basis is interpreted the words of God Most High, ﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾, meaning they persisted in steadfastness in a lasting manner with an extended duration. That steadfastness is the one that counts, not what is cut off by its opposite, such as deviation towards desire and appetites. Likewise His words, ﴿Then they do not follow what they spent with reproach or injury﴾, meaning they persist in forgetting the kindness and in not regarding it or boasting of it, and they do not abandon this forgetting for periods of time in order to harm and repeat reproach because of it, and then repent. And God knows best. Close to this, or similar to it, is that the sin (the particle *sa-*) accompanies the verb to extend the time of its occurrence and delay it. Then God Most High's words are reported about the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾. And God Most High has related in a similar verse, ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾. So there is no way to interpret the *sin* as indicating a delay in the time of his receiving guidance; therefore it must be understood as expressing the continuance of the guidance he had received, the persistence of its remaining, and the prolongation of its duration. Perhaps al-Zamakhshari also alluded to this meaning in the verse about Abraham, peace be upon him. This interpretation is preferable to what al-Zamakhshari applied to the verse of al-Baqarah. This verse keeps closer to the literal meaning and is nearer to the original usage in the best manner. And God is the Granter of success.]] *from the one who gives to his petitioner and reproaches, and from the one who withholds his gift and is stingy.* And in it: *The taste of blessings [[His words "and in it, the taste of blessings": In al-Sihah: al-ala' means blessings, its singular being ala with a fatha. Also in it: al-ala' (with a fatha) is a tree of pleasant appearance and bitter taste. The name for blessings is on the pattern of asbab. It seems that the name of the tree is on the pattern of sahab, so what is in Nawabigh should be verified. (ʿ)]] is sweeter than reproach, and it is more bitter than blessings together with reproach.* Al-adha (injury) is that he boasts over him because of what he has given him.

The meaning of "then" (thumma) is to show the gap between spending and abandoning reproach and injury, and that abandoning them is better than the spending itself, just as the steadfastness in faith has been made better than entering into it by His words, ﴿then they remained steadfast﴾.

If you ask: what is the difference between His words ﴿لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ﴾ [they have their reward] and His words later on, ﴿لَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ﴾ [they have their reward]? I answer: the relative clause (al-mawsul) here has not been given the meaning of a condition, whereas it has been given that meaning there. The difference between them in meaning is that the *fa'* (then) in the latter indicates that it was by the spending that they deserved the reward, whereas its omission is free of that indication.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 263–264:

﴿Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.﴾ A kind response (radd jamil) and forgiveness, pardoning the petitioner when he has done something that burdens the one asked; or it may mean obtaining forgiveness from Allah through the kind refusal, or pardon on the part of the petitioner, for if the one asked refuses him kindly, the petitioner excuses him. ﴿Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.﴾ The predicate is indefinite (nakirah) yet the statement is valid because it is specified by the descriptive phrase that follows. ﴿And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ He has no need of a spender who reminds of his favour and causes injury. ﴿Forbearing﴾ means He does not hasten to punish; this is a sign of His displeasure and a warning to the one who does so. Then He intensified this with what follows: ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ That is: do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like the nullification of the hypocrite who spends his wealth ﴿to be seen by people﴾, not intending by his spending the pleasure of Allah nor the reward of the Hereafter. ﴿So his example is like the example of a smooth rock﴾: his likeness and the fruitlessness of his spending, which yields no benefit at all, is like a smooth rock (safwan) with a layer of dust on it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib read it as ṣafwān, on the pattern of kurawān. ﴿Upon which heavy rain falls and leaves it bare﴾: heavy rain of great drops, which leaves it ﴿ṣaldan﴾, bare and clean of the dust that was on it. From this comes ṣalad, the smooth forehead of a bald man when it shines. ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned.﴾ Like His saying: ﴿And We made it scattered dust﴾. It is also permissible for the kaf (like) to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, do not nullify your charities while resembling the one who spends. If you ask: how does He say ﴿they have no power﴾ after ﴿like the one who spends﴾? I say: by "the one who spends" He means the category or the group that spends, and because "man" and "alladhi" are interchangeable, it is as if it were said: like those who spend.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 265:

﴿وَتَثْبِيتًا مِنْ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ — and for the firming (tathbit) of their own souls. Or: that they may firm themselves by spending wealth, which is the twin of the soul. Spending it is the hardest thing for the self, harder than the other burdensome acts of worship and harder than faith itself, because when the self is trained by pressing upon it and imposing on it what is difficult for it, it becomes humbled and submissive to its owner, and its appetite for following its desires diminishes; and the reverse is also true. Thus spending wealth is a firming of the self upon faith and certainty. It is also permissible that the meaning be: and as a confirmation of Islam, and a verification of the reward, from the very root of their souls, because when a Muslim spends his wealth in the way of God, he knows that his assent and his faith in the reward come from the root of his self and from the sincerity of his heart. The "min" (مِنْ, "from") in the first interpretation is partitive (lil-tab'id), like it is in their saying: "he shook from his bending" (هز من عطفه) and "he stirred from his vigor" (وحرك من نشاطه). In the second interpretation it denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿حَسَدًا مِنْ عِنْدِ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ — out of envy from their own selves. It may also be that the meaning is: and a firming from their souls in the eyes of the believers, that they are truthful in faith and sincere in it. The reading of Mujahid supports this: "wa-tabyinan min anfusihim" (and a clarifying from their souls). If you ask: what is the meaning of the partitive? I say: its meaning is that whoever spends his wealth for the face of God has firmed part of his self, and whoever spends his wealth and his soul together is the one who has firmed it entirely, ﴿وَتُجَاهِدُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ بِأَمْوَالِكُمْ وَأَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ — and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your souls.

The meaning: ﴿وَمَثَلُ نَفَقَةِ هَؤُلَاءِ فِي زَكَاتِهَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍ﴾ — the likeness of the spending of these people, in its growth before God, is like the likeness of a garden, and it is the orchard, ﴿بِرَبْوَةٍ﴾ on a raised place. He specified it because the trees in it are purer and better in fruit. ﴿أَصَابَهَا وَابِلٌ﴾ — a heavy rain struck it, great in its drops, ﴿فَآتَتْ أُكُلَهَا﴾ — so it yielded its produce, its fruit, ﴿ضِعْفَيْنِ﴾ — double, ﴿مِثْلَيْ مَا كَانَتْ تُثْمِرُ﴾ — twice what it used to bear, by reason of the heavy rain. ﴿فَإِنْ لَمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ﴾ — and if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light dew, a small-dropped rain, ﴿يَكْفِيهَا﴾ suffices it, because of the generosity of its ground. Or: the likeness of their state before God is the garden on the height, and their spending, much or little, is the heavy rain and the dew. And just as each of the two rains doubles the produce of the garden, so their spending, whether much or little, after it is sought for the face of God and they exert their utmost effort in it, is pure before God and increases their nearness to Him and the goodness of their standing with Him.

It has been read: "ka-mathali habbatin" (like the likeness of a grain), and "bi-rabwatin" with all three vowel-forms, and "ukulaha" with two dammas.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 266:

The hamza in ﴿أَيَوَدُّ﴾ (ayawaddu, "does one of you wish") is for denunciation (inkar). It has also been read as ﴿له جنات﴾ (lahu jannat, "for him are gardens") and ﴿ذرية ضعاف﴾ (dhurriyyatun ḍi'af, "offspring who are weak"). Al-I'sar (the whirlwind) is the wind that spins around the earth and then rises toward the sky like a column. This is a parable for one who does good deeds but does not seek thereby the Face of Allah. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he finds them nullified (muhbata), and so he is seized by a regret like the regret of one who had a garden, among the most splendid of gardens and the most complete in fruits, and then reached old age while he had weak offspring, and the garden was their livelihood and means of sustenance; then it was destroyed by a thunderbolt. It is narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked the Companions about it, and they said, "Allah knows best." He became angry and said, "Say 'we know' or 'we do not know'!" Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, "Within myself there is something about it, O Commander of the Faithful." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari from the hadith of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr: that ʿUmar asked ... and he mentioned it.]] He said, "Speak, my nephew, and do not belittle yourself." He said, "I have struck it as a parable for a deed." He said, "For what deed?" He said, "For a wealthy man who does good deeds, then Allah sends Satan to him, and he commits acts of disobedience until he drowns (aghraqa) all his deeds." [[The phrase "aghraqa a'malahu kullaha" (drowned all his deeds) is in some copies of al-Jalal: "ahraqa" (burned), with the ḥāʾ, and so is the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]] It is also narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "This is a parable, by Allah, few among people understand it: an old man whose body has grown weak and whose children have multiplied, and who is most in need of his garden, and by Allah, one of you is most in need of his deeds when the world has cut itself off from him." Now if you ask: how did He say ﴿جَنَّةٌ مِنْ نَخِيلٍ وَأَعْنابٍ﴾ (a garden of palm trees and grapevines) and then say ﴿لَهُ فِيها مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَراتِ﴾ (for him in it are of all the fruits)? [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say: why did He mention the palm trees and grapevines first ... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is from the category of repeating the mention of what is given attention twice, generally and then specifically, and similar to it is ﴿فِيهِما فاكِهَةٌ وَنَخْلٌ وَرُمَّانٌ﴾ (in them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates), except that in that verse He began with the general and in this verse He began with the specific; and the intended purpose is what we have pointed out, and Allah knows best.]] I say: since the palm trees and grapevines were the noblest of trees and the most abundant in benefits, He singled them out for mention and made the garden of them, even though it contains all other trees, by giving them precedence over others; then He followed them with the mention of all the fruits. It is also permissible that by "the fruits" He means the benefits that would accrue to him from it, as in His saying ﴿وَكانَ لَهُ ثَمَرٌ﴾ (and he had fruit) after His saying ﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ مِنْ أَعْنابٍ وَحَفَفْناهُما بِنَخْلٍ﴾ (two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with palm trees). Now if you ask: upon what is the phrase ﴿وَأَصابَهُ الْكِبَرُ﴾ (and old age had afflicted him) conjoined? I say: the "wa" is for the circumstantial clause (hal), not for conjunction. Its meaning is that he has a garden while old age has afflicted him. It has also been said that one says "wadadtu an yakuna kadhā" (I wished that it were so) and "wadadtu law kana kadhā" (I wished that if it were so), so the conjunction was carried over to the sense, as if it were said: "Does one of you wish that he had a garden and old age had afflicted him?"

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿مِنْ طَيِّبَاتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ﴾ means: from the good things of what you have earned, that is, from the finest of what you have acquired, "وَمِمَّا أَخْرَجْنَا لَكُمْ" means: and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth, namely grain, fruit, minerals and other things.

If you ask: why was it not said "وَمَا أَخْرَجْنَا لَكُمْ" (and what We have brought forth for you), coordinated with "مَا كَسَبْتُمْ", so that the good things would include both what is acquired and what is brought forth from the earth? I say: its meaning is "and from the good things of what We have brought forth for you," but the phrase has been elided because the good things have been mentioned (i.e., the word "طيبات" governs both clauses).

﴿وَلَا تَيَمَّمُوا الْخَبِيثَ﴾ means: do not aim at or intend the bad wealth, the inferior property, ﴿مِنْهُ تُنْفِقُونَ﴾ (that you spend from it), you single it out for spending. The phrase ﴿مِنْهُ تُنْفِقُونَ﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

ʿAbdullah (ibn Masʿud) read: "وَلَا تَأَمُّوا" (wa-lā ta'ammū). Ibn ʿAbbas read: "وَلَا تَيَمَّمُوا" with the letter tāʾ vowelled with a ḍamma. "يممه" and "تيممه" and "تأممه" are the same in meaning: they mean "قصده" (he intended it).

﴿وَلَسْتُمْ بِآخِذِيهِ﴾ means: while you yourselves would not take it, ﴿إِلَّا أَنْ تُغْمِضُوا فِيهِ﴾ except by being lenient in taking it and accepting it with indulgence. This is from your saying: "أغمض فلان عن بعض حقه" (so-and-so overlooked part of his right), when he lowered his gaze. It is said of a seller: "أغمض" (he overlooked), meaning he does not scrutinize, as if he does not see.

al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:

"لَمْ يَفُتْنَا بِالْوِتْرِ قَوْمٌ وَلِلضَّيْمِ رِجَالٌ يَرْضَوْنَ بِالإِغْمَاضِ"

[Footnote in the original: his saying "لم يفتنا بالوتر قوم": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-mawtūr" is the one whose slain kinsman was killed and he did not obtain retribution for his blood. One says from it: "وتره وتراً وترة". Likewise "وتره حقه" means he diminished his right. (ʿ)]

[Footnote in the original: The "bāʾ" in "بالإغماض" is for accompaniment or means "with". "al-Witr" (with kasra) is injustice and diminishment of part of a right, and "al-tirra" is similar. The verb is "وتر" like "وعد". "al-ḍaym" is injustice, and "al-ighmāḍ" is leaving part of a right and turning away from it, as if one does not see it. He says: no people have preceded us in taking our due by wronging us and gaining the upper hand over us; and "وللضيم رجال" is a new independent clause, meaning that we do not turn away from our rights as others do, out of our courage over them; or it is a circumstantial clause, meaning that while there are people who, out of their weakness, accept leaving their rights, the matter returns to the first sense.]

al-Zuhri read: "تُغْمِضُوا" (tughmiḍū). "أغمض" and "غمض" have the same meaning. From him also: "تُغَمِّضُوا" with the letter mīm vowelled with ḍamma and with kasra, from "غمض يغمض" and "غمض يغمض". Qatada read: "تُغْمَضُوا" in the passive form, meaning: unless you enter into it and are drawn towards it. It was also said: unless you are found with your eyes closed.

From al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him): "If you found it being sold in the market, you would not take it until a part of its price was reduced for you."

From Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "They used to give in charity the dried-up and worthless dates, so they were forbidden from that."

Satan promises you poverty in spending, and tells you that the outcome of your spending will be that you become poor. It was also read: "al-fuqr" (with a damma on the faa). "Al-faqr" with both letters vowelled with a fatha is also read, and "al-wa'd" (the promise) is used for both good and evil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Fire, Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾. "And he commands you to indecency" means he incites you and urges you toward stinginess and withholding charity, the urging of one who commands the one commanded.

In the speech of the Arabs, "al-fahish" means the stingy person. [[Regarding his saying "al-fahish 'inda al-'Arab al-bakhil" (the fahish, in the usage of the Arabs, is the stingy one), he said:

I see death taking the generous and choosing / the noblest of the wealth of the stingy, the stern one (Ibn ʿAbbas?)]] Allah promises you, in spending, forgiveness from Him for your sins and an expiation for them, and bounty, and that He will replace for you something better than what you spent, or a reward for it in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 269:

"He gives wisdom (al-hikmah)" means: He grants success in knowledge and in acting upon it. And the wise person (al-hakim) in the sight of Allah is the one who is knowledgeable and acts upon his knowledge. It has been recited as "and whoever is given (wa-man yu'ta) the wisdom," meaning: and whoever Allah gives the wisdom. Al-A'mash also recited it this way. And "much good" (khayran kathiran) is indefinite for the sake of magnification, as if He had said: then he has been given a great good of some kind. "And none remember except the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)," meaning the wise, the knowledgeable, and those who act. The purpose of this is to urge acting upon what the verses contain concerning spending (al-infaq).

Whatever you spend of expenditure in the way of Allah, or in the way of Satan, or whatever vow you vow in obedience to Allah, or in disobedience to Him, ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, nothing is hidden from Him, and He will recompense you for it. ﴿And the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾: those who withhold the charities, or spend their wealth in sins, or do not fulfill their vows, or vow in sins, will have no one to help them from Allah, to protect them from His punishment.

"Mā" in (ni'ammā) is an indefinite noun that is neither a relative pronoun nor a descriptive qualifier. The meaning of fa-ni'immā hiya is: how excellent is their giving (fa-ni'ma shay'an ibdā'uhā). It is read with the nūn both kasra and fatha (wa-quriʾa bi-kasr al-nūn wa-fathihā).

Wa-in tukhfūhā wa-tu'tūhā al-fuqarā' (and if you conceal them and give them to the poor), and you reach their proper recipients while concealing them: fa-huwa khayrun lakum (then it is better for you), concealment is better for you.

What is meant is voluntary charity (al-ṣadaqāt al-mutaṭawwa' bihā), for the better course in obligatory charity (al-farā'id) is to make it public (yujāhar bihā). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Secret voluntary charity is better than its public form by seventy times, and public obligatory charity is better than its secret form by twenty-five times" [[Narrated by al-Ṭabarī from the narration of Ibn 'Abbās, who said: "Allah made secret voluntary charity better than its public form by seventy times, and made public obligatory charity better than its secret form by twenty-five times, and likewise all obligations and supererogatory acts in all things."]]. The reason that public declaration is better for obligatory charity is to remove suspicion (li-nafy al-tuhma), so that if the giver is one not known for wealth, concealing it is better, while for the voluntary giver, if he wishes to be emulated, showing it is better.

Yukaffiru (and He will expiate): it is read with a nūn in the nominative (marfū'an), as coordination with the position of what follows the fā' (ʿaṭfan ʿalā maḥall mā baʿd al-fā'), or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and We expiate" (ay wa-naḥnu nukaffiru); or as a nominative verbal clause beginning a new sentence. It is also read in the jussive (majzūman) as coordination with the position of the fā' and what follows it, since it is the answer of the conditional. It is read as wa-yukaffiru with a yā' in the nominative, the verb being attributed to Allah or to the concealment. It is read as wa-tukaffiru with a tā', both nominative and jussive, the verb being attributed to the charities. Al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with him, read it with a yā' and in the accusative by implying "an" (bi-iḍmār an). Its meaning: "If you conceal them, it will be better for you, and that He expiate from you."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 272:

It is not incumbent upon you to make them guided [[Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is not incumbent upon you to make them guided..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may God have mercy on him, said: The correct belief is that God is the One who creates guidance for whomever He wills to guide, and that is divine grace (al-lutf), not as al-Zamakhshari claims, that guidance is not God's creation and that the servant creates it for himself. Even if God Most High attributes guidance to Himself, as in this verse, it is interpreted, according to al-Zamakhshari's view, as God's grace impelling the servant to create his own guidance. This is nothing but fabrication. This deviation is a consequence of their corrupt belief concerning the creation of acts. "It is not upon us to guide them, but God guides whomever He wills, and He is the one asked not to make our hearts swerve after He has guided us."]] to be guided to refraining from what they have been forbidden: stinginess (al-mann), harm (al-adha), spending from what is corrupt, and other things. Your duty is only to convey the prohibitions to them.

But God guides whomever He wills: He shows grace to whomever He knows the grace will benefit, so that he refrains from what he has been forbidden.

And whatever good you spend: from wealth, it is for your own selves. It benefits no one but you, so do not show favour to people by it nor harm them by acting superior toward them.

And you spend only seeking God's face: your spending is not except for seeking the face of God and desiring what is with Him. So why do you show favour by it and spend the corrupt, which would not be offered to God in this way?

And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full: its reward will be repaid to you manifold, so you have no excuse for being averse to spending it, and for it to be in the best and most beautiful manner.

It has been said:

Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may God be pleased with them both, performed the pilgrimage, and her mother came to her asking for something, while she was a polytheist. She refused to give her anything, so this verse was revealed.

And it is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God be pleased with him: "They were careful not to give a portion to their polytheist relatives." It is also narrated that some Muslims had in-laws among the Jews and foster relations, and they used to spend on them before Islam. When they became Muslims, they disliked spending on them [[His saying "they disliked spending on them" is perhaps an implicit inclusion of the verb with the meaning of giving. Or perhaps it is a corruption and the original is "yanfaʿūhum" from benefit. (ع)]].

It is also narrated from some scholars: "Even if they were the worst of God's creation, you would still have the reward for your spending."

There is disagreement concerning the obligatory charity. Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, permitted giving the zakat al-fitr (obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan) to the protected non-Muslim subjects (ahl al-dhimma), while others rejected this.

The jar (prepositional phrase) is connected to an omitted verb. The meaning is: "Aim at the poor, and make what you spend go to the poor," like His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾ (27:12). It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "your charities are for the poor."

﴿Those who are restricted in the way of God﴾ are those whom jihad has restricted, ﴿and cannot go about the land﴾ ﴿striving﴾ for livelihood, because they are occupied with it.

It is also said that they are the People of the Suffah (ahl al-suffah, "the people of the bench"), about four hundred men of the Quraysh emigrants who had no dwellings in Medina and no clans. They stayed in the Suffah of the mosque, which is its portico, learning the Qur'an at night and cracking date-stones during the day. Whenever the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent out a military expedition, they would go out with it. Whoever had a surplus would bring it to them in the evening.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) once stood over the People of the Suffah, saw their poverty, their hardship, and the goodness of their hearts, and said: "Rejoice, O People of the Suffah! Whoever of my community remains in the condition you are in, content with what it entails, will be among my companions in Paradise."

﴿The ignorant one thinks them rich because of their restraint﴾: they seem wealthy because of their abstention from asking. ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾: by the paleness of their faces and the shabbiness of their condition.

Al-ilhaf (persistent importunity) is al-ilhah, which is constancy, and that one does not leave until given something. From their saying: "He gave me from the surplus of his lahaf," meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God, exalted is He, loves the modest, forbearing, restrained one, and hates the rude, importunate asker."

[Footnote: Ibn Abi Shaybah recorded it in al-Adab from the narration of Maymun ibn Abi Shabib from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal report, except that he said "and hates the obscene, foul-mouthed one." It has also been transmitted as a connected report: al-Bazzar, by way of Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Malai, from Layth, from Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah, with a narration beginning "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest," and he said: "We do not know it from Abu Hurayrah except through this chain." Its isnad is weak. Al-Tabarani transmitted it from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud with a fuller text, and in its chain is Sawwar ibn Musʿab, who is weak. It has another route from Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Ishaq in his Musnad and by al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin by his route, who said: "Kulthum ibn Muhammad informed us, saying: ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Muslim al-Khurasani narrated to us from Abu Hurayrah," and he mentioned it, limited to what the author mentioned, in its meaning. Abu Nuʿaym in Tarikh Isfahan and Hamzah al-Sahmi in Tarikh Jurjan both recorded it through ʿIsa ibn Khalid al-Balkhi, from Waraqa, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "When God bestows a blessing upon a servant, He loves to see the effect of His blessing upon him, and He dislikes wretchedness and affected wretchedness, He hates the importunate asker, and He loves the chaste, restrained one."]

The meaning: if they ask, they ask gently and do not press. It is also said that this is a negation of both asking and importunity together, as in the poet's saying:

*ʿAlā lāḥibin lā yuhtadā bi-manārihi*
*On a worn, obscure track whose landmarks cannot be followed,*

[Footnote: ʿAlā lāḥib: a clear road (from al-Sihah). (ʿ)]

*Wa innī zaʿīmun in rajaʿtu mumallikan... bi-sayrin tarā minhu al-farānaqu azwarā*
*And I am a guarantor, if I return as a king... by a journey in which the farāniq are seen turning aside,*

*ʿAlā lāḥibin lā yuhtadā bi-mānārihi... idhā sāfahu al-ʿawdu al-nabāṭiyyu jarjaran*
*On a worn track whose landmarks cannot be followed, when the old camel of the Nabateans sniffs it and rumbles in protest.*

Imru' al-Qays. Al-zaʿīm is the guarantor. Al-farānaq (with a damma on the fa) are messengers who carry news of fear. Al-azwar is the one who leans aside.

He says: if they make me king over them as I was before, I am a guarantor of a difficult journey. Al-lahab and al-lahib are the wide road, from "lahabahu" when he trod it and passed along it, so its origin is malhub. Al-manar are the signposts of the road. Sāfahu yasūfuhu sawfan means he smelled it thoroughly; from it comes al-masāfah (distance). Al-ʿawd is the aged camel, and it is also applied to an old road. Al-sawdad is the ancient. Al-nabāṭī is ascribed to the Nabat, a people who inhabit the plains between the two ʿirāqs and extract water from them, like kimānī ascribed to Yemen. It is also narrated as al-ʿawd al-diyāfī. Dāfa yadūfu means he mixed, and Diyāf is a place in al-Jazāʾir where Syrian Nabateans live; al-diyāfī is ascribed to it. Al-jarjara is a sound a camel repeats in its throat. He means: it is a wide road with no landmarks by which one may be guided. In this line there is a figure of rhetoric that they call "negating a thing by affirming it," defined as an utterance whose outward form affirms something while its inner meaning negates it, by negating what belongs to its cause, which is the thing negated in the inner sense. In the line, the negation is of being guided by the landmarks, while the intended meaning is the negation of the landmarks themselves, as al-Suyuti mentioned in his commentary on ʿUqud al-Juman. When an old camel smells it, it knows the road is rough from its experience of roads, and it rumbles in fear because of its difficulty for it, especially if it is from Nabatean camels, due to their frequent travel. It is also possible that "sayr" (journey) is a metaphor for governance, as the request for kingship suggests, so that what follows it is a supporting element of the metaphor.

He intends the negation of the landmarks and of being guided by them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾ — they generalize the times and the circumstances with charity, out of their eagerness for good. So whenever a needy person comes to them with a need, they hasten to meet it and do not postpone it, nor do they make excuses of time or circumstance. It is said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) when he gave in charity forty thousand dinars: ten by night, ten by day, ten in secret, and ten openly. And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): it was revealed concerning 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who possessed only four dirhams, so he gave one dirham by night, one dirham by day, one dirham in secret, and one dirham openly.

It is also said that it was revealed concerning the fodder of horses and their tethering in the way of Allah. And from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): whenever he passed by a fat horse, he would recite this verse.

The Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari, commentary on surah 2, verses 275–276:

The word al-Ribā (usury) is written with a waw in the manner of those who pronounce the vowel emphatically, just as al-Ṣalāh (prayer) and al-Zakāh (almsgiving) are written, and an alif is added after it in imitation of the waw of the plural. ﴿Do not stand﴾ when they are raised from their graves. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) may Allah have mercy on him said: "It means when they are raised from their graves... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: His words "and the Devil's touch" are among the fabrications of the Arabs, that is, their lies and embellishments which have no reality, as is said of the ghoul and the phoenix and the like. This statement, in reality, is about the touch of the Devil on the Qadariyya (determinists) in their rejected claims, which are refuted by decisive texts of the Shari'a. For it is related: "Every child that is born is touched by the Devil, so it cries out loudly." In some chains it is: "except that the Devil pokes it in its side, and because of that it cries out, except Mary and her son, because of the saying of her mother: 'I seek refuge for her in You and her offspring from the accursed Devil.'" And his saying, peace be upon him: "Gather your children at the beginning of the night, for it is the time when the devils spread out; or, you have been spared, for it is the hour of their emergence, and in it they spread out, and in it occurs al-khabta." Shamir said: "There was a lisp in the tongue of Makhul, and he meant al-khabṭa (a striking) from the Devil, that is, an affliction of touch or madness." It is also reported in the hadith of the missing man whom the devils seized and who then returned in the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he related his account with them, saying: "Then a bird came to me, as if it were a camel, and it seized me and carried me upon one of its flight-feathers..." and other things too long to mention in this book. The belief of the early generations (al-salaf) and the People of the Sunna is that these are matters real in their actualities, as the Shari'a has reported about them. The Qadariyya are only enemies of the manifest, and so they inevitably deny much of what they claim to be contrary to their principles, such as sorcery, the Devil's touch, and most conditions of the jinn. And even if they acknowledge something of that, it is in a manner other than that which the People of the Sunna acknowledge and which the apparent Shari'a indicates, in a long confusion on their part; so beware of them. May Allah fight them; how are they turned away?]] except as he stands who is being struck by the Devil, that is, the one who is seized (al-maṣrū'). The Devil's touch is among the claims of the Arabs; they claimed that the Devil strikes a person and fells him.

Al-khabṭ is striking not in order, like the blind camel's striking (khabṭ al-'ashwā'), so the verse came in accordance with what they believed. Al-mass is madness.

A man is called "mamsūs" (touched), and this too is among their claims: that a jinn touches him and his intellect becomes confused. Likewise, "junna al-rajul" means the man was struck by jinn. They had among them tales, reports and wonders about the jinn, and denying these was for them like denying what is seen.

If you ask: with what does His saying ﴿from the touch﴾ connect? I say: with ﴿do not stand﴾, that is, they do not stand from the touch that is upon them except as the one seized stands. It is also permissible that it connects with ﴿stand﴾, that is, as the one seized stands from his madness. The meaning is that they will stand on the Day of Resurrection bewildered like the seized, a sign by which they are recognized by the people of the gathering. It was said: those who come out from the graves rush forward, except the devourers of usury, for they rise and fall like the seized, because they consumed usury, and Allah made it grow in their bellies until it weighed them down, so they cannot rush forward. ﴿That punishment is because they said: "Trade is only like usury."﴾ If you say: Why was it not said, "Usury is only like trade," since the discussion is about usury and not about trade? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did they not say: 'Usury is only like trade'... etc." Ahmad said: In my view there is another answer to the question raised, other than what was mentioned, namely that whenever the aim is to equate two things in establishing a ruling, the speaker may equate them by extension (qiyas al-ṭard, analogy of concomitance), saying for example: "Usury is like trade," and his purpose is to say: "Trade is permitted, so usury is permitted." He may also equate them by reversal (qiyas al-'aks, analogy of reversal), saying: "Trade is like usury," so that if usury were forbidden, trade would be forbidden by necessity of the likeness. Its conclusion, which the force of the speech indicates, is that he says: "Since trade is permitted by consensus and not forbidden, usury must be like it." The first follows the method of extension-analogy, and the second the method of reversal-analogy, and both lead to one purpose. Hence, according to this explanation, there is no need to depart from the apparent meaning for the sake of emphasis or any other reason. The purpose of all this is only to show what they imagined upon the model of correct arrangement, even though it is an analogy of faulty premise, for it is used to contradict what is known of Allah's ruling on the prohibition of usury and the permission of trade, and the cutting off of analogy between them. But if you use the two mentioned methods correctly, say in the first: "Nabidh (date-wine) is like wine in the cause of prohibition, which is intoxication, and wine is forbidden, so nabidh is forbidden." And say in the second: "Wine is only like nabidh; so if nabidh were permitted, wine would be permitted, and wine is not permitted by consensus, so nabidh is likewise, by necessity of the stated likeness." This interpretation is better for the verse to be understood by.) And Allah knows best.] So it must be said that they likened usury to trade and therefore made it lawful. Their argument was that they said: "If a man buys something worth only one dirham for two dirhams, it is permitted; so likewise if he sells one dirham for two dirhams?" I say: It is expressed as hyperbole, meaning that their belief in the permissibility of usury reached the point that they made it a principle and a rule of permissibility, so much so that they made trade resemble it.

His saying ﴿And Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ is a denial of their equating the two, and an indication that analogy is overturned by the text, because He made the proof of the falsity of their analogy the permission and prohibition of Allah.

﴿So whoever has received an admonition﴾ from Allah, that is, whoever has reached him an admonition from Allah and a warning by the prohibition of usury, ﴿and desists﴾, following the prohibition and refraining, ﴿he shall have what has passed﴾, so he is not taken to account for what has gone before, because he took it before the revelation of the prohibition; ﴿and his affair is with Allah﴾, who will judge concerning him on the Day of Resurrection, and nothing of his affair is up to you, so do not demand it of him. ﴿But whoever returns [to usury], those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ This is a clear proof [Mahmud said: "In this verse is a proof of the eternal abiding of the sinners... etc." Ahmad said, may Allah have mercy on him: It is built on the premise that what is threatened with eternal abiding is returning to the act of usury specifically, and the apparent meaning by which he (al-Zamakhshari) argued does not support that, for what they returned to is left unmentioned in the verse. Do you not see that He said ﴿and whoever returns﴾ without mentioning what is returned to? So it is taken as referring to what was previously mentioned, as if He said: "Whoever returns to what has been mentioned before, those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever." And what was previously mentioned is the act of usury, the belief in its permissibility, and the argument for it by analogy with trade. There is no doubt for us, the People of the Sunna and the Community, that whoever engages in a usurious transaction considering it lawful, obstinately contesting its prohibition, and attributing its permissibility to opposing Allah's clear verses with what he imagines of fancies, has disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief; and in that case the one promised eternal abiding in the verse is one who is said to be a disbelieving denier and not a believer, and there is no disagreement about this. So there is no proof for al-Zamakhshari in this verse for his Mu'tazilism. And Allah is the Granter of success. He is merely charged with loading the verses with false beliefs that they cannot bear. And how could he have that in the Mighty Book, to which falsehood does not come from before it or behind it, a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.] And the mention of the verb of admonition (fa-man jā'ahu mawʿiẓa) is because its feminine marking is not real, and because it has the sense of exhortation (al-waʿẓ).

Ubayy and al-Hasan recited: ﴿fa-man jā'atuh﴾.

﴿Allah destroys usury﴾, that is, He takes away its blessing and ruins the wealth into which it enters. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Usury, though it be abundant, ends in scarcity."

﴿And He makes charities grow﴾: what is given in charity, by multiplying its reward upon him, increasing the wealth from which the charity was taken out, and blessing it. In the hadith: "The zakat of any wealth has never decreased"* [*From the narration of al-'Ala' from his father from Abu Hurayra, with the wording "No charity has decreased any wealth... the hadith." al-Bazzar narrated it through this route, adding "ever" (qaṭṭ).]

﴿Allah does not love any ungrateful sinner﴾: this is an intensification regarding the matter of usury and a notice that it is an act of the disbelievers, not an act of the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 277–281:

They took what they had stipulated from the people of usury (al-riba), and some remainders were left to them. So they were commanded to leave them and not to demand them.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Thaqif, who had money owed to them by some people of Quraysh, and they demanded from them, when the term came due, the principal and the usury.

Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "ما بقي" (mā baqiya), converting the yā' into an alif, according to the dialect of Tayy. And from him (also): "ما بقي" with a silent yā'. Among its occurrences is the verse of Jarir:

هُوَ الْخَلِيفَةُ فَارْضَوْا مَا رَضِى لَكُمُو ... مَاضِى الْعَزِيمَةِ مَا فِى حُكْمِهِ جَنَفُ [[That is, he is the one known for justice. Or: he is the perfect caliph, so be pleased with what he has approved for you of rulings. The sukun on the final "radiya" and similar is an anomalous dialectal usage. "Mādī al-'azīmah": whose decision is executed; "laysa fī ḥukmihi janaf": there is no deviation in his judgment from the truth toward something else.]]

"In kuntum mu'minīn" (if you are believers): if your faith is sound. He means that the evidence of the soundness and steadfastness of faith is compliance with what you have been commanded in this matter. "Fa-'dhanū bi-ḥarb" (then be informed of a war): i.e., know of it and be aware of it, from "adhina bi'l-shay'" (he knew of the thing) when he came to know it. It has been read "fa-ādhanū" (then announce it), i.e., inform others of it; this derives from "al-idhn," which is hearing, because it is one of the paths of knowledge. Al-Hasan recited "fa-ayqinū" (then be certain), and this is evidence for the reading of the common readers. If you say: why was it not said "bi-ḥarbi Allāh wa-rasūlihi" (a war from Allah and His Messenger)? I say: this is more eloquent, because the meaning is: then announce a kind of war that is great in the sight of Allah and His Messenger. It is narrated that when this was revealed, Thaqif said: "We have no power against war with Allah and His Messenger."

"Wa-in tubtum" (and if you repent) from usury, "fa-lakum ru'ūs amwālikum" (then you shall have your principal), "lā taẓlimūna" (you shall not wrong) the debtors by demanding increase upon it, "wa-lā tuẓlamūna" (nor shall you be wronged) by reduction from it. If you say: this is their ruling if they repent; what is their ruling if they do not repent? I say: they said that their wealth becomes spoils (fay') for the Muslims. Al-Mufaddal narrated from 'Aṣim: "lā tuẓlimūna wa-lā tuẓlamūna" (you shall not wrong, nor be wronged) with the passive form in the second.

"Wa-in kāna dhū 'usrah" (and if one is in hardship): if one of your debtors is in hardship or straitened circumstances. 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "dhā 'usrah" according to: "wa-in kāna al-gharīmu dhā 'usrah" (and if the debtor is in hardship). It has been read: "wa-man kāna dhā 'usrah" (and whoever is in hardship), "fa-naẓirah" (then let there be postponement), i.e., the ruling or the matter is postponement, and it is the granting of respite (al-inẓār). It has been read "fa-naẓrah" with a sukun on the ẓā'. 'Aṭā' recited "fa-nāẓirah," meaning: then the creditor is one who waits for it, i.e., awaits it; or the possessor of its waiting, in the manner of the relative (nisba), as they say: "makān 'āshib" and "bāqil," meaning: a place with grass and a place with herbs. And from him (also): "fa-nāẓirah" as a command, meaning: then be lenient with him by granting respite and ease him through it. "Ilā maysarah" (until a time of ease): until prosperity. It has been read with a ḍammah on the sīn, like "maqbarah" and "maqburah," "mashrafah" and "mashrufah." It has also been read with both forms in construct with the tā' dropped in the iḍāfah, as in the verse:

وَأخْلَفُوكَ عِدَا الأَمْرِ الَّذِى وَعَدُوا [[Inna al-khalīṭ ajdaw al-bayna wa-injarradū ... wa-akhlafūka 'idā al-amri alladhī wa'adū

It belongs to Abū Umayyah al-Faḍl ibn al-'Abbās ibn 'Utbah ibn Abī Lahab. It is also said to be by Zuhayr. "Al-khalīṭ": the companion in close association, and he is like the 'ashīr (companion). It is said of the singular and the plural. "Ajdaw al-bayn": they strove toward separation. "Injarradū": they departed. "'Idā al-amr": its origin is "'iddat al-amr," and its origin is "waʿd"; the tā' was substituted for the wāw, then the tā' was dropped for the iḍāfah, like the tanwīn, according to one dialect. There is disagreement: it is said that it is transmitted (samā'ī), and it is said that it is analogical (qiyāsī). Their stipulation for the deletion, the absence of ambiguity—so it is forbidden in "shajarat Zayd" because of ambiguity with "shajr Zayd"—supports its being analogical.

In al-Murāḥ: the deletion of the substitute tā' is permissible here by consensus. As for Sibawayh, it is because substitution is among the permissible matters in his view. As for al-Farrā', it is because he requires the tā' only when there is no iḍāfah, and here the iḍāfah is realized, so it takes the place of the substitute. The returning pronoun of the relative is omitted, i.e., "al-amr alladhī wa'adūhu iyyāka" (the matter they promised you).]]

And His saying, the Exalted: "wa-aqāma al-ṣalāh" (and established prayer). "Wa-an taṣaddaqū khayrun lakum" (and that you give charity is better for you): this is an exhortation to give up their principal, or part of it, to whoever among their debtors is in hardship, like His saying, the Exalted: "wa-an ta'fū aqrabu lil-taqwā" (and that you pardon is nearer to piety). It has also been said: charity here means granting respite, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "No Muslim's debt is due and he postpones it except that he has for every day a charity." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah from the narration of al-A'mash from Abu Dawud Nafi' from Buraydah, raised: "Whoever grants respite to one in hardship, he has for every day a charity. And whoever grants him respite after it is due, he has the like of it every day as charity." Abu Dawud is weak, and there is disagreement concerning him: 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr narrated it from al-A'mash in this form, but Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash contradicted him, narrating it from al-A'mash from Abu Dawud from 'Imran ibn Husayn; Ahmad and al-Tabarani recorded it. Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman all recorded it from the narration of 'Abd al-Warith from Muhammad ibn Juhadah from Ibn Buraydah from his father, similarly. It has a supporting report from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas recorded by al-Tabarani.]] "In kuntum ta'lamūn" (if you knew): that it is better for you so that you would act upon it. He made one who does not act upon it, even though he knows it, as if he did not know it. It has been read "taṣaddaqū" with the ṣād lightened, by dropping the tā'.

"Turja'ūn": it has been read in the active and passive forms. "Yurja'ūn" with the yā' is read by way of iltifāt (shift of person). 'Abd Allah read "turaddūn," and Ubayy read "taṣīrūn."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was the last verse revealed by Jibril, peace be upon him, and he said: "Place it at the end of the two hundred and eightieth verse of al-Baqarah." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, lived after it twenty-one days. It is also said eighty-one days, and it is said seven days, and it is said three hours.
