"Wa-in tubtum" (and if you repent) from usury, "fa-lakum ru'ūs amwālikum" (then you shall have your principal), "lā taẓlimūna" (you shall not wrong) the debtors by demanding increase upon it, "wa-lā tuẓlamūna" (nor shall you be wronged) by reduction from it. If you say: this is their ruling if they repent; what is their ruling if they do not repent? I say: they said that their wealth becomes spoils (fay') for the Muslims. Al-Mufaddal narrated from 'Aṣim: "lā tuẓlimūna wa-lā tuẓlamūna" (you shall not wrong, nor be wronged) with the passive form in the second.

"Wa-in kāna dhū 'usrah" (and if one is in hardship): if one of your debtors is in hardship or straitened circumstances. 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "dhā 'usrah" according to: "wa-in kāna al-gharīmu dhā 'usrah" (and if the debtor is in hardship). It has been read: "wa-man kāna dhā 'usrah" (and whoever is in hardship), "fa-naẓirah" (then let there be postponement), i.e., the ruling or the matter is postponement, and it is the granting of respite (al-inẓār). It has been read "fa-naẓrah" with a sukun on the ẓā'. 'Aṭā' recited "fa-nāẓirah," meaning: then the creditor is one who waits for it, i.e., awaits it; or the possessor of its waiting, in the manner of the relative (nisba), as they say: "makān 'āshib" and "bāqil," meaning: a place with grass and a place with herbs. And from him (also): "fa-nāẓirah" as a command, meaning: then be lenient with him by granting respite and ease him through it. "Ilā maysarah" (until a time of ease): until prosperity. It has been read with a ḍammah on the sīn, like "maqbarah" and "maqburah," "mashrafah" and "mashrufah." It has also been read with both forms in construct with the tā' dropped in the iḍāfah, as in the verse:

وَأخْلَفُوكَ عِدَا الأَمْرِ الَّذِى وَعَدُوا [[Inna al-khalīṭ ajdaw al-bayna wa-injarradū ... wa-akhlafūka 'idā al-amri alladhī wa'adū

It belongs to Abū Umayyah al-Faḍl ibn al-'Abbās ibn 'Utbah ibn Abī Lahab. It is also said to be by Zuhayr. "Al-khalīṭ": the companion in close association, and he is like the 'ashīr (companion). It is said of the singular and the plural. "Ajdaw al-bayn": they strove toward separation. "Injarradū": they departed. "'Idā al-amr": its origin is "'iddat al-amr," and its origin is "waʿd"; the tā' was substituted for the wāw, then the tā' was dropped for the iḍāfah, like the tanwīn, according to one dialect. There is disagreement: it is said that it is transmitted (samā'ī), and it is said that it is analogical (qiyāsī). Their stipulation for the deletion, the absence of ambiguity—so it is forbidden in "shajarat Zayd" because of ambiguity with "shajr Zayd"—supports its being analogical.

In al-Murāḥ: the deletion of the substitute tā' is permissible here by consensus. As for Sibawayh, it is because substitution is among the permissible matters in his view. As for al-Farrā', it is because he requires the tā' only when there is no iḍāfah, and here the iḍāfah is realized, so it takes the place of the substitute. The returning pronoun of the relative is omitted, i.e., "al-amr alladhī wa'adūhu iyyāka" (the matter they promised you).]]

And His saying, the Exalted: "wa-aqāma al-ṣalāh" (and established prayer). "Wa-an taṣaddaqū khayrun lakum" (and that you give charity is better for you): this is an exhortation to give up their principal, or part of it, to whoever among their debtors is in hardship, like His saying, the Exalted: "wa-an ta'fū aqrabu lil-taqwā" (and that you pardon is nearer to piety). It has also been said: charity here means granting respite, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "No Muslim's debt is due and he postpones it except that he has for every day a charity." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah from the narration of al-A'mash from Abu Dawud Nafi' from Buraydah, raised: "Whoever grants respite to one in hardship, he has for every day a charity. And whoever grants him respite after it is due, he has the like of it every day as charity." Abu Dawud is weak, and there is disagreement concerning him: 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr narrated it from al-A'mash in this form, but Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash contradicted him, narrating it from al-A'mash from Abu Dawud from 'Imran ibn Husayn; Ahmad and al-Tabarani recorded it. Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman all recorded it from the narration of 'Abd al-Warith from Muhammad ibn Juhadah from Ibn Buraydah from his father, similarly. It has a supporting report from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas recorded by al-Tabarani.]] "In kuntum ta'lamūn" (if you knew): that it is better for you so that you would act upon it. He made one who does not act upon it, even though he knows it, as if he did not know it. It has been read "taṣaddaqū" with the ṣād lightened, by dropping the tā'.

"Turja'ūn": it has been read in the active and passive forms. "Yurja'ūn" with the yā' is read by way of iltifāt (shift of person). 'Abd Allah read "turaddūn," and Ubayy read "taṣīrūn."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was the last verse revealed by Jibril, peace be upon him, and he said: "Place it at the end of the two hundred and eightieth verse of al-Baqarah." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, lived after it twenty-one days. It is also said eighty-one days, and it is said seven days, and it is said three hours.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 282–283 (part 1 of 2):

"O you who believe, when you contract a debt..." (إِذا تَدايَنْتُمْ): when you deal with one another in debt. It is said: "dāyantu al-rajul" (I dealt with the man in debt), meaning I transacted with him in debt, whether as creditor or debtor, just as you say "bāya'tuhu" (I traded with him) when you sell to him or he sells to you. Ru'ba said:

"I dealt in debt with Arwā, and debts are paid,
so she delayed some of it and paid some of it."

[[Ru'ba's verse. He says: I transacted with my beloved Arwā with a debt I had on her, which arises from the requirements of affection. "Famaṭalat" means she postponed some of it and prolonged the period of its delay, and "paid some of it." His saying "wa-l-duyūnu tuqḍā" ("and debts are paid") is a circumstantial or parenthetical clause, explaining her injustice in delay. The root meaning of maṭl is stretching and extending.]]

The meaning is: when you deal in deferred debt, then write it down. If you say: why was it not said "when you deal in debt until a specified term" (ilā ajalin musammā)?

[[Maḥmūd said: "If you say, why was it not said 'when you deal in debt...' etc.?" Aḥmad said: the specified term (al-ajal al-musammā) is one whose end is known, and knowing the end has several ways: among them, fixing it by time itself, such as a year or a month. Among them, fixing it by something customarily occurring in a specific, conventionally fixed time, such as the harvest or the arrival of the pilgrims. Whatever way the term is known, it is valid to stipulate it; hence the Mālikī school permitted sale on credit until the harvest, since it is known to them. Then the consideration is the time of the occurrence of these markers, not the occurrence itself; so if the time of the pilgrims' arrival comes and some obstacle prevents their coming, for example, it carries no weight, and we rule that the debt's term has come due. And God knows best.]]

And what need is there to mention "debt" as he said, "I dealt with Arwā," and did not say "in debt"? I say: it was mentioned so that the pronoun can refer back to it in His saying "fa-ktubūhu" (then write it), for if it were not mentioned, it would have to say "fa-ktubū al-dayn" (then write the debt), and the composition would not have been so elegant. Also because it is clearer in distinguishing debt into deferred and immediate. If you say: what is the benefit of His saying "musammā" (specified)? I say: so that it is known that a term must be known, like being fixed by years, months and days; and if He had said "until the harvest," or "the threshing," or "the return of the pilgrims," it would not be permitted, for lack of specification. He commanded the writing of the debt because that is more secure, safer from forgetting, and further from denial, and the command is one of recommendation. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās that it refers to the salam (advance sale), and he said: when God forbade usury, He permitted the salaf (advance). And from him: "I bear witness that God permitted the guaranteed salam up to a known term in His Book, and revealed in it the longest verse."

[[Al-Ḥākim narrated it from the narration of Abū Ḥayyān al-A'raj from al-A'mash from Ibn 'Abbās, who said: "I bear witness that the guaranteed salam up to a specified term, God fixed its term in the Book and permitted it," and he recited this verse: "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, then write it down."]]

"Bi-l-'adl" (with justice) is attached to "kātib" (scribe) as its qualifier, meaning: a scribe trusted regarding what he writes, who writes with evenhandedness and caution, neither adding to what must be written nor reducing it. And in it: the scribe should be a jurist, knowledgeable in the conditions, so that what he writes comes out fair according to the Sharī'ah. It is a command to the contracting parties to choose the scribe, and that they should not appoint as scribe except a jurist of good religion. "Wa-lā ya'ba kātibun" (and let no scribe refuse), i.e., no one among the scribes should refuse, and this is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "kātib": "an yaktuba kamā 'allamahu Allāh" (to write as God taught him), i.e., like what God taught him of the writing of documents, without altering or changing. It was said it refers to His saying, "and do good as God has done good to you" (2:195 — cf. 28:77), i.e., he should benefit people with his writing as God benefited him by teaching it. It is reported from al-Sha'bī: it is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāya). "Kamā 'allamahu Allāh" may be attached either to "an yaktuba" or to "fa-l-yaktub."

If you say: what is the difference between the two views? I say: if you attach it to "an yaktuba," then he has forbidden refusing the restricted writing, and then he is told "fa-l-yaktub," meaning: let him write that writing, not deviating from it, for emphasis. And if you attach it to "fa-l-yaktub," then he has forbidden refusing writing in an unrestricted manner, and then commanded it in a restricted form.

"Wa-l-yumlil alladhī 'alayhi al-ḥaqq" (let the one upon whom the obligation lies dictate): the dictator must be none other than the one upon whom the right is due, for he is the one whose acknowledgment of it in his obligation and confession of it is witnessed. "Al-imlā'" and "al-imlāl" are two dialects, both of which the Qur'an has uttered: "fa-hiya tumlā 'alayhi" (25:5). "Wa-lā yabkhas minhu" (and let him not diminish from it) of the right "shay'an" (anything), and al-bakhs is reduction. It was recited "shay'an" with the hamza dropped, and "shayyan" with shadda.

"Safīhan" (foolish): one placed under restraint for his squandering and ignorance of dealing. "Aw ḍa'īfan" (or weak): a child, or a senile old man. "Aw lā yastaṭī'u an yumilla huwa" (or one unable to dictate himself) or unable to dictate for himself, due to incapacity of speech or muteness: "fa-l-yumlil waliyyuhu" (then let his guardian dictate), the one who manages his affairs, whether a guardian (waṣī) if he is foolish or a child, or an agent (wakīl) if he is unable, or an interpreter who dictates on his behalf while he confirms it. His saying "an yumilla huwa" implies that he is unable in himself but able through another, namely the one who translates for him.

"Wa-stashhidū shahīdayni" (and call two witnesses): seek that two witnesses bear witness for you concerning the debt, "min rijālikum" (from among your men), i.e., from among the men of the believers. Freedom and puberty are conditions along with Islam according to the general body of scholars. It is reported from 'Alī, may God be pleased with him: the testimony of a slave is not valid in anything. According to Sharīḥ, Ibn Sīrīn and 'Uthmān al-Battī, it is valid. According to Abū Ḥanīfa, the testimony of non-Muslims against one another is valid, despite differences of religion.

"Fa-in lam yakūnā" (but if they are not): if the two witnesses are not two men, "fa-rajulun wa-imra'atān" (then one man and two women) shall testify. The testimony of women with men is accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfa in matters other than the ḥudūd and retaliation (qiṣāṣ). "Mimman tarḍawna" (of those whom you approve): those whose uprightness you know. "An taḍilla iḥdāhumā" (that one of them may err): that one of them may not be guided to testimony by forgetting it, from ḍalla al-ṭarīq (he lost the way) when he is not guided to it. Its position is as an object of purpose: meaning, in the desire that one of them err. If you say: how can her erring be willed by God, Most High? I say: since error was the cause of reminding, and reminding was the effect of it, and they treat each of the cause and effect as the other because of their association and connection, the willing of the error that causes the reminding is willing of the reminding; so it is as if it were said: in the desire that one of them remind the other if she errs.

Its parallel is the saying of people: "I prepared the timber that the wall may lean, so I shore it up; and I prepared the weapon that an enemy may come, so I repel him."

It is read "fa-tudhakkira" with lightening and with doubling, both being dialects; and "fa-tadhākara." Ḥamza read "in taḍilla iḥdāhumā" in the conditional form, and "fa-tudhakkiru" with raf' and tashdīd, like His saying "wa-man 'āda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu" (5:95). It is also read "an tuḍalla iḥdāhumā" in the passive and feminine form.

Among the odd interpretations: "fa-tudhakkira" means that one of them makes the other a male, i.e., that when the two of them come together they are in the position of a male, "idhā mā du'ū li-yuqīmū al-shahāda" (when they are called to establish the testimony). It was said: "li-yastashhidū" (to be called as witnesses). It was said: they are called witnesses before bearing, treating what is about to occur as though it has occurred.

It is reported from Qatāda: a man would circle a great gathering-place in which there were people, and none of them would follow him; so this was revealed. "Al-sa'am" (weariness) is a metaphor for laziness, since laziness is a characteristic of the hypocrite. From the ḥadīth: "The believer should not say 'I am lazy'" (to be mentioned in Barā'a).

It is also permissible that it means one whose debts are many, so he needs to record a book for every debt, small or large, and perhaps he becomes weary of the multiplicity of books.

"Hu" in "taktubūhu" refers to the debt or the right, "ṣaghīran aw kabīran" (small or large), whatever state the right is, whether small or great. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the book, and that they write it abridged or full, without neglecting its writing "ilā ajalihi" (until its term), i.e., until its time upon which the two creditors agreed to name.

"Dhālikum" (that) is a reference to writing it, since it has the sense of the verbal noun, i.e., that writing "aqsaṭu" (more just) than the just, "wa-aqwamu li-l-shahāda" (more upright for testimony) and more helpful in establishing the testimony, "wa-adnā allā tartābū" (and nearer to avoiding doubt) and nearer to the absence of suspicion.

If you say: from what are the comparatives "aqsaṭu" and "aqwamu" formed? I say: it is permissible, according to the school of Sībawayh, that both are formed from aqsaṭa and aqāma, and that aqsaṭu is from qāsiṭ in the manner of the relative form, meaning dhū qisṭ, and aqwamu from qawīm.

It is read "wa-lā yasa'amū an yaktubūhu" with the yā' in both places.

If you say: what is the meaning of "tijāratan ḥāḍiratan" (present trade) and "tudīrūnahā baynakum" (you conduct it among yourselves)? Whether the transaction is in debt or in goods, the trade is present. And what is the meaning of conducting it among them? I say: by "trade" is meant what is traded in of exchanges. And the meaning of conducting it among them is their handling it hand to hand.

The meaning: except that you conduct a transaction that is immediate, hand to hand, then there is no harm in your not writing it, for there is no suspicion in it as there is in debt. It is read "tijāratun ḥāḍiratun" with raf' as the complete verb kāna. It was said: it is the incomplete, with the subject being "tijāratun ḥāḍiratun" and the predicate "tudīrūnahā"; and with naṣb, as in: "illā an takūna al-tijāratu tijāratan ḥāḍiratan," like the verse of the Kitāb:

"Banī Asad, do you know our affliction
when a day comes that is dhū kawākib (full of stars), appalling?"

[[From verses of the Kitāb. The purpose of this interrogation is threat and warning and reminder of what has passed, or affirmation; or "hal" means "qad." Al-balā' means war and every hardship. That is, O Banī Asad, do you know our war when the day is a day of stars, meaning the subject of kāna is elided. It is permissible that the subject of kāna is a pronoun for al-balā', and "yawman" is an adverbial complement attached to the elided predicate. Dhū kawākib is a metaphor for the dark, since many stars appear only at night; so the meaning: when the day resembles the night in darkness from the intensity of war and the raising of dust that veils the sun, so the stars seem to appear in it. Closer than that is that he metaphorically applies "kawākib" to the points of spears and swords for their gleam and their spreading on that day like stars, in the manner of explicit metaphor. "Ashna'" means ugly.]]

That is, when the day is a day...

"Wa-ashhidū idhā tabāya'tum" (and call witnesses when you trade): an order to call witnesses on every transaction, whether immediate or deferred, since it is more cautious and further from the disputes that may arise. It is also permissible that it means: and call witnesses when you conduct this trade, meaning the present trade, on the basis that witnessing suffices for it rather than writing. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: if he wills, he calls witnesses, and if he wills, he does not. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: it is a binding command from God, even for a bundle of herbs [[his saying "'alā bāqat baql" means a bunch of it, as the Ṣiḥāḥ states]].

"Wa-lā yuḍārr" (and let neither be harmed) may be in the active or passive voice. The evidence for this is the reading of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "wa-lā yuḍārir," with idhhār and kasra; and the reading of Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them: "wa-lā yuḍārar," with idhhār and fatḥa. The meaning is the prohibition of the scribe and the witness from refusing to respond to what is requested of them, or from alteration, addition and reduction; or the prohibition of harming them by making them hasten away from an important matter and be burdened; or the scribe is not given his right of wages, or the witness is made to bear the cost of his coming from a town [[his saying "from a town" probably means a distant town]].

Al-Ḥasan read "wa-lā yuḍārra" with kasra. "Wa-in taf'alū" (and if you do): and if you harm one another, "fa-innahu" (then indeed it), i.e., harm, "fusūqun bikum" (is a transgression in you). It was said: "and if you do something of what you were forbidden."

"'Alā safarin" (on a journey): travelers. Ibn 'Abbās and Ubayy, may God be pleased with them, read "kitāban" (a document). Ibn 'Abbās said: "Do you see if you find the scribe but not the sheet and the inkwell?" Abū al-'Āliya read "kutuban" (documents). Al-Ḥasan read "kitāban," the plural of kātib.

"Fa-rihānun" (then a pledge): then that by which the right is secured is a pledge. It is read "fa-rihun" with damma and with sukūn of the ha', and it is the plural of rahn, like suqf and suqf, and "fa-rihān." If you say: why was travel stipulated for pledging, when it is not restricted to travel rather than residence?

[[Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: why was travel stipulated for pledging, when it is not restricted to travel..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: restriction to travel on this basis follows the usual case, so it has no implicit restriction. And in this verse there is clear evidence for the school of Mālik, may God be pleased with him, that the establishment of a pledge at the time of dispute over the amount of the debt stands in place of a witness for the pledgee up to the full value of the pledge; so that if they dispute, and the debtor says: "I pledged it to you for a hundred," and the creditor says: "Rather, the pledge is for two hundred," the pledge would serve as a witness to its value. This is against al-Shāfi'ī, may God be pleased with him, who holds that the word of the debtor is accepted absolutely, because he is the one who pays. The evidence from the verse for Mālik, may God be pleased with him, is that God made the pledge, in securing the right, a substitute for witnessing and writing, and restricted it to travel because they are scarce at that time; and if the word of the debtor were legally decisive, the pledge would not stand in place of witnessing nor serve its function in any way, for if there were no pledge, the word of the debtor concerning the amount of the debt would be accepted, so the existence of the pledge adds no benefit over its absence in terms of its substitution for witnessing. Nor can it be said that its benefit is priority over the other creditors, for that is the benefit of witnessing, so that it stands in its place when it is unavailable; and there is no benefit then except making the word of the pledgee concerning the amount of the debt decisive in case of disagreement, which is the school of Mālik mentioned earlier. Hence he did not make it a witness except concerning its value, not beyond it, supported by custom that a creditor does not accept in his debt except what is fulfilled to its value. So the debtor's claim that the debt is more than the value is refuted by custom, and the debtor also does not permit handing over what is worth more for what is less, so his claim that the debt is less than the value is refuted by custom. Nothing remains except one matter, namely that for Mālik the value is considered on the day of judgment; so if both agree that the value on the day of the pledge was more or less, no attention is paid to that, whether it increased or decreased, and only the day of decision is considered. One might say: if you make the pledge stand in place of the witness when it is absent because custom requires that people pledge for debts equal in value to them, then you should consider the value on the day of the pledge, without regard to its increase or decrease on the day of decision; and at that point the discussion becomes entangled over whether the reason for its standing in place of the witness is the meaning mentioned earlier or something else. Our purpose is only that the verse guides to its standing in place of testimony in general. As for the details of the question, that belongs to the portion of jurisprudence.]]

"Wa-qad rahana rasūlu Allāh (ṣallā Allāhu 'alayhi wa-sallam) dir'ahu fī ghayri safar" (and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail when not traveling) [[agreed upon, from the narration of al-Aswad ibn Yazīd from 'Ā'isha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) bought food from a Jew on credit for a term and pledged him an iron coat of mail; and al-Bukhārī from the narration of Qatāda from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail in Medina with a Jew, and took barley from him for his family." End.]].

I say: the purpose is not to permit pledging only during travel, but since travel is the likely occasion for scarcity of documents and witnesses, He commanded, by way of guidance to preserve property for the one who is on a journey, that securing by pledge stand in place of securing by writing and witnessing. It is reported from Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk that they did not permit it except in a state of travel, taking the apparent meaning of the verse. As for taking possession (al-qabḍ), it must be taken into account [[Maḥmūd said: "As for taking possession, it must be taken into account..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: there is no dispute between Mālik and al-Shāfi'ī over the validity of pledging by offer and acceptance without possession; but according to Mālik, may God be pleased with him, it is valid by that, and the contract obliges the debtor to hand it over to the pledgee. According to al-Shāfi'ī, it is not binding by the contract. But for Mālik, possession has weight at the beginning and continuation; al-Shāfi'ī does not condition many of its rulings as Mālik does. For if the two agreed on possession and then the creditors appeared, the pledge would benefit the pledgee according to al-Shāfi'ī and be distinguished by it, but it would not benefit him according to Mālik, and he would be one among the creditors in it, unless the witnessing to their possession is accompanied by the witnesses' presence seeing it, because he suspects them of collusion to void the creditors' right, so their acknowledgment is not accepted without the addition of witnessing. Possession in this respect is thus more weighty in the view of Mālik than in the view of al-Shāfi'ī. This concerns the beginning. As for continuation, Mālik, may God be pleased with him, requires its remaining in the hand of the pledgee; so if it returns to the debtor's hand, by the pledgee depositing it with him, or renting it to him, or lending it to him in an unrestricted loan, it has left the pledge; and if the creditors appear while it is in the debtor's hand by any of the mentioned ways, he is one among the creditors regarding it. Al-Shāfi'ī, may God be pleased with him, does not require continuation of possession in this way, but for the debtor according to al-Shāfi'ī it is permissible to benefit from the pledge even if the pledgee dislikes it, provided that benefit does not harm the pledge, such as living in a house or employing a slave. And he may take its benefits himself, according to the sound opinion of his school, as stated in al-Umm, and that does not affect the pledge by invalidating or impairing it. You have known that possession is more weighty in Mālik's school in beginning and continuation, and the verse supports it, for "rahn" in the language means continuance. Abū 'Alī recited:

"So bread and meat are for them as a pledge,
and wine, its strainer poured out."]].

And perhaps the one who holds that the continuation of the pledge in the possession of the pledgee is a condition relied on what is in the word *rahn* (pledge) implying continuity, and he has a basis for that.

I only lengthened the account of Mālik's position on possession because what is understood from al-Zamakhsharī's words is that he dismisses possession according to Mālik, since he understood from the statement of his companions that possession is not a condition for the validity of the pledge or for its binding force, meaning that it is entirely disregarded in his view. And Allah knows best.

According to Mālik, the pledge is valid by offer and acceptance without possession. ﴿Then if some of you trust others﴾: that is, if some of the creditors trust some of the debtors [[The phrase "*al-madyūnīn*" (the debtors) "because of his good opinion of him": perhaps this is a rare transmitted reading, and the analogical form would be *al-madīnīn*; similarly, the singular *al-madyūn* would analogically be *al-madīn*. (ʿ)]] because of his good opinion of him. Ubayy recited: *fa-in ʾawmana* (then if he makes [them] secure), meaning: the people made him secure, [[The phrase "*ayy ʾāmanahu al-nās*" (that is, the people made him secure): the apparent reading is that it is from the causative form (*ʾif ʿāl*) with a kasra, not from the form (*mufāʿala*). That is, the people made one party, the creditor, such that he trusts the other party, the debtor, and this is by describing the debtor to him as trustworthy, etc., so the creditor became one who trusts the debtor. (ʿ)] and they described the debtor as trustworthy, faithful, and self-sufficient, so that he need not be secured by a pledge from someone like him. ﴿Then let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾: this urges the debtor to be what the creditor thinks of him, to be the one he trusts and in whom he places confidence, and to deliver to him the right he was entrusted with, since he did not give a pledge.

He called the debt a trust, though it is a guaranteed obligation, because the creditor entrusted him with it by forgoing a pledge from him. The reading is to pronounce a silent hamza after the *dhāl*, or a *yāʾ*, so you say: *al-ladhī ʾuttumina* or *al-ladhī tumina*. It is related from ʿĀṣim that he recited *al-ladhī ittaman*, assimilating the *yāʾ* into the *tāʾ*, by analogy with *ittasara* in the reflexive form (*ifti ʿāl*) from *yusr* (ease). This is not sound, because the *yāʾ* is converted from the hamza, so it has the status of the hamza. And *ittazara* is a colloquial form. Likewise *riyā* for *ruʾyā*.

﴿Sinful (*āthimun*)﴾ is the predicate of *inna* (indeed). And ﴿his heart﴾ (*qalbuhu*) is in the nominative as the agent of *āthimun*, as if it were said: "indeed his heart sins." It is also permissible for *qalbuhu* to be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with *āthimun* as a fronted predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of *inna*.

If you ask: why not limit it to his saying ﴿indeed he is sinful﴾? And what is the benefit of mentioning the heart, when it is the whole person who sins, not the heart alone? I answer: concealing testimony means that one hides it within oneself and does not speak it. Since it is a sin committed by the heart, the act is attributed to it, because attributing an action to the limb with which it is done is more emphatic. Do you not see that you say, when you want emphasis: "this is something my eye has seen, something my ear has heard, something my heart has known"? Also, the heart is the chief of the organs, the lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. So it is as if it were said: sin has taken firm root in the very core of his self, and has possessed the noblest place in it. And so that it may not be thought that concealing testimony is a sin related only to the tongue, and so that it may be known that the heart is the origin of what it relates to and the source of its commission, while the tongue is its interpreter. And because acts of the heart are greater than the acts of the other limbs, and they are for them like roots from which branches spread. Do you not see that the root of good and evil deeds is faith and disbelief, which are acts of the heart? So when concealing testimony is made a sin of the heart, it is thereby testified that it is among the greatest of sins.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the greatest of the major sins is associating partners with Allah, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾, and false testimony, and concealing testimony.

It is also recited *qalbahu* with a fatḥa (accusative), like the saying: ﴿he has made a fool of himself (*safiha nafsahu*)﴾. Ibn Abī ʿAblah recited *ʾathima qalbahu*, meaning he made it sinful. [[The phrase "*ʾathima qalbahu* meaning he made it sinful": this may be with the hamza prolonged, as a causative form (*ʾif ʿāl*), and it may be with the *tāʾ* doubled as a causative form (*tafʿīl*), so let it be examined. (ʿ)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verses 282–283 (part 1 of 2):

"O you who believe, when you contract a debt..." (إِذا تَدايَنْتُمْ): when you deal with one another in debt. It is said: "dāyantu al-rajul" (I dealt with the man in debt), meaning I transacted with him in debt, whether as creditor or debtor, just as you say "bāya'tuhu" (I traded with him) when you sell to him or he sells to you. Ru'ba said:

"I dealt in debt with Arwā, and debts are paid,
so she delayed some of it and paid some of it."

[[Ru'ba's verse. He says: I transacted with my beloved Arwā with a debt I had on her, which arises from the requirements of affection. "Famaṭalat" means she postponed some of it and prolonged the period of its delay, and "paid some of it." His saying "wa-l-duyūnu tuqḍā" ("and debts are paid") is a circumstantial or parenthetical clause, explaining her injustice in delay. The root meaning of maṭl is stretching and extending.]]

The meaning is: when you deal in deferred debt, then write it down. If you say: why was it not said "when you deal in debt until a specified term" (ilā ajalin musammā)?

[[Maḥmūd said: "If you say, why was it not said 'when you deal in debt...' etc.?" Aḥmad said: the specified term (al-ajal al-musammā) is one whose end is known, and knowing the end has several ways: among them, fixing it by time itself, such as a year or a month. Among them, fixing it by something customarily occurring in a specific, conventionally fixed time, such as the harvest or the arrival of the pilgrims. Whatever way the term is known, it is valid to stipulate it; hence the Mālikī school permitted sale on credit until the harvest, since it is known to them. Then the consideration is the time of the occurrence of these markers, not the occurrence itself; so if the time of the pilgrims' arrival comes and some obstacle prevents their coming, for example, it carries no weight, and we rule that the debt's term has come due. And God knows best.]]

And what need is there to mention "debt" as he said, "I dealt with Arwā," and did not say "in debt"? I say: it was mentioned so that the pronoun can refer back to it in His saying "fa-ktubūhu" (then write it), for if it were not mentioned, it would have to say "fa-ktubū al-dayn" (then write the debt), and the composition would not have been so elegant. Also because it is clearer in distinguishing debt into deferred and immediate. If you say: what is the benefit of His saying "musammā" (specified)? I say: so that it is known that a term must be known, like being fixed by years, months and days; and if He had said "until the harvest," or "the threshing," or "the return of the pilgrims," it would not be permitted, for lack of specification. He commanded the writing of the debt because that is more secure, safer from forgetting, and further from denial, and the command is one of recommendation. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās that it refers to the salam (advance sale), and he said: when God forbade usury, He permitted the salaf (advance). And from him: "I bear witness that God permitted the guaranteed salam up to a known term in His Book, and revealed in it the longest verse."

[[Al-Ḥākim narrated it from the narration of Abū Ḥayyān al-A'raj from al-A'mash from Ibn 'Abbās, who said: "I bear witness that the guaranteed salam up to a specified term, God fixed its term in the Book and permitted it," and he recited this verse: "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, then write it down."]]

"Bi-l-'adl" (with justice) is attached to "kātib" (scribe) as its qualifier, meaning: a scribe trusted regarding what he writes, who writes with evenhandedness and caution, neither adding to what must be written nor reducing it. And in it: the scribe should be a jurist, knowledgeable in the conditions, so that what he writes comes out fair according to the Sharī'ah. It is a command to the contracting parties to choose the scribe, and that they should not appoint as scribe except a jurist of good religion. "Wa-lā ya'ba kātibun" (and let no scribe refuse), i.e., no one among the scribes should refuse, and this is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "kātib": "an yaktuba kamā 'allamahu Allāh" (to write as God taught him), i.e., like what God taught him of the writing of documents, without altering or changing. It was said it refers to His saying, "and do good as God has done good to you" (2:195 — cf. 28:77), i.e., he should benefit people with his writing as God benefited him by teaching it. It is reported from al-Sha'bī: it is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāya). "Kamā 'allamahu Allāh" may be attached either to "an yaktuba" or to "fa-l-yaktub."

If you say: what is the difference between the two views? I say: if you attach it to "an yaktuba," then he has forbidden refusing the restricted writing, and then he is told "fa-l-yaktub," meaning: let him write that writing, not deviating from it, for emphasis. And if you attach it to "fa-l-yaktub," then he has forbidden refusing writing in an unrestricted manner, and then commanded it in a restricted form.

"Wa-l-yumlil alladhī 'alayhi al-ḥaqq" (let the one upon whom the obligation lies dictate): the dictator must be none other than the one upon whom the right is due, for he is the one whose acknowledgment of it in his obligation and confession of it is witnessed. "Al-imlā'" and "al-imlāl" are two dialects, both of which the Qur'an has uttered: "fa-hiya tumlā 'alayhi" (25:5). "Wa-lā yabkhas minhu" (and let him not diminish from it) of the right "shay'an" (anything), and al-bakhs is reduction. It was recited "shay'an" with the hamza dropped, and "shayyan" with shadda.

"Safīhan" (foolish): one placed under restraint for his squandering and ignorance of dealing. "Aw ḍa'īfan" (or weak): a child, or a senile old man. "Aw lā yastaṭī'u an yumilla huwa" (or one unable to dictate himself) or unable to dictate for himself, due to incapacity of speech or muteness: "fa-l-yumlil waliyyuhu" (then let his guardian dictate), the one who manages his affairs, whether a guardian (waṣī) if he is foolish or a child, or an agent (wakīl) if he is unable, or an interpreter who dictates on his behalf while he confirms it. His saying "an yumilla huwa" implies that he is unable in himself but able through another, namely the one who translates for him.

"Wa-stashhidū shahīdayni" (and call two witnesses): seek that two witnesses bear witness for you concerning the debt, "min rijālikum" (from among your men), i.e., from among the men of the believers. Freedom and puberty are conditions along with Islam according to the general body of scholars. It is reported from 'Alī, may God be pleased with him: the testimony of a slave is not valid in anything. According to Sharīḥ, Ibn Sīrīn and 'Uthmān al-Battī, it is valid. According to Abū Ḥanīfa, the testimony of non-Muslims against one another is valid, despite differences of religion.

"Fa-in lam yakūnā" (but if they are not): if the two witnesses are not two men, "fa-rajulun wa-imra'atān" (then one man and two women) shall testify. The testimony of women with men is accepted according to Abū Ḥanīfa in matters other than the ḥudūd and retaliation (qiṣāṣ). "Mimman tarḍawna" (of those whom you approve): those whose uprightness you know. "An taḍilla iḥdāhumā" (that one of them may err): that one of them may not be guided to testimony by forgetting it, from ḍalla al-ṭarīq (he lost the way) when he is not guided to it. Its position is as an object of purpose: meaning, in the desire that one of them err. If you say: how can her erring be willed by God, Most High? I say: since error was the cause of reminding, and reminding was the effect of it, and they treat each of the cause and effect as the other because of their association and connection, the willing of the error that causes the reminding is willing of the reminding; so it is as if it were said: in the desire that one of them remind the other if she errs.

Its parallel is the saying of people: "I prepared the timber that the wall may lean, so I shore it up; and I prepared the weapon that an enemy may come, so I repel him."

It is read "fa-tudhakkira" with lightening and with doubling, both being dialects; and "fa-tadhākara." Ḥamza read "in taḍilla iḥdāhumā" in the conditional form, and "fa-tudhakkiru" with raf' and tashdīd, like His saying "wa-man 'āda fa-yantaqimu Allāhu minhu" (5:95). It is also read "an tuḍalla iḥdāhumā" in the passive and feminine form.

Among the odd interpretations: "fa-tudhakkira" means that one of them makes the other a male, i.e., that when the two of them come together they are in the position of a male, "idhā mā du'ū li-yuqīmū al-shahāda" (when they are called to establish the testimony). It was said: "li-yastashhidū" (to be called as witnesses). It was said: they are called witnesses before bearing, treating what is about to occur as though it has occurred.

It is reported from Qatāda: a man would circle a great gathering-place in which there were people, and none of them would follow him; so this was revealed. "Al-sa'am" (weariness) is a metaphor for laziness, since laziness is a characteristic of the hypocrite. From the ḥadīth: "The believer should not say 'I am lazy'" (to be mentioned in Barā'a).

It is also permissible that it means one whose debts are many, so he needs to record a book for every debt, small or large, and perhaps he becomes weary of the multiplicity of books.

"Hu" in "taktubūhu" refers to the debt or the right, "ṣaghīran aw kabīran" (small or large), whatever state the right is, whether small or great. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the book, and that they write it abridged or full, without neglecting its writing "ilā ajalihi" (until its term), i.e., until its time upon which the two creditors agreed to name.

"Dhālikum" (that) is a reference to writing it, since it has the sense of the verbal noun, i.e., that writing "aqsaṭu" (more just) than the just, "wa-aqwamu li-l-shahāda" (more upright for testimony) and more helpful in establishing the testimony, "wa-adnā allā tartābū" (and nearer to avoiding doubt) and nearer to the absence of suspicion.

If you say: from what are the comparatives "aqsaṭu" and "aqwamu" formed? I say: it is permissible, according to the school of Sībawayh, that both are formed from aqsaṭa and aqāma, and that aqsaṭu is from qāsiṭ in the manner of the relative form, meaning dhū qisṭ, and aqwamu from qawīm.

It is read "wa-lā yasa'amū an yaktubūhu" with the yā' in both places.

If you say: what is the meaning of "tijāratan ḥāḍiratan" (present trade) and "tudīrūnahā baynakum" (you conduct it among yourselves)? Whether the transaction is in debt or in goods, the trade is present. And what is the meaning of conducting it among them? I say: by "trade" is meant what is traded in of exchanges. And the meaning of conducting it among them is their handling it hand to hand.

The meaning: except that you conduct a transaction that is immediate, hand to hand, then there is no harm in your not writing it, for there is no suspicion in it as there is in debt. It is read "tijāratun ḥāḍiratun" with raf' as the complete verb kāna. It was said: it is the incomplete, with the subject being "tijāratun ḥāḍiratun" and the predicate "tudīrūnahā"; and with naṣb, as in: "illā an takūna al-tijāratu tijāratan ḥāḍiratan," like the verse of the Kitāb:

"Banī Asad, do you know our affliction
when a day comes that is dhū kawākib (full of stars), appalling?"

[[From verses of the Kitāb. The purpose of this interrogation is threat and warning and reminder of what has passed, or affirmation; or "hal" means "qad." Al-balā' means war and every hardship. That is, O Banī Asad, do you know our war when the day is a day of stars, meaning the subject of kāna is elided. It is permissible that the subject of kāna is a pronoun for al-balā', and "yawman" is an adverbial complement attached to the elided predicate. Dhū kawākib is a metaphor for the dark, since many stars appear only at night; so the meaning: when the day resembles the night in darkness from the intensity of war and the raising of dust that veils the sun, so the stars seem to appear in it. Closer than that is that he metaphorically applies "kawākib" to the points of spears and swords for their gleam and their spreading on that day like stars, in the manner of explicit metaphor. "Ashna'" means ugly.]]

That is, when the day is a day...

"Wa-ashhidū idhā tabāya'tum" (and call witnesses when you trade): an order to call witnesses on every transaction, whether immediate or deferred, since it is more cautious and further from the disputes that may arise. It is also permissible that it means: and call witnesses when you conduct this trade, meaning the present trade, on the basis that witnessing suffices for it rather than writing. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: if he wills, he calls witnesses, and if he wills, he does not. It is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: it is a binding command from God, even for a bundle of herbs [[his saying "'alā bāqat baql" means a bunch of it, as the Ṣiḥāḥ states]].

"Wa-lā yuḍārr" (and let neither be harmed) may be in the active or passive voice. The evidence for this is the reading of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "wa-lā yuḍārir," with idhhār and kasra; and the reading of Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them: "wa-lā yuḍārar," with idhhār and fatḥa. The meaning is the prohibition of the scribe and the witness from refusing to respond to what is requested of them, or from alteration, addition and reduction; or the prohibition of harming them by making them hasten away from an important matter and be burdened; or the scribe is not given his right of wages, or the witness is made to bear the cost of his coming from a town [[his saying "from a town" probably means a distant town]].

Al-Ḥasan read "wa-lā yuḍārra" with kasra. "Wa-in taf'alū" (and if you do): and if you harm one another, "fa-innahu" (then indeed it), i.e., harm, "fusūqun bikum" (is a transgression in you). It was said: "and if you do something of what you were forbidden."

"'Alā safarin" (on a journey): travelers. Ibn 'Abbās and Ubayy, may God be pleased with them, read "kitāban" (a document). Ibn 'Abbās said: "Do you see if you find the scribe but not the sheet and the inkwell?" Abū al-'Āliya read "kutuban" (documents). Al-Ḥasan read "kitāban," the plural of kātib.

"Fa-rihānun" (then a pledge): then that by which the right is secured is a pledge. It is read "fa-rihun" with damma and with sukūn of the ha', and it is the plural of rahn, like suqf and suqf, and "fa-rihān." If you say: why was travel stipulated for pledging, when it is not restricted to travel rather than residence?

[[Maḥmūd, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: why was travel stipulated for pledging, when it is not restricted to travel..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: restriction to travel on this basis follows the usual case, so it has no implicit restriction. And in this verse there is clear evidence for the school of Mālik, may God be pleased with him, that the establishment of a pledge at the time of dispute over the amount of the debt stands in place of a witness for the pledgee up to the full value of the pledge; so that if they dispute, and the debtor says: "I pledged it to you for a hundred," and the creditor says: "Rather, the pledge is for two hundred," the pledge would serve as a witness to its value. This is against al-Shāfi'ī, may God be pleased with him, who holds that the word of the debtor is accepted absolutely, because he is the one who pays. The evidence from the verse for Mālik, may God be pleased with him, is that God made the pledge, in securing the right, a substitute for witnessing and writing, and restricted it to travel because they are scarce at that time; and if the word of the debtor were legally decisive, the pledge would not stand in place of witnessing nor serve its function in any way, for if there were no pledge, the word of the debtor concerning the amount of the debt would be accepted, so the existence of the pledge adds no benefit over its absence in terms of its substitution for witnessing. Nor can it be said that its benefit is priority over the other creditors, for that is the benefit of witnessing, so that it stands in its place when it is unavailable; and there is no benefit then except making the word of the pledgee concerning the amount of the debt decisive in case of disagreement, which is the school of Mālik mentioned earlier. Hence he did not make it a witness except concerning its value, not beyond it, supported by custom that a creditor does not accept in his debt except what is fulfilled to its value. So the debtor's claim that the debt is more than the value is refuted by custom, and the debtor also does not permit handing over what is worth more for what is less, so his claim that the debt is less than the value is refuted by custom. Nothing remains except one matter, namely that for Mālik the value is considered on the day of judgment; so if both agree that the value on the day of the pledge was more or less, no attention is paid to that, whether it increased or decreased, and only the day of decision is considered. One might say: if you make the pledge stand in place of the witness when it is absent because custom requires that people pledge for debts equal in value to them, then you should consider the value on the day of the pledge, without regard to its increase or decrease on the day of decision; and at that point the discussion becomes entangled over whether the reason for its standing in place of the witness is the meaning mentioned earlier or something else. Our purpose is only that the verse guides to its standing in place of testimony in general. As for the details of the question, that belongs to the portion of jurisprudence.]]

"Wa-qad rahana rasūlu Allāh (ṣallā Allāhu 'alayhi wa-sallam) dir'ahu fī ghayri safar" (and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail when not traveling) [[agreed upon, from the narration of al-Aswad ibn Yazīd from 'Ā'isha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) bought food from a Jew on credit for a term and pledged him an iron coat of mail; and al-Bukhārī from the narration of Qatāda from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail in Medina with a Jew, and took barley from him for his family." End.]].

I say: the purpose is not to permit pledging only during travel, but since travel is the likely occasion for scarcity of documents and witnesses, He commanded, by way of guidance to preserve property for the one who is on a journey, that securing by pledge stand in place of securing by writing and witnessing. It is reported from Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk that they did not permit it except in a state of travel, taking the apparent meaning of the verse. As for taking possession (al-qabḍ), it must be taken into account [[Maḥmūd said: "As for taking possession, it must be taken into account..." etc. Aḥmad, may God have mercy on him, said: there is no dispute between Mālik and al-Shāfi'ī over the validity of pledging by offer and acceptance without possession; but according to Mālik, may God be pleased with him, it is valid by that, and the contract obliges the debtor to hand it over to the pledgee. According to al-Shāfi'ī, it is not binding by the contract. But for Mālik, possession has weight at the beginning and continuation; al-Shāfi'ī does not condition many of its rulings as Mālik does. For if the two agreed on possession and then the creditors appeared, the pledge would benefit the pledgee according to al-Shāfi'ī and be distinguished by it, but it would not benefit him according to Mālik, and he would be one among the creditors in it, unless the witnessing to their possession is accompanied by the witnesses' presence seeing it, because he suspects them of collusion to void the creditors' right, so their acknowledgment is not accepted without the addition of witnessing. Possession in this respect is thus more weighty in the view of Mālik than in the view of al-Shāfi'ī. This concerns the beginning. As for continuation, Mālik, may God be pleased with him, requires its remaining in the hand of the pledgee; so if it returns to the debtor's hand, by the pledgee depositing it with him, or renting it to him, or lending it to him in an unrestricted loan, it has left the pledge; and if the creditors appear while it is in the debtor's hand by any of the mentioned ways, he is one among the creditors regarding it. Al-Shāfi'ī, may God be pleased with him, does not require continuation of possession in this way, but for the debtor according to al-Shāfi'ī it is permissible to benefit from the pledge even if the pledgee dislikes it, provided that benefit does not harm the pledge, such as living in a house or employing a slave. And he may take its benefits himself, according to the sound opinion of his school, as stated in al-Umm, and that does not affect the pledge by invalidating or impairing it. You have known that possession is more weighty in Mālik's school in beginning and continuation, and the verse supports it, for "rahn" in the language means continuance. Abū 'Alī recited:

"So bread and meat are for them as a pledge,
and wine, its strainer poured out."]].

And perhaps the one who holds that the continuation of the pledge in the possession of the pledgee is a condition relied on what is in the word *rahn* (pledge) implying continuity, and he has a basis for that.

I only lengthened the account of Mālik's position on possession because what is understood from al-Zamakhsharī's words is that he dismisses possession according to Mālik, since he understood from the statement of his companions that possession is not a condition for the validity of the pledge or for its binding force, meaning that it is entirely disregarded in his view. And Allah knows best.

According to Mālik, the pledge is valid by offer and acceptance without possession. ﴿Then if some of you trust others﴾: that is, if some of the creditors trust some of the debtors [[The phrase "*al-madyūnīn*" (the debtors) "because of his good opinion of him": perhaps this is a rare transmitted reading, and the analogical form would be *al-madīnīn*; similarly, the singular *al-madyūn* would analogically be *al-madīn*. (ʿ)]] because of his good opinion of him. Ubayy recited: *fa-in ʾawmana* (then if he makes [them] secure), meaning: the people made him secure, [[The phrase "*ayy ʾāmanahu al-nās*" (that is, the people made him secure): the apparent reading is that it is from the causative form (*ʾif ʿāl*) with a kasra, not from the form (*mufāʿala*). That is, the people made one party, the creditor, such that he trusts the other party, the debtor, and this is by describing the debtor to him as trustworthy, etc., so the creditor became one who trusts the debtor. (ʿ)] and they described the debtor as trustworthy, faithful, and self-sufficient, so that he need not be secured by a pledge from someone like him. ﴿Then let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾: this urges the debtor to be what the creditor thinks of him, to be the one he trusts and in whom he places confidence, and to deliver to him the right he was entrusted with, since he did not give a pledge.

He called the debt a trust, though it is a guaranteed obligation, because the creditor entrusted him with it by forgoing a pledge from him. The reading is to pronounce a silent hamza after the *dhāl*, or a *yāʾ*, so you say: *al-ladhī ʾuttumina* or *al-ladhī tumina*. It is related from ʿĀṣim that he recited *al-ladhī ittaman*, assimilating the *yāʾ* into the *tāʾ*, by analogy with *ittasara* in the reflexive form (*ifti ʿāl*) from *yusr* (ease). This is not sound, because the *yāʾ* is converted from the hamza, so it has the status of the hamza. And *ittazara* is a colloquial form. Likewise *riyā* for *ruʾyā*.

﴿Sinful (*āthimun*)﴾ is the predicate of *inna* (indeed). And ﴿his heart﴾ (*qalbuhu*) is in the nominative as the agent of *āthimun*, as if it were said: "indeed his heart sins." It is also permissible for *qalbuhu* to be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with *āthimun* as a fronted predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of *inna*.

If you ask: why not limit it to his saying ﴿indeed he is sinful﴾? And what is the benefit of mentioning the heart, when it is the whole person who sins, not the heart alone? I answer: concealing testimony means that one hides it within oneself and does not speak it. Since it is a sin committed by the heart, the act is attributed to it, because attributing an action to the limb with which it is done is more emphatic. Do you not see that you say, when you want emphasis: "this is something my eye has seen, something my ear has heard, something my heart has known"? Also, the heart is the chief of the organs, the lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. So it is as if it were said: sin has taken firm root in the very core of his self, and has possessed the noblest place in it. And so that it may not be thought that concealing testimony is a sin related only to the tongue, and so that it may be known that the heart is the origin of what it relates to and the source of its commission, while the tongue is its interpreter. And because acts of the heart are greater than the acts of the other limbs, and they are for them like roots from which branches spread. Do you not see that the root of good and evil deeds is faith and disbelief, which are acts of the heart? So when concealing testimony is made a sin of the heart, it is thereby testified that it is among the greatest of sins.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the greatest of the major sins is associating partners with Allah, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾, and false testimony, and concealing testimony.

It is also recited *qalbahu* with a fatḥa (accusative), like the saying: ﴿he has made a fool of himself (*safiha nafsahu*)﴾. Ibn Abī ʿAblah recited *ʾathima qalbahu*, meaning he made it sinful. [[The phrase "*ʾathima qalbahu* meaning he made it sinful": this may be with the hamza prolonged, as a causative form (*ʾif ʿāl*), and it may be with the *tāʾ* doubled as a causative form (*tafʿīl*), so let it be examined. (ʿ)]]

And if you show what is in your selves or conceal it, meaning evil, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills, meaning whoever deserves forgiveness through repentance for what he has shown or harboured, and punishes whom He wills, meaning whoever deserves punishment through persistence in sin. What a person conceals does not include whisperings (al-wasawis) and the mind's passing thoughts (hadith al-nafs), because these are beyond his power to be free of. Rather, it refers to what he believes and resolves upon. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited it and said: "If Allah holds us accountable for this, we will surely perish." Then he wept until his sobbing (nashij) was heard. [[Narrated by al-Tabari through al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn Murjana, from Ibn Umar. Al-Hakim also narrated it through another route from Ibn Umar.]] It was reported to Ibn Abbas, who said: "May Allah forgive Abu Abd al-Rahman. The Muslims experienced the same as he did, so the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾." [[The word "nashij" in al-Sihah (the lexicon by al-Jawhari): nashaja al-baki nashjan wa nashijan, when the weeping person chokes on tears in his throat without wailing. (Ibn Umar's? no: this note is by the editor, "ʿ".)]]

It was also read as "fa-yaghfiru" and "yu'adhdhibu" in the jussive, coordinated with the response of the conditional, and in the nominative, meaning "fa-huwa yaghfiru wa yu'adhdhibu" (then He forgives and punishes). If you ask: how does one recite the jussive? I answer: one makes the ra' clear and assimilates the ba'. As for one who assimilates the ra' into the lam, he is a mistaken reciter who has erred grossly. And the one who transmits it from Abu Amr has erred twice, because he commits a grammatical error and attributes to the most knowledgeable person in Arabic what indicates great ignorance. The reason for such transmissions is the scant precision of the narrators, and the reason for scant precision is scant understanding, and only the people of grammar (ahl al-nahw) can preserve such things.

Al-A'mash read "yaghfiru" without the fa', in the jussive, as a substitute (badal) for "yuhasibukum" (will call you to account), like the poet's words:

*"Whenever you come to us and descend upon us in our abodes, you will find thick firewood and a fire blazing."* [[The word "tulmim" is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it, meaning: whenever you come down at our place, you will find us kindling the fire with thick wood, and this is a metaphor for their generosity. "Ta'ajjaja" is predicated of the pronoun referring to the wood and the fire, meaning they blazed. It is predicated of the fire literally, and of the wood by way of attributing to the cause, so it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and in it there is a combination of the literal and the metaphorical in the attribution.]]

The meaning of this substitution is the detailing of the whole reckoning, because the detail is clearer than what is detailed. It therefore functions as a substitution of part from whole (badal al-ba'ad min al-kull) or a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), as in your saying: "I struck Zayd, his head," and "I loved Zayd, his intellect." This substitution occurs in verbs just as it occurs in nouns, because both kinds require clarification.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 2, verse 285:

And "the believers" (al-mu'minun): if it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the Messenger," then the pronoun, for which the tanwin (nunation) in kullun is a substitute, refers back to the Messenger and the believers, meaning: all of them believed in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, of those mentioned [[His saying "and His messengers, of those mentioned" — perhaps before it there is an omission, its sense being: "i.e., each of those mentioned." (ʿA.)]]. And he stopped at it (waqafa ʿalayhi). But if it is a subject (mubtada'), then the pronoun refers to the believers. The pronoun of kullun in "āmana" is made singular in meaning: each one of them believed. It would also have been permissible to make it plural, as in His saying: ﴿And all of them come to Him humbled﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas recited "wa-kitabihi" (singular), meaning the Qur'an, or the genus (al-jins) [[Mahmud said: "It is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he recited wa-kitabihi..." Ahmad said: Malik has said that the singular is more apt to comprehend the genus than the plurals of dates, for "the date" (tamr) extends over the genus without a verbal form, whereas "dates" (tumur) turns it toward the notion of individual units; then the comprehensiveness after that is by the plural form, and in the plural form there is disturbance. This statement of the Imam, had he found support for it in Ibn ʿAbbas's reading, would have made the obligation (farḍiyya) famous in citing it as evidence for the soundness of this view, so we will not repeat it.]]. And it is also reported from him: "al-kitab" is more comprehensive than "al-kutub" (the books). If you say: how can the singular be more comprehensive than the plural? I say: because when the singular is intended as the genus, and the genusness subsists in every individual unit of the genus, nothing is excluded from it. As for the plural, it includes only those plurals in which the genusness is present. ﴿We make no distinction﴾, they say, "lā nufarriqu" (we make no distinction). It is reported from Abu ʿAmr that he read "yufarriqu" with the yāʾ, taking the verb as referring to kull (each). ʿAbdullah recited "lā yufarriqūna" (they make no distinction). "Aḥad" (any one) carries the sense of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿So there is none of you who could withhold Him from us﴾, which is why "bayn" (between) was applied to it. ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ ("samiʿnā wa-aṭaʿnā"): "ajabnā" (we answered), "ghufrānaka" (Your forgiveness) is in the accusative by an implied verb. It is said: "ghufrānaka, not kufrānaka," meaning: we ask You for forgiveness and we do not disbelieve in You. And it was read "wa-kutubihi wa-rusulihi" with sukūn (the unvocalised form).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 2, verse 286**

*Al-wus'* (capacity): what a person can bear, which does not constrain or distress him and in which he is not burdened. That is, He does not burden a soul except with what is within its capacity and easy for it, not beyond its utmost ability and effort. This is information about His justice and mercy, like His saying: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ [2:185]. For it was within a person's capacity and power to pray more than the five prayers, to fast more than the month, and to perform more than one pilgrimage.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read *wus'ahā* with a fatha (on the *sīn*). ﴿It shall have what it earned, and it shall bear what it acquired.﴾ What it earned of good benefits it, and what it acquired of evil harms it. No one bears the sin of another, and no one is rewarded for another's obedience.

If you ask: why was good assigned to *kasaba* (earning) and evil to *iktasaba* (acquiring)? I answer: *iktisāb* (acquiring) implies exertion. Since evil is something the self desires, is drawn toward, and commands one to, it is more active and eager in obtaining it, so it was described with the form that implies acquisition. Since this is not the case in the matter of good, it was described with a form that does not imply exertion.

﴿Do not take us to task for forgetting or erring﴾, that is: do not hold us accountable for forgetfulness or error if we fall short in them.

If you ask: forgetfulness and error are overlooked, so what is the meaning of asking not to be held accountable for them? [Mahmud said: "If you ask, forgetfulness and error are overlooked..." etc.] Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: This question does not arise according to the principles of the People of the Sunna, for we say that the removal of accountability for these two is established by revelation, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Error and forgetfulness have been lifted from my community." If that is so, then perhaps the lifting of accountability for them was the answer to this supplication, for it is reported that Allah the Exalted said at each of these supplications: "I have done it." Al-Zamakhshari was obliged to hold that the question arises according to the principles of the Qadariyya, who hold it impossible on rational grounds to hold someone accountable for error and forgetfulness, because that would be imposing what cannot be borne, which they regard as impossible, following from their doctrine of *tahsin wa taqbih* (the rational goodness and badness of acts). All of these are false principles and baseless doctrines. Allah the Exalted grants us the greatest share in answering these supplications, inspires us with the true creed and the correct statement. Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Responding, and He is sufficient for us, and the best Guardian.

I say: Forgetfulness and error are mentioned, and what is meant by them is the negligence and inattentiveness that they cause. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan﴾ [18:63]? Satan cannot cause forgetfulness; rather he whispers, and his whisper becomes the cause of the negligence from which forgetfulness results. Also, they were people who feared Allah with due fear, so no lapse ever came from them except in the form of forgetfulness and error. Therefore describing them as supplicating with this was an announcement of their innocence regarding what they might be held accountable for, as if it were said: If forgetfulness and error were things one is held accountable for, then there is no cause for accountability in them except forgetfulness and error.

It is permissible for a person to supplicate with something he knows is already granted to him before the supplication, by Allah's grace, so as to ensure its continuance and to acknowledge the blessing in it.

*Al-işr* (burden): the load that pins its bearer in place, so that he cannot rise with it because of its weight. It is used metaphorically for a hard obligation, such as killing oneself, cutting off the part of skin or cloth that is soiled with impurity, and other things. It is also read as *āṣāran* in the plural. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿and do not lay upon us﴾ with the doubled letter (*tashdid*).

If you ask: what is the difference between this doubling and the one in ﴿and do not burden us﴾?

I answer: The one here is for emphasis in *ḥammala 'alayhi* (to lay upon), and the other is to transfer the verb's object from one object to two objects.

﴿And do not burden us with what we have no power to bear﴾: that is, the punishments that fell upon those before us. They asked to be relieved of the hard obligations that had been imposed on those before them, and then of the punishments that befell them because of their failure to maintain them. It was said: what is meant is the hard obligation that can barely be borne. This is a repetition of His saying: ﴿Do not lay upon us a burden﴾.

﴿Our Master, You are our Lord, and we are Your servants﴾, or: our Helper, or: the One who manages our affairs. ﴿So help us﴾, for it is the right of a master to help his servants.

Or: because that is Your custom. Or: because that is one of our affairs that You are responsible for managing.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made these supplications, it was said to him after each phrase: "I have done it." [It was narrated by Muslim through the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas: When the verse ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls...﴾ was revealed, something entered their hearts that had never entered them before. So he said: Say: "We hear and we obey"... the hadith, in which is: "I have done it." Al-Hakim overlooked this and added it to his *Mustadrak*, in several places.]

It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the last two verses of Surat al-Baqara in a night, they will suffice him." [Agreed upon from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. Its meaning has been disputed. It was said: they suffice him, i.e., they are enough for him in place of night prayer, as in the previous narration. It was said: they suffice him with reward and merit. It was said: they suffice him from every devil or from every calamity.]

It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "I have been given the closing verses of Surat al-Baqara from a treasure beneath the Throne, which no prophet before me was given." [This is part of a hadith whose beginning is from Hudhayfa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have been favored over the people in three ways: the whole earth has been made a mosque for us, its dust has been made a purifier for us, our rows have been made like the rows of the angels, and I have been given these verses, the end of Surat al-Baqara, from a treasure beneath the Throne, which none before me has been given, and none after me will be given from it." It was narrated by al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Khuzayma, and Ibn Hibban, through the narration of Abu Malik al-Ashja'i from Rib'i ibn Khirash from Hudhayfa. It was also narrated by Muslim, but in the third item he said: "and he mentioned another quality," so he left it unspecified. The compilers of the *Mustakhrajat* and others mention it through his teacher with its chain in it. Al-Hakim overlooked this and in the chapter on the virtues of the Qur'an in *al-Mustadrak* mentioned that Muslim narrated this clause. Perhaps Muslim left it unspecified because of the disagreement over it on the authority of Rib'i. Ahmad and Ishaq narrated it through the narration of Jarir from Mansur from Rib'i from Khirash from Zayd ibn Zabyan from Abu Dhar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given the closing verses of Surat al-Baqara from a treasure beneath the Throne." But Abu Malik was followed by Nu'aym ibn Abi Hind, narrated by al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* in *al-Muhammadun* from his route.]

It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "Allah sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Merciful wrote with His own hand two thousand years before He created creation. Whoever recites them after the night prayer, they suffice him in place of night prayer." [Narrated by Ibn 'Adi from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. In its chain is al-Walid ibn 'Abbad, who is unknown, from Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, who is abandoned.]

If you ask: is it permissible to say "I recited Surat al-Baqara" or "I recited al-Baqara"? I answer: There is no harm in that.

It has come in the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "from the end of Surat al-Baqara," "the closing verses of Surat al-Baqara," and "the closing verses of al-Baqara." [These have all been mentioned briefly above. In Muslim, from the hadith of Murra ibn Sharahil al-Tayyib from Ibn Mas'ud: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given three things: the five prayers, the closing verses of Surat al-Baqara... the hadith. And in Muslim from Ibn 'Abbas: While Jibril was with the Prophet (ﷺ), an angel descended... the hadith, in which is: "the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of Surat al-Baqara."]

It is also reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The closing verses of Surat al-Baqara are from a treasure beneath the Throne."

It is also reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he threw the pebble at the Jamra and then said: "From here, by Him besides whom there is no god, threw the one to whom Surat al-Baqara was revealed." [Agreed upon, from the narration of al-A'mash: I heard al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf on the pulpit say: "The sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned, and the sura in which Al 'Imran is mentioned, and the sura in which al-Nisa' is mentioned." I mentioned that to Ibrahim, and he said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid told me that he was with Ibn Mas'ud when he threw the pebble at Jamrat al-'Aqaba... the hadith.]

There is no difference between this and your saying "Surat al-Zukhruf," "Surat al-Mumtahana," and "Surat al-Mujadila." When one says "I recited al-Baqara," it is not unclear that what is meant is Surat al-Baqara, like His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [12:82]. It is reported from some of them that he disliked this and said: one should say "I recited the sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned is the tent-pole of the Qur'an, so learn it, for learning it is a blessing and abandoning it is regret, and the *baṭala* cannot master it." It was said: What is the *baṭala*? He said: "The sorcerers." [Abu Shuja' al-Daylami mentioned it in *al-Firdaws*, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The matter is in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Umama, raised: "Recite Surat al-Baqara, for taking it is a blessing and leaving it is regret, and the *baṭala* cannot master it." Mu'awiya, one of its narrators, said: the meaning is that the *baṭala* are the sorcerers. On this topic, from Buraydah, in al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi.

(Note) The author mentioned the hadith of Abu Sa'id as evidence for his saying "the sura in which such-and-such is mentioned," and the one before it as evidence for permissibility. It is among the raised narrations that al-Tabarani narrated in *al-Awsat* in *al-Muhammadun*, and Ibn Mardawayh in his tafsir, from the hadith of Musa ibn Anas ibn Malik from his father, raised: "Do not say Surat al-Baqara or Surat Al 'Imran, and likewise the whole Qur'an, but say the sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned and the one in which Al 'Imran is mentioned." And likewise the whole Qur'an. In the chain is 'Isa ibn Maymun Abu Salama al-Khawwas, who is discarded.]
